Alcestis (438 BC)

Alcestis

(Pherae, in Thessaly, before the house of Admetus. Apollo comes out of it, carrying his bow.)

Apollo. House of Admetus. I put up with a servant's table here, and I was a god when I did it. Zeus was the cause. He killed my son Asclepius, driving the lightning into his chest, and I lost my temper and killed the Cyclopes, who forge his fire for him, and for that my father made me work for wages in a mortal's house. So I came to this country and kept a stranger's cattle, and I have kept this house safe to this very day. I am a decent god, and I had found a decent man in the son of Pheres, and I saved him from dying. I cheated the Fates. The goddesses agreed with me that Admetus could slip out of the death that was waiting for him, if he gave the powers below another corpse in exchange. He went round everyone he loved and put the question to them, his father, the old mother who bore him, and he found nobody willing to die in his place and stop looking at the light, except his wife. She is in the house now, in his arms, gasping out her life. This is the day she is fated to die and leave the living. And I am leaving too. I love this roof, but I cannot let the pollution touch me inside it. And here is Death himself, already, close by. The priest of the dead. He is on his way to take her down to the house of Hades, and he has timed it exactly. He has been watching for this day, the day she has to die.

(Death comes in.)

Death.
	Ah. Ah.
	What are you doing at this house? Why are you hanging about here,
	Apollo? Cheating again, are you, snatching away the rights
	of the gods below and stopping them short?
	Was it not enough for you to block Admetus's death
	and trip the Fates with a dirty trick?
	And now here you are again, standing guard over her,
	with your bow in your hand,
	over the daughter of Pelias, who promised
	to die for her husband and set him free.

Apollo. Steady. I have justice on my side, and good arguments.

Death. Then what is the bow for, if you have justice?

Apollo. Habit. I always carry it.

Death. And you always help this house more than is right.

Apollo. I cannot bear it when a friend is in trouble.

Death. So you will rob me of this second body as well?

Apollo. I did not take the first one from you by force.

Death. Then how is he up here on the earth and not under it?

Apollo. He gave you his wife instead. The one you have come for now.

Death. And I will take her down under the ground.

Apollo. Take her, then. I doubt I could talk you out of it.

Death. Out of killing whoever is due? That is my job.

Apollo. No. Your job is to deal death to people who are about to die anyway.

Death. I see your argument. And I see what you want.

Apollo. Is there any way, then, for Alcestis to reach old age?

Death. There is not. I enjoy my rights too, you know.

Apollo. You cannot take more than one life either way.

Death. When the young die, the prize I win is bigger.

Apollo. If she dies old, she will get a rich funeral.

Death. You are writing the law to suit the rich, Apollo.

Apollo. What did you say? Have you been clever all this time, without my noticing?

Death. People with money would buy the right to die old.

Apollo. So you will not do me this one favour.

Death. No. You know my ways.

Apollo. I do. Mortals hate them, and the gods loathe them.

Death. You cannot have everything that is not yours to have.

Apollo. Well, you will be stopped, all the same, savage as you are. There is a man coming to the house of Pheres. Eurystheus has sent him after a team of horses, in the freezing country of Thrace. He will be a guest here, in Admetus's house, and he will take this woman away from you by force. You will get no thanks from me, then, and you will do exactly what I am asking anyway, and I will hate you for it.

Death. Talk all you like, you will get nothing more. This woman is going down to the house of Hades. I am going in for her now, to begin the rite with my sword. Once this blade has cut a lock of hair from a head, that head belongs to the gods below.

(Apollo goes. Death goes into the house. The Chorus, old men of Pherae, come in and gather at the door.)

Chorus.
	Why is it so quiet in front of the house?
	Why has the house of Admetus gone silent?
	And there is not one of the family near,
	to tell me whether I should be mourning
	the queen dead already, or whether she still lives
	and looks at this light, the daughter of Pelias,
	Alcestis, who to me, and to everyone,
	seemed the best wife
	a husband ever had.
Chorus.
	Does anyone hear a groan,
	or the sound of hands beating, inside the house,
	or a wail, as if it were over?
	No, and there is not a servant either
	posted at the gate. Oh, Healer,
	if only you would appear
	between the waves of this ruin.
Chorus.
	If she were dead they would not be silent.
	She is a corpse already.
	She has not been carried out of the house.
	How do you know? I am not so sure. What makes you confident?
	How could Admetus give a wife as good as that
	a funeral with nobody there?
Chorus.
	And in front of the gates I see
	no spring water, as custom has it,
	standing at the door of the dead.
	No lock of hair on the doorstep,
	cut off, the way it falls
	in mourning. No young women's hands
	beating out the grief.
Chorus.
	And yet this is the appointed day.
	What are you saying?
	The day she has to go under the earth.
	You have touched my heart. You have touched my mind.
	When the good are worn down to nothing,
	anyone who has ever
	been counted decent must grieve.
Chorus.
	There is nowhere on earth
	you could send a ship,
	not to Lycia,
	not to the waterless seat
	of Ammon in the desert,
	to save that poor woman's life.
	Death is coming for her, sheer as a cliff,
	and I do not know which god's altar
	I should go to now
	with a sheep to kill.
Chorus.
	Only one man, if he were still alive
	and his eyes saw this light,
	Apollo's son: then she might have left
	the dark seats
	and the gates of Hades and come back.
	He used to raise the dead,
	until the lightning Zeus throws struck him,
	the fire from heaven.
	But now, what hope of her life
	is there left for me to hold?
Chorus.
	The king and queen have done everything already.
	On the altars of every god
	the sacrifices stand, full and dripping blood,
	and there is no cure for the evil. None.

(A Maid comes out of the house, in tears.)

Chorus. But here comes one of the servants out of the house, crying. What am I going to hear? If something has happened to the master and mistress, grief is forgivable. But we would like to know whether the lady is still alive, or whether she is gone.

Maid. You could say she is alive, and you could say she is dead.

Chorus. How can the same woman be dead and still see?

Maid. She is sinking already. Her life is tearing loose.

Chorus. Poor man. To be the man he is, and lose a wife like that.

Maid. The master does not know it yet. He will not until it happens.

Chorus. Is there no hope any more of saving her life?

Maid. None. The appointed day is forcing its way in.

Chorus. Then is everything being done for her that should be?

Maid. The clothes are ready that her husband will bury her in.

Chorus. Then let her know this: she dies with a great name, and she is the best woman under the sun, by a long way.

Maid. Best? Of course she is the best. Who would argue with that? What would a woman have to be, to outdo her? How could anyone show more plainly that she put her husband first than by being willing to die for him? The whole city knows that much. But what she did inside the house, you will be amazed to hear.

When she realised the appointed day had come, she washed her white skin in water from the river, and took clothes and jewels out of the cedar chests and dressed herself beautifully, and stood in front of the hearth and prayed. "Lady, I am going under the earth, and this is the last time I will kneel to you, so I ask you: be a mother to my orphans. Find my boy a loving wife, and my girl a good husband. And do not let my children die before their time, as I their mother am dying, but let them live out a happy life in their father's country, and enjoy it." Then she went to every altar in Admetus's house and put wreaths on them and prayed, breaking the sprigs off the myrtle boughs, without a tear, without a sound, and the evil that was coming did not change the lovely colour of her skin at all.

And then she rushed into the bedroom, to the bed, and there she did cry, and this is what she said. "Bed, where I undid my virgin belt for the man I am dying for, goodbye. I do not hate you. But you have killed me, and only me: it was because I could not bear to betray you, and him, that I am dying. Some other woman will own you. Not a better one. A luckier one, perhaps." And she fell on it and kissed it, and the whole bed was soaked in the flood that ran out of her eyes. When she had had enough of crying, she tore herself off the bed and walked out, head down, and over and over as she was leaving the room she turned round and threw herself back down on the bed again. The children were hanging on their mother's dress, crying. She took them in her arms, first one and then the other, and kissed them, as a woman does who is about to die. And every slave in the house was crying, out of pity for the mistress. And she held out her right hand to each of them, and there was not one so low that she did not speak to him and get his answer back. That is the trouble in Admetus's house. If he had died, he would be gone, and that would be that. He has escaped death, and what he has instead is a pain he will never forget.

Chorus. Admetus must be groaning, surely, at this disaster, if he has to lose a wife as good as that.

Maid. He is crying, holding his dear wife in his arms, begging her not to leave him, asking for the impossible. She is wasting away. The sickness is withering her. She has gone limp, a pitiful weight on his arm. But even so, with what little breath she has left, she wants to look at the rays of the sun. She will never see them again. This is the very last time she will look at the sunlight and its disc. But I will go in and say you are here. Not everyone thinks well enough of their rulers to stand by them kindly when things go wrong. You have been my master's friend a long time.

(The Maid goes in.)

Chorus.
	Oh, Zeus, what way out of this evil can there be,
	how, from where? What release from the fate
	that has come down on the king and queen?
	Aiai. Is someone coming out? Should I cut my hair now,
	and put on the black
	clothes of mourning already?
	It is plain, friends, plain enough. But all the same
	let us pray to the gods. The gods' power
	is the greatest there is.
	Lord Healer,
	find Admetus some way out of this evil.
	Find it, find it. You found one before,
	for this man. Now
	be the one who sets her free from death.
	Stop Hades, the killer.
Chorus.
	Papai.
	Son of Pheres, what has been done to you,
	losing your wife?
	Aiai. Is this not reason enough to cut your throat,
	and more than reason enough to hang your neck
	from a rope in the air?
	For today you will watch her die,
	the woman who was not dear to you,
	but the dearest of all.
	Look. Look.
	Here she comes out of the house, and her husband with her.
	Cry out, groan, land of Pherae,
	for the best of women,
	withering away with sickness,
	going under the earth to Hades below.

(Alcestis is carried out of the house, with Admetus beside her and the two children.)

Chorus.
	I will never say that marriage brings
	more joy than grief. I judge by what has happened
	before, and by what I see now
	happening to the king, who loses
	the best of wives, and will live
	a life that is not a life from now on.
Alcestis.
	Sun, and light of day,
	and clouds racing in the whirl of the sky.

Admetus. The sun sees you and me, two people who have done badly, and who did nothing to the gods that you should die for.

Alcestis.
	Earth, and the roof of the house,
	and the bed I was married in, in Iolcus, where I was born.

Admetus. Lift yourself up, poor woman, do not leave me. Beg the gods who rule us to have pity.

Alcestis.
	I see the boat with the two oars. I see it, on the lake.
	The ferryman of the dead,
	Charon, with his hand on the pole,
	is calling me already. "What are you waiting for?
	Hurry up. You are holding me back." That is how
	he hurries me, in his impatience.

Admetus. Oh. That is a bitter voyage you are telling me about. Unlucky woman, what is happening to us?

Alcestis.
	Someone is taking me, taking me, someone is taking me. Can you not see him?
	To the courtyard of the dead.
	He is glaring at me from under dark brows,
	and he has wings. Hades.
	Let me go. What are you doing? Let go. What a road
	I am walking down, the most wretched woman alive.

Admetus. A road that is pitiful to everyone who loves you, and most of all to me and the children, who share this grief with me.

Alcestis.
	Let me go, let me go now.
	Lay me down, there is no strength in my feet.
	Hades is close.
	Dark night is creeping over my eyes.
	Children, children, there is no
	mother for you any more, no more.
	Goodbye, children. Enjoy this light. Look at it.
Admetus.
	Oh. That is a word of misery to hear,
	and worse to me than any death.
	By the gods, do not have the heart to leave me.
	By the children you will make orphans.
	Get up. Be brave.
	If you are dead, I am nothing.
	Living or not living, we depend on you.
	It is your love we worship.

Alcestis. Admetus, you can see how it is with me. I want to tell you what I want, before I die. I put you first. I set you up to go on looking at this light at the cost of my own life, and I am dying, when I did not have to die for you. I could have married any man in Thessaly I liked, and lived in a house that was rich with a throne in it. I did not want to live, torn away from you, with orphaned children. And I did not hold back my youth, though I had gifts in it I enjoyed. And yet your father and the mother who bore you betrayed you, when they had come to the time of life where dying is fine, where it would have been fine to save their son and die with honour. You were their only son. There was no hope, if you died, of their having other children. And you and I would have gone on living the rest of our time, and you would not be groaning over a wife you have lost, and bringing up children without a mother. But some god arranged it so that this is how things are.

Well. Now remember what you owe me for it. I am going to ask you for something. Never the equivalent, because nothing is worth more than a life. But something fair, as you will say yourself, because you love these children no less than I do, if you have any sense. Let them be the masters of my house, and do not marry again, and put a stepmother over these children. She would be a worse woman than me, and out of jealousy she would lift her hand against your children and mine. Do not do it. I am begging you. A stepmother who comes in after the first wife hates her children, and a viper is no gentler than she is. A boy has his father, a great tower to him, someone to talk to and to answer him back. But you, my daughter, how will you grow up decently? What kind of wife will you find at your father's side? She could fasten some filthy rumour on you, in the flower of your youth, and wreck your marriage. Your mother will never see you married, never be there at your side to give you courage when you are having your children, my child, when there is nothing kinder than a mother. Because I have to die. And this evil is not coming to me tomorrow, or the day after; in a moment I will be counted among the people who no longer exist. Goodbye. Be happy. And you, husband, can boast that you had the best of wives, and you, children, that you were born from the best of mothers.

Chorus. Do not be afraid. I am not ashamed to answer for him. He will do it, unless he has lost his mind.

Admetus. It will be so, it will be so, do not be afraid. You were the only wife I had while you were alive, and when you are dead you alone will be called my wife. No bride from Thessaly will ever take your place and speak to me as her husband. There is no woman so well born, or so outstandingly beautiful, that she could. And I have children enough. I pray to the gods that I get some good of them, because I have had none of you. I will not mourn you for a year. I will mourn you as long as my life lasts, wife, and I will loathe the woman who bore me and hate my father, because they loved me in words and not in deeds. You gave the dearest thing you had in exchange for my life, and saved it. Do I not have reason to groan, losing a wife like you?

I will put a stop to the drinking parties, and the company of men over the wine, and the garlands, and the music that used to fill my house. I will never touch the lyre again, or lift my heart to sing to the Libyan pipe. You have taken all my pleasure in life away with you. And craftsmen with clever hands will make a likeness of your body, and it will be laid out in my bed, and I will fall on it and wrap my arms round it and call your name, and think I am holding my dear wife in my arms, when I am not. A cold pleasure, I know. But still, I would be draining off some of the weight on my heart. And you might come to me in dreams and make me glad. It is sweet to see the people we love even at night, for as long as they stay.

If I had the tongue of Orpheus, and his music, so that I could charm the daughter of Demeter or her husband with my singing and take you back out of Hades, I would have gone down, and neither Pluto's hound nor Charon at his oar, the ferryman of souls, would have stopped me, until I had set your life back in the light. As it is, wait for me there, when I die, and get a house ready for us to live in together. I will give orders to these children to lay me in the same cedar coffin as you, and stretch my side out next to yours. Not even in death would I be parted from you, the only one who was faithful to me.

Chorus. And I will share this grief with you, friend with friend. It is hard, and she deserves it.

Alcestis. Children, you heard it yourselves. Your father said he will never marry another woman and set her over you, and never dishonour me.

Admetus. I say it again now, and I will keep to it.

Alcestis. On those terms, take the children from my hand.

Admetus. I take them. A dear gift, from a dear hand.

Alcestis. Now you be a mother to these children in my place.

Admetus. I will have to be, now they are robbed of you.

Alcestis. Children, I am going down below, when I ought to be living.

Admetus. Oh, what am I going to do without you?

Alcestis. Time will soften you. The dead are nothing.

Admetus. Take me with you, by the gods. Take me down.

Alcestis. It is enough that I am dying in your place.

Admetus. God, what a wife you are robbing me of.

Alcestis. My eyes are growing dark and heavy.

Admetus. Then I am finished, if you really leave me, wife.

Alcestis. You can speak of me as someone who no longer exists.

Admetus. Lift your face. Do not leave your children.

Alcestis. Not willingly, I promise you. But goodbye, children.

Admetus. Look at them. Look.

Alcestis. I am nothing now.

Admetus. What are you doing? Are you leaving us?

Alcestis. Goodbye.

Admetus. I am lost.

Chorus. She is gone. The wife of Admetus is no more.

Child.
	Oh, what has happened to me. Mother has gone
	down below. She is not here any more, father,
	not under the sun.
	She has left me behind, poor thing,
	and made my life an orphan's.
	Look, look at her eyes, and her hands hanging loose.
	Listen to me, hear me, mother, I am begging you.
	It is me, mother, me,
	your own chick, calling you, pressing
	my mouth against your lips.

Admetus. She cannot hear you, and she cannot see you. You two and I have been struck a heavy blow.

Child.
	I am so young, father, to be left
	alone like this, without my mother, without her love.
	Oh, it is a terrible thing
	that has been done to me,
	and you, my sister, you have gone
	through it with me. Oh, father,
	you married for nothing, for nothing. You never reached
	the end of old age with her.
	She died first. And with you gone,
	mother, the house is finished.

Chorus. Admetus, you have to bear this. You are not the first man, and you will not be the last, to lose a good wife. Remember: every one of us owes a death.

Admetus. I know it. This evil did not swoop down on me out of nowhere. I have known it was coming, and it has been wearing me down for a long time. But now I am going to carry this body out for burial, so stay here with me, and while you wait, sing back the hymn to the god below, the god who cannot be bargained with. And to every Thessalian I rule I say this: share the mourning for this woman, with your heads shaved and your clothes black. You who yoke four-horse teams, and you who ride single horses, cut the manes from their necks with iron. Let there be no sound of pipes in the city, and no lyre, until twelve full moons have passed. I will never bury anyone dearer to me than this body, or anyone better to me. She deserves honour from me. She, and nobody else, died in my place.

(Admetus and the children go into the house with the body.)

Chorus.
	Daughter of Pelias,
	go with my blessing to live in the house of Hades,
	the home that has no sun.
	Let Hades know it, the god with the black hair, and the old man
	who sits at his oar and his rudder
	ferrying the dead,
	that it is by far, by far the best woman
	he has carried over the lake of Acheron
	in his boat with the two oars.
Chorus.
	The servants of the Muses will sing of you
	many times, to the seven-stringed shell of the mountain tortoise
	and in hymns with no lyre at all, making you famous,
	at Sparta, when the circling year brings round the Carnean
	month, and the moon
	rides high all night long,
	and in shining Athens, the rich city.
	That is the song you left behind when you died,
	for the makers of songs.
Chorus.
	If only it were in my power,
	if only I could send you
	back to the light out of the halls of Hades
	and the streams of Cocytus,
	with an oar on the river of the dead.
	Because you, and you alone, dearest of women,
	you had the nerve
	to buy your husband out of Hades
	with your own life. May the earth
	lie light on you, lady. And if your husband
	ever takes a new bride to his bed, believe me, he will be hated
	by me, and by your children.
Chorus.
	His mother was not willing
	to hide her body in the earth
	for her son, and nor was his old father.
	They brought him into the world, and they would not save him,
	the pair of them, hard-hearted, with their grey hair.
	But you, in the flower
	of your youth, died for him, and are gone.
	May I find a wife like that
	to share my life and love me. It is
	a rare thing in this world. She would live
	beside me all my days
	and never once give me pain.

(Heracles comes in from the road.)

Heracles. Strangers, you people of this land of Pherae, would I find Admetus at home?

Chorus. The son of Pheres is in the house, Heracles. But tell us, what business sends you to Thessaly, to this town of Pherae?

Heracles. I am doing a job for Eurystheus of Tiryns.

Chorus. And where are you going? What wandering are you yoked to this time?

Heracles. I am after the four-horse chariot team of Diomedes the Thracian.

Chorus. How are you going to manage that? Have you never met the man who will be your host?

Heracles. Never. I have not been to the country of the Bistones yet.

Chorus. You cannot get hold of those horses without a fight.

Heracles. But I cannot refuse the labours, either.

Chorus. Then you will kill him and come back, or die and stay there.

Heracles. It would not be the first race of that kind I have run.

Chorus. And if you beat their master, what do you get out of it?

Heracles. I drive the horses away to the king of Tiryns.

Chorus. It is not easy to put a bit in those jaws.

Heracles. Easy enough, unless they breathe fire out of their nostrils.

Chorus. No, but they tear men to pieces with those quick jaws.

Heracles. That is fodder for mountain beasts you are talking about, not horses.

Chorus. You will see their mangers spattered with blood.

Heracles. And whose son does the man who feeds them boast of being?

Chorus. The son of Ares. He is lord of the golden shield of Thrace.

Heracles. This labour too is just the luck I was born with. It is always hard, and it always goes uphill, if I have to fight the sons Ares fathered, Lycaon first, then Cycnus, and now this third contest, going in against the horses and their master. But there is nobody alive who will ever see the son of Alcmena tremble at an enemy's hand.

Chorus. And here is Admetus himself, the king of this country, coming out of the house.

(Admetus comes out, his hair cut short in mourning.)

Admetus. Welcome, son of Zeus, of the blood of Perseus.

Heracles. And welcome to you, Admetus, king of Thessaly.

Admetus. I wish I could be. But I know you mean it kindly.

Heracles. Why are you showing yourself with your hair cut for mourning?

Admetus. I have to bury someone today.

Heracles. May a god keep harm away from your children.

Admetus. The children I fathered are alive, in the house.

Heracles. Your father, then. Well, he was ripe for it, if he is gone.

Admetus. He is alive, Heracles, and so is my mother.

Heracles. Surely it is not your wife who is dead? Not Alcestis?

Admetus. There are two things I could tell you about her.

Heracles. Do you mean she is dead, or still alive?

Admetus. She is, and she is not. And it hurts me.

Heracles. I am none the wiser. You are talking in riddles.

Admetus. Do you not know the fate she has to meet?

Heracles. I know. She undertook to die in your place.

Admetus. Then how is she still alive, if she agreed to that?

Heracles. Ah. Do not mourn your wife ahead of time. Put it off until then.

Admetus. The one who is about to die is dead. The dead no longer exist.

Heracles. Being and not being are counted as two different things.

Admetus. That is how you judge it, Heracles. I judge it the other way.

Heracles. Then why are you crying? Which of your people has died?

Admetus. A woman. It was a woman we were speaking of just now.

Heracles. An outsider, or someone related to you by blood?

Admetus. An outsider. But she was bound to this house all the same.

Heracles. Then how did she come to lose her life in your house?

Admetus. Her father died, and she lived here as an orphan.

Heracles. Ah. I wish I had found you without grief, Admetus.

Admetus. What are you planning to do, that you stitch a speech like that together?

Heracles. I will go to the hearth of some other host.

Admetus. That cannot happen, my lord. Never let an evil like that come on me.

Heracles. A guest is a nuisance to people in grief, if he turns up.

Admetus. The dead are dead. Come into the house.

Heracles. It is shameful for guests to feast beside people who are weeping.

Admetus. The guest rooms are separate. We will take you there.

Heracles. Let me go, and I will owe you ten thousand thanks.

Admetus. You are not going to another man's hearth. You there, lead the way for him. Open the guest rooms that face away from the house, and tell the stewards to have plenty of food there. And shut the doors to the inner courtyard, and shut them well. Guests at their dinner should not hear groaning, or be made unhappy.

(Heracles goes in, a servant leading the way.)

Chorus. What are you doing? With a disaster like this in front of you, Admetus, you have the heart to take in guests? What is this foolishness?

Admetus. And if I had driven him away from my house and my city, when he came to me as a guest, would you have praised me more? You would not. My disaster would have been no smaller, and I would have been less of a host. And on top of my troubles I would have had another trouble: my house getting the name of a house that hates its guests. And I find the man himself the best of hosts, whenever I go to the thirsty land of Argos.

Chorus. Then why did you hide the misfortune that is on you, if it was a friend who came, as you say yourself?

Admetus. He would never have been willing to come into the house if he had known anything of my troubles. And I suppose there are people who think I am a fool for doing this, and will not praise me for it. But my house does not know how to push a guest away, or treat one without honour.

Chorus.
	House that has always had room for guests, house of a free man,
	Pythian Apollo himself, the fine lyre-player,
	thought you worth living in,
	and brought himself to be a shepherd
	under your roof,
	down the slanting hillsides
	piping to your flocks
	the wedding songs of shepherds.
Chorus.
	And the spotted lynxes grazed alongside them, glad of his music,
	and the tawny pack of lions came
	down out of the glen of Othrys,
	and round your lyre, Apollo,
	the fawn with the dappled coat
	danced, stepping out past the tall pines
	on her light hooves,
	happy at the cheerful song.
Chorus.
	And so he lives in a house with more sheep than any other,
	by the lovely waters of Lake Boebe,
	and for his ploughed fields
	and his level plains he sets one border
	in the west, where the sun stables its horses
	in the dark sky of the Molossians,
	and the other at the Aegean, where he rules as far as
	the harbourless coast under Pelion.
Chorus.
	And now he has thrown open his house
	and taken in a guest, with his eyes wet,
	weeping for the body of his dear wife,
	dead in the house this very day. Good birth
	comes out as decency.
	In good men there is every kind of wisdom. I admire it,
	and in my heart the confidence sits firm
	that a man who honours the gods will do well.

Admetus. Men of Pherae, you are kind to be here. My servants are carrying the body out now, dressed with everything it needs, high on their shoulders, to the tomb and the pyre. And you, as custom asks, speak to the dead woman as she goes out on her last road.

(The body is carried out of the house. Pheres comes in, an old man, with servants behind him carrying robes and ornaments.)

Chorus. And I see your father coming, on his old man's feet, and attendants carrying in their hands finery for your wife, offerings for the dead below.

Pheres. I have come to share your pain, my son. You have lost a good wife, and a sensible one; nobody will deny it. But you have to bear these things, hard as they are to bear. Take these robes and ornaments, and let them go under the earth with her. Her body deserves to be honoured. She died for your life, my son, and she did not leave me childless; she did not let me lose you and wither away in a mourning old age. She has made life a more glorious thing for every woman, by daring this noble act. You who saved this man, who raised us up when we were falling, farewell, and may it go well with you even in the house of Hades. Marriages like that are a gain to men, I say. Otherwise marrying is not worth it.

Admetus. You did not come to this burial because I invited you, and I do not count your presence as a friend's. She will never wear that finery of yours. She will be buried needing nothing of yours. You should have shared my pain then, when I was dying. But you stood out of the way, and you let somebody else die, somebody young, when you were old, and now you are going to wail over this body? Then you were never really the father of this body of mine. And the woman who says she bore me, and is called my mother, did not give birth to me. I was born of slave's blood and slipped secretly to your wife's breast. You showed what you are when you were put to the test, and I do not consider myself your son.

You outdo everyone in cowardice. At your age, at the very end of your life, you would not die for your own son, you did not have the nerve to. You left it to this woman, an outsider, and I would be right to count her, and her alone, as my mother and my father both. And yet what a fine contest that would have been for you to enter, dying for your own son, and in any case the time you had left to live was short. And I would have lived, and so would she, for the rest of our time, and I would not be left alone, groaning over my troubles.

And you have had everything a happy man should have. You had your youth as a king. You had a son, me, to inherit this house, so you were not going to die childless and leave an orphaned house for strangers to loot. And you cannot say you gave me up to die because I dishonoured your old age. I was the most respectful son to you that there could be. And in return for that, this is the thanks you and my mother gave me. So you had better get on with fathering more children, and lose no time about it, children who will look after you when you are old, and lay you out when you are dead, and set out your body for burial. Because I am not going to bury you, not with this hand. As far as you are concerned, I am dead. If I found somebody else to save me, and I am looking at the light, then I say I am that person's child, and the loving supporter of that person's old age. It is all lies, then, when old men pray to die, complaining about old age and how long life is. When death comes near, not one of them wants to die, and old age is not a burden to them any more.

Chorus. Stop, both of you. The trouble that is here is enough. My boy, do not goad your father's temper.

Pheres. Boy, who do you think you are abusing? Some Lydian, some Phrygian, that you bought with your silver? Do you not know I am a Thessalian, and my father was a Thessalian, a free man, legitimately born? You are going too far. This is outrage. You fling a young man's words at me, and you are not going to hit me with them and walk off like that. I fathered you to be the master of this house, and I brought you up. I do not owe you my death. That is not a law I inherited from my fathers, that fathers die for their sons, and it is not a Greek one either. You were born for yourself, lucky or unlucky, and what you had a right to get from me, you have. You rule many people, and I will leave you broad acres, because I got them from my father. So how have I wronged you? What am I robbing you of? Do not die for this man here, and I will not die for you.

You love looking at the light. Do you think your father does not? Believe me, I count the time down below as long, and life as short, but sweet all the same. You, at any rate, fought shamelessly not to die, and you are alive, past the death that was appointed for you, because you killed her. And then you talk about my cowardice, you, the worst of men, beaten by a woman, who died for you, her fine young husband? What a clever scheme you have found for never dying at all: talk whatever wife you have at the time into dying for you, every time. And then you insult your own family for not being willing to do it, when you are the coward yourself? Be quiet. And think about this: if you love your own life, everyone loves theirs. And if you go on speaking ill of me, you will hear plenty of evil about yourself, and none of it false.

Chorus. Too much evil has been said, now and before. Stop, old man, abusing your son.

Admetus. Speak. I have had my say. If it hurts you to hear the truth, you should not have wronged me.

Pheres. I would have done you more wrong by dying for you.

Admetus. So it is the same thing for a young man to die and an old one?

Pheres. We owe one life. Not two.

Admetus. Then may you live longer than Zeus.

Pheres. You curse your parents, when they have done you no wrong?

Admetus. I saw you were in love with a long life.

Pheres. And this body you are carrying out, is it not in your place?

Admetus. A sign of your cowardice, you coward.

Pheres. She did not die at my hands. You cannot say that.

Admetus. Oh, may you come to need this man some day.

Pheres. Court plenty of wives, so there will be more of them to die.

Admetus. That is a reproach to you. You were the one who would not die.

Pheres. This light of the god is sweet. It is sweet.

Admetus. That is a mean spirit, and not a man's.

Pheres. You will not be laughing as you carry out an old man's corpse.

Admetus. You will die with a bad name, when you do die.

Pheres. A bad name does not bother me once I am dead.

Admetus. Oh, oh. How shameless old age is.

Pheres. She was not shameless. It was a fool you found in her.

Admetus. Go away, and let me bury this body.

Pheres. I am going. You bury her, you, her murderer. And you will still pay for it to her family. Acastus is no longer a man, if he does not make you answer for his sister's blood.

Admetus. Get out, you and the woman who lives with you. Grow old childless, though your son is alive, the way you deserve. You will never again come under the same roof as this man. If I had to renounce your hearth, my father's hearth, by heralds' proclamation, I would have renounced it.

(Pheres goes.)

And now, because the trouble in front of us has to be borne, let us go and lay the body on the pyre.

Chorus.
	Oh. Oh. What nerve you had, and what it cost you.
	Noble woman, best of all by far,
	goodbye. May Hermes of the world below receive you
	gladly, and Hades too. And if there, as well,
	the good have anything more, may you have your share of it
	and sit beside the bride of Hades.

(The funeral procession goes out. The Servant comes out of the house.)

Servant. I have known many guests already, from every kind of country, come to the house of Admetus, and I have set dinner in front of them. But I have never yet taken in a worse one at this hearth than this one. First of all, he saw the master was in mourning, and he came in anyway, and had the nerve to walk through the gates. Then, he did not take what hospitality we could give him with any decency, knowing our disaster. No. If there was anything we did not bring, he shouted for it. He took the ivy-wood cup in his hands and drank the black grape's dark juice, neat and strong, until the flame of the wine wrapped round him and heated him up, and he put myrtle branches on his head and howled, out of tune. And there were two kinds of music to hear: he was singing, caring nothing for the troubles in Admetus's house, and we slaves were crying for our mistress. But we did not let the guest see our wet eyes, because Admetus had ordered it so. And now here I am in the house, feeding a guest, some crook, a thief and a robber for all I know, while she has gone out of the house, and I did not follow her, or stretch out my hand to her, mourning my mistress, who was a mother to me and to every slave in the house. She saved us from ten thousand troubles, softening her husband's tempers. So am I not right to hate this guest, who came in the middle of our troubles?

(Heracles comes out of the guest rooms, with a wreath on his head and a cup in his hand.)

Heracles. You there. Why the solemn, worried look? A servant should not be sour-faced with the guests. He should welcome them with a friendly mind. You see a friend of your master's standing right in front of you, and you receive him with a sullen face and your brows knitted, because you are so taken up with a grief that belongs to somebody outside the house. Come here, so you can learn a little wisdom. Do you know what mortal life is really like, what its nature is? I do not suppose you do. How could you? Well, listen to me. Every mortal owes a death, and there is not a man alive who knows for certain whether he will be alive tomorrow. Where fortune will go next is hidden. It cannot be taught, and no skill can catch it. So now you have heard it, and learned it from me: cheer yourself up, drink, count the life you have today as yours, and the rest as fortune's. And honour the sweetest of all the gods to mortals, Aphrodite. She is a kind goddess. Let all the rest go, and take my advice, if you think I am talking sense, that is. I think I am. So will you not drop this excessive grief, and drink with us, and put these troubles behind you, with a garland on your head? I know for a fact that the splash of wine falling into the cup will carry you out of this sullen, knotted state of mind and into another harbour. We are mortals, and we should think mortal thoughts. Because for all the solemn ones with their knitted brows, if you take my judgement on it, life is not truly life. It is a disaster.

Servant. We know all that. But what we are going through right now does not call for partying and laughter.

Heracles. The dead woman is an outsider. Do not grieve too much. The masters of this house are alive.

Servant. Alive? Do you not know what has happened in this house?

Heracles. I do, unless your master lied to me about something.

Servant. He is too kind to his guests. Far too kind.

Heracles. Was I supposed to go without my dinner because some outsider died?

Servant. An outsider. Oh yes. She was a complete outsider, she was.

Heracles. Is there some trouble here that he did not tell me about?

Servant. Go and enjoy yourself. Our masters' troubles are our business.

Heracles. That does not sound like the start of a stranger's grief.

Servant. No. If it were, watching you carouse would not have hurt me the way it did.

Heracles. Have my hosts done something terrible to me, then?

Servant. You did not come at the right time for this house to take you in. We are in mourning. You can see the clothes, black, and the shorn hair.

Heracles. Who is it that is dead? One of the children gone? Or his old father?

Servant. It is the wife of Admetus who is dead, stranger.

Heracles. What did you say? And after that you still sat me down to dinner?

Servant. He was ashamed to turn you away from his door.

Heracles. Poor man. What a wife he has lost.

Servant. We are all lost, not just her.

Heracles. But I noticed. I saw it: his eyes streaming, his hair cut short, his face. But he talked me round. He said it was an outsider's funeral he was taking to the grave. So I forced myself through these gates, and I sat drinking in the house of a man who loves his guests, while he was in that state. And then I went on carousing, with garlands piled on my head? But you. To say nothing, with a disaster like this lying on the house. Where is he burying her? Where do I go to find her?

Servant. Straight along the road that leads to Larissa. You will see the tomb of cut stone, just outside the town.

Heracles. Heart of mine, you have put up with so much, and you, my hand: now show what kind of son Alcmene of Tiryns, the daughter of Electryon, bore to Zeus. I have to save this woman who has just died. I have to set Alcestis back in this house and pay Admetus back for what he did for me. I will go and watch for Death, the black-robed lord of the dead, and I think I will find him near the tomb, drinking the blood of the offerings. If I rush him out of hiding and get hold of him and lock my arms round him in a ring, there is nobody who will get him out of it, however his ribs ache, until he lets the woman go to me. And if I miss my quarry, and he does not come to the clotted blood, I will go down to the sunless house of Persephone and her Lord below, and I will ask them for her. I am confident I will bring Alcestis up, and put her into the hands of my host, who took me into his house and did not drive me away, though he had been struck a heavy blow. He hid it, because he is a noble man, out of respect for me. Who in Thessaly loves his guests more than this man does? Who in all Greece? He will never say that he did a good turn to a bad man, noble as he is.

(Heracles goes off toward the tomb, and the Servant goes into the house. Admetus comes back from the burial, with the Chorus.)

Admetus.
	Io. Hateful,
	the way in. Hateful, the sight of a house
	with the wife gone. Io moi moi. Ai ai.
	Where can I go? Where can I stand? What can I say? What not say?
	How can I die?
	The mother who bore me bore me under a heavy fate.
	I envy the dead. I want to be them.
	I long to live in those houses of theirs.
	I take no joy in looking at the light,
	or in setting my foot on the earth.
	That was the hostage Death took from me
	and handed to Hades.
Chorus.
	Go forward, go on. Go into the shelter of the house.
Admetus.
	Aiai.
Chorus.
	You have suffered things worth crying over.
Admetus.
	E, e.
Chorus.
	You have walked through pain, I know it well . . .
Admetus.
	Pheu, pheu.
Chorus.
	but you do nothing for the woman below.
Admetus.
	Io moi moi.
Chorus.
	Never to see your dear wife's face
	in front of you again. That is hard.
Admetus.
	You have named the thing that scars my heart.
	What worse can happen to a man than losing
	a faithful wife? I wish I had never married,
	never lived with her in this house.
	I envy the unmarried and the childless.
	They have one life. To ache for that
	is a burden a man can carry.
	But children falling sick, and marriage beds
	torn apart by death,
	no one can bear to watch it, when he could have been
	childless and unmarried all his life.
Chorus.
	Fate, fate has come, and there is no wrestling with it.
Admetus.
	Aiai.
Chorus.
	But you set no limit to your grief.
Admetus.
	E, e.
Chorus.
	Heavy to carry. And yet . . .
Admetus.
	Pheu, pheu.
Chorus.
	bear it. You are not the first man to lose . . .
Admetus.
	Io moi moi.
Chorus.
	a wife. Disaster shows itself
	to one mortal after another, and presses down.
Admetus.
	Long grief, long sorrow for the people we love
	under the earth.
	Why did you stop me throwing myself
	into the open trench of the tomb, to lie there dead
	with her, the best woman by far?
	Hades would have had two souls for one,
	the two most faithful, crossing
	the lake under the earth together.
Chorus.
	I had a kinsman
	whose son died in his house,
	a boy worth mourning,
	his only child. And yet
	he carried the evil, and carried it well enough, childless as he was,
	his hair already grey,
	already stooping forward,
	far along the road of his life.
Admetus.
	Shape of my house, how can I go in?
	How can I live here, when my luck
	has turned over? Oh. The distance is so wide.
	Then, with pine torches from Pelion
	and wedding songs, I walked in,
	holding my dear wife's hand,
	and a loud crowd of revellers came behind,
	calling the dead woman and me happy:
	two people well born, from noble stock
	on both sides, yoked together.
	Now, in place of the wedding songs, a wail,
	and black clothes in place of white,
	escort me in
	to an empty bed.
Chorus.
	On the heels of good fortune
	this pain came to you, who had never known evil.
	But you saved
	your life and your breath.
	Your wife died. She left her love behind her.
	What is new in that? Death has already
	unyoked many men
	from their wives.

Admetus. Friends, I think my wife's fate is luckier than mine, though it does not look it. No pain will ever touch her again. She has finished with all her troubles, and with glory. But I, who should not be alive, who slipped past my fated hour, I will live out a life of misery. I am only now learning it. How am I going to bear walking in through these doors? Who will I speak to, and who will speak to me, so that I get any pleasure from coming in? Where will I turn? The emptiness inside will drive me out, when I see my wife's bed empty, and the chairs she used to sit in, and the floor unswept under the roof, and the children falling at my knees and crying for their mother, and the slaves groaning for the mistress they have lost from the house.

That is how it will be at home. And outside, the weddings of Thessaly and the gatherings full of women will drive me away, because I will not be able to stand looking at women my wife's age. And whoever happens to be my enemy will say this about me: "Look at him, living in disgrace. He did not have the nerve to die. He gave the woman he married in his place, out of cowardice, and escaped Hades. And he thinks he is a man? He hates his own parents, when he was not willing to die himself." That is the name I will have, on top of my troubles. So what is the profit in living, friends, with a bad name and a bad life?

Chorus.
	I have gone up through the Muses' country
	and high into the air,
	I have taken hold of many arguments,
	and I have found nothing stronger
	than Necessity. There is no drug
	on the Thracian tablets
	that the voice of Orpheus wrote out,
	none among all the medicines Apollo gave the sons of Asclepius,
	cut from the roots to heal the pains of mortal men.
Chorus.
	She is the only goddess with no altar
	you can go to, no image,
	and she does not listen to sacrifice.
	Lady, do not come to me
	any harder than you have in my life before.
	Whatever Zeus nods his head to,
	he brings to its end with you.
	Even the iron of the Chalybes you break by force,
	and there is no mercy in you, no relenting in that sheer will.
Chorus.
	And you, Admetus: the goddess has caught you in the grip of her hands, and you cannot escape.
	Bear it. You will never bring the dead
	up from below by crying.
	Even the sons of gods fade
	into the dark of death.
	She was dear when she was with us,
	and dead, she will be dear still.
	The noblest wife of all women was the one you yoked to your bed.
Chorus.
	Do not let your wife's tomb be counted
	a mound of the dead, like the other dead.
	Let it be honoured like the gods,
	something travellers bow to.
	Someone stepping off the road
	onto the side path will say:
	"This woman died for her husband, once.
	Now she is a blessed spirit.
	Hail, Lady. Be good to us." That is how
	they will speak to her.

(Heracles comes back, leading a woman whose face is veiled.)

Chorus. And here, it seems, is the son of Alcmene, Admetus, on his way to your hearth.

Heracles. Admetus, a man should speak freely to a friend, and not keep his complaints down under his ribs and say nothing. I came to you when you were in trouble, and I thought I had earned the right to stand close and be counted as a friend. But you did not tell me your wife's body was laid out in the house. You gave me a guest's welcome instead, as if you were taken up with some outsider's grief. And I put a garland on my head and poured out wine to the gods, in your house, with that disaster in it. I blame you for that. I do blame you, after what I went through. But I do not want to hurt you when you are down.

What I have come back here for, I will tell you. Take this woman and keep her safe for me until I come back with the horses from Thrace, once I have killed the king of the Bistones. And if something happens to me that I hope does not happen, because I do hope to come home, I give her to you to serve in your house. She came into my hands with a lot of hard work. I found some people setting up a public contest, a real job for athletes, and that is where I got her: I took her as the prize. The men who won the light events led away horses, and the ones who won the bigger events, the boxing and the wrestling, got herds of cattle, and a woman went with the cattle. I happened to be there, and it would have been a disgrace to pass up a prize with glory in it. So, as I said, you must look after the woman. I did not steal her. I won her with hard work, and I have brought her here. And in time, maybe you will thank me for it too.

Admetus. It was not from any disrespect to you, or because I count you among people I am ashamed of, that I hid my wife's miserable fate from you. It would have been pain piled on pain if you had gone off to some other host's house. It was enough for me to cry over my own trouble. But the woman, my lord, if there is any way at all, I beg you, tell some other Thessalian to keep her, someone who has not suffered what I have. You have plenty of friends in Pherae. Do not remind me of my misery. I could not look at her in the house and keep my eyes dry. Do not put a sickness on top of the sickness I have. I am weighed down enough with what has happened to me.

And where in the house would a young woman live? She is young: her dress and her jewellery show it. Is she to live in the men's quarters? And how will she stay untouched, moving about among young men? A young man in his prime, Heracles, is not easy to hold back. I am thinking of your interests. Or do I take her into the dead woman's bedroom and keep her there? And how do I bring her into that woman's bed? I am afraid of blame from two sides. From the townspeople, in case someone accuses me of betraying the woman who saved me and falling into another young woman's bed. And from the dead woman herself. She deserves my respect. I have to be very careful.

And you, woman, whoever you are, know this: you have the same measure of body as Alcestis. You are her shape. Oh. By the gods, take this woman out of my sight. Do not take me when I am already taken. When I look at her I think I am looking at my wife. It churns my heart, and the springs have broken open in my eyes. Oh, I am a wretched man. Only now am I tasting how bitter this grief is.

Chorus. I could not call your luck good. But whoever you are, you have to bear what a god gives.

Heracles. If only I had the power to bring your wife up into the light from the houses below and do you that favour.

Admetus. I know you would want to. But how? The dead do not come back to the light.

Heracles. Then do not go too far. Carry it the way you should.

Admetus. It is easier to give advice than to suffer and hold out.

Heracles. What good will it do you if you want to groan for ever?

Admetus. I know that myself. But some longing drags me on.

Heracles. Yes. Loving the dead brings tears.

Admetus. She has destroyed me, more than I can say.

Heracles. You have lost a good wife. Who will deny it?

Admetus. So that this man takes no more pleasure in life.

Heracles. Time will soften it. The evil is still young.

Admetus. Time. Yes, you can say time, if time means dying.

Heracles. A woman will cure you. The longing for a new marriage.

Admetus. Be quiet. What a thing to say. I would not have believed it of you.

Heracles. What? You will not marry again? You will keep an empty bed?

Admetus. There is no woman who will lie in it.

Heracles. Do you expect that to do the dead woman any good?

Admetus. She has to be honoured, wherever she is.

Heracles. I approve. I do approve. But you are convicting yourself of foolishness.

Admetus. As long as you never call this man a bridegroom.

Heracles. I praised you because you are a faithful friend to your wife.

Admetus. May I die if I ever betray her, even though she is gone.

Heracles. Then take this woman into your noble house.

Admetus. No. I beg you, by Zeus who fathered you.

Heracles. And yet you will be making a mistake if you do not.

Admetus. And if I do, grief will gnaw at my heart.

Heracles. Do it. The favour may turn out to land just where it is needed.

Admetus. Pheu. If only you had never won her in that contest.

Heracles. But when I win, you win with me.

Admetus. Well said. But the woman must go.

Heracles. She will go, if she has to. But first, look at whether she has to.

Admetus. She has to, unless you mean to lose your temper with me.

Heracles. I know something, and that is why I am pressing it.

Admetus. Win, then. But what you are doing gives me no pleasure.

Heracles. There will come a time when you praise me. Just do it.

Admetus. Take her in, servants, if this woman has to be received in the house.

Heracles. I will not hand the woman over to servants.

Admetus. Then take her into the house yourself, if you like.

Heracles. No. I am going to put her into your hands.

Admetus. I will not touch her. She is free to go inside.

Heracles. I trust your right hand, and only yours.

Admetus. My lord, you are forcing me to do this against my will.

Heracles. Have the nerve. Stretch out your hand and touch the stranger.

Admetus. There. I am holding it out, as if I were cutting off the Gorgon's head.

Heracles. Have you got her?

Admetus. Got her? Yes.

Heracles. Then keep her safe. And one day you will say the son of Zeus was a noble guest.

(He lifts the veil from the woman's face.)

Look at her. See if she seems at all like your wife. You are a lucky man now; step out of your grief.

Admetus. Gods, what am I going to say? This is a wonder I never hoped for. Is this really my wife I am looking at? Or is some god mocking me, knocking me out of my senses with joy?

Heracles. No. It is your own wife you are looking at.

Admetus. Make sure it is not some ghost from below.

Heracles. The guest you took in was no conjuror of spirits.

Admetus. But am I looking at my wife, the woman I buried?

Heracles. Be sure of it. I am not surprised you cannot believe your luck.

Admetus. Can I touch her? Can I speak to her as my living wife?

Heracles. Speak to her. You have everything you wanted.

Admetus. Face and body of my dearest wife. I have you, past all hope, when I thought I would never see you again.

Heracles. You have her. Only let no god be jealous of it.

Admetus. Noble son of almighty Zeus, be happy, and may the father who begot you keep you safe. You alone have set my house back on its feet. How did you send her up from below into this light?

Heracles. I fought the god who had her in his power.

Admetus. Where did you fight this fight with Death, you say?

Heracles. Right beside the tomb. I sprang out of hiding and got my hands on him.

Admetus. But why is she standing there without a word?

Heracles. You are not allowed to hear her speak to you yet. Not until she has been purified from her consecration to the gods below, and the third day comes. Take her inside now. And in future, Admetus, be a just man and treat your guests with reverence. Goodbye. I have a job waiting, and I am going to do it for Eurystheus, the king, Sthenelus's son.

Admetus. Stay with us. Share our hearth.

Heracles. Another time. Now I have to hurry.

Admetus. Good luck to you, and may you come home again. And to the citizens, and to all four districts of my Thessaly, I give this order: set up dances for this good fortune, and make the altars smoke with the sacrifice of cattle and with prayers. Because now we have changed our life for a better one than the life before. I am a lucky man, and I will not deny it.

(Heracles goes. Admetus leads Alcestis into the house.)

Chorus.
	Many are the shapes of what the gods do,
	and many the things they bring about that no one expected.
	What we counted on did not happen,
	and for what no one counted on, a god found a way.
	That is how this business ended.

Medea (431 BC)

Medea

(Corinth, in front of the house where Jason and Medea have lived. The Nurse comes out alone.)

Nurse. If only the Argo had never flown through the dark Clashing Rocks to the land of Colchis. If only the pine had never been cut down in the glens of Pelion and fallen, to put oars in the hands of the best men alive, the ones who went to fetch the golden fleece for Pelias. Then my mistress Medea would never have sailed to the towers of Iolcus, her heart knocked flat by love for Jason. She would never have talked the daughters of Pelias into killing their father, and she would not be living here in Corinth with her husband and her children. And she was welcome here. The citizens of the country she came to as an exile liked her, and she herself went along with Jason in everything, which is the surest safety there is: a wife who does not stand apart from her husband. But now it is all hatred, and what was dearest is sick. Jason has betrayed his own children and my mistress, and he sleeps in a royal marriage. He has married the daughter of Creon, who rules this land. And Medea, poor woman, cast off and dishonoured, shouts about the oaths he swore. She calls up the right hand he gave her, the greatest pledge there is, and she calls the gods to witness what kind of return she is getting from Jason.

She lies there without eating, her body given up to pain, melting away the whole of her time in tears, ever since she found out her husband had wronged her. She does not lift her eyes; she does not raise her face off the ground. When her friends try to talk sense into her she listens the way a rock does, or a wave of the sea. Except that now and then she turns that white neck of hers away and cries to herself for her dear father, and her country, and the home she betrayed to come away with a man who has now thrown her aside. Now she knows, poor thing, from what has happened to her, what it is worth never to leave your own country. She hates the children. She takes no pleasure in seeing them. And I am afraid she is planning something new. She has a heavy mind, and she will not put up with being treated badly. I know her. I am frightened she will go quietly into the room where the bed is made and drive a sharpened sword through the liver, or kill the princess and the man who married her too, and then bring some greater disaster down on herself. She is dangerous. Nobody who picks a quarrel with that woman is going to come out of it singing the victory song easily.

But here come the children, finished with their running about. They have no idea of their mother's troubles. A young mind does not like to hurt.

(The Tutor comes in with the two boys.)

Tutor. Old servant of my mistress's house, why are you standing out here at the gate by yourself, groaning your troubles to yourself? How does Medea come to want to be left alone without you?

Nurse. Old man, you who walk behind Jason's children: when a master's affairs go wrong, that is a misfortune for good slaves as well. It takes hold of their hearts. I have come to such a pitch of grief that a longing came over me to come out here and tell the earth and the sky what has happened to my mistress.

Tutor. Has the poor woman not stopped crying yet?

Nurse. I envy you. The trouble is at its beginning. It is nowhere near the middle.

Tutor. The fool. If I may say that about a master. She knows nothing yet about the newer troubles.

Nurse. What is it, old man? Do not begrudge me the telling.

Tutor. Nothing. I take back even what I said already.

Nurse. No. By your beard, do not hide it from a fellow slave. I will keep quiet about it, if I have to.

Tutor. I heard someone talking, and pretended not to listen, as I came up to the draughts players, where the oldest men sit, by the holy water of Pirene. He said that Creon, the ruler of this land, is going to drive these children out of Corinth, and their mother with them. Whether the story is true I do not know. I would like it not to be.

Nurse. And Jason will put up with his sons being treated like that, even if he has quarrelled with their mother?

Tutor. Old ties lose out to new ones. That man is no friend to this house.

Nurse. Then we are finished, if we add a new trouble to the old one before we have bailed out the first.

Tutor. As for you, keep quiet and say nothing about it. This is not the moment for the mistress to know.

Nurse. Children, do you hear what kind of father you have? Curse him. No. He is my master. But he is caught being a bad man to the people he owes.

Tutor. Who is not? Are you only now learning that every man loves himself more than his neighbour, some of them honestly and some for gain, when their father does not love these children, all for the sake of a bed?

Nurse. Go inside the house, children. It will be all right. And you, keep them out of the way as much as you can. Do not bring them near their mother while she is in this black mood. I have already seen her glaring at them like a bull, as if she wanted to do something. She will not stop this rage, I know it, until she strikes somebody down. Let it be enemies she does something to, and not the people she loves.

(Medea's voice comes from inside the house.)

Medea.
	Oh.
	Unhappy, miserable, worn down with pain,
	oh, oh, how can I die?
Nurse.
	That is it, dear children. Your mother
	is stirring her heart, stirring her anger.
	Hurry into the house, quickly,
	and keep out of range of her eye,
	do not go near her. Watch out
	for the wild temper, the hateful nature
	of that stubborn mind.
	Go now, get inside as fast as you can.
	It is plain enough: the cloud of grief
	that is lifting off the ground will soon catch fire
	with a greater rage. What will she do,
	that great-hearted, hard-to-stop
	soul, bitten by her wrongs?

(The Tutor takes the children into the house.)

Medea.
	Aiai.
	I have suffered, suffered things
	worth loud crying. Accursed
	children of a hateful mother, die,
	you and your father, and let the whole house go to ruin.
Nurse.
	Oh, oh, poor woman.
	Why should your children share
	in their father's crime? Why hate them? Oh,
	children, I am sick with fear that something will happen to you.
	The tempers of kings are terrible. Somehow,
	taking few orders and giving many,
	they find it hard to shift their anger.
	Being used to living among equals
	is better. For my part, let me grow old
	in no great state, but safe.
	The middle way: first, its very name
	wins, and to live by it is far
	the best thing for mortals. Too much
	does nobody any good in the end,
	and when a god is angry with a house
	it pays back greater ruin.

(The Chorus, women of Corinth, come in.)

Chorus.
	I heard the voice, I heard the cry
	of the unhappy woman from Colchis. Is she still
	not calm? Old woman, tell me.
	At the double doors, from inside the house, I heard a cry,
	and I take no pleasure, woman, in the pains
	of this house. It has become dear to me.
Nurse.
	There is no house. It is gone already.
	A royal bed has him,
	and she is in her room wasting her life away,
	my mistress, and not one friend's word
	brings any warmth to her heart.
Medea.
	Aiai. Zeus, and Earth, and Light:
	let fire from heaven come down
	through my head. What good is living to me now?
	Ah, ah. Let me be done with it in death
	and leave a life I hate.
Chorus.
	Did you hear, Zeus and earth and light,
	what a cry that unhappy
	bride is singing?
	What is this longing of yours
	for the bed no one can go near, you fool?
	Death's ending will hurry on by itself.
	Do not pray for it.
	If your husband
	bows down to a new bed,
	that is his affair. Do not tear yourself over it.
	Zeus will plead your case for you. Do not
	waste yourself away crying over the man who shared your bed.
Medea.
	Great Themis, and lady Artemis,
	do you see what I suffer, I who bound
	that accursed husband
	with great oaths? One day let me see
	him and his bride ground to nothing, house and all,
	for daring to wrong me first.
	Father. City. I left you in shame,
	and killed my brother.
Nurse.
	Do you hear what she says, how she calls
	on Themis, who hears prayers, and on Zeus,
	whom men count the keeper of oaths?
	There is no way my mistress will lay down
	this anger over anything small.
Chorus.
	How could she come out
	where we can see her, and take in
	the sound of the words we would say?
	If only she would let go
	of the heavy anger and the stubbornness of her mind.
	Let my goodwill, at least,
	never fail the people I care for.
	Go and bring her
	out here, out of the house.
	Tell her we are her friends too.
	Hurry, before she does harm to the ones inside.
	This grief of hers is gathering speed.
Nurse.
	I will. But I am afraid I will not
	persuade my mistress.
	Still, I will give you the favour of the effort.
	And yet she glares at her slaves
	like a lioness with cubs, whenever one of us
	comes near her to say a word.
	You would not be wrong to call the men of old
	clumsy, and not clever at all,
	who invented songs for festivals,
	for banquets and for dinners,
	pleasant sounds for life to listen to,
	but nobody has found how to stop
	the hateful griefs of mortals with music
	and many-stringed song, the griefs
	that bring deaths and terrible turns of fortune down on houses.
	And yet it would be a gain if people
	could heal those with singing. Where the dinner is good
	and the tables full, why raise a useless noise?
	The full table in front of them
	has pleasure enough in itself for mortals.

(The Nurse goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	I heard the wail, heavy with groans,
	the shrill and bitter cry she raises
	against the traitor in her bed, the man whose marriage was a crime.
	Wronged, she calls on the gods,
	on Themis, who keeps oaths for Zeus,
	who brought her across
	to Greece on the far shore,
	through the salt sea at night, through the
	narrow lock of the endless deep.

(Medea comes out of the house.)

Medea. Women of Corinth, I have come out of the house so that you will not blame me. I know many people get a name for being haughty, some because they keep out of sight, and some in public; and others, because they go quietly, are called lazy. There is no justice in people's eyes. Before they have really learned what a man is inside, they hate him on sight, though he has done them no wrong. A foreigner especially must fit in with the city. And I have no praise for the citizen who is stubborn, either, and makes himself bitter to his fellow citizens out of ignorance.

But this thing that fell on me out of nowhere has destroyed my soul. I am finished. I have let go of any pleasure in living, and I want to die, my friends. The man who was everything to me, as he knows very well, has turned out to be the worst man alive: my husband.

Of all creatures that live and think, we women are the most wretched. First we have to buy a husband, at an enormous price, and take a master over our bodies, which is a worse evil on top of the first. And that is the greatest contest of all: getting a bad one or a good one. Divorce brings a woman no honour, and she cannot refuse a husband. She comes into new habits and new rules, and she has to be a prophet, since nobody taught her at home, to work out how best to handle the man she sleeps with. And if we work all this out well, and the husband lives with us and does not fight the yoke, our life is one to envy. If not, better to die. A man, when he is sick of the company indoors, goes out and clears his heart of its disgust, turning to some friend or someone his own age. We have to look to one soul alone. And they say we live a life without danger, at home, while they fight with the spear. What fools. I would rather stand behind a shield three times than give birth once.

But the same argument does not fit you and me. You have this city, and your fathers' houses, and the good things of life, and friends to be with. I am alone. I have no city, and my husband treats me with outrage, a woman carried off as loot from a barbarian country, with no mother, no brother, not one relative I can put in to shelter from this storm. So this much, and only this, I want from you. If I can find some way, some device, to pay my husband back for these wrongs, and the man who gave him his daughter, and the woman he married, keep silent. A woman is full of fear about everything else, a coward when it comes to a fight, and she cannot look at steel. But when she is wronged in her bed, there is no mind more murderous.

Chorus. I will. You will be right to make your husband pay, Medea. I do not wonder that you grieve at what has happened to you. But I see Creon, the king of this land, coming this way, with news of some new decision.

(Creon comes in with attendants.)

Creon. You, with the scowl and the fury at your husband. Medea. I order you out of this country, into exile, and take your two children with you. No delay. I am the judge of this sentence, and I am not going back into my house until I have thrown you outside the borders of the land.

Medea. Aiai. I am destroyed, poor woman, root and branch. My enemies are letting out every rope of sail, and there is no easy landing from this ruin. But I will ask, even in this state. Why are you sending me out of the country, Creon?

Creon. I am afraid of you. No need to dress it up in words. I am afraid you will do my daughter some harm that cannot be undone. A great many things add up to that fear. You were born clever, and you know a great deal about doing harm, and you are in pain, cheated of your husband's bed. And I hear you are threatening, so people tell me, to do something to the father who gave the bride, and the bridegroom, and the bride. So I am going to guard against it before it happens. Better for me to have you hate me now, woman, than to go soft and groan about it afterwards.

Medea. Ah, ah. This is not the first time, Creon. My reputation has hurt me many times and done me a great deal of harm. No man with any sense should ever have his children taught to be too clever. Apart from the name for idleness that they get, they earn the spite and ill will of their fellow citizens. If you bring new and clever ideas to fools, you will look useless, and not clever at all; and if the people who think they know something subtle decide you are better than they are, the city will find you painful to have around. I share this luck myself. Because I am clever, some people envy me, some think me withdrawn, some think the opposite, and some find me difficult. And I am not so very clever.

Anyway, you are afraid of me. Afraid I will do you some injury? I am not in a position, so do not tremble at me, Creon, to go committing offences against kings. What have you done to wrong me? You gave your daughter to the man your heart chose. It is my husband I hate. You, I think, acted sensibly. And now I do not begrudge you your good fortune. Make your marriage, and good luck to you all. But let me live in this country. I have been wronged, and I will keep quiet about it. I have been beaten by people stronger than me.

Creon. Soft words to listen to. But inside I am terrified you are planning something bad, and I trust you that much less than before. A quick-tempered woman, and a man too, for that matter, is easier to guard against than a clever one who keeps quiet. So get out, as fast as you can, and no speeches. It is settled, and you have no trick that will keep you here among us when you are my enemy.

Medea. No. By your knees, by your newly married daughter.

Creon. You are wasting words. You will never persuade me.

Medea. You will drive me out, and pay no respect to my prayers?

Creon. I do not love you more than my own house.

Medea. My country. How I think of you now.

Creon. Yes. After my children, it is what I love most, by far.

Medea. Ah, ah. What a great evil love is for mortals.

Creon. That depends, I imagine, on how things fall out.

Medea. Zeus, do not let the man who caused this escape you.

Creon. Go, you fool, and rid me of this trouble.

Medea. The trouble is mine. I have no shortage of it.

Creon. In a moment my servants' hands will push you out by force.

Medea. Not that, not that. I am asking you, Creon...

Creon. You are going to make a scene, it seems, woman.

Medea. I will go into exile. That is not what I begged you for.

Creon. Then why are you forcing me? Why will you not let go of my hand?

Medea. Let me stay this one day, and finish thinking out how we will go into exile, and find some start in life for my children, since their father does not care to arrange anything for his sons. Have pity on them. You are the father of children yourself. It is natural that you should feel kindly. I have no thought for myself, if we are exiled. It is them I weep for, meeting such a disaster.

Creon. There is nothing of the tyrant in my nature, and I have ruined a great deal by feeling sorry for people. And now I can see I am making a mistake, woman, but all the same you will have what you ask. But I warn you: if tomorrow's sun, the god's torch, sees you and your children inside the borders of this land, you die. That word is spoken and it will not lie. So now, if you have to stay, stay for one day. You will not do any of the terrible things I am afraid of in that time.

(Creon goes out with his attendants.)

Chorus.
	Unhappy woman,
	ah, ah, miserable in your sorrows.
	Where will you turn? To what stranger's house?
	What home, what country will you find
	to save you from these evils?
	Into what a hopeless sea of troubles, Medea,
	a god has carried you.

Medea. It has gone badly in every direction. Who will deny it? But it is not going to end this way. Do not think so yet. There are still trials ahead for the newlyweds, and for the ones who made the match, no small pains. Do you think I would ever have fawned on that man if I were not getting something out of it, or working some scheme? I would not have spoken to him. I would not have touched him with my hands. But he has gone so far into folly that when he could have wrecked my plans by throwing me out of the country, he has let me stay this one day, and in it I will make corpses of three of my enemies: the father, the girl, and my husband.

I have many roads to their deaths, and I do not know which to take first, my friends. Shall I set fire to the bridal house? Or go quietly into the room where the bed is made and drive a sharpened sword through the liver? One thing stands in my way. If I am caught going into the house and working my scheme, I will die, and give my enemies a laugh. Best to take the straight road, where we women are cleverest by nature: take them with poison.

Very well. Say they are dead. What city will take me in? What host will offer me a land of refuge and a house that stands good for me, and save my life? There is none. So I will wait a little while longer, and if some safe tower shows itself to me, I will go after this murder by stealth and in silence. But if hopeless circumstance drives me out, I will take the sword in my own hand, even if I am going to die for it, and kill them, and go the hard way of daring. For by the mistress I honour above all others and have chosen as my partner in the work, Hecate, who lives in the inmost corner of my hearth, not one of them is going to hurt my heart and enjoy it. Bitter and grievous I will make their marriage, bitter their match-making, bitter my exile from the land.

Come on, then. Spare nothing of what you know, Medea, plotting and scheming. Go to the terrible thing. Now is the trial of courage. You see what is being done to you. You are not to be laughed at over Jason's marriage into the house of Sisyphus, you, the daughter of a noble father, born from the Sun. You have the knowledge. And besides, we were born women: helpless when it comes to doing good, but of every kind of evil the cleverest builders.

Chorus.
	The springs of the holy rivers are running uphill.
	Justice and everything else are turned round backwards.
	It is men whose plans are treacherous, men
	whose oaths by the gods no longer hold.
	And the talk will turn, and my life will have its good name.
	Honour is coming to the race of women.
	No more will ugly rumour have women in its grip.
Chorus.
	The Muses of the poets of old will stop
	singing of my faithlessness.
	Apollo, lord of song, did not put
	the lyre's inspired music into our minds,
	or I would have sung a hymn back
	at the race of men. The long years have
	much to say about our lot, and about men's too.
Chorus.
	You sailed from your father's house
	with a mind gone mad, and passed between the twin
	rocks of the sea. Now in a strange
	land you live, the bed you slept in
	lost, no husband in it,
	poor woman, and driven out of the country
	in dishonour, an exile.
Chorus.
	The grace of oaths is gone. Shame
	no longer stays in great Greece. It has flown up into the sky.
	And you have no father's house,
	poor woman, to shelter in
	from your troubles, and another queen,
	stronger than you in your own bed,
	has taken over the house.

(Jason comes in.)

Jason. This is not the first time I have seen it. I have seen it often: a harsh temper is an evil nothing can be done about. You could have had this country and this house, if you had taken your betters' decisions lightly, and instead, for the sake of foolish talk, you are being thrown out of the country.
