It makes no difference to me. Never stop calling Jason the worst man alive, if you like. But for what you have said against the royal family, count it clear gain that exile is your only punishment. I kept trying to take the edge off the king's anger, all the time, and I wanted you to stay. But you would not let go of your folly, always speaking badly of the royal family, and so you are being thrown out. Even so, even after all this, I have not given up on the people I owe. I have come here looking after your interests, woman, so that you will not be thrown out with the children penniless, or short of anything. Exile drags a great many evils along with it. And even if you hate me, I could never wish you harm.

Medea. You utter, utter coward. That is the worst thing my tongue can call you: that you are no man. You have come to me? You come here, when you have made yourself the worst enemy of the gods, and of me, and of the whole human race? This is not courage. It is not daring, to wrong the people you owe and then look them in the face. It is the worst of all the sicknesses that live in human beings: shamelessness. But you did well to come. I will lighten my heart by telling you exactly how bad you are, and you will hurt, listening.

I will start at the beginning. I saved your life. Every Greek who boarded the Argo with you knows it. You had been sent to yoke the fire-breathing bulls and to sow the field of death. And the serpent that coiled round the golden fleece and guarded it, sleepless, in its many folds: I killed it, and held up the light that saved you. I betrayed my own father and my own house and came with you to Iolcus under Pelion, more eager than clever. And I killed Pelias, in the most painful way there is to die, at the hands of his own children, and I wiped out his whole house. That is what I did for you, and you, worst of men, betrayed me and took a new bed, when we had children. If you had still been childless, I could have forgiven you for wanting this marriage.

The trust in oaths is gone. I cannot make out whether you think the gods of those days no longer rule, or that new rules have been laid down for human beings now, because you know perfectly well you have not kept your oath to me. Ah, this right hand, which you took hold of so often, and these knees. How uselessly we were touched by a bad man, and how we missed what we hoped for.

Come, then. I will talk to you as if you were a friend, though what good do I expect to get from you? Still, I will do it. The questions will show you up as even more shameful. Where am I to turn now? To my father's house, which I betrayed for you, along with my country, to come here? To the poor daughters of Pelias? They would give me a fine welcome into their house, when I killed their father. That is how it stands. To the ones I loved at home I have become an enemy; and the ones I had no reason to harm, I have made my enemies, to do you a favour. And in return for all that, you have made me so blessed in the eyes of many a Greek woman. What a wonderful husband I have in you, and how faithful, poor me, if I am thrown out of the country and go into exile, without one friend, alone with my children, alone. A fine reproach to the new bridegroom: his children wandering as beggars, and the woman who saved his life. Zeus, why did you give people clear tests for gold, to tell the counterfeit from the true, when there is no mark stamped on a man's body to tell the bad one by?

Chorus. Anger like this is a terrible thing, and hard to heal, when people who were close to each other fall out and fight.

Jason. It seems I had better be a decent speaker after all. I will have to be like a good helmsman, who reefs his sail right down to the edges and runs out from under the storm, to get clear of this gale you keep blowing from your mouth, woman. As for me, since you pile your favour so high, I say it was Aphrodite who saved my voyage, and nobody else, god or mortal. You have a subtle mind, I grant you. But it would be an ungracious story to go through, how Love forced you, with arrows nobody can dodge, to save my skin. Still, I will not weigh it too finely. However you helped me, it was help, and I do not complain of it. But you took more for saving me than you ever gave, as I will now show you.

First, you live in Greece, instead of a barbarian country. You know what justice is, and how to live by law instead of by whoever is strongest. Every Greek has heard how clever you are, and you have a name. If you were still living out at the far edge of the world, nobody would ever have mentioned you. As for me, I would not want gold in the house, or a voice to sing more sweetly than Orpheus, if my luck did not make me famous with it. That is all I have to say about my labours, and I only say it because you were the one who set up this contest of speeches.

Now, the royal marriage you threw in my face. Here I am going to show you, first, that I was clever; second, that I kept myself in hand; and third, that I was a great friend to you and to my children. No, keep quiet. When I moved here from the country of Iolcus, dragging one hopeless disaster after another behind me, what luckier find could I possibly have found than this, an exile marrying a king's daughter? Not, as you keep stinging yourself with thinking, because I hated your bed and had been struck down with desire for a new bride. Not because I was eager to win some contest for having the most children, either. The ones I have are enough, and I have no complaint about them. No. I did it so that, first and most important, we could live well and not go short, because I know that a poor man's friends all get out of his way. So that I could bring the children up in a manner worthy of my house, and father brothers for the children I have by you, and put them all on the same footing, and join the family into one, and we would all be happy. What do you need more children for? For me, it pays to use the children still to come to help the ones I already have. Have I planned badly? You would not say so yourself, if your bed were not stinging you.

But you women have got to the point where, as long as the bed is going right, you think you have everything, and the moment something goes wrong in the bed, you turn on the best and finest things you have as though they were your worst enemies. Men should have found some other way of getting children, and there should have been no such thing as women. Then there would be no trouble in the world for anyone.

Chorus. Jason, you have dressed these words up very well. All the same, even if I am saying something you will not like, I think you have betrayed your wife, and what you are doing is not just.

Medea. I certainly differ from most people about a great many things. To my mind, a man who is in the wrong and is a clever speaker by nature deserves the heaviest penalty of all. He is so sure his tongue can dress up an injustice nicely that he has the nerve to try anything. And he is not so very clever, either. So do not put on your fine manners with me now, and your gift for speaking. One word will lay you flat. If you were not a bad man, you should have talked me round first and then made this marriage, instead of doing it behind the backs of the people who loved you.

Jason. Oh yes, you would have given that proposal a warm welcome, I am sure, if I had told you about the marriage. When even now you cannot bring yourself to let go of the great rage in your heart.

Medea. That is not what held you back. A barbarian wife was starting to look bad for you, as you got on towards old age.

Jason. Get this clear. It was not for the woman's sake that I married into the royal bed I have now. I told you before: I wanted to save you, and to father royal sons to be brothers to my own children, a wall round the house.

Medea. May I never have the kind of prosperity that hurts, or the kind of wealth that stings my heart.

Jason. Do you know how to change that prayer, and look wiser for it? Pray that good things never look painful to you, and that when your luck is in you do not think it is out.

Medea. Go on, add outrage to it. You have somewhere to turn. I am the one who goes into exile from this country alone.

Jason. You chose this yourself. Blame nobody else.

Medea. By doing what? Marrying someone and betraying you?

Jason. By calling down unholy curses on the royal house.

Medea. Yes, and I am a curse on your house too, as it turns out.

Jason. I am not going to argue any more of this with you. But if you want to take some of my money, to help the children or to help you in your exile, say so. I am ready to give with an open hand, and to send tokens to my friends abroad, who will treat you well. If you refuse this, woman, you are a fool. Let go of your anger and you will come out of it better.

Medea. I would not make use of those friends of yours, and I would not accept a thing. Do not offer it to us. A bad man's gifts do nobody any good.

Jason. Well then. I call the gods to witness that I am willing to do everything for you and for the children. But you do not like good things. You are so stubborn you push away the people who care about you, and so you will suffer all the more.

Medea. Go. You are aching for the girl you have just broken in, and you have been away from the house too long. Go and be a bridegroom. Because perhaps, with the god's help I will say it, you are making the kind of marriage you will wish you had never made.

(Jason goes off towards the palace.)

Chorus.
	Love that comes in too strong
	brings men no good name
	and no goodness either.
	But if Aphrodite comes in just enough,
	there is no god so gracious.
	Never, my lady, aim at me from your golden bow
	the arrow no one escapes, dipped in desire.
Chorus.
	Let a steady heart love me,
	the finest gift the gods give.
	Never let terrible Aphrodite
	strike my spirit into quarrelling tempers
	and fights that are never fed full, over some other woman's bed.
	Let her honour marriages that keep the peace,
	and judge with a sharp mind who should sleep with whom.
Chorus.
	My country. My home.
	Never let me be a woman without a city,
	dragging out a life of helplessness
	that there is no crossing,
	the most pitiful of griefs.
	Let death, let death bring me down first,
	when I have finished this day.
	There is no hardship worse
	than to lose the land you were born in.
Chorus.
	I have seen it. I do not need
	anybody else's story to tell it.
	No city, not one of your friends
	pitied you when you suffered
	the most terrible thing there is to suffer.
	Let him die unthanked, the man who could
	honour his friends and will not,
	will not unlock a clean mind to them.
	He will never be a friend of mine.

(Aegeus, the king of Athens, comes in, on his way through Corinth.)

Aegeus. Medea, be happy. Nobody knows a better opening than that for greeting a friend.

Medea. And you be happy too, Aegeus, son of clever Pandion. Where have you come from, to be setting foot in this country?

Aegeus. From Apollo's ancient oracle. I have just left it.

Medea. What sent you to the navel of the earth, where the god sings his answers?

Aegeus. I was asking how I might get the seed of children.

Medea. By the gods. Have you been living childless all this while?

Aegeus. We are childless. Some god has arranged it.

Medea. Do you have a wife, or have you never known a woman's bed?

Aegeus. I am not unyoked. I have a marriage bed.

Medea. Then what did Apollo tell you about children?

Aegeus. Words too clever for a man to piece together.

Medea. Am I allowed to know what the god said?

Aegeus. Certainly. It needs a clever mind, if anything does.

Medea. What did he say, then? Tell me, if I am allowed to hear it.

Aegeus. That I must not untie the foot of the wineskin that sticks out.

Medea. Until you have done what? Or reached what country?

Aegeus. Until I come home again to my father's hearth.

Medea. And what do you want here, that you have sailed to this country?

Aegeus. There is a man called Pittheus, the king of the land of Troezen.

Medea. The son of Pelops, they say, and a very godly man.

Aegeus. I want to share the god's answer with him.

Medea. Yes, he is a clever man, and used to handling things like this.

Aegeus. And to me the dearest of all the friends I have fought beside.

Medea. Well, good luck to you, and may you get everything you long for.

Aegeus. But why are your eyes like that? Why is your skin so wasted?

Medea. Aegeus, my husband is the worst man alive, to me.

Aegeus. What do you mean? Tell me plainly why you are so low.

Medea. Jason is wronging me, and I never did a thing to him.

Aegeus. What has he done? Tell me more clearly.

Medea. He has put another woman over us as mistress of the house.

Aegeus. Surely he has not had the nerve to do a thing as shameful as that?

Medea. Be sure of it. We who were dear to him before are nothing now.

Aegeus. Did he fall in love? Or did he come to hate your bed?

Medea. A great love, yes. He was born faithless to the people he owes.

Aegeus. Then let him go, if he is as bad as you say.

Medea. What he fell in love with was marrying into a king's family.

Aegeus. And who is giving him the bride? Finish the story for me.

Medea. Creon, who rules this land of Corinth.

Aegeus. Then you have every excuse for your grief, lady.

Medea. I am finished. And on top of it, I am being driven out of the country.

Aegeus. By whom? That is another new trouble you are telling me about.

Medea. Creon is driving me out of the land of Corinth as an exile.

Aegeus. And Jason allows it? I do not think much of that either.

Medea. Not in so many words. But he is willing to put up with it. Aegeus, I beg you, by this beard of yours, by your knees, I am your suppliant. Pity me. Pity me, the luckless woman. Do not stand and watch me thrown out alone. Take me into your country, into your house, at your hearth. If you do, may the gods bring your longing for children to fruit, and may you die a happy man yourself. You do not know what a find you have found in me. I will put an end to your childlessness. I will make you the father of children. I know the drugs for it.

Aegeus. There are many reasons, lady, why I am eager to do you this favour. First, for the sake of the gods. Second, for the children you promise me, because on that score I am completely at a loss. So this is how it stands with me. If you come to my country, I will try to protect you as your host, which is only just. But I give you this much warning in advance, lady. I will not be willing to take you out of this land myself. If you come to my house on your own, you will stay there safe from harm, and I will never hand you over to anyone. But it is your own feet that must carry you out of this country. I want to be blameless in the eyes of my hosts here as well.

Medea. So be it. But if I could have a pledge from you on this, I would have everything I want from you.

Aegeus. Do you not trust me? What is the difficulty?

Medea. I trust you. But the house of Pelias is my enemy, and so is Creon. If you were bound to me by oaths, you would not let them take me out of your country. If you had only made an agreement in words, and were not sworn before the gods, you might become their friend, and you might give in when their heralds came asking. No, you would not hold out. My side is weak, and they have wealth and a royal house.

Aegeus. There is a great deal of foresight in what you say. Well, if that is what you want, I do not refuse to do it. It is the safest thing for me too, to have some excuse I can show your enemies, and it puts your own position on firmer ground. Name the gods.

Medea. Swear by the floor of the Earth, and by the Sun, who was the father of my father, and by the whole race of the gods, all together in one oath.

Aegeus. To do what, or not to do what? Say it.

Medea. That you will never throw me out of your country yourself, and that if any enemy of mine wants to take me, you will never willingly let me go, as long as you live.

Aegeus. I swear by Earth, and by the holy light of the Sun, and by all the gods, that I will stand by what I hear from you.

Medea. That is enough. And if you do not stand by this oath, what should happen to you?

Aegeus. Whatever happens to men who do not keep faith with the gods.

Medea. Go, and be happy. Everything is well. I will come to your city as fast as I can, once I have done what I mean to do, and got what I want.

(Aegeus goes on his way.)

Chorus.
	May Hermes, the son of Maia, the lord who guides travellers,
	bring you safe to your house,
	and may you get the thing you are set on
	and hurrying after, Aegeus,
	because you have shown yourself a good man in my eyes.

Medea. Zeus. Justice, daughter of Zeus. Light of the Sun. Now, my friends, we are going to win a glorious victory over my enemies. We have set foot on the road. Now there is hope that the people I hate will pay what they owe. Because this man has appeared, right where I was struggling hardest, as a harbour for my plans. I will tie my stern cable to him, when I reach the town and the citadel of Pallas Athena.

Now I will tell you all my plans. Do not expect to enjoy them. I will send one of my slaves to Jason and ask him to come and see me. When he comes, I will speak softly to him. I will say that I think as he does, that this royal marriage he has betrayed us for is a good thing, that it is to our advantage and well thought out. And I will ask that my children stay here. Not that I would leave my children on enemy soil for my enemies to insult. No. I ask it so that I can kill the king's daughter by a trick. I will send them carrying gifts in their hands, gifts for the bride, so that they will not be exiled from this land: a fine-woven dress and a wreath of beaten gold. And if she takes the finery and puts it on her skin, she will die horribly, and so will anyone who touches the girl. That is the kind of drug I am going to smear on my gifts.

But there I leave that part of the story. I groan at the thing that has to be done after it. I am going to kill my children. My own. There is nobody who is going to take them from me. And when I have brought Jason's whole house down in ruins, I will leave this land, running from the murder of the children I love most, having found the nerve for the most unholy act there is. Because to be laughed at by my enemies is not something I can bear, my friends. Let it come. What good is living to me? I have no country, no home, no way out of my troubles. I went wrong the day I left my father's house, talked round by the words of a Greek man, and with the god's help he is going to pay me for it. He will never see the children I gave him alive again, and he will never father a child on his new-yoked bride, because she has to die, a bad woman dying badly, by my drugs. Let no one think me weak, or feeble, or the quiet kind. I am the other kind. Heavy on my enemies, and kind to my friends. People like that are the ones whose lives are remembered.

Chorus. Since you have shared this plan with us, I forbid you to do it. I want to help you, and I am taking the side of the laws that human beings live by.

Medea. There is no other way. You are forgiven for saying it. You are not suffering what I am suffering.

Chorus. But will you have the nerve to kill your own children, woman?

Medea. Yes. That is the way my husband will be bitten deepest.

Chorus. And you would become the most wretched woman alive.

Medea. Let it come. Every word between now and then is a waste. Now go, and fetch Jason here. When I need someone I can trust, I always use you. Say nothing about what I have decided, if you are loyal to your masters, and if you were born a woman.

(The Nurse goes to fetch Jason.)

Chorus.
	Children of Erechtheus, blessed since the old days,
	children of the blessed gods, from a holy land
	that no enemy has ever sacked, you feed on wisdom,
	the most glorious there is, and you walk delicately
	through the brightest of air, where once, the story goes,
	golden-haired Harmony gave birth to the nine holy Muses,
	the Muses of Pieria.
Chorus.
	And they sing that Aphrodite draws water
	from the streams of the lovely-flowing Cephisus,
	and breathes over the country
	the gentle, sweet-breathing breezes of the winds,
	and that she always sets a fragrant wreath of rose-blossom on her hair,
	and sends the Loves to sit beside Wisdom,
	to work with her at every kind of excellence.
Chorus.
	So how will the city of the holy rivers,
	how will the country that sees its friends safe on their way,
	take you in, the killer of your children,
	the unholy woman, to live among its people?
	Think of the blow that falls on your children.
	Think of the murder you are taking on.
	No. By your knees, every way there is,
	in every way we can, we beg you:
	do not murder
	your children.
Chorus.
	Where will you get the boldness for it,
	in your mind, or in your hand,
	or in your heart, bringing this terrible daring
	down on your own children?
	How will you look at your children
	and take on the murderer's part
	without a tear? You will not be able to.
	When your children fall at your feet and beg,
	you will not be able to wet your hand
	in their blood with a hardened heart.

(Jason comes in from the palace.)

Jason. I have come, as I was told to. Even though you hate me, you shall not go without this much at least. I will hear what new thing it is you want from me, woman.

Medea. Jason, I ask you to forgive what I said. It is only fair that you should put up with my tempers, after all the love there has been between the two of us. I have been going over it with myself, and I have been telling myself off. "You wretch, why are you raving like this, and picking fights with people who are planning well? Why are you making an enemy of the rulers of this land, and of your husband, who is doing the most useful thing he could do for us, marrying a princess and fathering brothers for my children? Am I not going to let go of my anger, when the gods are providing so well? What is the matter with me? Do I not have children? Do I not know that we are exiles from this land, and short of friends?" When I thought it through, I saw how badly I had been reasoning, and how pointless my anger was.

So now I approve. I think you kept your head, taking this marriage on for us, and I was the fool. I should have been in on these plans. I should have helped to arrange the wedding, and stood beside the bed, and enjoyed looking after your bride. But we are what we are, we women. I will not say bad. But you should not have sunk to matching us at it, or answered childishness with childishness. I give in. I admit I had it wrong then, but I have thought it through better now.

Children, children, come here. Leave the house, come out, and greet your father with me, and speak to him. Make up with him, along with your mother, and put away the old hatred against the people we owe. We have made a truce, and the anger is gone.

(The children come out of the house, with the Tutor.)

Take his right hand. Oh. How I keep thinking of the troubles that are hidden. Children, will you go on living a long time, and go on holding out a loving arm like this? Poor me. How close to tears I am, how full of fear. Now that I have finally ended this quarrel with your father, I have filled this soft face with tears.

Chorus. The tears have started pale from my eyes as well. I only hope the trouble goes no further than it has.

Jason. I approve of this, woman, and I do not blame you for what went before. It is natural for the female sex to lose their tempers when a husband smuggles in another marriage on the side. But your heart has changed for the better. You have recognised the winning plan, late, but you have recognised it. That is how a sensible woman acts. And for you, children, your father has been thinking hard, and with the gods' help he has set up a great deal of security. I think that one day you will be the first men in this land of Corinth, along with your brothers. Just grow up. Your father is working out the rest, and so is whichever of the gods is kind to us. I want to see you grow up strong and come to the end of your youth, standing over my enemies. You there, why are you wetting your eyes with pale tears? Why have you turned your white cheek away? Why are you not glad to hear this from me?

Medea. It is nothing. I was thinking about these children.

Jason. Then take heart. I am going to arrange things well for them.

Medea. I will. I will not doubt what you say. But a woman is a female thing, and she is born to tears.

Jason. Then why are you groaning so much over these children?

Medea. I gave birth to them. And when you prayed for the children to live, pity came over me, wondering whether it will happen. But about the reasons you came here to talk to me: some of it has been said, and I will mention the rest now. Since the rulers of this land have decided to send me away, and since it is best for me too, I see that well enough, not to live here in your way and in the way of the rulers of the land, because they think I am an enemy to their house, I am leaving this country and going into exile. But the children. So that they can be brought up by your hand, ask Creon not to send them into exile from this land.

Jason. I do not know if I could persuade him. But I must try.

Medea. Then at least tell your wife to ask her father not to send the children into exile from this land.

Jason. Certainly. And her, I think, I will persuade.

Medea. If she is a woman like the rest of us. And I will take a share in this job with you. I will send her gifts, by far the most beautiful things there are among human beings today, I know it: a fine-woven dress and a wreath of beaten gold, and the children will carry them to her. One of the servants must go and bring the finery out here, as quickly as possible. She is going to be happy not once but ten thousand times over, getting you for a husband, the best of men, and owning the finery that the Sun, my father's father, gave to his descendants.

(A servant brings the dress and the golden wreath out of the house.)

Take these wedding gifts in your hands, children, and carry them to the happy royal bride, and give them to her. They are not gifts anybody could find fault with.

Jason. What are you doing, you foolish woman, emptying your hands of these? Do you think the royal house is short of dresses? Short of gold? Keep them. Do not give them away. If the woman thinks I am worth anything at all, she will put me before money, I know that well enough.

Medea. Do not talk to me like that. Gifts persuade even the gods, they say, and gold does more with human beings than ten thousand words. Her luck is in. A god is making her fortune grow now. She is young, and she is a queen. And to save my children from exile I would give my life, not just gold. Now, children, go into the rich house, to your father's new wife, my mistress, and beg her. Beg her not to send you into exile from this land, and give her the finery. This is the thing that matters most: she must take these gifts into her own hand. Go, as fast as you can. And may you do it well, and come back to your mother with the good news she is longing to hear.

Chorus.
	Now I have no hope left for the children's lives,
	none. They are walking to their murder already.
	The bride will take the golden headband,
	the poor girl will take her ruin in her hands,
	and around her yellow hair she will set
	the finery of Hades, herself, with her own two hands.
Chorus.
	The loveliness of the robe, and its shine like a god's,
	will talk her into putting on the crown of worked gold,
	and she will dress as a bride for the dead below.
	That is the net she will fall into,
	that is the death that is her share, poor girl,
	and she will not slip out from under the ruin.
Chorus.
	And you, poor man, you married badly
	when you married into the king's house, and you do not see
	that you are bringing destruction on your sons' lives
	and a hateful death on your wife.
	Poor man. How wrong you are about what is coming to you.
Chorus.
	And I grieve for your pain too, poor mother
	of these children, who will murder
	your sons over a marriage bed,
	the bed your husband left, against all law,
	to live with another woman.

(The Tutor comes back from the palace with the two children.)

Tutor. Mistress, these children of yours are let off their exile, and the royal bride took the gifts gladly, in her own hands. From that side, the children have peace. Hey. Why are you standing there so upset, when things are going well for you? Why have you turned your face away, and why aren't you glad to hear this from me?

Medea. Aiai.

Tutor. That does not go with the news I have brought.

Medea. Aiai, again.

Tutor. Have I reported some misfortune without knowing it? Was I wrong to think my news was good?

Medea. You reported what you reported. I don't blame you.

Tutor. Then why are your eyes on the ground? Why are you crying?

Medea. I have to, old man. I have to. The gods and I, in my bad judgement, arranged all of this.

Tutor. Take heart. Your children will bring you home again some day too.

Medea. Before that I will bring others home. Down, into the ground. The misery of it.

Tutor. You are not the only woman who was ever parted from her children. When you are mortal you have to carry your troubles lightly.

Medea. I will. But go inside, and get the children what they need for the day.

Children, children. You two have a city now, and a house, where you will live for ever without me, leaving your wretched mother behind, robbed of her. And I am going to another country, an exile, before I have had any joy of you, before I have seen you happy, before I have dressed a bride for you and made the marriage bed beautiful and held up the wedding torch. Oh, my own stubborn will, and the misery it has brought me. So it was for nothing that I brought you up, children, for nothing that I laboured and was worn to shreds with work, and bore the hard pains of childbirth. There was a time, poor fool that I was, when I had great hopes of you: that you would look after me when I was old, and when I died you would wrap my body with your own hands, which is a thing people envy. Now that sweet thought is dead. Without you two I will drag out a life that is bitter and full of pain. And you will never see your mother again with those dear eyes. You are going away into another shape of life.

Oh. Oh. Why are you looking at me like that, children? Why are you smiling at me, that very last smile? Aiai. What am I going to do? My heart has gone out of me, women, now that I have seen my children's bright faces. I could not do it. Goodbye to the plans I made before. I will take my children out of the country with me. Why should I hurt their father through their suffering, and get myself twice as much suffering as he gets? No. Not I. Goodbye to my plans.

And yet, what is happening to me? Do I want to be laughed at, and let my enemies go unpunished? I have to have the nerve for this. What a coward I am, to let soft words into my heart at all. Go into the house, children. Anyone who has no right to be present at my sacrifice, let that be his own concern. I will not let my hand go weak.

Ah. Ah. No, my heart, don't. Don't you do this. Let them be, you poor thing. Spare the children. They will live there with us, and they will make you glad. No. By the avenging spirits down in Hades, there is no way, ever, that I will hand my children over to my enemies to be outraged. They have to die, whatever happens. And since they must, I will kill them, I who gave them birth. It is all done now, whatever happens, and she will not escape. The crown is on her head already; the royal bride is dying in the robe. I know it for certain.

But I am going down the most wretched road there is, and I am sending these two down one more wretched still, so I want to speak to my children. Give me, children, give your mother your right hand to kiss. Dearest hand, dearest mouth, and the shape of you, and the noble faces of my children. Be happy, both of you. But there, not here. Everything here your father has taken away. Oh, the sweetness of holding you, the soft skin, the sweet breath of my children. Go. Go in. I cannot look at you any longer. The evil is beating me. I know what evil I am about to do, but my anger is stronger than my plans, and anger is the cause of the greatest evils human beings suffer.

(The children go into the house. Medea stays where she is.)

Chorus.
	Often before now
	I have gone into finer arguments
	and taken on bigger questions
	than the female sex ought to look into.
	But we have a Muse of our own, too,
	who keeps us company for the sake of understanding.
	Not all of us. It is a small breed
	you would find among many women,
	but you might find it: women the Muse has not passed by.
	And I say this. Of all human beings,
	the ones who have never had children,
	who know nothing at all about it,
	are better off in happiness
	than the ones who are parents.
	The childless never had any, so they never learn
	whether children turn out a sweetness to people
	or a grief,
	and they are spared a great deal of hard work.
	But the ones who have in their house
	the sweet growth of children, I see them
	worn down with worry the whole time.
	First, how to bring them up well,
	and how to leave them enough to live on.
	And after all that, whether it is worthless children
	or good ones
	they have been working for, they cannot tell.
	And there is one evil more, the last of all,
	and I will name it now for every mortal.
	Say they have found enough to live on,
	and the children's bodies have come to their prime,
	and they have turned out good. Then, if their luck
	falls that way, Death is off to Hades,
	carrying the children's bodies away.
	So what is the good of it? Why, on top of everything else,
	should the gods throw this one grief, the bitterest of all,
	for the sake of children,
	on mortal men and women?

Medea. Friends, I have been waiting a long time for what happens next, watching for how things turn out over there. And now I see one of Jason's men coming. He is breathing hard, and that tells me he has some new evil to report.

(A messenger runs in from the palace, out of breath.)

Messenger. Medea. You have done a terrible thing, and a lawless one. Run. Run. Whatever will carry you, take it, a ship over the sea or a wagon over the plain.

Medea. And what has happened that deserves this running away?

Messenger. The princess is dead, just now, and Creon her father with her, killed by your poisons.

Medea. That is the most beautiful thing you could have said. From now on you count among my benefactors and my friends.

Messenger. What? Are you in your right mind, woman? Not mad? You have desecrated the king's hearth, and you are glad to hear it, and not afraid?

Medea. I have something to say to that too, an answer of my own. But don't rush, friend. Tell me. How did they die? You will give me twice the pleasure if they died horribly.

Messenger. When your two children came with their father and went into the bride's house, we were glad, we slaves who had suffered along with you in your troubles. At once the word went from ear to ear all through the house that you and your husband had made up your old quarrel. One of us kissed the children's hands, another their yellow hair, and I myself was so happy that I went along with the children into the women's rooms. Our mistress, the one we honour now in your place, had her eyes fixed eagerly on Jason, before she caught sight of your two boys. But then she covered her eyes and turned her white cheek away, disgusted that the children had come in. Your husband set about taking the girl's anger and her temper away, saying this: "You won't be unkind to people who love you, will you? Stop being angry and turn your head back this way. Count as your friends the people your husband counts. Take these gifts, and ask your father to let these boys off their exile, for my sake." And when she saw the finery, she couldn't hold out. She agreed to everything her husband asked, and before the father and the children were far from the house, she took the embroidered robe and put it on, and set the golden crown around her curls, and arranged her hair in a bright mirror, smiling at the lifeless image of her own body. Then she got up from her chair and walked through the rooms, stepping delicately on her white, white feet, overjoyed with the gifts, and over and over again she stretched out her leg and looked down at the line of her ankle.

But what came after that was a terrible thing to see. Her colour changed. She staggered back sideways, her legs shaking under her, and only just managed to fall into the chair instead of onto the floor. One of the servants, an old woman, thinking, I suppose, that a fit from Pan or some other god had come on her, raised the cry of prayer. Until she saw white foam coming out of the girl's mouth, and her eyes rolling back in their sockets, and no blood left in her skin. Then instead of that prayer she sent up a great shriek of grief. Straight away one servant ran for her father's house and another for the new husband, to tell him what had happened to his bride, and the whole house rang with feet running back and forth.

By the time a fast walker could have covered the length of a running track and been reaching the far end of it, the poor girl came to, out of her silence and her closed eyes, with a terrible groan. Two torments were attacking her at once. The golden band lying round her head let loose an astonishing stream of fire that ate everything, and the fine robe, your children's gift, was eating the poor girl's soft flesh. She got up from the chair and ran, on fire, shaking her hair and her head this way and that, trying to throw the crown off. But the gold held its fastenings tight, and every time she shook her hair the fire blazed twice as bright. She fell to the floor, beaten by the disaster, and nobody could have known her except her own father. You could not make out the set of her eyes any more, or her lovely face. Blood was dripping from the top of her head, mixed with fire, and the flesh was running off her bones under the invisible jaws of the poisons, the way resin drips from a pine. A terrible sight. And everyone was afraid to touch the body. What had happened had taught us that much.

Then her poor father, knowing nothing of what had happened, came suddenly into the room and fell on the corpse. He groaned at once, and wrapped his arms round her and kissed her, and said this to her: "My poor child. Which of the gods destroyed you like this, so shamefully? Who is making an old man, with one foot in the grave, an orphan, robbed of you? Oh. Let me die with you, child." When he had stopped his crying and his wailing and wanted to lift his old body up, he was stuck to the fine robe the way ivy sticks to the shoots of a laurel, and then there was a terrible wrestling. He wanted to get up on his knee, and she held him back. If he pulled hard, he tore his old flesh off his bones. In the end he gave out, and the poor man let his life go. He could not rise above the evil any longer. So they lie there dead, the daughter and the old father, side by side, a disaster that cries out for tears.

As for you, I leave your part out of my account. You will find out for yourself how to turn the punishment aside. Not for the first time, I think human life is a shadow. And I would say without fear that the people who pass for clever, the ones who work so hard on their words, are the ones found guilty of the greatest folly. No human being is happy. When wealth pours in, one man may be luckier than another. But happy? No.

Chorus. It looks as if the god is fastening a great many evils on Jason today, and fastening them with justice. Poor woman, daughter of Creon, how we pity your disaster, gone to the house of Hades because of your marriage to Jason.

Medea. Friends, the thing is decided. I will kill the children as fast as I can and leave this land. I will not delay and hand my children over to another hand to murder, a hand that hates them more. They have to die, whatever happens. And since they must, I will kill them, I who gave them birth. Come on, then, heart. Arm yourself. Why am I waiting to do the terrible thing that has to be done? Come, my wretched hand, take the sword. Take it. Go to the starting line of a life of grief. Do not turn coward. Do not remember the children, how much you love them, how you bore them. For this one short day forget your children, and grieve afterwards. Because even if you kill them, still, they were born your own dear ones. And I am an unlucky woman.

(Medea goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	Io, Earth, and you, ray of the Sun
	that lights everything, look down, look
	at this ruined woman before she lays
	a bloody hand on her children, her own.
	They grew from your golden seed,
	and for a god's blood to be spilled
	by human hands is a thing to fear.
	Light born of Zeus, hold her back,
	stop her, get her out of the house,
	this pitiful Fury of blood that the spirits of vengeance drive.
Chorus.
	The labour of your children has gone for nothing.
	Was it for nothing you bore your dear sons,
	you who left behind the dark Clashing Rocks,
	the Symplegades, the passage that welcomes no stranger?
	Wretched woman, why does this heavy anger
	fall on your mind, why is murder,
	hateful murder, taking the place of love?
	Pollution from the blood of your own kin
	is hard for human beings to bear on the earth. It brings
	griefs from the gods down on the killers' house, to match.
Children.
	Aiai.
Chorus.
	Do you hear the cry? Do you hear the children?
	Io, wretched, ill-starred woman.

(The children's voices come from inside the house, first one boy and then the other.)

Children. Oh. What do I do? Where can I run from my mother's hands?

I don't know, brother, dearest. We are being killed.

Chorus.
	Should I go into the house? I think
	I should keep the children from being murdered.

Children. Yes, by the gods, keep us from it. We need you now.

The net of the sword is closing on us already. We are that near.

Chorus.
	Wretched woman. Then you were stone,
	or iron, all along, to kill the children you bore,
	the crop of your own body, with a death dealt by your own hand.
Chorus.
	One, only one woman before this
	have I heard of who laid her hand on her own children:
	Ino, whom the gods drove mad, when the wife of Zeus
	sent her out of her house to wander.
	And the poor woman fell into the sea
	for the unholy murder of her children,
	stepping off the sea cliff over the water,
	and died there with her two sons.
	What is left that could be terrible now, after this?
	Oh, the marriage bed of women,
	how much pain it costs, how much evil it has done to people already.

(Jason comes in at a run.)

Jason. Women, standing near this house. Is she still inside, Medea, the one who did these terrible things, or has she run for it? She will have to hide under the earth or lift her body on wings into the depths of the sky, if she is not going to pay the royal house what she owes it. Does she think that after killing the rulers of this land she will get away from this house unpunished? But it is not her I am thinking of. It is the children. The ones she has hurt will hurt her back. I came to save my children's lives, in case the family of the dead does something to me, taking revenge for the unholy murder their mother did.

Chorus. Poor man. You do not know how far into evil you have come, Jason, or you would not have said that.

Jason. What is it? Does she want to kill me too?

Chorus. Your children are dead. Their mother's hand killed them.

Jason. Oh. What are you saying? You have destroyed me, woman.

Chorus. Your children no longer exist. Think of them that way now.

Jason. Where did she kill them? Inside the house, or outside?

Chorus. Open the doors, and you will see your children murdered.

Jason. Slaves, undo the bolts, quick as you can. Unfasten the bars. Let me see the double evil, the two dead, and her. I will make her pay for it.

(Medea appears above the house, in a chariot drawn by dragons. The bodies of the children are beside her.)

Medea. Why are you shaking the doors and prising at the bolts, hunting for the dead and for me, who did it? Save your effort. If you want something from me, say it, if you like. But your hand will never touch me. This chariot is what my father's father, the Sun, gives me: a wall against my enemies' hands.

Jason. You hateful thing. Woman most loathed by the gods, and by me, and by the whole human race. You had the nerve to drive a sword into your own children, you, their mother, and you have destroyed me, left me childless. And having done it, you look at the sun and the earth, after having the nerve to do the most unholy thing there is. Die. I am in my right mind now. I was not then, when I brought you out of your house and your barbarian country to a Greek home, a great evil, a traitor to your father and to the land that raised you. The gods have flung your avenging spirit at me. You had already killed your brother at the hearth when you stepped aboard the Argo with its lovely prow. That is how you began. Then you married me, and bore me children, and for the sake of a bed, of sex, you have destroyed them. There is not one Greek woman who would ever have had the nerve to do this, and I passed over every one of them to marry you, a marriage that was my enemy and my ruin: a lioness, not a woman, wilder by nature than the monster Scylla in the Tyrrhenian sea. But I could not bite you with ten thousand insults; that is how bold you are by nature. Go to hell, you filth, you murderer of your children. All that is left to me is to weep over my own fortune. I will get no joy of my new marriage bed, and the children I fathered and brought up I will never speak to alive again. I have lost them.

Medea. I would have made a long speech in answer to that, if Zeus the father did not already know what you had from me and what you did to me. You were not going to dishonour my bed and then live a pleasant life laughing at me. Nor was the princess. Nor was Creon, who arranged your marriage, going to throw me out of this land and get away with it. So call me a lioness if you like, and Scylla who lives on the Tyrrhenian shore. I have got my hands on your heart, the way I had to.

Jason. You are in pain too. You share the evil.

Medea. Be sure of it. But the pain is worth it, as long as you are not laughing.

Jason. Children, what an evil mother you got.

Medea. Boys, how your father's sickness destroyed you.

Jason. It was not my right hand that killed them.

Medea. No. Your outrage did, and your new marriage.

Jason. You thought a marriage bed a good enough reason to kill them?

Medea. Do you think that is a small hurt to a woman?

Jason. To a woman who keeps herself in hand, yes. To you everything is evil.

Medea. They no longer exist. That will bite you.

Jason. They exist. Oh, they exist, as avengers on your head.

Medea. The gods know who began this pain.

Jason. They know, yes. They know your disgusting mind.

Medea. Hate me. I loathe the bitter sound of your voice.

Jason. And I loathe yours. Parting is easy.

Medea. How, then? What do I do? I want it badly enough myself.

Jason. Let me bury these dead and weep over them.

Medea. No. I will bury them myself, with this hand. I will carry them to the sacred ground of Hera of the Heights, so that none of my enemies can outrage them by tearing up their graves. And on this land of Sisyphus, on Corinth, I will lay a solemn festival and rites for all time to come, to pay for this unholy murder. I myself am going to the land of Erechtheus, to Athens, to live with Aegeus, the son of Pandion. And you, as is only right, will die a coward's death, a bad man dying badly, your head struck by a piece of the wreck of the Argo, after you have seen the bitter end of your marriage to me.

Jason.
	May the children's Fury destroy you,
	and Justice that avenges blood.
Medea.
	What god or spirit listens to you,
	you who broke your oath and cheated the house that took you in?
Jason.
	Ah. Ah. Filthy woman. Child-killer.
Medea.
	Go home, and bury your wife.
Jason.
	I am going. Without either of my two sons.
Medea.
	You are not mourning yet. Wait until you are old.
Jason.
	Children, dearest children.
Medea.
	To their mother. Not to you.
Jason.
	And then you killed them?
Medea.
	Yes. To hurt you.
Jason.
	Oh. I want to kiss
	my children's dear mouths. The misery of it.
Medea.
	Now you talk to them, now you want to hold them.
	Then, you pushed them away.
Jason.
	By the gods, let me
	touch my children's soft skin.
Medea.
	No. Your words are thrown away on the wind.
Jason.
	Zeus, do you hear how I am driven off,
	what I am suffering from this filthy woman,
	this lioness who kills her children?
	But as far as I can, as far as I am allowed,
	I mourn them, and I call on the gods,
	I call them to witness that you killed
	my children and will not let me
	touch them with my hands or bury their bodies.
	I wish I had never fathered them
	to see them dead at your hands.

(The chariot rises and carries Medea away. Jason is left below.)

Chorus.
	Zeus on Olympus keeps the store of many things,
	and many the things they bring about that no one expected.
	What we counted on did not happen,
	and for what no one counted on, a god found a way.
	That is how this business ended.

The Children of Heracles (c. 430 BC)

The Children of Heracles

(Marathon, in the country of Athens, in front of the temple of Zeus. Iolaus, an old man, sits at the altar with the young sons of Heracles gathered around him.)

Iolaus. I made up my mind about this a long time ago. One kind of man is born fair to the people around him. Another kind has let his heart run loose after profit, and he is no use to his city and hard to deal with, and the only person he is any good to is himself. I know this. I did not learn it from talk. Out of respect, and because I honour the ties of blood, I gave up living quietly in Argos, which I could have done, and shared Heracles' labours instead, more of them than any other single man, while he was still among us. And now that he lives in the sky, I have his children here under my wings, and I keep them safe, when I need saving myself.

When their father left the earth, the first thing Eurystheus wanted was to kill us. But we got away. Our city is gone, but our lives were saved. And since then we have been on the run, wandering, driven over the border of one city after another. Because on top of everything else Eurystheus has done to us, he thought fit to add this outrage: wherever he heard we had settled, he sent heralds there, demanding us back and having us shut out of the country, holding out Argos to them, no small city to have as a friend or as an enemy, and his own good fortune along with it. And they look at me and see how little strength I have, and they see how small these children are, with no father, and they bow to the stronger side and shut us out of their land. And I share the children's exile with them, I share their bad luck with them, because I cannot bring myself to abandon them. I do not want anyone to be able to say, "Look. Now that the boys have no father, Iolaus, their own kinsman, did not stand up for them."

So, with no place left to us anywhere in Greece, we have come to Marathon and the country that goes with it, and we sit at the altars of the gods as suppliants, and ask them to help. Because they say two sons of Theseus live on the plains of this country, land that fell to them by lot out of the family of Pandion, and they are close kin to these children. That is why we have come this far, to the border of famous Athens. Two old people are the generals of this retreat. I fret over these boys here, and Alcmene, inside the temple, holds her son's daughters in her arms and keeps them safe, because we are ashamed to bring young unmarried girls near a crowd and stand them at an altar. And Hyllus and his brothers who are old enough are out looking for some walled place where we could make a home, if we are pushed out of this country by force.

Children, children, here, take hold of my robe. I can see a herald of Eurystheus coming towards us. He is the man who hunts us, the reason we are wanderers, shut out of every country on earth. You hateful thing. I hope you die, you and the man who sent you. Out of that same mouth you brought plenty of bad news to these children's noble father as well.

(The Herald comes in.)

Herald. I suppose you think you have found yourself a fine seat there, and arrived at a city that will fight on your side. You are a fool. There is not a man alive who will pick your useless strength over Eurystheus. Move. What is the point of all this effort? You have to get up and go to Argos, where the sentence waiting for you is death by stoning.

Iolaus. No, I will not. The god's altar will protect me, and so will the free ground we are standing on.

Herald. Do you want to give this hand of mine some work to do?

Iolaus. You will not take me by force. And you will not lay hands on these children and take them either.

Herald. You will find out. You were not much of a prophet about that, it seems.

(The Herald takes hold of the children and throws the old man to the ground.)

Iolaus. That will never happen while I am alive.

Herald. Out of the way. Whether you like it or not, I am taking these boys, because I count them as the property of Eurystheus, which is what they are.

Iolaus. You men who have lived in Athens so long, help us! We are suppliants of Zeus of the marketplace, and we are being dragged away by force, our wreaths defiled, a disgrace to your city and an insult to the gods.

(The Chorus, old men of Marathon, come hurrying in.)

Chorus. Ah. Ah. What is this shouting that has gone up beside the altar? What kind of trouble is it going to show us?

Chorus.
	Look at the old man, feeble, sprawled
	on the ground. Poor man.
	Who did this? Who threw you down so pitifully in the dirt?

Iolaus. This man, strangers. He shows your gods no respect, and he is dragging me by force from the steps of Zeus's altar.

Chorus.
	And where have you come from, old man, to the four towns
	that live here as one people? Have you put in
	from across the water with the oar that beats the sea,
	leaving the shore of Euboea behind?

Iolaus. I do not lead an islander's life, strangers. We have come to your country from Mycenae.

Chorus.
	And what name, old man,
	did the people of Mycenae call you by?

Iolaus. You know, I think, of the man who stood beside Heracles in battle, Iolaus. This body of mine is not unheard of.

Chorus.
	I know. I heard of you before now. But whose are these
	little boys you are carrying, holding them by the hand,
	still so young? Tell me.

Iolaus. These are the sons of Heracles, strangers. They have come as suppliants to you and to your city.

Chorus.
	What is it they want? Tell me. Is it a hearing
	with the city they are anxious to get?

Iolaus. Not to be handed over. Not to be torn from your gods by force and taken to Argos.

Herald. That will not satisfy your masters, though. They have rights over you, and they have found you here.

Chorus.
	It is right to respect the gods' suppliants, stranger,
	and not to make them leave the seats of the gods
	by force of your hand.
	Lady Justice will not put up with that.

Herald. Then send these people of Eurystheus's out of your country, and I will not use this hand on them at all.

Chorus.
	It is a godless thing for a city to let go
	of a suppliant's appeal, the plea of strangers.

Herald. It is a good thing, too, to keep your foot out of trouble, by taking the better piece of advice.

Chorus. Then you should have told the king of this land what you meant to do before you had the nerve to do it, instead of dragging strangers away from the gods by force, in a free country you ought to respect.

Herald. And who is the ruler of this land and this city?

Chorus. Demophon, son of Theseus, a good man's son.

Herald. Then it is with him that this argument really has to be fought out. Everything else has been said for nothing.

Chorus. And here he is himself, coming in a hurry, and Acamas his brother with him, to hear what is being said.

(Demophon and Acamas come in with attendants.)

Demophon. Since you got here before us, old as you are, running to help at this altar of Zeus ahead of younger men, tell me: what has happened to bring this crowd together?

Chorus. The sons of Heracles are sitting here as suppliants, my lord. They have put wreaths on the altar, as you can see. And with them is Iolaus, the man who stood faithfully at their father's side in battle.

Demophon. And why did that call for screaming?

Chorus. This man here. He was trying to drag them away from the altar by force, and he raised the shouting, and he knocked the old man's legs out from under him, so that I wept for pity.

Demophon. Well, he wears Greek clothes, and the cut of his robe is Greek, but this is the work of a barbarian's hand. Now it is your turn to speak, and no delay about it. What country's borders did you leave to get here?

Herald. I am an Argive. That is what you want to know. And I am willing to tell you what I have come for, and who sent me. Eurystheus, king of Mycenae, sends me here to bring these children back. And I have come, stranger, with plenty of justice on my side, for what I do and for what I say. I am an Argive myself, and it is Argives I am taking away, runaways from my own city, condemned to death by the laws there. We live in our own city and we have the right to pass sentences on our own people that hold good. They have come to the hearths of many other cities, and there we took our stand on these same arguments, and nobody had the nerve to bring trouble of his own making down on his own head.

So either they have spotted some foolishness in you and come here for it, or, out of sheer desperation, they are throwing the dice, whether it comes off or not. Because they surely do not expect that you, if you are in your right mind, alone in all the breadth of Greece they have travelled through, are going to pity their stupid troubles. Come on, then, weigh one thing against the other. Let them into your country, or let us take them out of it: what do you gain? Here is what you get from our side: the whole great hand of Argos, and the entire strength of Eurystheus, added to this city. But if you look at their speeches and their weeping and go soft, then this business is settled by a wrestling match of spears. Do not imagine we are going to give up this contest without cold steel.

So what will you say? What land have you been robbed of, what plunder taken off you, that you should go to war with the Argives? What allies are you defending? On whose behalf will you be burying your dead? You will get a bad name from your own citizens, if for the sake of an old man, a tomb, a nothing, to put it plainly, and these children, you wade into the bilge of a sinking ship. The best you can say is that you will find hope in them, only hope. And even that falls a long way short of what is needed now. These boys, once they are grown up, would make a poor showing in a fight against Argives under arms, if that is what raises your spirits. And there is a long stretch of time in between, in which you could be wiped out. No. Listen to me. Give me nothing. Just let me take what is mine, and you have Mycenae for a friend. And do not do the thing you Athenians love to do, taking the weaker side when you had the chance to choose the stronger as your friends.

Chorus. Who could judge a case, or understand an argument, before he has heard clearly what both sides have to say?

Iolaus. My lord, in your country I have this to begin with: I am allowed to speak and to be heard in turn, and no one will push me away before I have spoken, the way they did everywhere else. Between us and this man there is nothing in common. Since we have no share in Argos any more, since that was decided by vote and we are exiles from our own country, how can he justly take us away as Mycenaeans, when we are what we are, people they drove out of the land? We are foreigners. Or is your position that whoever is exiled from Argos is exiled from the whole of Greece? Not from Athens, at any rate. The Athenians will not drive the children of Heracles out of their country for fear of Argos. This is not Trachis, and it is not that town in Achaea, the places you drove these children from while they sat as suppliants at the altar. Not by any justice, but by puffing up Argos, exactly the way you are doing now. If that happens here, if they judge your arguments the winners, then I no longer know this Athens as a free city. But I know the spirit of these people, and their nature. They will be willing to die. Among decent men, shame is reckoned worse than death.

That is enough about the city. Too much praise is a thing people resent, and I know it myself, I have often felt the weight of being praised too much. But I want to explain to you why you are bound to save these children, since you are the one who stands at the head of this land. Pittheus was the son of Pelops. From Pittheus came Aethra, and from her your father Theseus was born. Now let me go back over these children's family for you. Heracles was the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and Alcmene was the daughter of Pelops' daughter. So your father and their father were the sons of first cousins. That is how you stand to them by blood, Demophon. But now I will tell you what you owe these children beyond what kinship demands. I say that I once sailed with their father, carrying his shield, when he went with Theseus after the Amazon queen's belt, the belt that cost so many lives. And he brought your father up out of the deep fortress of Hades. All Greece is witness to that.

In return for all this, they ask you for one favour: not to be handed over, not to be torn away from your gods by force and thrown out of the country. It would be shameful for you personally, and bad for the city, for suppliants, wanderers, your own kin, oh, look at them, look at them, to be dragged off by force. I beg you, I lay my suppliant wreath on you with my hands, I touch your beard: do not despise the children of Heracles now that you have them in your hands. Be a kinsman to them. Be their friend, their father, their brother, their master. Any one of those is better than falling into the hands of the Argives.

Chorus. Hearing what has happened to them, my lord, I pity them. Never have I seen noble birth beaten by fortune as plainly as now. These are the children of a great father, and they are suffering what they do not deserve.

Demophon. Three roads of reasoning force me, Iolaus, not to turn away these guests of yours. The greatest is Zeus. You are sitting at his altar with this flock of nestlings around you. Then there is the blood tie, and the old debt: these children have a claim on us, for their father's sake, to be treated well. And then there is the shame of it, and that is what I have to weigh most of all. If I let this altar be plundered by force, by a foreigner, then people will say the country I live in is not free, and that I handed suppliants over out of fear of Argos. That is near enough to hanging myself. I wish you had come here under a luckier star, but as it is, do not be afraid that anyone is going to tear you and these children away from this altar by force.

You. Go back to Argos and tell Eurystheus this, and tell him that if he has any charge against these strangers he will get justice. But you will never take them.

Herald. Not even if my case is just, and I win the argument?

Demophon. And how can it be just to take a suppliant by force?

Herald. Then the disgrace is mine, and no harm to you.

Demophon. Harm to me, if I let you drag them away.

Herald. Then you banish them, and we will take them from over the border.

Demophon. You are a fool by nature, thinking you know better than the god.

Herald. So it seems this is the place for criminals to run to.

Demophon. The seat of the gods is a shelter open to everyone.

Herald. The Mycenaeans may not see it that way.

Demophon. Am I not the master of what happens here?

Herald. As long as you do them no harm. If you have the sense to keep yourself in hand, you will not.

Demophon. Be harmed, then. I am not going to pollute the gods.

Herald. I do not want you at war with Argos.

Demophon. Neither do I. But I will not let go of these children.

Herald. All the same, I will take what is mine and go.

Demophon. Then you will not find it easy to get back to Argos.

Herald. I will try it and find out, right now.

Demophon. Touch them and you will be sorry, and not in a while, either. Now.

Chorus. By the gods, do not dare to strike a herald.

Demophon. I will, unless the herald learns to keep himself in hand.

Chorus. Go. And you, my lord, do not touch him.

Herald. I am going. One arm is a weak thing to fight with. But I will come back, and I will bring the whole bronze spearhead of Argive war with me. Ten thousand men with shields are waiting for me, and King Eurystheus himself in command. He is waiting on the borders of Megara, Alcathous's country, watching to see how things turn out here. When he hears of your outrage he will come down like a flash of light on you and on your citizens, on this land and on everything that grows in it. It would be a waste of all the young men we have in Argos if we did not punish you.

(The Herald turns and goes off the way he came.)

Demophon. Go to hell. I am not afraid of your Argos. You were never going to shame me and take these children out of here by force. This is not a city I hold as a subject of Argos. I hold it free.

Chorus.
	Now is the time to think ahead, before the Argive army
	comes near our borders.
	The war god of Mycenae is very sharp,
	and after this, sharper still than before.
	This is the way of every herald:
	to build what happened up to twice its size.
	What do you think he will tell his king,
	how terribly he suffered, how close he came
	to having the life scraped out of him?

Iolaus. There is no finer prize for children than this: to be born of a good and noble father, and to marry into good families. The man who gives in to desire and mixes his blood with the low-born, I have no praise for him. He leaves his children a disgrace for the sake of his own pleasure. Good birth stands up to misfortune better than bad birth does. Look at us. We fell to the very bottom of trouble, and we found friends and kinsmen here, the only people in the whole inhabited Greek world who stood up for these children.

Give them your right hands, children. Give them. And you, give yours to the boys, and come close to them. Children, we have put our friends to the test. If ever the day comes when you go home to your own country and live in your father's house and hold his honours, remember: these men are your saviours and your friends, always, and never lift a hostile spear against this land. Remember that for me. Count this city the dearest of all. They deserve your reverence. They took on themselves the enmity of a country as great as Argos and the whole Pelasgian people, for our sake, when they could see we were beggars and wanderers. And still they did not hand us over, and they did not drive us out of the land.

And I, alive and dead, when I die, will praise you loud and high, my friend, when I stand beside Theseus, and I will make him glad by telling him how well you took in the children of Heracles and protected them, how you are a nobleman all through Greece and keep your father's good name, and how, born of a great man, you have turned out no worse than your father. Very few can say that. Out of many men you might find one, perhaps, who is not worse than his father.

Chorus. This land has always wanted to help the helpless, where justice is on their side. That is why it has borne countless hardships for its friends, and now I see another struggle of that kind close at hand.

Demophon. You have spoken well, old man, and I promise you these children will turn out as you say. The favour will be remembered. I am going to call an assembly of the citizens and set them in order, so that I meet the Mycenaean army with a strong force. First I will send scouts out to meet it, so it does not fall on me unawares; every man in Argos is quick to answer a call to arms. And I will gather the prophets and make sacrifice. You go into the house with the children, and leave the altar of Zeus. There are people who will look after you, even if I am away. Go into the house, old man.

Iolaus. I will not leave the altar. Let us sit here as suppliants and wait, and pray the city does well. When you have come through this struggle with honour, we will go to the house. The gods on our side are no weaker than the Argives', my lord. Hera, the wife of Zeus, stands at the head of theirs. Athena stands at the head of ours. And I say that this too counts towards success, to have the better gods. Pallas Athena will not stand being beaten.

(Demophon and Acamas go off towards the city.)

Chorus.
	Boast as loudly as you like, there are others
	who care no more for you for it,
	stranger come from Argos.
	Your big talk will not
	frighten my heart.
	May it never come to that for great Athens,
	the city of beautiful dances.
	You are a fool, and so is the son of Sthenelus,
	the king in Argos,
Chorus.
	who comes into another city,
	one no smaller than Argos,
	and drags off suppliants of the gods, wanderers
	who are begging my land for help,
	a stranger using force,
	not giving way to our kings,
	not making one just argument.
	How could that look right
	to anyone with sense?
Chorus.
	Peace is what I like myself.
	But I tell you, wrong-headed king,
	if you come to my city,
	you will not get what you expect
	as easily as that. You are not the only one
	with a spear and a bronze-plated shield.
	No. You who love war,
	do not stir up with your spear
	this city that the Graces have blessed.
	Hold yourself back.

(Demophon comes back alone, with a troubled face.)

Iolaus. My boy, why have you come back with that worried look in your eyes? Is there news of the enemy? Are they on their way? Are they here? What have you heard? You are not going to tell me the herald lied. Their general has had good luck from the gods so far, and he will come against Athens, I know it, and with no small opinion of himself, either. But Zeus punishes the thoughts of people who think too much of themselves.

Demophon. The Argive army is here, and King Eurystheus with it. I saw him with my own eyes. A man who claims to know how to be a general should not look at the enemy through messengers. He has not sent his army down onto the plains of this country yet. He is sitting on a rocky ridge, looking things over, and, I am only telling you what I think, deciding which way to bring his army in without a fight, and where in this country he can pitch camp safely. As for my side, everything is already well in hand. The city is under arms, and the victims stand ready for the gods who are owed them, to turn the enemy back and save the city, and the prophets are filling the town with sacrifice.

I gathered every singer of oracles into one place and questioned them, and I went through the old prophecies, the public ones and the secret ones, the ones that keep this land safe. And the oracles differ from each other on many points, but on one thing they all say the same, and it stands out: they tell me to sacrifice a virgin to Persephone, Demeter's daughter, a girl whose father is of noble blood. Now, you can see how much goodwill I have towards you. But I will not kill my own child, and I will not force any citizen of mine to do it against his will. And who would be willing? Who is so far gone in his wits that he would hand over the children he loves most out of his own hands? Already you could see bitter meetings in the streets, some saying it was right to help strangers who are suppliants, others accusing me of folly. And if I actually do this thing, it is civil war, there and then.

So look at this yourself, and help me find a way for you to be saved, and this country too, without my being slandered before my citizens. I do not hold a tyrant's power, the way barbarians do. If I do what is just, I will be treated justly.

Chorus. Can it be that the god will not let this city help strangers, when it is eager to and wants to?

Iolaus. Children, we are like sailors who escaped the wild rage of a storm and came close enough to touch the land with their hands, and then were driven off the shore by the winds and back out to sea. That is how we are being pushed away from this country, when we were already at the shore and thought we were saved. Oh. Why did you make me so glad, then, hope, you wretched thing, when you never meant to finish the favour you started? I can forgive this man. He does not want to kill his own citizens' children. And I can find good things to say about how we were treated here. If this is what the gods want to happen to me, the thanks I owe you is not wiped out.

Children, I do not know what to do with you. Where can we turn? What god's altar have we not wreathed? What walled town have we not come to? We are finished, children. We are going to be handed over. For myself, I do not care whether I have to die, except that in dying I might please my enemies. But I weep for you, children, and I pity you, and your father's old mother Alcmene. Poor woman, for that long life of yours. And poor me, all the labour I have done for nothing. So it was our fate, after all, to fall into an enemy's hands and lose our lives in shame and misery.

But wait. Do you know how you can help me? All hope of saving these children has not left me yet. Hand me over to the Argives instead of them, my lord. Run no risk yourself, and let my children be saved. I have no business loving my own life. Let it go. Eurystheus would like nothing better than to get his hands on me, Heracles' comrade in arms, and outrage me. The man is a brute. A wise man should pray to have a wise man for his enemy, not a proud fool. From a wise enemy you would get plenty of respect, and justice.

Chorus. Old man, do not blame this city. It might be a lie, but it would still do us harm, the reproach that we betrayed strangers.

Demophon. That was nobly said, but it cannot be done. It is not for you that the king is marching his army here. What good is a dead old man to Eurystheus? It is these children he wants to kill. To an enemy, the young of a noble house are a danger as they grow up: young men, and remembering the outrages done to their father. He has to look ahead to all of that. But if you know of any other plan that fits the moment better, have it ready, because I am at a loss since I heard those oracles, and full of fear.

(Macaria, the eldest daughter of Heracles, comes out of the temple.)

Macaria. Strangers, do not put my coming out here down to boldness. That is the first thing I will ask of you. For a woman, silence and keeping herself in hand are the finest things, and staying quietly inside the house. But I heard your groaning, Iolaus, and I came out. Not because I have been appointed to take the lead in the family. But I am fit for it in a way, and my brothers matter to me more than anything, and about them and about myself I want to know: has some new pain been added to the old troubles, and is it eating at your heart?

Iolaus. My girl, it is nothing new for me to praise you, and justly, above all the children of Heracles. Our course seemed to be running well, and now it has swung back again to where there is no way out. This man says the singers of oracles are telling him to slaughter, not a bull or a calf, but a virgin of noble blood, to Demeter's daughter, if we are to live, and this city is to stand. That is what we have no answer to. He says he will not slaughter his own children, or anyone else's. And to me he says, not in so many words, but he says it all the same, that unless we find some way out of this we must go and find ourselves another country, because he wants to save this one.

Macaria. Is that the condition our safety hangs on? That one thing?

Iolaus. That is it. In everything else we have done well.

Macaria. Then stop being afraid of the enemy's Argive spear. I myself, before anyone orders me, old man, am ready to die and to stand at the altar for the knife. What are we going to say, if this city thinks it right to run a great risk for our sake, and we, who could save them, put our troubles onto other people's shoulders and run away from dying? No. It would be a joke, wouldn't it, to sit as suppliants of the gods and groan, and then, born of the father we were born of, to be seen to be cowards. Where among decent people does that look right? Better, I think, if this city were taken, and may that never happen, and I fell into the enemy's hands, and then, my noble father's daughter, suffered what I would suffer and looked on Hades all the same. Or shall I be thrown out of this country and wander? And will I not be ashamed when somebody says, "Why have you come here with your suppliant branches, when you love your own lives so much? Get out of the country. We do not help cowards."

And even if these boys died and I alone were saved, I have no hope of doing well. Many people before now have betrayed their friends in that hope. Who would want to take a girl with no family as his wife, or to have children by me? Is it not better to die than to meet with that, which I do not deserve? That might suit some other girl better, one who is not as marked out as I am.

Lead me to where this body has to die. Put the wreaths on me and begin the rite, if that is what you decide. And beat your enemies. This life is here for you, freely given and not under compulsion. I declare it: I will die for these brothers of mine and for myself. Because by not loving my life too much I have found the finest thing there is to find, a way to leave it with honour.

Chorus. Ah, ah. What am I to say, hearing this great speech from a girl who is willing to die before her brothers do? Who could speak more nobly than this? What human being could do more?

Iolaus. My child, your head comes from nowhere else. You are the seed of that godlike spirit. You are Heracles' own. I am not ashamed of your words. It is your fate that hurts me. But let me say how it could be done more fairly. All this girl's sisters should be called out here, and then the one who draws the lot should die for the family. It is not just for you to die without a lot being drawn.

Macaria. I will not die by the luck of a lot. There is no grace in that. Do not say it, old man. If you will accept me, and if you want to make use of my willingness, then I give my life for these children freely. Not because I was forced.

Iolaus. Ah. This speech of yours is nobler than the last, and the last was the best I ever heard. You outdo daring with daring, and one good speech with another. I am not ordering you to die, child, and I am not forbidding it. But your brothers are helped by your dying.

Macaria. That is a clever way to order it. Do not be afraid that you will share in the pollution of my death. Let me die free. Come with me, old man. I want to die in your arms. Be there, and cover my body with your robe. Because I am going to the horror of the knife, if I really am the daughter of the father I claim.

Iolaus. I could not stand by and watch you die.
