Macaria. Then at least ask this of the king for me: that I breathe out my life in women's hands, not men's.

Demophon. It will be so, poor girl. It would be a disgrace to me too if you were not honoured properly, for many reasons: for your courage, and because it is just. You are the bravest woman my eyes have ever seen. Now, if you have anything to say, go and speak to these children and to the old man. Your last words.

Macaria. Goodbye, old man, goodbye. And teach these boys for me to be like you, clever in everything. No more than that. That will be enough for them. And try to keep them from dying, as eagerly as you are doing now. We are your children. Your hands brought us up. You can see how I am giving up my own wedding day and dying in their place. And you, my brothers, all of you here with me now, be happy. And may everything come to you that my heart is going to be cut open for. Honour this old man, and the old woman inside the house, Alcmene, my father's mother, and these strangers. And if the gods ever find you a release from your troubles and a way home, remember to give the woman who saved you the burial she is owed. The finest you can give would be only fair. I did not fail you. I stood by you, and I died for the family. That is my treasure to keep, in place of children, in place of my girlhood, if there is anything at all under the earth. I hope there is nothing. Because if we who are about to die are going to have cares there too, I do not know where a person could turn. Death is supposed to be the greatest cure there is for evil.

Iolaus. You stand out above all women for courage. Know this: living, you will be the most honoured of all to us, and dead, far more. Goodbye. I shrink from saying an ill word against the goddess your body has been consecrated to, Demeter's daughter. Children, we are finished. My limbs are coming loose with grief. Take hold of me and set me down on the seat, right here, and cover me with these robes, children. I take no pleasure in what has been done, and if the oracle is not carried out, there is no living either. The ruin would be greater. But this too is a disaster.

Chorus.
	No man, I say, is blessed without the gods,
	and no man is crushed by fate without them either.
	And no house walks forever
	on the road of good fortune. One fate after another
	comes hunting it down.
	One man it brings down from a height to a small place;
	the wanderer it makes prosperous.
	What is fated, no one is allowed to escape.
	No one will push it away by being clever,
	and the man who keeps on trying will only
	have the labour of it, forever, for nothing.
Chorus.
	So do not throw yourself down. Carry what the gods send,
	and do not let grief wear your mind past bearing.
	The poor girl has a death that is honoured,
	dying for her brothers and for this land,
	and the name she has
	among people will not be one without glory.
	Courage walks through hardship.
	What she has done is worthy of her father,
	worthy of her noble birth. And if you honour
	the deaths of the good, I share that with you.

(A servant of Hyllus comes in and finds the old man on the ground with his cloak over his face.)

Servant. Children, good day to you. Where is old Iolaus? And your father's mother, why has she left her place at this altar?

Iolaus. I am here. Such as my being here amounts to.

Servant. Why are you lying there? Why is your face down like that?

Iolaus. A grief came, one of the family's own, and it has hold of me.

Servant. Then lift yourself up. Get your head up.

Iolaus. I am old. There is no strength left in me at all.

Servant. Well, I have come bringing you a great piece of joy.

Iolaus. Who are you? Where did I meet you? I do not remember.

Servant. I am one of Hyllus's serfs. You are looking right at me and do not know me?

Iolaus. Dearest man. Have you come to save the two of us from harm, then?

Servant. I have. And more than that: things are going well for you now.

Iolaus. Mother of a noble son, Alcmene, I am calling you: come out, and hear the best words you could hear from this man. You have been in labour a long time over the people who have come, wasting your heart away over whether they would ever get here.

(Alcmene comes out of the temple.)

Alcmene. What is this shouting? The whole house is full of it. Iolaus, is there another herald here from Argos, using force on you? My strength is feeble, but there is one thing you should know, stranger: you will never take these children while I am alive. If you do, let nobody count me his mother any more. And if you lay a hand on them, you will have a fight on your hands with two old people, and it will not do you any credit.

Iolaus. Courage, old woman, do not be frightened. It is not a herald with hostile words from Argos.

Alcmene. Then why did you raise a shout? A shout is a messenger of fear.

Iolaus. For you. So that you would come out here in front of the temple.

Alcmene. I do not understand any of this. Who is this man?

Iolaus. He brings news that your son's son has come.

Alcmene. Then good day to you too, for that news. But if he has set foot in this country, where is he now? Why is he not here? What has happened to keep him from appearing here with you and gladdening my heart?

Servant. He is settling the army he brought with him, and setting it in order.

Alcmene. Then that is a matter that no longer concerns us.

Iolaus. It concerns us. And it is my job to find out about it.

Servant. What is it you want to know about what has been done, then?

Iolaus. How large a force of allies has he brought with him?

Servant. A lot of men. I cannot give you a number beyond that.

Iolaus. The Athenian commanders know this, I suppose?

Servant. They know. And their left wing is already in position.

Iolaus. So the army is already armed and ready for action?

Servant. Yes. And the animals for the sacrifice have already been brought up, a little way off from the ranks.

Iolaus. And how far away is the Argive army?

Servant. Close enough for their general to be seen plainly.

Iolaus. Doing what? Marshalling the enemy's lines?

Servant. That was our guess. We could not hear. But I am going. I would not want my masters going into battle without me, whatever my part in it is worth.

Iolaus. And I am coming with you. We think alike, it seems: stand by your friends and help them.

Servant. Of all people, you are the last who should be talking nonsense.

Iolaus. And the last who should stay out of a hard fight when my friends are in it.

Servant. Looks do not wound anyone. Only a hand that does something.

Iolaus. What? Could I not put a spear through a shield, even now?

Servant. You could. But you would fall first yourself.

Iolaus. Not one of the enemy will be able to look me in the face.

Servant. My friend, the strength you once had is not there any more.

Iolaus. Well, at any rate they will have one more man to fight.

Servant. It is a small weight you are adding to your friends' side of the scale.

Iolaus. Do not hold me back. I am ready to act.

Servant. Act, you cannot. Want to, perhaps.

Iolaus. Say anything else you like to me, but not that I am staying here.

Servant. Then how will you show yourself to the soldiers with no armour?

Iolaus. There are captured arms inside this temple. I will use those, and if I live I will give them back. If I die, the god will not ask for them. Go inside, take a full set of armour down off the pegs and bring it out to me as fast as you can. This is a shameful way to keep house: some men fighting, and others hanging back out of cowardice.

(The Servant goes into the temple.)

Chorus.
	Time has not flattened your spirit yet.
	That is still young. It is your body that is gone.
	Why work for nothing at what will hurt you
	and do our city very little good?
	At your age you should know when you are beaten
	and let go of what cannot be done. There is no way
	you will get your youth back again.
Alcmene.
	What are you doing? Have you lost your mind,
	to leave me here alone with my children?

Iolaus. Fighting is men's work. Your job is to look after them.

Alcmene. And what if you are killed? How am I to be kept safe?

Iolaus. Your son's sons, the ones who are left, will look after you.

Alcmene. And if something happens to them, which the gods forbid?

Iolaus. These strangers will not give you up. Do not be afraid.

Alcmene. That is all the courage I have. I have nothing else.

Iolaus. Zeus cares about your troubles too, I know it.

Alcmene. Ah. Zeus will hear no bad word from me. But whether he has dealt righteously with me, he knows himself.

(The Servant comes back out with a full set of armour.)

Servant. Here is your full suit of armour, you can see it. Now hurry and get your body inside it. The fight is close, and Ares hates a man who dawdles more than anything. But if you are afraid of the weight, walk there without it for now, and put this gear on when you are in the ranks. I will carry it in the meantime.

Iolaus. Good idea. Carry the armour and keep it ready to my hand. Put the spear in my grip, and take my left arm to steady me, and guide my feet.

Servant. So I am to lead a soldier about like a child?

Iolaus. For the omen's sake, we must get there without a stumble.

Servant. If only you could do as much as you want to.

Iolaus. Hurry. If I miss the battle it will be terrible for me.

Servant. You are the one who is slow, not me. You just think you are doing something.

Iolaus. Can you not see how my legs are hurrying?

Servant. I see you thinking you are hurrying. That is not the same thing.

Iolaus. You will not say that when you see me there.

Servant. Doing what? Well, I hope it is winning, whatever it is.

Iolaus. Hitting one of the enemy straight through his shield.

Servant. If we ever get there. That is what worries me.

Iolaus. Ah. Arm of mine. If only you could be the ally to me now that I remember you being in your youth, when you sacked Sparta at the side of Heracles. What a rout I would make of Eurystheus. He is too much of a coward to stand and face a spear. There is this, too, that is wrong with prosperity: it gets a man a reputation for courage. We think that someone who is doing well must know how to do everything.

(Iolaus goes off toward the battle, leaning on the Servant.)

Chorus.
	Earth, and moon that shines all night,
	and brightest rays of the god
	that bring the light to mortals,
	carry the news to me.
	Shout it to the sky,
	and beside the throne of our ruler,
	and in the house of grey-eyed Athena.
	For my fatherland,
	for my home, because I took in
	people who came begging, I am about to cut
	through the danger with grey iron.
Chorus.
	It is a fearful thing that a city
	as prosperous as Mycenae, so much praised
	for the strength of its spear,
	should hide its anger against my land.
	But it would be a wrong, my city,
	to hand over strangers who came begging
	because Argos ordered it.
	Zeus fights on my side. I am not afraid.
	Zeus is grateful to me, and rightly.
	Never, because of me, will the gods
	be shown weaker than mortals.
Chorus.
	Lady, this ground is yours,
	and the city is yours, and you are its mother,
	its mistress and its guard,
	so turn him away down some other road,
	the man who is wrongly leading an army
	of shaking spears here from Argos. After what I have done,
	I do not deserve to be thrown out of my house.
Chorus.
	For you are honoured, always, with many sacrifices,
	and the waning day of the month is never forgotten,
	nor the songs of the young men, nor the music of the dancers.
	On the windy hill
	the cries of joy ring out all night
	to the beat of girls' feet.

(The Servant comes back.)

Servant. Mistress, I bring you a report. It is very short for you to hear, and for me, standing here, it is the finest news there is. We have beaten the enemy, and trophies are being set up with the full armour of your enemies hung on them.

Alcmene. Dearest man. This day has brought you your freedom, for that news. But there is one trouble you have not set me free from yet. I am afraid: are the people I want alive, alive?

Servant. They are alive, and covered in glory throughout the army.

Alcmene. And the old man, Iolaus. Is he alive too?

Servant. Very much so. And the gods have done the finest thing of all for him.

Alcmene. What is it? Did he do something brave in the fight?

Servant. He has turned from an old man back into a young one.

Alcmene. That is an astonishing thing to say. But first I want you to tell me about the battle, and how our friends won it.

Servant. One speech of mine will make all of it plain to you.

When we had stretched out our lines of armed men face to face with theirs, Hyllus stepped down from his four-horse chariot and stood in the middle, in the ground between the two armies, and he said: "General, you who have come from Argos, why do we not leave this land alone? You will do Mycenae no harm by losing it one man. Fight me, one man against one. If you kill me, take the children of Heracles and go. If you die, leave me my father's honours and my father's house." The army roared its approval: that was well said, as a way out of the trouble and as a piece of courage too. But he, with no shame in front of the people who had heard the challenge, and none at his own cowardice, and he the general, did not have the nerve to come anywhere near a good spear. He was a coward, plain and simple. And that is the sort of man who had come to make slaves of Heracles's children.

So Hyllus went back to his place in the line. And the prophets, when they saw there would be no settlement by single combat, shield against shield, did not wait: they cut the victims' throats and let the blood that promised good luck run straight from a human throat. Then some were climbing into chariots, and others were tucking flank against flank under the shelter of their shields. And the king of the Athenians gave his army the order a well-born man ought to give: "Fellow citizens, the land that feeds you and the land that bore you needs every man's help today." And the other one, for his part, was begging his allies not to let Argos and Mycenae be shamed. Then the signal went up, shrill, on the Etruscan trumpet, and they came together in battle, and how loud a crash of shields do you think there was, how much groaning and screaming all at once? At first the surge of the Argive spears broke us. Then they gave way in their turn. In the second round it was foot planted against foot, man standing against man, and the battle held hard, and many were falling. And the shouts went up: "Men of Athens!" and "You who sow the fields of Argos! Will you not keep disgrace off your city?" And by doing everything, and not without hard work, we finally turned the Argive spear to flight.

At that point the old man, Iolaus, saw Hyllus charging out, and he held out his right hand and begged him to take him up into his chariot. He took the reins in his hands and went after Eurystheus's horses. From here on I can tell you what I heard from others; up to here I saw it myself. As he was crossing the sacred hill of Pallene, which belongs to Athena, he saw Eurystheus's chariot, and he prayed to Hebe and to Zeus to let him be young for one single day and make his enemies pay. Now here is a marvel for you to hear. Two stars settled on the yoke of the horses and hid the chariot in a dark cloud. Your son and Hebe, the cleverer people say. And out of that murky darkness he showed the shape of a young man, with young arms. And the famous Iolaus caught Eurystheus's four-horse chariot at the Scironian rocks, and bound his hands in chains, and is coming here bringing the general who was so prosperous before, as the finest first-fruits of the battle. And with what has happened to him now he announces plainly, for every mortal to learn: do not envy the man who seems to be doing well until you have seen him dead. Fortune lasts a day.

Chorus. Zeus, who turns the battle, now I can look on a day that is free of terrible fear.

Alcmene. Zeus, you took your time to look at my troubles, but I thank you all the same for what has been done. And my son: I did not believe before that he lived among the gods. Now I know it for certain. Children, now, now at last you will be free of your troubles, free of Eurystheus, who is going to die a bad death. You will see your father's city, and walk onto the land that is yours by lot, and sacrifice to your fathers' gods, which you were shut out from, living the miserable life of wanderers in foreign places. But tell me: what clever plan was Iolaus keeping to himself when he spared Eurystheus and did not kill him? Tell me. Because the way we see it, that is not clever, to take your enemies and not make them pay.

Servant. He was thinking of you: so that you could see him with your own eyes, beaten and under your hand. Not that Eurystheus came willingly. He yoked him by force, whether he liked it or not, because he did not want to come alive into your sight and pay the penalty. But goodbye, old lady, and remember what you said to me first, when I was beginning my story: that you would set me free. In matters like this, the mouth of the well-born should tell no lies.

(The Servant goes off to rejoin the army.)

Chorus.
	Dancing is sweet to me, when the clear grace
	of the pipe is at the feast,
	and may Aphrodite be there, with her grace.
	And it is a sweet thing, too, to see
	friends doing well
	who never expected to before.
	For Fate, who brings things to pass,
	and the long years, the children of Time,
	give birth to a great deal.
Chorus.
	You have a road that is just, my city,
	and you must never let go of it:
	honouring the gods. Anyone who says you do not
	is driving close to madness,
	with proof like this on show.
	For the god gives clear notice:
	he strips the unjust
	of their pride, always.
Chorus.
	Your son is in heaven, old woman.
	He has gone there. He escapes the story
	that he went down to the house of Hades,
	his body eaten by the terrible flame of the fire.
	He has Hebe's lovely bed
	in the golden court.
	Hymen, god of weddings, you have honoured
	two children of Zeus.
Chorus.
	Many things fall in with many others.
	They say Athena stood by the father
	of these children, and now the goddess's city
	and the goddess's people have saved them too,
	and checked the outrage of a man
	whose temper put violence before justice.
	May my heart never be like that,
	may my spirit never want more than it has.

(Eurystheus is brought in, bound and guarded. The Servant is with him.)

Servant. Mistress, you can see for yourself, but I will say it anyway: we have come bringing Eurystheus here to you, a sight you never hoped for, and a turn of fortune he never expected either. He never imagined he would fall into your hands when he marched out of Mycenae with his long-suffering shield-men, thinking himself too big for justice, to sack the city of Athena. But a god set things the other way round and turned his fortune upside down. Hyllus and brave Iolaus were setting up a statue of Zeus who turns the battle, for a glorious victory, and they sent me to bring this man to you, wanting to gladden your heart. It is the sweetest thing there is: to see an enemy who was prosperous fall into misery.

Alcmene. You. Hateful thing. Have you come? Has Justice caught you at last? First, turn your head this way to me, and bear to look your enemies in the face. You are the one who is ruled now, not the ruler. Are you the man, I want to know, who thought it right to heap so many outrages on my son, wherever he is now, you villain? What outrage did you not have the nerve to put on him? You sent him down alive into Hades. You sent him out with orders to kill hydras and lions. The other evils you devised I pass over; it would make a long story. And it was not enough for you to have dared that much: no, you drove me and the children out of the whole of Greece, when we were sitting as suppliants of the gods, some of us old, some still babies. But here you found men, and a free city, who were not afraid of you. You have to die, and die badly, and even then you come out ahead every way: you ought not to die just once, after all the suffering you have caused.

Chorus. It is not possible for you to kill this man.

Servant. Then we took him prisoner for nothing?

Alcmene. What law is there that stops this man from dying?

Chorus. The rulers of this land do not approve of it.

Alcmene. What does that mean? They do not think it right to kill enemies?

Chorus. Not one they have taken alive in battle.

Alcmene. And Hyllus put up with a decision like that?

Chorus. He should have disobeyed this land, I suppose?

Alcmene. This man should not be alive, or looking at the light any more.

Chorus. The first wrong done to him was that he did not die then.

Alcmene. So is it no longer the right moment for him to pay the penalty?

Chorus. There is no one who would kill him.

Alcmene. I would. And I count myself as someone, too.

Chorus. You will get a great deal of blame if you do it.

Alcmene. I love this city; there is no arguing with that. But this man, now that he has come into my hands, there is no mortal alive who will take him out of them. Let anyone who likes call me the bold woman, the one who thinks bigger than a woman should. This piece of work will be done by me.

Chorus. Your quarrel with this man is a terrible one, lady, and it is forgivable. I understand that well.

Eurystheus. Woman, understand this clearly: I am not going to flatter you, or say anything else to save my life that would earn a man the name of coward. I did not take up this quarrel by my own choice. I knew I was your cousin, and a blood relation of your son Heracles. But whether I wanted it or not, and she is a god, Hera made me sick with this sickness. And once I had taken up hostility against him, and knew that this was the contest I was going to have to fight, I became an expert in troubles. I sat up with the night and gave birth to plan after plan, for pushing my enemies aside and killing them, so that I would not have to live with fear for the rest of my life. Because I knew your son was not a mere number: he was a real man. Enemy or not, he will hear good things from me, because he was a good man.

And once he was gone, hated as I was by these children, and knowing the feud I had inherited from my father, was I not forced to move every stone, killing, banishing, plotting? As long as I did that, my position was safe. And you: if you had taken over my fortunes, would you not have hounded the hostile lion's cubs, that bad brood, with every evil you could? Would you have kept yourself in hand and let them live in Argos? You will not convince anyone of that. So now, since they did not destroy me then, when I was ready to die, by the laws of the Greeks my death is a pollution on the man who kills me. The city let me go, and kept itself in hand when it did: it honours the god far more than its hatred of me. You have spoken; you have had your answer. From here on you will have to call me two things: the avenging ghost, and the man of honour. That is how it stands with me. I do not want to die. But if I leave my life behind, I will not mind at all.

Chorus. I want to give you a small piece of advice, Alcmene. Let this man go. It is what the city wants.

Alcmene. And what if he dies, and we obey the city too?

Chorus. That would be best of all. But how could that happen?

Alcmene. I will teach you, easily. I will kill him, and then I will give the body to whichever of his friends come for it. As far as his body goes, I will not disobey this land. But he will pay me the penalty by dying.

Eurystheus. Kill me. I am not begging you. But this city, since it let me go and was too decent to kill me, I will give a present: an old oracle of Apollo, which will do it more good in time than you would think. When I am dead, you will bury me where it is fated, in front of the temple of the divine virgin at Pallene. And I will lie under the ground there forever, a foreigner settled among you, kind to you and a protection to the city, and the deadliest enemy of these children's descendants when they come here with a great army, betraying this kindness you have done them. That is the kind of strangers you have stood up for. Then why did I come here, if I knew all this, instead of respecting the god's oracle? Because I thought Hera was far stronger than any prophecy, and would not give me up. But do not let them pour drink offerings on my grave, or let blood drip on the place where I lie. I will give them a bad homecoming in return for all this. And you will have a double profit from me: by dying I will help you and I will hurt them.

Alcmene. Then what are you waiting for, when you have heard this, if you have to make the city safe, and our children after us? Kill the man. He is showing you the safest road himself. He is an enemy, and dead he is useful. Take him away, slaves. Then kill him and throw him to the dogs. Do not hope that you will live to throw me out of my father's land again.

(Eurystheus is led away.)

Half-Chorus.
	I think the same. Go, attendants.
	Nothing that comes from us
	will leave a stain on our kings.

Hippolytus (428 BC)

Hippolytus

(Trozen, in front of the house of Theseus. A statue of Aphrodite stands on one side of the door and a statue of Artemis on the other. Aphrodite appears.)

Aphrodite. I am a great power among mortals, and not a nameless one. My name is Cypris, the goddess of Cyprus: Aphrodite. In heaven, too. And of all the people who live between the Black Sea and the bounds of Atlas in the far west and look at the light of the sun, the ones who respect my power I put first, and the ones who think themselves too big for me I trip up. Because gods are like this too: we enjoy being honoured by human beings. And I will show you how true that is, and soon.

The son of Theseus, the boy the Amazon bore him, Hippolytus, whom holy Pittheus brought up, is the only person in this land of Trozen who says I am the vilest of all the gods. He refuses the bed. He will have nothing to do with marriage. It is Artemis he honours, the sister of Apollo, the daughter of Zeus. He counts her the greatest of the gods, and he is always with the virgin in the green woods, clearing the land of wild animals with his fast hounds, keeping company that is too high for a mortal. I do not begrudge him that. Why should I? But for the wrong he has done me, I will punish Hippolytus this very day. I cleared most of the ground a long time ago. It will not take much work.

Once, he came from Pittheus's house to the land of Pandion, to Athens, to see the holy mysteries and be initiated, and his father's noble wife saw him. Phaedra. And her heart was seized with a terrible love. That was my plan. And before she ever came to this land of Trozen, she built a temple to Cypris right beside the rock of Pallas, on the Acropolis, where it looks out over this country, because she was in love with someone who lived across the water. She named the temple after Hippolytus, and people will say for ever that the goddess was set up there for him. Then Theseus left the land of Cecrops, to escape the pollution of the blood of the sons of Pallas, whom he had killed, and sailed here to this country with his wife, accepting a year's exile from home. And here she is, groaning, struck to the heart by the goads of love, the poor woman, dying, and in silence. Not one of the household knows what her sickness is.

But this love is not going to end that way. I will reveal the matter to Theseus, and it will all come out. And the young man who is my enemy will be killed by his father, with curses. The lord of the sea, Poseidon, gave Theseus a gift: three prayers to the god that would never go to waste. As for Phaedra, she keeps her good name, but she dies all the same. I will not rate her suffering so high that I let my enemies off paying me a penalty big enough to satisfy me.

But here is the son of Theseus coming now, Hippolytus, back from the hard work of the hunt, so I will leave this place. A loud crowd of his men is coming behind him, shouting out, singing hymns in honour of the goddess Artemis. He does not know that the gates of Hades stand open for him, and that this light he is looking at is his last.

(Aphrodite goes. Hippolytus comes in with his huntsmen.)

Hippolytus.
	Follow me, singing, follow,
	for Artemis, daughter of Zeus, who lives in heaven,
	whose care we are.
Huntsmen.
	Lady, lady, most holy,
	child of Zeus,
	hail, hail to you, daughter
	of Leto and of Zeus, Artemis,
	by far the loveliest of virgins,
	you who live in the wide sky
	in your noble father's court,
	the golden house of Zeus.
	Hail to you, loveliest, loveliest
	of all the virgins on Olympus,
	Artemis.

Hippolytus. For you, mistress, I have made this woven crown of flowers from an untouched meadow, and I bring it to you. No shepherd thinks fit to graze his flock there. The iron of the scythe has never come there. Only the bee crosses that meadow in spring, untouched as it is, and Modesty tends it like a garden, watering it with river dew. Nobody who had to be taught may pick flowers there. Only those who have it in their nature, as their portion, to keep themselves in hand in everything alike. For the bad, it is not allowed. So, dear mistress, take this band for your golden hair, from a hand that reveres you. I alone of mortals have this privilege. I am with you, I talk with you and you answer me, I hear your voice, though I do not see your face. And may I round the last turn of my life the way I began it.

Servant. My lord, since only the gods should be called masters, would you take a piece of good advice from me?

Hippolytus. Of course. I would look a fool otherwise.

Servant. Then you know the rule that holds among human beings?

Hippolytus. No. What rule are you asking me about?

Servant. To hate what is stiff and proud, and does not make itself a friend to everyone.

Hippolytus. Quite right. What stiff and proud man is not a burden?

Servant. And is there a certain charm in people who are easy to talk to?

Hippolytus. A great deal of it. And profit, for very little trouble.

Servant. Do you think the same holds among the gods?

Hippolytus. Yes, if we mortals take our rules from the gods.

Servant. Then how is it that you are so stiff and proud yourself, and do not greet a goddess?

Hippolytus. Which goddess? Careful. Do not let your tongue slip.

Servant. This one. Cypris, who stands here at your gate.

Hippolytus. I greet her from a distance. I am pure.

Servant. She is a great goddess, all the same, and famous among men.

Hippolytus. Different gods for different men, and different men for different gods.

Servant. I wish you luck, and as much sense as you need.

Hippolytus. No god that is worshipped at night has any appeal for me.

Servant. The gods have their honours, boy, and we have to give them.

Hippolytus. Go on in, men, into the house, and see to the food. A full table is a pleasure after a hunt. And rub down the horses, so that when I have eaten my fill I can yoke them to the chariot and give them the exercise they need. As for your Cypris, I bid her a long goodbye.

(Hippolytus goes into the house with his huntsmen. The Servant stays behind and turns to the statue of Aphrodite.)

Servant. As for us, since the young are not to be copied when they think like that, we will speak the way slaves should speak, and pray to your image, Lady Cypris. You should forgive him. If somebody with the hot young blood in his belly talks nonsense about you, pretend you did not hear it. Gods ought to be wiser than men.

(The Servant goes in. The Chorus, women of Trozen, come in.)

Chorus.
	There is a rock, they say, that drips the water of Ocean,
	pouring a running stream from its cliff face
	where the pitchers are dipped.
	A friend of mine was there,
	soaking purple clothes
	in the river water
	and laying them out on the back
	of a warm rock in the sun.
	It was from her
	that the first word of my mistress came to me:
Chorus.
	that she is worn down on a bed of sickness,
	keeping her body inside the house,
	a thin veil shading her golden head.
	This is the third day, I hear,
	that she has kept her body pure
	of the bread of Demeter,
	her mouth taking nothing,
	wanting, with a grief she hides,
	to run herself aground
	on the wretched shore of death.
Chorus.
	Is a god in you, girl?
	Is it Pan who drives you wandering, or Hecate,
	or the holy Corybantes,
	or the Mother of the mountains?
	Or is it Dictynna, mistress of wild things,
	you have offended? Are you wasting away
	because you owe her offerings you never made?
	She ranges over the lakes
	and over the dry land, and across the sea,
	in the whirlpools of the salt water.
Chorus.
	Or is it your husband, the chief
	of the sons of Erechtheus, the well-born man,
	that some woman in the house is shepherding
	into a bed hidden from yours?
	Or has some sailor come from Crete
	and put in at the harbour
	that is kindest to seamen,
	bringing the queen news,
	so that grief over her troubles
	has tied her soul to her bed?
Chorus.
	A bad helplessness likes to live
	with the awkward temper of women,
	the helplessness of birth pains and of folly.
	That wind blew through my own womb once.
	And I cried out to the heavenly one who eases childbirth,
	Artemis, the mistress of arrows,
	and she comes to me always, and I envy no one,
	with the gods on her side.
Chorus.
	But here is the old nurse at the door,
	bringing her out of the house.
	The hateful cloud on her brows is growing.
	My soul longs to know what it is,
	what has ruined
	the queen's body and changed its colour.

(The Nurse comes out of the house with Phaedra, who is carried on a couch by her women.)

Nurse.
	Oh, the troubles of mortals, the hateful sicknesses.
	What am I to do for you? What am I not to do?
	Here is the bright light you wanted, here is the open sky.
	Your sickbed is outside the house now.
	Every word you spoke was about coming out here,
	and soon you will be in a hurry to get back to your room.
	You change your mind in a moment. Nothing pleases you.
	What you have does not please you; whatever you have not got
	you think you would like better.
	Better to be sick than to nurse the sick.
	The one is simple. The other joins
	grief in the mind to labour with the hands.
	The whole of human life is painful,
	and there is no rest from the labour.
	If there is anything dearer than living,
	darkness wraps it in clouds and hides it.
	And so we show ourselves badly in love
	with whatever this is that glitters on the earth,
	because we have no experience of another life,
	and no proof of what is under the ground.
	We are carried along by stories, nothing more.
Phaedra.
	Lift my body, hold my head up.
	The joints of my poor limbs have come undone.
	Take my arms, my lovely arms, women.
	The headdress is too heavy for my head.
	Take it off. Let my hair fall over my shoulders.
Nurse.
	Courage, child. Do not throw
	your body about so.
	You will bear the sickness more easily with quiet
	and a noble spirit.
	Mortals have to suffer.
Phaedra.
	Aiai.
	If only I could draw a drink of pure water
	from a dewy spring,
	and lie down under the poplars
	in a long-grassed meadow, and rest.
Nurse.
	Child, what are you saying?
	Do not talk like that in front of a crowd,
	flinging out words with madness riding on them.
Phaedra.
	Send me to the mountain. I will go to the woods,
	to the pine trees, where the hounds that kill
	go treading, hard on the dappled deer.
	By the gods, I long to shout the hounds on,
	to hold a Thessalian spear
	and throw it past my golden hair,
	the barbed point in my hand.
Nurse.
	Child, why are you fretting after these things?
	What do you care about hunting?
	Why do you long for water from a spring?
	There is a dewy slope right by the walls
	where you could have your drink.
Phaedra.
	Artemis, lady of the salt lagoon of Limna
	and of the racing grounds that thunder with hooves,
	if only I were on your level fields,
	breaking in Venetian colts.
Nurse.
	What is this now, another wild word flung out?
	A moment ago you were off to the mountain,
	longing to hunt; now it is colts you long for
	on the sand where there are no waves.
	It would take a great prophet to say
	which god is pulling on your reins
	and knocking your mind off its course, child.
Phaedra.
	I am wretched. What have I done?
	Where have I wandered, away from good sense?
	I went mad. I fell. A god's ruin struck me down.
	Pheu, pheu. Poor me.
	Nurse, cover my head again.
	I am ashamed of what I have said.
	Cover me. Tears run down from my eyes
	and my face is turned towards my shame.
	Getting your mind straight again hurts.
	Madness is bad. But it is better
	to be destroyed without knowing it.
Nurse.
	I cover you. And when will death
	cover my own body?
	A long life has taught me a great deal.
	People ought to mix their friendships
	in moderation, one with another,
	and not to the very marrow of the soul.
	The heart's affections should be easy to untie,
	easy to push away and easy to draw tight.
	For one soul to be in labour over two
	is a hard weight, as I am
	in pain over this one.
	People say that a life held to strict rules
	trips you up more than it delights you,
	and makes war on your health.
	So I have less praise for too much
	than for nothing in excess,
	and the wise will agree with me.

Chorus. Old woman, faithful nurse of Phaedra our queen, we see her wretched state, but we cannot tell what the sickness is. We would like to hear it from you.

Nurse. I have asked and I know nothing. She will not say.

Chorus. Not even how these troubles began?

Nurse. You come to the same answer. She is silent about all of it.

Chorus. How weak she is. How her body has been worn away.

Nurse. What do you expect? This is the third day she has eaten nothing.

Chorus. Is it ruin, some madness struck into her, or is she trying to die?

Nurse. To die. She is starving herself to be rid of life.

Chorus. That is astonishing, if her husband is content with it.

Nurse. She hides the trouble. She says she is not ill.

Chorus. And he does not read it in her face?

Nurse. He happens to be out of the country.

Chorus. And you do not force her? You do not try to find out what her sickness is, and where her mind has wandered?

Nurse. I have tried everything, and I have got nowhere. But I will not let up, even now. You are here; you can be my witness to what I am like to my master and mistress when things go badly for them.

Come, dear child. Let us both forget what was said before. You be gentler; unknot that hateful brow, and change the road your mind is on. And I, where I followed you badly before, will let that go and find a better line of talk. If your sickness is one of the ones that cannot be spoken about, here are women to help you set it right. But if your trouble can be carried out to men, say so, so that it can be told to doctors.

Well? Why are you silent? You should not be silent, child. Either correct me, if what I say is wrong, or agree with what is said well. Say something. Look over here.

Oh, I am wretched. Women, we are wasting our labour. We are as far off as we were before. Words did not soften her then, and she is not persuaded now.

But know this, and go on being more stubborn than the sea about it, if you like. If you die, you betray your children. They will get no share of their father's house. I swear it by the horse-riding queen, the Amazon, who bore a master to rule over your children: a bastard with a legitimate son's ideas of himself. You know him well. I mean Hippolytus, the one who

Phaedra. Oh.

Nurse. That touched you, did it?

Phaedra. You have destroyed me, nurse. By the gods, I beg you again: about that man, be silent.

Nurse. You see? You are in your right mind. And in your right mind, you still will not help your children and save your own life.

Phaedra. I love my children. It is another storm I am caught in.

Nurse. Your hands are clean of blood, child?

Phaedra. My hands are clean. It is my mind that carries the pollution.

Nurse. Not from some enemy's spell, brought in from outside?

Phaedra. Someone I love is destroying me. Neither of us wants it.

Nurse. Has Theseus done you some wrong?

Phaedra. May I never be seen doing wrong to him.

Nurse. Then what is this terrible thing that is driving you to die?

Phaedra. Let me do my wrong. It is not you I am wronging.

Nurse. Not willingly, no. And if I fail, the fault will lie with you.

Phaedra. What are you doing? Forcing me, hanging on to my hand?

Nurse. And your knees. And I will never let go.

Phaedra. It will be bad for you, poor woman, if you find out. Bad.

Nurse. What could be worse for me than to lose you?

Phaedra. It will kill you. And yet the thing brings me honour.

Nurse. And then you hide it, when what I beg for is good?

Phaedra. Yes. Out of what is shameful I am building something noble.

Nurse. Then if you tell it, you will look more honourable still.

Phaedra. Go away, by the gods. Let go of my right hand.

Nurse. No. Because you are not giving me the gift you should.

Phaedra. I will give it. I respect the reverence owed to your hand.

Nurse. Then I will be quiet now. From here on it is yours to speak.

Phaedra. Poor mother, what a love you loved.

Nurse. The love she had for the bull, child? Or what do you mean?

Phaedra. And you, my poor sister, wife of Dionysus.

Nurse. Child, what is wrong with you? Are you speaking ill of your own family?

Phaedra. And I am the third. Look how I am being destroyed.

Nurse. You have struck me dumb. Where is this going?

Phaedra. That is where our misfortune comes from. It is not new.

Nurse. I know no more of what I want to hear than I did.

Phaedra. Pheu. If only you could say for me what I have to say.

Nurse. I am no prophet, to know for certain what is hidden.

Phaedra. What is this thing people talk about, being in love?

Nurse. The sweetest thing there is, child, and the most painful, both at once.

Phaedra. I would say I have found the second one.

Nurse. What are you saying? You are in love, child? With whom?

Phaedra. Whoever he is, the Amazon's...

Nurse. Hippolytus, you mean?

Phaedra. You heard that from yourself, not from me.

Nurse. Oh. What are you going to say, child? You have destroyed me. Women, this is unbearable. I will not bear it and live. Hateful day, hateful light I look at. I will throw myself down, I will let my body go, I will be rid of life and die. Goodbye. I no longer exist. Because people who keep themselves in hand fall in love with evil too. Not willingly, but they do. Cypris is not a god after all. She is something greater than a god, if there is such a thing, and she has destroyed this woman, and me, and the house.

Chorus.
	Did you hear? Oh, did you hear
	the queen crying out
	her wretched suffering, not to be listened to?
	Let me die, dear one, before I come
	to the state of your heart. Io moi. Pheu, pheu.
	Poor woman, for these pains.
	Oh, the troubles that feed mortals.
	You are destroyed. You have brought your evil out into the light.
	What does this day, the whole long day of it, hold for you?
	Something new will come to its end in this house.
	It is no longer unclear where the fortune
	Cypris sends is setting, poor daughter of Crete.

Phaedra. Women of Trozen, who live here on the furthest edge of the land of Pelops, before now, in the long hours of the night, I have thought about other things: about how human life comes to be destroyed. And it seems to me that it is not by the nature of their judgement that people go wrong. Plenty of people have good sense. No, you have to look at it this way. We know what is right, and we recognise it, and we do not work it out in practice. Some from laziness. Some because they put some other pleasure ahead of what is right. And life has many pleasures: long talks, and leisure, a pleasant evil, and shame. There are two kinds of shame. One is not bad; the other is a weight on a house. If it were clear which was which, and when, there would not be two things spelt with the same letters.

Since that is what I think, then, there was no drug that could have made me change my mind and fall the other way. And I will tell you the road my judgement took. When love wounded me, I looked for the way I could carry it best. So I began with this: to be silent and hide my sickness. Because the tongue cannot be trusted. It knows how to lecture other people about their attitudes, out of doors, and it gathers the most evil of all to itself. Second, I planned to bear the madness well, and to beat it by keeping myself in hand. And third, when I could not master Cypris by those means, I decided to die. The best of my plans; nobody will say otherwise. Because I want my good acts to be seen, and when I do wrong, not to have many witnesses. I knew the act and the sickness were disgraceful, and I knew very well, on top of that, that I was a woman, a thing everyone hates. May she die the worst of deaths, whoever she was, the first woman who started shaming her bed with men from outside it. It was in noble houses that this evil began among women. Because when what is shameful looks right to the good, it will certainly look right to the bad. And I hate the women too who keep themselves in hand in words, but who have the nerve, in secret, for things that are not right. How do they ever, Lady Cypris, queen of the sea, look their husbands in the face? How do they not shudder at the darkness, their accomplice, and at the timbers of the house, in case they find a voice?

Because this is the very thing that is killing me, friends: that I never be caught shaming my husband, or the children I bore. Let them live as free men, flourishing in freedom of speech, in the city of glorious Athens, with a good name because of their mother. It makes a slave of a man, even a bold one, when he knows his mother's or his father's evil. There is only one thing, they say, that can hold its own against life: a just and good judgement, in whoever has it. Time shows up the bad among mortals when it happens to, holding up a mirror to them as if to a young girl. May I never be seen among those.

Chorus. Pheu, pheu. How beautiful self-control is, everywhere, and what a good name it harvests among men.

Nurse. Mistress, your misfortune, when I heard it a moment ago, gave me a terrible sudden fright. But now I realise I was being stupid. Among human beings, too, second thoughts are somehow wiser. Nothing has happened to you that is out of the ordinary or beyond explanation. A goddess's anger has fallen on you. You are in love. What is so astonishing about that? So are a great many people. And then you are going to destroy your life because of love? That is a poor bargain for everyone who loves their neighbour, and everyone who is going to, if they have to die for it. Cypris is not to be borne when she comes in full flood. The one who gives way she goes after gently; but whoever she finds proud and thinking himself too big, she takes hold of him and, how do you think, humiliates him. Cypris goes through the air, she is in the swell of the sea, everything is born from her. She is the one who sows love and gives it, and every one of us on the earth is her offspring.

People who have the writings of the old poets, and who live among the Muses themselves, know how Zeus once longed for the bed of Semele, and know how the lovely shining Dawn once carried Cephalus off to live among the gods, for love. And yet they live in heaven still, and do not run away from the other gods. They put up with it, I think, beaten by what happened to them. And you will not put up with it? Then your father should have begotten you on special terms, or under different gods for masters, if you will not accept these laws. How many men do you think, with perfectly good sense, see their beds sick and pretend not to see? How many fathers help their sons carry Cypris when they have gone astray? Because this is part of human wisdom: to keep what is not good out of sight. Human beings should not work too hard at getting life exactly right. They cannot even finish the roof that covers a house to the last detail. And you have fallen into a misfortune as deep as this, and think you can swim out of it? No. If you have more good in you than bad, being human, you are doing very well indeed.

Dear child, stop thinking these evil thoughts. Stop your outrage. That is all this is, outrage: wanting to be stronger than the gods. Have the nerve to love. A god has willed it. You are sick; find some good way to turn the sickness. There are charms, and words that soothe. Some cure for this sickness will be found. Men would take a long time finding it, if we women did not find the way.

Chorus. Phaedra, what she says is more useful for the trouble you are in now. But it is you I praise. And this praise is harder to hear than her words, and hurts you more.

Phaedra. This is the thing that destroys well-run cities and human houses: words that are too fine. You should not say what pleases the ear. You should say what will bring a person a good name.

Nurse. Why the solemn speech? It is not fine words you need. It is the man. We have to see it through as fast as we can, and tell him the truth about you, straight out. If your life were not in a crisis like this, if you happened to be a woman who kept herself in hand, I would never be leading you this way for the sake of your bed and your pleasure. But now it is a great struggle to save your life, and nobody can begrudge that.

Phaedra. You have said a terrible thing. Will you not shut your mouth and stop letting out these shameful words again?

Nurse. Shameful, yes. But better for you than fine ones. The deed is better, if it saves you, than the name you will die boasting of.

Phaedra. By the gods, and because what you say is well said but shameful, do not go a step further. My soul is ploughed and ready for love already, and if you dress up what is shameful in fine words, I will be spent on the very thing I am running from now.

Nurse. If that is how you see it, then you ought not to have done wrong. But since you have, listen to me. That is the next best favour. I have love charms in the house that soothe it. It has just this moment come into my head. They will end this sickness for you without disgrace and without harm to your mind, if you do not lose your nerve. But we need something from him, the one you long for, a token, a word or a scrap of his clothes, to tie the two of you into one love.

Phaedra. Is the drug something to rub on, or something to drink?

Nurse. I do not know. Want to be helped, child; do not want to be told.

Phaedra. I am afraid you will turn out too clever for me.

Nurse. Then you would be afraid of everything, believe me. What are you frightened of?

Phaedra. That you might tell any of this to the son of Theseus.

Nurse. Leave it, child. I will arrange it all well. Only you, Lady Cypris, queen of the sea, be my partner in the work. As for the rest of what I have in mind, it will be enough to tell it to our friends inside.

(The Nurse goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	Eros, Eros, you who drip desire
	down through the eyes, who bring sweet pleasure
	into the souls of the people you march against,
	never come to me with evil in your hands,
	never come out of measure.
	No shaft of fire, no shaft of the stars, hits harder
	than the arrow of Aphrodite
	that Eros, the child of Zeus,
	lets fly from his hands.
Chorus.
	It is all for nothing, all for nothing, that beside the Alpheus
	and at Apollo's Pythian shrine
	the land of Greece piles up the slaughtered oxen,
	while Eros, the tyrant of men,
	who holds the keys
	to Aphrodite's dearest bedrooms, we do not worship,
	though he lays waste, and drags mortals
	through every kind of disaster
	when he comes.
Chorus.
	The girl in Oechalia,
	a filly never yoked to a bed,
	no husband yet, no wedding:
	Cypris unhitched her from the house of Eurytus
	and drove her off like a running Naiad, like a Bacchant,
	with blood, with smoke,
	with murder for her wedding song,
	and gave her to Heracles, Alcmene's son.
	What a wretched wedding that was.
Chorus.
	Holy wall of Thebes,
	and mouth of the spring of Dirce, you could tell
	how Cypris comes creeping in.
	With the double-flamed thunderbolt
	she put Semele to bed, the mother of Dionysus,
	the god who was born twice, and the bed she made her
	was a bloody death.
	Terrible, the breath she blows on everything,
	and she flits from one to the next like a bee.

(Phaedra has gone to the door of the house and is listening. She turns to the women.)

Phaedra. Be quiet, women. It is all over for me.

Chorus. What is it, Phaedra? What is so terrible inside your house?

Phaedra. Wait. Let me hear what they are saying in there.

Chorus. I am quiet. But this is a bad beginning.

Phaedra. Io moi. Aiai. Oh, what I am suffering. What a wretched woman I am.

Chorus.
	What is that cry? What are you shouting?
	Tell me, lady, what word has rushed in
	on your mind and frightened you?

Phaedra. I am destroyed. Stand here at the doors and listen to the noise that is breaking over the house.

Chorus.
	You are at the door. It is for you to catch
	the words that the house sends out.
	Tell me, tell me, what evil has happened?

Phaedra. It is Hippolytus, the son of the horse-loving Amazon. He is shouting. He is calling my servant terrible names.

Chorus.
	I hear a cry, but nothing I can make out.
	Call out to me
	what came, what came through the door to you.

Phaedra. Clearly enough. He is calling her a matchmaker for evil, a woman who has betrayed her master's bed.

Chorus.
	Oh, this is evil. You are betrayed, my dear.
	What can I plan for you now?
	What was hidden is out in the light. You are destroyed by it,

Phaedra. Aiai. E, e.

Chorus. betrayed by the people who love you.

Phaedra. She has destroyed me by telling my trouble. She meant it kindly. It was no good way to cure this sickness.

Chorus. What now, then? What will you do? There is no way out of this.

Phaedra. I only know one thing. To die, as fast as I can. It is the only cure for the pain I am in now.

(Hippolytus bursts out of the house. The Nurse comes after him, clutching at him.)

Hippolytus. Mother Earth. Open sky, and the sun. What words have I heard? Words that should never be said.

Nurse. Quiet, boy, before somebody hears you shouting.

Hippolytus. I cannot hear things like that and keep quiet.

Nurse. Please. By your right hand, your beautiful arm.

Hippolytus. Take your hand off me. Do not touch my clothes.

Nurse. By your knees, I beg you. Do not destroy me.

Hippolytus. Why should I, if what you said was nothing evil, as you claim?

Nurse. This story, boy, is not one for everybody to hear.

Hippolytus. Good things sound even better said in front of a crowd.

Nurse. Child, do not dishonour your oath. Never.

Hippolytus. My tongue swore the oath. My mind swore nothing.

Nurse. Boy, what are you going to do? Destroy the people who love you?

Hippolytus. I spit on them. No one who does wrong is a friend of mine.

Nurse. Forgive. People make mistakes. That is what people are, child.

Hippolytus. Zeus, why did you ever settle women in the light of the sun, this counterfeit coin of an evil, for men to live with? If you wanted to sow the human race, you should not have had it come from women. Men should have been able to put down gold or iron or a weight of bronze in your temples and buy the seed of children, each man a child worth what he paid, and then live in their houses free, with no females in them. As it is, the first thing we do is fetch the evil home, and to do it we drain the wealth out of the house.

Here is the proof that a woman is a great evil. The very father who sired her and raised her adds a dowry and ships her off, to be rid of the trouble. And the man who takes the ruinous plant into his house is delighted, and hangs ornaments on his statue, a pretty face on a worthless thing, and works himself to the bone dressing it in robes, poor fool, draining his house of its wealth. And he is caught either way. Either he has married into a good family, and he is so pleased with his in-laws that he holds on to a wife who is bitter to him; or he has a good wife and useless in-laws, and presses the bad luck down with the good. The man who has it easiest is the one with a nobody in his house, a useless woman set in her home by her own simplicity.

I hate a clever woman. I will not have one in my house who thinks more than a woman should. Cypris breeds mischief more readily in the clever ones. A woman who is helpless, with only a little judgement, is kept out of folly by her own lack of wit.

Servants should never have been allowed near a wife. Women should be housed with dumb beasts that bite, so they could not speak to anyone and no one could answer them back. As it is, the bad women inside plot their bad plans, and the servants carry them out of doors. And that is how you came to me, you evil head, to bargain over my father's bed, which no one may touch. I will wash it off with running water, pouring it into my ears. How could I be evil, when just hearing about it makes me feel unclean?

Understand this, woman: it is my piety that saves you. If you had not caught me off my guard with oaths to the gods, nothing would have stopped me telling all of this to my father. As it is, I am leaving the house for as long as Theseus is out of the country, and I will keep my mouth shut. When my father comes home, I will come back with him, and I will watch how you look at him, you and your mistress. I have had a taste of your nerve already. I will know it when I see it.

Damn you both. I will never get my fill of hating women, not even if somebody says I never talk about anything else. Because they are always evil too, one way or another. Either let somebody teach them to keep themselves in hand, or let me go on trampling on them forever.

(Hippolytus goes out.)

Phaedra.
	Wretched, ill-fated,
	the lot of women.
	What skill do we have now, what words,
	when we have slipped, to untie the knot?
	I have got what I deserved. Io, earth and light.
	Where can I escape what has happened to me?
	How do I hide my pain, friends?
	What god would come to help me, what mortal
	would sit beside me, or lend a hand
	in wrong that I have done? This suffering of mine
	has come to the edge of my life, and there is no crossing it.
	Of all women I am the most unlucky.

Chorus. Pheu, pheu. It is done. Your servant's schemes have gone wrong, mistress, and things are bad.

Phaedra. You worst of all women, you destroyer of the people who loved you, look what you have done to me. May Zeus, my ancestor, blast you with his fire and wipe you out, root and all. Did I not tell you, did I not see your mind coming, to keep quiet about the very thing that is now my shame? But you could not hold back. And so I will not die with a good name after all. Now I need new plans. That man, with his mind whetted sharp on anger, will tell his father your sins and call them mine. He will tell old Pittheus what has happened. He will fill the whole country with the ugliest talk. Damn you, and damn everyone who is so eager to do good to people who do not want it, and does it badly.

Nurse. Mistress, you can blame me for the harm I have done. The sting of it is stronger than your judgement. But I have something to say to that, if you will let me. I brought you up, and I want the best for you. I went looking for a medicine for your sickness and I found what I was not looking for. If it had worked, I would have been counted very clever. We are as wise as our luck lets us be.

Phaedra. Is that fair? Is it enough for me, that you wound me first and then want to argue about it?

Nurse. We are talking too long. I did not keep myself in hand, I admit it. But there is a way to be saved even from this, child.

Phaedra. Stop talking. Your advice before was bad, and what you tried was evil. Get out of my way and go and look after yourself. I will put my own affairs in order.

(The Nurse goes into the house.)

And you, noble daughters of Troezen, grant me this one thing I ask of you. Cover what you have heard here in silence.

Chorus. I swear by holy Artemis, the daughter of Zeus, that I will never bring any of your troubles into the light.

Phaedra. Well said. I have turned it over and over, and I have found one way out of this disaster: to leave my children a life with a good name, and to get some good for myself out of the way things have fallen. I will never shame my Cretan house, and I will never come before Theseus's face with this ugly business on me, to save one life.

Chorus. What do you mean to do? Something there is no curing?

Phaedra. To die. How, I will work out for myself.

Chorus. Do not say such things out loud.

Phaedra. And you, give me good advice. As for me, I will give Cypris, the goddess who is destroying me, her pleasure today, when I am rid of my life. I will be beaten by a bitter love. But in dying I will be an evil to someone else as well, so that he learns not to stand tall over my misfortunes. When he has his share of this sickness of mine, he will learn to keep himself in hand.

(Phaedra goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	I wish I could hide under the sheer cliffs,
	I wish a god would make me a bird with wings
	and set me among the flying flocks.
	I would rise over the sea-wave
	of the Adriatic shore
	and the water of the Eridanus,
	where the poor girls, Phaethon's sisters,
	grieving for their brother,
	drip into their father's dark swell
	the amber-shining light
	of their tears.
Chorus.
	I wish I could reach the apple-sown shore
	of the Hesperides, the singers,
	where the lord of the sea
	grants sailors no passage over the dark water any more,
	where he touches the holy edge of the sky,
	the one Atlas holds up,
	and springs of ambrosia pour
	beside the beds in the halls of Zeus,
	where the holy earth that gives life
	makes the happiness
	of the gods grow.
Chorus.
	White-winged ship from Crete,
	that carried my queen
	through the salt sea, the beating waves,
	away from a happy house,
	to the joy of a wedding that was the worst of weddings.
	Bad omens flew with her from both shores,
	from the land of Crete to glorious Athens,
	and at the shore of Munychus, the harbour,
	they tied the twisted ends of the cables
	and stepped out
	onto the mainland.
Chorus.
	And that is why her mind was broken
	by the terrible sickness of Aphrodite,
	an unholy love.
	She is swamped by hard disaster,
	and from the beams of her bridal room
	she will fasten a hanging noose
	and fit it round her white neck,
	in shame before her hateful fate,
	choosing a good name instead,
	and ridding her heart
	of a love that hurts.

(The Nurse cries out from inside the house.)

Nurse. Iou, iou. Everyone near the house, come and help. The mistress has hanged herself, the wife of Theseus.

Chorus. Pheu, pheu. It is done. The queen is no more. She is hanging in a noose.

Nurse. Hurry, will you? Will somebody bring a two-edged blade, so we can cut this knot from her neck?

Chorus. Friends, what do we do? Do we think we should go into the house and get the queen down out of the noose she pulled tight?

Why should we? Are there not young servants in there? Doing too much is not a safe way to live.

Nurse. Lay her out straight, the poor dead woman. This is a bitter piece of housekeeping for my master to come home to.

Chorus. She is dead, the poor woman, from what I hear. They are already laying her out like a corpse.

(Theseus comes in, a garland of leaves on his head, back from the oracle.)

Theseus. Women, do you know what that shouting is, in the house? A heavy sound of servants has reached me. The house does not think it worth opening its doors and greeting me kindly, a man coming home from the oracle. Has something happened to old Pittheus? His life is far along already, but even so, it would hurt me if he left this house.

Chorus. This blow of yours is not aimed at the old, Theseus. It is the young who have died and will give you pain.

Theseus. Oh. Not my children. Nobody has robbed me of their lives?

Chorus. They are alive. Their mother is dead. That is the worst of it for you.

Theseus. What are you saying? My wife is dead? How did it happen?

Chorus. She fastened a hanging noose round her neck.

Theseus. Frozen with grief? Or did something happen to her?

Chorus. That is all we know. I have only just come to the house myself, Theseus, to mourn your troubles.

Theseus. Aiai. Then why is my head crowned with these woven leaves? I went to the oracle and I have come back to this. Undo the bolts on the doors, servants, unfasten them, and let me see the bitter sight of the woman who has destroyed me by dying.

(The doors open. Phaedra's body is carried out and laid down.)

Chorus.
	Io, io. Poor woman, your misery, your evil.
	What you suffered, what you did,
	was enough to bring this whole house down.
	Aiai, the daring of it. Killed by violence,
	an unholy end, wrestled down
	by your own poor hand.
	Who put your life out, poor woman?
Theseus.
	Oh, the pain. I have suffered, my city,
	the greatest of my evils. Fortune,
	how heavily you have set your foot on me and on my house,
	a stain from some avenging spirit, past all telling.
	It is the destruction of my life. No life is left.
	I see an ocean of evils, wretched man that I am,
	so wide I will never swim out of it again,
	never cross the wave of this disaster.
	What word for you, poor woman, what name for your fate,
	so heavy, could I find to say?
	You are gone from my hands like a bird,
	with one quick leap away from me into Hades.
	Aiai, aiai. Misery, misery, this.
	From somewhere far back I am reaping
	a fate the gods sent
	for the sins of somebody who came before me.

Chorus. Lord, these evils have not come to you alone. Many other men have lost a good wife.

Theseus.
	Under the earth, under the earth, in the dark,
	that is where I want to live, dead, in my misery,
	robbed of your company, the dearest I had.
	You have destroyed me more than you have died.
	Who can tell me? Where did the deadly stroke,
	poor woman, come from, that reached your heart?
	Will somebody say what happened, or is it for nothing
	that my royal house shelters a crowd of servants?
	Oh, oh, for you.
	The misery, what pain I have seen in this house,
	not to be borne, not to be spoken. I am destroyed.
	The house is empty, and the children are orphans.
	You left them, the children you bore, you left them, dearest
	and best of women, of all
	the light of the sun looks on,
	and the starry glow of the night.
Chorus.
	Io, poor man. Poor man. How much evil this house holds.
	My eyes are wet,
	flooded with tears at your fate.
	And the trouble after this, I have been shuddering at it a long time.

Theseus. Wait. What is this? What is this letter, hanging from her dear hand? Does it want to tell me something new? Did she write me instructions, poor woman, about my marriage and the children, asking me for something? Do not be afraid, poor girl. No woman will ever come into Theseus's bed, or into his house. But look, the marks pressed by her gold ring, and she is gone, are fawning on me, coaxing me to read. Come, let me unwind the wrapping from the seals and see what this letter wants to say to me.

Chorus.
	Pheu, pheu. One more new evil the god brings on,
	one after another. As for me, after what has happened,
	life is not worth living. Let it come, if it comes.
	I say the house of my king and queen is destroyed,
	pheu, pheu, it is no more.
	God, if there is any way, do not bring the house down.
	Hear me, I am begging you. I see something coming,
	like a prophet reading a bird, an omen of evil.

Theseus. Oh. Here is another evil on top of the evil, one that cannot be borne, cannot be spoken. Misery. I am a wretched man.

Chorus. What is it? Tell us, if we may share in it.

Theseus.
	It cries out, the letter cries out things that cannot be forgotten.
	Where can I run from the weight of these evils?
	I am gone, destroyed, finished.
	Such a song, such a song I have seen
	speaking in the writing, poor wretch that I am.
Chorus.
	Aiai. The word you bring into the light begins the evil.
Theseus.
	I will not hold it any longer behind the gates of my mouth,
	this evil there is no crossing over,
	this evil that destroys. Io, my city.
	Hippolytus has dared to touch my bed
	by force. He has dishonoured the holy eye of Zeus.
	Father Poseidon, you promised me once
	three curses. Use one of them
	to finish my son. Let him not escape this day,
	if the curses you gave me were real.

Chorus. Lord, by the gods, take that prayer back. You will find out later that you were wrong. Listen to me.

Theseus. It cannot be done. And more: I will drive him out of this country as well, and one of two fates will strike him down. Either Poseidon will honour my curses and send him dead to the house of Hades, or he will be thrown out of this land to wander, and drain out a miserable life on foreign soil.

Chorus. And here he is himself, your son Hippolytus, just in time. Let go of this evil anger, lord Theseus, and think what is best for your house.

(Hippolytus comes in with his companions.)

Hippolytus. I heard you shouting, father, and I came as fast as I could. But what you are groaning about, I do not know, and I would like to hear it from you. Wait. What is this? Your wife, father. I see her dead. This is past all wondering at. I left her only a moment ago; she was looking at this light not long since. What happened to her? How did she die? Father, I want to hear it from you. You say nothing. Silence does no good when things are bad. The heart that wants to know everything is caught being greedy even in trouble, I know. But it is not right, father, to hide your misfortunes from the people who love you, and more than love you.

Theseus. Human beings, you make so many mistakes, and all for nothing. Why do you teach ten thousand skills, and contrive everything, and discover everything, and there is one thing you do not know and have never yet hunted down: how to teach sense to people who have none?

Hippolytus. That would be a formidable expert, the man who could force sense into people who have none. But this is no time for hairsplitting, father. I am afraid your tongue is running away with you, in your trouble.

Theseus. Pheu. There should be some clear test for men to tell their friends by, some way of seeing into their minds, which one is a true friend and which one is not. Every man should have two voices, an honest one and the other one, whatever it happened to be, so that the one thinking dishonest thoughts could be caught out by the honest one, and we would never be deceived.

Hippolytus. Has one of your friends been whispering slander about me in your ear? Am I sick with it, when I have done nothing? I am stunned. Your words are stunning me. They wander, they are off the track of any sense.

Theseus. Pheu, the human mind. How far will it go? What limit will there be to daring and to sheer face? If it swells like this with each generation of men, and every one that comes after outdoes the one before in wickedness, the gods will have to bolt another earth onto this one to hold the people born unjust and evil.

Look at this man. My own son, and he has shamed my bed, and the dead woman convicts him, openly, as the worst of men. Show your face, then, since you have already come into pollution. Show it here, to your father. So you are the man who is too good for the rest of us, and keeps company with gods? You are the one who keeps himself in hand and is untouched by evil? I will not believe your boasting and think so badly of the gods as to credit them with stupidity. Go on, then, boast now. Peddle your meatless diet, take Orpheus for your master and rave in his rites, honouring the smoke of all his books, now that you have been caught. I warn everyone to run from men like that. They hunt you down with holy words while they are plotting filth.

She is dead. Do you think that saves you? That is what convicts you most of all, you worst of men. What oaths, what words could be stronger than she is, so that you could escape the charge? You will say she hated you, and that a bastard is born the natural enemy of the legitimate children. Then you are calling her a bad trader with her own life, if she destroyed what she loved most out of hatred of you. Or will you say that folly is not in men, but is born into women? I know young men. They are no steadier than women when Cypris shakes a young mind. Being male helps them; it is on their side. But why am I arguing against your words like this, when the corpse is here, the clearest witness there could be? Get out of this land, into exile, as fast as you can. Do not go to god-built Athens, and do not go to the borders of any land my spear rules. If I let you beat me after what you have done to me, Sinis, the robber I killed on the Isthmus, will never bear witness that I killed him. He will say I was bragging, and it was nothing. And the rocks of Sciron that live beside the sea will never say I am a hard man to the wicked.

Chorus. I don't know how I could ever call any mortal happy. What was on top has been turned over and is upside down again.

Hippolytus. Father, the anger in you, the way your mind has locked itself shut, is frightening. But this business of yours, for all it has fine arguments on its side, is not fine at all once somebody unfolds it. I am no good at making speeches to a crowd. Among people my own age, and few of them, I am cleverer. And there is a fairness in that too: the men who are nothing among the wise are the ones who sing sweetest to a mob. Still, with disaster here, I have no choice. I have to let my tongue go. I will begin where you first came at me, meaning to finish me off without my getting a word in. You see this light, and this earth. In all of it there is no man, whatever you say, who keeps himself in hand better than I do. I know, first, how to revere the gods. I know how to have friends who do not try to do wrong, friends who would be ashamed to propose anything bad or to pay back the people they deal with in shameful favours. I am not a man who laughs at his companions, father. I am the same man to my friends when they are away as when they are standing next to me. And there is one thing I have never touched, and it is the very thing you think you have caught me in. To this day my body is clean of the bed. I do not know that act at all, except by hearing it talked about and seeing it in pictures, and I am not eager to look even at those. I have a virgin's soul.

Very well. Suppose my self-control does not convince you. Let it go. Then you have to show how I was corrupted. Was her body more beautiful than every other woman's? Or did I hope to live in your house by marrying into a bed with an inheritance attached? Then I was a fool. No, worse: I was out of my mind entirely. Or is it that "being king is sweet"? Not to a man who keeps himself in hand, not in the least, unless being sole ruler has already rotted the minds of the mortals it pleases. I would want to be first at winning the games of Greece, but second in the city, and happy for ever there with the best men for my friends. You can get things done in that position, and the absence of danger gives a pleasure that no throne can match.

One of my points has not been made. You have all the others. If I had a witness to the kind of man I am, and if I were fighting this case with her alive and looking at the light, you would have gone through the facts and seen who the guilty were. As it is, I swear to you by Zeus, who keeps oaths, and by the floor of the earth, that I never touched your marriage, never wanted to, never once had the thought. If I am a bad man, let me die without fame and without a name, with no city and no home, an exile wandering the earth, and let neither sea nor land take my flesh when I am dead. Whether she was frightened and destroyed her own life, I do not know. I am not allowed to say more than that. She kept herself in hand, though she did not have it in her to. I had it in me, and I have not used it well.

Chorus. You have given a good enough answer to the charge. You have offered oaths by the gods, and that is no small pledge.

Theseus. Isn't this man a spell-singer and a sorcerer? He has dishonoured the father who made him, and he is confident he can master my spirit with his even temper.

Hippolytus. And I am astonished at the very same thing in you, father. If you were my son and I were your father, I would have killed you, not punished you with exile, if I thought you had laid a hand on my wife.

Theseus. How fitting, what you have just said. But you will not die like that. A quick death is the easiest thing for a man in trouble. No. You will wander in exile from your father's land, exactly the sentence you laid down for yourself, and drain out a bitter life on foreign soil. That is the wage for a man who has no piety.

Hippolytus. Oh. What are you going to do? You won't even wait for time to give its evidence against me? You will drive me out of the country?

Theseus. Beyond the sea. Beyond the lands of Atlas, if I had the power. That is how much I hate the sight of your face.

Hippolytus. Without testing my oath, or my pledge, or a word from the seers, you will throw me out of the land untried?

Theseus. This tablet here drew no lot for the right to speak, and it accuses you, and it is believable. As for the birds that flit about over our heads, I wish them a long goodbye.

Hippolytus. Gods. Why don't I unlock my mouth, when I am being destroyed by you, the very ones I revere? No. I won't. I would not persuade the people I need to persuade in any case, and I would be breaking the oaths I swore for nothing.

Theseus. Oh, this holiness of yours will be the death of me. Get out of your father's land. Now.

Hippolytus. Where am I supposed to turn, in the state I am in? Whose house will take me in as a guest, an exile on a charge like this?

Theseus. Somebody who enjoys entertaining the corrupters of other men's wives, and keeping house with their crimes.

Hippolytus. Aiai. That one went to the liver. It is close to tears, this, if I really look like a bad man, and you really think I am one.

Theseus. The time to groan and think ahead was when you had the nerve to outrage your father's wife.

Hippolytus. House, if only you could find a voice and speak for me, and give your evidence whether I am a bad man.

Theseus. You run to witnesses that cannot talk. Clever. But the deed does not need to talk. It informs on you, and it says you are bad.

Hippolytus. Pheu. If only I could stand opposite myself and look at me, so that I could weep at what I am suffering.

Theseus. Yes, you have practised worshipping yourself far more than you have practised being just and doing right by your parents.

Hippolytus. My poor, unhappy mother. What a bitter birth. May no friend of mine ever be a bastard.

Theseus. Drag him out of here, slaves. Didn't you hear me? I proclaimed him banished long ago.

Hippolytus. Any one of them who touches me will be sorry for it. You do it yourself, if you have the stomach for it. Push me out of the land.

Theseus. I will, if you don't obey what I have said. No pity for your exile is creeping over me.

(Theseus goes into the house.)

Hippolytus. It is fixed, then, it seems. Oh, I am wretched. I know the truth, and I do not know how to say it. Daughter of Leto, dearest to me of all the gods, you who sit beside me and hunt beside me, I am to leave glorious Athens. Goodbye, then, city and land of Erechtheus.
