Ground of Troezen, you have so much happiness in you for a boy to grow up in, goodbye. This is the last time I will look at you and speak to you. Come, young men of this country, my own age, say goodbye to me and see me out of the land. You will never see another man who keeps himself in hand better than I do, even if my father does not think so.

(Hippolytus goes out. His huntsmen stay behind.)

Huntsmen.
	Truly, when the care the gods take of us comes into my mind,
	it takes a great weight of grief away.
	But I keep a hope, deep down, that I understand something,
	and then I look at what happens to mortals, and at what they do,
	and I am left behind.
	One thing gives way to another, from every side,
	and men's lives shift, forever wandering.
Chorus.
	If I could pray, and fate would grant me this from the gods:
	luck, and wealth with it, and a heart that grief has never touched.
	An opinion of things neither too exact
	nor stamped with the false coin's mark,
	but easy ways, changing with tomorrow as tomorrow comes,
	and so, always,
	a life that goes well.
Huntsmen.
	My mind is not clear any more. What I see is past all hope.
	The brightest star of Athens, of the whole Greek land,
	we have seen him, we have seen him, driven by a father's anger
	away to another country.
	Sands of the city's shore,
	oak-woods on the mountain, where he killed the wild things
	running with his quick-footed hounds,
	in the company of holy Dictynna, Artemis of the nets.
Chorus.
	No more will you mount behind your yoked Venetian colts
	and hold the track round Limna
	under the hooves of your trained horse.
	The music that never slept under the frame of the strings
	will stop in your father's house.
	No garlands now at the resting places of Leto's daughter
	in the deep green grass.
	And with your exile the contest is over,
	the girls' race for your bed.
Chorus.
	And I, for your misfortune,
	will spend a fate that is no fate in tears.
	Poor mother, you gave birth for nothing.
	Pheu. I am raging at the gods.
	Io, io.
	Graces, who go yoked together, why do you send
	this poor man out of his father's land,
	guilty of none of this ruin,
	away from this house?

Chorus. And here comes one of Hippolytus's attendants, hurrying toward the house with a dark look on his face.

Messenger. Women, where would I find Theseus, the king of this land? If you know, tell me. Is he inside the house here?

Chorus. Here he is himself, coming out of the house.

Messenger. Theseus, I bring news that is worth your worry, for you and for the citizens who live in the city of Athens and within the borders of Troezen.

Theseus. What is it? Has some new disaster caught up with the two neighbouring cities?

Messenger. Hippolytus is no more. That is one way to put it. He is still looking at the light, but the scales are tipping.

Theseus. Who did it? Did somebody come at him out of hatred, somebody whose wife he had disgraced by force, the way he did his father's?

Messenger. His own chariot destroyed him. That, and the curses from your mouth, the ones you prayed to your father, the ruler of the sea, against your son.

Theseus. Gods. Poseidon. So you really are my father: you heard my prayers. How did he die? Tell me. How did the club of Justice come down on the man who disgraced me?

Messenger. We were near the shore where the waves come in, combing out the horses' manes with brushes, and crying while we did it, because a messenger had come and told us that Hippolytus would never set foot in this land again; you had sentenced him to a miserable exile. Then he came down to the beach to us himself, singing the same tearful song, and behind him walked an enormous crowd of friends and young men his own age. After a while he stopped groaning and said, "Why am I raving like this? My father's orders have to be obeyed. Harness the horses to the chariot, slaves. This city is not mine any more." From then on every man was hurrying, and faster than you could say it we had the mares harnessed and standing beside the master. He snatched the reins off the rail and fitted his feet into the footholds, boots and all. And first he spread out his hands and said to the gods, "Zeus, let me stop living if I am a bad man. And let my father come to understand how he is dishonouring me, whether I am dead by then or still looking at the light." With that he took the goad in his hands and laid it on all the mares together, and we, his servants, followed close to the chariot, by the horses' heads, along the road that runs straight to Argos and Epidaurus.

When we struck into empty country, where there is a stretch of shore beyond the border of this land, lying toward the Saronic gulf, a sound came out of the ground there, like the thunder of Zeus, a deep roar, horrible to hear. The horses put their heads straight up and their ears to the sky, and a raw panic went through us: where could that noise be coming from? We looked toward the shore where the surf pounds, and we saw a wave, unholy, propped against the sky, so high that it took the cliffs of Sciron out of my sight. It hid the Isthmus and the rock of Asclepius. Then it swelled up, foam boiling round it, the sea's breath blowing through it, and came on toward the shore where the four-horse chariot was standing. And with the surge itself, with the third wave, the great one, the sea put out a bull on the sand: a savage monster. The whole land filled with its bellowing and roared back, a horrible sound, and to us who were watching it was a sight too big for our eyes to hold.

At once a terrible fear fell on the mares. The master, who had lived with horses and their ways all his life, grabbed the reins in both hands and pulled, the way a sailor pulls an oar, throwing his body back against the straps. But the mares bit down on the fire-forged bits with their jaws and carried him off by force, not turning for the helmsman's hand or the harness or the jointed car. And if he took the steering and pointed their run toward the soft ground, the bull showed itself in front of them, to turn them back, maddening the four-horse team with terror. And if they rushed toward the rocks, out of their minds, it came up close, in silence, keeping pace with the chariot rail, until it tripped them and threw them over, driving the rim of the wheel against a stone. Everything went together in one heap. The hubs of the wheels jumped into the air, and the pins out of the axles. And he himself, poor man, tangled in the reins, was dragged along, tied in a knot he could not undo, his dear head pounded against the rocks, his flesh breaking, and he was shouting things that were terrible to hear: "Stop, you that I fed at my own mangers. Do not wipe me out. Oh, my father's wretched curse. Who is here who wants to save the best of men?" Many of us wanted to, but we were left behind, too slow. Then somehow, I do not know how, he came loose from the cut leather straps and fell, with a little life still breathing in him. And the horses vanished, and that cursed monster of a bull with them, somewhere in the rocky ground, I do not know where.

I am a slave of your house, my lord. But there is one thing I will never be able to do, and that is believe that your son is a bad man. Not if the whole race of women hanged itself, and somebody filled every pine tree on Mount Ida with writing. I know he is good.

Chorus. Aiai. The disaster has come to pass, new evils on top of the old, and there is no escape from fate and from what has to be.

Theseus. Out of hatred for the man this has happened to, I was glad of your story. But now, out of respect for the gods, and for him, because he is my son, I take no pleasure in these evils and no pain either.

Messenger. Then what? Should we bring him here, or what do we do with the poor man to please your mind? Think about it. If you take my advice, you will not be cruel to your son in his misfortune.

Theseus. Bring him here. I want to see him with my own eyes, the man who denied he had defiled my bed, and prove him wrong with words and with what the gods have done to him.

Chorus.
	You lead the unbending mind of gods and of mortals,
	Cypris, and with you
	goes the one with the painted wings, who wraps them round his prey
	on the quickest feather there is.
	He flies over the earth and over the loud salt sea,
	and Love casts his spell on whatever maddened heart
	he swoops down on, winged, shining gold:
	on the nature of the cubs in the mountains, and the creatures of the deep,
	and everything the earth feeds,
	and everything the blazing sun looks down on,
	and men. Over all of them the royal honour,
	Cypris, is yours alone. You rule them.

(Artemis appears above the house.)

Artemis.
	You, well-born son of Aegeus, I command you
	to listen.
	It is Leto's daughter, Artemis, who is speaking to you.
	Theseus, poor man, why do you take pleasure in this,
	when you have killed your son against everything holy,
	persuaded by your wife's lying words
	about a thing you never saw? The ruin you took on is plain enough to see.
	Why don't you hide your body in the pit under the earth
	for shame,
	or change your life for a bird's and go up into the air
	and lift your foot out of this pain?
	Because among good men there is no
	share of life you can call yours any more.
	Listen, Theseus, to how your troubles stand.
	And yet I will get nothing done by it. I will only hurt you.
	But this is what I came for: to show that your son's mind
	was just, so that he can die with a good name,
	and to show your wife's frenzy, or, in a way,
	her nobility. She was stung by the goads of the goddess
	most hateful to those of us who take our pleasure in staying virgin,
	and she fell in love with your son.
	She tried to beat Cypris with her judgement,
	and against her will she was destroyed by her nurse's scheming.
	The nurse bound your son by oaths, and told him the sickness.
	He, being the just man he is, did not go along with her words,
	and even when you abused him he would not
	tear up the pledge of his oath. He is a god-fearing man.
	And she, afraid she would be found out and put to the test,
	wrote a lying letter and destroyed your son
	by trickery. And she convinced you all the same.

Theseus. Oh.

Artemis. Does the story bite, Theseus? Keep still. Hear the rest, and you will have more to groan about. You know you had three curses from your father, with a sure result? You took one of them, you utter villain, and used it on your own son, when you could have used it on some enemy. Your father the sea-god meant well by you, and he gave what he had to give, since he had promised. But you have shown yourself a bad man, in his eyes and in mine. You did not wait for proof or for the voice of the seers. You did not put it to the test. You did not give it a long time's thought. Faster than you should have, you let the curse go at your son, and you killed him.

Theseus. Lady, let me die.

Artemis. What you did is terrible. But even so, you can still be forgiven for it. Cypris wanted this to happen; she was filling up her anger. And this is the law among the gods: none of us chooses to stand in the way of another god's will when that god is set on something. We always stand aside. Because, you can be sure of this, if I were not afraid of Zeus I would never have come to such shame as to let the man I loved best of all mortals die. As for your fault: not knowing, first of all, clears you of wickedness. And then your wife, by dying, used up every chance of testing her words, and so convinced your mind. These evils have broken over you most of all, but there is grief in it for me too. The gods take no pleasure when the god-fearing die. The bad, though, we destroy, children and house and all.

(Hippolytus is carried in by his huntsmen, broken, and barely alive.)

Chorus.
	And here he comes, the poor man,
	his young flesh and his fair head
	torn to pieces. Oh, the pain of this house.
	What a double grief has come down on these halls,
	sent by the gods, and gripping them.
Hippolytus.
	Aiai, aiai.
	I am wretched. An unjust father's
	unjust curse has torn me apart.
	I am destroyed, poor man. Oh, oh.
	Pains shoot through my head,
	a spasm jumps through my brain.
	Stop. Let me rest my body. It has given up.
	E, e.
	Hateful team of horses, that I fed
	with my own hand,
	you have wrecked me, you have killed me.
	Pheu, pheu. By the gods, slaves, gently.
	Touch my torn skin gently with your hands.
	Who is standing there on my right side?
	Lift me carefully. Pull me along evenly,
	the man the god hates, cursed
	by his father's mistakes. Zeus, Zeus, do you see this?
	This is me, the holy one, the worshipper of gods.
	This is me, who outdid everyone at keeping himself in hand,
	going down to Hades with my eyes open, my life
	destroyed from the top down. All my labours of piety
	toward mankind
	were for nothing.
Hippolytus.
	Aiai, aiai.
	And now the pain, the pain comes over me again.
	Let go of me, you poor men.
	Let death come to me now, death the Healer.
	Finish me, finish off the man
	the god hates. I long for a two-edged spear
	to cut me in pieces
	and lay my life down to sleep.
	Oh, my father's wretched curse.
	The evil of old blood-stained kinsmen,
	of ancestors long ago, is coming out past its boundary
	and does not wait,
	and it has come for me. Why, when I am
	guilty of none of it?
	Io moi moi.
	What can I say? How can I get my life free
	of this pain that has no pity? If only
	the black night-necessity of Hades
	would lay me down to sleep, the man the god hates.

Artemis. Poor man. What a disaster you have been yoked to. It was the nobility of your mind that destroyed you.

Hippolytus. Ah. A breath of divine fragrance. Even in this agony I felt you, and my body grew lighter. The goddess Artemis is here in this place.

Artemis. Poor man, she is. The dearest of the gods to you.

Hippolytus. Do you see me, lady, the state I am in, the wretch I am?

Artemis. I see you. But it is not lawful for tears to fall from my eyes.

Hippolytus. You have no huntsman now, and no servant.

Artemis. No. But you are dear to me even as you die.

Hippolytus. No one to drive your horses, or guard your statues.

Artemis. It was Cypris who plotted this. She stops at nothing.

Hippolytus. Oh. Now I understand which god destroyed me.

Artemis. She blamed you for the honour you did not pay her, and she hated you for keeping yourself in hand.

Hippolytus. Three of us. She destroyed three of us, Cypris. I see it now.

Artemis. Your father, and you, and third, his wife.

Hippolytus. Then I groan for my father's bad luck as well as mine.

Artemis. He was deceived by a goddess's design.

Hippolytus. Father, how wretched this disaster has made you.

Theseus. I am finished, child. There is no joy left in life for me.

Hippolytus. I grieve for you more than for myself, for the mistake you made.

Theseus. If only I could be the corpse, child, instead of you.

Hippolytus. Bitter gifts, the gifts of your father Poseidon.

Theseus. I wish they had never come into my mouth.

Hippolytus. Why? You would have killed me anyway, as angry as you were then.

Theseus. Yes. The gods had knocked my judgement off its feet.

Hippolytus. Pheu. If only the race of mortals could lay a curse on the gods.

Artemis. Let it be. Not even under the darkness of the earth will the angry will of the goddess Cypris come down on your body and go unavenged. You are owed that, for your piety and your good mind. I will take my revenge on her with my own hand: whichever mortal man she loves best of all, I will punish him with these arrows, which nothing escapes. And to you, poor suffering man, in return for these evils, I will give the greatest honours in the city of Troezen. Girls not yet yoked in marriage will cut their hair for you before their weddings, and through the long ages you will harvest the deepest grief of their tears. The girls will always make you their care and put you in their songs, and Phaedra's love for you will not fall nameless and be passed over in silence.

And you, child of old Aegeus, take your son in your arms and hold him close. You destroyed him without meaning to. When the gods arrange it, it is natural for human beings to go wrong. And you, Hippolytus, I advise you not to hate your father. You had a fate, and this is how it broke you. Goodbye. It is not lawful for me to look at the dead, or to stain my eye with the last breaths of the dying. And I see you are already close to that.

(Artemis is gone from above the house.)

Hippolytus. Goodbye to you too. Go, blessed virgin. You leave a long friendship easily. I end the quarrel with my father, since you want it. Before now I always obeyed what you said. Aiai. The darkness is reaching my eyes already. Take hold of me, father, and hold my body straight.

Theseus. Oh, child, what are you doing to me, the man the god hates?

Hippolytus. I am gone. I can see the gates of the dead.

Theseus. And you leave my hand unclean?

Hippolytus. No. I set you free of this killing.

Theseus. What are you saying? You let me go free of your blood?

Hippolytus. I call Artemis to witness it, Artemis who tames with the bow.

Theseus. Dearest boy. How noble you show yourself to your father.

Hippolytus. Pray for legitimate sons like this one.

Theseus. Oh, your mind, so god-fearing and so good.

Hippolytus. Goodbye to you too. Goodbye, father, many times over.

Theseus. Don't desert me now, child. Hold on.

Hippolytus. My holding on is done. I am gone, father. Cover my face with my robes, quickly.

Theseus. Glorious Athens, and the land that Pallas marked out for her own, what a man you will have lost. Oh, I am wretched. How many times, Cypris, I will remember what you have done.

Chorus.
	This grief has come to every citizen alike,
	and nobody expected it.
	There will be a beating of many tears.
	When the great fall, the news of it
	deserves grief, and takes a stronger hold.

Andromache (c. 425 BC)

Andromache

(Phthia, in Thessaly, before the house of Neoptolemus. Beside the house stands the shrine of Thetis, with the statue of the goddess and an altar. Andromache is sitting at the altar.)

Andromache. City of Thebe, the pride of Asia. That is where I came from, once, to Priam's royal hearth, with a dowry heavy with gold, given to Hector as his wife, to bear his children. Andromache. In those days it was a name other women envied. Now, if any woman ever was, I am the unluckiest woman alive. There is nobody born, and nobody who ever will be, who has been through what I have. I watched my husband Hector killed by Achilles. I watched the son I bore him, Astyanax, thrown from the high towers, on the day the Greeks took the plain of Troy. And I myself, who was counted a daughter of the freest house there was, came to Greece a slave, handed over to the islander Neoptolemus as his prize of war, picked out of the Trojan plunder specially for him. So here I live, on the flat land where Phthia's ground runs into the ground of the city of Pharsalus, the place where Thetis the sea-goddess lived with Peleus, away from other people, keeping clear of the crowd. The Thessalians call it Thetideion, the goddess's ground, in memory of her wedding. This is where the son of Achilles made his home. He lets Peleus go on ruling Pharsalus: he does not want to take the sceptre from the old man while he is alive. And in this house I have given birth to a boy, by the son of Achilles. My master.

Before, bad as things were, I always had one hope to lead me on: if my child lived, I might find some defence in him, some help against my troubles. But since my master married the Spartan woman, Hermione, and pushed my slave's bed to one side, she has hounded me with cruelties. She says I am making her childless with secret drugs, and making her husband hate her, and that I want to live in this house in her place and throw her out of her own marriage bed by force. I never wanted that bed in the first place, and now I have left it altogether. Great Zeus be my witness: I did not share that bed by choice. But I cannot make her believe it. She wants to kill me, and her father Menelaus is helping his daughter do it. He is in the house right now. He came from Sparta for exactly this. I was terrified, so I have come to the shrine of Thetis, next door to the house, and here I sit, hoping it will stop them killing me. Peleus and the family of Peleus hold it sacred: it is the monument of his marriage to the Nereid. My only son I have smuggled away in secret to another house, because I am afraid they will kill him. His father is not here to help me, and he is no use to the child at all. He is away in the country of Delphi, paying Apollo for his madness: the day he went to Pytho and demanded that Apollo pay for killing his father. Now he is asking pardon for those old offences, hoping to make the god kind to him from here on.

(The Maid, one of the Trojan slaves of the house, comes out.)

Maid. Mistress. I am not afraid to call you by that name, because I thought it was your due in your own house too, when we lived in the land of Troy. I was loyal to you, and to your husband while he lived, and now I have come to you with fresh news. I am frightened, in case one of the masters notices, but I pity you. Menelaus and his daughter are planning terrible things against you, and you must be on your guard.

Andromache. Dearest fellow slave. Because that is what you are now, a fellow slave to the woman who used to be your queen, and is now in misery. What are they doing? What plots are they weaving this time, wanting to kill me, wretched as I already am?

Maid. Your son, poor woman. They are going to kill your son, the one you smuggled out of the house.

Andromache. Oh. She has found out that I sent my child away? How? From where? Oh, this is misery. I am finished.

Maid. I do not know how. But I heard it from them myself. And Menelaus has left the house to go and fetch him.

Andromache. Then I am finished. My child, the two vultures will take you and kill you, and the man they call your father is still in Delphi.

Maid. Yes. I do not think you would be treated like this if he were here. As it is, you have no friends left.

Andromache. Has there been no word about Peleus, that he is coming?

Maid. He is old. Too old to help you, even if he were here.

Andromache. And yet I have sent for him, and not just once.

Maid. You do not really think any of your messengers cares about you?

Andromache. Why would they? Well then. Will you go, as my messenger?

Maid. And what do I say, when I have been so long away from the house?

Andromache. You will find plenty of excuses. You are a woman.

Maid. It is dangerous. Hermione does not keep a careless watch.

Andromache. You see? You back out on your friends when they are in trouble.

Maid. No, I do not. Do not throw that at me. I will go. A slave woman's life is not much looked at anyway, whatever happens to me.

(The Maid goes off to find Peleus.)

Andromache. Go, then. And I will do what I always do: stretch out to the sky the laments and groans and tears I live in. It is born in women, to take a kind of pleasure in the troubles they have, keeping them always in the mouth and on the tongue. And I have not one thing to groan over but many: my father's city, Hector dead, the hard fate I was yoked to when I fell into the day of slavery, and did not deserve it. Never call any mortal happy until he is dead, and you have seen how he got through his last day and went down below.

Andromache.
	It was no bride Paris brought home to high Ilium. It was ruin
	he brought to bed in his room, when he brought Helen.
	For her sake, Troy, the swift war-god of Greece came with a thousand ships
	and took you, a prey to the spear and the fire,
	and took my husband, Hector, mine, unhappy woman, whom the son of Thetis of the sea
	dragged behind his chariot round the walls.
	And I was led out of my room to the edge of the sea,
	slavery, the hateful thing, thrown over my head.
	Many tears ran down my face, when I left
	the city and my room and my husband in the dust.
	Oh, unhappy me. Why did I have to go on seeing the light,
	as Hermione's slave? Worn down by her,
	I have come to this statue of the goddess and thrown my arms round it, begging,
	and I melt like a spring of water trickling out of the rock.

(The Chorus, women of Phthia, come in.)

Chorus.
	Lady, you have sat so long on the floor of Thetis's shrine
	and you will not leave it.
	I am a woman of Phthia, but I have come to you, a daughter of Asia,
	to see if there is anything I can do,
	any cure I can cut for these troubles no one can untie,
	the troubles that have locked you and Hermione in a hateful quarrel,
	poor woman, over a bed
	shared by two,
	over the son of Achilles.
Chorus.
	Know your luck. Reckon up the evil you have come to, where you stand.
	Are you a match for your masters,
	a girl from Ilium against a daughter born in Sparta?
	Leave the house where the sheep are offered,
	the house of the goddess of the sea. What good does it do you,
	terrified, to waste your body with weeping,
	when your masters hold the power?
	Power will come down on you. Why labour,
	when you are nothing, at a labour that comes to nothing?
Chorus.
	Come. Leave the shining seat of the goddess, the Nereid.
	Know what you are: a slave on foreign ground,
	in another people's city,
	where you see not one friend
	of your own, unluckiest of women,
	a bride of every sorrow.
Chorus.
	You were the most pitiful thing I ever saw, Trojan woman, when you came
	to my masters' house. But out of fear
	we keep quiet.
	I do pity what has happened to you,
	but I am afraid the child of Zeus's daughter
	might find out that I wish you well.

(Hermione comes out of the house, richly dressed.)

Hermione. This gold ornament on my head, and this embroidered dress on my body: I did not come out here wearing them as the first-fruits of the house of Achilles or of Peleus. They came from Sparta, in Laconia. My father Menelaus gave me them, with a great dowry besides, so that I can say what I like. That is my answer to you women. As for you: you are a slave, a woman won at spear-point, and you want to throw us out and take possession of this house. My husband hates me because of your drugs. My womb is dying, barren, because of you. The women of Asia have a terrible gift for that kind of thing. But I will put a stop to it, and this house of the Nereid will do you no good, not the altar, not the temple. You are going to die. And if some man or god does want to save you, then instead of the proud thoughts of your rich old days you will have to cower, and go down on your knees at my feet, and sweep my house, and sprinkle water from the river Achelous out of gold jugs with your own hand, and learn where on earth you are. There is no Hector here, no Priam, no gold. This is a Greek city. And you, you wretched creature, have come to such a pitch of ignorance that you have the nerve to sleep with the son of the father who killed your husband, and bear children to the murderer's blood. That is the whole barbarian race. Father sleeps with daughter, son with mother, sister with brother; the nearest and dearest kill each other, and no law stops any of it. Do not bring that in among us. Here it is not thought decent for one man to hold the reins of two women. Men here look to one wife's bed and are content with it, any man who does not want a house that is a disgrace.

Chorus. A woman's mind is a jealous thing, and always hardest on the women who share her marriage.

Andromache. Pheu, pheu. Youth is a bad thing in a human being, when youth comes with injustice in it. What I am afraid of is that my being your slave will push my arguments aside, however many good ones I have; and if I win, I am afraid I will pay for winning. People who breathe big do not take it kindly when the better argument comes from someone beneath them. Still, I will not be caught betraying my own case.

Tell me, young woman: what solid ground could have persuaded me to push you out of your lawful marriage? That Sparta is a smaller city than Phrygia? That my luck outruns yours? That you see a free woman when you look at me? Am I so puffed up with a young, firm body, a great city, and friends, that I want your house instead of you? Why, so that I can bear children in your place, slaves, a wretched string of them dragging behind me? Or will anyone put up with my sons as kings of Phthia if you have none? The Greeks love me so much, for Hector's sake? And I was a nobody, was I, no queen in Phrygia? It is not my drugs that make your husband hate you. It is that you are not fit to live with. That is a love-charm too: it is not beauty, lady, it is goodness that pleases the man in your bed. But if anything scratches you, then Sparta is a great city and Scyros is nowhere; you are rich among people who are not; Menelaus is a bigger man than Achilles. That is what your husband hates in you. A woman, even if she is given to a bad husband, has to be content, and not set herself up against him. If you had a king for a husband in Thrace, the country the melting snow pours through, where one man shares his bed with many wives in turn, would you have killed them all? You would have been caught fastening a charge of insatiable lust on every woman alive. A disgrace. And yet it is true we suffer this sickness worse than men do. But we put a good face on it. Dearest Hector, for your sake I even loved alongside you, whenever Aphrodite tripped you up, and many a time I put my breast to your bastards, so that I would never give you cause for bitterness. By doing that I bound my husband to me, by being good. But you will not let a drop of the sky's dew settle on your husband, you are so afraid. Do not try to outdo your mother, lady, in a weakness for men. Children with any sense should run from the ways of a bad mother.

Chorus. Mistress, as far as it comes easily to you, let yourself be persuaded, and come to terms with her.

Hermione. Why the high-minded speeches? Why turn this into a debate, as if you were the one who kept herself in hand, and I were the one who did not?

Andromache. You certainly do not, on the arguments you have just been standing on.

Hermione. May your kind of mind never live in my house, woman.

Andromache. You are young, and you are talking about shameful things.

Hermione. You do not talk about them. You do them to me, as far as you can.

Andromache. Can you not suffer your love-troubles in silence?

Hermione. What? Is that not the first thing for women, everywhere?

Andromache. Yes, for women who handle it well. Otherwise it is not decent.

Hermione. We do not run our city by barbarian laws.

Andromache. What is shameful there is shameful here too.

Hermione. Clever. Very clever. And you are still going to die.

Andromache. Do you see the statue of Thetis, looking straight at you?

Hermione. Yes. Hating your country, for the killing of Achilles.

Andromache. Helen destroyed him, not I. Your mother.

Hermione. Are you going to keep on poking at my wounds?

Andromache. There. I am silent. I am holding my mouth shut.

Hermione. Tell me the one thing I came out here for.

Andromache. I tell you that you have less sense than you need.

Hermione. Will you leave this holy ground of the goddess of the sea?

Andromache. If I am not going to die. Otherwise, never.

Hermione. Then that is settled. I will not wait for my husband to come.

Andromache. And I will not give myself up to you before he does.

Hermione. I will bring fire against you, and I will not stop for anything of yours.

Andromache. Burn away, then. The gods will know it.

Hermione. And the pain of terrible wounds on your skin.

Andromache. Cut my throat. Bloody the goddess's altar. She will come after you.

Hermione. You barbarian thing, hard and bold. So you will stand up to death, will you? Well, I will get you up off that seat, and soon, and you will get up willingly. I have the right bait for you. But I will keep the words to myself; the thing itself will show you soon enough. Sit tight. Even if molten lead were holding you there, I will have you up before the son of Achilles comes, the man you trust so much.

(Hermione goes back into the house.)

Andromache. I do trust him. It is a strange thing: some god found cures for men against savage snakes, but the thing that is worse than a viper, worse than fire, a bad woman, nobody has yet found a drug for that. That is how great an evil we are to human beings.

Chorus.
	Great griefs began, then,
	on the day the son of Maia and Zeus
	came to the glen on Ida
	driving the lovely three-horse team of goddesses,
	harnessed for a hateful quarrel over beauty,
	to the herdsman's steading,
	to the young man alone with his cattle,
	and the lonely
	hearth of his hut.
Chorus.
	And when they came to the wooded glen,
	they washed their bodies till they shone
	in the streams of the mountain springs,
	and went to the son of Priam,
	outbidding each other with spiteful words,
	and Aphrodite won with treacherous words,
	sweet to hear,
	and bitter: the wreck of a life
	for the luckless city of the Phrygians
	and the towers of Troy.
Chorus.
	If only the mother who bore him
	had struck Paris a deathblow over the head
	before he settled
	on the rock of Ida,
	when Cassandra at the holy laurel
	screamed out to kill him,
	the great ruin of Priam's city.
	Whom did she not go to? Which of the city's elders
	did she not beg
	to put the baby to death?
Chorus.
	Then the yoke of slavery would never have come
	on the women of Ilium, and you, lady,
	would have kept
	your seat in a royal house;
	and Greece would have been spared the painful
	labours of the ten years her young men
	wandered round Troy with their spears.
	Beds would never have been left empty,
	and old men
	robbed of their children.

(Menelaus comes in with attendants, leading Andromache's small son.)

Menelaus. I have come, and I have your son, the one you smuggled out to another house behind my daughter's back. You were so sure this image of the goddess would save you, and the people who hid him would save him. But you have been found out, woman, less clever than Menelaus here. And if you do not get up and clear out of this ground, his throat will be cut instead of yours. So reckon it up: do you want to die, or do you want him to die for the wrong you are doing to me and my daughter?

Andromache. Reputation. Reputation. You have puffed up ten thousand nobodies into great lives. The people whose good name rests on the truth, I call them happy; the ones who have it by lies, I will not allow that they have anything but the luck of seeming clever. So it was you, was it, who led the picked men of Greece and took Troy from Priam? A man as feeble as this? A man who has worked himself into such a rage over the words of a daughter who is barely more than a child, and gone into the ring against an unlucky slave woman? I do not think you were worthy of Troy any more, or Troy of you. The people who seem clever are bright on the outside; inside they are the same as everybody else, except perhaps in money, and money is a great strength.

Menelaus, come on, let us take this argument through to the end. Suppose I am dead at your daughter's hands, and she has destroyed me. She will never escape the stain of murder; and in most people's eyes you will stand trial for this blood too. You helped her, and the debt of it will drag you in. And suppose I slip out of dying myself: will you kill my son? Then how will his father take his child's death lightly? Troy does not call him that much of a coward. No, he will go where he must, and he will show himself worthy of Peleus and of his father Achilles in what he does, and he will throw your daughter out of his house. And you, when you are offering her to another man, what will you say? That her decency ran away from a bad husband? That is a lie, and he will find it out. Who will marry her? Or will you keep her in your house without a man, a grey-haired widow? Poor man, do you not see the flood of evils pouring in on you? How many wrongs against her marriage bed would you rather your daughter had found, than suffer what I am telling you? You should not build great evils on small grounds; and if we women are a deadly evil, men should not make their nature like ours. Because if I am drugging your daughter and aborting her womb, as she says, then willingly, not against my will, and without crouching at any altar, I will submit to justice myself at the hands of your son-in-law, to whom I owe no smaller damages for making him childless. That is what I am. But as for your mind, there is one thing I am afraid of in you: it was a quarrel over a woman that made you destroy the poor city of the Phrygians too.

Chorus. You have said too much, for a woman speaking to men. The sense that should keep you in hand has shot its last arrow.

Menelaus. Woman, these are small matters, not worth my throne, as you say, and not worth Greece. But understand this: whatever a man happens to need, that is a bigger thing to him than taking Troy. And I stand by my daughter as her ally, because I count it a great thing, being robbed of her marriage. Anything else a woman suffers comes second. When she loses her husband she loses her life. Neoptolemus should have command of my slaves, and my people and I of his, because friends, if they are really friends, have nothing of their own; everything is held in common. And if I wait for the absent instead of arranging my affairs as well as I can, I am a fool, not a wise man. So get up out of the goddess's shrine. If you die, this boy escapes his death; if you refuse to die, I kill him. One of the two of you has to leave life.

Andromache. Oh. That is a bitter lottery you are setting me, a bitter choice of life. If I draw the lot I am wretched; if I do not draw it I am destroyed. You, who are doing something enormous for a small cause: listen to me. Why are you killing me? For what? What city have I betrayed? Which of your children have I killed? What house have I burned? I was forced into bed with my masters. And then it is me you will kill, not him, the man who is to blame? You let the beginning go and rush for the end that came after it? Oh, these evils. My poor country. What terrible things I suffer. Why did I have to give birth as well, and add a second weight on top of this one? But why do I weep over that, and not wring out the evils at my feet and reckon them up? I saw Hector butchered and dragged behind the chariot wheels. I saw Ilium burning, a pitiful sight. And I went aboard the Argive ships myself, a slave, dragged by the hair, and when I got to Phthia I was married off to Hector's killers. What is sweet in life to me? What am I supposed to look at? My present luck or my past? I had one child left, this one, the eye of my life, and the people who have decided this are going to kill him. No. Not to save my miserable life. In him there is hope, if he lives; and for me it is a disgrace not to die for my son. Look. I leave the altar. I am in your hands, to cut my throat, to murder, to bind, to hang by the neck. Child, the mother who bore you is going to Hades so that you will not die. And if you slip out of your death, remember your mother, what I endured, how I died, and go to your father with kisses, pouring tears, with your arms round his neck, and tell him what happened to me. So it is true: for everyone alive, children are their life. Whoever has none and sneers at that feels less pain, but his happiness is a poor thing.

Chorus. I pitied you as I listened. Bad luck is pitiable to everyone alive, even when it falls on a stranger. But you should have brought your daughter and this woman to terms, Menelaus, and set her free of her troubles.

Menelaus. Take hold of her, slaves. Twist her arms behind her. What she is about to hear will not be to her liking. You: it was to get you off the goddess's holy altar that I held your child's death up in front of you, and that is how I drew you into my hands to be killed. So that is how matters stand with you. Understand it. As for this boy, my daughter will decide whether she wants him killed or not. Now get into the house, and learn, slave that you were born, never to insult free people again.

Andromache. Oh. You crept up on me with a trick. I have been cheated.

Menelaus. Announce it to the world. I do not deny it.

Andromache. Is this what passes for clever among you people by the Eurotas?

Menelaus. And among the people of Troy too: when you have been hurt, you hurt back.

Andromache. Do you think the gods are not gods, and that there is no justice in them?

Menelaus. When that comes, I will bear it. But you I am going to kill.

Andromache. And this chick too, that you have dragged out from under my wing?

Menelaus. No, not I. I will hand him to my daughter to kill, if she likes.

Andromache. Oh. Then why am I not mourning for you already, my child?

Menelaus. It is true that the hope waiting for him is not a bold one.

Andromache. You people of Sparta, most hated of all human beings by all human beings. Council chambers of treachery. Lords of lies. Stitchers of evil schemes. Twisted, nothing sound in you, all your thinking goes round corners: you prosper in Greece and you do not deserve to. What is there that is not found among you? The most murders? Money made by shameful means? Saying one thing with your tongue and thinking another, and being found out at it, every time? I hope you die. For me, death is not as heavy as you have decided it should be. What destroyed me was that other thing, the day the poor city of the Phrygians was wiped out, and my famous husband with it, the man whose spear so often turned you from a coward on land into a coward at sea, running for your ship. And now you show yourself a fearsome man-at-arms against a woman, and you kill me. Then kill me. You will get no flattery from my tongue, you or your daughter. You were born great in Sparta; well, I was born great in Troy. And if things are going badly for me now, do not brag about it. It could happen to you.

Chorus.
	Never will I praise a man for having two wives,
	or sons with two different mothers:
	feuds in the house, and hatred, and grief.
	Let my husband be content with one marriage,
	one bed,
	and share it with no one.
Chorus.
	Nor is a city easier to bear
	with two kings than with one:
	burden on burden, and the citizens divided.
	And when two poets are making one song,
	the Muses love
	to set them quarrelling.
Chorus.
	When a fast wind is carrying the sailors,
	two minds at the steering oar,
	a whole crowd of clever men in a heap,
	are weaker than one plainer head with sole command.
	One man's power, in a house
	and in a city, whenever people
	want to find the right moment.
Chorus.
	The Spartan woman has shown it, the daughter
	of Menelaus the general. She went through fire
	against another woman's bed,
	and she is killing the poor woman from Troy
	and her child, for the sake of a spiteful quarrel.
	Godless, lawless, graceless, this murder.
	Lady, the tide will turn on you yet
	for what you have done.
Chorus.
	And here I see them,
	the pair yoked together, in front of the house,
	condemned to death by a vote.
	Unhappy woman, and you, poor child,
	dying for your mother's bed,
	you who had no part in it
	and did no wrong to the king's family.
Andromache.
	Here I am, my hands bleeding,
	tied tight with the cords,
	being sent down under the earth.
Child.
	Mother, mother, I am going down with you,
	under your wing.
Andromache.
	A cruel sacrifice, you rulers
	of the land of Phthia.
Child.
	Father,
	come and help the people you love.
Andromache.
	You will lie, my darling child,
	at your mother's breast,
	a corpse under the earth, beside a corpse.
Child.
	Oh, oh, what is going to happen to me? We are lost,
	you and I, mother.
Menelaus.
	Go down below the earth. You came here
	from towers that were our enemies. Two of you,
	and you die for two reasons: my vote
	takes your life, and my daughter Hermione's
	takes the boy's. It is great folly
	to leave your enemies' children alive
	when you could kill them
	and take the fear out of your house.
Andromache.
	Husband, husband, if only I had
	your hand and your spear to fight beside me,
	son of Priam.
Child.
	Poor me, what song can I find
	to turn my death aside?
Andromache.
	Beg him, my child. Go up close
	and touch the master's knees.
Child.
	Friend,
	friend, let me off my death.
Andromache.
	My eyes are running with tears,
	I drip like a sunless spring
	off a smooth rock face. Poor woman that I am.
Child.
	Oh, oh, what way out of this evil
	can I ever find?
Menelaus.
	Why fall at my feet, begging me
	as if you were praying to a rock in the sea, or a wave?
	I have been a help to my own people;
	for you I have no love-charm at all. I spent
	a great share of my life
	taking Troy, and your mother with it.
	That is your inheritance from her:
	you go down to Hades under the ground.

(Peleus comes in, leaning on a staff, with an attendant.)

Chorus. And here I see Peleus close by, hurrying this way on his old legs.

Peleus. I am asking you, and the man in charge of this slaughter: what is this? How did it come to this? What is the story that has the house sick like this? What are you doing, scheming away without a trial? Menelaus, stop. Do not rush ahead of justice. You there, boy, lead me faster. This is no business for taking one's time, it seems to me. If I ever wanted my youth back, and the strength that came with it, I want it now. First of all, then, I will blow into this woman like a following wind into a sail. Tell me: by what right have these men tied your hands with cords and are marching you off, you and your child? You are being led to the slaughter like a ewe with the lamb under her, while I was away and so was your master.

Andromache. Old sir, these men are taking me, with my child, to be killed, just as you see. What can I tell you? It was not one urgent message I sent for you by, but thousands of messengers. You have heard, I expect, about the quarrel in this house with this man's daughter, and why I am being destroyed. And now they have dragged me from the altar of Thetis, who bore you your noble son, whom you worship and wonder at, and they are taking me away, with no trial to judge me, without waiting for the men who are away from home, because they knew I was alone, and this child too, who has done nothing, and whom they mean to kill along with me, his wretched mother. I beg you, old man. I fall at your knees. I cannot take hold of your dear beard with my hand. Save me, in the gods' name. If you do not, we will die, and it will be a disgrace to your house and a misery to me, old man.

Peleus. I order you to loosen those ropes before someone is sorry, and free her two hands.

Menelaus. And I forbid it. I am a second man here, no less than you, and I have far more authority over her.

Peleus. How so? Have you come here to run my house? Is it not enough for you to rule what is in Sparta?

Menelaus. I took her prisoner out of Troy.

Peleus. And my son's son received her as his prize.

Menelaus. Is not what I own his, and what he owns mine?

Peleus. Yes. To do good with, not harm. Not to kill by force.

Menelaus. You will never take her out of my hands.

Peleus. Shall I bloody your head with this staff?

Menelaus. Touch me and find out. Come one step closer.

Peleus. You, count as one of the men? You worst of men, from a family of the worst. What claim have you to a place in the company of men? A man who let a Phrygian take his wife off him. You left your house and your hearth unlocked and unguarded, as if the woman you had at home were a chaste one, when she was the worst of them all. A Spartan girl could not keep herself in hand if she wanted to. They leave home with the young men, their thighs bare and their dresses hanging loose, and they share the running tracks and the wrestling grounds with them, which I cannot stomach. And then is it any wonder that you do not bring up your women to keep themselves in hand? Helen was the one to ask that question, the woman who walked out of your house, and out from under the Zeus who guards the love between husband and wife, and went carousing off with a young man to another country. And then, for her sake, you collected that enormous crowd of Greeks and led them to Troy? You should have spat her out and never lifted a spear, once you found out what she was; you should have let her stay where she was, paid a price for the privilege, and never taken her back into your house. But that was not the way your mind's wind was blowing. Instead you destroyed many good lives, and left old women childless in their homes, and robbed grey-haired fathers of their noble sons. I am one of those wretched fathers. And I look at you as the killer of Achilles, a man polluted with his blood. You alone came home from Troy without a wound, and brought your fine armour back in its fine cases just the way it went out. And I told the boy when he was marrying: do not make a marriage tie with this man, do not take into your house the filly of a bad mother. They carry their mothers' shame out of the house with them. You young men who are looking for wives, mark this for me: get a daughter from a good mother. And besides all that, what an outrage you did to your own brother, when you told him to cut his daughter's throat, and he was fool enough to do it. That is how afraid you were of being left without your worthless wife. And when you took Troy, since I will follow you there too, you did not kill the woman when you had her in your hands. No: the moment you saw her breast, you threw your sword away and took her kiss, and fawned on the bitch who had betrayed you, because Aphrodite is stronger than you are, you worst of men. And then you come to my children's house while they are away and ransack it, and kill a poor unlucky woman without honour, and a child who will one day make you weep, you and that daughter of yours in the house, even if he were three times a bastard. Dry ground has beaten deep soil for a crop many a time, and many a bastard is a better man than the legitimate sons. Take your daughter and go. It is better for a man to have a poor honest man for a son-in-law and a friend than a rich bad one. And you are nothing.

Chorus. From a small beginning the tongue supplies people with a great quarrel. Sensible people take care about that: they do not start a fight with the people they owe.

Menelaus. Then why would anyone call old men wise, or the men the Greeks once thought had sense? When you, Peleus, born of a famous father and tied to me by marriage, say things that shame you and insult me, and all over a barbarian woman. You should have driven her out beyond the streams of the Nile, beyond the river Phasis, and cheered me on the whole way. She is a woman from the mainland of Asia, where more Greek dead fell to the spear than anywhere else, and she had a share in your own son's blood. Paris, who killed your son Achilles, was Hector's brother, and this woman was Hector's wife. And you go in under the same roof with her, and think it fit to eat at the same table with her, and let her bear children in the house who will be your worst enemies. I saw all this coming, old man, for your sake and for mine, and when I try to kill her she is snatched out of my hands. Come now. There is no shame in laying hands on the argument itself. If my daughter has no child and this woman's children grow up, will you set them up as kings of this land of Phthia, barbarians by birth, ruling Greeks? And then I am the one with no sense, because I hate injustice, and you are the one with brains? Consider this too. If you had given your daughter to some citizen and she had then been treated like this, would you have sat there in silence? I doubt it. Yet for the sake of a foreign woman you scream this at the family you are bound to. And another thing: a wife who is wronged by her husband grieves as much as a man does, and so, just the same, does a man with a wife playing the fool in his house. But he has great strength in his own hands. Her affairs rest with her parents and the people who owe her. Is it not right, then, that I should help my own? You are old, old. As for my generalship, you would help me more by talking about it than by keeping quiet. Helen's trouble was not her own choice; it came from the gods, and it did Greece the greatest good. They knew nothing of arms and battle, and they went on to manly deeds. Practice is the teacher of everything for human beings. And when I came face to face with my wife and held back from killing her, that was keeping myself in hand. I wish you had not wanted to kill your brother Phocus either. I have gone at you with all this in good sense, not out of anger. If you fly into a temper, you get a sore tongue from all your talking, and I get the profit of having looked ahead.

Chorus. Stop now, both of you. That is far the best thing: stop these useless words, before the two of you go wrong together.

Peleus. Oh, what a bad custom Greece has. When the army sets up a trophy over the enemy, people do not count it the work of the men who did the labour. The general carries off the credit. He was one man among ten thousand shaking a spear, he did no more than any one of them, and he gets more of the glory. And they sit in high office in the city, very solemn, and think themselves greater than the people, and they are nobodies. The people are ten thousand times cleverer than they are, if they had the daring and the will at the same time. That is how you and your brother sit puffed up over Troy and the generalship you had there, lifted up by other men's labour and other men's pain. I will teach you to think Paris of Ida a smaller enemy than Peleus, unless you take yourself off from under this roof as fast as you can, you and your childless daughter, whom the son of my blood will drive through this house by the hair. She is a barren heifer and she will not put up with other women bearing children when she has none of her own. But if she is unlucky about children, must we be left with none at all? Get away from her, slaves, so I can find out whether anyone is going to stop me untying her hands. Lift yourself up. I am shaking, but I will undo these plaited leather knots. Is this how you tore up her hands, you worst of men? Did you think you were tying up a bull or a lion? Or were you afraid she would grab a sword and fight you off? Come here, little one, under my arm. Help me untie your mother. In Phthia I will raise you to be a great enemy to these people. If the Spartans had not their reputation for the spear and the contest of battle, in everything else, be sure of it, you are no better than anyone.

Chorus. Old men are a thing let off the leash, and hard to hold back when their temper is up.

Menelaus. You are far too quick to rush into abuse. As for me, I came to Phthia, and I am not going to do anything shabby here by force, or have it done to me. And now, since I have no spare time to waste, I am going home. There is a city not far from Sparta which used to be friendly and is now acting as an enemy. I want to march on it with an army and bring it under my hand. When I have settled things there the way I want, I will come back. Then, face to face with my son-in-law, I will make my case and hear his. If he punishes this woman and keeps himself in hand towards us from now on, he will find us keeping ourselves in hand. If he loses his temper, he will find us losing ours, and deed will answer deed. Your speeches I can bear easily. You stand there like a shadow with a voice. You cannot do anything; all you can do is talk.

(Menelaus goes out with his men.)

Peleus. Lead the way, my child. Stand here under my arm. And you too, poor woman. You ran into a savage storm, and you have come into a harbour out of the wind.

Andromache. Old sir, may the gods be good to you and yours, for saving my child and me, the unluckiest of women. But watch out that these men do not crouch in wait for the two of us on a lonely stretch of road and take me by force, seeing that you are old and I am weak and this child is a baby. Think about that, in case we escape now and are caught later.

Peleus. Do not bring me a woman's cowardly talk. Walk. Who is going to lay a hand on you? He will be sorry if he touches you. Thanks to the gods, I command a crowd of horsemen and many armed men in Phthia. And I still stand straight. I am not the old man you think. A man like that, I need only look at him and I will set up a trophy over him, old as I am. One old man with a good heart is stronger than a lot of young ones. What use is a fine body to a coward?

(Peleus goes out, with Andromache and the child.)

Chorus.
	Let me not be born, or let me be born
	of good fathers, and share a house with plenty in it.
	If anything comes that cannot be mended,
	the well-born never lack defenders;
	when a man is proclaimed the son of a noble house,
	there is honour and glory in it. Time
	does not wear away what good men leave behind.
	Their excellence shines on when they are dead.
Chorus.
	Better a victory nobody thinks badly of
	than to trip up justice with power and spite.
	It tastes sweet at the time, to human beings,
	but in time it goes dry
	and hangs on the house as a reproach.
	This is the life I praise, this is the life I hold to:
	to have no power beyond what is right,
	in the marriage bed or in the city.
Chorus.
	Old son of Aeacus,
	I believe it: you stood with the Lapiths
	against the Centaurs with your spear,
	the most famous spear of all; and on the Argo
	you passed the unfriendly water of the Clashing Rocks
	on that famous voyage;
	and when, long ago, the son of Zeus, Heracles,
	threw a ring of slaughter round the glorious city of Troy,
	you came home to Europe
	with an equal share of the glory.

(The Nurse comes out of the house.)

Nurse. Dear women, what a train of evils this day is laying out for us, one on the heels of another. My mistress inside the house, Hermione I mean, deserted by her father and realising at the same time what she has done, planning to kill Andromache and her child, wants to die. She is terrified of her husband: that for what she has done he will send her out of this house in disgrace, or kill her, for trying to kill people it was wrong to kill. The slaves standing guard over her can barely stop her hanging herself, and they snatch the swords out of her right hand and take them off her. That is how sorry she is now, and she knows that what she did before was not well done. I am worn out, friends, keeping my mistress from the noose. You go in, into the house, and get her out of death. New faces persuade better than the friends people are used to.

Chorus. Yes, and we can hear the servants shouting in the house, about the very thing you came to tell us. The poor woman looks about to show how bitterly she grieves for the terrible things she did. She is coming out of the house, out of the servants' hands, wanting to die.

(Hermione comes out, tearing at her hair and her veil.)

Hermione.
	Io moi moi.
	I will tear my hair out in handfuls
	and rake my nails through my face.
Nurse.
	Child, what are you doing? Are you going to disfigure your own body?
Hermione.
	Aiai, aiai.
	Off my hair with you, up into the air,
	fine-woven veil.
Nurse.
	Child, cover your breasts. Fasten your dress.
Hermione.
	Why should I cover
	my breasts with a dress? What I did
	to my husband is plain, and in the open,
	and cannot be hidden.
Nurse.
	Does it hurt, that you stitched up a murder for the woman who shares your husband?
Hermione.
	Yes, I groan for it,
	for the cruel thing I dared to do.
	I am cursed. Cursed
	in the eyes of every human being.
Nurse.
	Your husband will forgive you this mistake.
Hermione.
	Why did you hunt the sword
	out of my hand?
	Give it back, dear, give it back, so I can drive
	a blow straight home. Why do you keep me from the rope?
Nurse.
	And if I let you go, out of your mind as you are, so that you could die?
Hermione.
	Oh, my fate.
	Where is a fire I could love, a flame for me?
	Where can I climb, up onto the rocks,
	over the sea, or into the woods on the mountains,
	so that I can die and belong to the dead below?

Nurse. Why are you torturing yourself like this? The blows the gods send come to everyone, sooner or later. Today, or some other day.

Hermione.
	You left me, you left me, father, alone on the shore,
	like a boat with no oar, stranded, by myself.
	He will kill me, he will kill me. I will never live again
	under this roof I was married in.
	Whose statue can I run to and cling to for protection?
	Or shall I fall at a slave's knees, a slave myself?
	If only I could fly out of the land of Phthia,
	a bird with dark wings,
	or be that ship of pine
	that was the first to row through the Clashing Rocks,
	the dark ones, on its first voyage.

Nurse. My child, I did not like the excess in you before, when you went too far against that Trojan woman, and I do not like it now, this terror you are working yourself into. Your husband is not going to throw away his marriage to you because a barbarian woman talked him round with some flimsy arguments. You are not a prisoner he brought back from Troy. You are a great man's daughter, and he took you with a rich dowry, out of a city that has done more than well for itself. And your father is not going to betray you and let you be thrown out of this house, whatever you are afraid of. Now go inside, and stop making a show of yourself in front of the doors. If people see you out here in front of the house, child, it will be held against you.

(The Nurse goes into the house. A young man comes in quickly, worn from the road and foreign-looking. It is Orestes.)

Chorus. Look. Here is a stranger, from some other country by the look of him, hurrying towards us as fast as he can walk.

Orestes. Women of this foreign land, is this the house of Achilles's son, the king's palace?

Chorus. It is. But who are you, to ask?

Orestes. The son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra. My name is Orestes. I am on my way to the oracle of Zeus at Dodona. And since I have reached Phthia, I thought I would find out about a kinswoman of mine, whether she is alive and well: Hermione, from Sparta. She lives a long way from us, but she is dear to me all the same.

Hermione. Son of Agamemnon, you are a harbour in a storm to a sailor. By these knees of yours, I beg you, pity me. You were asking how I am. I am not doing well. And I wrap my arms round your knees, and they are as good as the wool bands a suppliant lays on an altar.

Orestes. Wait. What is this? Am I wrong, or is this the mistress of the house I am looking at, the daughter of Menelaus?

Hermione. The only daughter Helen, the child of Tyndareus, ever bore my father in his house. Have no doubt of it.

Orestes. Apollo, Healer, grant us a release from our troubles. What is the matter? Is it gods or men who are hurting you?

Hermione. Some of it is my own doing. Some of it is the man who has me. Some of it is a god's. Whichever way I look, I am destroyed.

Orestes. What disaster can happen to a woman who has no children yet, unless it has to do with her bed?

Hermione. That is exactly where I am sick. You led me straight to it.

Orestes. Your husband loves another bed instead of yours?

Hermione. The prisoner. Hector's wife.

Orestes. That is a bad thing you are telling me. One man with two beds.

Hermione. That is how it is. So I fought back.

Orestes. You plotted against the woman? The way a woman does?

Hermione. Death. For her and for her bastard child.

Orestes. And did you kill them, or did something happen and take them out of your hands?

Hermione. Old Peleus did. He took the side of the people beneath him.

Orestes. Did anyone share this killing with you?

Hermione. My father. He came from Sparta for exactly that.

Orestes. And then he was beaten by an old man's arm?

Hermione. By shame. And he is gone, and left me alone.

Orestes. I understand. You are afraid of your husband, because of what you did.

Hermione. You have it. He would be right to kill me. What is there to say? But I beg you, in the name of Zeus who watches over our family, send me as far from this country as you can, or to my father's house. Because the very walls here seem to have found a voice and are driving me out, and the whole land of Phthia hates me. And if my husband comes home from Apollo's oracle before that, he will kill me on the most shameful charge there is, or I will be a slave to a bastard bed that I used to be mistress of.

So how, as somebody is going to ask, did you go so wrong? It was women coming into the house that ruined me. Bad women. They puffed me up with this kind of talk. "You are going to put up with her? That prisoner, the lowest of the low, a slave, in your house, sharing your bed with you? By the Queen of heaven, if it were my house she would not be alive to look at the daylight and get the harvest of my marriage." And I listened to what those Sirens said, the clever, scheming, twisty chatter of them, and I filled up with folly like a sail with wind. What did I need to watch my husband for? I had everything I could want. Wealth, plenty of it. I was mistress of the house. Any children I had would be legitimate, and hers would be bastards, half slaves, and mine would own them.

Never, never, and I will not say this only once, should a man with any sense who has a wife let women come into his house to visit her. They are the teachers of everything bad. One of them is making something out of it, and helps to spoil the marriage. Another has slipped herself and wants company in her sickness. And a great many of them are simply lewd, and that is how the houses of men get infected. So guard the doors of your houses well, with bolts and bars. Nothing healthy ever comes of women visiting from outside. Only a great deal of harm.

Chorus. You have let your tongue run too freely against your own kind. We can forgive you for it, in your position. But even so, a woman ought to dress up the sickness of women, not expose it.

Orestes. It was a clever man who taught people to listen to the argument from the other side too. I knew about the turmoil in this house, and about the quarrel between you and Hector's wife, and I kept watch and waited, to see whether you would stay here, or whether you were frightened enough by the killing of a captive woman to want out of this house.

I did not come because I had any great respect for the messages you sent me. I came so that if you gave me an opening, as you are giving me one now, I could take you away from this house. Because you were mine, before. You are living with this man now because your father is a coward. Before he ever crossed into Trojan territory he gave you to me as my wife, and then afterwards he promised you to the man who has you now, if he took the city of Troy. And when Achilles's son came home here, I forgave your father, and I pleaded with the bridegroom to give up his marriage to you. I told him what had happened to me, and the god that was on me at the time: that I could marry from among my friends, but not easily from outside, being in exile from my home the way I am. And he was an outrage to me. He threw my mother's murder in my face, and the goddesses with blood in their eyes who hunt me for it. And I was low, because of what had happened to my house, and I hurt, I hurt badly, but I bore what had happened, and I went away robbed of my marriage to you, against my will.

So now, since your luck has turned upside down, and you have fallen into this disaster and have no way out, I will take you away from this house and put you in your father's hands. Blood is a strong thing. And when things go wrong there is nothing better than one of your own.

Hermione. As for my marriage, that is my father's business. It is not for me to decide. But take me out of this house as fast as you can, before my husband gets here first and comes home, or before old Peleus finds out that I am deserting the house and comes after me with horses.

Orestes. Never mind the old man's arm. And do not be afraid of Achilles's son, for all the outrage he did me. There is a machine built for him, a death trap, knotted with knots that will not slip, and this hand built it. I will not say what it is before it is done, but when it is being done, the rock of Delphi will know. If my allies in the Pythian country keep their oaths, the mother-killer will teach him that nobody marries the woman who should have been mine. He will pay bitterly for demanding that Lord Apollo answer for his father's blood. It will do him no good to have changed his mind, and to be making his peace with the god now. Between Apollo and my slanders he will die a bad death, and he will learn what my hatred is. When men hate a god, the god turns their fate upside down and does not let them think big.

(Orestes and Hermione go out together.)

Chorus.
	Apollo, who towered up the strong walls on the hill of Troy,
	and you, god of the sea, who drive your dark horses
	over the salt water,
	why did you take the work of your own hands
	and give it, dishonoured, to Ares,
	the master of the spear,
	and let go of Troy,
	poor Troy, poor Troy?
Chorus.
	So many chariots with fine horses you yoked
	on the banks of the Simois,
	so many bloody races of men you set going
	with no wreath for the winner.
	And the kings of Troy are dead and gone,
	and the fire no longer blazes on the altars in Troy
	for the gods,
	with the sweet smoke of incense.
Chorus.
	The son of Atreus is gone, by the hands of his wife,
	and she paid for his murder with her own death.
	Her children took it from her.
	A god's, a god's command turned against her, out of the oracle,
	when Agamemnon's son travelled from Argos
	and stood in the holy of holies,
	and became his mother's killer.
	God, Apollo, how am I to believe it?
Chorus.
	And through the market squares of Greece many women
	sang their groans for children lost,
	and wives left their homes
	for another man's bed.
	Not on you alone, and not on the people you love,
	did the heavy grief come down.
	Greece bore the plague, the plague. And it crossed over
	to the rich fields of the Phrygians too,
	a thunderbolt raining down the blood that Hades loves.

(Peleus comes in, hurrying.)

Peleus. Women of Phthia, I am asking, so tell me. I heard a report, nothing clear, that the daughter of Menelaus has left this house and gone, and I have come in a hurry to find out whether it is true. When friends are away, the people at home have to look after their affairs.

Chorus. Peleus, what you heard is right. And it would not be decent of me to hide the trouble I find myself in. The queen has fled from this house.

Peleus. Afraid of what? Tell me the whole thing.

Chorus. Afraid of her husband. That he would throw her out of the house.

Peleus. For plotting the death of his child? Surely not.

Chorus. Yes. And she was afraid of the prisoner too.

Peleus. Did she leave the house with her father, or with somebody else?

Chorus. Agamemnon's son came and took her out of the country.

Peleus. And what does he hope to get out of it? Does he mean to marry her?

Chorus. Yes. And he is arranging the death of your son's son.

Peleus. Lying in wait for him, or meeting him face to face in a fight?

Chorus. In the holy sanctuary of Apollo, with the men of Delphi.

Peleus. Oh. This is dangerous, and it is now. Will somebody go, as fast as he can, to the Pythian hearth and tell our friends there what is happening here, before Achilles's son is killed by his enemies?

(A Messenger comes in.)

Messenger. Oh, oh. What news I am bringing, and I am the unlucky one who has to bring it, to you, old man, and to everyone who loved my master.

Peleus. Aiai. My heart knows already. It is expecting something.

Messenger. You have no grandson, old Peleus. I am telling you plainly. That is how he is, cut with swords, by the men of Delphi and by the stranger from Mycenae.

Chorus. Ah, ah. What are you doing, old man? Do not fall. Hold yourself up.

Peleus. I am nothing. I am destroyed. My voice is gone, and the strength is gone out of my legs.

Messenger. Listen. If you want to avenge your own, straighten yourself up and hear what was done.

Peleus. Fate, how tightly you have wrapped me up, a miserable old man at the very end of his life. How did I lose him, the only son of my only son? Tell me. I do not want to hear it, and I want to hear it all the same.

Messenger. When we reached the famous ground of Apollo, we spent three bright circuits of the sun filling our eyes with the sights. And that, it turns out, was already suspicious. The people who live round the god's shrine began to gather in knots and circles, and Agamemnon's son went through the town whispering poison into every ear. "Do you see this man, walking in and out of the god's hollow chambers, the ones full of gold, the treasuries of the whole world? He is here for the second time, on the same errand he came on before. He wants to sack the temple of Apollo." And from that an angry surge ran through the city. The magistrates crowded into their council chambers, and the men who have charge of the god's property quietly posted a guard among the colonnades.

We knew nothing of any of this yet. We took sheep, reared on the leafy slopes of Parnassus, and went and stood at the altars, with our Delphian sponsors and the Pythian seers. And somebody said, "Young man, what shall we pray to the god for, on your behalf? What have you come for?" And he said, "I want to make amends to Apollo for a fault I committed before. I once demanded that he pay me for my father's blood." And right there Orestes's story showed how strong it was: that my master was lying, that he had come for something shameful.

He goes up inside the temple, onto its stone platform, to pray to Apollo in front of the oracle, and he is at the burnt offering. And there was an ambush waiting for him, men with swords, in the shade of the laurel, and Clytemnestra's son was one of them, the one who had stitched the whole plot together. My master stood in full view of everyone, praying to the god, and they, with their sharpened swords, stabbed Achilles's son from behind, and he had no armour on. He stepped back. He had not been hit anywhere that killed. He drew his sword, and he snatched the armour that was hanging on pegs on a pillar, and he stood on the altar, a soldier terrible to look at, and shouted at the sons of Delphi, asking them this: "Why are you killing me? I came here on a holy errand. What am I dying for?" And of all those thousands standing near, not one man said a word. They threw stones at him, instead, out of their hands.

Pounded from every side by a thick snowstorm of them, he held his armour out in front of him and guarded against the hits, stretching his shield out on this side and on that. It did no good. Everything was coming at him at once: arrows, javelins with throwing straps, spits with two points pulled loose from the fire, the butcher's knives they kill oxen with, landing in front of his feet. You would have seen your boy dance a terrible war dance then, dodging what they threw. And when they had him ringed round and were giving him no room to breathe, he left the altar hearth where the sheep are laid, and he leapt, the leap he leapt at Troy, straight at them. And they turned their backs and ran, like doves when they see the hawk. Many of them fell in the crush, from wounds, or trampled by each other in the narrow doorways, and a scream that had no holiness in it rose in that holy house and echoed off the rocks. And in a kind of calm my master stood there, shining in his bright armour.

Until a voice came out of the middle of the inner shrine, something terrible, something that made your skin creep, and it roused that crowd and turned them back to fight. Then Achilles's son fell. A Delphian struck him in the ribs with a sharpened sword, a Delphian killed him, with plenty of others to help. And when he fell to the ground, who did not bring a blade to him, who did not bring a stone, throwing, battering? That whole beautiful body was ruined with savage wounds. And when he was dead and lying beside the altar, they threw him out of the temple where the incense burns.

We snatched him up as fast as we could and we are bringing him to you, old man, to wail over and weep over, and to honour with a grave in the earth. That is what the lord who gives oracles to everyone else, the judge of right for all mankind, did to Achilles's son, when he was there to make amends. He remembered an old quarrel, the way a bad man does. So how can he be wise?

(The Messenger goes. The body of Neoptolemus is carried in on a bier.)

Chorus.
	And look, here is the king already, carried in,
	come from the land of Delphi to his home.
	Wretched the man it happened to, and wretched too,
	old man, are you. This is Achilles's cub
	you are taking into the house, and not the way you wanted.
	You have met with evil yourself,
	and fallen into one fate with him.
Peleus.
	Oh, what evil is this I am looking at,
	taking it into my hands and my house.
	Io moi moi. Aiai.
	City of Thessaly, we are destroyed,
	we are finished. There is no family left me now, no children
	left in the house.
	I am cursed with what I have suffered. Who is left,
	what friend, that I can turn my eyes to and be glad?
	Dear mouth, dear cheek, dear hands,
	if only a god had killed you under the walls of Troy
	beside the bank of the Simois.

Chorus. Then he would have died with honour, old man, and you would have been the happier for it.

Peleus.
	Marriage, marriage, you have destroyed
	this house and my city. Aiai.
	E, e. My child,
	if only that marriage with its cursed name
	had never wrapped my family, my children and my house,
	in the death that Hermione brought
	down on you, child.
	If only the lightning had killed her first.
	And if only you, a man, had never fastened
	on a god, on Apollo, the blame for the arrow that killed
	your father, the son of a god.
Chorus.
	Ottototoi. My master is dead. I begin the lament,
	the way the custom is
	for those who are gone below.
Peleus.
	Ottototoi. And I take it up after you, wretched as I am,
	an old man
	with no luck left, and I weep.
Chorus.
	It was a god's decree. A god brought this disaster about.
Peleus.
	Dear one,
	you have left the house empty.
	Oh, oh, and left me wretched,
	an old man with no children.
Chorus.
	You should have died, old man, died before your children.
Peleus.
	Shall I not tear my hair?
	Shall I not bring down on my head
	the deadly blow of my own hand? City,
	Apollo has robbed me
	of both my children.
Chorus.
	You have suffered so much evil, and seen so much, unlucky old man.
	What life
	will you have from now on?
Peleus.
	No children. Alone. No end to the evil.
	I will drain out
	my sorrows to the last drop, down to Hades.
Chorus.
	For nothing, then, the gods blessed you on your wedding day.
Peleus.
	Flown away,
	all of it gone. It lies
	far short of the high boasts.
Chorus.
	Alone, in a lonely house, you go up and down.
Peleus.
	You are gone, city, city.
	And this sceptre, let it go, down on the ground.
	And you, daughter of Nereus, in your cave in the dark,
	you will see me
	utterly destroyed, falling to the earth.
Chorus.
	Io, io.
	What is that moving? What god am I feeling near?
	Girls, look, look up.
	Some god is being ferried through the white air
	and coming down onto the plains of Phthia,
	where the horses graze.

(Thetis appears above the house.)

Thetis. Peleus, for the sake of the marriage we made long ago, I have come. I am Thetis, and I have left the house of Nereus. First, I tell you not to take the trouble you are in too hard.
