I too, who ought to have borne children I would never have to weep for, have lost the son I had by you, Achilles, the fast runner, the first man in Greece. Now I will tell you why I have come, and you listen.

Take this dead man, Achilles's son, to the Pythian hearth and bury him there, a reproach to Delphi, so that his grave announces the violent murder done by Orestes's hand. As for the prisoner, Andromache I mean, she must go and live in the land of the Molossians, old man, joined in a lawful marriage to Helenus, and this boy with her, the last of the line of Aeacus. From him a line of kings must come down, one after another, and rule Molossia in prosperity. Because your family and mine, old man, is not to be uprooted like this. Nor is Troy's. The gods care about Troy too, even though it fell, because Pallas Athena was set on it.

And you, so that you will know what it was worth to have shared my bed, I, a goddess born and the daughter of a god, will set free from everything that mortals suffer, and make you a god, immortal and unfading. And from then on you will live with me in the house of Nereus, a god with a goddess, for the rest of time. From there you will walk out of the sea with dry feet and see the son you and I loved best, Achilles, living in his island home on the White Shore, inside the Black Sea. But now go to Delphi, the city the gods built, and take this body with you, and when you have buried him in the earth, come back and sit down in the hollow of the old rock of Sepias, in the cave there, and wait, until I come out of the sea with fifty daughters of Nereus, dancing, to escort you. What is fated must be carried through. This is what Zeus has decided. And stop grieving for the dead. This is the vote the gods have passed on every human being. Everyone owes a death.

Peleus. Lady. Noble wife who shared my bed, daughter of Nereus, I salute you. What you are doing is worthy of you, and of the children who came from you. I stop my grieving, goddess, since you order it, and when I have buried this boy I will go to the glens of Pelion, where I first took your beautiful body in my arms.

So. Should a man with any sense not marry out of a good family, and give his daughter to good men, and have no appetite for a bad wife, not even if she brings a fortune into the house with her? Then the gods would never make things go badly for him.

(Thetis vanishes. Peleus follows the body out.)

Chorus.
	Many are the shapes of what the gods do,
	and many the things they bring about that no one expected.
	What we counted on did not happen,
	and for what no one counted on, a god found a way.
	That is how this business ended.

Hecuba (c. 424 BC)

Hecuba

(The Greek camp on the shore of the Thracian Chersonese, in front of Agamemnon's tent. The Ghost of Polydorus appears.)

Ghost of Polydorus. I have come from the hiding place of the dead and the gates of darkness, where Hades lives apart from the other gods. I am Polydorus, the son of Hecuba, the daughter of Cisseus, and of Priam. When the city of the Phrygians was in danger of falling to the Greek spear, my father was afraid, and he sent me secretly out of the land of Troy to the house of Polymestor, his Thracian guest-friend, who sows this rich flat country of the Chersonese and rules a horse-loving people with his spear. And my father sent a great deal of gold out with me, in secret, so that if the walls of Ilium ever fell, the children who survived him would not go short of the means to live. I was the youngest of Priam's sons, and that was why he smuggled me out of the country: with a boy's arm I could carry neither armour nor spear. So as long as the boundary stones of our land stood upright, and the towers of Troy were unbroken, and my brother Hector was winning with his spear, I grew up well in the house of the Thracian, my father's guest-friend, and did well on his care, like a young shoot. Poor fool that I was. But when Troy was destroyed, and Hector's life with it, and my father's hearth was dug up out of the ground, and he himself fell at the god-built altar, butchered by the murderous son of Achilles, then my father's guest-friend killed me, for the sake of the gold. He killed a helpless boy, and when he had killed me he threw me into the swell of the sea, so that he could keep the gold in his own house. I lie on the beach, and then again in the surge of the sea, carried up and down on the long back-and-forth of the waves, unwept, unburied. And now I have left my body behind and I am hovering over my dear mother Hecuba, and this is the third day I have hung in the air, all the time my poor mother has been here in this land, the Chersonese, since she came from Troy.

All the Achaeans are sitting quietly by their ships on the shore of this Thracian country, because the son of Peleus, Achilles, appeared above his tomb and held back the whole Greek army as they were steering their oars for home across the sea. He is asking for my sister Polyxena, to have her slaughtered at his tomb as his victim and his prize of honour. And he will get it. The men who were his friends will not send him away without his gift. Fate is leading my sister to her death this very day. So my mother will look on the corpses of two children at once, mine and my poor sister's. Because I am going to appear, so that I can get the grave I am so wretched without: I will show up in the shallows at the feet of a slave woman. I begged this from the powers below, that I might get a tomb and fall into my mother's hands. So what I wanted for myself will come about. Now I will get out of the way of old Hecuba. Here she comes, stepping out from under Agamemnon's tent, terrified by my ghost.

Ah. Mother. You came from a king's house and lived to see the day of slavery. You are as badly off now as you were once well off. Some god is weighing your old good fortune against you, and destroying you to balance the scale.

(The Ghost goes. Hecuba comes out of Agamemnon's tent, held up by captive Trojan women.)

Hecuba.
	Lead the old woman out in front of the tent, children,
	lead her, hold her upright, Trojan women,
	your fellow slave now, and once your queen.
	Take me, carry me, guide me, lift me up,
	hold me by my old hand,
	and I will lean on the crooked staff of your arm
	and hurry my slow-footed
	walk along, one joint in front of the other.
	Oh lightning of Zeus. Oh darkness of night.
	Why am I lifted up like this in the night
	by terrors, by phantoms? Oh lady Earth,
	mother of the black-winged dreams,
	I send this vision of the night away from me,
	the one about my son, who is being kept safe in Thrace,
	and about Polyxena, my dear daughter,
	the terrible sight I saw in my dreams and learned and understood.
	Gods of the earth below, keep my son safe.
	He is the only anchor my house has left,
	and he is in snowy Thrace,
	in the keeping of his father's guest-friend.
	Something new is coming.
	A song of grief is coming for women who grieve.
	Never before has my heart been so relentless,
	shivering, afraid.
	Where, Trojan women, can I find
	the inspired soul of Helenus, or Cassandra,
	to read my dreams for me?
	I saw a dappled deer with a wolf's bloody claw in its throat,
	dragged from my knees without pity, and slaughtered.
	And this frightens me too: over the very top
	of his tomb
	came the ghost of Achilles, and he asked for a prize,
	one of the Trojan women who have suffered so much.
	Away from my child, away from my child, send this thing,
	you powers, I beg you.

(The Chorus of captive Trojan women comes in.)

Chorus.
	Hecuba, I have slipped away to you in a hurry,
	leaving my master's tent,
	where the lot assigned me and posted me
	as a slave, driven out of the city
	of Ilium, hunted down at the point
	of the Achaeans' spears.
	I bring nothing to lighten what you suffer.
	I have picked up a heavy load of news
	for you, lady, and I am the herald of your pain.
	In the full assembly of the Achaeans, they say,
	it was decided to make your daughter
	a sacrifice to Achilles. You know how he stood
	on his tomb and appeared in his golden armour
	and held back the sea-going ships,
	with their sails already straining at the ropes,
	and shouted this:
	"Where are you off to, Greeks, leaving
	my tomb without its prize?"
	And a wave of quarrelling broke,
	and opinion split in two through the Greek
	army of spearmen, some for giving
	the tomb its victim, some against.
	There was one man working hard for your good,
	Agamemnon, who keeps the bed
	of the god-possessed prophetess.
	But the two sons of Theseus, shoots of Athens,
	made two different speeches
	and agreed on one judgement:
	to crown the tomb of Achilles
	with fresh blood. They said they would never
	put Cassandra's bed
	ahead of the spear of Achilles.
	The heat of the argument, pulled tight,
	was about equal, until that shifty-minded
	chatterer, that sweet-talker, that pleaser of crowds,
	the son of Laertes, persuaded the army
	not to push aside the best of all the Greeks
	for the sake of a slave's throat,
	and not to have one of the dead
	standing beside Persephone
	say that the Greeks had left the plains of Troy
	ungrateful to the Greeks
	who died for Greece.
	Odysseus will be here any moment now,
	to drag the foal from your breast
	and tear her out of your old hand.
	Go to the temples, go to the altars,
	sit at Agamemnon's knees as a suppliant,
	call on the gods, the ones in heaven
	and the ones under the earth.
	Either your prayers will keep you
	from being robbed of your poor child,
	or you must watch a girl fall forward on the tomb,
	reddened with blood
	from her gold-hung throat
	in a dark, shining stream.
Hecuba.
	Oh, I am wretched. What sound can I make?
	What cry, what wail,
	miserable in a miserable old age,
	in a slavery that cannot be endured,
	cannot be borne? Oh.
	Who will defend me? What family,
	what city? The old man is gone,
	the children are gone.
	Which way am I to go, this way or that?
	Where can I hurry to? Where is any god
	or power to help me?
	Oh, you who have brought me evil,
	Trojan women, you who have brought me
	evil and pain, you have destroyed me, destroyed me. Life
	in the light is nothing I want any more.
	Poor foot, lead me,
	lead an old woman
	to this tent. Oh child, oh daughter
	of the most wretched mother alive, come out, come out
	of the tent. Hear your mother's voice.
	Oh child, so that you know what it is, what it is
	I am hearing said about your life.
Polyxena.
	Io.
	Mother, mother, why are you shouting? What news
	have you cried out, that you have scared me out of the tent
	like a bird, with this fright?
Hecuba.
	Oh, my child.
Polyxena.
	Why do you speak to me in that voice of bad omen? It is an evil beginning.
Hecuba.
	Aiai, your life.
Polyxena.
	Say it. Do not hide it any longer.
	I am afraid, I am afraid, mother,
	of why you are groaning like this.
Hecuba.
	Oh child, child of a wretched mother.
Polyxena.
	What is this you are going to tell me?
Hecuba.
	The Greeks have made up one mind
	and are straining to cut your throat at the tomb
	for the son of Peleus.
Polyxena.
	Oh, mother, how can you say
	such unenviable evils? Tell me,
	tell me, mother.
Hecuba.
	I am telling you, child, a report of bad omen.
	They bring me word that the Argives have voted
	and decided about your life.
Polyxena.
	Oh, you who have suffered terrible things, oh, all-wretched,
	oh, mother of a miserable life,
	what is this, what is this outrage now,
	most hateful, unspeakable,
	that some power has stirred up against you?
	No longer is this daughter yours, no longer
	will I share your slavery, wretched beside
	your wretched old age.
	Like a cub, like a calf reared on the mountain,
	you will see me, wretched woman, wretched girl,
	torn out of your hand,
	my throat cut, sent down to Hades
	under the dark of the earth, where among the dead
	I will lie, poor thing.
	And for you, mother, in your misery,
	I cry with every lament I have,
	but for my own life, its outrage and its ruin,
	I shed no tear. For me, dying
	has turned out the better fortune.

Chorus. And here is Odysseus, walking fast, Hecuba, coming to tell you something new.

(Odysseus comes in with attendants.)

Odysseus. Lady, I think you already know what the army has decided and the vote that has been passed, but I will tell you all the same. The Achaeans have voted to slaughter your daughter Polyxena on the high mound of Achilles' grave. They have appointed me to escort the girl and bring her there. The son of Achilles will preside over the sacrifice and act as priest. So you know what to do? Do not make us tear her away by force, and do not get into a wrestling match with me. Know how much strength you have, and know the trouble you are in. Even in bad times, it is clever to think the thoughts you have to think.

Hecuba. Aiai. So a great struggle is here, it seems, full of groaning and not short of tears. And so I did not die where I should have died. Zeus did not destroy me. He is keeping me alive, so that I can look at evils worse than the evils before, wretch that I am.

But if slaves may put questions to free men, questions that do not hurt them or bite at their hearts, then you should speak now and answer, and we who are asking should hear.

Odysseus. You may. Ask. I do not grudge you the time.

Hecuba. Do you remember when you came to Troy as a spy, ugly in filthy rags, with drops of blood running from your eyes down your chin?

Odysseus. I remember. It touched more than the surface of my heart.

Hecuba. And Helen recognised you, and told me, and only me?

Odysseus. I remember. I was in great danger.

Hecuba. And you took hold of my knees, and made yourself humble?

Odysseus. So humble that my hand went dead, gripping your dress.

Hecuba. And I saved you, and I sent you out of the country?

Odysseus. You did. That is why I see this light of the sun.

Hecuba. And what did you say then, when you were my slave?

Odysseus. I found a great many things to say, so as not to die.

Hecuba. Then are you not a coward, with these plans of yours? You had from me exactly what you say you had, and you do us no good in return and all the harm you can. You are an ungrateful breed, all of you who chase the honours of a public speaker. I wish I had never known you. You hurt your friends and think nothing of it, as long as you can say something to please the crowd.

But tell me, what kind of clever move did they think it was, when they voted death for this child? Was it duty that pushed them to slaughter a human being at a tomb, where an ox is the proper thing to kill? Or is it that Achilles wants to kill the people who killed him, and is aiming at her, with justice on his side? But she never did him any harm. It is Helen he should have asked for, as the victim for his grave. She destroyed him. She is the one who brought him to Troy. And if some prisoner has to be picked out to die, one who is outstanding in beauty, that does not point to us. The daughter of Tyndareus is the most striking to look at, and she was found to have done him no less wrong than we did. That is the argument I set against him, on the question of justice.

Now hear what you owe me in return, since I am asking for it. You took hold of my hand, by your own account, and you fell at my feet and touched this old cheek. Now I take hold of you in the same way, at the same places, and I ask for the favour I did you then, and I beg you: do not tear my child out of my arms. Do not kill her. There are dead enough. She is my joy, and I forget my troubles in her. She is my comfort for everything I have lost. She is my city, my nurse, my walking stick, my guide on the road. Those who have power should not use it for what is wrong, and those who are doing well should not think they will do well forever. I was somebody once, and now I am not any more. One day took all my happiness away.

Oh, by your beard, my friend, have some respect for me, have some pity. Go to the Achaean army and talk them round. Tell them how hateful it is to kill women you did not kill the first time, when you dragged them from the altars, but pitied instead. Among you the law about bloodshed is the same for the free and for slaves. Your standing will persuade them, even if you argue badly. The same speech from a nobody and from a man of reputation does not carry the same weight.

Chorus. No human nature is so hard that it could hear your groans, your long laments, your cries of grief, and not let fall a tear.

Odysseus. Hecuba, let me teach you something, and do not, because you are angry, make an enemy in your mind of a man who is talking sense. Your life, the body that did me a good turn, I am ready to save, and I say nothing different. But what I said in front of everybody I will not deny: that when Troy was taken, your daughter should be given as a victim to the first man of the army, since he asked for her. Here is where most cities go wrong: when a man who is good and willing gets nothing more than worse men do. To us, lady, Achilles is worth honouring. He died for the land of Greece, and died as well as a man can. Is it not a disgrace, if we use a man as a friend while he can see, and once he is dead, use him no more? Well then. What will people say, if once again the army musters and there is a fight with an enemy? Will we fight, or will we love our own lives, seeing the dead man gets no honour? As for me, while I live, if I had only a little to live on each day, I would have enough. But I would want my tomb to be seen to be honoured. That gratitude lasts a long time.

You say you suffer pitiably. Here is my answer. On our side there are old women and old men no less wretched than you, and young wives robbed of the best of husbands, whose bodies this dust of Ida covers. Bear it. As for us, if we are wrong to think we should honour the brave, we will be charged with stupidity. But you barbarians, go on not counting your friends as friends, and go on not admiring the men who died well, so that Greece may prosper, and you may have what your policies deserve.

Chorus. Aiai. To be a slave is always an evil thing. It puts up with what it should not, because force wins.

Hecuba. Daughter, my words about your death are gone, thrown into the air for nothing. But you, if you have some power greater than your mother's, hurry, let out every note like a nightingale's mouth, and do not be robbed of your life. Fall at the knee of this man Odysseus and make him pity you, and beg him. You have a reason to give: he has children too. Make him pity what has happened to you.

Polyxena. I see you, Odysseus, hiding your right hand under your cloak and turning your face away, so that I cannot touch your beard. Do not worry. You have escaped my Zeus, the god of suppliants. I will follow you, because I must, and because I want to die. If I were unwilling, I would show myself a coward, a woman in love with her own life. Why should I live? My father was king of all the Phrygians. That was the start of my life. Then I was brought up on fine hopes, a bride for kings, with no small rivalry over my marriage, over whose house and hearth I would come to. And I was mistress, poor thing, of the women of Ida, a girl that women and girls looked up to, equal to a goddess except for one thing: death. And now I am a slave. First of all the name makes me want to die. It is not a name I am used to. And then I might get a master with a savage heart, whoever buys me for silver, me, the sister of Hector and of so many others. He would put me to grinding grain in his house whether I liked it or not, and sweeping his floors, and standing at the loom, dragging through wretched days. And some slave, bought from who knows where, would dirty my bed, the bed that was once thought worthy of kings. No. I give up this light with eyes that are still free, and I hand my body over to Hades. Take me, Odysseus, and finish me off when you have taken me. I see nothing here, no hope and no expectation, to give me any confidence that I will ever be happy again. Mother, do not stand in my way, not with a word, not with an act. Agree with me that I should die before I meet with shameful things I do not deserve. Someone who is not used to tasting evils bears it, but it hurts to put her neck in the yoke. She would be far luckier dead than alive. To live without honour is heavy labour.

Chorus. It is a wonderful stamp, and a plain one, among mortals, to be born of good parents, and the name of good birth goes further still in those who deserve it.

Hecuba. You spoke well, daughter, but there is pain in the fine words. Odysseus, if you must do the son of Peleus a favour and escape blame, do not kill this girl. Take me to the pyre of Achilles and stab me. Do not spare me. I bore Paris, who shot the son of Thetis with his arrows and destroyed him.

Odysseus. It was not your death, old woman, that Achilles' ghost asked the Achaeans for. It was hers.

Hecuba. Then at least kill me together with my daughter, and there will be twice as much blood to drink for the earth and for the dead man who demands it.

Odysseus. Your daughter's death is enough. We need not add one death to another. I wish we did not owe this one.

Hecuba. I am absolutely bound to die with my daughter.

Odysseus. How? I did not know I had a master.

Hecuba. Like ivy on an oak. That is how I will hold on to her.

Odysseus. Not if you listen to people who are wiser than you.

Hecuba. I will not let go of this child of my own free will.

Odysseus. And I will not go away and leave her here either.

Polyxena. Mother, listen to me. And you, son of Laertes, go easy on a parent who has every reason to be angry. And you, poor mother, do not fight the people who have power over us. Do you want to be thrown to the ground, and tear your old skin, pushed about by force, and to be dragged off shamefully by a young man's arm? That is what will happen. Do not. It is not worthy of you. No, my dear mother, give me your sweet hand, and let me lay my cheek against your cheek. Because never again, but now for the very last time, I will look at the rays of the sun and its round disc. You are hearing the last of my words to you. Oh mother, oh you who bore me, I am going down below now.

Hecuba. Oh daughter. And I will go on living in the light, as a slave.

Polyxena. No bridegroom, no wedding song, none of what should have been mine.

Hecuba. You are pitiful, child, and I am a wretched woman.

Polyxena. And there in Hades I will lie apart from you.

Hecuba. Oh. What am I going to do? Where will I end my life?

Polyxena. I will die a slave, and my father was a free man.

Hecuba. And I, of fifty children, have not one.

Polyxena. What shall I say for you to Hector, or to your old husband?

Hecuba. Tell them I am the most wretched of all women.

Polyxena. Oh breast, oh the breasts that fed me so sweetly.

Hecuba. Oh daughter, oh your wretched fate, before your time.

Polyxena. Goodbye, you who bore me. Goodbye, Cassandra, from me.

Hecuba. Others say goodbye and fare well. There is no faring well for your mother.

Polyxena. And my brother Polydorus, among the horse-loving Thracians.

Hecuba. If he is alive. I doubt it. I have no luck in anything.

Polyxena. He is alive, and when you die he will close your eyes.

Hecuba. I am dead already. My troubles have killed me before my death.

Polyxena. Take me, Odysseus, and put my robe over my head. Before my throat is cut, my mother's laments have melted my heart already, and I am melting hers with my crying. Oh light. I can still speak your name, but I have no share in you except the time it takes me to walk between the sword and the pyre of Achilles.

(Odysseus and his men lead Polyxena away.)

Hecuba. Oh, I am fainting. My limbs are giving way. Daughter, touch your mother, reach out your hand, give it to me. Do not leave me childless. I am destroyed, friends. If only I could see the Spartan woman like this, Helen, sister of the sons of Zeus. With her beautiful eyes she brought Troy down, Troy that was happy once, in the ugliest way there is.

(Hecuba sinks to the ground.)

Chorus.
	Breeze, breeze off the sea,
	you who carry the quick ships
	over the swell of the water,
	where will you take me, in my misery?
	Whose house will I come to, bought,
	to be a slave in it? To a harbour
	in the Dorian land?
	Or to Phthia, where they say
	the Apidanus, father of the loveliest waters,
	makes the plains fat and rich?
Chorus.
	Or to the islands, sent on my miserable way
	by an oar that sweeps the salt,
	to a pitiful life in someone's house,
	where the first palm tree ever born, and the laurel,
	lifted their holy branches
	for Leto, whom they loved,
	the glory of her labour, when she bore the children of Zeus?
	And there, with the girls of Delos,
	will I sing of the golden headband
	and the bow of Artemis, their goddess?
Chorus.
	Or in the city of Pallas,
	on the saffron robe of Athena
	of the lovely chariot,
	will I yoke her horses, working them
	into the web in threads of many colours,
	bright as flowers? Or the race of the Titans,
	that Zeus, the son of Cronos,
	puts to sleep with his fire
	that burns from both ends?
Chorus.
	Oh, my children,
	oh, my fathers, and my country,
	crumbling in smoke,
	smouldering, taken by the spear
	of the Argives. And I, on foreign
	soil, am called a slave now,
	leaving Asia behind
	for a house in Europe,
	which is a bedroom in Hades.

(Talthybius, the herald of the Greek army, comes in. He is an old man.)

Talthybius. Where can I find Hecuba, who was queen of Troy once, girls of Troy?

Chorus. Here, Talthybius, close by you. She is lying on her back on the ground, wrapped up in her clothes.

Talthybius. Zeus, what am I to say? That you watch over human beings? Or that we hold this belief for nothing, and it is false, and there is no race of gods at all, and it is chance that oversees everything that happens to mortals? Was this not the queen of the Phrygians, with all their gold? Was this not the wife of Priam, the greatly blessed? And now the whole city has been torn up by the spear, and she lies on the ground, a slave, an old woman with no children, fouling her poor head in the dust. Pheu, pheu. I am an old man, but let me die before I fall into some shameful piece of luck like this. Get up, poor woman. Lift your side off the ground, and that head, all white.

Hecuba. Ah. Who is this, who will not let my body lie? Whoever you are, why are you moving me, when I am grieving?

Talthybius. I am Talthybius, the servant of the Greeks. Agamemnon sent me to fetch you, lady.

Hecuba. Dearest man. Have the Achaeans decided to kill me too, at the grave? Is that what you have come for? What a welcome thing to say. Let us hurry. Let us be quick. Lead the way, old man.

Talthybius. I have come to fetch you so that you can bury your daughter, lady. She is dead. The two sons of Atreus sent me, and the Achaean people.

Hecuba. Oh. What are you going to say? So you did not come to fetch us to die, but to bring bad news? You are gone, child, snatched away from your mother. And I have no children now, as far as you are concerned. Oh, wretched woman that I am. How did you finish her? Did you show her any respect? Or did you come at the terrible thing as if she were an enemy, old man, and kill her that way? Tell me, even though what you say will not be kind.

Talthybius. Lady, you want me to earn a double set of tears, out of pity for your daughter. I will wet these eyes now, telling the bad news, as I did at the tomb when she was dying.

The whole crowd of the Achaean army was there, at full strength, in front of the tomb, for your daughter's slaughter. The son of Achilles took Polyxena by the hand and stood her on the top of the mound, and I was close by. Picked young men, the pick of the Achaeans, came behind, to hold your young heifer down with their hands if she kicked. Then Achilles' son took a full cup, all gold, in his hands and lifted it, a drink offering to his dead father, and he signalled to me to proclaim silence to the whole Achaean army. I took my place in the middle of them and said this: "Silence, Achaeans. Let the whole people be silent. Silence. Quiet." And I settled the crowd until there was not a breath of wind in it. Then he spoke. "Son of Peleus, my father, accept from me these offerings that soothe the dead and draw them up. Come, and drink the black, unmixed blood of a girl, which the army and I are giving you. Be kind to us. Let us loose the sterns and the cables of our ships, and grant us all a kind homecoming from Troy, and let us all come home to our own country." That is what he said, and the whole army prayed with him.

Then he took his sword, with the gold on the hilt, by the handle, and drew it from the sheath, and nodded to the picked young men of the Argive army to take hold of the girl. And she, when she realised, spoke these words: "Argives, who sacked my city, I die of my own free will. Let no one touch my body. I will offer my neck with a good heart. By the gods, let me go free when you kill me, so that I die free. I am a king's daughter, and I am ashamed to be called a slave among the dead." The people roared their approval, and King Agamemnon told the young men to let the girl go. And as soon as they heard that last word from the man whose power was greatest, they let go. And when she heard what her masters had said, she took her dress at the top of the shoulder and tore it down to the middle of her side, beside the navel, and showed her breasts and her chest, lovely as a statue's, and she sank on one knee to the ground and spoke the bravest words of all: "Look. Here. If it is my chest you want to strike, young man, strike. If you want it under the neck, here is my throat, ready." And he, not wanting to and wanting to, out of pity for the girl, cut through the channels of her breath with the iron, and the springs ran. And she, even as she died, took great care to fall decently, hiding what should be hidden from the eyes of men.

When she had let go her breath in the deadly slaughter, no two Argives had the same task. Some of them threw leaves on the dead girl from their hands. Others were heaping up a pyre, carrying logs of pine, and the man who carried nothing heard things like this from the man who did: "Are you standing there, you worthless man, with no dress and no ornament in your hands for the girl? Are you not going to give something to the girl with the great heart beyond all others, the best in spirit?" That is what I have to say about your daughter's death, and I see you as the most blessed of all women in your children, and the most unlucky.

Chorus. Some terrible trouble has boiled over onto the sons of Priam and onto my city. The gods forced it on us.

Hecuba. Daughter, I do not know which of my evils to look at. There are so many here. If I take hold of one, this one will not let me, and then another grief calls me over from there, evil taking over from evil. And now I cannot wipe what happened to you out of my mind so as not to groan for it. But you have taken the edge off it, reported to me as noble. Is it not strange? Bad soil, if it gets its season from the gods, bears a good crop, and good soil, if it misses what it ought to get, gives bad fruit. But among human beings the worthless man is never anything but bad, and the good man is good, and no disaster ruins his nature: he is decent always. Is it the parents that make the difference, or the upbringing? Being brought up well does teach a man goodness, though; and if someone learns that lesson well, he knows what is shameful, because he has learned it by the measuring rod of the good. My mind has been shooting those arrows into the air for nothing.

You, go and tell the Argives this: no one is to touch my daughter. Keep the crowd away. In an army of tens of thousands the mob has no discipline, and sailors' lawlessness is stronger than fire, and the man who does no harm is the bad one.

(Talthybius goes.)

And you, old servant, take a jar, dip it in the salt sea and bring it here, so that I can wash my child in her last bath, a bride who is no bride, a virgin who is no virgin, and lay her out. As she deserves? Where would I get the means? I could not. But as I can. What else is there for me? And I will gather ornaments from the captive women who live beside me inside these tents, if any of them has stolen something out of her own house without her new masters knowing.

(The old Maid goes off towards the shore with the jar.)

Shape of a house. House that was happy once. Priam, who had the most of everything and the finest of it, the most blessed of fathers, and I, this old woman, the mother of your children: how we have come to nothing, stripped of the pride we had. And then we puff ourselves up, one of us in a rich house, another with a name for honour among the citizens. Those things are nothing. Plans in the mind, and boasting with the tongue. The happiest man is the one who meets nothing bad, day by day.

(Hecuba goes into the tent.)

Chorus.
	It had to come to me, disaster,
	it had to come to me, grief,
	the day Paris first cut
	the pine on Mount Ida
	to sail over the swell of the sea
	to Helen's bed, the loveliest woman
	the Sun with his golden light
	shines on.
Chorus.
	Because troubles, and harder than troubles,
	necessities, are wheeling round,
	and out of one man's folly came an evil
	shared by all, and deadly, to the land of Simois,
	and disaster from other men's hands.
	The quarrel was judged, the one that Paris,
	a cowherd then, judged on Ida
	between three daughters of the blessed gods,
Chorus.
	and it ended in the spear, and killing, and the wrecking of my house.
	And a Spartan girl is groaning too,
	weeping her eyes out, at home
	beside the lovely stream of the Eurotas,
	and a mother whose sons are dead
	lays her hand on her grey head
	and tears at her cheeks,
	and her nails are bloody with the tearing.

(The Maid comes back from the shore. Women come with her, carrying a body under a cloth.)

Maid. Women, where is Hecuba? Where is the most miserable woman alive, who beats every man and every woman ever born at suffering? Nobody is going to take that crown from her.

Chorus. What now, you poor woman, with your ugly shouting? Your painful announcements never sleep.

Maid. I am bringing Hecuba this pain. In evil times it is not easy for a mortal mouth to speak good words.

Chorus. Look, she is just coming out of the tent. She is appearing at the right moment for what you have to say.

(Hecuba comes out of the tent.)

Maid. Mistress. Wretched beyond everything, and more than I can say. You are destroyed, you no longer exist, though you are looking at the light. No children, no husband, no city. Wiped out.

Hecuba. That is nothing new. You are throwing it at people who know. But why have you come, bringing me this corpse, Polyxena's, when I was told the whole Achaean army was busy with her burial, hand to hand?

Maid. She knows nothing. She is mourning Polyxena to me, and she has not touched the new trouble.

Hecuba. Oh, wretched woman. You are not bringing me the frenzied head of Cassandra, the god-singer, here?

Maid. The one you cry out for is alive. It is the dead one here you are not groaning for. Look at the body, uncovered, and see if it strikes you as a wonder, and past all your hopes.

(She draws back the cloth.)

Hecuba. Oh. I see my son dead. Polydorus, whom the Thracian was keeping safe for me in his house. I am destroyed, wretched woman, I no longer exist. Child, child, aiai, I begin the dirge, a frenzied song I learned just now from an avenging spirit.

Maid. So you knew your son's ruin, poor woman?

Hecuba. Unbelievable, unbelievable, new, new, what I see. Evils are coming one out of another, evils out of evils. Never a day without a groan, without a tear, will hold me again.

Chorus. Terrible, poor woman. Terrible, what we are suffering.

Hecuba.
	Child, child of a miserable mother,
	how did you die? What death
	lays you here?
	At whose hands, of all men?
Maid.
	I do not know. I found him on the shore of the sea.
Hecuba.
	Thrown up by the waves, or fallen there,
	killed by a bloody spear,
	on the smooth sand?
Maid.
	The open swell of the sea carried him out onto the beach.
Hecuba.
	Oh, aiai. I understand the dream my eyes saw
	in my sleep. It did not pass me by,
	the black-winged ghost, the one I saw around you,
	child, no longer alive in the light of Zeus.

Chorus. Then who killed him? Can you read your dream and say?

Hecuba. My guest. Mine. The Thracian horseman, in whose house his old father put him away and hid him.

Chorus. Oh. What are you going to say? He killed him to keep the gold?

Hecuba.
	Unspeakable. Unnameable. Past all wondering at.
	Not holy, not to be borne. Where is the justice between guest and host?
	Cursed man, worst of men, how you carved up
	his flesh, cutting with an iron sword
	the limbs of this child, and felt no pity.

Chorus. Poor woman. Whatever god is heavy on you has made you the most suffering of mortals. But I see the shape of our master, Agamemnon, coming. From here on, friends, let us be quiet.

(Agamemnon comes in.)

Agamemnon. Hecuba, why are you delaying? Why have you not come to hide your daughter in her grave, on the terms Talthybius brought me from you, that none of the Argives should touch your girl? We let her be, then, and we did not touch her. But you are taking your time, and I am amazed at it. I have come to send you on your way. Everything over there has been well done, if any of this is well. Ah. What man is this I see by the tents, a dead Trojan? He is no Argive. The clothes wrapped round his body tell me that.

Hecuba. Wretched woman. I mean myself, Hecuba, when I say you. What am I to do? Fall at Agamemnon's knees here, or carry my troubles in silence?

Agamemnon. Why have you turned your back to my face? Why are you crying, and not saying what has happened? Who is this?

Hecuba. But if he thinks of me as a slave and an enemy, and pushes me away from his knees, I would be adding pain to pain.

Agamemnon. I was not born a prophet. If I am not told, I cannot trace the road your thoughts are taking.

Hecuba. Am I reckoning this man's mind as more hostile than it is, when he is not hostile at all?

Agamemnon. If you want me to know nothing about this, we have arrived at the same place. I have no wish to hear it either.

Hecuba. Without this man I could not avenge my children. Why am I turning it over and over? I have to have the nerve, whether I win or not. Agamemnon, I beg you, by these knees, and by your beard, and by your fortunate right hand.

Agamemnon. Looking for what? Not to make your life free? That is easy enough for you.

Hecuba. No, not that. Let me punish the wicked, and I am willing to be a slave for the whole of my life.

Agamemnon. Well then, what are you calling on us to help with?

Hecuba. None of the things you are thinking of, my lord. Do you see this corpse, that I am dripping tears on?

Agamemnon. I see it. But what comes next I cannot make out.

Hecuba. I gave birth to him once. I carried him under my belt.

Agamemnon. Which of your children is this, poor woman?

Hecuba. Not one of Priam's sons who died under the walls of Troy.

Agamemnon. You had another son, then, besides them, lady?

Hecuba. For no good, as it turns out. This one, that you are looking at.

Agamemnon. Where did he happen to be when the city was being destroyed?

Hecuba. His father sent him away, for fear he would die.

Agamemnon. Where did he send him, alone, apart from the children he had then?

Hecuba. To this country, where he was found dead.

Agamemnon. To the man who rules this land? Polymestor?

Hecuba. He was sent here to keep gold. The bitterest gold there ever was.

Agamemnon. And who killed him? What death did he meet?

Hecuba. Who else? His Thracian host destroyed him.

Agamemnon. Poor woman. Was he so greedy to get the gold?

Hecuba. Exactly that, once he learned of the Phrygians' disaster.

Agamemnon. Where did you find him? Or did someone bring the body?

Hecuba. This woman. She came upon him on the seashore.

Agamemnon. Looking for him, or busy with some other work?

Hecuba. She had gone to fetch water from the sea, to wash Polyxena.

Agamemnon. So his host killed him, it seems, and threw him out.

Hecuba. To drift in the sea. After cutting up his body like this.

Agamemnon. Cruel, what you have suffered. Troubles without measure.

Hecuba. I am destroyed, Agamemnon. There is no evil left.

Agamemnon. Pheu, pheu. What woman was ever born so unlucky?

Hecuba. There is none, unless you mean Luck herself. But hear why I am falling at your knees. If you think what I have suffered is what the gods allow, I will put up with it. But if you think the opposite, then be my avenger on this man, the most godless of hosts, who feared neither the gods below the earth nor the gods above, and did the most godless thing. He sat at my table many times. He was counted first among my friends in the tally of guest-friendship. He had everything he should have had, and then he took his precautions and killed my son. And having chosen to kill him, he did not think him worth a grave, but threw him into the sea.

We are slaves, then, and weak, perhaps. But the gods are strong, and so is what rules over them: Law. It is by law that we believe in the gods at all, and live our lives with right and wrong marked out. If that law comes up to you for judgement and is destroyed, if the men who kill their guests, or have the nerve to carry off the holy things of the gods, do not pay for it, then there is nothing fair left anywhere among human beings. Count this as a disgrace, then, and have some respect for me. Pity us. Stand back from me like a painter from his picture, and look at me, and look closely at the evils I have. I was a queen once, and now I am your slave. I had fine children once, and now I am old, and childless at the same time, with no city, alone, the most wretched of mortals.

(Agamemnon turns away.)

Oh, wretched woman. Where are you drawing your foot away from me? It seems I will get nothing. Oh, poor woman that I am. Why is it that we mortals labour at all the other kinds of knowledge, as we should, and search them out, but Persuasion, the one thing that rules human beings absolutely, we take no more trouble to learn to the end, and pay fees for it, so that a man could persuade people of whatever he wanted and get it at the same time? How can anyone hope to do well after this? The sons I had are no longer mine, and she, my daughter, is a captive, in shame. I am gone. I see the smoke of my city leaping up over there.

And then, perhaps this is an empty part of the argument, to put Aphrodite forward, but all the same it is going to be said. At your side sleeps my daughter, the god-possessed girl, the one the Phrygians call Cassandra. Where will you show that those nights were dear to you, my lord? What thanks will my daughter have for the loving embraces in your bed, and I for hers? It is out of the dark, and the love-charms of the night, that mortals get their greatest gratitude. Listen, then. Do you see this dead man? If you do right by him, you do right by a kinsman of your own bed. My speech is short of one thing still. If only I had a voice in my arms, and in my hands, and in my hair, and in the tread of my feet, by the arts of Daedalus or some god, so that all of them together could take hold of your knees, weeping, and press every kind of argument on you. Master, greatest light of the Greeks, be persuaded. Lend the old woman your hand for her revenge, even if she is nothing. Do it anyway. It is a good man's part to serve justice, and to do evil to the evil, always, everywhere.

Chorus. It is strange how everything falls together for mortals, and how the laws mark out what has to be, making friends of the bitterest enemies, and enemies of the people who used to be kind.

Agamemnon. Hecuba, I pity you, and your son, and your fortunes, and the hand you hold out to me. And for the gods' sake, and for justice, I want this godless host to pay you this penalty, if only some way could be found for it to go well for you, and for me not to look, to the army, as if I had planned this killing of the king of Thrace for Cassandra's sake. There is a point where confusion has come over me. The army counts this man a friend, and the dead man an enemy. If he is dear to you, that is a separate matter, and the army has no share in it. Think about that. You have me willing to share your work and quick to help, but slow, if I am going to be slandered to the Achaeans.

Hecuba. Pheu. There is no mortal who is free. He is a slave to money, or to luck, or the mass of the city or the written laws keep him from acting the way his own judgement tells him. Since you are afraid, and give the mob too much weight, I will set you free of that fear. Know about it, if I plan some evil against the man who killed this boy, but do not do it with me. And if there is an uproar among the Achaeans, or an attempt to rescue the Thracian while he is suffering what he is going to suffer, hold them back, without seeming to do it for my sake. The rest, take heart, I will arrange it all well.

Agamemnon. How? What will you do? Take a sword in your old hand and kill the barbarian? Or with poisons, or with somebody's help? What hand will be with you? Where will you get friends?

Hecuba. These tents hide a crowd of Trojan women.

Agamemnon. You mean the captives? The Greeks' catch?

Hecuba. With them I will punish the man who murdered my son.

Agamemnon. And how are women going to get the better of men?

Hecuba. Numbers are a terrible thing, and with cunning added, hard to fight.

Agamemnon. Terrible. Still, I have a low opinion of the female race.

Hecuba. Why? Did women not kill the sons of Aegyptus, and empty Lemnos of men, every one of them? But let it be so. Drop this argument, and send this woman safely through the army for me.

(She turns to the Maid.)

And you, go up to my Thracian guest-friend and say this: "Hecuba, who was queen of Troy once, calls for you, on your own business no less than hers, and for your children too. Your children must hear what she has to say as well."

(The Maid goes off through the camp to find Polymestor.)

And hold back the burial of Polyxena, Agamemnon, slaughtered so lately, so that these two, brother and sister, can be hidden in the earth side by side, in one flame, a double grief for their mother.

Agamemnon. It shall be so. If the army could sail, I could not have given you this favour. But as it is, since the god is sending no favouring wind, we have to wait, and watch for a calm crossing. May it turn out well, somehow. This much is common to everyone, to each man privately and to the city: that the bad man suffers something bad, and the good man prospers.

(Agamemnon goes. Hecuba waits beside the body.)

Chorus.
	Troy, my country, you will never again
	be counted among the cities nobody has sacked.
	Such a cloud of Greeks has closed over you,
	spear upon spear, and laid you waste.
	Your crown of towers has been cut from your head,
	and you are smeared with soot,
	a filthy, pitiful stain. Poor city,
	I will never walk your streets again.
Chorus.
	It was midnight when my ruin came,
	the hour when sleep after supper
	spreads sweetly over the eyes.
	The songs were over, and the sacrifice, and the dancing,
	and my husband lay in our bedroom
	with his spear hung on its peg,
	no longer watching for the crowd of sailors
	who had set foot on Trojan ground.
Chorus.
	And I was doing up my hair
	in its band, looking into the endless
	gleam of a golden mirror,
	ready to fall into my bed.
	And a noise went up through the city,
	and this was the shout that ran down the streets of Troy:
	"Sons of Greece, when, oh when
	will you sack the citadel of Troy
	and get home to your houses?"
Chorus.
	I left the bed I loved in nothing but a shift,
	like a Dorian girl,
	and sat down at the altar of holy Artemis,
	and it did me no good, poor woman.
	I saw my husband dead, and I am being carried away
	over the salt sea,
	looking back at my city, when the ship
	set its foot for home
	and cut me off from the land of Troy.
	Wretched. I gave in to the pain,
Chorus.
	cursing Helen, the sister of the twin sons of Zeus,
	and the cattleman of Ida,
	Paris, the ruin of us,
	because it was a marriage, a marriage that was no marriage
	but misery sent by some avenging spirit,
	that destroyed me, and tore me from my father's land,
	and threw me out of my home.
	May the salt sea never carry her back again,
	and may she never
	come to her father's house.

(Polymestor comes in with his two young sons and an armed escort. Hecuba comes out of the tent to meet him.)

Polymestor. Priam, the dearest man I knew, and you, Hecuba, dearest of women, I weep to look at you, and at your city, and at your daughter, killed just now. Pheu. There is nothing a man can trust. Not a good name. Not the idea that someone doing well will not come to do badly. The gods themselves stir everything up, backwards and forwards, throwing in confusion, so that we will worship them because we cannot understand them. But what is the use of crying over all that? It does not get us one step ahead of our troubles. As for you, if you have any complaint about my being away, hold it. I happened to be off in the middle of Thrace when you came here. When I got back, I was just lifting my foot over my own doorstep when this slave of yours ran straight into me with your message, and I heard it and came.

Hecuba. I am ashamed to look you in the face, Polymestor, lying in troubles like these. You saw me when I was doing well, and shame takes hold of me now that I have come to this, to where I am now. I could not look at you with a steady eye. But do not take it for ill will towards you, Polymestor. There is another reason besides: the custom that women do not look men in the face.

Polymestor. No wonder at all. But what do you need me for? What made you send for me to come out of my house?

Hecuba. There is something private, something of my own, that I want to say to you and to your sons. Order your attendants to stand off, away from these tents.

Polymestor. Go. There is no danger in being alone here.

(The escort goes.)

You are my friend, and this Greek army is a friend to me. But you must say what it is. How should a man who is doing well help friends who are not? I am ready.

Hecuba. First tell me about the boy you have in your house, Polydorus, from my hand and his father's. Is he alive? The rest I will ask you after.

Polymestor. Certainly. On his account, at least, you are lucky.

Hecuba. Dearest of friends, how well you speak, and how like you.

Polymestor. So what is the second thing you want to learn from me?

Hecuba. Does he remember me at all, his mother?

Polymestor. Yes. He was looking for a way to slip off and come to you here in secret.

Hecuba. And the gold he came from Troy with, is it safe?

Polymestor. Safe. Under guard in my house.

Hecuba. Then keep it safe, and do not covet what belongs to your neighbours.

Polymestor. Never. Let me enjoy what I have, lady.

Hecuba. Do you know, then, what I want to tell you and your sons?

Polymestor. I do not. Your words will show me.

Hecuba. There is, my friend, and you are as dear to me now as I am to you, there is...

Polymestor. What is it that I and my children have to know?

Hecuba. Gold. Old vaults of it, dug down under the ground by Priam's house.

Polymestor. This is what you want to pass on to your son?

Hecuba. Yes, and through you. You are a god-fearing man.

Polymestor. Then why do these children have to be here?

Hecuba. Better that they know, in case you die.

Polymestor. Well said. That is the cleverer way, too.

Hecuba. Do you know where the temple of Athena of Troy stands?

Polymestor. The gold is there? What is the mark?

Hecuba. A black rock sticking up out of the ground.

Polymestor. Is there anything else you want to tell me about that place?

Hecuba. I want you to keep safe the money I came away with.

Polymestor. Where is it? Inside your dress, or have you got it hidden somewhere?

Hecuba. It is kept safe in these tents, among a heap of spoils.

Polymestor. Where? These are the Greeks' shelters, all round their ships.

Hecuba. The captive women have tents of their own.

Polymestor. And inside, can I trust it? No men about?

Hecuba. No Greeks inside. Only us women. Come into the tent. The Argives are longing to cast off their ships and get home from Troy. Then, when you have done everything you need to, you can go back with your sons to wherever it was you settled my child.

(Hecuba takes Polymestor and his sons into the tent.)

Chorus. You have not paid yet. But perhaps you will pay.

Chorus.
	Like a man who falls into the bilge with no harbour near,
	you will pitch sideways out of everything your heart holds dear,
	robbed of your life. For where what is owed
	to Justice and what is owed to the gods fall together,
	there is ruin. Deadly, deadly ruin.
	The hope that led you down this road will cheat you.
	It has led you to death and to Hades, poor fool,
	and you will lose your life to a hand that never went to war.

(Polymestor screams from inside the tent.)

Polymestor. Oh. Oh. I am blinded. The light of my eyes. Misery.

Chorus. Did you hear the Thracian howling, friends?

Polymestor. Oh, again, again. My children. Butchered. Misery.

Chorus. Friends, something new and terrible has been done inside the tent.

Polymestor. You will not get away from me, not on your quick feet. I will smash my way in. I will break open the inner rooms of this house.

Chorus. Look. There goes a missile from a heavy hand. Shall we burst in? This is the moment. Hecuba and the women of Troy need us at their side.

(Hecuba comes out of the tent.)

Hecuba. Pound away. Spare nothing. Batter the doors down. You will never put the bright sight back in your eyes, and you will never see your sons alive. I killed them.

Chorus. Have you really brought the Thracian down, mistress? Is the stranger in your power? Have you done what you say?

Hecuba. You will see him in a moment in front of the tent, blind, coming out on blind and stumbling feet, and the bodies of his two sons, whom I killed, with the best of the women of Troy. He has paid me what he owed. Here he comes out of the house, as you see. I will get out of his way and stand clear of the Thracian while his anger is running. There is no fighting him now.

(Polymestor crawls out of the tent on his hands and knees, blood running from his eyes.)

Polymestor.
	Oh, oh, where can I go,
	where can I stand, where can I put in to shore?
	Down on all fours like a mountain beast,
	hands and feet on the track? Which way
	shall I take, this one or that one,
	hunting to catch the Trojan women, the killers of men,
	the women who destroyed me?
	Wretched daughters of Phrygia, wretched,
	cursed women,
	which corner have they run to, cowering from me?
	Sun, if only you would heal my eyes,
	heal the bleeding lids, the blindness,
	and give me back the light.
	Ah. Ah.
	Quiet. I can hear them, the women,
	their hidden step. Where can I spring
	and fill myself with flesh and bone,
	and make a wild beast's feast of them,
	and win back my ruin,
	their maiming for mine? Oh, misery.
	Where, where am I rushing, leaving my children
	alone for the Bacchants of Hades to tear in pieces,
	butchered, a bloody meal for dogs,
	thrown out on the mountainside like a savage's leavings?
	Where can I stand, where turn, where go,
	like a ship hauling in its sea ropes, furling
	the linen sail, rushing to that bed
	of death, to guard my children?

Chorus. Poor man. Unbearable things have been done to you. But you did shameful things, and the penalty is terrible. The god who is heavy on you, whoever he is, has given it.

Polymestor.
	Aiai. Io, Thrace, my people, spear in hand,
	armed, riding fine horses, in the grip of Ares.
	Io, Greeks. Io, sons of Atreus. I am shouting, shouting, I shout.
	Come. Come here, by the gods.
	Does anyone hear? Will nobody help? Why are you waiting?
	Women have destroyed me, captive women.
	Terrible, terrible things have been done to us.
	Oh, my ruin.
	Where can I turn, where can I go?
	Shall I fly up to the high roof of heaven,
	where Orion and Sirius shoot
	blazing fire from their eyes,
	or shall I plunge down, wretched, to the black
	ferry-crossing of Hades?

Chorus. When a man suffers evils too great to bear, it is forgivable if he takes himself out of a wretched life.

(Agamemnon comes in with his men.)

Agamemnon. I heard shouting and came. Echo, the daughter of the mountain rock, was not quiet about it: she shrieked it through the whole army and set off a commotion. If we did not know that the Phrygians' towers had fallen to the Greek spear, this noise would have given us a real fright.

Polymestor. Dearest of friends. I know you, Agamemnon. I heard your voice. Do you see what has been done to us?

Agamemnon. What is this? Polymestor. Poor man, who has destroyed you? Who blinded your eyes and bloodied the pupils, and killed these children? Whoever he was, he had a great anger against you and your sons.

Polymestor. Hecuba, with the captive women. She has destroyed me. Not destroyed. Worse than that.

Agamemnon. What are you saying? You did this, as he says? You, Hecuba, had the nerve for this, a thing nobody could have thought possible?

Polymestor. Oh. What are you saying? Is she near here somewhere? Show me, tell me where she is, so that I can grab her in my hands and tear her apart and bloody her flesh.

Agamemnon. You. What is the matter with you?

Polymestor.
	By the gods I beg you,
	let me loose my raging hand on her.

Agamemnon. Stop. Throw the barbarian out of your heart and speak. I will hear you and her in turn, and judge fairly why you are suffering this.

Polymestor. I will speak, then. There was a son of Priam's, the youngest, Polydorus, Hecuba's boy, and his father Priam sent him to me out of Troy to bring up in my house, because he already suspected Troy would fall. I killed him. But hear why I killed him, and how well and how cleverly I thought it out. I was afraid that if the boy was left alive as your enemy he would gather Troy together and settle it again, and that the Greeks, once they knew a son of Priam was living, would raise another expedition against the Phrygians' country, and then they would be trampling these plains of Thrace and plundering them, and the neighbours of Troy would have the same trouble we were labouring under just now, my lord.

Hecuba found out about her son's death, and she brought me here with a story: she was going to show me the hidden vaults of the house of Priam's gold in Troy. She took me into the tent alone with my children, so that nobody else would know about it. I sat down on a couch in the middle of them, with my knees bent. There were a lot of hands. The girls of Troy had their seats on my left and on my right, as if beside a friend, and they were praising the weaving of Edonian hands, holding this cloak up to the light to look at it. Others were admiring my Thracian spear, and between them they stripped me of both my defences. And the ones who were mothers were making a great fuss over my children, tossing them in their arms and passing them from hand to hand, to get them away from their father. And then, out of that calm talk, would you believe it, all at once they pull daggers from somewhere in their dresses and stab the children, and the rest of them grab me like enemies and hold my arms and legs. I wanted to help my sons, and if I lifted my face, they held me down by the hair; if I moved my hands, I could do nothing, poor man, against that crowd of women. And at the last, pain on top of pain, they did the worst of all. They took their brooches and stabbed the pupils of my eyes, my poor eyes, and made them run with blood, and then they scattered through the tent and ran. I leapt up like a wild beast and went after the murdering bitches, hunting along every wall like a huntsman, striking, battering.

That is what I have suffered for trying to do you a favour, Agamemnon, and for killing an enemy of yours. And so as not to spin out a long speech: if any man in the old days has spoken ill of women, or if any man is speaking ill of them now, or is going to, I will put it all in one sentence. Neither the sea nor the land breeds a race like them. Anyone who has ever had dealings with them knows it.

Chorus. Do not be so bold, and do not lump the whole female sex in with your own troubles and blame us all together. There are many of us. Some of us deserve to be hated, and some of us are born to be counted among the bad. But not all.

Hecuba. Agamemnon, men's tongues should never have been given more power than their deeds. If a man had done good, he should have spoken well; if he had done wrong, his words should have been rotten, and it should never have been possible to make injustice sound good. The people who have worked that art out to a fine point are clever, but they cannot go on being clever to the end. They come to a bad end. Nobody has escaped it yet.

That is my opening, and it was for you. Now I will go to this man and answer him. You say you killed my son to save the Greeks a second war, and for Agamemnon's sake. But first, you worst of men: the barbarian race never could be friends with the Greeks, and never will be. It is not possible. And what favour were you so eager to do? Were you marrying into some family? Were you a relative? What reason did you have? Or were they going to sail back here and cut down the crops of your land? Who do you think is going to believe that? If you wanted to tell the truth, it was the gold that killed my son. The gold, and your profit.

Then explain this to me. When Troy was doing well, when the wall still stood round the city, when Priam was alive and Hector's spear was in flower, why did you not kill the boy then, if you really wanted to do this man a favour? You had him in your house, you were bringing him up. Or why not come to the Argives with him alive? No. It was when we were no longer in the light, when the smoke showed that the city belonged to the enemy, that you murdered a guest who had come to your hearth.

And on top of that, listen to this, so you can be shown for what you are. If you were really a friend to the Greeks, you should have taken the gold, which you say is not yours but his, and brought it and given it to them, when they were poor and had been exiles from their own country so long. But even now you cannot bring yourself to let it out of your hand. You keep hold of it and hang on to it in your house. And consider: if you had brought up my boy the way you were bound to bring him up, and kept him safe, you would have had a fine name. It is in trouble that good men show most clearly as friends; good luck finds friends of its own accord, every time. If you had run short of money and he had prospered, my son would have been a great treasure for you to draw on. As it is, you no longer have him for your friend, the good of the gold is gone, your sons are gone, and you yourself are as you are.

And I say this to you, Agamemnon. If you help this man, you will be shown for a bad man. You will be doing good to a guest who was not god-fearing, not faithful where he should have been faithful, not holy, not just. And we shall say that you take pleasure in bad men because you are one yourself. But I do not abuse my masters.

Chorus. Pheu, pheu. A good cause always gives a man the start of a good speech.

Agamemnon. It is a heavy thing for me to judge other people's evils, but I have to all the same. It would be a disgrace to take this business into my hands and then push it away. As for my opinion, so that you know it: it does not look to me as if you killed your guest as a favour to me, or to the Greeks. It looks as if you did it to have the gold in your own house. Now that you are in trouble, you say what suits you. Perhaps among your people it is an easy thing to kill a guest. Among us Greeks it is a disgrace. How can I judge you not guilty and escape the blame? I cannot. You had the nerve to do what was not right. Now bear what you will not like.

Polymestor. Oh. Beaten by a woman, it seems, and a slave, I am to pay the penalty to people who are beneath me.

Agamemnon. And is it not just, if you did the evil?

Polymestor. Oh, my children. Oh, my eyes. Misery.

Hecuba. You are in pain? And what about me? Do you think I feel no pain for my son?

Polymestor. It makes you happy, does it, this outrage against me, you criminal?

Hecuba. And why should I not be happy, when I have my revenge on you?

Polymestor. Not for long. Not once the salt spray of the sea...

Hecuba. Carries me by ship to the borders of Greece, you mean?

Polymestor. Closes over you, when you fall from the masthead.

Hecuba. And who is going to force me to make that jump?

Polymestor. You will climb the ship's mast yourself, on your own feet.

Hecuba. With wings on my back? Or how?

Polymestor. You will turn into a dog, with eyes of fire.

Hecuba. And how do you know about this change in my shape?

Polymestor. Dionysus, the prophet of the Thracians, told me.

Hecuba. And he told you nothing about the evils you have now?

Polymestor. No. Or you would never have caught me with a trick like this.

Hecuba. Dead or alive, is it here that I will finish my life?

Polymestor. Dead. And your tomb will be given a name...

Hecuba. After my shape, you will say? Or what?

Polymestor. The Grave of the Miserable Dog. A landmark for sailors.

Hecuba. I do not care, so long as you have paid me the penalty.

Polymestor. And your daughter Cassandra will have to die too.

Hecuba. I spit on that. I give it back to you, to keep for yourself.

Polymestor. This man's wife will kill her. The bitter keeper of his house.

Hecuba. May the daughter of Tyndareus never go so mad as that.

Polymestor. And she will kill this man too, with an axe raised high over her head.

Agamemnon. You there. Are you mad? Are you asking for trouble?

Polymestor. Kill me. A bath of blood is waiting for you in Argos.

Agamemnon. Slaves, drag him out of my sight, by force.

Polymestor. Does it hurt to hear it?

Agamemnon. Shut his mouth.

Polymestor. Shut it. It has been said.

Agamemnon. Now, as fast as you can, throw him out on some deserted island, since his mouth is so very bold. And you, Hecuba, poor woman, go and bury your two dead. And you women of Troy must go to your masters' tents. I can see the wind already, the wind that will carry us home. May we sail safely home to our own country, and find everything well in our houses, set free from all this trouble.

(Agamemnon's men drag Polymestor away. Agamemnon goes. Hecuba goes to her dead.)

Chorus.
	Go to the harbour, friends, and to the tents,
	to taste the labour of slaves
	under masters. Necessity is hard.

The Suppliants (c. 423 BC)

The Suppliants

(Eleusis, in front of the temple of Demeter. Aethra, the mother of Theseus, sits at the altar. Around her, in a ring, stand the old women of Argos, dressed in mourning, holding out olive branches. Adrastus lies on the ground by the gateway with his head covered, and a group of boys stands near him.)

Aethra. Demeter, keeper of the hearth of this land of Eleusis, and you servants of the goddess who look after her temple: give happiness to me, and to my son Theseus, and to the city of Athens, and to the country of Pittheus, where my father brought me up, Aethra, in a rich house, and gave me as a wife to Aegeus, the son of Pandion, because the oracle of Apollo told him to. I am making this prayer because I have been looking at these old women. They have left their homes in the land of Argos and fallen at my knees with the suppliant's olive branch in their hands, and a terrible thing has happened to them. Their seven noble sons died around the gates of Cadmus's city, and they are childless. Adrastus, the king of Argos, led those men there once. He wanted to win a share of the inheritance of Oedipus for his son-in-law Polyneices, who was an exile. Now their mothers want to bury the dead, the men the spear killed, in the earth, and the winners are stopping them. They will not allow the bodies to be taken up. They are treating the laws of the gods with contempt.

Adrastus shares the load of this appeal to me. There he lies, his eyes wet with tears, groaning over his spear, and over the most disastrous expedition he ever sent out of his house. He keeps pressing me to persuade my son with my prayers to become the man who recovers the dead and helps to bury them, either by talking or by the strength of his spear. He lays this one task on my son and on the city of Athens.

I happen to be here because I had come out of my house to this precinct to offer the first sacrifice for the ploughing of the land, here where the fruitful ear of grain first showed itself, bristling above this earth. And I am waiting, at the holy altars of the two goddesses, Persephone and her mother Demeter, holding these leaves that tie me down though they are no rope, out of pity for these grey-haired mothers whose children are gone, and out of respect for the sacred garlands. My herald has gone to the city to call Theseus here, so that he can either lift these women's grief off the land, or release me from this suppliant's hold on me, by doing something the gods approve of. For women, if they have any sense, it is right to do everything through men.

Chorus.
	I beg you, old woman,
	an old mouth begging,
	down on my knees at your knee.
	Free my children. Lawless men
	have left the limbs of the dead, unstrung by death,
	as food for the wild beasts of the mountains.
Chorus.
	Look at the pitiful tears
	welling out of my eyes and lying on the lids,
	the grey skin of my old flesh
	torn by my own fingernails. What else can I do?
	I never laid my dead sons out in my house,
	and I do not see the earth heaped up over their graves.
Chorus.
	You too, lady, once bore a son.
	You made your bed dear to your husband.
	So give me a share of your mind,
	share it with me, as much as I ache,
	miserable, for the dead that I bore.
	Persuade your son, oh, we beg you, to go
	to the river Ismenus and put into my arms
	the bodies of the dead, young men in their strength, lying about unburied.
Chorus.
	Not as holy custom allows, but under force,
	I have come, falling down and begging
	at the altars of the gods, where the fire is lit.
	My cause is just, and you have
	the power, in the good luck of your own child, to lift
	the misfortune off me. I suffer pitifully and I beg you,
	put my dead son into my wretched hands,
	let me wrap my arms round the poor limbs of my boy.
Chorus.
	Here comes another contest of wailing, wailing
	taking up the wailing. The hands of the servant women are ringing.
	Come, beating in time with the song,
	come, you who share the pain,
	the dance that Hades honours.
	Drag the white nail down the cheek
	and bloody it, bloody the skin.
	What is done for the dead
	is an ornament to the living.
Chorus.
	This pleasure in wailing is never satisfied. It carries me away,
	so much labour, like a wet drop
	running down a steep rock face,
	never stopping, forever. Wailing.
	When children die, it is a woman's nature
	to suffer it out in cries. That labour is laid on us.
	E, e.
	If I were dead, I could forget
	these pains.

(Theseus comes in.)

Theseus. What wailing was that I heard, and the beating of breasts, and dirges for the dead, echoing out of this temple? Fear gives me wings. My mother has been away from home a long time, and I have come on foot to find her, in case something has happened to her. Ah. What is this? I see a strange opening for talk. My old mother sitting at the altar, and foreign women with her, and their trouble is not all of one kind. From their old eyes they are driving pitiful tears down to the ground. Their hair is cut, and their clothes are not clothes for a festival. What is this, mother? It is yours to tell me, and mine to listen. I am expecting news.

Aethra. My son, these women are the mothers of the seven generals who died around the gates of Cadmus's city. They are holding me under guard with their suppliant branches, in a ring, child, as you can see.

Theseus. And who is this man groaning so pitifully in the gateway?

Aethra. Adrastus, they tell me. The king of Argos.

Theseus. And the boys round him? Are they his children?

Aethra. No. They are the sons of the dead men.

Theseus. Then why have they come to us, with the suppliant's hand held out?

Aethra. I know why. But from here on the story is theirs to tell, child.

Theseus. You, the man wrapped up in his cloak. I am asking you. Uncover your head and speak, and let the groaning go. Nothing gets done except by way of the tongue.

Adrastus. Glorious victor, king of the land of Athens, Theseus, I have come as a suppliant to you and to your city.

Theseus. What are you hunting for? What do you need?

Adrastus. You know about the expedition I led, and how it ended in ruin.

Theseus. You did not exactly cross Greece in silence.

Adrastus. There I lost the best men of Argos.

Theseus. That is what miserable war does.

Adrastus. I went to the city and asked for these dead men.

Theseus. Trusting to heralds, Hermes's men, so that you could bury them?

Adrastus. Yes. And even then the men who killed them would not let me.

Theseus. What do they say, when what you ask for is holy?

Adrastus. Say? They are winning, and they do not know how to carry it.

Theseus. So have you come to me for advice? Or for what?

Adrastus. I want you, Theseus, to bring the sons of Argos home.

Theseus. And where is Argos now? Was all that boasting for nothing?

Adrastus. We stumbled, and we are finished. We have come to you.

Theseus. Is this your own private idea, or the whole city's?

Adrastus. All the sons of Danaus beg you to bury the dead.

Theseus. And what made you march seven companies against Thebes?

Adrastus. I was doing a favour for my two sons-in-law.

Theseus. Which of the Argives did you give your daughters to?

Adrastus. I made no marriage for my house inside the family.

Theseus. You gave Argive girls to foreigners?

Adrastus. Yes. To Tydeus, and to Polyneices, the Theban-born.

Theseus. What made you want a marriage like that?

Adrastus. Riddles from Apollo, hard to make out. They crept up on me.

Theseus. What did Apollo say, when he settled the girls' marriage?

Adrastus. To give my two daughters to a boar and a lion.

Theseus. And how did you unwind the god's oracle?

Adrastus. Two exiles came to my gates one night, and they were both...

Theseus. Who and who? Say it. You are talking about two men at once.

Adrastus. Tydeus and Polyneices. They started fighting each other.

Theseus. And you gave your daughters to them, as if they were the beasts?

Adrastus. Yes. Watching them fight, I saw the two animals.

Theseus. And how had they come to leave the borders of their own countries?

Adrastus. Tydeus was in exile for shedding a kinsman's blood.

Theseus. And the son of Oedipus? Why had he left Thebes?

Adrastus. Because of his father's curse. So that he would not kill his brother.

Theseus. That was a sensible exile you describe, and a voluntary one.

Adrastus. But the ones who stayed at home wronged the one who was away.

Theseus. You do not mean his brother robbed him of his property?

Adrastus. I went to settle that account. And then I was destroyed.

Theseus. Did you go to the seers? Did you look at the flame of the burnt offerings?

Adrastus. Oh. You are driving me right to the place where I stumbled worst.

Theseus. You did not go, it seems, with the goodwill of the gods.

Adrastus. Worse. I went against Amphiaraus, over his head.

Theseus. You turned your back on the divine as easily as that?

Adrastus. The shouting of young men knocked the sense out of me.

Theseus. You went for courage instead of good counsel.

Adrastus. Yes. And that has destroyed many a general. But listen, bravest head in all Greece, king of Athens. I am ashamed to be falling to the ground and wrapping my hand round your knee, a grey-haired man, a king, and a fortunate one, once. But I have no choice. I have to give way to what has happened to me. Save the dead for me. Pity my troubles, and pity these women, the mothers of the men who died, whose grey old age has come to them with no children in it. They found the strength to come here and set a stranger's foot on foreign soil, barely able to move their old limbs, and not as an embassy to the mysteries of Demeter, but to bury their dead, when they themselves should have been buried by the hands of those sons, in their prime.

It is wise for a rich man to look at poverty, and for a poor man to look up at the rich, admiring them, so that the love of money takes hold of him; and for people who are not in trouble to look at pitiful things and be afraid. And a man who makes songs should be happy when he brings the songs he makes into the world. If he is not, if he is hurting at home, there is no way he can give pleasure to others. It would not even be right.

Now perhaps you will say: why pass over the land of Pelops and lay this labour on Athens? I ought to explain that. Sparta is cruel, and her ways are shifty. The other cities are small and weak. Your city is the only one that could take this labour on. It looks at what is pitiful, and it has you for a shepherd, young and good; and many cities have been destroyed for the want of one, with no general to lead them.

Chorus. And I say the same as this man does, Theseus. Take my troubles to heart, out of pity.

Theseus. I have argued this same point with other people before, and worked at it. Someone said that there is more bad than good in the lives of mortals. I hold the opposite opinion: that for human beings the good outweighs the bad. If it did not, we would not be alive in the light. I praise whichever of the gods it was who took our life out of the muddle, out of living like beasts, and set it in order. First he put understanding in us. Then he gave us a tongue, the messenger of speech, so that we could recognise words. Then food from the crops, and for the crops drops of water out of the sky, to feed what grows from the earth and water its belly. And on top of that, shelter against winter, and ways of keeping off the burning heat the god sends down; and sailing the sea, so that we could exchange with one another whatever a country lacks. And where things are unclear and we have no certain knowledge, the seers look into the fire, and into the folds of the entrails, and read the birds, and tell us in advance. Are we not spoiled, when a god has fitted life out for us like this, if it is not enough for us? But our cleverness wants to be stronger than the god, and with pride settled in our hearts we think we are wiser than the gods.

You seem to me to belong to that company. You were not born clever. You were yoked to the oracles of Apollo and gave your daughters to foreigners on the strength of them, as if the gods were real, and you mixed a bright house with a muddy one and left a running sore on your own. A wise man should never mix unjust bodies with just ones. He should get prosperous friends for his family. Because the god treats their fortunes as one, and by the pains of the sick man he destroys the man who shares his sickness and did nothing wrong. You led all the Argives out to war when the seers were telling you what the gods said, and then you dishonoured them, forced your way past the gods, and destroyed your city.
