You were led astray by young men, the kind who enjoy being honoured and swell wars without any justice in them, ruining the citizens: one so that he can command an army, one so that he can get power into his hands and commit outrage with it, another for profit, never looking to see whether the people are harmed by any of it.

There are three classes of citizens. The rich are useless, and always want more. The have-nots, short of a living, are dangerous. They give too big a share to envy, and they shoot evil stings at the men who have something, fooled by the tongues of bad leaders. Of the three parts, it is the one in the middle that saves cities, by keeping whatever order the city lays down. And after all that, am I to become your ally? What fine thing could I say to my citizens? Go, and good luck to you. If you did not plan well, press down on your own fortune yourself, and leave us alone.

Chorus. He went wrong. But that is in young men, and he should be forgiven. And we have come to you as a healer of these things, my lord.

Adrastus. I did not choose you as a judge of my troubles, my lord, nor, if it turns out that I did something badly, as the man to punish and correct me. I came so that I might get some good of you. If you will not, I have to be content with your decision. What else can I do? Come, old women. Go. Leave the grey-green leaves here where they lie, lay the branches down, and call the gods to witness, and the earth, and Demeter, the goddess who carries the torch, and the light of the sun, that our prayers in the gods' name did us no good at all.

Chorus. Your mother's father Pittheus was a son of Pelops, and we come from the land of Pelops. The blood of your fathers is the blood of ours. What are you doing? Will you betray these branches, and throw old women out of your land with nothing of what they had a right to? Do not. A wild beast has the rock for a refuge, and a slave has the altars of the gods, and a city, when the storm hits it, cowers up against another city. Nothing in human life is happy all the way to the end.

Chorus.
	Get up, poor woman, from the holy floor of Persephone,
	get up and go to him, lay your hand on his knees,
	beg him to bring home the bodies of your dead children. Oh, my misery,
	the boys I lost under the walls of Cadmus's city.
	Io moi. Take me, carry me, lead me, guide these poor old hands.
	By your beard, friend, most honoured man in Greece,
	I beg you, falling round your knee and your hand, wretched as I am.
	Pity me, for my children. I am a suppliant, a wanderer
	pouring out a pitiful lament, a pitiful one.
	Do not stand by, child, and let my sons lie unburied in the land of Cadmus,
	a joy for the wild beasts, young men your own age. I beg you.
	Look at the tears on my eyelids, as I fall like this
	at your knees, to win a grave for my children.

Theseus. Mother, why are you crying, with your thin veil pulled over your eyes? Is it because you heard these women's miserable wailing? Something went through me too. Lift your white head. Do not sit weeping at the holy altar of Demeter.

Aethra. Aiai.

Theseus. Their troubles are not yours to groan over.

Aethra. Poor women.

Theseus. You were not born one of them.

Aethra. May I say something, child, that would be good for you and for the city?

Theseus. Yes. Plenty of wisdom comes from women too.

Aethra. But the thing I am keeping back makes me hesitate.

Theseus. That is a shameful thing to say. Hiding good words from your own people.

Aethra. Then I will not keep quiet now and blame myself later for the silence I kept today, and call it a bad silence. And I will not throw away the fine thing I have to say out of the fear that it is useless for women to speak well. My son, first I tell you to look to the gods' side of this, so that you do not fall by dishonouring them. You think well about everything else. This is the one place where you have stumbled.

Beyond that: if there were no duty to have the nerve to act for people who are wronged, I would have kept very quiet. But as it is, you should understand how much honour this brings you, and it costs me no fear to advise it, child. There are men of violence keeping the dead from their share of a grave and the rites of burial. Force them, with your own hand, to do what they have to do. Stop men who are throwing the laws of all Greece into confusion. Because what holds human cities together is this: a man keeping the laws well.

And someone will say it was cowardice in your hands. That when your city could have won the crown of glory you were afraid, and stood back. That you took on the fight with a wild boar and worked hard at a cheap job, and where you should have looked at a helmet and a spear point and worked it through, you were found to be a coward. Do not do it, child. Not if you are mine. Do you see how your country, when they mock her for having no plan, looks back at the mockers with a fierce eye? Because she grows in her labours. Cities that keep quiet and do things in the dark see in the dark too, from being so careful. Will you not go, child, and help the dead, and these wretched women who need you? I am not afraid for you, since you are setting out with justice on your side. And though I see Cadmus's people doing well, I am confident they will throw the dice differently yet. The god turns everything upside down again.

Chorus. Dearest woman, you have spoken well for him and for me. This is a double joy.

Theseus. Mother, the words I said to this man were right, and I gave my opinion of the plans that made him fall. But I also see what you are warning me about: that it does not suit my character to run from danger. I have done many fine things, and I have chosen this as my habit before the Greeks: always to stand as the punisher of the wicked. So I cannot refuse labours. What will my enemies say of me, when you, my mother, who fear for me more than anyone does, are the first to tell me to take this labour on?

I will do it. I will go and free the dead by persuading them with words. If not, then by force of the spear, right away, and the gods will not begrudge it. But I want the whole city to approve of this as well. It will approve, because I want it; still, if I add an argument, I will have the people better disposed. I made the people the sole ruler here, when I set this city free and gave every man an equal vote. I will take Adrastus as the proof of what I say and go to the assembly of the citizens. When I have persuaded them, I will gather picked young Athenians and come back here, and sitting under arms I will send word to Creon, asking for the bodies of the dead.

And you, old women, take the holy garlands off my mother, so that I can take her dear hand and lead her to the house of Aegeus. A man is wretched who does not serve his parents in return. It is the finest of all repayments. What he gives, he gets back from his own children, the same as he gave to the ones who bore him.

(Theseus leads Aethra away. Adrastus and the boys stay by the altar.)

Chorus.
	Argos, land of horses, my father's ground,
	did you hear this, did you hear
	what the king means to do, holy toward the gods
	and great, for all Pelasgia,
	and all through Argos?
Chorus.
	If only he could come to the end of my troubles and past it,
	and still take up the mother's
	treasure, bloodied as it is,
	and make the land of Inachus his friend
	by helping her.
Chorus.
	A fine ornament for cities, a labour done in reverence,
	and it keeps its thanks forever.
	What will the city decide for me? Will it cut
	a treaty of friendship with me, and will we get graves for our children?
Chorus.
	Defend a mother, city of Pallas, defend her,
	so that the laws of mortals are not defiled.
	You honour justice, and you give
	the lesser share to injustice, and you always rescue the unlucky.

(Theseus comes back with an Athenian herald.)

Theseus. You have always served the city and me with this skill of yours, carrying my proclamations. Go across the Asopus and the water of the Ismenus and tell the high and mighty king of the Cadmeans this: Theseus asks you, as a favour, to let him bury the dead. He lives in the land next to yours, he thinks it a fair thing to be granted, and he would make the whole people of Erechtheus your friends. If they agree, thank them and come straight back. If they refuse, here is the second message: they can expect my revellers, and my revellers carry shields. My army is sitting here ready, round the holy spring of Callichorus, and it is being reviewed as we speak. And the city took this labour on willingly, gladly, once it saw that I wanted it.

Ah. Who is this, coming to interrupt my talk? A Cadmean, it seems, a herald, though I am not sure of it. Wait. He may save you the trouble. He has come to meet my plans halfway.

Herald. Who is the king of this country? Who do I deliver my message to? I bring the words of Creon, who rules the land of Cadmus now that Eteocles is dead at the seven gates, killed by his own brother's hand, by Polyneices.

Theseus. You have started off with a mistake, stranger, looking for a king here. This city is not ruled by one man. It is free. The people rule it, taking their turn in office year by year, and wealth does not get the biggest share. The poor man has an equal one.

Herald. Well, that is one point you hand to us, like a piece given away in a board game. The city I come from is governed by one man, not by a crowd. There is nobody there who puffs the people up with speeches and turns them this way and that for his own private profit, sweet as honey for the moment and handing out favours, and then doing them harm later, and then covering his old blunders with fresh slanders and slipping clean out of justice. Besides, how can the people steer a city straight when they cannot even judge an argument straight? Time is a better teacher than haste. A poor man who works the land, even if he happens not to be stupid, has his hands too full to keep an eye on public business. And it makes the better sort sick, I can tell you, when some worthless man who was nothing yesterday gets a position by getting hold of the people with his tongue.

Theseus. A polished herald. He does a little speech-making on the side. Well, since you have entered this contest of your own accord, listen. You set up the debate. There is nothing more hostile to a city than a tyrant. Under a tyrant, first of all, there are no laws that belong to everyone. One man rules, and the law is his private property, and right there equality is gone. When the laws are written down, the weak man and the rich man have equal justice. The weaker can answer the man who is doing well in the same terms he is spoken to in, and the little man beats the great one if he has right on his side. This is freedom: "Who has good advice for the city and wants to bring it before us?" The man who wants to speak, shines. The man who does not, keeps silent. What is fairer to a city than that?

And there is this. Where the people are masters of the land, they take pleasure in the young men coming up under them. A king sees them as enemies. He kills the best men, and any man he thinks has a mind of his own, because he is afraid for his throne. So how can a city go on being strong when someone is cutting the daring out of it, like a man scything the ears off a spring meadow, and plucking its young men away? Why gather wealth and a livelihood for your children, so a tyrant can live better on your labour? Why bring your daughters up decently at home, to be a sweet treat for a tyrant whenever he feels like it, and tears for the parents who raised them? I would rather be dead than see my children married off by force.

That is my volley, fired back at yours. Now: what do you want from this country? If your city had not sent you, you would have paid in tears for all this extra talking. A messenger's job is to say what he was told to say and get back as fast as he can. Next time Creon can send my city a messenger who talks less than you.

Chorus. Pheu, pheu. When a god gives good fortune to bad men, they turn to outrage, as if their luck would last forever.

Herald. Now I will say my piece. On the points we have been arguing, you think what you think and I think the opposite. I forbid you, I and the whole people of Cadmus, to let Adrastus into this land. If he is in it, then before the sun's light goes down, untie the holy suppliant wreaths and drive him out of it, and do not take up the dead by force. You have no business with the city of Argos. If you listen to me, you will steer your city on a calm sea. If you do not, there will be a great surge of war, for us, for you, and for your allies.

Think about it. Do not lose your temper at my words and, because you have a free city, answer me with a speech that flexes its arms. Hope is not to be trusted. It has thrown many cities into war by driving their spirit too far. When war comes up for a vote before the people, nobody reckons on his own death. He assumes that piece of bad luck belongs to somebody else. If death stood before each man's eyes as he cast his vote, Greece would not be dying of spear-madness. And yet every one of us knows which of two arguments is the better, and what is good and what is bad, and how much better peace is for human beings than war. Peace is the dearest friend the Muses have, and the enemy of the Spirits of Vengeance. She delights in fine children. She rejoices in wealth. And we throw all that away, we bad men, and take up wars, and enslave whoever is weaker, man enslaving man and city enslaving city.

And you: you are helping men who are your enemies even in death, burying them and carrying them home, when it was their own outrage that destroyed them? Then was it wrong that Capaneus's body still smokes where the lightning struck him? He set the uprights of his ladder against our gates and swore he would sack the city whether the god liked it or not. Was it wrong that the earth opened and swallowed the seer Amphiaraus, chariot and four horses and all? And that the other captains lie at the gates with the seams of their skulls torn open by rocks? So either boast that you know better than Zeus, or admit that the gods are right to destroy bad men.

A sensible man loves his children first, and then his parents and his country, and his country is something to build up, not to break down. A bold leader is a dangerous thing. A sailor who keeps quiet and knows his moment is the wise one. And to my mind that is courage: forethought.

Chorus. Zeus has punished us. That was enough. You had no need to add this outrage on top of it.

Adrastus. You worthless, worthless —

Theseus. Quiet, Adrastus. Hold your tongue. Do not put your words in front of mine. This man has not come with his proclamation to you but to me, and it is for me to answer him.

I will take your first points first. I am not aware that Creon is my master, or that he has more power than I have, so that he can force Athens to do this. Rivers would be running uphill if we took our orders that way. And I am not the one starting this war. I did not go with these men to the land of Cadmus. What I claim is the right to bury the men who have died, doing no harm to your city and bringing no man-killing battle to it, but keeping the law of all the Greeks. What is wrong with that? If the Argives did something to you, they are dead for it. You beat off your enemies with honour, and with shame to them, and justice has run its course. Let the dead be covered with earth now. Let each part of them go back where it came from when it came into the light: the breath to the air, the body to the ground. We do not own our bodies. We live in them for a while, and afterwards the earth that fed them has to take them back.

Do you think it is Argos you are hurting by refusing to bury the dead? Not at all. This is the common business of all Greece, if a man keeps the dead from what they are owed and leaves them lying unburied. Make that a law, and it will put cowardice into brave men. And you have come to me hurling dreadful threats, while your own people are afraid of a few corpses, if they are hidden in the ground? Afraid of what? That they will dig up your country from underneath, once they are buried? Or breed children in the hollows of the earth, and one of them will grow up to be an avenger? That is a stupid waste of breath, being frightened of fears that are wretched and empty.

You fools. Learn what human beings are up against. Our life is a wrestling match. Some men are lucky soon, some later, some right now, and Fortune is a pampered god. The unlucky man honours her and pays her court so that his luck will turn, and the prosperous man praises her to the sky because he is afraid her breeze will drop. Knowing that, we should bear a moderate wrong without rage, and do only such wrong as does no harm to a city. So how will it be? Give us the fallen dead to bury, since we are the ones who want to do what is right. Or else the next step is plain: I will go and bury them by force. It will never be reported around Greece that the ancient law of the gods came to me, and to the city of Pandion, and was destroyed there.

Chorus. Take heart. Keep the light of Justice burning and you will escape most of what men find to blame.

Herald. Do you want me to put your whole speech in a few words?

Theseus. Say what you like. You are not going to be silent anyway.

Herald. You will never take the sons of Argos out of our land.

Theseus. Then hear my answer to that, if you like.

Herald. I will hear it. Not that I want to, but I have to give you your turn.

Theseus. I will bury the dead. I will take them out of the land of Asopus and bury them.

Herald. You will have to risk it among the shields first.

Theseus. I have been through plenty of other labours before this.

Herald. Did your father breed you to be a match for everybody?

Theseus. For everybody who commits outrage, yes. We do not punish good behaviour.

Herald. Meddling in everything. That is your habit, and your city's.

Theseus. Which is why she works so hard, and why she does so well.

Herald. Come, then, and let the spear of the men sown in our soil catch you inside our city.

Theseus. What kind of furious war god could ever come out of a snake?

Herald. You will learn that the hard way. You are still a boy.

Theseus. You will not needle me into losing my temper with your boasting. Get out of this country, and take the empty words you brought here with you. We are getting nowhere.

(The Herald goes out, back the way he came.)

Every man in armour must move out now, and every man who rides a chariot, and the horses' bits must start to move, dripping foam on the land of Cadmus. I am going to the seven gates of Cadmus myself, with sharp iron in my hands, and I will be my own herald. You I order to stay here, Adrastus. Do not mix your luck with mine. I am going to lead this army with my own fortune beside me, a new general with a new spear. I need one thing only: to have the gods on my side, the ones who honour justice. Have those together and you have victory. Courage means nothing to human beings unless the god is willing.

(Theseus goes out to gather the army.)

Chorus.
	Unhappy mothers of unhappy captains,
	how the pale fear crouches under my heart.
	What is this new cry you are raising?
	Where will the army of Pallas be judged?
	Judged by the spear, do you mean, or by an exchange of words?
	Words would be a gain. But if the killing of battle,
	the fighting, the blows of hands on breasts, break out
	through the city again, then, poor wretch,
	what will they say of me, what blame will I carry, who am the cause?
Chorus.
	But a man who shines with good luck can be taken down
	by fate again. That is the thought that gives me courage.
	You are talking as if the gods were just.
	Who else deals out what happens to us?
	I see a great deal in the gods' dealings with us that does not agree.
	It is the old fear that is destroying you.
	Justice has called for justice, and blood for blood,
	and the gods give human beings a breathing space from evil.
	The end of everything is in their hands.
Chorus.
	How could we reach the plains under those fine towers,
	leaving the goddess's water here, the well of Callichorus?
	If one of the gods would give you wings,
	so I could come to the city of the two rivers, Thebes.
	Then you would know, you would know how your friends have fared.
	What fate, what end
	is waiting for the brave man
	who is king of this land?
Chorus.
	The gods we called on before, we call on again.
	Yes. When we are afraid, that is the first thing we trust.
	Io, Zeus, who fathered a child on the heifer long ago,
	our first mother, the daughter of Inachus:
	be kind to this city of mine. Fight beside it.
	Your pride, your foundation stone,
	the men on whom you built our city,
	I am carrying to the pyre, outraged.

(A Messenger comes in.)

Messenger. Women, I come with a great deal of good news to tell you, and I have come through alive myself. I was taken prisoner in the battle that the seven companies fought beside the stream of Dirce, the companies of the seven dead masters. And I come to announce the victory of Theseus. I will save you a long round of questions. I was the servant of Capaneus, the man Zeus burned to ash with his fiery lightning.

Chorus. Dearest of men, it is good news that you have come back, and good news about Theseus. If the army of Athens is safe as well, then everything you tell us will be good.

Messenger. Safe, and it has done what Adrastus should have done with the Argives, when he led them out from the river Inachus against the city of the Cadmeans.

Chorus. How did the son of Aegeus and the men who shared the fight with him set up Zeus's trophy? Tell us. You were there, and we were not, and you will make us glad.

Messenger. The bright ray of the sun, a clear straight line, was striking the earth. I stood by the Electran gates to watch, from a tower with a clear view. And I saw three divisions of three armies. The men in armour were stretched out up towards the hill of Ismenus, so I was told, and the king himself, the famous son of Aegeus, and the men with him, the people of the old city, were drawn up on the right wing. The men from the coast were on the left, equal in number, equipped with spears, right beside the spring of Ares, with the chariots, and the mass of the cavalry was drawn up on the edges of the camp. The people of Cadmus were sitting in front of the walls, with the dead, who were what the fight was about, placed behind them, under the holy tombs of Amphion. Horsemen were armed against horsemen, and four-horse chariots stood against chariots.

Then Theseus's herald spoke to everyone. "Silence, peoples. Silence, ranks of the Cadmeans, and listen. We have come for the dead. We want to bury them, keeping the law of all the Greeks. We have no wish to draw out the slaughter." Creon made no proclamation in answer to that. He sat there by his arms in silence. Then the drivers of the four-horse chariots began the battle. They drove their chariots through past one another and set down the fighting men who rode beside them into the line of battle. Some of these fought it out with iron, while the drivers wheeled the horses back into the fight to pick their men up again. Phorbas, who commanded the cavalry for the sons of Erechtheus, saw the mass of chariots, and so did the men guarding Cadmus's horse, and they joined battle, and they won and they lost by turns.

I saw all this. I did not hear about it. I was there, right where the chariots and the men who rode them were fighting, and out of all the misery that was there I do not know what to tell you first. The dust going up to the sky, there was so much of it? Or the men being dragged up and down in their reins, and the streams of red blood, as some fell and others were thrown headfirst out of their smashed chariots and slammed into the ground, and left their lives lying among the wreckage of the cars?

When Creon saw that our side was winning with the horse, he took a shield in his hand and went forward himself, before despair could reach his allies. And they crashed together in the middle of the whole army, and killed and were killed, and passed the order along to one another with a great shout: "Strike! Hold your spears against the sons of Erechtheus!" And Theseus's side was not lost through hesitation. He snatched up his shining armour and went straight at them. The company that grew to manhood from the serpent's teeth was a terrible wrestler. It bent our left wing back. But their left was beaten by our right and ran, so the fight was evenly balanced. And there the general deserved his praise. He did not simply take his profit from the part that was winning. He went to the part of his own army that was giving way, and he broke out in a shout that made the ground ring: "Boys, if you do not hold the stubborn spear of these sown men, the cause of Pallas is lost." That put heart into the whole army of Athens. And he took up his own weapon, the club he carried from Epidaurus, that terrible thing, and swung it round and round, and swept off necks and the heads that sat on them together, harvesting helmets and snapping them off at the stalk with the wood. Even then they barely turned and ran.

I shouted for joy and danced and clapped my hands. They were streaming for the gates. There was shouting and wailing through the city, young and old, and they crowded the temples in their fear. And though he could have gone inside the walls, Theseus held back. He said he had not come to sack the city but to ask for the dead. That is the kind of general a people should choose: a man who is brave in danger, and who hates a people that turns to outrage, that does well and then goes looking for the top rung of the ladder, and throws away the good fortune it could have used.

Chorus. Now that I have seen this day I never hoped to see, I believe in the gods. And I think my misfortune weighs less, now that these men have paid the penalty.

Adrastus. Zeus, why do they say that wretched human beings have any sense? We hang from you. We do whatever you happen to want. To us Argos was irresistible, and we were many, and young, with strong arms. When Eteocles offered terms, and moderate terms, we would not take them, and then we were destroyed. And then the winners, the ill-minded people of Cadmus, behaved like a poor man who has just come into money: they turned to outrage, and their outrage destroyed them in their turn. You men who draw the bow past the mark. You empty things, who suffer so many evils, and deserve to, who will not listen to friends but only to events. And you cities, who could bend your troubles aside with talk, and settle your business with slaughter instead of speech.

But why go on about that? What I want to know is how you got away, and then I will ask the rest.

Messenger. When the fighting threw the city into confusion, I walked out through the gates, the same gates the army was coming in by.

Adrastus. And the dead, the men the whole fight was about: are you bringing them?

Messenger. The ones who commanded the seven famous companies, yes.

Adrastus. What do you mean? The rest of the dead, all those others: where are they?

Messenger. They have been given burial in the folds of Cithaeron.

Adrastus. On that side of the mountain or this? And who buried them?

Messenger. Theseus. Where the shady rock of Eleutherae stands.

Adrastus. And the ones he did not bury: where did you leave them when you came?

Messenger. Close by. Anything you are eager for is close.

Adrastus. I suppose the servants hated bringing them in from the slaughter.

Messenger. Not one slave was set to that work.

Messenger. You would say the same if you had been there, when he tended the dead.

Adrastus. He washed those poor men's wounds himself?

Messenger. And laid out their beds, and covered their bodies.

Adrastus. That was a dreadful load to carry, and there was shame in it.

Messenger. What is shameful to men about other men's suffering?

Adrastus. Oh. How gladly I would have died with them.

Messenger. You are grieving for nothing, and you are drawing tears from these women.

Adrastus. I suppose I am. They are the ones who taught me. Well then. I raise my hand to meet the dead, and I pour out the tearful songs of Hades, calling to my friends. They have left me behind, and I am the wretch who weeps alone. This is the one expense human beings can never recover once it is spent, a human life. For money there are always ways.

Chorus.
	Some of it is good, some of it is grief.
	For the city, glory,
	and for the generals of the spear,
	honour doubled.
	For me, to see my children's limbs
	is bitter, and a fine sight, if I do see it,
	having seen the day I never hoped for,
	the greatest grief of all.
Chorus.
	Unmarried. Old Time, the father,
	should have made me that,
	and left me so to this day.
	What did I need children for?
	I thought it would be some terrible thing to suffer,
	if I were never yoked in marriage.
	Now I see the evil plain as day,
	stripped of the children I loved most.

(The bodies of the dead captains are carried in.)

Chorus.
	But now I see them, the bodies
	of my children who are gone. Wretched woman,
	how can I die with these children of mine,
	and go down to Hades with them together?
Adrastus.
	Mothers, the groan
	for the dead under the earth:
	cry it out, shout it back, in answer to mine,
	when you hear me groaning.
Chorus.
	Sons. Oh, sons. A bitter word
	for the mothers who loved you to call you by.
	I am speaking to you, and you are dead.
Adrastus.
	Io. Io.
Chorus.
	And I for griefs of my own.
Adrastus.
	Aiai.
Adrastus.
	We have suffered, oh,
Chorus.
	the cruellest pains there are.
Adrastus.
	City of Argos, do you not see what has become of me?
Chorus.
	They see me too, a wretched woman
	with no children, my children gone.
Adrastus.
	Bring them near, the bodies of the unlucky men,
	dripping with blood,
	killed as they did not deserve, by men who did not deserve to kill them,
	the men on whom the whole contest was decided.
Chorus.
	Give them to me, so that I can fold
	my arms around them
	and hold my children in my embrace.
Adrastus.
	You have him. You have him.
Chorus.
	Grief enough, and the weight of it.
Adrastus.
	Aiai.
Chorus.
	And for the parents, nothing to say?
Adrastus.
	Listen to me.
Chorus.
	You groan for the pain of us both.
Adrastus.
	I wish the Theban ranks had cut me down in the dust.
Chorus.
	And I wish my body had never been yoked
	to a husband's bed.
Adrastus.
	Look at this sea of evils,
	mothers, poor mothers of these children.
Chorus.
	We have ploughed our cheeks with our nails,
	we have poured ashes over our heads.
Adrastus.
	Io. Io moi moi.
	Let the floor of the earth take me down,
	let a whirlwind tear me in two,
	let the flame of Zeus's fire fall on my head.
Chorus.
	Bitter the marriages you saw made,
	bitter the word Apollo spoke.
	The Fury of Oedipus, heavy with groans,
	left his house empty and came to you.

Theseus. I was going to ask you something, while you were pouring out your laments to the army, but I let it go; I left the words unsaid where they were. Now I turn to Adrastus. Where did these men come from, who stood out among mortals for their courage? Tell it, since you are wiser, to the young men of this city. You know these things. I saw for myself their deeds of daring, more than words could describe, the deeds they hoped would take the city. But there is one thing I will not ask you, or I would make myself a laughing-stock: which enemy each of them stood against in the battle, or whose spear gave him his wound. Those are empty stories, for the ones listening and for the one telling them: a man who stood in the fight, with spears flying thick in front of his eyes, and reported clearly who the brave one was. I could not ask that, and I could not believe the men who have the nerve to say it. When you stand face to face with the enemy you can barely see even what you have to see.

Adrastus. Listen, then. You give me a task I take on gladly: to speak the truth about these friends, and speak it fairly, which is what I want to do.

Do you see that fine-looking man, the one the bolt flew through? That is Capaneus. He had a great deal to live on, and he was the last man to be proud of his wealth. He thought no more of himself than a poor man does, and he kept clear of anyone who puffed himself up over his dinner table and looked down on having enough. Goodness does not live in stuffing the belly, he used to say; a moderate amount will do. He was a true friend to his friends, whether they were there or not, and there are not many of those. A character without a lie in it, a courteous way of speaking, and no promise left unkept, to his own household or to his fellow citizens.

The second I name is Eteoclus, who practised a different kind of goodness. He was a young man short of money, and he held more offices of honour than anyone in the land of Argos. His friends kept offering him gold, and he would not let it into his house: he would not put his character under the yoke of money and make a slave of it. It was the men who did wrong that he hated, not the city, because a city is not to blame if it gets a bad name through a bad pilot.

The third of them, Hippomedon, was like this. From boyhood he had the nerve not to turn to the pleasures of the Muses and the soft side of life. He lived in the fields, gave his body hard things to do, and enjoyed it for the manliness of it: out hunting, delighting in horses, bending a bow in his hands, because he wanted to give the city a body it could use.

Then the son of Atalanta the huntress, the boy Parthenopaeus, the handsomest of them all. He was an Arcadian, but he came to the streams of Inachus and was brought up in Argos. And when he was grown, first, as a foreigner living in another people's city should, he was no nuisance to the city and gave nobody cause to resent him, and he was no wrangler in arguments, which is what makes a man hardest to bear, citizen or foreigner. He stood in the ranks like a born Argive and defended the country. When the city did well he was glad, and when anything went badly he took it hard. He had many lovers, men and as many women, and he took care to do nothing wrong.

Tydeus I will praise greatly, and briefly. He was no shining speaker, but behind a shield he was a formidable expert, clever at finding many clever things. In judgement he fell short of his brother Meleager, but he made his name the equal of his brother's through his skill with the spear, because he had worked out an exact science of fighting. An ambitious nature, and rich in ambition; a spirit that showed itself in deeds, not in words.

So from what I have told you, Theseus, do not wonder that these men had the nerve to die in front of the towers. To be brought up well brings a sense of shame with it, and every man who has practised what is good is ashamed to turn coward. Courage can be taught, if a baby can be taught to speak, and to hear things it does not yet understand. And what a person learns, he tends to keep into old age. So bring up your children well.

Chorus.
	Io, my child. It was for misery
	I raised you, carried you under my heart,
	bore the pains of labour. And now
	Hades has all my work,
	all my wretched labour, and I have no one
	to look after my old age,
	I who bore a son. Poor woman.

Theseus. And then there is the noble son of Oecles, Amphiaraus: the gods snatched him alive into the depths of the earth, chariot and four horses and all, and that is their praise of him, in plain sight. And the son of Oedipus, Polyneices I mean: we would not be lying if we praised him. He was my guest-friend before he left the city of Cadmus and crossed over to Argos, an exile by his own choice. But do you know what I want to do about these men?

Adrastus. I know only one thing: to do what you tell me.

Theseus. Capaneus, the one Zeus's fire struck down,

Adrastus. You want to bury him apart, as a holy corpse?

Theseus. Yes. All the others on one pyre.

Adrastus. Then where will you set his tomb, apart from them?

Theseus. Right here, beside this temple. I have built the grave.

Adrastus. That is work for the slaves, and they should be at it now.

Theseus. And these men are our work. Let the dead be carried forward.

Adrastus. Go to your children, poor mothers. Go close to them.

Theseus. Adrastus, that is the last thing you should be saying.

Adrastus. Why? Must the mothers not touch their children?

Theseus. It would kill them to see them changed like this.

Adrastus. Yes. The blood and the wounds of the dead are a bitter sight.

Theseus. Then why do you want to add to their grief?

Adrastus. You win. You must wait, and bear it. Theseus is right. When we have put them on the fire, you will gather up the bones. Wretched human beings. Why do you get yourselves spears and deal out death to one another? Stop it. Give up this labour, and keep your cities in peace, quiet people among quiet people. Life is a small thing. We should get through it as easily as we can, and not with pain.

Chorus.
	No longer blessed in children, no longer
	blessed with sons; no share for me now
	in the good fortune of the Argive women who have borne boys.
	Artemis who watches over childbirth
	would not speak a word to women with no children.
	Life is an ill wind,
	and like some wandering cloud
	I am driven along by winter storms.
Chorus.
	Seven mothers, and seven sons
	we bore, we wretched women,
	the most famous men in Argos.
	And now, no son, no child,
	I grow old in utter misery,
	counted neither among the dead
	nor among the living,
	with a fate of my own, apart from both.
Chorus.
	What is left to me is tears.
	In my house the sad memorials of my son
	lie stored: hair cut in mourning,
	garlands for his head,
	drink-offerings for the dead and gone,
	and songs, songs that golden-haired
	Apollo will not accept.
	I will wake at dawn to wail,
	and the fold of my dress at my breast
	will be wet with tears for ever.
Chorus.
	And look: I see the burial chamber now,
	the holy tomb of Capaneus,
	and outside the temple
	the offerings Theseus has set for the dead,
	and near this man the lightning killed
	his famous wife, Evadne,
	the daughter King Iphis fathered.
	Why is she standing high on the rock
	that towers over this temple,
	walking out along that path?

(Evadne appears on the rock above the temple, over the pyre of Capaneus. She is dressed as she was for her wedding.)

Evadne.
	What light, what brightness
	did the sun drive across the sky that day,
	and the moon through the upper air,
	where the swift-running nymphs
	ride through the dark with their torches,
	the day the city of Argos
	built the wedding songs high,
	the songs of my happiness, for my marriage
	to my husband in his bronze armour, aiai, Capaneus.
	To you I have come, running from my house,
	driven wild, out of my mind,
	to step into the light of your pyre
	and into the same grave,
	to end my toiling life in Hades
	and the labours of living.
	The sweetest death there is
	is to die with the ones you love as they die,
	if a god decrees it.

Chorus. There. You see the pyre, the one you are standing over, the treasure-house of Zeus: your husband is inside it, struck down by the torches of the lightning.

Evadne.
	I see the end,
	from where I stand. May luck
	go with my feet. For honour's sake
	I will launch myself from here,
	leap from this rock
	into the fire,
	and mix my body with my husband's
	in the blazing flame,
	my dear skin laid against his skin,
	and come to Persephone's bridal chambers,
	never betraying you, dead
	under the earth, to save my own life.
	Let the light go, and marriage with it.
	And in Argos, let honest weddings
	and honest marriages appear
	for my children to see. And let the husband
	who shares the bed be true, true,
	melted into one with the guileless spirit
	of a noble wife.

Chorus. And look, here is your own father coming this way, old Iphis, to hear news he has not heard before. It will hurt him to hear it.

Iphis. Poor women. And I am a poor old man too. I have come with a double grief in my own blood. One is my son Eteoclus, killed by the Theban spear: I have come to ship his body home to his own country. And I am looking for my daughter, the wife of Capaneus, who has rushed out of the house and gone, because she is in love with dying with her husband. Up to now she was watched, in the house. But when I let the guard drop, because of the troubles on us, she went. We think she is most likely to be here. Tell me if you have seen her.

Evadne. Why ask them? Here I am, on the rock, father, above the pyre of Capaneus, hovering like a bird, a wretched thing hanging in the air.

Iphis. Child, what wind blew you here? What journey is this? Why did you slip out of the house and come to this country?

Evadne. You would be angry if you heard my plans. I do not want you to hear them, father.

Iphis. What? Is it not right for your own father to know?

Evadne. You would not be a wise judge of my decision.

Iphis. And why have you dressed yourself up like this?

Evadne. This dress means something glorious, father.

Iphis. You do not look like a woman in mourning for her husband.

Evadne. No. I am dressed for something new.

Iphis. And you show yourself like that, beside a tomb and a pyre?

Evadne. Yes. This is where I come as the winner, wearing the crown.

Iphis. Winning what? What victory? I want to learn that from you.

Evadne. Over every woman the sun looks down on.

Iphis. In Athena's handiwork, or in good sense?

Evadne. In courage. I am going to lie down dead beside my husband.

Iphis. What are you saying? What is this rotten riddle you are hinting at?

Evadne. I am going to jump into this pyre, where Capaneus lies dead.

Iphis. Daughter, do not say that in front of all these people.

Evadne. That is exactly what I want. For every Argive to know it.

Iphis. But I will not let you do it. I will not stand for it.

Evadne. It makes no difference. You will never catch me, never get your hand on me. There. My body is let go. Not dear to you, but dear to me, and to the husband who burns with me.

(She leaps from the rock into the pyre.)

Chorus. Io. Woman, what a terrible thing you have done.

Iphis. I am finished. Daughters of Argos, I am destroyed.

Chorus.
	E, e. You have suffered a cruel thing,
	and now you will look at what she dared, poor man, the whole of it.
Iphis.
	You could not find another man more wretched.
Chorus.
	Io, poor man.
	You have taken your share of the fortune of Oedipus, old man,
	you and my poor city both.

Iphis. Oh. Why is this one thing not given to mortals: to be young twice, and old again a second time? Inside a house, if something is not right, we straighten it out with second thoughts; but a life we cannot. If we were young twice, and old twice, then whenever someone went wrong he would have a second life to put it right in. Look at me. I saw other men having children and I fell in love with children; I was dying of the longing for them. If I had come to this first, had been through it and learned what it is for a father to be robbed of his children, I would never have come to the evil I am in now: I fathered a son, and raised him to be the best young man there was, and now I am robbed of him.

Well. What should a wretched man like me do now? Go home? And look at the emptiness of all those rooms, and no way forward for my life? Or go to the house of Capaneus here? I loved to go there before, when my daughter was alive. But she is gone now. She used to draw my beard to her lips, and take this head of mine between her hands. There is nothing sweeter to an old father than a daughter. Sons have bigger spirits, but they are less sweet when it comes to fondness.

Take me home, quickly. Put me in the dark. There I will starve this old body of mine, waste it away and destroy it. What good will it do me to touch my child's bones? Old age, you are a hard wrestler. How I hate having you. And I hate the men who want to stretch out their lives, who use food and drink and magic to turn the stream aside so that they will not die. When they are no use to the earth any more they should die and be gone, and get out of the young people's way.

Chorus.
	Io. Io.
	Here they come, the bones
	of my dead children, carried in. Take hold of me, servants,
	a feeble old woman. There is no strength
	left in her, for grief over her sons.
	She has lived out the measure of a long time
	and wasted away with many sorrows.
	What greater suffering could you find
	for mortals than this:
	to see your children dead?

(The sons of the Seven come in, each carrying an urn of his father's ashes.)

Children.
	I carry them, I carry them,
	poor mother, my father's limbs out of the fire,
	a weight that is not light, for the pain of it,
	though all I have is packed into this little space.
Chorus.
	Io. Io.
	Where are you carrying tears
	to the loving mother of the dead?
	A little heap of ash, in place of the bodies
	of men once so well thought of in Mycenae?
Children.
	No child. No child.
	And I, robbed of my poor father, wretched,
	will take an empty house and be an orphan in it,
	not in the arms of the father who made me.
Chorus.
	Io. Io.
	Where is the labour I spent on my children,
	where the thanks for bearing them,
	a mother's nursing, the nights my eyes did not sleep,
	the loving kisses on their faces?
Children.
	They are gone. They are no more. Oh, father.
	They are gone.
Chorus.
	The air holds them now,
	melted to ash in the fire.
	On wings they have finished the journey to Hades.
Children.
	Father, do you hear your children crying?
	Will I ever stand in the line with a shield
	and avenge your killing? If only it could be.
Children.
	One day, if the god is willing, justice will come
	for my father.
Chorus.
	This evil is not asleep yet.
	Aiai, the wailing. I have had enough of fortune,
	enough of pain already.
Children.
	One day the bright water of the Asopus will receive me
	in bronze armour, leading the army of the Argives,
	the avenger of my dead father.
Children.
	I think I still see you, father, before my eyes,
Chorus.
	laying your loving kiss against your son's cheek.
Children.
	But the encouragement of your words
	is carried off on the wind and gone.
Chorus.
	He left his grief to two: to his mother,
	and the pain for your father will never leave you.
Children.
	I carry a weight as heavy as what destroyed me.
Chorus.
	Come. Let me lay the dear ash against my breast.
Children.
	I wept to hear that word,
	the most hateful of all. It touched my heart.
Chorus.
	Child, you are gone. Never again will I see you,
	your loving mother's darling.

Theseus. Adrastus, and you women of the Argive race: you see these boys holding in their hands the bodies of their fathers, the best of men, whom I recovered. I and the city give them to you as a gift. You must remember this and keep your gratitude for it safe, looking at what you have had from me, and say the same words to these boys: to honour this city, and to hand on from children to children for ever the memory of what you received. Let Zeus be the witness, and the gods in heaven, of the treatment you had from us as you leave.

Adrastus. Theseus, we know everything you have done, all the good to the land of Argos when it needed help, and our gratitude will never grow old. We have been treated nobly, and we owe you the same in return.

Theseus. Then what else is there that I must do for you?

Adrastus. Goodbye. You deserve it, and so does your city.

Theseus. So be it. And may the same come to you.

(Athena appears above the temple.)

Athena. Listen, Theseus, to these words from Athena: what you must do, and by doing it help this city. Do not hand these bones over to the boys to carry to the land of Argos, letting them go as lightly as that. In return for your own labours and the city's, first take an oath. Adrastus must be the one to swear it: he has the authority, being king, to swear for the whole land of the Danaans. And this is what the oath will be: that the Argives will never bring an army in full armour against this land, and that if others come, they will put their spears in the way. And if they break the oath and come, pray that the land of Argos may be destroyed again, and miserably.

Now hear me on where you must cut the throats of the victims. You have a bronze-footed tripod in your house, which Heracles once, when he had torn up the foundations of Troy and was setting off on another labour, charged you to set up at the Pythian hearth, at Delphi. Cut the throats of three sheep over it, and engrave the oath inside the hollow bowl of the tripod, and then give it to the god who cares for Delphi to keep, a memorial of the oath and a witness for all Greece. And the sharp-edged knife you open the victims with, and make the wound that kills them: hide it in the depths of the earth, right beside the seven pyres of the dead. If ever they come against the city, it will be shown to them, and it will put fear in them, and send them home the worse for it. When you have done all this, send the dead out of the land. And the sacred ground where their bodies were purified by fire, give up to the god, at the place where the three roads meet on the way to the Isthmus.

That is what I have to say to you. To the sons of the Argives I say this. When you are grown you will sack the city on the Ismenus, avenging the killing of your dead fathers: you, Aegialeus, standing in your father's place as a young general, and the son of Tydeus, coming from Aetolia, the boy his father named Diomedes. As soon as the beard shadows your cheeks you must launch the army of the Danaans, heavy with bronze, against the seven-gated fortress of the Cadmeans. You will come to them bitter, lion cubs grown up, and sack their city. It cannot be otherwise. Through all Greece you will be called the After-born, the Epigoni, and you will give the men who come after you something to sing. That is the kind of army you will lead, with the god's help.

Theseus. Lady Athena, I will do as you say. You set me straight, so that I do not go wrong. I will bind this man with oaths. Only keep me on the straight road. As long as you are kind to the city, we will live in safety from now on.

Chorus.
	Let us go, Adrastus, and give our oaths
	to this man and his city. What they have laboured for,
	on our behalf, deserves our reverence.

Electra (c. 420 BC)

Electra

(Before a farmer's cottage in the hill country on the border of Argos. It is still dark. The Farmer comes out of the house.)

Farmer. Old plain of Argos, streams of Inachus. This is where King Agamemnon set out from, when he raised an army and sailed a thousand ships to make war on the land of Troy. He killed Priam, who ruled the land of Ilium, and took the famous city that Dardanus founded, and came home here to Argos, and hung the high temples with more plunder from the barbarians than any man before him. Over there he did well. At home, he died. His wife Clytemnestra laid the trap, and Aegisthus, the son of Thyestes, did it with his own hand. So he is gone, and the old sceptre of Tantalus went with him, and Aegisthus is king of this country, with Agamemnon's wife, the daughter of Tyndareus, for his own.

As for the children he left in the house when he sailed for Troy, a boy, Orestes, and a girl, the young shoot Electra: Orestes was about to die at Aegisthus's hands, but his father's old tutor stole him away and gave him to Strophius to bring up in the land of the Phocians. Electra stayed on in her father's house, and when she came into the full bloom of her youth, the first men of Greece were asking for her. Aegisthus was afraid she would bear a son to one of those lords, an avenger for Agamemnon, so he kept her in the house and would not match her with any bridegroom. And when even that turned out to be full of fear, because she might bear children to some nobleman in secret, he made up his mind to kill her. Her mother stopped him. Cruel as she is, her mother saved her from Aegisthus's hand. For killing her husband she had an excuse. For killing her children, she was afraid, she would be hated.

So out of all this, here is what Aegisthus worked out. Agamemnon's son had got away, an exile out of the country; Aegisthus put up gold for any man who kills him. And Electra he gave to me, to have as my wife. My people were Mycenaeans, and on that score nobody can fault me. The family was bright enough in blood, but poor in money, and that is where good birth goes to die. He gave her to a weak man so that his fear would be weak too. Because if a man of standing had got her, he would have woken the murder of Agamemnon out of its sleep, and justice would have come for Aegisthus then.

And this man here has never shamed her in bed. Aphrodite is my witness: she is still a virgin. I would be ashamed to take a rich man's daughter and outrage her, when I was not born her equal. And I grieve for poor Orestes, my brother-in-law in name, if he ever comes home to Argos and sees what a miserable marriage his sister has made. Whoever calls me a fool for having a young girl in my house and not touching her can know this: he is measuring good sense with a crooked ruler, and he is the fool himself.

(Electra comes out of the house with a water jar on her head.)

Electra. Black night, nurse of the golden stars. Under you I go to the river for water with this jar balanced on my head, not because I have come down to such need, but to show the gods what Aegisthus's outrage looks like, and I send my cries up into the wide sky, to my father. Because that murderous daughter of Tyndareus, my mother, has thrown me out of the house to please her husband. She has other children now, by Aegisthus, and Orestes and I are the leftovers of the family —

Farmer. Why do you do this, you poor thing? Why work yourself like this for my sake, taking all this labour on, when you were brought up soft? And why don't you stop when I tell you to?

Electra. To me you are as good as a god, the friend you have been to me. You did not take advantage of me when I was down. When things go badly, it is a great piece of luck for a mortal to find a healer for it, and that is what I have found in you. So even if nobody asks me to, I ought to do all I have strength for to lighten your load and carry the work alongside you, so you bear it more easily. You have enough to do out of doors. The house is my business, to keep it straight. When a working man comes in from outside, it is a pleasure to find things right indoors.

Farmer. Go, then, if that is what you want. The springs are not far from this house anyway. And I will go out at first light and put the oxen in the fields and sow the ground. No idler, however much he keeps the gods' names in his mouth, ever got a living together without work.

(The Farmer goes off to his fields, and Electra towards the river. Orestes and Pylades come in along the road.)

Orestes. Pylades, you are the first man I would name as loyal to me, a friend and a guest. You alone of my friends have stood by Orestes here, treated the way I have been treated by Aegisthus, who killed my father, he and my mother, that destroyer. I have come from the god's holy shrine to Argive soil, and nobody knows it, to pay my father's murderers back murder for murder. Last night I went to my father's grave and gave him my tears, and cut him the first lock of my hair, and killed a sheep over the mound and let its blood run, unseen by the tyrants who hold this land. And I am not setting foot inside the walls. I have come to the edge of the country with two aims at once. If some watcher recognises me, I can step over the border into another country. And I am looking for my sister. They say she is living here, yoked in marriage, no virgin any more. I want to meet her and get her to work with me on the killing, and find out for certain how things stand inside the walls.

So now, since dawn is lifting her white eye, let us step off this path. Some ploughman or some slave woman will show herself, and we can ask whether my sister lives round here. And look. I can see one now, some servant, carrying a jar of water on her cropped head. Let us sit down, and put our question to this slave woman, Pylades, in case she gives us a word about the business we came to this country for.

(They step aside and sit down out of sight. Electra comes back with the jar of water on her head, singing.)

Electra.
	Move your feet. It is time. Faster.
	Go on, go on, and weep as you go.
	Io moi moi.
	I was born Agamemnon's child,
	and Clytemnestra bore me,
	the hateful daughter of Tyndareus,
	and the people of the town call me
	Electra, the wretched one.
	Pheu, pheu, for the hard work
	and the life I loathe.
	Father, you lie in Hades,
	butchered by your wife
	and Aegisthus. Agamemnon.
Electra.
	Come, wake the same cry again,
	raise up the pleasure of long weeping.
Electra.
	Move your feet. It is time. Faster.
	Go on, go on, and weep as you go.
	Io moi moi.
	What city, what house, my poor brother,
	are you wandering in,
	when you left your sister behind
	in her father's rooms, to be pitied,
	with the worst of griefs on her?
	Come, and set me free from this work,
	miserable as I am.
	Zeus, Zeus, come and stand by my father
	against that most hated blood. Bring the wanderer
	to shore in Argos.
Electra.
	Take this jar off my head and set it down,
	so I can cry the night-cries for my father
	before the dawn,
	a wail, a song of Hades,
	Hades, father, for you
	under the earth. I say the laments
	I live in every day, all day,
	tearing my dear throat with my nails
	and beating my hand on my cropped head,
	for your death.
Electra.
	Ai ai. Tear your face.
	Like a swan crying clear
	by the river's streams,
	calling to its dearest father,
	dead in the treacherous meshes of a net,
	so I cry for you, my wretched
	father,
Electra.
	washed in your last bath,
	in the most pitiful bed of death.
	Io moi, io moi,
	for the bitter cut of the axe on you,
	father, and the bitter plan
	that met you on the road home from Troy.
	Not with garlands did your wife receive you,
	not with crowns,
	but with a two-edged sword. She made you
	the sorry victim of Aegisthus
	and took a traitor into her bed.

(The Chorus, country women of Argos, come in.)

Chorus.
	Daughter of Agamemnon,
	Electra, I have come
	to your country yard.
	A man has come, a man has come from Mycenae,
	a milk-drinker who walks the mountains,
	and he brings news: the Argives are announcing
	a sacrifice for the day after tomorrow,
	and all the unmarried girls
	are to walk in procession to Hera's temple.
Electra.
	It is not for finery, friends,
	that my heart goes flying out of me,
	not for necklaces of gold,
	and I will not stand in the dance
	with the young women of Argos
	and beat out the turns with my foot.
	I pass my nights in tears,
	and tears, poor thing that I am,
	are all my care by day.
	Look at my hair, filthy,
	and these rags I wear for a dress,
	and ask if they are fit for a princess,
	Agamemnon's daughter,
	or for Troy, which fell to my father once
	and has not forgotten him.
Chorus.
	The goddess is great. Come.
	Borrow from me a thick-woven robe to wear,
	and gold, do me the favour,
	to set off your finery.
	Do you think your tears will beat your enemies,
	if you give the gods no honour?
	Not with groans, child. Honour the gods
	with prayers, and you will see good days.
Electra.
	No god hears the cry
	of a woman the gods hate,
	or remembers my father, slaughtered so long ago.
	Oh, for the dead man,
	and for the living one, the wanderer,
	who is somewhere in another country,
	poor man, drifting
	to a hired man's hearth,
	and he the son of that famous father.
	And I live in a labourer's house,
	my life melting away,
	driven out of my father's home
	onto these mountain crags.
	And my mother, in a bed stained with blood,
	lives married to another man.

Chorus. Your mother's sister Helen is to blame for a great deal of evil, both to the Greeks and to your own house.

Electra. Oh. Women, I have broken off my lament. There are strangers by the house. They were lying low at the altar and now they are getting up out of their hiding place. Run. You down the path, and I into the house. Let us get away from these criminals while we can.

(Orestes and Pylades come out of hiding. Orestes has his sword drawn.)

Orestes. Stay where you are, poor woman. You have nothing to fear from my hand.

Electra. Apollo, help me. I am on my knees to you. Do not kill me.

Orestes. There are others I would rather kill. People I hate more than you.

Electra. Get away. Do not touch what you have no right to touch.

Orestes. There is nobody I have a better right to touch.

Electra. Then why are you lying in ambush at my house with a sword?

Orestes. Stay and listen, and you will soon say the same.

Electra. I am standing still. I am yours in any case. You are the stronger.

Orestes. I have come with a message for you from your brother.

Electra. Dearest of men. Is he alive, or dead?

Orestes. Alive. I want to give you the good news first.

Electra. Good luck to you, for the sweetest words I ever heard. That is your fee.

Orestes. I will take that as a gift for the two of us to share.

Electra. Where on earth is he, poor man, in his poor exile?

Orestes. He wears himself out drifting, with no one city's laws to live by.

Electra. Surely he is not short of his daily bread?

Orestes. He has that. But a man in exile is a weak man.

Electra. And what message have you come with from him?

Orestes. Whether you are alive, and if you are, how you are faring.

Electra. Well, you can see for yourself, first, how my body has dried up.

Orestes. Yes, wasted with grief. It makes me groan to look at it.

Electra. And my head, my hair, cropped with a razor like a Scythian's.

Orestes. Your brother gnaws at you, I suppose, and your dead father.

Electra. Oh. What is dearer to me than those two?

Orestes. Pheu, pheu. And what do you think you are to your brother?

Electra. He loves me from far away. He is not here to be a friend to me.

Orestes. And why do you live out here, so far from the town?

Electra. I am married, stranger. A marriage that is death.

Orestes. I groan for your brother. To which of the Mycenaeans?

Electra. Not to the one my father ever hoped to give me to.

Orestes. Tell me, so I can hear it and tell your brother.

Electra. This is his house. I live in it, far from everything.

Orestes. A ditch-digger or a cowherd would be the right man for a house like this.

Electra. A poor man, but well born, and he treats me with reverence.

Orestes. What kind of reverence does this husband of yours have?

Electra. He has never brought himself to touch my bed.

Orestes. Some holy vow he keeps? Or does he think you beneath him?

Electra. He did not think he had the right to outrage my parents.

Orestes. How could he get a marriage like that and not be delighted?

Electra. He does not think the man who gave me away had the right to, stranger.

Orestes. I see. He is afraid Orestes will make him pay for it one day.

Electra. He is afraid of that, yes. But he is also a man who keeps himself in hand.

Orestes. Pheu. That is a noble man you are describing. He should be treated well.

Electra. Yes, if the one who is away ever comes home.

Orestes. And your mother, who bore you, put up with this?

Electra. Women love their husbands, stranger, not their children.

Orestes. And why did Aegisthus do you this outrage?

Electra. He wanted me to bear weak children, so he gave me to a man like this.

Orestes. So you would never bear sons to punish him, of course.

Electra. That was his plan. And may he pay me for it.

Orestes. Does your mother's husband know you are a virgin?

Electra. He does not. We keep quiet and steal that from him.

Orestes. These women listening to us, are they friends of yours?

Electra. Friends enough to keep your words and mine well hidden.

Orestes. Then what could Orestes do about it, if he came to Argos?

Electra. You ask that? Shame on you for asking. Is now not the moment?

Orestes. And if he did come, how could he kill his father's murderers?

Electra. By having the nerve to do to them what his enemies had the nerve to do to my father.

Orestes. And would you have the nerve to kill your mother, with him?

Electra. Yes. With the same axe my father died by.

Orestes. Am I to tell him that? And that you will not waver?

Electra. Let me die, once I have spilled my mother's blood.

Orestes. Pheu. If only Orestes were standing here to hear that.

Electra. But stranger, I would not know him if I saw him.

Orestes. No wonder. You were both children when you were torn apart.

Electra. There is only one of my friends who would recognise him.

Orestes. The man they say stole him away from being murdered?

Electra. Yes. My father's tutor. An old man now, from the old days.

Orestes. And your father, when he died, did he get a grave?

Electra. He got what he got. Thrown out of the house.

Orestes. Oh. What a thing to say. It bites a man, hearing of suffering, even when the trouble is somebody else's. Tell me, so that I can know it and carry the story to your brother: not pleasant to hear, but he has to hear it. There is no pity in a stupid man. Pity lives in the wise. And even for the wise it costs something, to have a mind that is too wise.

Chorus. And we have the same longing in our hearts as this man. We live far from the town, and we do not know the evils in the city. Now we would like to learn them too.

Electra. I will tell it, if I must, and one must, to a friend: the heavy luck of my father and me. And since you are the one setting the story going, I beg you, stranger, tell Orestes what has happened to me, and to him. First, the clothes I bed down in, like an animal in a stall. The dirt I am weighed down with. The kind of roof I live under, after a king's palace. I weave my own clothes at the loom, working myself to the bone, or else I go naked and do without. I carry the water from the river myself. I have no festivals, no holy rites, no share in the dances. I turn away from the married women, because I am a virgin, and I turn away from Castor, who courted me before he went up among the gods, because I was his kin.

And my mother sits on her throne among the plunder of Troy, and beside her seat stand slave women from Asia, my father's prizes of war, their Trojan robes pinned with golden brooches. And my father's blood is still there on the walls of the house, gone black and rotten, and the man who killed him climbs into the same chariot my father rode and drives out in it, and takes the sceptre my father commanded the Greeks with in his bloodstained hands and swaggers with it. Agamemnon's grave lies dishonoured. It has never once had a drink poured on it, or a sprig of myrtle. His pyre is bare of every offering. And my mother's husband, the famous one, when he is soaked with drink, jumps on the grave, so they say, and throws stones at my father's stone monument, and has the nerve to say this about us: "Where is your boy Orestes? Is he here doing a fine job of guarding your tomb?" That is how Orestes is outraged, and he is not here to hear it.

So, stranger, I beg you, take this report back. Many voices are sending it, and I am only their interpreter: these hands, this tongue, this worn-out heart, my shaven head, and the man who fathered him. Because it is a disgrace if his father wiped out the Trojans and he cannot kill one man, one against one, when he is young and comes from a better father.

Chorus. And look, we can see him, your husband, I mean, on his way home, his work done for the day.

(The Farmer comes back from the fields.)

Farmer. What is this? Who are these strangers I see at my door? What brings them to a farmyard gate like mine? Do they want something from me? It does not look right, you know, for a woman to stand about with young men.

Electra. Dearest, do not get suspicious of me. You will hear the true story. These strangers have come to me as messengers, with news of Orestes. And strangers, forgive him for what he said.

Farmer. What are they saying? The man is alive? He sees the light of day?

Electra. So they say, and I do not think they are lying to me.

Farmer. And does he remember anything of your father's wrongs, and yours?

Electra. That is something to hope for. A man in exile is weak.

Farmer. What message from Orestes have they come to deliver?

Electra. He sent them to see for themselves how badly I am treated.

Farmer. Then they see some of it, and I suppose you are telling them the rest.

Electra. They know. There is nothing they lack of it.

Farmer. Then should the doors not have been opened to them long ago? Go inside, both of you. In return for your good news you will find whatever hospitality my house has in it. Servants, take their baggage inside. And do not argue with me: you are friends, come from a friend. I may be poor, but I will not show you the manners of a low-born man.

Orestes. By the gods, is this the man who keeps up the pretence of your marriage, the one who does not want to bring shame on Orestes?

Electra. This is the man they call my husband. Mine, in my misery.

Orestes. Pheu. There is no exact way to measure a man's worth. Human nature is a muddle. I have seen the son of a noble father turn out to be nothing, and good children come out of bad parents. I have seen famine in a rich man's mind and a great judgement in a poor man's body. So how does anyone sort them out and judge them rightly? By wealth? Then he is using a rotten judge. By having nothing? But poverty has a sickness in it: it teaches a man to be bad because he is in need. Shall I go to war for my test, then? Who, with a spear pointed at him, could stand witness to which man is brave? Best to let all that go, and leave it to chance.

Because this man here is nobody great among the Argives, and he is not puffed up with the reputation of his family. He is one of the many, and he has turned out to be the best. Will you not stop being fools, you people who wander about stuffed with empty notions, and judge men by the company they keep, and judge the noble by their habits? Men like that run cities well, and households too. The lumps of flesh with no mind in them are statues in the marketplace. A strong arm does not stand up to the spear any better than a weak one: that is a matter of a man's nature, and of his courage.

But since the son of Agamemnon deserves it, the one who is here and not here, the one we have come for, let us accept the shelter of this house. Inside, slaves. We must go in. I would rather have a poor man for my host who wants to have me than a rich one. So I am grateful for the welcome this man gives me into his house, though I would have wished your brother could have led me, prosperous himself, into a prosperous house. And perhaps he will come. Apollo's oracles are sure. It is the prophecy of men I say goodbye to.

(Orestes and Pylades go into the house with their servants.)

Chorus. Now more than ever before, Electra, our hearts are warm with joy. Perhaps our luck, after its hard slow progress, is coming to a good standing place.

Electra. You reckless man. You know how poor your house is. Why did you take in these strangers, men so far above you?

Farmer. Why not? If they are as well born as they look, will they not be just as content with small things as with great?

Electra. Well, since you have made this mistake, small man that you are, go to my father's dear old tutor. He is out by the river Tanaus, where it cuts the border between the land of Argos and the land of Sparta. He was thrown out of the city, and he keeps sheep there. Tell him these men have arrived at my house, and to come, and bring something for the strangers' meal. He will be glad, and he will pray to the gods when he hears that the child he saved once is alive. From my father's house, from my mother, we would get nothing. And it would be bitter news we brought, if that hard woman ever found out that Orestes is still alive.

Farmer. All right. If that is what you want, I will take the message to the old man. But you get into the house as fast as you can and get things ready inside. A woman who wants to can always find plenty to add to a meal. And there is still enough in the house to fill these men with food for one day at least. It is at times like this, when I fall short of what I meant to do, that I see what great power money has: to give to strangers, and to spend on saving a body when it falls ill. But when it comes to the day's food, money does not go far. Every man who has eaten his fill, rich or poor, carries the same load.

(The Farmer goes off towards the river Tanaus. Electra goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	Famous ships, that went to Troy once
	with oars past counting,
	leading the dance with the Nereids,
	where the dolphin that loves the pipe
	leapt at your dark-blue prows
	and rolled,
	carrying Thetis's son,
	Achilles, light on his leaping feet,
	with Agamemnon to the banks
	of Simois, the river of Troy.
Chorus.
	And the Nereids left the headlands of Euboea
	and carried the shield, the toil of Hephaestus's anvils,
	the golden armour,
	up Pelion, up the glens
	at the foot of holy Ossa,
	the Nymphs' lookouts, searching for the place
	where Chiron, the horseman who was a father to him,
	was raising him, the light of Greece,
	Thetis's son from the sea,
	swift-footed for the sons of Atreus.
Chorus.
	I heard it from a man who came from Troy
	and landed in the harbour at Nauplia:
	that on the round of your famous shield,
	son of Thetis,
	these were the signs worked in it,
	terrors for the Phrygians.
	Running round the rim, on its base,
	Perseus the throat-cutter, over the sea
	on his winged sandals,
	holding up the Gorgon's head,
	with Zeus's messenger Hermes beside him,
	Maia's son, the god of the countryside.
Chorus.
	And in the middle of the shield blazed
	the bright circle of the sun
	on his winged horses,
	and the dancing stars of the sky,
	the Pleiades and the Hyades,
	to turn Hector's eyes and put him to flight.
	On the helmet of beaten gold
	were Sphinxes carrying in their claws
	the prey their singing had won,
	and on the breastplate, round his ribs,
	a lioness breathing fire ran hard,
	claws out,
	at the sight of Pegasus, the colt of Pirene's spring.
Chorus.
	And on the murderous sword
	horses pranced on four feet,
	and black dust rose about their backs.
	The lord of warriors like these, spearmen like these,
	you killed, daughter of Tyndareus,
	with your adultery, evil-minded woman.
	For that the gods of heaven
	will send you one day to your death.
	Yes, and I will see it yet, I will see
	the blood run under your throat,
	spilled by the iron.

(The Old Man, who was Agamemnon's tutor, comes slowly up the path to the farmhouse, carrying a lamb, a wineskin and a basket.)

Old Man. Where is she? Where is my young lady, my mistress, Agamemnon's child, the girl I brought up once? What a steep climb this house has, for an old man with a wrinkled foot to get up. Still, when it is for the people you love, you drag the bent old spine along, and the knee that keeps giving way under you. Daughter. I have only just seen you there at the door. Here I am, and look what I have brought you from my own flock: this newborn lamb, pulled away from its mother, and garlands, and cheeses I took out of the presses, and this old treasure of Dionysus, ripe with the smell of it. Not much of it, but sweet to pour a cup of into something weaker. Someone take these into the house for the guests. As for me, I want to wipe my eyes on this rag of a cloak. They are wet.

Electra. Why are your eyes wet, old man? Have my troubles reminded you of themselves, after all this time? Or are you groaning over Orestes and his miserable exile, and over my father, whom you once held in your arms and brought up, and all for nothing: no good to you, and none to the people you love?

Old Man. For nothing. Yes. But all the same there was one thing I could not bear. I went by his grave on the way here, a little off the road, and when I found it deserted I fell on it and cried. And I opened the wineskin I am bringing for your guests and poured him an offering, and I laid sprigs of myrtle round the tomb. And on the altar itself I saw a sheep with a black fleece, slaughtered, and blood that had not been spilled long, and curls of yellow hair, cut off. And I wondered, child, who on earth had the nerve to go near that tomb. It was not any Argive, that much is certain. But perhaps your brother has come, in secret, somehow, and found his father's poor grave and paid it honour. Look at the hair. Hold it against your own and see whether the colour of the cut lock is the same as yours. It usually happens that people who share a father's blood come out alike in most parts of the body.

Electra. That is not worthy of a clever man, old man, what you are saying. Do you think my brother would come sneaking into this country, afraid of Aegisthus? Him? He has more courage than that. And then, how is a lock of hair going to match: one grown in the wrestling schools, on a well-born man, and the other soft, a woman's hair, made with combing? It is impossible. And you could find plenty of people, old man, with curls of hair exactly alike, who are no blood relations at all.

Old Man. Then go and stand in the footprint. See whether the print of his boot measures the same as your foot, child.

Electra. How could there be any print of a foot on rocky ground? And if there is one, a brother's foot and a sister's would not be the same size, a man's and a woman's. The male is bigger.

Old Man. Is there nothing, then, even if your brother has come to this country, nothing by which you could recognise the weaving of your own shuttle, the cloth I once stole him away in and saved his life?

Electra. Do you not know I was still a little girl when Orestes was driven out of the country? And even if I had woven him clothes, how could he, a child then, still be wearing the same ones now, unless his clothes grew along with his body? No. Either some stranger took pity on the grave and cut his hair for it, or else someone slipped past the watchmen of this country and —

Old Man. And where are the guests? I want to see them and question them about your brother.

Electra. Here they are, coming out of the house. Quickly, too.

(Orestes and Pylades come out of the house.)

Old Man. Well, they look well-born. But that can be counterfeit. Plenty of well-born men are bad. Still. Greetings to the guests. I wish them well.

Orestes. Greetings, old man. Electra, which of your friends does this ancient relic of a man belong to?

Electra. This is the man who brought up my father, stranger.

Orestes. What? This is the one who smuggled your brother out?

Electra. This is the man who saved him, if he is still alive.

Orestes. Ah. Why is he staring at me like that, as if he were examining the bright stamp on a silver coin? Is he comparing me to somebody?

Electra. Perhaps he is glad to see someone the same age as Orestes.

Orestes. Yes, a man I love. But why is he walking round and round me?

Electra. I am looking at it too, stranger, and I am amazed.

Old Man. My lady. Daughter. Electra. Pray to the gods.

Electra. For what? Something I have, or something I have not?

Old Man. To take hold of a treasure you love, which a god is showing you.

Electra. There. I call on the gods. Or what do you mean, old man?

Old Man. Now look at this man, child. The man you love most.

Electra. I have been looking for a while, wondering whether you have lost your mind.

Old Man. Lost my mind? When I am looking at your brother?
