Electra. What did you say, old man? That is a word I never hoped to hear.

Old Man. That I see Orestes here. Agamemnon's son.

Electra. What mark have you seen, that I should believe you?

Old Man. A scar by his eyebrow. He fell and cut himself, once, in his father's house, chasing a fawn with you, and it bled.

Electra. What are you saying? I see it. I see the mark of the fall.

Old Man. And you are still slow to throw your arms round the one you love most?

Electra. Not any more, old man. My heart is convinced by your proofs. You have appeared at last. I am holding you. I never hoped —

Orestes. And I am holding you, at last.

Electra. I never thought it would happen.

Orestes. I never hoped it would either.

Electra. Are you really him?

Orestes. The one ally you have. If I can haul in the catch I have come for. And I am confident I can. Or else we should stop believing in gods at all, if wrong is going to win out over justice.

Chorus.
	You have come, you have come, oh, day so long in coming,
	you have blazed up, you have shown the city
	a beacon to see by: the man who long ago
	went out of his father's house into exile,
	poor wretch, and wandered.
	A god, my dear, a god is bringing
	our victory home.
	Lift up your hands, lift up your voice, send prayers
	to the gods, that with luck, with luck,
	your brother may walk into the city.

Orestes. Well. I have had the sweet pleasure of your welcome, and later on we will give it back to each other. But you, old man, you have come at exactly the right time, so tell me: what should I do to pay back my father's murderer, and my mother, his partner in an unholy marriage? Is there anyone in Argos who still wishes me well? Or am I bankrupt all round, the way my fortunes are? Who do I join up with? By night, or in daylight? Which road do I take against my enemies?

Old Man. Child, when you are down on your luck you have no friend. It is a rare find, believe me, someone who will share the bad with you as well as the good. As for you, you have been torn out by the roots as far as your friends are concerned, and you have left them no hope, so hear me and understand: everything you have is in your own right arm and in your luck. Your father's house and your city are yours to take with those.

Orestes. Then what do I do, to get there?

Old Man. Kill Thyestes's son, and your mother.

Orestes. That is the crown I came for. But how do I get my hands on it?

Old Man. Not by going inside the walls, even if you wanted to.

Orestes. He is well supplied with guards, and spearmen at his side?

Old Man. You have it. He is afraid of you, and he does not sleep well.

Orestes. Well. It is for you to plan the next move, old man.

Old Man. Then listen to me. Something has just come into my head.

Orestes. I hope it is something good, and I hope I see it.

Old Man. I saw Aegisthus as I was crawling along here.

Orestes. I like the sound of that. Where was he?

Old Man. Near these fields. By his horse pastures.

Orestes. Doing what? I see a hope coming out of nowhere.

Old Man. Getting up a feast for the Nymphs, it looked like to me.

Orestes. For children already born and reared, or for a birth on the way?

Old Man. I know only one thing. He was getting ready to slaughter an ox.

Orestes. With how many men? Or alone, with his slaves?

Old Man. There was no Argive there. Only his own household.

Orestes. There is nobody who will know me when he sees me, old man?

Old Man. They are slaves. Slaves who have never seen you.

Orestes. Would they be on our side, if we won?

Old Man. That is the way with slaves. And a good thing for you.

Orestes. So how do I ever get near him?

Old Man. Walk where he will see you while he is killing the ox.

Orestes. His fields are right by the road, then?

Old Man. Yes, and when he sees you there he will invite you to share the feast.

Orestes. A bitter guest he will find at his table, if a god is willing.

Old Man. From there, work it out for yourself, as it falls.

Orestes. Well said. And the woman who bore me. Where is she?

Old Man. In Argos. But she will join her husband for the feast.

Orestes. Why did my mother not set out with her husband?

Old Man. She stayed behind. She is frightened of what the people say.

Orestes. I understand. She knows the city looks at her sideways.

Old Man. Something like that. An unholy woman is hated.

Orestes. So how do I kill her and him at the same time?

Electra. I will arrange my mother's murder myself.

Orestes. And as for the other one, luck will set it right.

Electra. Let this man help us with both.

Old Man. It will be done. But how do you find a way to kill your mother?

Electra. Go to Clytemnestra, old man, and tell her this. Tell her I have had a child. A boy.

Old Man. Had it some time ago, or just now?

Electra. Ten days ago. The time a new mother keeps herself pure.

Old Man. And how does that bring your mother's death any nearer?

Electra. She will come, when she hears I have been through childbirth.

Old Man. Come? Why? Do you think she cares about you, child?

Electra. Yes. And she will cry over my child's low birth.

Old Man. Perhaps. Now bring your story round the turn again, to the finish.

Electra. Well then, if she comes, obviously, she dies.

Old Man. Yes. She will come right up to the doors of your house.

Electra. And then, is it not a small step from there to Hades?

Old Man. Let me die once I have seen that.

Electra. First of all, then, old man, take my brother the way —

Old Man. To where Aegisthus is sacrificing to the gods right now?

Electra. Then go and find my mother and tell her my news.

Old Man. So that it sounds as if the words came from your own mouth.

Electra. Your work starts now. You drew the first turn in the killing.

Orestes. I would go, if someone would show me the road.

Old Man. I will take you myself. And gladly.

Orestes. Zeus of my fathers, be the one who turns my enemies to flight —

Electra. and pity us. We have suffered pitiful things —

Old Man. Yes, pity them. They are your own descendants.

Electra. And Hera, you who rule over the altars of Mycenae —

Orestes. give us victory, if what we ask for is just.

Old Man. Yes, give them justice for their father. Give them their revenge.

Orestes. And you, father, living under the earth by an unholy act —

Electra. and Earth, our queen, whom I strike with my hands —

Old Man. defend them, defend these children. You love them best.

Orestes. Now come, and bring every dead man with you as an ally.

Electra. all the men who wiped out the Phrygians at Troy beside you, spear in hand —

Old Man. and everyone who hates unholy men with pollution on them.

Electra. Do you hear me, you who suffered dreadful things from my mother?

Old Man. Your father hears all of it, I know. But it is time to go.

Electra. And I say this to you now, in front of everyone: Aegisthus is to die. Because if you are thrown in this wrestling match and go down dead, then I am dead too. Do not call me a living woman any more. I will drive a two-edged sword through my liver. I am going into the house to get things ready. If good news comes from you, the whole house will ring with women's cries of joy. If you die, it will be the opposite. That is what I have to say to you.

Orestes. I know. All of it.

Electra. Then you must be a man now. And you, women, light me the signal fire of a shout, when this fight is decided. I will stand guard with a sword ready in my hand. Because if I am beaten, I will never let my enemies take their satisfaction out of me, and outrage my body. (Orestes and Pylades go out with the Old Man. Electra goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	Under the Argive hills, once,
	a lamb, still at its soft mother's side:
	the story keeps its place in the grey old tales,
	how Pan, who breathes sweet music
	on his well-fitted reeds,
	Pan the steward of the fields,
	brought it down, a lamb with a fleece
	of gold, beautiful curls of gold.
	And a herald stood up on the stone steps
	and cried, "To the assembly, Mycenaeans,
	to the assembly, come and see
	the wonder, the terror, that has come
	to our blessed kings." And the dancers
	paid their honours to the house of Atreus.
Chorus.
	Altars of beaten gold were set out,
	and through the town the fire
	blazed on the altars of the Argives.
	The pipe, the servant of the Muses,
	rang out its loveliest note,
	and lovely songs went swelling up
	in praise of the golden lamb: Thyestes's, they sang,
	Thyestes's luck. For he had talked
	the dear wife of Atreus into a secret bed,
	and carried the wonder off to his own house,
	and went into the assembly and shouted
	that he had the horned sheep
	with the golden fleece at home. His.
Chorus.
	Then, it was then, that Zeus changed
	the shining roads of the stars,
	and the light of the sun,
	and the white face of the dawn,
	and drove the sun across the western
	back of the sky with a hot flame from heaven's fire;
	the rain-clouds went north,
	and the seat of Ammon dried up
	and withered, knowing no dew,
	robbed of the lovely rain that Zeus sends.
Chorus.
	That is what they say. I put small
	faith in it myself: that the sun
	turned his hot golden throne around
	and changed his course, for the misfortune of mortals,
	because of one man's crime and his punishment.
	But stories that frighten people
	are good for the worship of the gods.
	You never gave them a thought when you killed
	your husband, you, the sister
	of the famous brothers, Castor and Polydeuces.

Chorus. Ah. Ah. Friends, did you hear a shout? Or is it an empty fancy that has crept over me? Like the thunder of Zeus, under the ground. Listen. There is a wind rising, and it is not without meaning. Mistress. Electra. Come out of the house.

(Electra comes out.)

Electra. Friends, what is it? How do we stand in the fight?

Chorus. I know one thing only. I hear a cry, and it is a cry of killing.

Electra. I heard it too. A long way off, but I heard it.

Chorus. Yes, the sound is coming from far away. But it is clear enough.

Electra. That groan was an Argive's. Was it one of ours?

Chorus. I cannot tell. The whole tune of the shouting is mixed together.

Electra. That is my death you are calling out. Why am I waiting?

Chorus. Hold on. Wait until you know your fortune for certain.

Electra. No. We have lost. Where are the messengers?

Chorus. They will come. It is no small thing to kill a king.

(A Messenger runs in.)

Messenger. Women of Mycenae, girls in glory, I bring news to all his friends: Orestes has won, and Agamemnon's murderer, Aegisthus, is lying on the ground. Now we must pray to the gods.

Electra. Who are you? How do I know this news of yours is true?

Messenger. Do you not know your brother's servant when you look at him?

Electra. Dearest of men. I was so frightened I could not place your face. Now I know you. What are you saying? Is he dead, my father's hateful murderer?

Messenger. Dead. I say it twice, since it is what you want to hear.

Electra. Gods. And Justice, who sees everything: you have come at last. How did he do it? What kind of death did he give Thyestes's son? I want to hear it.

Messenger. When we left this house we came out onto the wide cart-road, the one with the two ruts, and walked to where the famous king of Mycenae was. He turned out to be walking in a garden full of running water, picking sprays of tender myrtle to make a wreath for his head, and when he saw us he called out, "Welcome, strangers. Who are you? Where have you come from, and what country are you from?" And Orestes said, "Thessalians. We are on our way to the Alpheus to sacrifice to Olympian Zeus." When Aegisthus heard that, he said, "Then you must stay and share the feast with me, as my guests. As it happens I am sacrificing an ox to the Nymphs. Get up at dawn tomorrow and you will be no worse off. Come, let us go inside." And even while he was saying it he had taken us by the hand and was leading us off the road. "I will not have you refuse."

And when we were in the house he said, "Somebody fetch water for the guests, quickly, so they can stand round the altar by the basin." But Orestes said, "We have just purified ourselves, in clean water, in the running stream of a river. If strangers may sacrifice alongside citizens, Aegisthus, we are ready. We will not refuse you, my lord." So they let that conversation drop, out of the middle of things. The slaves who made up the master's bodyguard put down their spears, and every one of them set his hands to the work. Some brought the bowl for the blood, others lifted the baskets, others lit the fire and set the cauldrons upright round the hearth, and the whole roof rang with it.

Then your mother's bedfellow took the barley grains and threw them on the altars, and this is what he said as he did it: "Nymphs of the rocks, grant that I and my wife at home, the daughter of Tyndareus, may sacrifice like this many times over, doing as well as we are doing now, and that my enemies do badly." Meaning Orestes and you. And my master prayed for the opposite, not speaking the words out loud: to take back his father's house. Aegisthus took a long straight knife out of the basket, cut off some of the calf's hair and laid it on the holy fire with his right hand, and when the slaves had lifted the calf up on their shoulders he cut its throat. And he said this to your brother: "One of the fine things Thessalians boast of, they say, is this: a Thessalian knows how to cut up a bull properly, and how to break horses. Take the knife, stranger, and show us that the talk about Thessalians is true."

He grabbed the well-hammered Dorian blade in his hands, threw the handsome pinned cloak off his shoulders, picked Pylades to help him with the work and pushed the slaves back. Then he took the calf by the hoof and stripped the white flesh bare, arm outstretched, and he had the hide off it quicker than a runner does two laps of the horse-track, and laid the flanks open. Aegisthus took the sacred parts in his hands and studied them. And the liver had no lobe. And the portal vein and the gall-bladder beside it showed the man who was reading them bad things coming his way. He scowled, and my master asked him, "Why so downhearted?" "Stranger, I am afraid of some treachery from outside. Of all men alive the one I hate most is Agamemnon's son, and he is my house's enemy." And Orestes said, "You are afraid of treachery from an exile? You, the ruler of a city? Come. So that we can feast on the innards, will somebody bring me a Thessalian cleaver instead of this Dorian knife, and let me break the breastbone open?" He took it and chopped. Aegisthus picked up the innards and was studying them, sorting them out. And as he bent his head down, your brother rose up on the tips of his toes and struck him on the spine, and broke the joints of his backbone apart. His whole body heaved up and down, he thrashed, he screamed, he died hard, in his blood.

When the slaves saw it they ran straight for their spears, a crowd of them to fight two men. But Pylades and Orestes stood their ground like men, facing them head on, shaking their weapons. And he said, "I have not come as an enemy to this city, or to my own servants. I have paid back my father's murderer. I am Orestes, the wretched Orestes. Do not kill me, old slaves of my father's." And when they heard what he said they held their spears back, and an old man who had been in the household a long time recognised him. And at once they were putting a wreath on your brother's head, cheering, shouting for joy. And now he is coming to show you a head. Not the Gorgon's. The man you hate: Aegisthus. Blood for blood. The dead man has paid off a bitter loan today.

Chorus.
	Set your feet dancing, my dear,
	like a fawn leaping high as heaven,
	light with joy.
	Your brother has won a crown, and it outshines
	any that was ever won beside the streams of Alpheus.
	Come, sing a song of glorious victory
	to go with my dance.

Electra. Light. Blaze of the sun and his four horses. Earth, and the night that was all I could see before. Now my eyes are free, and I can open them, because Aegisthus, my father's murderer, has fallen. Come, friends. Whatever I own, whatever the house has hidden away, to make hair beautiful, let me bring it out, and I will crown my brother's head. He has won.

(Electra goes into the house. Orestes and Pylades come in, and behind them slaves carrying the body of Aegisthus.)

Chorus.
	You bring out the ornaments
	for his head. Our dance goes on,
	the dance the Muses love.
	Now the kings we loved before
	will rule this land again, and justly,
	having brought down the unjust.
	Let the shout go up, and the pipe with it, for joy.

(Electra comes out again with garlands in her hands.)

Electra. Glorious winner. Orestes, son of a father who won the war under Troy, take these bands for the curls of your hair. You have come home from the race, and it was not a useless one, not a sprint down the track for a prize: you killed our enemy, Aegisthus, who destroyed your father and mine. And you, his shield-mate, Pylades, brought up by the most god-fearing of men, take a garland from my hand. You carried an equal share of this contest with him. May I always see the two of you as lucky as you are today.

Orestes. First, Electra, think of the gods as the leaders of this good luck of ours, and then, after them, praise me, the servant of the gods and of fortune. I have come back having killed Aegisthus, and not in words. In deeds. And so that you may know it for certain, I have brought you the dead man himself. Do what you like with him. Put him out for the wild animals to tear, or drive a stake through him and set him up as a prize for the birds, the children of the air. He is your slave now, the man who used to be called your master.

Electra. I am ashamed to. But I want to say it all the same.

Orestes. Say what? Speak. You are out of reach of fear now.

Electra. To outrage the dead. I am ashamed to. Someone might throw it back in my face out of spite.

Orestes. There is no one who would blame you.

Electra. Our city is hard to please, and it loves finding fault.

Orestes. Say what you need to say, sister. The war we had with this man was one with no truce in it.

Electra. Well then. Where do I begin with your evils, and where do I end, and what do I put in the middle? Every morning, before it was light, I never once stopped going over what I wanted to say to your face, if only I were ever free of the terrors I used to live in. Well, now I am free. So I will pay you back now with everything I wanted to say to you while you were alive.

You destroyed me. You made me and my brother here orphans of a father we loved, and we had never done you any wrong. You married my mother, shamefully, and you killed her husband, the man who led the Greeks to war, when you never went near Troy yourself. And you were fool enough to hope that, marrying my mother, you would get a faithful wife, when you had been in my father's bed with her. Let every man know this: when he ruins another man's wife in secret and then finds he has to marry her, he is a miserable man if he thinks the self-control she did not have with the first husband she will suddenly have with him. You lived in misery and did not know it. You knew perfectly well you had made an unholy marriage, and my mother knew she had a godless husband. Two bad people: she took on your fortune, and you took on hers, and each of you got the other's evil. And everywhere in Argos this is what you heard: "the woman's husband," never "the man's wife." And that is a shameful thing, for the wife to be the head of the house and not the husband. I hate children who are known in the city by their mother's name and not their father's. When a man makes a grand marriage, above himself, nobody talks about the husband. The talk is all about the wife.

And here is what deceived you most, and you never saw it. You boasted that you were somebody, because you had money behind you. Money is nothing, except to keep company with for a little while. It is nature that lasts, not money. Nature stays at your side always and lifts your troubles off you; but wealth that was got unjustly, and lives with fools, flies out of the house after a short season in flower. As for what you did with women, a girl should not talk about it, so I will keep quiet; but I will hint plainly enough. You behaved with outrage, because you had a king's house and you were so good-looking. Give me a husband who does not have a girl's face but a man's ways. The sons of men like that grow up to hang on Ares and the spear; the pretty ones are only decoration at a dance.

(She kicks the corpse.)

Go to hell. You never understood what you were, until time found you out and made you pay for it. So let no criminal think, because he ran the first stretch well, that he has beaten Justice, before he comes up to the finishing line and rounds the last turn of his life.

Chorus. He did terrible things, and he has paid terribly for them, to you and to your brother. Justice has great strength.

Electra. Well then. You must carry his body inside and give it to the dark, slaves, so that when my mother comes she does not see a corpse before her own throat is cut.

Orestes. Wait. Let us talk about something else.

Electra. What is it? Those are not rescuers from Mycenae I see, are they?

Orestes. No. It is the mother who bore me.

Electra. Then she is walking beautifully into the middle of the net. And look at her, shining in her carriage and her fine clothes.

Orestes. What do we do now? Are we going to murder our mother?

Electra. Has pity taken hold of you, now that you have seen your mother in the flesh?

Orestes. Pheu. How can I kill her? She bore me. She brought me up.

Electra. The same way she killed your father and mine.

Orestes. Apollo, that was a great stupidity you prophesied.

Electra. If Apollo is a fool, who is wise?

Orestes. You told me to kill my mother, when I should not.

Electra. How are you harmed by avenging your father?

Orestes. I will be hunted as a mother-killer. I was clean before.

Electra. And if you do not defend your father, you will be godless.

Orestes. But my mother. Who will I pay the penalty to, for her blood?

Electra. And who will you pay, if you let your father's vengeance go?

Orestes. Was it some avenging spirit that said this, dressed up as the god?

Electra. Sitting on the holy tripod? I do not think so.

Orestes. I cannot believe this oracle was well prophesied.

Electra. Do not turn coward and fall into unmanliness.

Orestes. So. Am I to lay the same trap for her?

Electra. The one you brought her husband down with, when you killed Aegisthus.

Orestes. I will go in. This is a terrible business I am beginning, and I will do terrible things. If this is what the gods want, so be it. This contest is bitter to me, and sweet too.

(Orestes goes into the house. Clytemnestra's carriage comes up the road, with Trojan slave women walking beside it.)

Chorus.
	Io.
	Queen of the land of Argos,
	daughter of Tyndareus,
	sister of the two noble sons of Zeus
	who live in the flaming sky among the stars
	and hold the honour of saving mortals
	in the breaking waves of the sea:
	welcome. I worship you as I worship the blessed gods,
	for your wealth and your great good fortune.
	Now is the time to pay our court
	to your fortunes. Welcome, my queen.

Clytemnestra. Get down from the wagon, women of Troy, and take my hand, so that I can step out of this carriage. The temples of the gods are decorated with the spoils of Phrygia; and I have these women, the pick of the land of Troy, in exchange for the daughter I lost. A small prize, but a fine one, for my house.

Electra. Then may I, mother, since I am a slave, thrown out of my father's house and living in this wretched place, may I take that blessed hand of yours?

Clytemnestra. These slaves are here for that. Do not trouble yourself on my account.

Electra. Why not? You sent me away from home like a prisoner of war. My house was captured, and I was captured with it, like these women, and left without a father.

Clytemnestra. Well, that is what comes of the plans your father made, against the people he should least of all have made them against, his own family. I will speak. Though when a bad reputation has hold of a woman, there is a bitterness on her tongue. Wrongly, in my view. The right thing is to learn the facts, and then, if she deserves to be hated, hate her; and if not, why hate at all?

Tyndareus gave me to your father, not so that I should die, nor the children I bore. But that man took my daughter out of the house, talking her into it with a marriage to Achilles, and went off to Aulis where the fleet lay at its moorings, and there he stretched her over the altar fire and cut Iphigenia's white cheek. If he had killed one for the sake of many, to save the city from being captured, or to benefit his house, or to save his other children, he could have been forgiven. But it was because Helen could not keep herself in hand, and the man who married her had no idea how to punish a wife who betrayed him. That is why he destroyed my child. Even so, wronged as I was, I would not have gone savage over it; I would not have killed my husband. But he came home to me with a girl, a raving prophetess with a god inside her, and put her into his bed, and there we were, two brides kept in the same house.

Women are foolish. I will not say otherwise. But granted that, when a husband goes wrong and pushes away the bed he has at home, a woman wants to copy her husband and get a lover of her own. And then the blame shines out on us, and the men who caused it get no bad word. If Menelaus had been carried off from his home in secret, should I have killed Orestes to get back my sister's husband Menelaus? How would your father have stood for that? So was he not to die, for killing what was mine, while I was to suffer at his hands? I killed him. I turned the only way that was open to me: to his enemies. Which of your father's friends would have joined me in murdering him? Speak, if you want to, and answer me freely: how did your father die unjustly?

Chorus. What you say is just, but the justice is a shameful one. A woman should give way to her husband in everything, if she has any sense. Anyone who does not think so does not count in what I am saying.

Electra. Remember, mother, the last thing you said. You gave me leave to speak freely to you.

Clytemnestra. I say it again, and I do not take it back, child.

Electra. Then when you have heard it, mother, will you make me suffer for it?

Clytemnestra. No. It will be a pleasure to me to let your heart have its say.

Electra. Then I will speak. And this is where my preface begins: I wish, mother, that you had a better mind. Your looks, and Helen's, deserve the praise they get; but the two of you were born true sisters, both empty-headed, and neither of you worthy of Castor. She was carried off and was glad to be ruined; and you destroyed the best man in Greece, and you hold out the excuse that you killed a husband for the sake of a child. People do not know you as well as I do. You, before your daughter's killing had even been decided, when your husband had only just left home, were sitting at the mirror arranging the golden curls of your hair. A woman who works at her beauty while her husband is away from home, cross her off as a bad one. She has no need to show a pretty face out of doors unless she is looking for trouble. You were the only woman in all Greece, that I know of, who was glad when things went well for Troy and clouded over when they went badly, because you did not want Agamemnon to come home from Troy. And yet you had every chance to keep yourself in hand, and honourably. You had a husband who was no worse a man than Aegisthus, one whom Greece chose to be its general. And when your sister Helen had done what she did, you could have won a great name for yourself, because bad conduct gives good conduct a standard to be measured by, and something to look at.

And if, as you say, my father killed your daughter, what wrong did I do you, or my brother? Why, when you had killed your husband, did you not hand our father's house over to us? Instead you brought into your bed what belonged to someone else, and bought your marriage with wages. And why is your husband not in exile in place of your son, and why has he not died in place of me, when he has killed me, alive, twice as thoroughly as my sister was killed? If murder gives judgement, and murder answers murder, then I will kill you, and your son Orestes with me, to avenge our father. If that was just, then this is just too. Any man who looks at wealth or noble birth and marries a wicked woman is a fool. A humble wife who keeps herself in hand is better in a house than a grand one.

Chorus. Marriage is luck for women. Some, I see, fall out well, and some badly, among mortals.

Clytemnestra. Child, you were always made to love your father. That is how it is: some children belong to the men, and others love their mothers more than their father. I will forgive you. I am not really so very pleased, child, with what I did. But you, unwashed like this, in these poor clothes, when you have only just come through childbirth? Oh, I am wretched, and it is my own planning that did it. I went further in my anger against my husband than I should have.

Electra. You groan too late, when there is no cure left. Well, my father is dead. But the one outside the country, your son, wandering the world, why do you not bring him home?

Clytemnestra. I am afraid. I am looking to my own interest, not his. They say he is angry over his father's murder.

Electra. And why do you keep your husband so savage against me?

Clytemnestra. That is his way. And you were born stubborn too.

Electra. Because I am in pain. But I will stop being angry.

Clytemnestra. And then he will stop being hard on you.

Electra. He thinks he is a great man. He is living in my house.

Clytemnestra. You see? You are fanning up new quarrels again.

Electra. I am silent. I am afraid of him, exactly as afraid as I am.

Clytemnestra. Enough of this talk. Why did you send for me, child?

Electra. You have heard, I think, that I have had a child. Make the sacrifice for me, because I do not know how, on the tenth moon after the birth, the way it is done for a child. I have no experience of it. I never had a child before.

Clytemnestra. That is a job for someone else, the woman who delivered you.

Electra. I delivered myself. I gave birth to the baby alone.

Clytemnestra. Is this house set so far from any friendly neighbour?

Electra. Nobody wants poor people for friends.

Clytemnestra. Well, I will go in and make the sacrifice to the gods for the child's full count of days. And when I have done you this favour, I will go on to the field where my husband is sacrificing to the Nymphs. Attendants, take this team away and put them in the stalls. And when you judge that I have finished this sacrifice to the gods, be back here. I have to please my husband as well.

(Clytemnestra goes into the house.)

Electra. Go into my poor house. And be careful, please, that the smoke-blackened roof does not smear soot on your dress. You will make the sacrifice you owe to the gods. The basket is begun and the knife is sharpened, the same knife that brought down the bull; you will fall beside him, struck down. And in the house of Hades you will be the bride of the man you slept with in the light. That is the favour I will do you, and you will pay me justice for my father.

(Electra follows her in.)

Chorus.
	Evil paid back for evil. The winds of the house
	have turned and blow the other way. Once, in his bath,
	my king, my own king, fell,
	and the roof cried out, and the stone coping of the house,
	as he said: "Cruel woman, why are you murdering me,
	come home to my own dear country after ten years of harvests?"
Chorus.
	Justice flows back like the tide and drags her under,
	the wife who ran from her bed, who killed her husband
	when at last he came home
	to the towering walls the Cyclopes built. With her own hand,
	with a sharp-edged weapon, the axe in her two hands, she killed him.
	Poor husband, whatever the evil was that had hold of that wretched woman.
	Like a mountain lioness that ranges
	the oak woods in the meadows, she did this thing.

(Clytemnestra's voice is heard from inside the house.)

Clytemnestra.
	Children, by the gods, do not kill your mother.
Chorus.
	Do you hear a cry under the roof?
Clytemnestra.
	Io moi moi.
Chorus.
	I groan too, for a woman overpowered by her children.
	A god deals out justice, when the time comes.
	You suffered cruelly, but what you did to your husband
	was unholy, poor woman.

Chorus. But here they come out of the house, spattered with their mother's fresh blood, trophies on show of a pitiful sacrifice. There is no house more wretched than the descendants of Tantalus, and there never was.

(Orestes and Electra come out of the house. The two bodies are carried out after them and laid on the ground.)

Orestes.
	Io, Earth, and Zeus who sees everything
	that mortals do, look at this bloody,
	polluted work: two bodies
	lying on the ground, struck down
	by my hand, the price I have paid
	for my sufferings.
Electra.
	Too many tears, brother, and I am the cause.
	I came through fire in my rage at this woman, wretched that I am,
	at the mother who bore me, her daughter.
Chorus.
	Io, your fate, your fate,
	mother who bore unforgettable griefs,
	unforgettable and worse,
	and suffered them at your own children's hands.
	But you paid for their father's murder, and justly.
Orestes.
	Io, Apollo, the justice you sang of
	was dark, and the griefs you have brought about
	are plain to see, and the lot you gave me is a killer's,
	far from the land of Greece.
	What other city can I go to?
	What host, what god-fearing man
	will look me in the face,
	a man who killed his mother?
Electra.
	Io, io moi. And where can I go, to what dance,
	to what wedding? What husband will take me
	into a bride's bed?
Chorus.
	Again, again your mind
	has shifted with the wind.
	What you think now is holy; it was not then,
	and you did terrible things,
	my dear, to a brother who did not want to.
Orestes.
	Did you see how she threw open her dress, poor woman,
	and showed her breast as she was being killed,
	io moi, letting the limbs that gave me birth
	sink to the ground? And her hair, I —
Chorus.
	I know it well. You went through agony,
	hearing the wail of grief
	from the mother who bore you.
Orestes.
	She screamed this, and put her hand
	on my chin: "My child, I beg you."
	And she hung from my cheeks,
	so that the weapon fell out of my hands.
Chorus.
	Poor woman. How could you bear to see
	with your own eyes the blood
	of your mother as she breathed out her life?
Orestes.
	I threw my cloak over my eyes
	and began the sacrifice with my sword,
	driving it into my mother's throat.
Electra.
	And I urged you on,
	and I took hold of the sword with you.
Chorus.
	You have done the most terrible thing anyone can suffer.
Orestes.
	Take her. Cover our mother's limbs with her dress
	and close up the wounds.
	So it was your own killers you gave birth to.
Electra.
	There. Loved and not loved,
	we wrap this cloak around you.
Chorus.
	The end of the great evils of the house.
Chorus.
	But look, over the top of the roof,
	who are these appearing? Spirits, or gods
	from heaven? This is no road
	for mortals. Why are they coming
	into the open sight of men?

(Castor and Polydeuces, the Dioscuri, appear above the house.)

Castor. Son of Agamemnon, listen. The twin sons of Zeus, your mother's brothers, are calling you: Castor, and this is my brother Polydeuces. We had just stilled a swell in the sea that was terrible for ships when we came to Argos, because we saw the killing of our sister here, your mother. She has her justice now; but what you did was not just. And Apollo, Apollo. But he is my lord, so I keep quiet. He is wise, but the oracle he gave you was not. Still, we have to accept it. From here on you must do what Fate and Zeus have settled for you.

Give Electra to Pylades, to take home as his wife. You, leave Argos. You cannot set foot in this city; you have killed your mother. The terrible Fates, the goddesses with the faces of dogs, will drive you round and round like a wheel, a madman wandering. Go to Athens, and hold on to the holy image of Pallas Athena. She will keep them off you, fluttering as they are with their terrible snakes, so that they cannot touch you, holding her round shield with the Gorgon's face over your head. There is a hill of Ares there, where the gods first sat to vote on a killing, when savage Ares killed Halirrhothius, the son of the lord of the sea, in anger at the unholy rape of his daughter; and from that day the vote given there is the most god-fearing and the most secure that exists. There you too must run your risk for this murder. An equal count of votes will save you from dying by the verdict, because Apollo will take the blame on himself, since it was his oracle that commanded your mother's murder. And this law will be laid down for everyone who comes after: an equal vote always acquits the defendant. Then the terrible goddesses, struck with grief at that, will sink into a cleft in the earth beside that very hill, and it will be a holy oracle, revered by mortals. You must go and live in a city of the Arcadians, by the streams of the Alpheus, near the sanctuary of Zeus of Mount Lycaeon; and the city will be called after your name.

That is what I have to say to you. As for this corpse, Aegisthus, the citizens of Argos will cover it in the earth with a grave. Your mother will be buried by Menelaus, who has only now reached Nauplia, all this time after he took the land of Troy, and by Helen with him. She has come from the house of Proteus, leaving Egypt; she never went to Troy. Zeus, to make strife and slaughter among mortals, sent a phantom of Helen to Troy in her place. So let Pylades take the girl who is also a wife, and go home from the land of Achaea, and let him take the man who is your brother-in-law in name only to the land of Phocis, and give him riches by the weight. And you, set out along the neck of the Isthmus, and go to the blessed hill of Cecrops, in Athens. Once you have filled up the measure of murder that was fated for you, you will be happy, released from these troubles.

Chorus.
	Sons of Zeus, is it lawful for us
	to come near enough to speak with you?
Castor.
	It is lawful. You are not polluted by this killing.
Electra.
	May I have a share in the talk too, sons of Tyndareus?
Castor.
	You too. I lay this bloody deed
	at Apollo's door.
Chorus.
	How is it that you, two gods, brothers
	of the woman who lies dead here,
	did not keep the Fates away from her house?
Castor.
	Fate, and necessity, led to what had to be,
	and the unwise sounds from Apollo's tongue.
Electra.
	But what Apollo, what oracles,
	made me my mother's murderer?
Castor.
	Shared deeds, shared dooms:
	one ruin, handed down from your fathers,
	has ground you both to pieces.
Orestes.
	Sister, I have seen you again after so long,
	and at once I lose your love,
	and I will leave you, and be left by you.
Castor.
	She has a husband and a house. She has suffered nothing
	to pity, except that she is leaving
	the city of the Argives.
Electra.
	And what greater thing is there to groan for
	than leaving the borders of your own country?
Orestes.
	But I am going out of my father's house,
	and I will stand trial for my mother's blood
	before the votes of strangers.
Castor.
	Courage. You will come
	to the holy city of Pallas. Only hold out.
Electra.
	Press your chest against my chest,
	dearest brother.
	The bloody curses of our mother are cutting us apart
	from our father's house.
Orestes.
	Throw your arms around me. Hold me. And mourn over me
	as you would over a dead man's grave.
Castor.
	Pheu, pheu. That is a terrible thing you have said,
	even for gods to hear.
	Because in me too, and in the gods of heaven,
	there is pity for mortals, who suffer so much.
Orestes.
	I will never see you again.
Electra.
	And I will never come near your eyes again.
Orestes.
	These are the last words I will ever say to you.
Electra.
	Goodbye, my city.
	Goodbye, and goodbye again, women of my city.
Orestes.
	Most faithful of all, are you going already?
Electra.
	I am going, and the tears are wetting my soft eyes.
Orestes.
	Pylades, go, and be happy. Marry her.
	Take Electra as your bride.
Castor.
	Their marriage will be their concern. But you, run from these dogs
	and go on to Athens.
	They are on your trail, and it is terrible,
	the snake-handed ones with the black bodies,
	carrying the fruit of terrible pains.
	And we two must hurry over the Sicilian sea
	to save the prows of ships in the water.
	As we go across the plain of the sky
	we do not help the polluted;
	but those who hold holiness and justice
	dear in their lives, those we set free
	from hard troubles, and save.
	So let no one choose to do wrong,
	or sail with men who break their oaths.
	I am a god, and I say this to mortals.
Chorus.
	Goodbye. And whoever among mortals can fare well,
	and is not worn down by some blow of fortune,
	that is the one who lives a happy life.

Heracles (c. 416 BC)

Heracles

(Thebes, in front of the house of Heracles. Amphitryon, an old man, sits at the altar of Zeus the Saviour with Megara and her three small sons. Their clothes are in rags.)

Amphitryon. Is there anyone alive who has not heard of the man who shared his wife with Zeus? Amphitryon of Argos, the son Alcaeus fathered, and Alcaeus was the son of Perseus. The father of Heracles. That is me. I settled here in Thebes, where the crop of Sown Men sprang up out of the ground, grown from the dragon's teeth. Ares spared a handful of that race, and their children's children fill the city of Cadmus now. Creon came from that stock, the son of Menoeceus, the king of this country, and Creon is the father of Megara here, the woman every Theban once sang the wedding song for, to the sound of the pipe, on the day the famous Heracles brought her home to my house.

Then my son left Thebes, where I had settled, left Megara and her family, and set his heart on living in Argos, inside the walls the Cyclopes built. I am an exile from that city, because I killed Electryon. So to lighten my troubles, and because he wanted to live in his own country, he offered Eurystheus a great price for my return: he would clear the earth of its monsters. Whether Hera's goad drove him to it or whether it was simply what had to be, I cannot say. He worked his way through all the other labours, and for the last of them he went down through the mouth of Taenarus into the house of Hades, to bring the three-bodied dog up into the light. And from there he has not come back.

There is an old story the Thebans tell, that once upon a time a man called Lycus was Dirce's husband and ruled this city of seven towers, before Amphion and Zethus, the two sons of Zeus who rode the white horses, became kings of the land. That Lycus had a son with his father's name. He is no Theban; he came here from Euboea. He killed Creon, and having killed him he rules the country, because he fell on a city that was sick with civil strife. So our tie to Creon by marriage is turning out, it seems, to be the worst thing that could have happened to us. With my son deep in the earth, this new master of the land, Lycus, means to wipe out Heracles' children, and kill his wife, to put out one killing with another, and kill me too, if a useless old man still counts as a man at all, so that these boys never grow up and make him pay in blood for what he did to their mother's family.

So here I am. My son left me in this house when he went down into the black dark under the earth, to keep it and to look after his children. And so that Heracles' children should not die, I have sat down with their mother at this altar of Zeus the Saviour, which my noble son set up as a monument to his victorious spear when he beat the Minyans. We keep our place here in want of everything: food, drink, clothes. We lay our ribs on the bare ground. The house is sealed against us, and we sit here because there is nowhere else safe to go. As for friends, some of them I can see now were never real friends, and the ones who are real cannot do anything to help us. That is what bad luck does to a person. I hope it never comes to anyone who has even half a kind thought for me. There is no truer test of your friends.

Megara. Old soldier, who once took the city of the Taphians, leading the Theban army in a famous campaign: how little we humans can be sure of about what the gods are doing. Take me. On my father's side, fortune never shut me out. He was counted a great man once, for his wealth. He had a throne, and a throne is the thing long spears go leaping at, aimed at the lives of the lucky men who hold one, out of love for it. And he had children. And he gave me to your son. He married me to Heracles, a brilliant match. Now all that has died and flown away, and you and I are about to die, old man, and Heracles' children with us, the ones I am keeping safe under my wings like a bird crouched over her chicks. And they keep coming at me, one from this side and one from that, with their questions. "Mother, where has Father gone? What is he doing? When is he coming back?" They are too young to understand, and they look for their father everywhere. I put them off with words. I make up stories. But every time the doors creak they are startled, and every one of them is up on his feet, ready to run and throw himself at his father's knees.

So now, old man, what hope, what road to safety are you working out for us? I am looking to you. We cannot get across the border unseen: there are guards at every way out, and they are too strong for us. And there is no hope of rescue from our friends any more. Whatever your judgement is, say it, out loud, for all of us. Otherwise our death is as good as ready.

Amphitryon. Daughter, it is not easy to give offhand advice in a case like this, to be serious without doing the work. But we are weak, and let us make the time last.

Megara. Do you need more grief? Or are you that fond of the daylight?

Amphitryon. I enjoy the light. And I am fond of my hopes.

Megara. So am I. But you must not expect what cannot be expected, old man.

Amphitryon. In putting evils off there is a cure for them.

Megara. It is the time in between that bites me. It hurts.

Amphitryon. Daughter, there could still be a fair wind for you and me out of this trouble. My son, your husband, could still come. So be quiet, and dry the streams of tears running from your children's eyes, and soothe them with words, tell them stories, steal their fear away. A poor kind of theft, but steal it anyway. Even human misfortunes get tired, you know. The winds do not always blow at full strength, and the people who are doing well do not do well to the end. Everything changes places with everything else. The best man is the one who trusts in his hopes, always. Giving up is the mark of a bad one.

(The Chorus, old men of Thebes, come in slowly, leaning on their sticks.)

Chorus.
	To the high roof, to the old man's bed,
	propped on my stick, I have set out,
	a singer of wailing songs,
	like a grey old bird.
	I am nothing but words, a shape
	seen at night in a night-time dream,
	trembling, yes, but willing.
	Children, children with no father,
	old man, and you, poor mother,
	groaning for your husband
	in the house of Hades.
Chorus.
	Do not let your feet give out,
	or your heavy legs, like a colt
	under the yoke, dragging the weight
	of a wheeled cart up a rocky slope.
	Take hold of a hand, take hold of a cloak,
	whoever feels his dim footsteps failing.
	Old man, help an old man along,
	the one whose young spear stood by your young spear
	long ago, in the labours of your age-mates,
	and was never a shame to a country
	whose glory was second to none.
Chorus.
	Look. The fierce flash of their eyes,
	how like their father's.
	The bad luck has not left these children,
	and neither has the grace.
	Greece, what allies,
	what allies you will be robbing yourself of
	if you lose these boys.

(Lycus comes in with armed men.)

Chorus. But I see Lycus, the ruler of this land, coming past the house towards us.

Lycus. The father of Heracles, and his wife. I have a question for you, if I may. And I may, since I have made myself your master, and I ask what I like. How long do you mean to spin out your lives? What hope, what defence do you see that will keep you from dying? Do you believe the father of these children, who is lying dead in the house of Hades, is going to come back? You make far more of dying than it deserves, both of you, if you have to die. You, who scattered your empty boasts across Greece, that Zeus shared your wife and had a child with you. And you, who were called the wife of the finest man alive.

What was the great thing your husband did, after all? He killed a water-snake in a marsh? Or the beast of Nemea, which he caught in a snare and then said he strangled with his bare arms? Is that what you are fighting me with? Is that why Heracles' children should not die? The man made a name for courage he never had, fighting animals. In everything else he was nothing. He never held a shield on his left arm, never came near a spear. He carried a bow, the most cowardly weapon there is, and he was always ready to run. A bow is no proof of a man's courage. The proof is the man who stands his ground in the ranks and looks straight at the fast furrow the spear cuts, and does not blink.

And what I am doing, old man, is not shamelessness. It is caution. I know that I killed Creon, this woman's father, and that I hold his throne. So I have no wish to let these boys grow up and be left behind to take vengeance on me for what I did.

Amphitryon. Let Zeus defend the part of his son that is Zeus's. As for my part, Heracles, it falls to me to show, with words, on your behalf, what an ignorant man this is. I cannot let you be spoken of like that. First, then, the thing that should never be said at all, because calling you a coward, Heracles, is among the things that cannot be said. I have to clear you of that, and the gods are my witnesses. I call on the thunderbolt of Zeus, and on the four-horse chariot he rode in when he drove his winged arrows into the ribs of the Giants, the earth's children, and then sang the victory song with the gods. Or go to Pholoe, you worst of kings, and ask that four-legged outrage, the tribe of Centaurs, whom they would pick as the bravest man alive. Would it not be my son, the one you say only seems to be brave? Ask Dirphys, the mountain of the Abantes that raised you, and it would not sing your praises. There is nowhere in your own country you could point to and say, here I did one brave thing, and call the land as a witness.

Then you sneer at the cleverest invention there is, the archer's gear. Listen to me now and learn something. A man who fights in armour is the slave of his weapons. If the men in line beside him are not brave, he dies himself, through his neighbours' cowardice. And if he breaks his spear, he has nothing to keep death off his body: one defence, and that is all. But every man with a good aim and a bow in his hand has the one best thing, which is this. He can let fly ten thousand arrows, and there are still others to keep his body from death. He stands well back and fights the enemy off, wounding men who can see with shafts they cannot see coming, and he never gives the other side his body. He keeps it well guarded. And that is the cleverest thing in battle: to hurt the enemy and keep yourself alive, and not be anchored to luck. So much for that. My argument and yours take opposite views of the matter in hand.

And now, these children. Why do you want to kill them? What have they done to you? I will grant you are clever in one thing: you are a coward yourself, and you are afraid of the children of the best. But it is hard on us all the same, if we have to die for your cowardice, when you should have suffered that at our hands, since we are the better men, if Zeus had any fair feeling towards us. If you want the sceptre of this land for yourself, then let us go, let us leave the country as exiles. Do nothing by force, or you will suffer force yourself, when the god's wind changes for you.

Pheu. Land of Cadmus, because I am coming to you too, I am handing out my share of blame: is this how you defend Heracles and his children? The man who went alone into battle against the whole Minyan army and made it possible for Thebes to look out at the world with a free eye? And I cannot praise Greece either, and I will never keep quiet about it: I have found her at her worst towards my son. She should have come to these chicks with fire and spears and armour, to pay him back for clearing the sea and the land of their filth. That was the labour, and that was the thanks he earned. But you get none of that, children, not from the city of Thebes and not from Greece. You look to me, a feeble friend, and I am nothing but the noise of a tongue. The strength I had once is gone; old age has left my limbs shaking and my power dim. If I were young, if I still had my body under me, I would have picked up a spear and reddened that yellow hair of his with blood, so that he would be running from my spear this minute, out past the borders of Atlas, for cowardice.

Chorus. Do good men not find an opening for speech, even when they are slow to start?

Lycus. Go on, say what you like about me with the words you have built your tower out of. I will answer your words with something worse. You men, go, some of you to Helicon, some to the folds of Parnassus. Tell the woodcutters to fell oak logs and bring them into the city. Then stack the wood round the altar on every side, and light it, and burn their bodies, all of them, so that they learn that it is not the dead man who rules this land now. It is me.

And you, old men, you have set yourselves against my wishes. You will not only be mourning Heracles' children. You will be mourning what happens to your own houses too, whenever anything happens to them, and you will remember that you are slaves, and that I am your king.

Chorus. You children of the Earth, you men Ares sowed, when he tore the teeth out of the dragon's greedy jaw: will you not lift up the staffs your right hands lean on and bloody the unholy head of this man, who is no Theban, a foreigner, the lowest of the low, and lords it over the young men here? You will never be my master and enjoy it.

You will not have what I sweated for with my own hands either. Go back where you came from and do your outrages there. As long as I live you will never kill Heracles' children. He is not buried so deep under the ground as all that, when he left his children behind.

You hold this land, and you ruined it to get it. The man who did it good gets nothing that he deserves.

And am I meddling, because I do good to my friends when they are dead, when a friend is needed most?

Right hand, how you long to take hold of a spear. But you are weak, and the longing has died. Otherwise I would have stopped you calling me a slave, and we would have lived in this city of Thebes with honour, the city you are enjoying now. Because a city that is sick with civil strife and bad counsel is not in its right mind. If it were, it would never have taken you for its master.

Megara. Old men, thank you. It is right for friends to feel a just anger on their friends' behalf. But do not get yourselves hurt on our account, raging at your masters. Amphitryon, listen to my judgement, if you think there is anything in what I say. I love my children. How could I not love the ones I bore, the ones I laboured for? And I think dying is a terrible thing. But a person who strains against what has to be, I count a fool. Since we must die, we should die without being shredded by fire, giving our enemies something to laugh at, and to me that is a worse evil than the dying. We owe this house a great deal, and all of it fine. You have a glorious name as a soldier, so it is not to be borne that you should die a coward's death. And my husband needs no witness to his good name. He would never want these children saved at the price of a bad one. Noble men suffer when their children shame them, and I will not push my husband's example aside.

And look at your hope, the way I reckon it. You think your son is coming back from under the ground? Who ever came back out of Hades from among the dead? Or do we soften this man with words? Never. An enemy who is a brute, you run from. It is clever men, men who were raised well, that you give way to: touch their sense of shame and you can cut a friendly bargain more easily. It has already crossed my mind to beg him for exile for the children. But that is misery too, to wrap their rescue in pitiful poverty. They say a host's face is sweet to look at for exactly one day, when the friend at his door is a fugitive. Have the nerve to die with us. Death is waiting for you anyway. I am calling on your noble blood, old man. Whoever struggles against what the gods have fixed is keen, but the keenness is madness. What must be, no one will ever make not be.

Chorus. If my arms were strong and someone were insulting you, it would have been easy to stop him. Now we are nothing. From here on, Amphitryon, it is for you to see how to push this fate aside.

Amphitryon. It is not cowardice, and it is not any love of life, that keeps me from dying. I want to save my son's children. But it seems I am in love with the impossible. Look. Here is my neck, ready for the sword, to stab, to kill, to throw off a rock. One favour for the two of us, king. We beg you. Kill me and this poor woman before you kill the children, so we do not have to watch them, an unholy sight, gasping out their lives and calling for their mother and their father's father. The rest, if you are set on it, do. We have no defence against dying.

Megara. And I beg you to add a second favour to the first, so that one man can do both of us a double service. Let me put on my children the dress of the dead. Open the house, because we are locked out of it now, so that at least they have that much of their father's house.

Lycus. It shall be done. I tell my men to undo the bolts. Go in and dress yourselves. I do not begrudge you clothes. And when you have put your finery on your bodies, I will come back and give you to the world below.

(Lycus goes out with his men. The doors of the house are opened.)

Megara. Children, follow your poor mother's steps into your father's house. Other men own what is in it. The name is still ours.

(Megara goes in with the children.)

Amphitryon. Zeus, it was for nothing, then, that I had you as a partner in my marriage. For nothing that we called you the joint father of my son. You turned out to be less of a friend than you seemed. I am a mortal and you are a great god, and I beat you in goodness, because I did not betray Heracles' children. You knew how to sneak into a bed, to take another man's wife with nobody's leave. But your own friends you do not know how to save. You are a stupid god, or you were born unjust.

(Amphitryon goes in.)

Chorus.
	Ai. Linus: Apollo sings the lament for him,
	after the happy song, dead
	in his beauty, driving the strings
	with his golden pick.
	But I want to sing of the man
	who went down into the dark
	of the earth and the dead below,
	call him the son of Zeus
	or the child of Amphitryon,
	and put a crown of praise on his labours.
	The courage of noble work is the glory of the dead.
Chorus.
	First he emptied the grove of Zeus
	of its lion, and wrapped his back
	in the tawny hide, his yellow head
	hooded in the terrible
	gape of the beast's jaws.
Chorus.
	And the mountain tribe of wild Centaurs
	he laid low one day with his murderous bow,
	killing them with winged arrows.
	Peneus knows it, the river of beautiful eddies,
	and the long fields of the plain
	that bear no crop, and the farms on Pelion,
	and the glens of Homole next door,
	where they filled their hands with pine trees
	and rode down on the land of Thessaly
	and broke it
	under their horses' hooves.
Chorus.
	And the golden-horned deer
	with the dappled back, that plundered
	the farmers, he killed, and gave
	the glory to the goddess who kills wild beasts,
	Artemis of Oenoe.
Chorus.
	He mounted the four-horse chariot
	and tamed with the bit the horses of Diomedes,
	that champed at their bloody mangers
	unbridled, greedy, meat with the blood still on it
	between their jaws, an ugly table,
	glad to be eating men.
	Then over the banks of the Hebrus
	that runs with silver he crossed,
	still labouring for the king of Mycenae.
Chorus.
	And on the shore under Pelion,
	by the springs of Anaurus,
	he killed Cycnus with his arrows,
	the murderer of guests, who lived at Amphanae
	and mixed with no one.
Chorus.
	And he came to the singing girls
	in their garden in the west,
	to pick with his hand the golden fruit
	from the leaves of the apple tree,
	killing the dragon with the fiery back
	that coiled round it, guarding it,
	a thing no one could come near.
	And he went into the deep places of the salt sea
	and made it calm for the oars of men.
Chorus.
	And under the middle of the sky
	he drove his hands to hold up its seat,
	when he came to the house of Atlas,
	and with a man's strength he carried
	the starry homes of the gods.
Chorus.
	And the mounted army of the Amazons
	round the Maeotic lake,
	fed by so many rivers,
	he went to find, through the swell of the Black Sea
	that welcomes no one,
	gathering a company of friends from all Greece.
	Who did he leave out?
	After the gold-worked cloak of the war-god's daughter,
	the deadly hunt for a belt.
	Greece took the famous spoils of the barbarian girl,
	and they are kept safe in Mycenae.
Chorus.
	And the hound of Lerna with its thousand heads,
	the many-murdering water-snake,
	he burned out with fire,
	and dipped his arrows in its poison,
	and with those he killed the three-bodied
	herdsman of Erytheia.
Chorus.
	And other races he ran, and came through them
	with glory and good luck. And then he sailed
	to Hades, the place of many tears,
	the end of his labours,
	and there, poor man, he finishes
	his life, and has not come back.
	The house is empty of friends,
	and Charon's oar is waiting
	for his children, a road out of life
	with no return, godless, unjust.
	The house looks to your hands, and you are not here.
Chorus.
	If I had the strength of my youth
	and could shake a spear in the fight,
	with the Thebans who were young with me,
	I would have stood in front of these children
	and defended them. But now
	I am left behind by my lucky youth.

(Megara comes out of the house with the children, all dressed for burial, and Amphitryon behind them.)

Chorus.
	But look. I see them coming, dressed
	in the clothes of the dead, the children
	of the man who was so great once, Heracles,
	and his dear wife, dragging
	the children along at her feet
	like a team on a rope, and Heracles' old father.
	I am wretched. I cannot hold back
	the springs of tears in my old eyes any more.

Megara. Well, then. Who is the priest? Who is the butcher for these unlucky children? Who is the murderer of my miserable life? The victims are ready. Lead them to the house of Hades. Children, we are being led away, an ugly team of corpses, old men and young and mothers all together. My poor fate, and my children's. I am looking at you for the very last time. I gave you birth, and I raised you for our enemies, to be their outrage and their laughing-stock and their prey.

Pheu. How far my hopes have knocked me from what I expected, the things I once hoped for from your father's words. To you, your father who is dead was giving Argos. You were going to live in Eurystheus's house and rule the rich fields of the Pelasgian land, and he used to throw the lion's skin over your head, the beast's hide that he armed himself with. And you were going to be king of Thebes, the city that loves its chariots, with my land, the plains that came to me, for your inheritance, because that is what you talked your father into. And into your right hand he used to lower the carved club, the wood that kept him safe, pretending to give it to you. And you: he promised he would give you Oechalia, the city his far-shooting arrows once destroyed. Three of you, and three kingdoms your father was building up for you, proud of his own courage. And I was picking out the best brides, tying you by marriage to Athens and Sparta and Thebes, so that you would ride at anchor on stern-cables and live a happy life. All gone. Fortune has turned round and given you Deaths for brides instead, and given me tears for the wedding bath. I was a fool to hope. And your grandfather here is hosting the wedding feast, with Hades for the father of the brides. A fine match.

Oh. Which of you do I take to my breast first, which last? Which of you do I kiss? Which do I hold? If only I were a bee with brown wings and could gather up the grief from all of you and carry it into one place and give it back as one flood of tears. Dearest, if any mortal voice is heard in the house of Hades, I am saying this to you, Heracles. Your father is dying, and your children, and I am done for, I who was once called blessed among mortals because of you. Help us. Come. Show yourself, even as a shadow. Your coming would be enough, even as a dream, because the men who are killing your children are cowards.

Amphitryon. You see to the things below, woman. And I, Zeus, throw up my hand to the sky and call on you: if you mean to do anything for these children, help them now, because very soon you will be no use at all. And yet you have been called on many times. I am working for nothing. It seems we have to die.

Well, old men. Life is a small thing. Get through it as pleasantly as you can, and do not grieve from morning to night. Time does not know how to keep our hopes safe. It hurries about its own business and flies away. Look at me. Everyone looked at me once. I did things men talked about. And in one day fortune took it all from me, like a feather blown up into the sky. Great wealth and a great name: I do not know anyone whose are certain. Goodbye. You are looking at your old friend, my age-mates, for the very last time.

(Heracles comes in along the road, carrying his bow and his club. Megara sees him first.)

Megara. Ah. Old man, am I looking at the people I love most? Or what am I to say?

Amphitryon. I do not know, daughter. I cannot find my voice either.

Megara. This is the man they told us was under the earth. Unless we are seeing some dream in broad daylight. What am I saying? What kind of dreams am I seeing, in my fear? This is nobody else, old man. This is your son. Come here, children, hang on to your father's clothes. Go on, quickly, and do not let go. He is every bit as good to you as Zeus the Saviour himself.

Heracles. Greetings, my house, and the gates of my hearth. How glad I am to see you, coming back into the light. Ah. What is this? I see my children in front of the house with their heads wreathed in the dress of the dead, and my wife in a crowd of men, and my father in tears. What has happened? Let me go closer to them and find out. Wife, what new trouble has come to the house?

Megara. Dearest of men.

Amphitryon. Light, come back to your father.

Megara. You are here? You are safe? You have come in time for the people you love?

Heracles. What are you saying? What is this confusion I have walked into, father?

Megara. We are being destroyed. Old man, forgive me if I have snatched first what was yours to tell him. A woman is somehow quicker to cry than a man, and it was my children who were dying, and I was dying with them.

Heracles. Apollo. What an opening to your story.

Megara. My brothers are dead, and my old father.

Heracles. What? What did he do? Whose spear did he meet?

Megara. Lycus killed them. The new master of the country.

Heracles. In open battle, or was the land sick?

Megara. Civil war. He holds the power now, over Cadmus's city of the seven gates.

Heracles. Then why did the fear come to you and the old man?

Megara. He was going to kill your father, and me, and the children.

Heracles. What? What did he have to fear from my fatherless children?

Megara. That one day they would make him pay for Creon's death.

Heracles. And this dress the children are wearing, fit for the dead?

Megara. We have already put on the wrappings of death.

Heracles. And you were being put to death by force? Oh, this is hard to bear.

Megara. With no friends left. And we heard that you were dead.

Heracles. Where did that despair come from? Who told you?

Megara. The heralds of Eurystheus kept announcing it.

Heracles. And why did you leave my house and my hearth?

Megara. By force. Your father was thrown out of his bed.

Heracles. And he had no shame? He could treat an old man like that?

Megara. Shame? He lives a long way from that goddess.

Heracles. Were we so short of friends while I was away?

Megara. What friends does a man have when his luck turns?

Heracles. The battles I fought against the Minyans. They spat on those?

Megara. Bad luck has no friends. I will say it to you again.

Heracles. Throw those wrappings of Hades off your heads, and look up at the light. Instead of the dark down there, your eyes are getting a welcome exchange. And I, since now this is work for my own hand, will first go and tear down the house of the new king, cut off his unholy head and throw it to the dogs to drag about. And every Theban I find who turned bad after I did him good, I will bring down with this club that has won so many victories. The rest I will scatter with feathered arrows and fill the whole Ismenus with the corpses of the dead, and the white stream of Dirce will run with blood. Who should I defend, if not my wife and my children and my old father? Goodbye to my labours. I did them for nothing, if I did them instead of this. And I must die defending them, if they were going to die for their father. Or what will we call fine in going to fight a hydra and a lion on Eurystheus's orders, if I do not work to save my own children from death? Then I will not be called Heracles the glorious victor any more, the way I was before.

Chorus. It is right that children help the people who made them, and an old father, and the woman who shares a man's marriage.

Amphitryon. It is like you, my boy, to be a friend to your friends and to hate what is hateful. But do not be in too much of a hurry.

Heracles. And what am I doing faster than I should, father?

Amphitryon. The king has a lot of allies, poor men who pass for rich by the way they talk. They started the civil war and wrecked the city so they could plunder their neighbours, because what they had at home was gone, spent, run through by idleness. You were seen coming into the city. And since you were seen, watch out that you do not gather your enemies together and fall when you never expected it.

Heracles. I do not care if the whole city saw me. But I saw a bird sitting in an unlucky quarter of the sky, and I knew some trouble had fallen on the house. So I came into the country secretly, on purpose.

Amphitryon. Good. Now go in and greet your hearth, and let your father's house see your face. The king is coming here himself, to drag out your wife and children and butcher them, and to cut my throat over them. If you stay right here, everything will fall into your hands, and you gain safety into the bargain. And do not stir up your city before you have settled this well, child.

Heracles. I will do that. You are right. I will go into the house. I have come back at last from the sunless corners of Hades and of Persephone, down below, and I will not fail to greet the gods under my own roof first.

Amphitryon. Did you really go to the house of Hades, child?

Heracles. Yes, and I brought the three-headed beast up into the light.

Amphitryon. Did you beat him in a fight, or was he a gift from the goddess?

Heracles. A fight. And I was lucky: I had already seen the rites of the mysteries, the ones the initiated see at Eleusis.

Amphitryon. And is the beast in Eurystheus's house now?

Heracles. The grove of Demeter of the Underworld has him, and the town of Hermione.

Amphitryon. And Eurystheus does not know you have come back up onto the earth?

Heracles. He does not. I came here first, to find out how things stood.

Amphitryon. And why were you so long under the earth?

Heracles. I stayed to bring Theseus back out of Hades, father.

Amphitryon. And where is he? Has he gone off to his own country?

Heracles. He has gone to Athens, glad to have escaped from down below. But come, children, walk into the house with your father. Your going in is going to be a better thing than your coming out was. Take heart, and stop letting the streams run from your eyes. And you, wife, gather your courage, stop trembling, and let go of my clothes. I have no wings, and I have no wish to run away from the people I love. Ah. They will not let go. They cling to my clothes all the harder. Were you standing so close to the edge of the razor? Then I will take these little boats by the hand and tow them along, the way a ship tows its dinghies. I do not refuse to take care of my children. Everything human is the same. The best of men love their children, and so do men who are nothing at all. Money makes them different, some have it and some do not, but the whole race loves its children.

(Heracles goes into the house, leading the children by the hand. Megara and Amphitryon follow him.)

Chorus.
	Youth is what I love, always.
	Old age is a weight on my head,
	heavier than the crags of Etna,
	and it lays a dark veil
	over the light of my eyes.
	Never let me have the wealth
	of an Asian king's throne,
	never a house piled with gold,
	if the price is my youth.
	Youth is the loveliest thing there is when you are rich,
	and the loveliest when you are poor.
	But old age, grim and deadly,
	I hate it. Let it sink under the waves.
	It should never have come
	to the houses and cities of men.
	It should be out over the sky forever,
	carried along on wings.
Chorus.
	If the gods had any understanding,
	any wisdom, as men reckon such things,
	they would have given a second youth,
	a visible mark of goodness,
	to whoever had goodness in him, and when they died
	they would have run back up into the sunlight
	on a second lap of the course,
	while a bad nature had to make do
	with a single stretch of life.
	That way you could tell
	the bad from the good,
	the way sailors can count the stars
	through a gap in the clouds.
	As it is, the gods have set no clear line
	between good men and bad.
	Time turns and turns,
	and only piles up wealth.
Chorus.
	I will not stop mixing the Graces
	in with the Muses,
	the sweetest pairing there is.
	Let me not live without music.
	Let me always wear a garland.
	The old singer still sings
	of Memory, the mother of the Muses.
	I still sing the glorious victory
	of Heracles,
	beside Dionysus the giver of wine,
	beside the song of the seven-stringed shell
	and the Libyan pipe.
	Not yet will I put down the Muses,
	who set me dancing.
Chorus.
	The girls of Delos sing their hymn
	around the temple gates
	for Leto's lovely son,
	whirling in their beautiful dance.
	And I, an old singer, like a swan,
	will sing my hymns at your doors
	out of a grey-bearded throat.
	There is good matter here for a song:
	he is the son of Zeus.
	But his goodness rises
	higher than his birth. He laboured,
	and he made life calm for men,
	and killed the beasts they were afraid of.

(Lycus comes in with his men. Amphitryon comes out of the house to meet him.)

Lycus. Amphitryon. You are coming out of the house just in time. It is a long while now that you have been dressing your bodies in the clothes and ornaments of the dead. Come on. Tell the children and the wife of Heracles to show themselves outside this house, on the terms you offered, of your own free will, to die.

Amphitryon. My lord, you hound me when I am already broken, and you heap outrage on me on top of my dead. You should be more measured in your eagerness, even if you do hold the power. But since you lay the necessity of dying on us, we have to accept it. What you decide has to be done.

Lycus. Where is Megara, then? Where are the children of Alcmene's son?

Amphitryon. I think she, as far as I can guess from out here.

Lycus. What is this guess of yours? What proof have you got?

Amphitryon. Is sitting as a suppliant at the holy steps of the hearth.

Lycus. Begging, and getting nothing for it. It will not save her life.

Amphitryon. And calling on her dead husband. For nothing.

Lycus. Who is not here, and who will never come.

Amphitryon. No. Unless some god should raise him up.

Lycus. Go to her and bring her out of the house.

Amphitryon. If I did that I would be a partner in the murder.

Lycus. Then since you have that on your conscience, we will do it, we who are past being afraid. We will bring the children out, and their mother with them. Follow me, men. Let us cut this delay short and get the work done, and gladly.

(Lycus goes into the house with his men.)

Amphitryon. Go on, then. Go where you have to go. The rest, perhaps, someone else will see to. You have done evil; expect some evil to come to you. Old men, he is walking in beautifully. He is going to be tangled in the nooses of a net with swords in it, when he thought he was going to kill his neighbours, the vilest man alive. I am going in to watch him fall dead. There is pleasure in an enemy dying and paying the penalty for what he has done.

(Amphitryon goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	The evil has changed sides. The great king of before
	turns his life back round, up out of Hades.
	Io.
	Justice, and the tide of the gods, turning back.
	You have come at last to where you will pay for it with your death,
	for the outrages you did to your betters.
	Joy has made my tears break out.
	He has come back,
	the thing I never once, in my heart, hoped
	to live to see: the king of this land.
	But come, old friends, let us watch what is going on inside the house too,
	and see whether a certain man is faring the way I want him to.
Lycus.
	Io moi moi.
Chorus.
	This is the song, beginning now, that I love
	to hear inside the house. Death is not far off.
	The king cries out,
	groaning the first notes of his murder.
Lycus.
	Oh, all the land of Cadmus, I am being killed by a trick.
Chorus.
	Yes, because you killed. Endure it, as you pay it back,
	pay the penalty for what you did.
	Who was he, a mortal man, who stained the gods with his lawlessness,
	who threw a mindless slander
	at the blessed ones in heaven, that the gods, after all,
	have no strength?
	Old men, the godless man is no more.
	The house is silent. Let us turn to the dance.
	The friends I want to prosper are prospering.
Chorus.
	Dances, dances
	and feasting are what matter now
	all through the holy town of Thebes.
	A change from tears,
	a change of fortune,
	has given birth to new songs.
	The new king is gone, and the old one
	rules, back from the harbour of Acheron.
	Hope has come
	beyond anything I counted on.
Chorus.
	The gods, the gods
	take care to notice the unjust
	and the holy.
	Gold and good luck
	drag men out of their right minds
	and haul unjust power along after them.
	No one dared to look at what Time brings round again.
	He left the law behind, he gave his favour to lawlessness,
	and he smashed
	the black chariot of his prosperity.
Chorus.
	Ismenus, put on your garlands.
