	Polished streets of the seven-gated city,
	break out into dancing,
	and Dirce with your lovely stream,
	and you, the daughters of Asopus,
	leave your father's water and come and sing with us,
	nymphs, of the glorious victory
	Heracles has won.
	Wooded rock of Pythian Apollo,
	and you houses of the Muses on Helicon,
	oh, come with glad shouting
	to my city, to my walls,
	where the Sown Men sprang out of the ground,
	the crop that grew from the dragon's teeth Cadmus planted,
	a troop with bronze shields, who hand this land
	down to their children's children,
	a holy light for Thebes.
Chorus.
	Oh, the two beds that shared one marriage,
	a mortal's and Zeus's, who came to the bed
	of the bride descended from Perseus.
	How I believe now, Zeus, in that old story
	of your bed; it turned out true beyond my hope,
	and time has shown bright and clear
	the strength of Heracles,
	who came up out of the earth's chambers,
	leaving the house of Pluto
	down below.
	You are a better king to me
	than that low-born lord,
	as anyone can see now
	from this contest of drawn swords, which showed
	whether justice still pleases
	the gods.

(Iris and Madness appear above the house.)

Chorus. Ah. Ah. Have we come into the same fit of fear again, old men? What is that thing I see over the house? Run, run. Lift your slow legs and get out of the way. Lord Healer, turn this disaster away from me.

Iris. Courage, old men. The one you are looking at is Madness, the daughter of Night, and I am Iris, the servant of the gods. We have not come to do the city any harm. Our campaign is against one man's body, the man they say was born from Zeus and Alcmene. Until he had finished his bitter labours, what had to be kept him safe, and his father Zeus never let me or Hera hurt him. But now that he has come through the tasks Eurystheus set him, Hera wants to fasten fresh blood on him: he is to kill his own children. And I want it too. Come, then, daughter of black Night, who never married, take your heart and make it hard. Drive madness into this man, a child-killing confusion of the mind, and set his feet leaping. Drive him, shake him, let out the murderous sail. When he has ferried his fine garland of children across the strait of Acheron, killed by his own hand, then let him know what Hera's anger against him is like, and learn what mine is. Otherwise the gods are nowhere, and mortal men will be great, if he does not pay.

Madness. I come from a noble father and a noble mother. I am of the blood of Night and of Heaven. And the office I hold is not one to turn against friends in anger, and I take no joy in visiting the houses of men. I want to give Hera some advice, before I see her stumble, and you too, if you will listen to what I say. This man, whose house you are sending me into, is no nobody, on earth or among the gods. He tamed the trackless country and the wild sea, and by himself he set the honours of the gods back on their feet when they were falling, brought down by unholy men. So I advise you: do not wish great evils on him.

Iris. Do not lecture us about Hera's plans and mine.

Madness. I am setting your foot on the better path instead of the evil one.

Iris. It was not to keep yourself in hand that the wife of Zeus sent you here.

Madness. I call the Sun to witness that I am doing what I do not want to do. But if I really must serve Hera and you, and follow you at full speed, in full cry, like hounds after the huntsman, then I will go. Not the sea, groaning so wildly with its waves, not the earthquake, not the sting of the thunderbolt breathing out its pangs, will be anything like the sprint I am going to make into the chest of Heracles. I will smash the roof and bring the house down on top of him, once I have killed his children first. And the killer will not know that he is cutting down the children he fathered, until my madness lets him go. Look, there. Already he is tossing his head at the starting line, and rolling his eyes, twisted, glaring like a Gorgon, without a word. He cannot keep his breathing in hand; he is like a bull about to charge, terrible, and he bellows, calling up the Fates out of Tartarus. Soon I will make you dance harder still, and pipe terror into your ears. Go up to Olympus, Iris, lift your noble foot. I am going down into the house of Heracles, where no one will see me.

(Iris goes. Madness goes down into the house.)

Chorus.
	Ototototoi. Groan. He is being cut down,
	the flower of your city, the son of Zeus.
	Poor Greece, you are going to throw away
	the man who did you good, and destroy him, dancing
	to the mad pipes of Madness.
	She is off in her chariot, the lady of many groans,
	she puts the goad to her horses
	as if to outrage them,
	the Gorgon daughter of Night, with the hissing
	of a hundred snake heads, Madness with the flashing eyes.
	Quickly the god has turned his good luck over,
	quickly the children will breathe out their lives at their father's hand.
Amphitryon.
	Io moi. Wretched man that I am.
Chorus.
	Io, Zeus. Your child will have no children now;
	the mad, unjust Avengers who eat raw flesh
	are about to lay him out flat in misery.
Amphitryon.
	Io, roof of my house.
Chorus.
	The dance begins, without the drums,
	without the wand Dionysus loves,
Amphitryon.
	Io, my house.
Chorus.
	for blood, and not for the pouring
	of Dionysus's wine, the juice of the grape.
Amphitryon.
	Run, children. Get out of there.
Chorus.
	Deadly, this
	deadly tune the pipe is playing.
	He is hunting his children down like game. Never in vain
	will Madness run wild through a house.
Amphitryon.
	Aiai. The evil of it.
Chorus.
	Aiai indeed. How I groan for the old man,
	the father, and for the mother who raised the children,
	who bore them for nothing.
	Look. Look.
	A storm is shaking the house. The roof is falling in.
Heracles.
	E, e. What are you doing, daughter of Zeus, to my house?
	You are sending the turmoil of Tartarus into my house, Pallas,
	the way you did once against Enceladus.

(The Messenger comes out of the house.)

Messenger.
	Old men, bodies white with age.
Chorus.
	What is this cry you are calling me
	with?
Messenger.
	Unspeakable things in the house.
Chorus.
	I need no other
	prophet to tell me that.
Messenger.
	The children are dead.
Chorus.
	Aiai.
Messenger.
	Groan. There is reason to groan.
Chorus.
	Deadly murders,
	deadly hands of a parent. Oh.
Messenger.
	No one could say more than what we have suffered.
Chorus.
	How can you show us this ruin, this ruin of a father
	over his children, that we must groan for?
	Tell us how these evils rushed down, sent from a god,
	onto the house,
	and how the children met what they suffered.

Messenger. The sacrifice was set out in front of the altar of Zeus, to purify the house, because Heracles had killed the king of the land and thrown him out of this house. The children stood there, a beautiful group, with his father and Megara. The basket had already gone round the altar, and we were keeping the holy silence. Alcmene's son was about to take up the torch in his right hand, to dip it in the water of purification, when he stood still without a word. And as their father went on standing there, the children looked up at him. He was not himself any more. He was gone, ruined, in the rolling of his eyes; the roots of his eyes stood out bloodshot, and foam ran down into his thick beard. And he spoke, with a laugh that had gone wrong. "Father, why am I sacrificing and lighting the purifying fire before I have killed Eurystheus? Why have the work twice over? It is a job for one hand of mine to settle all this. When I bring the head of Eurystheus back here, I will wash my hands clean for the men who have just died, and for him together. Pour out the water. Throw the baskets out of your hands. Who is giving me my bow? Who is giving me the weapon for my hand? I am going to Mycenae. I need crowbars and pickaxes, to smash back down with bent iron the foundations the Cyclopes fitted together with their red plumb-line and their hammers."

Then he set off. He had no chariot, but he said he had one, and he stepped up onto the rail of a chariot that was not there and struck with his hand, as if he were holding a goad. The servants felt two things at once, laughter and fear together. And one man looked at another and said, "Is the master playing with us, or is he mad?" And he went pacing up and down through the house, and burst into the middle of the men's hall and said he had reached the city of Nisus, Megara, on the road south. Then, going further inside, he lay down on the floor, just as he was, and set about preparing himself a feast. And after he had passed a short while there, he said he was coming to the wooded flats of the Isthmus. And there he stripped his body of its clothes and their fastenings and wrestled with nobody, and had himself proclaimed the glorious victor over no one, by himself, to himself, after calling for silence from a crowd that was not there. Then, roaring terrible threats at Eurystheus, he was in Mycenae, by his own account. But his father took hold of his strong hand and said this to him. "My son, what is the matter with you? What is this strange journey you are on? It is not the blood of the men you have just killed that has driven you into this frenzy?" But he thought it was the father of Eurystheus, frightened, touching his hand to beg for mercy, and he pushed him away, and got his quiver ready, and his bow, against his own children, thinking he was killing the sons of Eurystheus. And they were terrified, and bolted, one this way and one that: one into the dress of his poor mother, one into the shadow of a pillar, and the other crouched under the altar like a bird. And their mother screamed, "You, their father, what are you doing? Are you killing your children?" And the old man screamed, and the whole crowd of slaves.

But he chased the boy round and round the pillar, a terrible circling of feet, and came face to face with him and shot him in the liver. He fell on his back, and soaked the stone pillars with his blood as he breathed out his life. And Heracles shouted in triumph and boasted. "There. One of Eurystheus's chicks is dead, fallen at my feet, paying for his father's hatred." Then he aimed the bow at another, who had crouched down at the base of the altar, thinking he was hidden. But the poor boy got to him first. He fell at his father's knees and threw his hand up to his beard and his neck, and said, "Dearest father, do not kill me. I am yours. I am your boy. It is not Eurystheus's son you are killing." But he turned that wild Gorgon eye on him, and since the boy was standing too close for the deadly bow, he lifted his club over his head, like a smith striking hot iron, and brought it down on the child's fair head and broke the bones. With the second boy taken, he goes for the third, to butcher him on top of the other two. But the poor mother was too quick for him. She snatched the child away inside the house and shut the doors. And he, as if he really were at the walls the Cyclopes built, dug and levered at the doors, tore the doorposts out, and laid his wife and his child flat with a single arrow. Then he goes galloping off to kill the old man. But an image came, or so it looked to us who were watching: Pallas, shaking her spear, the crest of her helmet nodding, and she threw a rock at Heracles's chest, and it stopped him in the middle of his frenzy for killing and sent him down into sleep. He fell to the floor, and hit his back against a pillar that had broken in two when the roof fell in and was lying across its base. Then we got our feet free of running away, and with the old man we tied him with bonds of knotted rope to the pillar, so that when he woke from his sleep he could not add anything to what he had done. He is sleeping, poor man, a sleep that is no blessing, after murdering his children and his wife. And I do not know any mortal more wretched than he is.

Chorus.
	The murder that the rock of Argos remembers,
	the daughters of Danaus killing their husbands in one night,
	was once the most famous crime in Greece, the hardest to believe.
	This has gone past it. It has outrun
	those old horrors, and it fell on the wretched son of Zeus.
	I could tell of Procne, who had one child
	and killed him, and made a sacrifice of him to the Muses.
	But you, you butcher, fathered three,
	and a raging fate worked beside you and finished them all.
	Aiai. What groan, what wail,
	what song for the dead,
	what dance of Hades am I to sound?
	Pheu, pheu.
	Look. The bolts are drawn, the doors are parting,
	the doors of the high-gated house.
	Io moi.
	Look at the children lying in front of their father,
	pitiful, in front of that wretched man,
	who sleeps a terrible sleep after murdering his sons.
	And round him the bonds, the ropes with all their knots,
	propping up the body of Heracles,
	lashed to the stone pillars of the house.

(The doors of the house stand open. Heracles lies asleep, roped to a broken pillar, with the bodies of his wife and children round him. Amphitryon comes slowly towards him.)

Chorus. And here is the old man, like a bird crying over a nest of young that never flew. He comes after his son on slow old feet, down a bitter road. Here he is.

Amphitryon.
	Old men of Thebes, quiet. Quiet.
	Will you not let him lie there, gone limp with sleep,
	and forget his evils?
Chorus.
	I weep for you, old man, and I groan,
	and for the children, and for that head that won every victory.
Amphitryon.
	Go further off. Do not
	stamp, do not shout, do not
	wake him. He is sleeping easy,
	sunk deep in sleep, on his bed.
Chorus.
	Oh.
	All this blood, that he...
Amphitryon.
	Ah. Ah.
	You will be the death of me.
Chorus.
	...spilled, is rising up against him.
Amphitryon.
	Can you not keep your dirge quiet,
	old men, when you cry Aiai?
	Or he will wake and burst his bonds and destroy the city,
	and tear his father apart, and bring the house down.
Chorus.
	I cannot. I cannot.
Amphitryon.
	Quiet. Let me learn how he is breathing.
	Here. Let me put my ear to him.
Chorus.
	Is he asleep?
Amphitryon.
	Yes. He is asleep,
	a sleep that is no sleep, a deadly sleep, the man who killed his wife,
	who killed his children, shot them down to the twang of his bow.
Chorus.
	Groan, then...
Amphitryon.
	I am groaning.
Chorus.
	...for the children's destruction...
Amphitryon.
	Omoi.
Chorus.
	...and for your son's.
Amphitryon.
	Aiai.
Chorus.
	Old man...
Amphitryon.
	Quiet. Quiet.
	He is turning over, he is waking, he is turning round. Here,
	let me hide myself out of sight, under the roof.
Chorus.
	Courage. Night still holds your son's eyes.
Amphitryon.
	Look. Look. To leave the light
	after evils like these, I do not
	shrink from it, wretched as I am. But if he kills me, his father,
	he will pile evil on evil,
	and on top of the Furies he has already, he will carry a father's blood.
Chorus.
	You should have died back then, when you went out
	to take payment for your wife's murdered brothers
	and sacked the Taphians' city, the city ringed by the sea.
Amphitryon.
	Run, run, old men, away from the house,
	get away. Run from a raving
	man as he wakes.
	Or soon he will throw fresh murder on the old murder
	and run wild through the city of the Thebans again.

Chorus. Zeus, why did you hate your own son so much, with such rage? Why did you lead him into this sea of evils?

Heracles. Ah. I am breathing. And I can see what I ought to see: the sky, and the earth, and these arrows of the Sun. But I have fallen into some kind of surge, some terrible churning of the mind, and the breath I breathe comes up hot from my lungs, in gasps, and will not hold steady. Look at this. Why am I sitting here, moored with ropes like a ship, my strong young chest and my arm tied fast to a half-smashed block of cut stone, with corpses for neighbours? And here are winged shafts, and my bow, scattered over the floor, the ones that used to stand beside my arms like shield-bearers, and kept my ribs safe, and were kept safe by me. Surely I have not gone down to Hades again? Run Eurystheus's double course a second time? To Hades? How? No. I do not see the rock of Sisyphus, or Pluto, or the sceptre of Persephone, Demeter's daughter. I am stunned. Where on earth am I, so helpless? Hey. Is any of my friends near, or far off, who can cure me of this not knowing? Because I know nothing clearly. Nothing of the things I used to know.

Amphitryon. Old men, shall I go closer to my own evils?

Chorus. And I will go with you. I will not desert you in your trouble.

Heracles. Father, why are you crying, and covering your eyes, standing so far away from the son you love best?

Amphitryon. My child. You are mine, even when things go badly for you.

Heracles. And what is going badly for me, that you are pouring out tears?

Amphitryon. Something even a god would groan over, if he learned of it.

Heracles. Big words. But you still have not said what has happened.

Amphitryon. You can see it for yourself, if you are in your right mind by now.

Heracles. Speak, if you are sketching some new turn in my life.

Amphitryon. If you have stopped raving, like one of Hades' own madmen, I will tell you.

Heracles. Papai. There it is again, that riddle. It makes me suspicious.

Amphitryon. And I am still watching to see whether you are steadily in your senses.

Heracles. I do not remember going out of my mind, if that is what you mean.

Amphitryon. Old men, shall I untie my son's bonds? Or what should I do?

Heracles. Yes, and tell me who tied me. It shames me.

Amphitryon. Know this much of your evils, and let the rest go.

Heracles. Is silence enough to teach me what I want to know?

Amphitryon. Zeus, do you see this, done from Hera's throne?

Heracles. Has something hostile come at us from there?

Amphitryon. Leave the goddess alone and look after your own evils.

Heracles. Then I am finished. You are going to tell me of some disaster.

Amphitryon. Look. Look at these. Your children, fallen.

Heracles. Oh. What sight is this I am looking at? What is this?

Amphitryon. My boy, you rushed into a war on your children that was no war.

Heracles. War? What do you mean, war? Who killed these?

Amphitryon. You, and your bow, and whichever of the gods is to blame.

Heracles. What are you saying? What did I do? Father, what evil news you bring.

Amphitryon. You were mad. It is a wretched explanation you are asking for.

Heracles. Am I my wife's murderer too?

Amphitryon. All of this is the work of one hand. Yours.

Heracles. Aiai. A cloud of groaning is closing round me.

Amphitryon. That is why I groan for what has happened to you.

Heracles. Did I smash my house as well, in my madness?

Amphitryon. I know one thing only. Everything of yours is ruined.

Heracles. Where did the madness take hold of me? Where did it destroy me?

Amphitryon. When you were purifying your hands with fire at the altar.

Heracles. Oh. Then why am I sparing my own life, when I have become the murderer of the children I loved most? Why do I not go and jump from some sheer rock, or drive a sword into my liver and be the judge who avenges my children's blood, or burn this flesh that she drove mad, and push away from my life the disgrace that is waiting for me? But here is Theseus, coming to stand in the way of my plans for dying, my kinsman and my friend. I will be seen. The pollution of a child-killer will come before the eyes of the dearest of my friends. Oh, what am I going to do? Where can I find a place empty of evils? Grow wings, or go under the ground? Here, let me throw some darkness over my head. I am ashamed of the evils I have done, and I have taken this blood on me that cries out for vengeance, and I do not want to harm anyone who is innocent.

(He covers his head with his robe. Theseus comes in.)

Theseus. I have come with others, armed young men of the land of Athens, who are waiting by the streams of the Asopus. I am bringing your son an allied spear, old man. Word came to the city of Erechtheus's people that Lycus had snatched the sceptre of this country and set himself against you in war and open battle. So I came, to pay something back for what Heracles did for me first, when he saved me from the world below, in case you need anything, old man, from my hand or my allies. Ah. Why is the floor so thick with these dead? Surely I have not been left behind, arrived too late for some newer evil? Who killed these children? Whose wife is this I am looking at? Boys do not stand anywhere near the spear. No, this is some other, some strange new evil I have found here.

Amphitryon. King, whose home is the hill where the olive grows.

Theseus. Why do you call on me with such a pitiful opening?

Amphitryon. We have suffered. Wretched sufferings, from the gods.

Theseus. These children. Whose are they, that you are crying over them?

Amphitryon.
	My son fathered them, my wretched son,
	and having fathered them he killed them. He had the heart for that blood.
Theseus.
	Do not say such things. Speak well.
Amphitryon.
	You are telling people who wish they could.
Theseus.
	You have said a terrible thing.
Amphitryon.
	We are gone, gone, flown away.
Theseus.
	What are you saying? What did he do?
Amphitryon.
	He went astray in a stroke of madness,
	with arrows dipped in the hundred-headed hydra.
Theseus.
	This is Hera's fight. But who is this among the dead, old man?
Amphitryon.
	Mine. He is mine, this son of mine, who has laboured so much,
	who went with the gods to the plain of Phlegra
	with his shield, to the spear-fight that killed the giants.
Theseus.
	Pheu, pheu. Was any man ever born so hated by his god?
Amphitryon.
	You could not find another
	among mortals who has laboured more,
	or been driven further.
Theseus.
	Why is he hiding his wretched head in his robe?
Amphitryon.
	He is ashamed to meet your eye,
	ashamed before a kinsman's love,
	and the blood of his children.
Theseus.
	But I came to share his pain. Uncover him.
Amphitryon.
	My child, take the robe away from your eyes,
	throw it off, show your face to the sun.
	A grief as heavy as yours is wrestling with your tears.
	I beg you, at your beard, at your knee,
	at your hand, falling before you, letting fall
	an old man's grey tears. Io, my boy,
	hold down the wild lion's temper in you.
	You are being driven to a roar of unholy bloodshed,
	wanting to join evils to evils, child.

Theseus. Well then. You, sitting there in that wretched posture. I am calling to you: show your face to your friends. There is no darkness with a cloud black enough to hide the disaster of your evils. Why are you waving your hand at me, signalling murder? So that the pollution of speaking to you will not fall on me? It is nothing to me to share in your bad fortune. I had good fortune with you once. I have to carry my mind back to that, to the time you brought me safe up from the dead into the light. I hate a friend's gratitude that grows old. I hate the man who wants to enjoy his friends' good things and will not sail in the same ship with them when they are in trouble. Stand up. Uncover your wretched head. Look at us. A man who is well born bears what the gods throw down on him, and does not refuse it.

Heracles. Theseus, did you see this struggle? My children?

Theseus. I heard of it. And now you are showing evils to a man who can see.

Heracles. Then why have you uncovered my head to the sun?

Theseus. Why not? You are mortal. You cannot pollute what belongs to the gods.

Heracles. Run, you poor man, from my unholy pollution.

Theseus. No avenging spirit passes from friend to friend.

Heracles. Thank you for that. And I do not regret the good I did you.

Theseus. And I, who had good done to me then, pity you now.

Heracles. I am to be pitied. I killed my own children.

Theseus. I weep for you, now that your fortune has turned to this.

Heracles. Have you ever found another man in greater evils?

Theseus. Your misfortune reaches from the earth up to the sky.

Heracles. Then I am ready. I mean to die.

Theseus. Do you think the gods care anything for your threats?

Heracles. The god is stubborn. So I will be stubborn with the gods.

Theseus. Hold your tongue. Big talk brings bigger suffering.

Heracles. I am full of evils already. There is no room left to stow another.

Theseus. What will you do, then? Where is this anger carrying you?

Heracles. I will die, and go back under the earth, where I came from.

Theseus. That is the talk of any ordinary man.

Heracles. And you are standing outside the disaster, lecturing me.

Theseus. Is this Heracles talking, who has endured so much?

Heracles. Not this much. Not if suffering is measured by any scale.

Theseus. The benefactor of mankind? Their great friend?

Heracles. Mankind is no help to me. Hera is winning.

Theseus. Greece would never stand by and let you die of your own folly.

Heracles. Listen to me, then, so I can compete in argument against your lectures. I will unfold it for you: my life was unlivable, now and before. First, I was born from this man, who killed my mother's old father and had that blood on him when he married Alcmene, who bore me. When the foundation of a family is not laid straight, the descendants are bound to come to grief. And Zeus, whoever Zeus is, begot me as an enemy to Hera. Do not be hurt, old man. I count you my father, not Zeus. While I was still at the breast, the woman who shares Zeus's bed slipped snakes with Gorgon eyes into my swaddling clothes, to kill me. And when I got the covering of flesh a grown man has, the labours I endured, what need to tell them? What lions, what three-bodied Typhons, what Giants, what war against the four-legged crowd of Centaurs did I not finish? And the hydra, the dog with heads all round that grew back as I cut them, I killed it, and I went through herds of countless other labours and came to the dead, to bring Hades' gatekeeper, the three-headed dog, up to the light, at Eurystheus's orders. And this last labour I endured, wretched man: I killed my children, and set the coping stone of evils on my house.

I have come to this by necessity. It is not holy for me to live in Thebes, which I love. And if I do stay, what temple or gathering of friends can I go to? The curses I carry do not invite greetings. Shall I go to Argos? How, when I am in exile from my country? Well then, shall I rush off to some other city? And then be looked at sideways as a marked man, and held in check by the bitter goads of tongues: "Isn't this the son of Zeus, who once killed his children and his wife? Won't he get himself out of this land and perish?" For a man who was once called happy, changes are painful. The man who is always badly off feels nothing; he was born to be wretched. And I think I will come to this point of misfortune: the earth will send out a voice forbidding me to touch the ground, and the sea and the springs of the rivers will forbid me to cross, and I will be an Ixion, driven round in chains on his wheel. And so this is best: that none of the Greeks see me, the people I lived among when I was happy and fortune was good. Why should I live? What gain is there in owning a useless, unholy life? Let the famous wife of Zeus dance, then, and stamp her shoe on the floor of Olympian Zeus. She has done what she wanted. She has turned the first man in Greece upside down, foundations and all. Who would pray to a goddess like that? A goddess who, because of a woman, out of jealousy over Zeus's bed, destroyed the benefactors of Greece, who were guilty of nothing.

Chorus. This fight is no other god's than the wife of Zeus's. You have judged that rightly.

Theseus. I would rather advise you than watch you suffer. No mortal is untouched by fortune, and no god either, if what the poets sing is not false. Have they not gone to bed with each other in ways no law allows? Have they not put their fathers in chains and disgraced them, to get a throne? And yet they live on Olympus all the same, and they have put up with their own wrongdoing. And what will you say, then, if you, born a mortal, take your fortunes too hard, and the gods do not? Leave Thebes, then, for the law's sake, and come along with us to the city of Pallas. There I will purify your hands of the pollution, and I will give you a house and a share of what I own. And the gifts I have from the citizens for saving the fourteen children, when I killed the bull of Cnossos, I will give to you. Everywhere in the country I have been allotted precincts of land, and from now on people will call them by your name while you live. And when you die and go down to Hades, the whole city of the Athenians will raise you up in honour with sacrifices and monuments of stone. It is a fine crown for citizens to win from the Greeks, a good name, for helping a good man. And I will give you this in return for saving me. Because now you need friends. When the gods honour a man, he has no need of friends. The god's help is enough, when he chooses to give it.

Heracles. Oh. All this is beside the point of my evils. I do not believe the gods love beds that are not lawful. I never thought it worth believing that they fasten chains on one another's hands, and I will not be persuaded of it now, or that one god is born the master of another. A god, if he is truly a god, needs nothing. These are the wretched tales of poets. But I have considered, even in my evils, whether I would be convicted of cowardice if I left the light. Whoever cannot stand up under disasters could not stand up to a man's weapon either. I will hold out. I will endure life. I will go to your city, and I owe you thanks for countless gifts.

Well. I have tasted countless labours, and I refused none of them, and I never let a spring run from my eyes. I never thought I would come to this, to let tears fall. But now, it seems, I must be a slave to fortune. So be it. Old man, you see me going into exile. You see that I am the murderer of my own children. Give them to the tomb and lay them out, and honour them with your tears, since the law does not let me. Lay them against their mother's breast and put them in her arms, a wretched partnership, which I in my wretchedness destroyed without meaning to. And when you have hidden the dead in the earth, live on in this city, wretchedly, but all the same force your soul to carry my evils with me. Children, the father who begot you and fathered you has destroyed you, and you got no good from my fine deeds, from all the labour and the force I spent to lay up a good name for you, a fine thing to have from a father. And you, poor woman, I destroyed you too, and not as you deserved, you who kept my bed safe and faithful, and bore the long watch of keeping my house. Oh, my wife and my children. Oh, myself, how wretchedly I have done, and how I am unyoked from my children and my wife. Bitter, the sweetness of these kisses. Bitter, the partnership of these weapons. I do not know whether to keep them or let them go. They will knock against my side and say this to me: "With us you took your children and your wife. You are keeping us. Your children's killers." Then am I to carry them on my arm? Saying what? But strip myself of the weapons I did the finest things in Greece with, throw myself under my enemies' feet, and die in shame? I must not leave them. Wretchedly, I must keep them. In one thing, Theseus, share the labour with me: come with me to Argos and help me settle the business of the wretched dog I have to deliver there, so that grief for my children does not make me do something, if I am alone. Land of Cadmus, and all the people of Thebes, cut your hair, mourn with me, come to my children's burial. You will mourn all of us together, in one word: the dead, and me. We have all perished, all of us wretched, struck down by one blow of Hera's.

Theseus. Stand up, you poor man. Enough of tears.

Heracles. I cannot. My joints have frozen.

Theseus. Yes. Misfortune brings down the strong as well.

Heracles. Pheu. I wish I could turn to stone right here, and forget my evils.

Theseus. Stop that. Give your hand to a friend who wants to help.

Heracles. No. I will wipe the blood off on your clothes.

Theseus. Wipe it off. Do not spare them. I do not refuse you.

Heracles. I have lost my sons, and I have you for a son.

Theseus. Put your arm round my neck, and I will lead you.

Heracles. A loving pair we make. And one of us is broken. Old man, this is the kind of man to have for a friend.

Amphitryon. The country that bore him is blessed in her sons.

Heracles. Theseus, turn me round again, so I can see my children.

Theseus. What for? Do you think that is a charm that will make you feel better?

Heracles. I long for it. And I want to hold my father to my chest.

Amphitryon. Here I am, my boy. What you want is what I want.

Theseus. Have you no memory left of your labours, that you carry on like this?

Heracles. Everything I endured then was less than this.

Theseus. If anyone sees you acting like a woman, they will not admire it.

Heracles. Am I so low in your eyes, alive? I don't think I was before.

Theseus. Far too low. Sick like this, you are not the famous Heracles.

Heracles. And what were you like, down below, in your evils?

Theseus. When it came to nerve, I was the least of men.

Heracles. Then how can you still say that I have been shrunk by my evils?

Theseus. Walk on.

Heracles. Goodbye, old man.

Amphitryon. And goodbye to you, my child.

Heracles. Bury the children as I told you.

Amphitryon. And who will bury me, my child?

Heracles. I will.

Amphitryon. When will you come back for me?

Heracles. When you have buried the children.

Amphitryon. How will you manage that?

Heracles.
	I will send for you, from Thebes to Athens.
	But carry the children in. The earth will find them a heavy load.
	And I, who have wasted my house in shame,
	will follow Theseus like a little boat towed behind, a total wreck.
	Whoever wants wealth or strength
	more than good friends has not thought it through.

(Heracles goes out, leaning on Theseus. Amphitryon and the Chorus turn to the bodies.)

Chorus.
	We go, pitiful, with many tears,
	having lost the greatest of our friends.

The Trojan Women (415 BC)

The Trojan Women

(The Greek camp on the shore at Troy, the morning after the city fell. Smoke rises from the ruins behind. In front of the tents where the captured women are kept, Hecuba lies on the ground. Poseidon appears.)

Poseidon. I am Poseidon. I have come up from the salt depths of the Aegean, where the Nereids dance in their choruses and their feet trace the loveliest of patterns. Ever since the day Apollo and I set the stone towers round this land of Troy, straight and true to the line, my heart has never once lost its goodwill towards the city of my Phrygians. And now it is smoking. It has been sacked and destroyed by the Argive spear. Epeius of Phocis, from under Parnassus, built a horse by Athena's contrivance, pregnant with weapons, and sent the deadly image in through the towers; and men in later days will call it the Wooden Horse, for the spears it hid inside it.

The groves are deserted, and the temples of the gods are running with blood. Priam has fallen dead on the steps of the altar of Zeus who guards the courtyard. Gold in heaps and Phrygian plunder are being carried down to the Achaean ships, and the Greeks who came against this city are waiting for a wind at their sterns, so that after ten seasons of sowing they can see their wives and children again and be glad. And I am leaving famous Troy and my altars, because I have been beaten, by Hera, the Argive goddess, and by Athena, who destroyed the Phrygians between them. When a cruel emptiness takes hold of a city, the worship of the gods sickens, and nobody wants to honour them any more.

The Scamander is loud with the wailing of the captive women as their masters are allotted. Some have gone to the Arcadians, some to the men of Thessaly, some to the sons of Theseus, the leaders of the Athenians. The Trojan women not yet allotted are under these roofs here, set aside for the chief men of the army, and with them Helen, the Spartan, Tyndareus's daughter, quite rightly counted as a captive. And if anyone wants to look at misery, here it is. Hecuba, lying in front of the gates, crying many tears for many reasons. Her daughter Polyxena has been killed at the mound of Achilles's tomb, a wretched death, and in secret; Hecuba does not know it. Priam is gone, and her children. And the girl the lord Apollo let run wild, Cassandra: Agamemnon is going to force her into his bed in the dark, and never mind the god, or what piety requires.

Goodbye, city that was happy once. Goodbye, towers of smooth-cut stone. If Athena, Zeus's daughter, had not destroyed you, you would be standing on your foundations still.

(Athena appears.)

Athena. Am I allowed to speak to my father's nearest kinsman, a great god, honoured among the gods, if I set aside the hatred between us?

Poseidon. You are. Talk between relatives, Lady Athena, is no small charm on the heart.

Athena. I am glad you are in a gentle mood. I bring proposals, my lord, that concern us both, and I want to put them between us.

Poseidon. Is it a new word from some god? From Zeus, or from one of the other powers?

Athena. No. It is about Troy, whose ground we are standing on. I have come to your power, to make it one with mine.

Poseidon. Don't tell me you have thrown away the old hatred and come round to pitying the city, now that it is burned to ashes?

Athena. Go back to the first point. Will you share in my plans, and help me do what I want done?

Poseidon. Certainly. But I want to know your side of it too. Have you come here for the Achaeans, or for the Phrygians?

Athena. I want to give my old enemies the Trojans some joy, and to give the Achaean army a bitter journey home.

Poseidon. Why do you leap about like this, from one mood to another? You hate too hard and you love too hard, whoever it happens to be.

Athena. Do you not know the outrage that was done to me, and to my temples?

Poseidon. I know. When Ajax dragged Cassandra away by force.

Athena. And the Achaeans did nothing to him. Said nothing to him.

Poseidon. And yet it was your strength that sacked Troy for them.

Athena. Which is exactly why I want to hurt them, with your help.

Poseidon. Whatever you want from me is ready. What will you do?

Athena. I want to give them a homecoming that is no homecoming.

Poseidon. While they are still on land, or out on the salt sea?

Athena. When they have sailed from Troy for home. Zeus will send rain, and hail past counting, and black blasts of wind out of the sky. And he says he will give me his lightning-fire, to strike the Achaeans and burn their ships. You do your part. Make the Aegean crossing roar with towering waves and whirlpools of brine, and fill the hollow bay of Euboea with corpses, so that from now on the Achaeans learn to respect my temples, and to honour the other gods as well.

Poseidon. It will be done. A favour like this does not need long speeches. I will stir up the open Aegean. The beaches of Myconos, the reefs of Delos, Scyros and Lemnos and the headlands of Caphereus will hold the bodies of many dead men. Go to Olympus, take the lightning bolts from your father's hands, and watch for the moment when the Argive army lets out its cables.

He is a fool, whoever among mortals sacks cities, and temples, and tombs, the holy places of the dead. He gives them over to emptiness, and later he is destroyed himself.

(The gods go. Hecuba stirs on the ground and lifts her head.)

Hecuba.
	Up, unlucky woman. Lift your head off the ground.
	Lift your neck. This is not Troy any more,
	and we are not the royal family of Troy.
	The god's luck has turned. Bear it.
	Sail with the current, sail with the luck you have,
	do not set the prow of your life
	against the wave. Sail as chance takes you.
	Aiai. Aiai.
	What is there for me not to groan about, in my misery,
	when my country is gone, and my children, and my husband?
	The great swollen pride of my ancestors,
	shrunk down to this. So you were nothing all along.
	What should I keep quiet about? What should I not keep quiet about?
	What should I sing a dirge for?
	Wretched woman that I am, my heavy-fated limbs
	lie the way they lie,
	my back stretched out on a hard bed.
	Oh, my head. Oh, my temples,
	and my ribs. How I long to roll over
	and shift my back and my spine
	from one side to the other, always
	to the sound of my own weeping.
	But even this is music to the wretched,
	to sing of ruin without a dance.
Hecuba.
	Prows of the ships, that came with your quick oars
	to holy Troy over the purple sea,
	past the good harbours of Greece,
	with the hateful war-song of the pipes
	and the sweet voice of the flutes,
	and hung out your hawsers of woven Egyptian rope,
	aiai, in the bays of Troy.
	You came after the hated wife of Menelaus,
	the shame of Castor, the disgrace of the river Eurotas,
	the woman who cut the throat
	of Priam, the father of fifty children,
	and ran me, wretched Hecuba, aground
	on this ruin.
	Oh. What a seat I sit on,
	camped here beside the tents of Agamemnon.
	I am being led away as a slave,
	an old woman out of her house, my head
	shorn pitifully in mourning.
	Wretched wives of the bronze-speared Trojans,
	and girls, girls, unlucky brides,
	Troy is smouldering. Let us cry aiai.
	Like a mother bird over her winged
	nestlings, I will lead the cry,
	the song, and not the same song
	as once, when I leaned on Priam's sceptre
	and led the Phrygian gods their proud music,
	my foot beating the time, the first in the dance.

(Some of the captive women come out of the tents.)

First Half-Chorus.
	Hecuba, why are you crying out? Why are you shouting?
	What does it mean? Through the walls
	I heard the pitiful sounds you were making,
	and fear shot through the breasts
	of the Trojan women who sit inside these tents
	and cry aiai for their slavery.
Hecuba.
	My children, already, at the ships of the Argives...
First Half-Chorus.
	The rowers' hands are moving?
	Oh, no. What do they want? Are they really going to
	ship me away from my own country now?
Hecuba.
	I do not know. But I can guess. Ruin.
First Half-Chorus.
	Io. Io.
	Wretched Trojan women, come out of the tents
	and hear what is going to happen to you.
	The Argives are making ready to sail home.
Hecuba.
	Ai, ai.
	Not her. Do not send
	Cassandra out to me,
	raving, out of her mind,
	a shame in front of the Argives,
	a madwoman. Do not add pain to my pain.
	Io.
	Troy, Troy, unlucky Troy, you are gone,
	and unlucky the people who are leaving you,
	the living and the dead alike.

(The rest of the women come out.)

Second Half-Chorus.
	Oh. I have left the tents of Agamemnon,
	trembling, to hear from you,
	my queen. Have the Argives decided
	to kill me, wretched as I am?
	Or are the sailors at the sterns already
	getting ready to move the oars?
Hecuba.
	My child, you woke before dawn and your heart woke with you.
Second Half-Chorus.
	I came out because I was shaking with terror.
	Has a herald come already from the Greeks?
	Whose slave am I to be, poor wretch?
Hecuba.
	You are not far, I think, from being allotted.
Second Half-Chorus.
	Io. Io.
	Which of the Argives, or the men of Phthia,
	or some island country, is going to take me,
	unlucky as I am, far from Troy?
Hecuba.
	Ah. Ah.
	And I, poor wretch,
	whose slave will I be, and where, in what country,
	an old woman, useless as a drone,
	the shape of a corpse,
	the feeble image of the dead,
	aiai,
	set to keep the watch at somebody's front door,
	or to nurse their children, I who held
	the highest honours in Troy?
Chorus.
	Aiai, aiai. What laments can you find
	to cry aiai for the ruin they have made of you?
	No more will I twirl the shuttle
	back and forth on the looms of Ida.
	I look my last on the bodies of my children,
	my last.
	And there is worse work coming.
	Either I am forced into some Greek's bed,
	and may that night be damned, and the luck that brings it,
	or I fetch the water from Peirene,
	a pitiful servant of the holy spring.
	If only we could come to the famous
	blessed country of Theseus.
	But never, never the swirl of the Eurotas,
	the hateful home of Helen,
	where I would meet Menelaus as his slave,
	the man who sacked Troy.
Chorus.
	The holy country of the Peneus,
	the loveliest footstool of Olympus,
	I have heard is heavy with wealth
	and with fine harvests.
	That would be my second choice, after the holy,
	sacred country of Theseus.
	And the land of Hephaestus under Etna,
	across the water from Phoenicia,
	the mother of the Sicilian mountains, I hear
	is proclaimed for its crowns of courage.
	And the land that sailors find nearest
	on the Ionian sea,
	watered by the Crathis, that loveliest river,
	that turns the hair red-gold
	and feeds a country of good men
	with its holy springs, and makes it rich.
Chorus.
	And here, from the army of the Greeks,
	comes a herald, carrying fresh news,
	hurrying, making his quick feet fly.
	What is he bringing? What is he going to say?
	We are slaves of the Dorian land already.

(Talthybius comes in from the camp, with soldiers.)

Talthybius. Hecuba, you know me. I have come many times to Troy as a herald from the Achaean army, and you knew me before this, lady. I am Talthybius, and I have come with fresh news.

Hecuba.
	Aiai. It has come,
	friends, Trojan women. It has come, the thing I have been afraid of
	for so long.
Talthybius.
	You have been allotted already, if that was what you were afraid of.
Hecuba.
	Aiai. Which city
	did you say? Somewhere in Thessaly,
	or Phthia, or the land of Cadmus?
Talthybius.
	You have gone to your masters one by one, not all together.
Hecuba.
	Then who has drawn whom? Which of the women of Troy
	has a lucky fate waiting for her?
Talthybius.
	I know. But ask me one at a time, not all at once.
Hecuba.
	Then my child. Who
	drew her? Tell me. Poor Cassandra.
Talthybius.
	King Agamemnon took her, as a prize set apart for himself.
Hecuba.
	As a slave for his Spartan
	wife? Io moi moi.
Talthybius.
	No. For his bed, in the dark, as a bride nobody will speak of.
Hecuba.
	Apollo's virgin? The girl the god with the golden hair
	gave the gift of a life with no man in her bed?
Talthybius.
	Desire shot him. Desire for the god-possessed girl.
Hecuba.
	Throw them away, child, the holy keys,
	tear off your body the sacred wreaths
	you wear, the garlands you are dressed in.
Talthybius.
	What, is it nothing to her, to win a king's bed?
Hecuba.
	And the child you took from me the other day, the youngest? Where is she?
Talthybius.
	You mean Polyxena? Or who is it you are asking about?
Hecuba.
	Her. Who did the lot yoke her to?
Talthybius.
	She has been appointed to serve at Achilles's tomb.
Hecuba.
	Oh. I gave birth to a servant for a grave.
	But what law is this, what custom
	of the Greeks is this, my friend?

Talthybius. Count your daughter lucky. She is well off.

Hecuba. What is that you said? Tell me, does she still see the sun?

Talthybius. Her fate has her now. She is free of all her troubles.

Hecuba. And the wife of Hector, the master of bronze? Poor Andromache. What fortune has she got?

Talthybius. Achilles's son took her too, as a prize set apart.

Hecuba.
	And I, whose servant am I,
	I who need a stick in my hand
	for a third foot, with my old grey head?
Talthybius.
	Odysseus, the king of Ithaca, drew you, to have as his slave.
Hecuba.
	E, e.
	Beat the shorn head,
	tear both cheeks with your nails.
	Io moi moi.
	I have drawn a slave's lot under a filthy, treacherous man,
	the enemy of justice, a beast with no law in him,
	who turns everything from there to here, and then
	back from here to there again, with his two-faced tongue,
	and makes every friend he had before into an enemy.
	Weep for me, women of Troy.
	I am gone, and my luck has gone. I am finished,
	poor wretch. The lot I have fallen on
	is the worst of all.

Chorus. You know your own fate, my queen. But mine? Which of the Achaeans, which of the Greeks, holds my fortune in his hands?

Talthybius. Go, slaves. Bring Cassandra out here to me as fast as you can, so that I can put her into the general's hands, and then take the rest of the captive women to the other chiefs, whoever drew them.

Hold on. What is that light of pine torches blazing inside there? Are they setting fire to the tents? What are the Trojan women doing? Are they burning themselves alive because they are about to be taken away from this country to Argos? Do they want to die? People who have been free take very badly to trouble like this. It is a stiff neck that cannot bend. Open up. Open up. What suits them may not suit the Achaeans, and I do not want the blame for it landing on me.

Hecuba. No. Nobody is setting fires. It is my daughter Cassandra. She is running this way, out of her mind.

(Cassandra bursts out of the tents, carrying a lighted torch and dressed as a priestess of Apollo, with garlands in her hair.)

Cassandra.
	Lift it high. Bring it here.
	Bring the light. Oh. I worship. I set it blazing, look, look,
	this holy place, with torches.
	Lord Hymen.
	Blessed is the bridegroom,
	and blessed am I, to be married
	into a royal bed in Argos.
	Hymen, oh Lord Hymen.
	Since you, mother, with your tears
	and your groans keep mourning
	my dead father and the country we loved,
	I light the fire for my own wedding,
	and set its light blazing
	into brightness, into glory,
	giving it, Hymen, to you,
	giving it, Hecate, a light
	for a virgin's marriage bed,
	as the custom is.
	Lift your foot. Dance.
	Lead the dance up to the sky. Euan, euoi.
	As if it were for my father's
	happiest of fortunes.
	The dance is holy.
	Lead it, Apollo, now. In your temple
	among the laurel trees I serve as your priestess.
	Hymen, oh Hymen, Hymen.
	Dance, mother, laugh out loud,
	twine your feet with mine, this way, that way,
	carrying the step I love best.
	Shout Hymen, oh,
	with blessed songs
	and cries for the bride.
	Come, girls of Phrygia in your fine dresses,
	sing of my marriage, sing
	the husband fate has laid down
	for my bed.

Chorus. My queen, will you not take hold of the girl? She is possessed. She will go running with those light feet of hers straight into the Argive army.

Hecuba. Hephaestus, you carry the torch at the weddings of mortals, but this is a miserable flame you are fanning up here, and nothing like the great hopes we had. Oh, my child. I never dreamed you would be married like this, at the point of a spear, by an Argive's sword. Give me the light. You are not carrying the fire straight, running about in your madness, and your troubles have not brought you to your senses, child. You are just as you were. Take the torches inside, women of Troy, and answer her wedding songs with your tears.

Cassandra. Mother, crown my head. I have won. Be glad for me, for my royal wedding. Send me off, and if you find me at all unwilling, push me there by force. Because if Apollo is any prophet at all, Agamemnon, the famous king of the Achaeans, is marrying a wife who will cost him more than Helen did. I am going to kill him. I am going to wreck his house in return for mine, and take the price of my brothers and my father.

But I will let that go. I will not sing about the axe that is going to come down on my neck, and on other necks; or the killing of a mother that my marriage will set going; or the overturning of the house of Atreus. What I will do is show you that this city is luckier than the Achaeans. I am possessed by the god, yes, but for this much I will step outside my raving.

They came hunting Helen, and for one woman, for one bout of desire, they lost men by the tens of thousands. Their general, the clever one, destroyed what he loved most for the sake of what he hated most: for a woman, he gave up to his brother the joy of his own children at home. And she went of her own free will. Nobody carried her off by force. Then, when they reached the banks of the Scamander, they started dying, and not because anyone was robbing them of their frontiers or their high-towered homeland. The men Ares took never saw their children again. No wife's hands wrapped them in their shrouds. They lie in a foreign country. And at home it was the same story. Women died widows; fathers died childless in their houses, having brought up sons for other people; and there is nobody at their graves to pour blood on the ground for them. That is the praise their army has earned. Better to say nothing about the shameful part. I would not want my Muse to be a singer of evil things.

The Trojans, now. First, they were dying for their country, and there is no finer glory than that. The ones the spear took were carried home dead by the people who loved them, and lay wrapped in the earth of their fathers' land, laid out by the hands that should have laid them out. And the Phrygians who did not die in battle lived every day with their wives and children beside them, which is a joy the Achaeans went without. As for Hector, and the grief you feel about him, listen to how it really stands. He is dead and gone, and he is known as the best man there was, and it was the Achaeans' coming that did that. If they had stayed at home, nobody would ever have found out how good he was. And Paris married the daughter of Zeus. If he had not, nobody would ever have talked about the marriage he made.

So anyone with any sense should keep clear of war. But if it comes to war, it is no shameful crown for a city to die well, and dying badly is the disgrace. So do not pity your country, mother, and do not pity my bed. With this marriage of mine, I am going to destroy the people you and I hate most.

Chorus. How sweetly you laugh at the disasters of your own house. And how sweetly you sing of things that you may not be able to show are true.

Talthybius. If Apollo had not driven your wits wild, you would not be sending my commanders out of this country with prophecies like that and getting away with it free of charge. But there it is. The grand people, the ones with the reputation for cleverness, turn out to be no better than the nobodies. The greatest king of all the Greeks, the dear son of Atreus, has fallen for a passion he set apart for himself: for this madwoman. And I am a poor man, but I would not have taken her into my bed. As for you, since your wits are not all there, your insults to Argos and your praises of the Phrygians I hand over to the winds to carry off. Follow me to the ships, a fine bride for the general.

And you, when the son of Laertes wants to take you, go with him. You will be the servant of a woman who keeps herself in hand, or so they say, the ones who came to Troy.

Cassandra. A clever servant, this one. Why do heralds have the name they have, these errand boys of kings and cities, the one thing the whole human race agrees on hating? You say my mother is going to end up in the halls of Odysseus? Then where are Apollo's words, the ones he made clear to me, that she will die here? I will not throw the rest of it in her face.

Poor man. He does not know what suffering is waiting for him. The day will come when my troubles and the Phrygians' look like gold to him. On top of his ten years here, he will fill out another ten before he reaches his own country, and he will reach it alone. He will come to the narrow passage between the rocks where the terrible Charybdis lives; and the Cyclops, who walks the mountains and eats men raw; and Circe of Liguria, who turns men into pigs; and wrecks on the salt sea; and the lotus, and the longing to eat it; and the holy cattle of the Sun, whose flesh will one day find a voice and speak, and Odysseus will not like what it says. To cut it short: he will go down alive into the house of Hades, and when he has escaped the water of the lake he will come home and find ten thousand troubles waiting in his house.

Cassandra. But why am I shooting off Odysseus's troubles like arrows? Go, as fast as you can. Let me marry my bridegroom in the house of Hades. You are a bad man and you will get a bad burial, at night, not in the daylight, you commander of the Greeks who thinks he is doing something grand. And me, the gullies will throw out my corpse naked, running with the winter rains, near my bridegroom's grave, for the wild beasts to tear at. Apollo's servant.

Garlands of the god I loved best, holy ornaments of my ecstasy, goodbye. I have left your festivals behind, where I used to be so glad. Off my body, go, I tear you off, so that while my flesh is still pure I can give them to the racing winds to carry to you, lord of prophecy. Where is the general's ship? Where must I go to board her? You cannot be too quick now in watching for a wind for your sails, since when you carry me out of this country you carry one of the three Furies with you. Goodbye, mother. Do not cry. Oh, my dear country, and my brothers under the earth, and my father who begot us, it will not be long before you welcome me. I will come down to the dead in victory, when I have destroyed the house of the sons of Atreus, who destroyed us.

(Talthybius leads Cassandra away towards the ships. Hecuba sinks to the ground.)

Chorus. You women who attend old Hecuba, do you not see your mistress has fallen full length, without a word? Will you not take hold of her? Are you going to let an old woman lie where she fell, you useless things? Lift her up.

Hecuba. Let me lie where I fell, girls. Help I do not want is no help. What I am suffering, and have suffered, and am still going to suffer, has earned me the right to lie here. Gods. They are poor allies, the ones I am calling on. But there is a certain form to it, calling on the gods, when one of us falls into bad luck. So first I want to sing of the good things. That way I will stir up more pity for the bad ones.

I was royal, and I married into royalty, and there I had children, the best of men, not just a number to be counted, but the finest in all Phrygia. No woman in Troy or in Greece, no barbarian woman either, could ever boast of giving birth to sons like them. And I saw them fall to the Greek spear, and I cut off this hair of mine at their graves. And Priam, who fathered them, I did not weep for him because somebody brought me the news. I saw him with these eyes, myself, his throat cut at the altar of the courtyard, and I saw the city taken. And the girls I brought up to be prizes worth having for bridegrooms of the highest rank, I brought them up for other men, and they were torn out of my hands. There is no hope that they will ever see me, and I will never see them again.

And the last thing, the coping stone on all my wretched troubles: I am going to Greece, a slave, an old woman. And they will set me to the work that suits old age worst of all: to keep the door and mind the keys, I, the mother of Hector, or to bake the bread, and to sleep on the floor with my wrinkled back, after a royal bed, in torn rags wrapped round a torn body, in scraps of a dress that the fortunate would not think fit to wear. Oh, poor wretch that I am. All this I have had, and all this I have coming, because one woman got married once.

Oh, my child. Oh, Cassandra, who danced with the gods in their ecstasy, what a disaster has undone your purity. And you, poor girl, where are you, Polyxena? Of all the children I bore, the sons and the daughters, so many of them, not one is any help to their wretched mother now. So why lift me up? What is there to hope for? Take me, the feet that once stepped so delicately in Troy and are a slave's feet now, to a bed of straw on the ground and a pillow of stone, so that I can fall on it and be destroyed, worn away with crying. Of all the people who are fortunate, count none of them lucky until he is dead.

Chorus.
	Sing me a song of Troy, Muse,
	a new kind of song, a song for a funeral, with tears in it.
	Now I will raise my voice for Troy
	and tell how the four-footed thing on wheels, the Argives' horse,
	destroyed me, a wretched woman, taken by the spear:
	when the Achaeans left that horse at the gates,
	rumbling up to the sky, its harness gold,
	and armed men inside it.
	And the people shouted, standing up on the rock of Troy,
	"Go on, your troubles are over,
	take this holy carving up the hill
	to the virgin daughter of Zeus, who watches over Troy."
	Which of the young women did not go?
	Which old man stayed in his house?
	And singing for joy
	they took in the trick that was their ruin.
Chorus.
	Every soul in Phrygia hurried to the gates
	to give the goddess her present:
	the Argive ambush, hidden in the polished mountain pine,
	the ruin of Dardanus's land,
	a gift for the virgin goddess whose horses never die.
	They put twisted ropes of flax around it
	and hauled it, like the dark hull of a ship,
	up to the stone seat and the stone floor
	of Pallas's temple, the floor that was going to drink
	our country's blood, and set it there.
	And on top of the work and the joy
	the darkness of night came down,
	and the Libyan pipe was sounding,
	and Phrygian songs, and the girls
	lifted their feet high and beat the ground and sang
	a happy song, and in the houses
	the bright blaze of the fire
	threw its dark glow
	and gave everyone over to sleep.
Chorus.
	And I was dancing then, round the house,
	singing for the virgin of the mountains,
	the daughter of Zeus, when a shout,
	a shout of blood, went through the town
	and took hold of the citadel of Pergamum.
	Babies threw their frightened arms
	round their mothers' dresses.
	War came out of its hiding place:
	the work of the virgin Pallas.
	Phrygians were slaughtered round the altars,
	and in the beds, where men lay with their heads cut off,
	the emptiness gave Greece a crown
	of young women, to breed her sons,
	and gave the fatherland of the Phrygians grief.

(A cart is drawn in, piled with Hector's bronze armour and the spoils of Troy. Andromache sits on it, holding the child Astyanax.)

Chorus.
	Hecuba, do you see Andromache there,
	carried along in a foreigners' cart?
	And at her heaving breast, held close,
	dear Astyanax, Hector's son.
	Where are they taking you on the back of that cart,
	poor woman, sitting beside Hector's
	bronze armour and the spoils of the Phrygians,
	hunted down at spear-point,
	the ones Achilles's son will hang up
	in the temples of Phthia, brought home from Troy?
Andromache.
	The Achaeans, my masters, are taking me away.
Hecuba.
	Oh.
Andromache.
	Why are you groaning? That is my song of grief, not yours.
Hecuba.
	Aiai.
Andromache.
	For these pains.
Hecuba.
	Oh, Zeus.
Andromache.
	And for this disaster.
Hecuba.
	Children.
Andromache.
	We were your children, once.
Hecuba.
	Gone, the happiness. Gone, Troy.
Andromache.
	Poor Troy.
Hecuba.
	And the noble blood of my children.
Andromache.
	Pheu, pheu.
Hecuba.
	Pheu, yes, for my
Andromache.
	sufferings.
Hecuba.
	Pitiful, the luck
Andromache.
	of the city,
Hecuba.
	which is going up in smoke.
Andromache.
	Come to me, husband, come to me.
Hecuba.
	You are calling for my son, and he is in Hades,
	poor woman.
Andromache.
	Come and shield your wife.
Hecuba.
	And you, scourge of the Achaeans,
	master of my children and their father,
	old Priam, first of my house,
	lay me down to sleep in Hades.
Andromache.
	This is a great longing,
Hecuba.
	Poor woman. These are the pains we suffer,
Andromache.
	for a city that is gone,
Hecuba.
	and pain lies on top of pain.
Andromache.
	because the gods turned against us, from the day that son of yours, Paris,
	cheated the death he was meant for, the one who, for a hateful bed,
	destroyed the towers of Troy. And the bloody bodies of the dead
	lie stretched out beside the goddess Pallas
	for the vultures to carry off, and Troy has been brought
	under the yoke of slavery.
Hecuba.
	Oh, my country. Oh, poor
Andromache.
	I am crying for you, left behind,
Hecuba.
	now you see the pitiful end,
Andromache.
	and for my house, where I gave birth.
Hecuba.
	Children, your mother has no city, and now she is losing you.
	What a wailing there is, what grief,
	tears falling out of tears
	in our houses. But the dead
	forget their pain. The dead do not cry.

Chorus. How sweet tears are to people who have come to grief, and the wailing of the dirge, and the music that has sorrow in it.

Andromache. Mother of the man who once killed more Argives with his spear than anyone alive, mother of Hector, do you see this?

Hecuba. I see the way the gods work. What was nothing they build up into a tower, and what looked like something they destroy.

Andromache. We are being led away as plunder, my child and I. Nobility has come down to slavery. That is how great the change is.

Hecuba. Necessity is a terrible thing. Just now Cassandra was torn from me too, dragged off by force.

Andromache.
	Pheu, pheu.
	It seems your daughter has found a second Ajax, another man
	to drag her off by force. But you are sick in other ways as well.

Hecuba. Yes, and there is no measure to my sicknesses, and no number. Evil comes racing against evil.

Andromache. Your daughter is dead. Polyxena. They cut her throat at Achilles's tomb, a gift to a dead man who cannot feel it.

Hecuba. Oh, I am wretched. So that is what Talthybius meant, the riddle he told me a while ago, so unclearly, and so clearly.

Andromache. I saw her myself. I got down from this cart and covered her body with my dress and beat my breast for her.

Hecuba. Aiai, child, for that unholy slaughter. Aiai, again and again, for the evil way you died.

Andromache. She died the way she died. But even so, dying like that, she got a happier fate than I have, alive.

Hecuba. Being dead and looking at the light are not the same thing, my child. One is nothing. The other has hope in it.

Andromache. Mother, you who gave birth to her, listen to the best argument I have. I want to put a little pleasure into your heart. I say that never to have been born is the same thing as being dead, and that dying is better than living in misery. The dead feel no pain. They know nothing of their troubles. But the man who was happy once and has fallen into unhappiness, his mind wanders off, back to the good life he had before. Polyxena is dead, and it is as if she had never seen the light: she knows nothing of what has happened to her. But I aimed at a good name, and I hit it, and I won more of it than most women ever do, and that is exactly how I missed my luck.

Everything that has ever been found out to help a woman keep herself in hand, I worked at, in Hector's house. First: whether or not there is any real blame in it for a woman, the mere fact of not staying at home brings a bad name with it, so I put the wish to go out of my mind and stayed in the house. And I did not let the clever talk of women in through the door either. I had my own mind as a teacher, a good one, from home, and that was enough for me. I gave my husband a quiet tongue and a calm eye. I knew where I should win against my husband, and where I should let him have the victory.

And the report of all this went out to the Achaean army and destroyed me. Because when I was taken, Achilles's son wanted me for his wife. I am going to be a slave in the house of the men who murdered mine. And if I push away my dear Hector's face and open my heart to the husband I have now, I will look like a traitor to the dead man. And if I hate this one, my own masters will hate me. And yet they say a single night undoes a woman's dislike of a man's bed. I spit on the woman who throws away the husband she had for a new bed and loves another man. Not even a horse, if it is separated from the one it grew up with, will pull the yoke easily. And a horse is a dumb beast: it has no reason, and nature has given it less than us.

But you, Hector, my dear, you were a husband who was enough for me, great in understanding, in birth, in wealth, in courage. You took me untouched from my father's house, and you were the first to yoke my virgin bed. And now you are dead, and I am being shipped off to Greece, a prisoner of war, to the yoke of slavery. So tell me: the death of Polyxena, that you are groaning for, is it not less to bear than what I have? I do not even have the one thing that is left to every human being alive, hope. I do not fool myself into thinking that I will ever do well again. And even the thinking would have been sweet.

Chorus. You have come to the same point of disaster we have. Mourning your own troubles, you are teaching us where we stand in ours.

Hecuba. I have never set foot on the hull of a ship myself, but I have seen them in pictures and heard about them, and so I know. When the storm is moderate enough to bear, sailors have the will to work their way out of trouble: one at the tiller, one up on the sails, one keeping the bilge water out of the ship. But when the sea is thrown into a great confusion and comes over them, they give in to luck and let themselves go to the running of the waves. And that is how I am. I have so many troubles that I am dumb. I have let go. I leave my mouth alone. The wretched wave the gods have sent is too strong for me.

But, my dear child, let Hector's fate alone. Your tears will not save him. Honour the master you have now. Offer the man the sweet bait of your ways. If you do that, you will make everyone who loves you glad, all of us together, and you may bring up this child, my son's son, to be the greatest help Troy could have, so that one day, perhaps, children born from you might settle Troy again, and there might still be a city. But one thing leads to another. Who is this Achaean servant I see coming now, bringing news of new decisions?

(Talthybius comes in, with soldiers.)

Talthybius. Wife of Hector, who was once the best of the Phrygians, do not hate me. I am not bringing this news because I want to. The Greeks, and the sons of Pelops with them, have a joint decision to announce.

Andromache. What is it? The way you are starting sounds like the beginning of something bad.

Talthybius. It has been decided that this boy, how am I going to say this?

Andromache. Not that he is to have a different master from mine?

Talthybius. No Achaean will ever be this boy's master.

Andromache. Then they are leaving him here, the last remnant of the Phrygians?

Talthybius. I do not know how to tell you the bad news gently.

Andromache. I thank you for your decency. Unless what you have to tell is good.

Talthybius. They are going to kill your son. There. Now you know the worst of it.

Andromache. Oh. That is a worse evil than my marriage.

Talthybius. Odysseus won the argument, speaking in front of the whole Greek army.

Andromache. Aiai, again. What we suffer is beyond all measure.

Talthybius. He said that the son of so great a father should not be brought up.

Andromache. May he win arguments like that about his own children.

Talthybius. And that he must be thrown from the towers of Troy. Let it happen that way, and you will show yourself the wiser for it. Do not cling to him. Grieve for your troubles like the well-born woman you are, and do not imagine you are strong when you have no strength at all. You have no defence anywhere. You must look at it clearly: your city is destroyed and your husband is dead, you are in our power, and we are quite able to fight one woman. So I do not want you to want a fight, or to do anything shameful or hateful, or to throw curses at the Achaeans. If you say anything that angers the army, this child will not be buried, and there will be no pity for him. But if you keep quiet and take what has happened to you as it should be taken, you will not leave his body unburied, and you will find the Achaeans kinder to you.

Andromache. My darling. My child, honoured beyond all children. You are going to die at the hands of your enemies and leave your miserable mother behind. Your father's nobility is killing you, the thing that saves other people. Your father's greatness came at the wrong time for you. My unlucky bed, my unlucky marriage, that brought me once into Hector's house. I did not come there to bear a son for the Greeks to slaughter, but a king of Asia with its rich harvests.

Child, are you crying? Do you understand what is happening to you? Why are you gripping me with your hands and holding on to my dress, like a chick huddling under my wings? Hector is not going to come up out of the ground with his famous spear in his fist and save you. No kinsman of your father's is coming, no Phrygian army. You will fall from the height, a hideous drop, headfirst onto your neck, with nobody to pity you, and the breath will be broken out of you. Little body in my arms, the dearest thing your mother has. The sweet smell of your skin. You smell so sweet. So it was for nothing that this breast fed you in your baby clothes. For nothing I laboured and wore myself to rags with work. Now, never again, hold your mother. Fall on the woman who bore you, wind your arms round my back, and put your mouth to mine.

Greeks. You have invented barbarian cruelties. Why are you killing this child? He has done nothing. And you, seed of Tyndareus, you were never Zeus's daughter. I say you had many fathers: the Avenging Spirit first, and then Envy, and Murder, and Death, and every evil the earth breeds. I will never boast that Zeus fathered you, you who have been death to so many barbarians and Greeks. Damn you. Out of those beautiful eyes of yours you have brought a shameful ruin on the famous plains of Phrygia. Go on, then. Take him. Carry him off. Throw him, if throwing him is what you have decided. Feast on his flesh. The gods are destroying us, and I cannot keep death away from my own child. Cover up my wretched body and throw it in the ship. I am going to a fine wedding, now that I have lost my child.

Chorus. Poor Troy. You have lost thousands of men, for one woman and her hateful bed.

Talthybius.
	Come, boy. Let go of your poor mother,
	let go of her arms around you, and walk
	to the very top of your father's towers,
	where the vote has decided
	you are to let your breath go.
	Take him.
	This kind of message should be carried
	by a man with no pity in him,
	a man who is a better friend to shamelessness
	than my mind is.

(The soldiers take the child from her. Talthybius goes out with Andromache and Astyanax.)

Hecuba.
	Child. Son of my poor son.
	They are robbing your mother and me
	of your life, and it is not just.
	What can I do? What can I do for you,
	unlucky boy? All we can give you
	is this: blows on the head, fists on the breast.
	That much is ours to give.
	Oh, for my city. Oh, for you.
	What do we not have?
	What is missing now, to make our ruin
	total, and complete, and fast?
Chorus.
	Telamon, king of Salamis, where the bees are kept,
	you made your home on an island the waves wash round,
	leaning against the holy hills
	where Athena first showed the branch of the grey olive,
	a crown from heaven and a glory for shining Athens.
	You came, you came, sharing the glory
	with the archer, the son of Alcmene, Heracles,
	to sack Troy, Troy, our city,
	long ago, when you came from Greece.
Chorus.
	That was when he led the first flower of Greece,
	furious over the horses Laomedon had promised him and never paid,
	and at the broad-flowing Simois he rested the oar
	that had carried him across the sea, and tied the ship's cables to the stern,
	and took out of the ship the sure aim of his hand, his bow,
	to be the death of Laomedon.
	And the stonework Apollo had squared to the line
	he brought down with the red breath of fire
	and sacked the land of Troy.
	Twice now, with two strokes, around the walls
	of Dardanus's country, the bloody spear has brought them down.
Chorus.
	So it was for nothing, then, that you walk so delicately
	among the golden wine-jugs, Ganymede, Laomedon's boy,
	filling the cup of Zeus, the loveliest of services.
	The city that bore you is burning in the fire,
	and the shores of the sea
	cry out, the way a bird
	shrieks over her young:
	here for husbands, here for children,
	here for old mothers.
	Your dewy baths, the running tracks
	where you exercised, are gone,
	and you, beside the throne of Zeus,
	keep your young face calm and lovely
	with its graces, while the spear of Greece
	has destroyed the land of Priam.
Chorus.
	Love, Love, who came once to the halls of Dardanus,
	when the gods in heaven had you on their minds,
	how high you built Troy then,
	binding her to the gods by marriage.
	I will not say it as a reproach to Zeus any more.
	But the light of the white-winged Dawn,
	which is dear to mortals, looked on this land
	and saw it die, saw the towers destroyed,
	she who had a husband from this land
	in her bedroom, Tithonus, the father of her children,
	the one the golden chariot of the stars, four horses,
	snatched up and carried off,
	a great hope for his fatherland. But the love the gods had
	for Troy is gone.

(Menelaus comes in, with his men.)

Menelaus. Bright light of the sun, this day, when I get my hands on my wife. Helen. I am Menelaus, the man who has done all the work, and this is the Achaean army. I came to Troy not, as people think, for a woman, but after a man: the man who cheated his host and robbed my house of my wife. Well, he has paid the price, with the gods' help, he and his country, fallen to the Greek spear. And I have come to take the wretched woman away. I do not enjoy saying the word "wife" of a woman who was once mine. She is in these prisoners' tents, counted in with the other Trojan women. The men who fought for her with the spear have given her to me to kill, or, if I choose not to kill her, to take back to the land of Argos. And I have decided to let Helen's death in Troy go, and to carry her by ship to Greece, and there hand her over to be killed, as payment to all the men whose friends died at Troy. Right. In you go, men, into the tent. Bring her out here by that hair of hers, foul with murder. And when the winds blow fair, we will send her to Greece.

Hecuba. You who carry the earth, and have your seat on the earth, whoever you are, hard to guess at and hard to know, Zeus, whether you are the necessity of nature or the mind of mortal men, I pray to you. You go along a soundless road, and you guide everything human toward justice.

Menelaus. What is this? You have found a new way to pray to the gods.

Hecuba. I praise you, Menelaus, if you will kill your wife. But do not look at her. Run from the sight of her, or she will take you with longing. She takes men's eyes. She takes cities. She burns down houses. That is the kind of spell she has. I know her. So do you. So does everyone who has suffered by her.

(Helen is brought out of the tent by Menelaus's men.)

Helen. Menelaus, this is an opening that might well frighten me. Your servants have laid hands on me and driven me out in front of these tents by force. Still, I am fairly sure you hate me. But I want to ask, all the same: what have the Greeks decided, and you, about my life?

Menelaus. Your case did not need a precise ruling. The whole army, the army you wronged, has given you to me to kill.

Helen. Then am I allowed to answer that, and argue that if I die, I am dying unjustly?

Menelaus. I did not come here to argue. I came to kill you.

Hecuba. Hear her out, Menelaus. Do not let her die without that. And then give us the other side, the case against her. You know nothing of what she did in Troy. Put the whole story together and it will kill her. There will be nowhere for her to run.

Menelaus. That is a gift that takes time. Still, if she wants to speak, she may. Understand that I am giving her this for the sake of what you have to say, so that she can hear it. Not as a favour to her.

Helen. Perhaps you will not answer me at all, whether you think I argue well or badly, because you have made up your mind that I am your enemy. Very well.
