I will guess at the charges you would bring against me if we went through it point by point, and I will set my answers against them, my accusations against yours.

First. This woman here gave birth to the beginning of all the trouble, when she gave birth to Paris. Second, it was the old man who destroyed Troy, and me with it: Priam, who did not kill the baby, the child his wife had dreamed of as a burning torch, a bitter dream and a true one, the child who was Alexander then. Now hear how the rest of it goes. This man was made the judge of three goddesses, a team of three. And Athena's gift to Alexander was this: he would lead the Phrygians in war and root Greece out of the ground. Hera promised he would hold Asia, and the farthest edges of Europe, as his kingdom, if Paris judged for her. And Aphrodite went into raptures over my looks, and promised him me, if she outran the other goddesses in beauty. Now look where the argument goes from there. Aphrodite beat the goddesses. And this is how much my marriage did for Greece: you are not ruled by barbarians. You did not go down in battle, and you do not live under a tyrant. What was good luck for Greece was my ruin. I was sold for my beauty, and I am reviled for the very thing that should have set a crown on my head.

You will say I have still not come to the point, the thing in front of us: how I slipped away from your house in secret. He came with no small goddess at his side, this woman's curse, the ruin of her house, call him Alexander if you like, or Paris, whichever name you please. And you, you worst of men, you left him behind in your house and sailed off from Sparta to Crete.

Well, then.

It is not you I will put the next question to. It is myself. What was I thinking, when I left my home and followed a stranger, betraying my country and my house? Punish the goddess. Be stronger than Zeus. He has power over every other god, and he is her slave. So forgive me.

Here is a respectable argument you might use against me next. When Paris was dead and gone down into the earth, and my marriage was no longer the gods' doing, then I should have left his house and gone to the Argive ships. I tried. That is exactly what I tried to do. My witnesses are the gatekeepers on the towers and the sentries on the walls. Time and again they caught me letting my body down from the battlements to the ground on knotted ropes. And then this new husband took me by force, Deiphobus, and kept me as his wife, against the wishes of the Phrygians. So how could you justly put me to death, husband, and be in the right, when one man married me by force, and my life here, instead of a victor's prize, was a bitter slavery? If you want to be stronger than the gods, then wanting it shows how little you understand.

Chorus. Queen, defend your children and your country. Break this woman's persuasion. She speaks well, and she is a criminal. That is a dangerous thing.

Hecuba. First I will take the goddesses' side, and show that what she says about them is not just. I do not believe Hera and the virgin Athena could ever have been so foolish, one of them to sell her Argos to barbarians, and Athena to make her Athens a slave of the Phrygians one day, if they came to Ida over their looks, as if for a game, out of vanity. Why would the goddess Hera have fallen so in love with beauty? So she could get herself a better husband than Zeus? And Athena, which of the gods was she hunting for a husband, she who begged her father to let her stay a virgin, because she wanted no man's bed? Do not make the goddesses fools to dress up your own crime. You will not persuade anyone with sense.

And then you said, and this is the laughable part, that Aphrodite came with my son to the house of Menelaus. Could she not have stayed quietly in heaven and brought you to Troy, and all Amyclae along with you? No. My son was extraordinarily handsome, and when your mind saw him, your mind turned into Aphrodite. Every piece of foolishness people commit, they call Aphrodite, and rightly: her name is the beginning of the word for having no sense. You looked at him, blazing in his barbarian clothes and his gold, and you went out of your mind. In Argos you had lived on little. Once you were free of Sparta, you hoped to drown the Phrygians' city, flowing with gold as it was, under your spending. Menelaus's house was not big enough for you to run riot in with your luxuries.

Well, then. You say my son took you by force. Which Spartan noticed? What cry did you ever raise? Castor was still alive, a young man, and his twin brother too, not yet among the stars. Then when you came to Troy, with the Argives on your track, and the struggle was on, spear against spear, whenever the news that came to you said this man was winning, you praised Menelaus, so that my son would suffer, having so great a rival in love. And if the Trojans were doing well, this man was nothing. You kept your eye on luck, and you made a practice of following wherever she went. Virtue you did not want.

And then you say you let yourself down from the towers on ropes, stealing your body away, as if you were staying against your will? Where were you ever caught knotting a noose, or sharpening a sword, the things a noble woman would do if she missed her first husband? And yet I told you, over and over. "Daughter, leave. My sons will find other brides. I will help you slip away and send you to the Achaean ships. End this war between the Greeks and us." But that was bitter to you. In Alexander's house you did as you pleased, and it was outrage, and you wanted barbarians bowing down to you. That was a great thing to you. And after all that, you have come out with your body groomed, and you look at the same sky as your husband. You disgusting thing. You should have come out humble, in rags, shaking with fear, your head shaved, with more decency about you than shamelessness, after everything you did before. Menelaus, so that you know where my speech ends: crown Greece, as you deserve to, and kill this woman. And make it a law for every other woman: whoever betrays her husband dies.

Chorus. Menelaus, be worthy of your ancestors and your house. Punish your wife. Clear yourself, before Greece, of the charge that you are soft, and show your enemies you are well born.

Menelaus. You have come round to the same conclusion as I have: that she left my house of her own free will for a stranger's bed, and Aphrodite has been dragged into the speech for show. Go on. Go to the men who will stone you. Pay back the long labours of the Achaeans in one short death, and learn not to bring shame on me.

Helen. No. By your knees, do not lay the gods' sickness on me and kill me for it. Forgive me.

Hecuba. And do not betray the allies this woman killed. I beg you for their sake, and for my children's.

Menelaus. Enough, old woman. I am not thinking about her. I am telling my men to take her to the sterns of the ships, where she will sail.

Hecuba. Then do not let her set foot on the same ship as you.

Menelaus. What is this? Does she weigh more than she used to?

Hecuba. There is no lover who does not go on loving.

Menelaus. That depends on how the minds of the ones we loved turn out. But you shall have what you want. She will not board the same ship as I do. What you say is not bad. And when she gets to Argos she will die badly, as she deserves, a bad woman, and she will teach every woman to keep herself in hand. That is not easy. But her destruction will throw a fright into their folly, even if they are worse than she is.

(Menelaus goes out, and his men take Helen after him.)

Chorus.
	So this is how you handed over
	the temple in Troy and the altar
	smoking with incense to the Achaeans,
	Zeus, and the flame of the offering cakes,
	and the smoke of myrrh rising into the sky,
	and holy Pergamos, the citadel,
	and Ida, the glens of Ida thick with ivy,
	running with rivers of melting snow,
	the edge of the world, first struck by the sun,
	a holy place, shining, where the gods were served.
Chorus.
	Gone, the sacrifices to you, gone the dancers'
	glad singing, gone the all-night
	vigils for the gods in the dark,
	the images shaped in gold,
	and the Phrygians' holy moons,
	twelve of them, twelve full moons together.
	I wonder, I wonder, lord, whether you think of this,
	seated on your throne in the sky,
	in the upper air, while the city dies,
	brought down by a rush of blazing fire.
Chorus.
	My love, my husband,
	you are dead and you wander,
	unburied, unwashed, and a ship on the sea
	will carry me, darting on its wings,
	to Argos, where horses graze, where stone walls
	built by Cyclopes reach up to the sky.
	And the crowd of children at the gates
	hang on us and cry, they weep and weep,
	and one cries out, cries out:
	"Mother, oh, the Achaeans are taking me
	alone, out of your sight,
	onto a dark ship
	with oars for the sea,
	to holy Salamis
	or the ridge between two seas,
	the Isthmus, where the gates
	of Pelops's land stand."
Chorus.
	And when Menelaus's boat
	is out in the middle of the sea,
	may the holy fire of the Aegean, the two-forked lightning,
	fall between the banks of oars,
	as he takes me from Troy in tears,
	uproots me from my country, a slave for Greece,
	while the daughter of Zeus
	still holds her golden mirrors,
	the toys of girls.
	May he never reach the land of Laconia,
	his father's hearth and his bedroom,
	nor the town of Pitane,
	nor the goddess with the bronze gates,
	now he has taken back the disgrace
	whose marriage shamed great Greece
	and brought miserable suffering
	to the streams of Simois.

(Talthybius comes in with soldiers, who carry the body of Astyanax on Hector's shield.)

Chorus.
	Io, io.
	New disasters, one on top of another,
	changing places on this land. Look, wives of Troy,
	miserable women, look at Astyanax, dead,
	the bitter thing the Greeks threw from the towers
	like a discus, killed, and now they bring him here.

Talthybius. Hecuba, one ship is still here, its oars waiting. It is about to carry the rest of the spoils of Achilles's son to the coast of Phthia. Neoptolemus himself has already put out to sea. He had news of fresh trouble for Peleus: Acastus, the son of Pelias, has driven him out of the country. So he is gone, faster than that, with no time to spare for waiting, and Andromache with him. She drew a great many tears from me when she set out from this land, crying for her country and speaking to Hector's tomb. And she asked him to let this body be buried, your Hector's son, who fell from the walls and gave up his life. And this shield, the terror of the Achaeans, backed with bronze, that the boy's father used to sling round his side: she asked him not to carry it to the hearth of Peleus, nor into the same bedroom where she, the mother of this dead child, is to be married, so that she will not have to look at it and grieve. Instead of a cedar coffin and a ring of stone, the boy is to be buried in this. And it is to be put into your arms, so that you can wrap the body in robes and garlands, as far as you have the means, given how things are with you. Because she is gone, and her master's hurry kept her from burying the child herself. So then, when you have dressed the body, we will heap earth over him and raise our spears. Do what you have been told, as fast as you can. One task I have spared you already: as I crossed the streams of the Scamander there, I washed the body and cleaned the wounds. Now I will go and break open a grave in the ground for him, so that my work and yours between them are finished quickly, and the ship can start for home.

(Talthybius goes.)

Hecuba. Set Hector's round shield down on the ground. A painful sight, and not one I love to see. Achaeans. Your spears weigh more than your minds. What were you afraid of in this child, that you committed a murder never seen before? That some day he would raise fallen Troy up again? Then you were nothing, after all. When Hector had the luck in battle, and ten thousand other hands with him, we were still being destroyed. And now the city is taken and the Phrygians are dead, and you were frightened of a baby this size. I have no praise for a fear that is afraid without ever reasoning it through.

My darling, what a wretched death came to you. If you had died for the city, once you had had your youth, and marriage, and the kingship that makes a man like a god, you would have been blessed, if any of those things is a blessing. As it is, you saw them and you knew them in your soul, child, but you do not know them. You had them in your house and got no use of them. Poor boy. How cruelly your father's walls have shorn your head, the towers Apollo built. The curls your mother tended so often and kissed, and now, where they were, murder grins out from the broken bones. I will not say the ugly thing. Hands, how sweetly you keep the likeness of your father's hands, and you lie in front of me loose at every joint. Dear mouth, that threw out so many big promises: you are gone, and you lied to me. You used to fall into my dress and say, "Mother, I will cut a great lock of my hair for you, and I will bring my friends in a procession to your tomb, and speak to you with love." But you are not burying me. I am burying you, the young one, and I am old, with no city and no children, and you are a pitiful corpse. Oh, all those kisses, all my nursing of you, those sleeps we had. Gone. What would a poet ever write on your tomb? "The Argives killed this child once, because they were afraid of him"? An inscription that shames Greece. Still, you did not get your father's property, but you will have his bronze-backed shield to be buried in. Shield, you kept Hector's beautiful arm safe, and you have lost your best guardian. How sweet the print of him lies in your handle, and on your well-turned rim, the sweat that Hector let drip from his brow so often in the thick of the work, when he pressed you to his chin.

Bring things, bring what you can, to dress this pitiful body out of what we have. The god is not giving us the luck for anything beautiful. But what I have, you will get. Anyone is a fool who thinks he is doing well and takes it for safe and is glad. Luck is like a man with a wild temper: she jumps this way one moment and that way the next, and nobody is lucky all the way through.

Chorus. Here are the women, ready at hand, bringing you ornaments out of the Phrygian spoils to hang on the dead.

Hecuba. Child, it is not for winning a horse race, or for beating your friends with the bow, the customs the Phrygians honour without chasing them to excess, that your father's mother puts these fine things on you, out of what once was yours. Helen, whom the gods hate, has robbed you of them now, and killed your life besides, and destroyed your whole house.

Chorus.
	E, e. You touched my heart,
	you touched it. You, who would have been to me one day
	the great lord of the city.

Hecuba. What you should have put on your body at your wedding, marrying the highest-born woman in Asia, these Phrygian robes, the pride of our weaving, I hang on your body. And you, who were glorious in victory once, mother of ten thousand trophies, Hector's beloved shield: take your crown. You will die with this body without dying. You are far more worth honouring than the arms of Odysseus, clever and evil.

Chorus.
	Aiai, aiai. The earth will take you, child,
	a bitter thing to mourn.
	Cry out, mother,

Hecuba. Aiai.

Chorus. the song for the dead.

Hecuba. Oh, oh.

Chorus. Oh, yes. For your evils that cannot be forgotten.

Hecuba. Some of your wounds I will heal with bandages, a wretched doctor, a doctor in name and not in fact. The rest your father will see to, among the dead.

Chorus.
	Beat, beat your head,
	your hands falling like oars,
	io moi moi.

Hecuba. Dearest women.

Chorus. Hecuba, say what is yours to say. What is the cry you are making?

Hecuba. So the gods had nothing in mind but my suffering, and Troy, the one city out of all of them they hated. We slaughtered oxen for them for nothing. And yet, if the god had not turned everything upside down and thrown us under the earth, we would have been nobodies, unsung, never giving the Muses of later generations a song to sing. Go and bury the body in its poor tomb. It has the garlands the dead need. I think it makes little difference to the dead whether anyone gets rich funeral gifts. That is empty pride, and it belongs to the living.

(The women carry the body away to be buried.)

Chorus.
	Io, io.
	Miserable mother, who has seen the great
	hopes of her life torn to rags in you.
	Counted so happy in your birth
	from noble fathers,
	you have died a terrible death.
	Ea, ea.
	Who are those I see on the heights of Troy,
	hands darting to and fro
	with blazing torches? Some new evil
	is about to fall on Troy.

Talthybius. Captains, you who have been ordered to burn this city of Priam's, I am speaking to you. Do not keep the flame idle in your hands any longer. Throw the fire in, so that we can raze the city of Troy to the ground and set off for home from Troy, glad to go. And you, so that one order does two things, daughters of Troy, when the leaders of the army sound the trumpet, loud and high, go to the Achaean ships and be taken out of this land. And you, old woman, most unlucky of women, come. These men have come for you from Odysseus. The lot sends you out of your country as his slave.

Hecuba. Oh, I am wretched. So this is the last thing, the very end of all my evils. I am leaving my country, and the city is being set alight. Old foot, hurry, hard as it is, so that I can say goodbye to my poor city. Troy, you who once breathed so grandly among the barbarians, they will soon take away your famous name. They are burning you, and they are leading us out of the land already, as slaves. Io, gods. But why do I call on the gods? They did not hear us before, when we called. Come. Let us run into the fire. The finest thing for me would be to die with my country as it burns.

Talthybius. You are out of your mind with your own sorrows, poor woman. Take her, men, do not hold back. She has to be put into Odysseus's hand and sent to him as his prize.

Hecuba.
	Ottototototoi.
	Son of Cronos, lord of Phrygia, father
	who begot our race, do you see what we suffer,
	things the blood of Dardanus never deserved?
Chorus.
	He sees. And the great city
	is no city. It is destroyed. Troy is no more.
Hecuba.
	Ottototototoi.
	Troy is blazing, the roofs
	of Pergamos are burning in the fire,
	the city, and the tops of the walls.
Chorus.
	Like smoke on a wing of wind, rising
	to the sky, the land fallen to the spear wastes away.
	The houses are overrun with raging fire
	and the enemy's spear.
Hecuba.
	Io, land that nursed my children.
Chorus.
	E, e.
Hecuba.
	Children, hear me, know your mother's voice.
Chorus.
	You are calling the dead with a song of grief.
Hecuba.
	Yes, laying my old limbs on the ground
	and beating the earth with both my hands.
Chorus.
	After you I set my knee on the earth,
	calling my own miserable husband
	up from below.
Hecuba.
	We are led, we are carried off,
Chorus.
	Pain, it is pain you cry.
Hecuba.
	under a slave's roof.
Chorus.
	Out of my country.
Hecuba.
	Io.
	Priam, Priam, dead,
	unburied, without a friend,
	you know nothing of my ruin.
Chorus.
	Black death has closed his eyes,
	a holy man, an unholy slaughter.
Hecuba.
	Io, houses of the gods, and my dear city,
Chorus.
	E, e.
Hecuba.
	the murdering flame is yours, and the point of the spear.
Chorus.
	Soon you will fall to the dear ground, and have no name.
Hecuba.
	And the dust, rising to the sky on a wing like smoke,
	will hide my own house from my eyes.
Chorus.
	The name of the land will vanish. Everything
	is gone, one thing here and one thing there,
	and poor Troy is no more.
Hecuba.
	Did you feel that? Did you hear?
Chorus.
	The citadel crashing down.
Hecuba.
	The earth shaking, shaking, the whole
Chorus.
	city, it will wash over the whole city like a wave.
Hecuba.
	Io.
	Trembling limbs, carry my steps.
	Go on, poor limbs,
	to the day of slavery that is your life.
Chorus.
	Io, poor city. And still,
	set your foot forward, to the Achaean ships.

Iphigenia Among the Taurians (c. 414 BC)

Iphigenia Among the Taurians

(The land of the Taurians, on the shore of the Black Sea. In front of the temple of Artemis stands an altar, stained dark, with trophies hung on the wall above it. Iphigenia, the priestess, comes out of the temple.)

Iphigenia. Pelops, the son of Tantalus, came to Pisa with his fast horses and married the daughter of Oenomaus. From her Atreus was born, and the sons of Atreus were Menelaus and Agamemnon. Agamemnon is my father. I am Iphigenia, his child, and my mother was the daughter of Tyndareus. And my father killed me. Or so he believes. He cut my throat for Artemis, for Helen's sake, in the famous bay of Aulis, beside the narrows where the Euripus spins in its whirlpools and twists the dark blue water round in the constant winds.

That is where lord Agamemnon gathered his fleet, a thousand Greek ships, wanting to take the victor's crown of Troy for the Achaeans and to punish the outrage done to Helen's marriage. He was doing Menelaus a favour. But the winds turned terrible and the ships could not sail, and he went to the burnt offerings to find out why, and Calchas told him this. "Agamemnon, commander of this Greek army, you will not get your ships off this shore until Artemis has your daughter Iphigenia, with her throat cut. You made a vow once, to sacrifice to the goddess who carries the torch the most beautiful thing the year brought forth. Well, that year your wife Clytemnestra bore you a child in your house" (and there he was handing the prize for beauty to me) "and that child you must sacrifice." So Odysseus worked one of his tricks, and they took me away from my mother on the pretext that I was to marry Achilles.

I came to Aulis. Poor girl. They lifted me high over the altar and were killing me with the sword. But Artemis stole me away. She gave the Achaeans a deer in my place, and carried me through the bright air and set me down to live here, in the land of the Taurians, where a barbarian rules barbarians: Thoas, whose name means Swift, and who earned it because he runs as fast as a bird flies. She made me priestess in this temple. And so, by the customs Artemis takes pleasure in, I preside at a festival whose name is the only fine thing about it. The rest I keep quiet about; I am afraid of the goddess. I sacrifice, by a law this city had before I came, any Greek man who lands in this country. I begin the rite, that is all. The killing itself is other people's business, inside the goddess's temple, and it is not to be spoken of.

But the night has brought me strange visions, new ones, and I will tell them to the open air, if telling them is any cure. I dreamed I had left this country and was living in Argos, sleeping among the unmarried girls, and the back of the earth shook and heaved, and I ran, and stood outside, and watched the cornice of the house come down and the whole roof thrown to the ground in ruins from its high pillars. One pillar was left standing, I thought, one, out of my father's whole house, and yellow hair came down from its capital and it took a human voice. And I, keeping up this trade of mine, this killing of strangers, sprinkled it with the holy water as if it were about to die, and I was crying.

This is how I read the dream. Orestes is dead, and I was the one who began the rite over him. The pillars of a house are its sons; and whoever my holy water touches, dies. I cannot make the dream fit anyone else I love: Strophius had no son when I was killed. So now I want to pour the offerings for my brother, he far away and I here, since that much at least I can do, with the attendants the king gave me, Greek women. But why are they not here yet? What is keeping them? I will go inside, into the goddess's temple, where I live.

(She goes into the temple. Orestes and Pylades come in cautiously from the direction of the shore.)

Orestes. Look. Watch out. Make sure there is nobody on the path.

Pylades. I am looking. I am turning my eyes every way and checking.

Orestes. Pylades, do you think this is the goddess's house? The one we launched the ship from Argos to find?

Pylades. I do, Orestes. And you had better think so too.

Orestes. And the altar, where Greek blood drips down?

Pylades. Well, the hair hanging on it is red with blood, at any rate.

Orestes. And do you see the spoils hanging under the cornice itself?

Pylades. Trophies. The first pickings from the strangers who died here. But we ought to keep our eyes moving and look carefully all round.

Orestes. Apollo, where have you led me this time, into what net, with your oracles? Ever since I avenged my father's blood by killing my mother, I have been hunted by Furies, relay after relay of them, an exile driven off my own land, and I have run many a long lap of the course. I came to you and asked you how I could reach the end of this madness that spins me like a wheel, and of the labours I had worked through, wandering all over Greece. And you told me to go to the borders of the Taurian country, where your sister Artemis has her altars, and take the statue of the goddess, which they say here fell into this temple from the sky; and when I had taken it, by cunning or by some stroke of luck, and come through the danger, to give it to the land of Athens. What came after that, you did not say. And if I did this, I would have a breathing space from my labours.

So I have come, obedient to what you said, to a country I do not know and that does not welcome strangers. And I am asking you, Pylades, because you are my partner in this labour: what do we do? You see how high the walls are all round. Do we climb the steps up to the house? And how would we not be seen? Or do we break the bronze-forged bolts of the doors with crowbars, when we know nothing about them? If we are caught opening the gates and rigging a way in, we die. No. Before we die, let us run for the ship, the one we sailed here in.

Pylades. Running is not to be borne, and we are not in the habit of it. And the god's oracle is not to be turned into a coward's excuse. Let us leave the temple and hide ourselves in the caves, where the black sea washes in with its spray, well away from the ship, so that nobody sees the hull and tells the king, and then we are taken by force. And when the eye of dark night comes on, then we have to have the nerve to take the polished statue out of the temple, whatever it takes. Look there, between the triglyphs: there is a gap where a man could let himself down. Good men have the nerve for hard labours. Cowards are nothing, anywhere.

Orestes. No. We did not row all this way to turn round at the finish line and head for home. You are right; we do as you say. We must go wherever on this land we can hide ourselves and not be seen. It will not be the god's fault that his sacred oracle falls useless to the ground. We must have the nerve. No labour is an excuse when you are young.

(They go out toward the shore. The Chorus, Greek women who are slaves of the temple, come in.)

Chorus.
	Keep holy silence,
	you who live by the twin rocks
	that clash together over the Unfriendly Sea.
	Daughter of Leto,
	Artemis of the nets, goddess of the mountains,
	to your court, to the gold cornices
	of your temple with its beautiful pillars,
	I bring my virgin step, holy to the holy one,
	I, the slave of the holy keeper of your keys.
	I have left the towers and the walls
	of Greece, the land of fine horses,
	and Europe, with its forests and its pastures,
	the home of my fathers.
	I am here. What is it? What is on your mind?
	Why have you called me, called me to the temple,
	daughter of the man who went against the towers of Troy
	with his famous fleet,
	a thousand ships,
	ten thousand spears, the son of Atreus, that famous house?
Iphigenia.
	Io, women, slaves of this house,
	how I am caught in dirges that are hard to sing,
	in the cry of a song no Muse would own,
	in laments with no lyre, aiai,
	aiai, in wails for the dead.
	Ruin has come down on me.
	I am mourning my brother, mourning his life.
	Such a sight, such a sight I saw in my dreams
	in the night whose darkness has just gone out.
	I am lost. I am lost.
	My father's house is no more.
	Oh. Oh. The family is gone.
	Ah, ah, for the sorrows of Argos.
	Io, fate,
	who rob me of my only brother
	and send him to Hades. For him
	I am going to pour these offerings,
	the bowl of the dead, over the back of the earth:
	streams of milk from the cows on the mountain,
	the wine that Dionysus gives, poured out,
	and the labour of the tawny bees.
	These are the things that soothe the dead.
	Give me the golden vessel now,
	and the offering for Hades.
	Child of Agamemnon under the earth,
	I send you these, as to a dead man.
	Take them. To your grave I will never bring
	my yellow hair, or my tears.
	I live too far, far from your country
	and mine, where they believe I lie,
	poor woman, with my throat cut.
Chorus.
	I will answer you, mistress, song for song,
	a barbarian cry, the hymns of Asia,
	I will sing it out for you:
	the music that belongs to the dead
	in laments, the music Hades sings
	in his songs, with no note of triumph in it.
	Oh, for the house of the sons of Atreus.
	The light of the sceptre is gone, oh,
	the light of your father's house.
	Once there was a rule in Argos
	of kings the gods had blessed,
	and now trouble darts out of trouble:
	Pelops on his wheeling winged horses,
	and the man he threw into the sea;
	and the Sun, who moved out of his seat
	the holy, holy eye of his light.
	And pain came on pain to the house,
	for the golden lamb,
	killing on killing, grief on grief,
	and out of the Tantalids who died before
	the punishment comes down on the house,
	and fate hurries against you
	what no one would hurry to meet.
Iphigenia.
	From the beginning my fate went wrong,
	from my mother's belt undone
	and that first night; from the beginning
	the Fates who stand by at a birth
	pulled my upbringing tight and hard,
	the girl the Greeks came courting,
	the first-born child in the house,
	whom Leda's unhappy daughter
	bore and reared, because of her father's outrage,
	as a victim, a sacrifice with no joy in it,
	the answer to a vow.
	In a chariot drawn by horses
	they set me down on the sands of Aulis,
	a bride, oh, no bride at all
	for the son of Nereus's daughter, aiai.
	And now I live a stranger by the Unfriendly Sea,
	the sea that is no friend to strangers,
	in a house on barren ground,
	no husband, no child, no city, no friend,
	not singing to Hera at Argos,
	not weaving on the sweet-sounding loom
	with my shuttle the picture of Athenian Pallas
	and the Titans. No. I stain the altars
	with the blood of strangers, a ruin
	that drips blood and no lyre could play,
	and they cry out, and the cry is pitiful,
	and the tears they shed are pitiful.
	And now I forget all of that,
	and I weep for the brother who died in Argos,
	the one I left at the breast,
	still a baby, still small, still a young shoot
	in his mother's arms, at her breast,
	Orestes, who holds the sceptre in Argos.

Chorus. Look, here comes a herdsman. He has left the shore of the sea, and he is coming to tell you something new.

Herdsman. Daughter of Agamemnon and of Clytemnestra, hear the news I am bringing. It is strange.

Iphigenia. What is there in it to startle anyone?

Herdsman. Two young men have come to this country in a ship, escaping the dark Clashing Rocks. An offering the goddess will love, a sacrifice for Artemis. You cannot be too quick getting the holy water ready, and the first cuttings for the rite.

Iphigenia. Where are they from? What country's dress do the strangers wear?

Herdsman. Greeks. That one thing I know, and nothing beyond it.

Iphigenia. You did not hear a name? You cannot tell me what the strangers are called?

Herdsman. One of them was called Pylades by the other.

Iphigenia. And his partner, the other stranger, what was his name?

Herdsman. Nobody knows. We did not hear it.

Iphigenia. How did you see them? How did you come across them and catch them?

Herdsman. On the edge of the breakers, on the Unfriendly Sea.

Iphigenia. And what do herdsmen have to do with the sea?

Herdsman. We went down to wash the cattle in the salt water.

Iphigenia. Go back to what I asked. How did you catch them, and in what way? That is what I want to know. They have been a long time coming. Not once yet has the goddess's altar been reddened with streams of Greek blood.

Herdsman. We were driving our cattle, the ones that feed in the woods, into the sea that flows in through the Clashing Rocks. There is a cleft there, a hollow in the rocks broken open by the constant pounding of the waves, where the men who dive for purple shellfish shelter. And there one of our herdsmen saw two young men, and came tiptoeing back to us, ferrying his footsteps on the very tips of his toes, and said, "Don't you see them? Those are gods, of some kind, sitting there." And one of us, a god-fearing man, lifted his hands when he saw them and prayed. "Son of Leucothea the sea-goddess, guardian of ships, lord Palaemon, be kind to us. Or is it you two sitting on our shore, the twin sons of Zeus? Or the darlings of Nereus, who fathered the noble chorus of the fifty Nereids?"

But another man, an idiot, with the nerve that comes from having no respect for any law, laughed at the prayers and said they were shipwrecked sailors sitting in the cleft, afraid of our custom, because they had heard that we sacrifice strangers here. Most of us thought he was talking sense, and that we should hunt down the victims the goddess is owed by the custom of the country.

And just then one of the two strangers left the rock and stood up, and shook his head up and down, and groaned, and his hands shook to the fingertips, wandering in a fit of madness, and he shouted like a hunter: "Pylades, do you see her? This one? Don't you see her, the she-dragon of Hades, how she wants to kill me, with her terrible vipers, mouths open at me? And that one, breathing fire and slaughter out of her robes, rowing the air with her wings, with my mother in her arms, a mass of rock, to throw down on me. Oh, she is going to kill me. Where can I run?" There were no such shapes there to see. He was turning the lowing of the calves and the barking of the dogs into what he said were the noises the Furies send out.

We huddled together, and sat there in silence, amazed. And he drew his sword and rushed into the middle of the calves like a lion and struck at them with the iron, into their flanks, driving it into their ribs, thinking that this was how he was fighting off the Furies, the goddesses, until the sea itself blossomed red with blood. Then every man of us, seeing the herd falling and slaughtered, armed himself, and blew the conch shells, and gathered the neighbours; because we thought herdsmen would make a poor fight of it against strangers who were young and well fed. It took a long time, but we filled our numbers. And the stranger fell. The pulse of the madness let go of him, and the foam ran down from his chin. And when we saw him fallen, so conveniently, every man went to work, throwing, battering. The other stranger wiped the foam away and looked after his body and covered him with the fine weave of his cloak, watching for the blows as they came and doing everything he could for his friend, tending him. Then the stranger came to his senses and leapt up from where he had fallen, and saw the wave of enemies breaking over them, and the disaster that was on the two of them right there, and he groaned. And we did not let up. We kept throwing stones, pressing in from every side. And then we heard that terrible cry of his: "Pylades, we are going to die. But let us die the best way we can. Draw your sword and follow me."

When we saw the two enemy swords swinging, we ran and filled the rocky gullies. But if some ran, others pressed in and threw at them; and if they drove those off, the ones who had just given way came back and pelted them with stones again. And it was unbelievable: with all those thousands of hands, not one of us managed to hit the goddess's victims. In the end we got them, but hardly by courage. We circled round and with the stones we knocked the swords out of their hands, and they sank on their knees to the ground, worn out. And we brought them to the king of this land. He looked at them, and as fast as he could he sent them to you, for the holy water and the slaughter. This is what you have been praying for, lady, strangers like these, for victims. Kill strangers like these, and Greece will have paid for your murder. It will be justice done for the slaughter at Aulis.

Chorus. That is an amazing story you have told about the madman, whoever he is, who has come from Greece to the Unfriendly Sea.

Iphigenia. Well. You go and bring the strangers here. We will see to the holy business at this end.

(The Herdsman goes back toward the shore to fetch the prisoners.)

Poor heart of mine. Until now you were calm with strangers, and always full of pity, and you measured out your tears for our shared blood whenever Greek men came into your hands. But now, because of the dreams that have made me savage, believing Orestes no longer looks at the sun, you will find me hard, whoever you are who have come here. And this is true, I see it now, my friends: people who are unlucky, when they are doing badly themselves, have no kind thoughts for people who are more unlucky still.

But no wind from Zeus has ever come, no ship, that carried Helen here through the Clashing Rocks, the woman who destroyed me, and Menelaus with her, so that I could pay them back, and set an Aulis here against the one there, where the Greeks took hold of me like a calf and cut my throat, and the priest was my own father, the man who begot me. Oh. I have not forgotten the evils of that day. How many times I threw my hands at his beard, and clung to his knees, the knees of the father who made me, and said things like this: "Father, this is a shameful wedding you are marrying me into. While you are killing me, my mother and the women of Argos are singing wedding hymns, and the whole house is full of flutes, and I am being destroyed by you. Achilles was Hades after all, then, not the son of Peleus, the husband you offered me, when you brought me in your chariot to a bloody marriage by a trick." And I was looking out through a fine veil, and I did not take my brother up in my arms, and now he is dead, and I did not kiss my sister, out of modesty, because I was going to the house of Peleus. I put off so many embraces until later, thinking I would come back again to Argos.

Poor Orestes. If you are dead, what good things you have lost, what a father's greatness you had coming to you.

And the goddess: I blame her cleverness. Any mortal who touches blood, or lays a hand on a woman in childbed or on a corpse, she bars from her altars, and calls him polluted. And she herself takes pleasure in sacrifices of human beings. It is not possible that Leto, Zeus's bride, gave birth to anything so stupid. For my part, I do not believe the story of the feast Tantalus gave the gods, that they enjoyed eating his son. And I think the people here, who are killers of men themselves, put their own vile behaviour onto the goddess. I do not believe any god is evil.

Chorus.
	Dark, dark, the meeting-place
	of two seas, where the gadfly
	that flew from Argos drove Io
	across the unfriendly swell,
	when she changed the land of Europe
	for the land of Asia.
	Who can they be, who left
	the reedy green waters of the Eurotas
	or the holy streams of Dirce,
	and came, came to this land that mixes with no one,
	where for the daughter of Zeus
	the blood of mortals wets
	the altars and the pillared temples?
Chorus.
	Was it to the double beat
	of pinewood oars in the surf
	that they sailed over the waves of the sea,
	a ship for a chariot, in breezes that fill the linen sails,
	racing each other for riches,
	to make their houses greater?
	Hope is a sweet thing, and it never has enough,
	and it is the ruin of human beings,
	the ones who carry off the weight of wealth,
	wandering over the swell, crossing to barbarian cities,
	all with the one idea.
	And for some the thought of wealth comes at the wrong time,
	and for others it comes in due measure.
Chorus.
	How did they pass the rocks that run together,
	how did they pass the sleepless shores
	of the sons of Phineus,
	running along the salt beach
	on the surf of Amphitrite,
	where the fifty daughters of Nereus
	dance in a ring and sing,
	with the wind filling the sails
	and the rudder creaking
	in its bed at the stern,
	on the south wind,
	or on the breath of the west wind,
	to the land of many birds,
	the white beach,
	the beautiful race-course of Achilles,
	along the Unfriendly Sea?
Chorus.
	If only, as my mistress prays,
	Helen, Leda's darling child,
	would leave the city of Troy
	and come here, and here,
	with the bloody water wound round her hair,
	die by my mistress's hand,
	her throat cut,
	and pay the penalty that matches her crime.
	But the sweetest news I could hear
	would be that someone had come
	from the land of Greece, a sailor,
	to put an end to my miserable slavery.
	Even in dreams let me be
	in my home, in my father's city,
	enjoying the pleasure of sleep,
	a happiness that belongs to everyone.
Chorus.
	But here they come, the two of them,
	their hands tied tight together, a fresh
	offering for the goddess. Be quiet, my friends.
	The first pickings of Greece
	are walking up to the temple now.
	The herdsman's report was no lie.
	Lady, if this city does these things
	in a way that pleases you, accept the sacrifice
	that the custom here holds out to you,
	the sacrifice that Greeks call unholy.

(Orestes and Pylades are brought in by the temple guards, their hands bound. Iphigenia comes out of the temple.)

Iphigenia. Well. First I must see that the goddess's business is done properly. Untie the strangers' hands. They are consecrated now, and they should not be in chains any longer. Go inside the temple and get ready what is needed, and what the custom is, for what we have to do.

(The guards free the prisoners' hands and go into the temple.)

Ah. Who was the mother who bore you two, who was your father? And your sister, if you happen to have one: what a pair of young men she is going to lose, and be left without a brother. Who knows whom fortunes like these will fall on? Everything the gods do creeps along in the dark, and nobody knows what evil is coming; luck leads us off where we cannot see. Where have you come from, poor strangers? You sailed a long way to reach this country, and you will be a long way from home for a long time. For ever. Down below.

Orestes. Why are you crying over this, woman, whoever you are, and grieving in advance for the evils that are coming to the two of us? I do not call it clever, when a man is about to be killed, to try to conquer his fear of dying by crying about it. Nor when a man with Hades this close and no hope of safety pities himself; he makes two evils out of one, he gets convicted of foolishness and he dies all the same. Let fate be. Do not mourn for us. We know the sacrifices they do here. We understand them.

Iphigenia. Which of the two of you is the one they call Pylades? That is the first thing I want to know.

Orestes. This man. If knowing it gives you any pleasure.

Iphigenia. And a citizen of what Greek city, by birth?

Orestes. What would you gain by learning that, woman?

Iphigenia. Are you brothers, from one mother?

Orestes. In love, yes. We are not brothers by birth, woman.

Iphigenia. And you, what name did your father give you?

Orestes. If I got my rights, I would be called Unlucky.

Iphigenia. That is not what I asked. Put that down to fortune.

Orestes. If we die without a name, nobody can laugh at us.

Iphigenia. Why so grudging about it? Are you so proud?

Orestes. It is my body you will be sacrificing, not my name.

Iphigenia. Will you not even tell me what city is yours?

Orestes. There is no profit in what you are asking. I am going to die.

Iphigenia. And what stops you doing me this one favour?

Orestes. Famous Argos. That is the country I claim as mine.

Iphigenia. By the gods, stranger, is it true? You were born there?

Orestes. From Mycenae, yes. It was a rich place once.

Iphigenia. Did you leave your country as an exile? Or what happened to you?

Orestes. I am in exile, in a way. Against my will, and willingly.

Iphigenia. Then would you tell me some things I want to know?

Orestes. It would be a small thing, beside my own bad luck.

Iphigenia. I am so glad you have come from Argos. I have longed for it.

Orestes. I have not. If you have, enjoy it.

Iphigenia. Perhaps you know Troy. Everyone everywhere talks about it.

Orestes. I wish I did not. Not even in a dream.

Iphigenia. They say it is gone. Nothing left. Taken by the spear.

Orestes. That is how it is. What you heard was not empty talk.

Iphigenia. And Helen has come home again to Menelaus's house?

Orestes. She has. And her coming was an evil to someone I love.

Iphigenia. And where is she? She owes me an evil turn as well.

Orestes. She lives in Sparta, with the man whose bed she shared before.

Iphigenia. Thing that all Greece hates. Not only me.

Orestes. I have had a taste of that woman's marriage myself.

Iphigenia. And the Achaeans came home, as they are saying?

Orestes. You bundle everything up and ask me all of it at once.

Iphigenia. Before you die, I want to get some good out of you.

Orestes. Cross-examine me, then, since you want it so much. I will tell you.

Iphigenia. A prophet called Calchas: did he come back from Troy?

Orestes. He is dead. That was the story in Mycenae.

Iphigenia. Lady goddess, how good that is. And Odysseus, the son of Laertes?

Orestes. He has not come home yet. But he is alive, they say.

Iphigenia. Let him die. Let him never reach his country.

Orestes. Do not curse him. Everything he has is sick.

Iphigenia. And is the son of Thetis, the Nereid, still living?

Orestes. He is not. The marriage he made at Aulis was for nothing.

Iphigenia. It was a trick. The people it was done to know that.

Orestes. Who are you, anyway? You know exactly what to ask about Greece.

Iphigenia. I am from there. I was lost when I was still a child.

Orestes. Then you have every right to want to know what happened there, woman.

Iphigenia. And the general? The one they say is so fortunate?

Orestes. Which one? The one I knew was not one of the fortunate.

Iphigenia. There was a king, they used to say. Agamemnon, the son of Atreus.

Orestes. I do not know. Leave that subject alone, woman.

Iphigenia. No, by the gods. Tell me, stranger. Let me have the pleasure of it.

Orestes. He is dead. Poor man. And he took somebody else down with him.

Iphigenia. Dead? How? What happened to him? Oh, I am wretched.

Orestes. Why did you groan at that? Was he something to you?

Iphigenia. I am groaning for the good fortune he used to have.

Orestes. Yes. He died horribly. A woman cut his throat.

Iphigenia. Oh, pitiful. Pitiful, the woman who killed him, and the man she killed.

Orestes. Stop now. Do not ask me any more.

Iphigenia. Just this one thing. Is the poor man's wife alive?

Orestes. She is not. The son she bore killed her. He did it.

Iphigenia. Oh, a house turned upside down. What did he want with that?

Orestes. To pay her back for his father's death.

Iphigenia. Ah. How thoroughly he collected the debt. A just thing, and an evil one.

Orestes. Just he may be. The gods have given him no luck for it.

Iphigenia. Did Agamemnon leave any other child in the house?

Orestes. One. Electra. A girl, unmarried.

Iphigenia. And what about the daughter who was sacrificed? Is there any word of her?

Orestes. None. Only that she is dead and does not see the light.

Iphigenia. Poor girl. And the father who killed her, poor man.

Orestes. She died for a worthless woman. A favour that earned no thanks.

Iphigenia. And the dead man's son. Is he in Argos?

Orestes. He is alive. Miserable. Nowhere, and everywhere.

Iphigenia. Lying dreams. Goodbye to you. You were nothing after all.

Orestes. And the gods, the ones people call wise, are no more truthful than dreams with wings. There is a great deal of confusion in the affairs of the gods, and in the affairs of men too. Only one thing really hurts: a man who was no fool listened to what the prophets said, and it destroyed him. How completely, the people who know can tell you.

Chorus. Ah, ah. And what about us? And the parents who bore me? Are they alive? Are they dead? Who could tell us?

Iphigenia. Listen. I have come round to a plan that would help you, strangers, and at the same time help me. A good thing is best of all when the same business pleases everyone. Would you be willing, if I saved your life, to go to Argos and take a message to the people I love there, and to carry a letter? A prisoner wrote it for me, out of pity. He did not think of my hand as the murderer. He thought the goddess's victims die by the law, and that the goddess holds it just. Because I have had nobody who could go back to Argos and take my message, nobody who might be saved and send my letter on to somebody I love. But you: you are not, it seems, my enemy, and you know Mycenae and the people I want you to know. So be saved. And take a reward that is nothing to be ashamed of: your life, for the sake of a little writing. But this man, since the city demands it, must be the goddess's sacrifice, apart from you.

Orestes. That was all well said, stranger, except one thing. For this man to be slaughtered is a heavy weight on me. I am the captain of this voyage of misfortunes; he only sailed with me for the sake of my troubles. So it is not right that I should do you a favour at the price of his death and slip out of trouble myself. No. Do it this way. Give him the letter. He will take it to Argos, and you will have what you want. And me, let anyone who wants to kill me kill me. It is the most shameful thing there is, for a man to throw his friends' lives into disaster and save his own. This man is my friend, and I want him to see the light every bit as much as I want to see it myself.

Iphigenia. What a spirit. What noble root you must have grown from, to be so true a friend to your friends. I hope the one brother I have left is a man like you. Because I am not without a brother either, strangers, except that I do not see him. Since this is what you want, we will send this man with the letter, and you will die. It seems you have a great longing for it.

Orestes. And who will sacrifice me? Who will have the nerve for something so terrible?

Iphigenia. I will. I hold the office of this goddess.

Orestes. No one would envy you that, young woman. No one would call it blessed.

Iphigenia. But I am bound to a necessity, and I have to keep it.

Orestes. You yourself, with a sword? A woman, sacrificing men?

Iphigenia. No. I sprinkle the holy water round your hair.

Orestes. And who does the killing? If I may ask that.

Iphigenia. Inside this temple there are men whose business it is.

Orestes. What sort of grave will take me, when I am dead?

Iphigenia. The holy fire inside, and a wide cleft in the rock.

Orestes. Ah. If only my sister's hand could lay my body out.

Iphigenia. That was a useless prayer, poor man, whoever you are. She lives a long way from this barbarian land. Still, since you happen to be an Argive, I will not leave undone any favour I can do. I will put a great deal of ornament on your grave. I will quench your body with yellow oil, and I will throw onto your pyre the honey of the tawny mountain bee, the gleaming stuff that streams from flowers. Now I will go and bring the letter out of the goddess's temple. Do not hold any of this against me. Guard them, attendants. Without chains. Perhaps I am about to send news nobody hoped for to someone I love in Argos, the one I love most of all, and the letter, telling him that the people he thinks are dead are alive, will bring him a joy he can believe.

(Iphigenia goes into the temple.)

Chorus.
	I mourn for you,
	the one the drops of holy water
	will claim, mixed with blood.
Orestes.
	This is no case for pity. Goodbye to you, strangers.
Chorus.
	And you, young man,
	we honour you for your blessed luck:
	one day you will set foot
	on your own country again.
Pylades.
	No friend would envy it, when his friend is dying.
Chorus.
	Oh, cruel journeys.
	Ah, ah. You are being destroyed.
	Aiai, aiai. Which of you is worse off?
	My mind is still torn two ways, in doubt:
	shall I groan first for you, or for you?

Orestes. Pylades, by the gods, do you feel what I feel?

Pylades. I do not know. You are asking a man who has no answer.

Orestes. Who is that young woman? How Greek her questions were: the labours at Troy, the Achaeans' journey home, Calchas the reader of birds, Achilles by name; and how she pitied poor Agamemnon, and asked me about his wife and children. This stranger is an Argive by birth. She is from there. Otherwise she would never be sending a letter and finding all this out, as if Argos doing well were her own business.

Pylades. You got there a little ahead of me. You have said what I was going to say, except one thing: everyone who has moved about in the world knows what has happened to kings. But I have been going over another thought as well.

Orestes. What? Share it, and you will understand it better yourself.

Pylades. It is shameful for me to go on looking at the light when you are dead. I sailed with you. I ought to die with you. I will be called a coward and a wretch, in Argos and in the folded hills of Phocis. Most people will think, because most people are bad, that I betrayed you and came home alone, saved; or even that I murdered you, while your house was sick, and stitched up your death for the sake of your throne, since I married your sister, the heiress. That is what I am afraid of, and it shames me. There is no way round it. I must breathe my last with you, be slaughtered with you, and have my body burned with yours. I am your friend, and I am afraid of what people would say.

Orestes. Do not talk like that. I have to carry my own troubles, and when the grief could be single I will not carry it double. What you call painful and shameful, that is what it would be for me, if I got you killed, you who have shared every labour with me. As for me, it is no bad thing, doing as badly as I am at the gods' hands, to let go of my life. But you are fortunate. Your house is clean; it is not sick. Mine is impious and unlucky. If you are saved, and get sons from my sister, whom I gave you for a wife, my name would live on, and my father's house would never be wiped out for want of a child. Go. Live. Live in my father's house. And when you come to Greece, and to Argos, the land of horses, by this right hand I charge you: heap up a grave mound for me and set a memorial on it, and let my sister give her tears and her hair to the tomb. Tell them I died at the hand of an Argive woman, at an altar, purified for the slaughter. And never betray my sister, when you see how lonely the house is, my father's house, that you married into.

And goodbye. I found you the dearest of all my friends, you who hunted with me and grew up with me, you who carried so much of the weight of my troubles. Apollo the prophet lied to me. He worked out his scheme and drove me as far from Greece as he could, ashamed of what he had prophesied before. I gave him everything I had, I trusted what he said, I killed my mother, and now I am destroyed in my turn.

Pylades. You will have your grave, and I will never betray your sister's bed, poor friend, since I will hold you dearer dead than I did living. But the god's prophecy has not destroyed you yet, though you are standing very close to the slaughter. There are, there really are, great changes that come out of trouble when the trouble is too great. When luck allows.

Orestes. Quiet. Apollo's words are no help to me. Here is the woman, coming out of the temple.

(Iphigenia comes out of the temple with the letter in her hand.)

Iphigenia. You, go inside and get things ready for the men who are in charge of the slaughter. Here is the letter, strangers, folded, with all its leaves. But listen to what I want as well. No man is the same when he is in trouble and when he has fallen out of fear into confidence. I am afraid that the one who is going to carry this letter to Argos will get away from this country and then count my message as nothing.

Orestes. What do you want, then? What is the difficulty?

Iphigenia. Let him give me his oath that he will ferry this writing to Argos, to the people I want to send it to.

Orestes. And will you give him the same words back?

Iphigenia. To do what, or not do what? Tell me.

Orestes. To send him out of this barbarian land alive.

Iphigenia. That is fair. How else could he deliver it?

Orestes. And will the king agree to it?

Iphigenia. Yes. I will persuade him, and I will put this man aboard the ship myself.

Orestes. Swear, then. And you, lady, lead him in an oath that a god would respect.

Iphigenia. You must say: I will give this to your friends.

Pylades. I will give this letter to your friends.

Iphigenia. And I will bring you safe out past the dark rocks.

Pylades. What god do you swear by, to witness this oath?

Iphigenia. Artemis. I hold my office in her house.

Pylades. And I by the lord of heaven, holy Zeus.

Iphigenia. And if you abandon your oath and wrong me?

Pylades. May I never get home. And you, if you do not save me?

Iphigenia. May I never set foot in Argos alive.

Pylades. Now listen. There is one point we passed over.

Iphigenia. Then let it be a new one. As long as it is good.

Pylades. Grant me this one exception. If something happens to the ship, and the letter goes down in the waves with the cargo, and I save nothing but my own body, then let this oath no longer bind me.

Iphigenia. Do you know what I will do? Many attempts hit many marks. I will tell you in words everything that is in there, written in the folds of the letter, so you can report it to my friends. That way it is safe. If you save the writing, it will tell them what is written in it by itself, silently. And if this writing is lost in the sea, then by saving your body you will save my words.

Pylades. Well said, for the gods' sake and for mine. Tell me who I am to take this letter to, in Argos, and what I am to say, once I have heard it from you.

Iphigenia. Take this message to Orestes, the son of Agamemnon. "The girl who was slaughtered at Aulis sends you this. Iphigenia, alive, though to the people there she is alive no longer."

Orestes. Where is she? Has she come back from the dead?

Iphigenia. The woman you are looking at. Do not confuse me with your talk. "Bring me to Argos, my brother, before I die. Take me away from this barbarian land and from the goddess's sacrifices, where my office is the killing of strangers."

Orestes. Pylades, what am I to say? Where are we? Where have we found ourselves?

Iphigenia. "Or I will be a curse on your house."

Pylades. Orestes?

Iphigenia. Yes. So that you learn the name, hearing it twice.

Pylades. Oh, gods.

Iphigenia. Why are you calling on the gods in my business?

Pylades. No reason. Go on. My mind was somewhere else. If I keep asking you questions I will probably come out at something impossible to believe.

Iphigenia. Tell him that the goddess Artemis saved me. She put a deer in my place; my father sacrificed it, thinking he was driving the sharp sword into me, and she settled me in this country. That is my message. That is what is written in the letter.

Pylades. Oh, what an easy oath you have bound me with. And how beautifully you swore your own. I will not take long. I will make good the oath I swore. Here, Orestes: I bring you a letter, and I hand it over to you, from your sister. This woman here.

Orestes. I take it. And I will let the folds of the letter wait, and take my joy first, not in words. Dearest sister, I am stunned, and still I am going to put my arms round you, arms that cannot believe it, and have my delight, now that I have learned things that astonish me.

(He goes to take her in his arms.)

Chorus. Stranger, you are wrong to pollute the goddess's servant, putting your arm round robes that must not be touched.

Orestes. My own sister, born from the same father, Agamemnon, do not turn away from me. You have your brother, and you never thought you would.

Iphigenia. I have you? My brother? Will you stop talking like that? Argos is full of him, and so is Nauplia.

Orestes. Your brother is not there, poor woman.

Iphigenia. But the Spartan woman, the daughter of Tyndareus, was your mother?

Orestes. And my father was the grandson of Pelops. That is where I come from.

Iphigenia. What are you saying? Do you have any proof of this to give me?

Orestes. I do. Ask me something about our father's house.

Iphigenia. Then you must talk, and I must learn.

Orestes. I will say first what I heard from Electra. You know about the quarrel between Atreus and Thyestes?

Iphigenia. I heard of it. The dispute was over a golden ram.

Orestes. And you know you wove it, in a fine-spun cloth?

Iphigenia. Oh, dearest. You are steering very close to my heart.

Orestes. And the sun, in the middle of the loom, turning back in its course?

Iphigenia. I wove that picture too, in fine threads.

Orestes. And you got the wedding bath from your mother, for Aulis?

Iphigenia. I know. The marriage was not so happy that it took the memory away.

Orestes. And this? You gave your mother a lock of your hair to take home?

Iphigenia. As a memorial to put in a tomb, instead of my body.

Orestes. And now what I have seen myself, I will tell you as proof. Pelops's old spear, in our father's house, the one he shook in his hand when he won Hippodamia, the girl from Pisa, and killed Oenomaus. It was hidden in your rooms, in the girls' quarters.

Iphigenia.
	Oh, dearest. Nothing else: you are the dearest.
	I have you, Orestes, my darling, from far away,
	from our father's country, from Argos, my love.

Orestes. And I have you, the one who was thought dead. Tears, and groaning mixed with joy, are wetting your eyes, and mine the same way.

Iphigenia.
	You were still a baby
	when I left you, tiny in the nurse's arms,
	tiny in the house.
	Oh, my soul, you are luckier than words can say.
	What can I say? This has gone past wonder,
	past anything words can reach.
Orestes.
	From now on, may we be lucky, together.
Iphigenia.
	A joy I have no place for has taken hold of me, my friends.
	I am afraid he will fly out of my hands
	up into the sky and be gone.
	Io, hearth the Cyclopes built. Io, my country,
	Mycenae, my dear,
	I thank you for his life, I thank you for his rearing,
	because you raised this brother for me
	in your house, this light of the family.

Orestes. In our birth we are lucky, sister. In what has happened to us, our life was born unlucky.

Iphigenia.
	I know it, wretched as I am, I know it: when my father,
	with wretchedness in his heart, put the sword to my throat.
Orestes.
	Oh. I was not there, and I think I see you there.
Iphigenia.
	No wedding song, brother, when I was led
	to the tent of Achilles,
	to a marriage bed that was a trick.
	Beside the altar there were tears and groans.
	Ah, ah, for the holy water there.
Orestes.
	I groaned too, for the daring our father dared.
Iphigenia.
	Fatherless, fatherless, the lot I drew.
	One thing comes out of another,
	by the luck some god sends.
Orestes.
	Yes: if you had killed your brother, poor woman.
Iphigenia.
	Oh, wretched, for the terrible thing I dared. Terrible, what I dared,
	terrible, oh, my brother. By a hair
	you escaped an unholy death, cut down
	by my hands.
	And what is the end of all this to be?
	What luck will come my way?
	What road can I find for you,
	to send you back from this city, away from the slaughter,
	to your Argive homeland,
	before the sword comes near your blood?
	This, this is your task, poor soul,
	to find that out.
	By land, not by ship?
	But then, on the rush of your own feet,
	you will come near to death, among barbarian tribes
	and along roads that are no roads. And through the dark
	rocks of the narrow strait it is a long way
	for a ship to run.
	Wretched, wretched woman.
	Who, then, what god, or what mortal, or what
	thing that nobody expects,
	could work a way out where there is no way, and show
	the last two children of Atreus's house
	a release from evil?

Chorus. Among wonders, beyond anything in the stories: I saw this with my own eyes, and I will tell it not as something I heard.

Pylades. When friends come into the sight of friends, Orestes, it is reasonable to throw your arms round each other. But now you must leave off the weeping and come to this: how we are going to win the glorious name of safety and get out of this barbarian land. That is what clever men do. They do not step outside their luck; they seize the moment when it comes, and leave their other pleasures for later.

Orestes. Well said. But I think luck will look after that part, along with us. When a man is eager, the gods' strength is likely to be the greater for it.

Iphigenia. Nothing is going to stop me, nothing is going to keep me from speaking, until I have first found out what lot in life Electra has drawn. You are all dear to me.

Orestes. She lives with this man. She has a happy life.

Iphigenia. And where is he from, and whose son is he?

Orestes. Strophius of Phocis is his father's name.

Iphigenia. Then he is the son of Atreus's daughter. My own kin.

Orestes. A cousin. And my one certain friend.

Iphigenia. He was not born yet when my father killed me.

Orestes. He was not. Strophius was childless for a while.

Iphigenia. Greetings, husband of my sister.

Orestes. And my saviour. Not only a relation.

Iphigenia. But that terrible business with our mother. How did you have the nerve?

Orestes. Let us say nothing about it. I was avenging my father.

Iphigenia. And her reason? Why did she kill her husband?

Orestes. Leave our mother's affairs alone. It is not good for you to hear them either.

Iphigenia. I am silent. And does Argos look to you now?

Orestes. Menelaus rules there. I am an exile from my country.

Iphigenia. Surely our uncle has not done our sick house an outrage?

Orestes. No. It is fear of the Furies that drives me out of the land.

Iphigenia. That was the madness they reported, on the shore here?

Orestes. It is not the first time I have been seen in my misery.

Iphigenia. I understand. The goddesses were hounding you, for our mother.

Orestes. To force a bloody bit between my teeth.

Iphigenia. And why did you ferry your steps to this land?

Orestes. I came at the command of Apollo's oracles.

Iphigenia. To do what? Can it be spoken, or must it be kept silent?

Orestes. I will tell you. This is where my many labours began. When my mother's evil, the evil we are keeping silent about, came into my hands, I was driven into exile, hounded by relay after relay of Furies, until Apollo sent my steps to Athens, to stand trial before the goddesses who are not to be named. There is a holy court there, which Zeus once set up for Ares when his hands were polluted with a killing.

I went there. At first not one host would take me in willingly; I was a man the gods hated. Then some who felt ashamed set out a guest's table for me, a table by myself, under the same roof as themselves but apart, and by their silence they built a wall round me so that I could not speak, so that I would be separate from them in food and in drink; and they filled a separate cup for every man there with an equal measure of wine, and enjoyed themselves. And I did not think it right to call my hosts to account. I suffered in silence and pretended not to notice, groaning deep down because I was my mother's murderer. I hear that my misfortune has become a festival at Athens, and that the custom still stands: the people of Pallas honour the cup of the Feast of Pitchers.

Then when I came to the hill of Ares I stood my trial. I took one platform, and the eldest of the Furies took the other. I spoke, and I heard the case against me, about my mother's blood, and Apollo saved me by giving evidence, and Pallas counted out the votes with her arm, equal on both sides, and I left the trial for murder a winner. Those Furies who sat there and were persuaded by the verdict marked out a holy place for themselves right beside the court. But those who were not persuaded by the law hounded me on and on, in a chase that never settled, until I came again to Apollo's holy ground and stretched myself out in front of his inner shrine, fasting, and swore that I would break off my life and die there if Apollo, who had destroyed me, did not save me. Then Apollo cried out a voice from the golden tripod and sent me here, to take the statue that fell from the sky and set it up in the land of Athens.

So help me to the safety he marked out for me. If we get hold of the goddess's image, I will be free of my madness, and I will put you aboard my ship with its many oars and settle you back in Mycenae. Sister, my love, my own sister, save our father's house, and save me. Because I am finished, all of me, and the whole line of Pelops with me, unless we take the goddess's image that came down from heaven.

Chorus. Some terrible anger of the gods has boiled up against the seed of Tantalus and drives them through labour after labour.

Iphigenia. The wish was mine before you ever came here, to be in Argos and to see you, brother. I want what you want: to release you from your labours and set our father's sick house upright again. I hold no anger against the man who killed me. I want it. It would take my hand out of your slaughter, and it would save our house. But how am I to hide it from the goddess, and from the king, when he finds the stone base standing empty with no statue on it? That is what I am afraid of. How can I not be killed? What excuse could I have? But if the one thing happens, if it all happens together, and you carry off the statue and take me away on your fine ship, then the risk is a fine one. If I am cut off from that, then I am lost, but you might settle your own business well and get home. Not that I am running from it. Not even if I have to die to save you. No. When a man dies and is gone from a house, he is missed. A woman is a weak thing.

Orestes. I will not be your murderer as well as my mother's. Her blood is enough. I want to be of one mind with you, and either live with you or, dying, share the same lot. I will take you home, if I get out of here myself, or I will die and stay here with you. But listen to my judgement. If this were against Artemis's will, how could Apollo have prophesied that I would bring the goddess's statue to Pallas's city, and see your face? Putting all of that together into one, I have hope that we will get home.

Iphigenia. Then how can we arrange it so that we do not die, and still get what we want? That is where our journey home is sick. The wanting is there.

Orestes. Could we kill the king?

Iphigenia. That is a terrible thing to say. Strangers who have landed in a country, murdering the man who rules it.

Orestes. But if it will save you and me, we have to risk it.

Iphigenia. I could not do it. But I admire the spirit.

Orestes. What if you hid me secretly in the temple?

Iphigenia. So that we could take the dark and slip away?

Orestes. Night belongs to thieves. The light belongs to truth.

Iphigenia. There are temple guards inside. We would never get past them.

Orestes. Oh. Then we are finished. How can we be saved?

Iphigenia. I think I have found something. Something new.

Orestes. What kind of thing? Share the idea, so I can learn it too.

Iphigenia. I am going to use your sufferings as my trick.

Orestes. Women are terribly good at inventing schemes.

Iphigenia. I will say that you have come from Argos, and that you killed your mother.

Orestes. Use my troubles, if you can make a profit on them.

Iphigenia. And that it is not lawful to sacrifice you to the goddess.

Orestes. On what grounds? I have a suspicion.

Iphigenia. Because you are not clean. Their sense of what is holy I will turn into fear.

Orestes. And how does that get us any nearer to taking the goddess's image?

Iphigenia. I will say I want to wash you clean in the springs of the sea.

Orestes. The statue we sailed here for is still inside the house.

Iphigenia. I will say that has to be washed too, because you touched it.

Orestes. Where? Do you mean the wet inlet where the sea runs out?

Iphigenia. Where your ship rides at anchor on its linen cables.

Orestes. And will you carry the image in your own hands, or someone else?

Iphigenia. I will. I am the only one who may touch it.

Orestes. And Pylades here, where does he fit into our labour?

Iphigenia. He will be said to carry the same pollution on his hands as you do.

Orestes. Will you do all this behind the king's back, or with his knowledge?

Iphigenia. I will talk him into it. I could never hide it from him.

Orestes. Well, the ship is there, and her oars are ready to strike.

Iphigenia. The rest is yours to see to. Make sure it goes well.

Orestes. One thing more is needed: these women have to keep the secret with us. Go to them and find the words that will persuade them. A woman has power when it comes to pity. As for the rest, perhaps. May it all turn out well.

Iphigenia. My dearest women, I am looking to you. Everything I am is in your hands now: whether I come through this, or become nothing and lose my country, and my dear brother, and my dearest sister. Let me begin what I have to say with this. We are women, a race that loves its own kind, and there is nobody safer at keeping a common secret safe. Keep silent for us, and work with us for our escape. A tongue that can be trusted is a fine thing for the one who has it.

You see how one fortune holds three people who love each other more than anyone: either we reach our fathers' land, or we die. And if I am saved, you will share my fortune. I will bring you safely home to Greece. So I beg you, by your right hand, and you, and you; you by your dear cheek, and you by your knees, and by everything you love at home, mother and father and children, whoever has them. What do you say? Which of you says yes to this, and which of you is not willing? Speak. If you do not agree to what I ask, I am destroyed, and my poor brother with me.

Chorus. Take heart, dear mistress. Only save yourself. Everything you charge us with will be kept silent, as far as I am concerned. Great Zeus be my witness.

Iphigenia. May you have joy of those words, and be happy. Now it is your work, and yours, to go into the house. The ruler of this land will be here any moment, to check whether the strangers' sacrifice has been done.

Lady, you who saved me in the terrible clefts of Aulis from my father's murdering hand, save me now too, and these men. Or else, because of you, mortals will never again believe that Apollo's mouth tells the truth. Come away kindly from this barbarian land to Athens. It is not right for you to live here, when a happy city is yours to have.

(Orestes and Pylades go into the temple. Iphigenia follows them.)

Chorus.
	Bird by the rocky ridges of the sea,
	halcyon, sea-kingfisher,
	who sing your fate as a lament,
	a cry the wise understand,
	always calling in your songs for your husband:
	I set my own dirges beside yours,
	a bird without wings,
	longing for the gatherings of Greece,
	longing for Artemis who helps women in childbirth,
	who lives by the Cynthian hill on Delos,
	by the palm with its soft leaves
	and the strong young laurel
	and the holy shoot of the grey-green olive,
	the tree Leto held when her pains came,
	and the lake that rolls its water round in a ring,
	where the singing swan
	serves the Muses.
Chorus.
	Oh, the streams of tears
	that fell on my cheeks
	when the towers came down and I went
	in the enemy's ships, among oars and spears.
	Bought and sold for gold,
	I came to a barbarian home,
	where I serve the girl who attends
	the goddess who kills the deer,
	Agamemnon's daughter, and altars
	where it is not sheep that die,
	and I envy the woman whose luck was bad
	from the start: if you grow up in hardship
	you do not tire under it.
	Bad luck changes.
	It is being brought low after happiness
	that is a heavy life for mortals.
Chorus.
	And you, lady, the Argive ship
	with its fifty oars will carry home.
	The wax-bound reed of Pan of the mountains
	will whistle and call the time to the rowers,
	and Apollo the prophet, with the ring
	of his seven-stringed lyre,
	will sing you all the way
	to the shining land of the Athenians.
	You will leave me here
	and go with the oars splashing.
	In the breeze the forestays will spread
	the sail's foot over the prow, past the beak
	of the fast ship.
Chorus.
	If only I could walk the bright race-course
	where the fire of the sun goes,
	and over the rooms of my own home
	fold the wings on my back
	and stop beating them.
	If only I could stand in the dances again,
	where I stood as a girl at glorious weddings,
	whirling beside my dear mother's feet
	with the bands of girls my own age,
	rising up to the contest of grace,
	the rich rivalry of hair,
	and shadowed my cheeks
	with my many-coloured veil
	and the curls I wound about them.

(Thoas comes in with his attendants.)

Thoas. Where is the woman who keeps the gate of this house, the Greek? Has she begun the rite on the strangers yet? Are their bodies blazing in the fire in the holy inner room?

Chorus. Here she is, my lord. She will tell you everything plainly.

(Iphigenia comes out of the temple with the image of the goddess in her arms.)

Thoas. Ah. Daughter of Agamemnon, why are you lifting the goddess's image in your arms, off the base it is never moved from?

Iphigenia. My lord, stop where you are. Stay in the doorway.

Thoas. What is it, Iphigenia? What is new in the house?

Iphigenia. I spit it out. Pollution. That word I give to Holiness, the goddess.

Thoas. What is this strange opening of yours? Say it plainly.

Iphigenia. The victims you caught for me are not clean, my lord.

Thoas. What taught you that? Or are you just telling me your opinion?

Iphigenia. The goddess's image turned round on its base and faced the other way.

Thoas. By itself? Or did an earthquake turn it?

Iphigenia. By itself. And it closed its eyes.

Thoas. And the cause? Was it the filth on the strangers?

Iphigenia. That, and nothing else. They have done terrible things.

Thoas. What, did they kill one of our barbarians on the shore?

Iphigenia. They came here with a murder from home already on them.

Thoas. What murder? I want to know. I have fallen in love with knowing.

Iphigenia. They cut their mother down. The two of them, with one sword.

Thoas. Apollo. Not even among barbarians would anyone have dared that.

Iphigenia. They have been hunted and driven out of the whole of Greece.

Thoas. And is that why you are carrying the image outside?

Iphigenia. Yes, under the holy open sky, to move it away from the blood.

Thoas. How did you find out the strangers' pollution?

Iphigenia. I questioned them, when the goddess's image turned its back.

Thoas. Greece has brought you up clever. How well you saw it.

Iphigenia. And yet they dangled a sweet bait for my heart.

Thoas. Bringing you some charm of news from Argos?

Iphigenia. That Orestes, my only brother, is doing well.

Thoas. So that you would save them, for the pleasure of their news.
