Iphigenia. And that my father is alive and prospering.

Thoas. But you swam back to the goddess's side, and rightly.

Iphigenia. Yes. I hate all Greece. It destroyed me.

Thoas. Then what do we do about the strangers? Tell me.

Iphigenia. We are bound to respect the law as it stands.

Thoas. Then why are the holy water and your sword not at work?

Iphigenia. First I want to wash them clean, with a holy purification.

Thoas. In spring water, or the spray of the sea?

Iphigenia. The sea washes away all the evils of mankind.

Thoas. They would certainly fall holier for the goddess that way.

Iphigenia. And my own business would go better that way too.

Thoas. But does the surf not break against the temple itself?

Iphigenia. It needs solitude. There are other things we have to do as well.

Thoas. Take them wherever you want. I have no wish to see what may not be seen.

Iphigenia. The goddess's image must be purified too.

Thoas. Yes, if the stain of a mother's blood has fallen on it.

Iphigenia. I would never have lifted it off its base otherwise.

Thoas. Your piety is right, and so is your forethought.

Iphigenia. Now, do you know what I need done?

Thoas. It is for you to tell me.

Iphigenia. Put chains on the strangers.

Thoas. Where could they run from you?

Iphigenia. Greece knows nothing about keeping faith.

Thoas. Go and fetch chains, attendants.

Iphigenia. And have them bring the strangers out here.

Thoas. It will be done.

Iphigenia. With their heads covered in their robes.

Thoas. Out of the sun's blaze.

Iphigenia. And send some of your servants with me.

Thoas. These men will go with you.

Iphigenia. And send someone to the city to announce...

Thoas. Announce what?

Iphigenia. That everyone is to stay indoors.

Thoas. So that they do not run into the murder?

Iphigenia. Yes. Things like this are polluting.

Thoas. You. Go and announce it.

Iphigenia. That nobody is to come near the sight.

Thoas. You take good care of the city.

Iphigenia. And of the friends I owe the most to.

Thoas. You mean me by that.

Thoas. The whole city admires you, and it has good reason.

Iphigenia. And you, stay here in front of the temple, and for the goddess...

Thoas. Do what?

Iphigenia. Purify the house with a torch.

Thoas. So that it is clean when you come back.

Iphigenia. And when the strangers come out through the door...

Thoas. What must I do?

Iphigenia. Hold your robe in front of your eyes.

Thoas. So that I do not take the killer's stain.

Iphigenia. And if I seem to be taking too long...

Thoas. How long should I allow?

Iphigenia. Do not be surprised at anything.

Thoas. Do the goddess's business well. There is no hurry.

Iphigenia. If only this purification would fall out as I want it.

Thoas. I pray for that with you.

(Orestes and Pylades are brought out of the temple by the guards, in chains, their heads covered, with attendants carrying lambs and torches.)

Iphigenia. Here they come, the strangers, out of the house now, and the goddess's ornaments, and the new-born lambs, so that I can wash polluted blood away with blood, and the blaze of the torches, and everything else I set out to purify the strangers and the goddess. I proclaim to the citizens: keep clear of this pollution. Any keeper of the temple who keeps his hands clean for the gods, anyone on his way to make a marriage, any woman heavy with a child: run, stand back, so that this filth does not fall on anyone.

Lady, virgin daughter of Zeus and Leto, if I wash the blood off these men and make the sacrifice where it should be made, you will live in a clean house, and we will be fortunate. The rest I do not say. But I signal it to the gods, who know more, and to you, goddess.

(Iphigenia goes out toward the shore, carrying the image, with the prisoners and Thoas's men behind her. Thoas goes into the temple.)

Chorus.
	A fine child, the son of Leto,
	whom the Delian mother bore once
	in the fruitful valleys, golden-haired,
	clever with the lyre; and with him the sister
	who glories in the true aim of her arrows.
	And the mother left the famous place of her labour
	and carried him from the ridge by the sea
	to the peak of Parnassus, with its rushing waters,
	where the dances run wild for Dionysus.
	There the wine-dark serpent
	with the dappled back,
	armoured in bronze under the shady, leafy laurel,
	the earth's enormous monster,
	kept guard over the oracle of Earth.
	Still a baby, still a baby, still leaping
	in your dear mother's arms,
	you killed him, Apollo, and stepped into the holy oracle,
	and you sit on the golden tripod, on the throne that never lies,
	dealing out to mortals the prophecies the gods send,
	up from the inner shrine, neighbour of Castalia's streams,
	holding the house at the centre of the earth.
Chorus.
	But when he came and drove Themis,
	the daughter of Earth, away from the holy oracle of Pytho,
	Earth gave birth to phantoms, dreams of the night,
	which told the cities of men
	what had been, and what came after,
	and everything that was going to happen,
	in the dark beds of sleep on the ground.
	So Earth took the honour of prophecy
	away from Apollo, out of jealousy for her daughter.
	And the lord ran fast to Olympus
	and wound his baby arm round the throne of Zeus,
	to have the earth-goddess's anger lifted
	from the Pythian house, and the night voices silenced.
	And Zeus laughed, that the child had come so quickly
	wanting the worship that pays in gold.
	He shook his hair, and the voices of the night stopped,
	and he took away from mortals
	the truth that shows its face in the dark,
	and gave the honours back to Apollo,
	and to mortals confidence in the songs of prophecy
	at the throne where so many strangers come.

(A Messenger, one of the king's men, runs in from the shore.)

Messenger. You, guards of the temple, you who stand by the altar, where has Thoas, the lord of this land, gone? Open the well-bolted gates and call the ruler of the country out of this house.

Chorus. What is it, if I may speak without being told to?

Messenger. The two young men are gone. Away. By the plotting of Agamemnon's daughter they are escaping from this country, and they have the holy image with them, in the hold of a Greek ship.

Chorus. That is an unbelievable story. But the man you want to see, the lord of this country, has left the temple in a hurry.

Messenger. Where? He has to know what is being done.

Chorus. We do not know. But go and chase after him, and wherever you find him, give him your news.

Messenger. Look at that. What a faithless race you women are. You have your share in what has been done as well.

Chorus. You are out of your mind. What do we have to do with the strangers' escape? Go to the king's door, as fast as you can.

Messenger. No. Not until this interpreter tells me the word: is the ruler of the land inside, or is he not? Hey there. Undo the bolts, I am talking to you inside, and tell the master I am at the gates with a cargo of fresh bad news.

(Thoas comes out of the temple.)

Thoas. Who is raising this shouting round the goddess's house, hammering on the gates and sending the noise inside?

Messenger. Ah. These women told me you had gone out, and they were driving me away from the house. And you were inside all along.

Thoas. What profit were they expecting? What were they hunting?

Messenger. I will explain about them later. Hear what is at your feet now. The young woman who stood at these altars, Iphigenia, has gone out of the country with the strangers, and she has the goddess's holy image with her. The purification was a fraud.

Thoas. What are you saying? What wind of fortune got into her?

Messenger. She is saving Orestes. That will amaze you.

Thoas. Which Orestes? The one the daughter of Tyndareus bore?

Messenger. The one the goddess had consecrated to herself at these altars.

Thoas. A wonder. What bigger name can I find for it?

Messenger. Do not turn your mind to that. Listen to me. Look at it clearly, hear it out, and then think out a pursuit that will hunt the strangers down.

Thoas. Speak. You are right. It is no short crossing they are running for, no voyage that will get them out of range of my spear.

Messenger. When we came to the shore of the sea, where Orestes's ship had been moored out of sight, Agamemnon's daughter signalled to us, the men you sent along holding the strangers' chains, to stand well back, as if she were about to make the secret fire-sacrifice and the purification she had come for. And she went on alone behind them, holding the two strangers' chains in her hands. It looked suspicious, my lord. But your servants let it pass.

After a while, so that we would think she was doing something, she raised the ritual cry, and chanted barbarian songs, working her witchcraft, as if she were really washing away the murder. When we had been sitting a long time, it came into our minds that the strangers might have got loose, killed her, and run for it. But we were afraid of seeing what we were not supposed to see, and we sat still and kept quiet. In the end we all said the same thing: go to where they were, whether we were allowed or not.

And there we saw the hull of a Greek ship, winged with the oar-blades fitted along her sides ready for the stroke, and fifty sailors at the tholes with their oars in their hands, and the two young men standing free of their chains at the stern. Some were holding the bow steady with poles. Others were hauling the anchor up to the cat-heads. Others were running the stern-cables through their hands and hurrying to let down the ladders and drop them into the sea for the strangers.

We did not spare ourselves. When we saw the trick they had worked, we grabbed the woman and the stern-cables, and we tried to pull the steering-oars out through the sockets of that fine stern. And words went back and forth. "What right have you to carry off images and priestesses, stealing them out of this land? Whose son are you? Who are you, to smuggle this woman out of the country?" And he said, "Orestes, her brother, so you know it. The son of Agamemnon. I am taking my sister home, the sister I lost from my house." But we held on to the woman just the same, and were trying to force her to come with us to you. And that is where the terrible blows to my face came from. They had no iron in their hands, and neither did we. But there were fists, pounding, and the two young men's legs came at us together, kicking at our ribs and our livers, so that the moment we got to grips with them our limbs were done for. Stamped with terrible marks, we ran for the cliff, some with bloody wounds on their heads, some in their eyes. When we stood on the heights we fought more carefully, and threw rocks. But there were archers standing on the stern who kept us off with their arrows and drove us further back.

And then a terrible swell ran the ship aground towards the land, and the girl was afraid to wet her feet. So Orestes took her on his left shoulder, walked into the sea, jumped onto the ladder, and set his sister down inside that well-marked ship, with the thing that fell out of the sky, the image of the daughter of Zeus. And from the middle of the ship a voice shouted, "Sailors of Greece, take hold of the ship with your oars and whiten the surf. We have what we sailed through the unfriendly strait for, in past the Clashing Rocks." And they gave a deep, glad groan, and struck the salt water.

The ship, while she was inside the harbour, made for the mouth. But as she was crossing out she met a violent swell and was thrown hard, because a terrible wind came up all at once and drove the sails back stern-first. The men held on, kicking against the wave. But the swell, running back, was carrying the ship towards the land again. And Agamemnon's daughter stood up and prayed. "Daughter of Leto, bring me, your priestess, safe to Greece out of this barbarian land, and forgive me my thefts. You love your brother too, goddess. Believe that I love my own blood as well." And the sailors answered the girl's prayer with the Healer's hymn, and set their shoulders, bare out of their clothes, to the oar at the word of command. But nearer and nearer to the rocks the hull kept going. One man jumped into the sea, another was making loops of rope fast.

And I was sent straight off here to you, my lord, to tell you what has happened down there. Go. Take chains and nooses in your hands. Unless the swell goes calm, there is no hope of safety for the strangers. Holy Poseidon, the lord of the sea, watches over Troy, and he is the enemy of the house of Pelops. Now, it seems, he will give the son of Agamemnon into your hands, and the people's, and his sister with him, the woman who forgot the slaughter at Aulis, and betrayed the goddess, and is caught.

Chorus. Poor Iphigenia. You will die with your brother, if you come back into your masters' hands.

Thoas. All you citizens of this barbarian land, go on, throw the reins on your horses. Ride along the coast and take whatever the Greek ship throws up. Hurry, with the goddess beside you, and hunt down these godless men. And the rest of you, drag the fast ships down to the sea. By sea, and by land on horseback, we will take them, and throw them down the rough rock, or fix their bodies on stakes.

And you women, who knew about these plots, I will punish you later, when I have the time. Now, with this business in front of us, we will not sit still.

(Athena appears above the temple.)

Athena. Where, where are you carrying this pursuit, lord Thoas? Listen to the words of Athena. I am here. Stop hunting them. Stop pouring out this flood of an army. Orestes came here because Apollo's oracles ordained it, running from the anger of the Furies, to bring his sister home to Argos and carry the holy image to my land, and so find a breathing space from the sufferings he has now. That is my word to you. And Orestes, whom you think you will catch in the sea's swell and kill: Poseidon, as a favour to me, is already making the sea's back smooth and waveless for his oars to cross.

And you, Orestes, learn my orders, because you can hear the goddess's voice even where you are. Go, and take the image and your sister with you. When you come to Athens, the city the gods built, there is a place at the farthest borders of the Attic land, next to the ridge of Carystus across the water, a holy place, and my people call it Halae. Build a temple there and set the image up in it, and let it carry the name of the Taurian land, and of the labours you toiled through, wandering all over Greece under the Furies' goads. From now on mortals will sing hymns to her there as Artemis Tauropolos, the goddess of the Taurians. And lay down this law: whenever the people keep her festival, in payment for your slaughter let a sword be held to a man's throat, and let blood be drawn, so that holiness is satisfied and the goddess keeps her honours.

And you, Iphigenia, must keep the keys for this goddess on the holy steps of Brauron. There you will die, and there you will be buried, and they will dedicate to you, as an ornament, the fine-woven robes that women who die in childbirth leave behind in their houses. And I charge you to send these Greek women out of this land, because their judgement was right. I saved you once before, Orestes, on the hill of Ares, when I judged the votes equal. And that will be the custom from now on: whoever gets an equal count of votes wins. Now take your sister out of this country, son of Agamemnon. And you, Thoas, do not be angry.

Thoas. Lady Athena, whoever hears the words of the gods and does not believe them is not thinking straight. I am not angry with Orestes for going off with the goddess's image, or with his sister. What good is there in wrestling with the gods, who have the strength? Let them go to your land with the goddess's image, and let them set it up there, and good luck to them. I will send these women too to happy Greece, as your command lays it on me. And I will lower the spear I was raising against the strangers, and the ships' oars, since that is how you judge it, goddess.

Athena. Good. Necessity rules you, and it rules the gods too. Go, winds, carry the son of Agamemnon over the sea to Athens. I will travel with them, and keep my sister's holy image safe.

Chorus.
	Go, and be happy in your luck,
	in the destiny that has saved you.
	Pallas Athena, holy among the immortals
	and holy among mortals,
	we will do as you command.
	For the news that has come to my ears
	is glad beyond anything I hoped.
	Great Victory, holy one,
	stay with me all my life,
	and never stop crowning me.

Ion (c. 413 BC)

Ion

(Delphi, in front of the temple of Apollo. It is not yet light. Hermes comes in.)

Hermes. Atlas, who wears down the sky, that old house of the gods, on his bronze back, fathered Maia on one of the goddesses, and Maia bore me, Hermes, to great Zeus, to run the gods' errands. I have come to this country, Delphi, where Apollo sits on the navel of the world and sings to mortals, forever telling them what is and what is coming. There is a city in Greece that is not without a name, the city called after Pallas Athena of the golden spear. There Apollo took Creusa, the daughter of Erechtheus, by force, under the hill of Pallas in the land of Athens, at the rocks that face north, the ones the lords of Attica call the Long Rocks, the Macrae. Her father never knew. The god wanted it that way. She carried the weight in her belly to term, and when her time came she gave birth to a boy in the house, and then she carried the baby out to the same cave where the god had bedded her, and she put him out there to die, in the rounded hollow of a cradle, keeping an old custom of her ancestors and of Erichthonius, who was born from the earth. When Athena, the daughter of Zeus, gave that child to the daughters of Aglaurus to keep safe, she set two snakes beside him to guard his body, and that is why the descendants of Erechtheus still have a custom of raising their children with snakes of beaten gold. But Creusa tied what finery a girl had on her baby, and left him to die.

Then Apollo, who is my brother, asked me this. "Brother, go to the people who grew out of the soil of famous Athens, you know the goddess's city, and take a newborn baby out of a hollow rock, cradle and swaddling clothes and all, and bring him to my oracle at Delphi, and set him down right at the entrance to my house. The rest, because the boy is mine, you should know that, will be my business." So I did my brother Apollo the favour. I picked up the woven cradle and brought it here, and I set the boy down on the steps of this temple, and I opened the lid of the curved wicker cradle, so the child could be seen.

And it happened that just as the sun's chariot was setting out on its round, the priestess was going into the god's shrine. Her eye fell on the little baby, and she was amazed that any girl of Delphi would have the nerve to throw the child of a secret labour into the god's house, and she was all for putting him out beyond the altar. But pity got the better of her hardness, and the god was working alongside her, so that his child would not be thrown out of his own house, and she took him up and raised him. She does not know that Apollo fathered him, or who the mother was, and the boy does not know his parents either. While he was small he wandered and played round the altars that fed him, and when his body grew to a man's, the Delphians made him keeper of the god's gold and trusted steward of everything, and he lives here in the god's halls to this day, a holy life.

Creusa, meanwhile, the young man's mother, is married to Xuthus, and this is how that came about. A wave of war broke between Athens and the people of Chalcodon, who hold the land of Euboea. Xuthus fought it through with the Athenians and helped them win it with his spear, and his reward was the honour of marrying Creusa, though he was not Athenian-born but an Achaean, a son of Aeolus, who was a son of Zeus. He has been sowing that marriage bed for years and has no child, and neither has Creusa. That is why they have come here, to this oracle of Apollo: they want children. And Apollo is driving their luck to this point. Nothing has escaped him, whatever people think. When Xuthus goes into this oracle, the god will give him his own son and say the boy is Xuthus's, so that the boy can go to his mother's house and be known to Creusa, and Apollo's bed stays a secret, and the boy gets what is coming to him. And he will see to it that all Greece calls the boy Ion, the founder of a country in Asia.

But I will step into this laurel grove and find out what is decided about the boy. I can see Apollo's son coming out now, to make the doorway in front of the temple bright with sprigs of laurel. And the name he is about to have, Ion: I am the first of the gods to call him by it.

(Hermes hides among the laurels. Ion comes out of the temple with a broom made of laurel branches and a bow over his shoulder. Temple servants follow him out.)

Ion.
	Here it comes, the bright chariot and the four horses:
	the Sun is already shining down on the earth,
	and the stars are running from this fire in the sky
	into holy night.
	The peaks of Parnassus, where nobody may walk,
	are catching the light, and taking the first arch of day
	on behalf of mortals.
	The smoke of dry myrrh flies up
	to the roof of Apollo.
	The woman of Delphi sits on the holy tripod,
	singing out to the Greeks whatever cries
	Apollo sounds in her.
	But you, Delphians, servants of Apollo,
	go down to the silver swirl of Castalia,
	wash yourselves in its clean dew,
	and then walk up to the temple.
	Guard your mouths. Say nothing of bad omen.
	Give a good word from your own tongues
	to the people who want to ask the god a question.
	And I will do the work I have done since I was a child,
	the work I never stop doing. With sprigs of laurel
	and holy garlands I will make Apollo's doorway clean,
	and wet the floor with drops of water,
	and the flocks of birds
	that foul the sacred offerings
	I will put to flight with my bow.
	Because I was born with no mother and no father,
	and it is the temple of Apollo I serve,
	the temple that brought me up.
Ion.
	Come, fresh-grown shoot
	of the most beautiful laurel,
	come and do your service to the god.
	You sweep the altar of Apollo under his temple.
	You come from gardens that never die,
	where holy dews are always wetting
	the sacred foliage of the myrtle,
	sending out a stream from a spring that never fails.
	With you I sweep the god's floor
	all day long, from the moment the sun
	lifts its swift wing,
	my service, every day.
	Healer, Healer,
	be blessed, be blessed,
	son of Leto.
Ion.
	It is fine work I do for you, Apollo,
	here in front of your house,
	honouring the seat of your prophecy.
	And it is a glorious thing to me, this work,
	to give my hands as a slave gives them, to gods,
	not to mortals, but to the deathless ones.
	I never tire of working
	at work that is holy.
	Apollo is my father. It was Apollo who begot me,
	because I bless the one who feeds me,
	and it is that helpful name, father,
	that I give to Apollo, who lives in the temple.
	Healer, Healer,
	be blessed, be blessed,
	son of Leto.
Ion.
	But now I will let the laurel broom rest,
	and from golden jugs I will fling out
	the spring water of Earth,
	the water the eddies of Castalia
	pour down. I throw the wet drops
	and I am clean: no one has ever shared my bed.
	Let me go on serving Apollo like this forever,
	and never stop, or stop only when my luck is good.
	Ah. Ah.
	Here they come already, the birds,
	leaving their beds on Parnassus.
	I am telling you, do not come near the cornices,
	do not go into the golden house.
	I will catch you with my arrows again, herald of Zeus,
	you who beat the strength of every other bird
	with those hooked claws.
	Here is another one rowing towards the altar,
	a swan. Will you not take
	those red feet somewhere else?
	Apollo's lyre, that sings along with your song,
	will never save you from my bow.
	Turn your wings aside.
	Go and settle on the lake at Delos.
	If you do not do as I say, you will bleed,
	and your beautiful songs will end in blood.
	Ah. Ah.
	What is this? A new bird coming?
	Are you going to build a nest of dry straw for your chicks
	under the eaves?
	The twang of my bowstring will keep you off.
	Will you not listen? Go and raise your young
	in the swirling water of the river Alpheus,
	or in the wooded valley at the Isthmus,
	so that the offerings and Apollo's temple
	come to no harm.
	I hate to kill you.
	You carry the gods' messages to mortals.
	But I am bound to my work.
	I will slave for Apollo, and I will never stop
	serving the ones who feed me.

(The Chorus, Creusa's Athenian serving women, come in as sightseers, and go from sculpture to sculpture on the temple front.)

Chorus.
	So it is not only in holy Athens
	that the gods have courtyards with fine columns,
	and the god of the roadways gets his worship.
	Here too, at the house of Apollo, Leto's son,
	the two faces of the temple
	shine with the light of beautiful eyes.
	Look at this one. Look:
	the son of Zeus is killing the water snake of Lerna
	with a golden sickle.
	Look at it, my dear, with your own eyes.
Chorus.
	I see it. And next to him another man
	is lifting a blazing torch.
	Is it the one whose story I weave at my loom,
	Iolaus with his shield,
	who took up the labours alongside the son of Zeus
	and bore them with him?
	And look at this one too,
	the man on the winged horse.
	He is killing the fire-breathing thing
	with the three bodies.
Chorus.
	I am chasing my eyes everywhere.
	Look at the battle of the Giants
	on the stone walls.
	We are looking, friends, right here.
	Do you see her, then, over Enceladus,
	shaking her shield with the Gorgon's face on it?
	I see Pallas, my own goddess.
	And what about this? The thunderbolt, fire at both ends,
	heavy, in the far-shooting hands of Zeus?
	I see it. He is burning Mimas, his enemy, to ash.
	And Dionysus is killing another of Earth's children
	with his staff of ivy,
	a stick that was never made for war.
Chorus.
	You there, by the temple. I am talking to you.
	Is it allowed to step inside the shrine,
	with our white feet?
Ion.
	It is not allowed, strangers.
Chorus.
	Could we have a word from you, then,
	and ask you something?
Ion.
	What is it you want?
Chorus.
	Is it true that the house of Apollo
	really holds the very navel of the earth?
Ion.
	It does. Wrapped in garlands, with Gorgons all round it.
Chorus.
	That is what people say, too.
Ion.
	If you have offered the holy cake in front of the house
	and there is something you want to ask Apollo,
	come up to the altar. But do not go
	into the inner house unless sheep have been slaughtered.
Chorus.
	I understand. We will not step over
	the god's law.
	What is outside will be a feast for the eyes.
Ion.
	Look at everything your eyes are allowed to see.
Chorus.
	Our masters let me come
	and look at these shrines of the god.
Ion.
	And whose house do you belong to? Whose slaves are you called?
Chorus.
	The house that raised the lords I serve
	shares its roof with Pallas.
	But the one you are asking about is here herself.

(Creusa comes in. She stops at the sight of the temple, in tears.)

Ion. There is breeding in you, and the way you carry yourself is proof of your character, whoever you are, lady. You can usually tell about a person, whether they were born well, just by looking at how they hold themselves. Oh, but you have startled me. You shut your eyes, and your well-bred cheek is wet with tears, the moment you saw Apollo's holy oracle. What is it, lady, that has brought you to this point of worry? Everyone else who looks at the god's shrine is glad. And here your eye is streaming.

Creusa. Stranger, there is nothing ill-bred in your surprise at my tears. When I saw this house of Apollo, I measured out an old memory all over again, and my mind was at home, though I am standing here. Poor women. Poor us. And the gods, and the things they have the nerve to do. What then? Where are we to take our case for justice, if it is the injustice of the ones in power that destroys us?

Ion. What is this, lady? Why so low, over something you will not explain?

Creusa. Nothing. I have shot my arrow, and that is all. About the rest I say nothing, and you stop thinking about it.

Ion. Who are you? Where have you come from? What country were you born in? What name should we call you by?

Creusa. My name is Creusa. I am the daughter of Erechtheus, and my country is the city of Athens.

Ion. A famous city to live in, and noble fathers to be raised by. How I admire you, lady.

Creusa. That is as far as my luck goes, stranger. No further.

Ion. By the gods, is it true, the story mortals tell?

Creusa. What are you asking, stranger? What do you want to know?

Ion. Your father's grandfather grew out of the earth?

Creusa. Erichthonius did, yes. My family is no help to me.

Ion. And Athena really lifted him up out of the ground?

Creusa. Into the hands of unmarried girls, yes. She had not given birth to him.

Ion. And she handed him over, the way the paintings usually show it?

Creusa. To the daughters of Cecrops, yes, to keep him and never look at him.

Ion. I have heard that the girls opened the goddess's chest.

Creusa. And so they died, and their blood stained the face of the rock.

Ion. I see. And what about this one? Is it true, or an empty story?

Creusa. What are you asking? I have the time. I am not tired of it.

Ion. Your father Erechtheus sacrificed your sisters?

Creusa. He had the heart to kill them, girls, as victims for the country's sake.

Ion. And how was it that you alone of the sisters were saved?

Creusa. I was a newborn baby in my mother's arms.

Ion. And is it true that a chasm in the earth hides your father?

Creusa. The blows of the sea god's trident destroyed him.

Ion. And there is a place there they call the Long Rocks?

Creusa. Why are you asking about that? You have reminded me of something.

Ion. The Pythian god honours it, and the Pythian lightning.

Creusa. Honours it. Honours it. I wish I had never set eyes on it.

Ion. What? You hate the thing the god loves most?

Creusa. No. But that cave and I know something shameful together.

Ion. And which Athenian married you, lady?

Creusa. Not a citizen. A man brought in from another country.

Ion. Who? He must be someone of good birth.

Creusa. Xuthus. He is descended from Aeolus, and from Zeus.

Ion. And how did he, a foreigner, get you, when you were born in the country?

Creusa. Euboea is a city next door to Athens.

Ion. With a boundary of water between them, so they say.

Creusa. He sacked it, sharing the war with the sons of Cecrops.

Ion. He came as an ally? And then married into your bed?

Creusa. Yes. It was his dowry from the war, the prize for his spear.

Ion. Have you come to the oracle with your husband, or alone?

Creusa. With him. But he is going round the shrine of Trophonius, the oracle in the cave.

Ion. As a sightseer, or for the sake of an oracle?

Creusa. He wants to hear one and the same word from him and from Apollo.

Ion. Have you come about the crops of the land, or about children?

Creusa. We have no children, though we have shared a bed for years.

Ion. You have never given birth? Never at all? You are childless?

Creusa. Apollo knows about my childlessness.

Ion. Poor woman. Lucky in everything else, and not in this.

Creusa. But who are you? What a lucky woman your mother is.

Ion. I am called the god's slave, lady, and that is what I am.

Creusa. An offering from a city, or sold to him by someone?

Ion. I know only one thing. I am called Apollo's.

Creusa. Then it is my turn to pity you, stranger.

Ion. Because I do not know who bore me or who my father is.

Creusa. Do you live in this temple, or under a roof of your own?

Ion. The whole house of the god is mine, wherever sleep catches me.

Creusa. Did you come to the temple as a child, or as a young man?

Ion. A baby, say the people who think they know.

Creusa. And which woman of Delphi fed you her milk?

Ion. I never knew a breast. But the one who raised me —

Creusa. Who, poor boy? I came here sick, and I have found sickness.

Ion. Apollo's priestess. I think of her as my mother.

Creusa. And till you came to be a man, how did you live?

Ion. The altars fed me, and whatever stranger came along.

Creusa. Poor woman, your mother. Who could she have been?

Ion. Some wrong done to a woman, perhaps. That is what I was born from.

Creusa. But you have a living. You are well dressed.

Ion. I am dressed in the god's clothes. I am his slave.

Creusa. And you never rushed to search out your birth?

Ion. I have nothing to go on, lady. No proof at all.

Creusa. Ah. Another woman has suffered what your mother did.

Ion. Who? If she would share the work with me, I would be glad.

Creusa. She is the reason I came here ahead of my husband.

Ion. What does she want? Tell me, lady, and I will help.

Creusa. She wants to learn a secret answer from Apollo.

Ion. Tell me, then. I will see to the rest, as your host here.

Creusa. Then listen to the story. But I am ashamed.

Ion. Then you will get nothing done. Shame is a lazy goddess.

Creusa. A friend of mine says she went to bed with Apollo.

Ion. Apollo, with a mortal woman? Do not say that, stranger.

Creusa. And she had a child by the god, without her father knowing.

Ion. Impossible. Some man wronged her, and she is ashamed of it.

Creusa. She says not. And she has suffered terribly.

Ion. Suffered how, if a god took her to bed?

Creusa. The child she bore, she put out of the house.

Ion. And the child who was put out, where is he? Is he looking at the light?

Creusa. Nobody knows. That is exactly what I am here to ask the oracle.

Ion. And if he is not alive, how did he die?

Creusa. She supposes that wild animals killed him, poor thing.

Ion. What proof did she use to decide that?

Creusa. She went to the place where she left him, and he was not there any more.

Ion. Was there any drop of blood on the path?

Creusa. She says not. And she went over the ground many times.

Ion. How long is it since the boy was done away with?

Creusa. If he were alive, he would be just your age.

Ion. The god has wronged her. And the mother, poor woman.

Creusa. And she never had another child after that.

Ion. But what if Apollo took him and is raising him in secret?

Creusa. Then he is doing wrong, enjoying alone what should be shared.

Ion. Oh. Her luck sings the same tune as my own trouble.

Creusa. And you too, stranger, I think: somewhere a poor mother misses you.

Ion. No. Do not lead me back to a grief I had forgotten.

Creusa. I am quiet. Finish what I am asking you about.

Ion. Do you know where your story limps worst?

Creusa. What is there in that poor woman's case that is not sick?

Ion. How is the god going to prophesy the very thing he wants hidden?

Creusa. He will, if he sits on a tripod that belongs to all Greece.

Ion. He is ashamed of the business. Do not put him on trial.

Creusa. And the woman it happened to is in pain at her luck.

Ion. There is nobody who will prophesy this for you. If Apollo were shown up as a villain in his own house, he would be right to do some harm to the man who gave you the answer. Go away, lady. We must not ask the oracle for things the god does not want. Think how far we would have gone in stupidity, if we worked the gods over against their will to tell us what they do not want to tell, whether by slaughtering sheep in front of the altars or by the flight of birds. The good things we chase by force, when the gods do not want it, we hold against their will, lady. What they give us willingly, that does us good.

Chorus. Many are the things that happen to the many kinds of mortals, and the shapes of them are all different. But one piece of good luck in a human life: you would hardly find that anywhere.

Creusa. Apollo, there and here you are unjust to the woman who is not here, whose words are. You did not save your son, when you were bound to save him, and you are a prophet, and you will not tell his mother when she asks, so that if he is no longer alive he could be given a mound of a grave, and if he is alive —

But I have to let this be, if the god blocks me from learning what I want to know. Stranger. I can see my husband, the noble Xuthus, close by, coming from the chambers of Trophonius. Say nothing to him about what has been said. I do not want the shame of being caught running secret errands, or the story going off in some direction other than the one we have been unwinding it in. Things go hard for women with men. The good ones are mixed in with the bad, and we are hated for it. That is the luck we were born to.

(Xuthus comes in.)

Xuthus. First, the god: let him have the first fruits of my greeting, and good day to him. And to you, wife. Did I take so long that I frightened you?

Creusa. Not at all. But you have come at an anxious moment. Tell me, what oracle do you bring from Trophonius? How are we two going to mix our seed and make children?

Xuthus. He did not think it right to get ahead of the god's prophecies. But he did say one thing: that I will not go home from the oracle childless, and neither will you.

Creusa. Lady Leto, mother of Apollo, let us come to a good end, and let the dealings we had with your son before change to something better.

Xuthus. It will be so. But who speaks for the god here?

Ion. I do, stranger, for the outside. Inside is other men's business, the ones who sit close to the tripod, the best men of Delphi, the ones the lot chose.

Xuthus. Good. Then I have everything I needed. I will go in. I am told a victim has been slaughtered in front of the temple, on behalf of all the visitors together, and I want to take the god's oracle today, because it is a lucky day. You, wife, take laurel branches and go round the altars, and pray to the gods that I bring an answer out of Apollo's house that promises children.

Creusa. It will be so. It will. And if Apollo is willing now, at last, to make up for his old wrongs, he could never be a complete friend to us. But whatever he is willing to give, he is a god, and I will take it.

(Xuthus goes into the temple. Creusa goes off to pray at the altars.)

Ion. Why does this foreign woman keep dropping hints against the god, in secret words, abusing him? Is it out of love for the woman she is consulting the oracle for? Or is she keeping quiet about something that had better be kept quiet? But what is the daughter of Erechtheus to me? Nothing. She is nothing to do with me. I will go and fill the basins for the sprinkling, with water from the golden jugs.

But I have a word to say to Apollo. What is the matter with him? He rapes girls and then abandons them? He fathers children in secret and lets them die, and does not care? Not you. No. You have the power, so go after goodness. Any mortal who turns out bad, the gods punish him. So how can it be just that you, who write the laws for mortals, should stand guilty of breaking the law yourselves? And if — it will never happen, but I will follow the argument — you paid mortals the penalty for rape, you and Poseidon and Zeus who rules the sky, you would empty your temples paying the fines for your injustice. You chase pleasure before you think, and that is wrong. It is no longer fair to call human beings bad, when we are only copying the fine things the gods do. Blame the ones who teach us.

(Ion goes.)

Chorus.
	You who were born without the pains of labour,
	with no goddess of childbirth to help,
	my Athena, I beg you,
	you whom the Titan Prometheus
	delivered from the very crown
	of the head of Zeus. Blessed Athena, Lady of Victory,
	come to the Pythian house.
	Fly from the golden chambers of Olympus
	down to these streets,
	where Apollo's hearth, at the navel of the earth,
	beside the tripod and the dancing round it,
	makes the prophecies come true.
	You, and Leto's daughter with you,
	two goddesses, two virgins,
	the holy sisters of Apollo.
	Girls, pray with me
	that the old house of Erechtheus
	hears at last, in clear oracles,
	that children are coming.
Chorus.
	Because there is a happiness beyond all others,
	a footing that does not shift, for mortals
	in whose fathers' halls
	the young lives of children
	shine, ripening like fruit,
	to take over the wealth from their fathers
	and pass it on to children of their own.
	A child is a defence in trouble,
	a joy when luck is good,
	and brings his father's country
	the saving strength of a spear.
	Give me, before wealth,
	before the bedchambers of kings,
	the loving work of raising good children.
	The childless life I loathe,
	and anyone who thinks well of it, I blame.
	Let me have what I need, and no more,
	and a life with good children in it.
Chorus.
	Seat of Pan, and rock
	that stands beside the caves,
	the hollows of the Long Rocks,
	where the three daughters of Aglaurus
	tread out their dances with their feet
	on the green ground in front of Pallas's temple,
	to the shifting cry of your pipes,
	when you, Pan, are piping
	in your sunless caves:
	there a girl who had a baby by Apollo,
	poor girl, put it out
	as a feast for the birds,
	a bloody meal for the beasts,
	the outrage of a bitter bed.
	Not at the loom, not in any story,
	have I heard it said that children
	born to mortals from the gods
	get any share of happiness.

(Ion comes back.)

Ion. Women in service, you who stand guard here at the steps of this house of incense and keep watch for your mistress: has Xuthus left the holy tripod and the oracle yet, or is he still inside, asking about his childlessness?

Chorus. He is inside, stranger. He has not crossed this threshold yet. But he must be at the door. We can hear the doors knocking, and now you can see the master coming out.

(Xuthus comes out of the temple and goes straight to Ion.)

Xuthus. My child. Good day to you. That is the right way for me to begin.

Ion. Good day to you too. Keep your head, and we will both do fine.

Xuthus. Give me your hand to kiss, and your body to put my arms round.

Ion. Are you in your right mind? Or has some god struck you and driven you mad, stranger?

Xuthus. I am in my right mind. I have found what I love most, and I am not going to run from it.

Ion. Stop. Do not touch the god's garlands. You will tear them with your hand.

Xuthus. I will touch. I am not stealing. I am finding what is mine, and I love it.

Ion. Get away from me, before you get an arrow in the lungs.

Xuthus. Why are you running from me? When you have found what is dearest to you —

Ion. I do not enjoy teaching manners to boorish strangers who have gone mad.

Xuthus. Kill me, then, and burn me. If you kill me, you will be your father's murderer.

Ion. Where is my father? You? Is that not a joke, to make me laugh?

Xuthus. No. If the story runs on, it will show you what I mean.

Ion. And what are you going to tell me?

Xuthus. I am your father, and you are my child.

Ion. Who says so?

Xuthus. Apollo, who raised you, when you were mine.

Ion. You are your own witness, then.

Xuthus. I have learned the god's oracle, yes.

Ion. You heard a riddle and got it wrong.

Xuthus. Then I am not hearing straight.

Ion. And what did Apollo say?

Xuthus. That the man who met me —

Ion. Met you how?

Xuthus. — as I came out of this house of the god —

Ion. What was going to happen to him?

Xuthus. — he was my son by birth.

Ion. Born yours, or a gift from somewhere else?

Xuthus. A gift. But born from me.

Ion. And I am the first person you set foot near?

Xuthus. Nobody else, child.

Ion. Where does this luck come from?

Xuthus. Two of us wondering at the same thing.

Ion. Ah. And what mother did you have me by?

Xuthus. I cannot tell you that, child.

Ion. Apollo did not say either?

Xuthus. I was so pleased with this that I did not ask that.

Ion. Then I was born from the earth, and she is my mother.

Xuthus. The ground does not bear children.

Ion. Then how could I be yours?

Xuthus. I do not know. I refer it to the god.

Ion. Come. Let us take hold of the question another way.

Xuthus. This way is better, child.

Ion. Did you ever go to a bed that was not your wife's?

Xuthus. In the foolishness of youth, yes.

Ion. Before you married the daughter of Erechtheus?

Xuthus. Never since, anyway.

Ion. So that is where you fathered me?

Xuthus. The time fits, at any rate.

Ion. And then how did I get here —

Xuthus. That I cannot work out at all.

Ion. — travelling such a long road?

Xuthus. That puzzles me just as much.

Ion. Did you ever come to the Pythian rock before?

Xuthus. Yes. For the torchlight festival of Dionysus.

Ion. Did you stay with one of the official hosts?

Xuthus. Yes. A man who, with some girls of Delphi —

Ion. Got you into the revels? Or what are you saying?

Xuthus. Into the Maenads of Dionysus, yes.

Ion. Were you sober, or in your wine?

Xuthus. In the pleasures of Dionysus.

Ion. That was it. That is where I was sown.

Xuthus. Fate found you out, child.

Ion. And how did I get to the temple?

Xuthus. Some girl's cast-off, perhaps.

Ion. So I have escaped being a slave's child.

Xuthus. Then take your father, my boy.

Ion. Well, it makes no sense to doubt the god.

Xuthus. Now you are thinking straight.

Ion. And what more could I want—

Xuthus. Now you are seeing what you ought to see.

Ion. —than to be the son of a son of Zeus?

Xuthus. Which is exactly what you are.

Ion. Then may I really touch the man who fathered me?

Xuthus. Yes. Trust the god.

Ion. Father. I greet you—

Xuthus. That is a word I am glad to hear.

Ion. —and this day—

Xuthus. —has made me a happy man.

Ion. Mother. My dear mother, when will I see your face as well? I long to look at you now more than ever, whoever you are. But perhaps you are dead, and there is nothing at all we can do.

Chorus. The good luck of the house is ours to share. All the same, I wish my mistress had been lucky in children too, and the house of Erechtheus with her.

Xuthus. My son, the god has brought his oracle out true as far as finding you goes. He has joined you to me, and you have found the thing you love most without ever knowing it before. And the thing you rushed at just now, quite rightly, is the thing I long for too: that you should find your mother, boy, and that I should find out what woman gave you to me. Give it time and perhaps we will find that out as well. But now leave the god's floor and your wandering life and come to Athens, of one mind with your father. Your father's sceptre is waiting for you there, and it is a fortunate one, and great wealth with it. You will not be sick with one of the two diseases, low birth and poverty, and called both names at once. You will be a nobleman, and rich. You are silent? Why do you keep your eyes fixed on the ground? You have gone off into your thoughts, and by swinging back like this from joy you are frightening your father.

Ion. Things do not look the same when they are far off and when you see them close up. I welcome what has happened. I have found a father in you. But listen, father, to what I am working out.

They say that the famous Athenians are born from their own soil, not a race brought in from somewhere else. So I will land among them carrying two diseases: a father who is an import, and myself a bastard. With that reproach on me, while I am still weak, I will be called a nobody, and a nobody's son. And if I push my way toward the front bench of the city and try to be somebody, the people with no power will hate me, because a man above you is galling. And the good men, the men who could be clever if they chose, but who keep quiet and do not rush into public business: among them I will be a laugh, and a fool, for not keeping my head down in a city full of fear. And as for the speakers, the men who use the city and make their careers in it, the higher I climb in rank the more they will guard against me with their votes. That is how it goes, father. The men who hold the cities and the offices are deadliest of all to anyone who competes with them.

Then there is the house. I come into another man's house as an outsider, and to a childless woman, who shared your troubles with you before, and who now has lost her share and will bear her fate alone and bitterly. How can she help hating me, and fairly, when I stand there at your elbow, and she, with no child, looks at the thing you love with bitter eyes? And then you must either betray me and look to your wife, or honour me and throw your whole house into confusion. How many killings, how many deadly poisons, women have found to destroy their husbands with. And besides, I pity your wife, father, growing old without a child. She comes from noble fathers, and she does not deserve to sicken with childlessness.

And kingship, which everybody praises for no reason: its face is sweet, but inside the house it is misery. Who is blessed, who is happy, who spins out his life afraid, glancing sideways? I would rather live as a happy commoner than as a tyrant, who takes pleasure in having bad men for friends and hates the good ones because he is afraid of being killed. You will tell me gold outweighs all that, and that being rich is pleasant. I do not like hearing noises in the night while I clutch my fortune in both hands, and I do not like the work of it either. Let me have a moderate amount, and no grief.

Now listen, father, to the good things I had here. First, leisure, the dearest thing a man can have, and not much of a crowd. No villain ever shoved me off the road, and that is the one unbearable thing, to give way and step aside for men worse than yourself. I was either at my prayers to the gods or in talk with people, and the people I served were happy people, not people in mourning. I was always seeing one set of strangers off as the next set arrived, so I was always welcome, a new face among new faces. And the thing people pray for even when they do not want it, to be honest: custom and my own nature together made me honest in the god's sight. When I add all that up, father, I think things are better here than there. Let me live here. The pleasure is the same either way: to enjoy great things, or to have small ones and like them.

Chorus. Well said, so long as the people I love find their happiness in what you say.

Xuthus. Stop this talk and learn how to be happy. I want to begin right here, my boy, where I found you: a shared table, a feast we sit down to together, and the birth-sacrifice for you that I never made before. For now I will bring you to my hearth as if you were a guest, and give you a good dinner, and take you to the land of Athens as a visitor, supposedly, and not as my own son. I do not want to hurt my wife with my own good luck while she has no child. In time, when the moment is right, I will bring her round to letting you hold my sceptre over the land. And I name you Ion, to fit what happened: you were the one coming toward me, the first to meet my step, as I came out of the god's shrine. Now gather the whole company of your friends, and over the pleasure of a roasted ox say your goodbyes, since you are about to leave the city of Delphi.

And you slave women, I am telling you: keep silent. Say one word of this to my wife and it is death.

Ion. I will go. But one piece of my luck is still missing. If I do not find the woman who bore me, father, my life is not worth living. And if I may pray for it, let the mother who bore me be a woman of Athens, so that I get the right to speak my mind from my mother's side. When a stranger lands in a city that keeps its blood pure, he may be a citizen in name, but his mouth is a slave's mouth, and he cannot speak freely.

(Xuthus and Ion go out together. The Chorus are left alone.)

Chorus.
	I see tears, and cries of mourning,
	and the first breaking-out of groans,
	when my queen learns that her husband
	has a fine son,
	and she herself is childless, left without children.
	What song was that you prophesied,
	prophetic son of Leto?
	Where did this boy come from, this foster-child
	raised around your temple? What woman's son is he?
	The oracle does not win me over. There may be a trick in it.
	I am afraid of what is coming,
	wherever it is going to land.
	A strange god is giving me strange things,
	and what he says still sounds fair,
	but the boy raised from another's blood
	is a trick and a stroke of luck together.
	Who will not agree with me?
Chorus.
	Friends, shall we say it plainly,
	straight into our mistress's ear?
	Her husband, in whom she had everything,
	whose hopes she shared, poor woman—
	and now she is wrecked by misfortune, and he is prospering,
	she is sliding into grey old age, and her husband
	has no honour for the people he owes.
	A wretch, who came into the house from outside,
	into great wealth, and did not hold to her fortune,
	who tricked my lady. Let him die. Let him die.
	And may the gods never accept from him
	the fair-flamed cake he burns
	on their fire. He will find out what I am,
	how much I was born a friend
	to my queen's royal house.
	Now they are near the feast already,
	father and son, the new man and the new.
Chorus.
	Io, ridges of Parnassus,
	you rock that holds the peak and the seat in the sky,
	where Bacchus lifts his two flaring pine-torches
	and leaps, light-footed, with the Bacchants who roam the night:
	may that boy never come to my city.
	Let him die and leave his young day behind him.
	Our city would have every reason to groan
	at a foreigner pushing in,
	the city that lord Erechtheus,
	our first ruler, gathered into one.

(Creusa comes in, leading the Old Man who was her father's servant slowly up the steep path.)

Creusa. Old man, you were tutor to my father Erechtheus once, when he was still in the light. Climb up to the god's oracle with me, so that you can share my joy, if lord Apollo has given any word about the birth of children. It is sweet to do well when your friends are with you, and if something bad turns up, which I pray it does not, it is sweet to look into the eyes of someone who wishes you well. You looked after my father once. I am your mistress, but all the same I look after you now, in his place.

Old Man. Daughter, you keep the ways your parents kept, and they were worthy of you and you of them. You have never shamed your ancestors, the children of this soil. Pull, pull me toward the temple, carry me up. The oracle is a steep place. Work with my old age. Be the doctor for my leg.

Creusa. Follow me, then. Watch where you put your feet.

Old Man. There. The foot is slow. The mind is quick.

Creusa. Lean on your stick. The path winds round.

Old Man. The stick is blind too, when I see so little.

Creusa. True. But do not give up because you are tired.

Old Man. Not willingly. But I am not master of what I no longer have.

Creusa. Women, faithful slaves of my loom and my shuttle, what fortune did my husband take away with him about the children we came here for? Tell me. If you bring me good news, you will not be throwing your favour to masters who forget it.

Chorus. Io. Our fate.

Old Man. That is not a lucky opening to a speech.

Chorus. Io. Poor lady.

Old Man. Is there something in the masters' oracles that hurts me too?

Chorus. Well then. What do we do? There is death hanging over this.

Creusa. What is this tune? And what is the fear about?

Chorus. Do we speak or keep silent? What are we going to do?

Creusa. Speak. You have some misfortune for me. I can see it.

Chorus. Then it will be said, even if I have to die twice for it. Mistress, you will never take a child in your arms, or hold one to your breast.

Creusa. Oh. Let me die.

Old Man. Daughter.

Creusa.
	Poor me, and my misfortune.
	I have taken it, I have suffered it, a pain
	no one could live with, friends.
	We are finished.
Old Man.
	Child.
Creusa.
	Aiai. Aiai.
	The pain has gone straight through me,
	deep inside my lungs.

Old Man. Do not groan yet—

Creusa. But the grief is here already.

Old Man. —until we learn—

Creusa. Learn what? What news is there for me?

Old Man. —whether the master is in the same case and shares the misfortune with you, or whether you are unlucky alone.

Chorus. To him, old man, Apollo has given a son. He is lucky on his own account, apart from her.

Creusa. This on top of that. The very peak of evil you have cried out, a pain for me to groan over.

Old Man. This boy you speak of: is he still to be born, from some woman, or did the god prophesy one already born?

Chorus. Already born, and fully grown, a young man. Apollo gives him to him. I was there.

Creusa. What are you saying? Unspeakable. Unspeakable. A word that should never be spoken, and you cry it at me.

Old Man. And at me. But how is the oracle being carried out? Tell me more clearly. And who is the boy?

Chorus. Whoever your husband met first as he came hurrying out from the god, that man the god gave him for a son.

Creusa. Ottotottotoi. Then it is a childless life, childless, that he has cried out for me? And I will live in a lonely house, with no one to come after me.

Old Man. Then who was the oracle about? Whose step did the poor woman's husband fall in with? How, and where, did he see him?

Chorus. Dear mistress, you know the young man who was sweeping this temple? He is the son.

Creusa. Let me fly up through the wet air, far from the land of Greece, out to the evening stars. Such pain, such pain I have suffered, friends.

Old Man. And what name does his father call him? Do you know, or is that still unsettled, and unsaid?

Chorus. Ion, because he was the first to meet his father coming out.

Old Man. And what mother is he—

Chorus. I cannot tell you. But so that you know everything I know, old man, her husband has gone off to the sacred tents, without telling her, to make the guest-offerings and the birth-offerings for the boy, and to sit down to a feast with his new son.

Old Man. Mistress, we are betrayed. I say we, because I am sick with the same sickness as you. Betrayed by your husband. It was planned. We are being outraged and thrown out of the house of Erechtheus. And I do not say this because I hate your husband. I say it because I love you more than him. He came into this city as a stranger, married you, took over your house and your whole inheritance, and now it turns out he has been secretly harvesting children from another woman. How secretly? I will tell you. When he saw you were childless, he was not content to be like you and carry an equal share of your fortune. He took a slave to his bed, married her in secret, and fathered the boy, and then he sent him out of the way and gave him to some Delphian to raise. And the boy was let loose in the god's house, so nobody would notice, and brought up there. Then when he heard the boy had grown to be a young man, he persuaded you to come here about your childlessness. So the god did not lie. He lied. He had been raising the boy all these years, and he wove his plots like this: if he was caught, he would put it all down to the god; if he got away with it, he would come home, and take his time about it, and wrap the kingship of the land round the boy. And the new name, shaped to fit after all this time: Ion, because supposedly he met him coming.

Chorus. Oh, how I have always hated wicked men, who put an injustice together and then dress it up with schemes. I would rather have a plain honest man for a friend than a bad one who was cleverer.

Old Man. And of all these evils you will suffer the last and worst: to bring into your house as its master a nobody with no mother and no name, some slave woman's child. The evil would have been a simple one if he had talked you round, pleading your childlessness, and settled a nobly born mother's son in the house. And if that was too bitter for you, he should have gone and asked for a marriage among the daughters of Aeolus. So now you must do something, and do it the way a woman does. Take a sword, or use some trick, or poison, and kill your husband and the boy before death comes to you from them. If you hold back from this, you will lose your life. When two enemies come under one roof, one of them has to go down, or the other. I am willing to work at this with you, and to share in killing the boy. I will go into the house where he is laying on his feast, and pay my masters back for my keep, and either die or live to look at the light. There is one thing, and one only, that brings shame on a slave, and that is the name. In everything else a slave is no worse than a free man, if he is a good one.

Chorus. And I too, dear mistress, want to share in this fortune with you, and either die or live with honour.

Creusa.
	My soul, how can I keep silent?
	But how can I bring that dark bed into the light
	and be left with no shame at all?
	What is there still standing in my way?
	Who is it I am competing with, to be the better woman?
	Has my husband not turned traitor to me?
	I am robbed of my house, robbed of children,
	and the hopes are gone, the hopes I wanted
	to settle well and could not,
	keeping silent about that coupling,
	silent about that birth, with all its tears.
	No. By the starry seat of Zeus,
	and by the goddess who stands on my cliffs,
	and by the holy shore of the Tritonian lake,
	I will hide that bed no longer.
	Once I have taken it off my chest I will breathe easier.
	My eyes are streaming with tears,
	my soul is in pain from the evil that was planned against me
	by men and by immortals both,
	and I will show them up for what they are,
	traitors to the bed, and ungrateful.
	You who sing to the voice
	of the seven-stringed lyre,
	who make the Muses' hymns ring sweet
	on horns from the fields, on dead horn,
	son of Leto, it is you I will accuse,
	out loud, here in this daylight.
	You came to me with your hair shining gold,
	when I was gathering saffron petals
	into the folds of my dress,
	flowers that flashed the gold back at the sun.
	You gripped my white wrists,
	you dragged me to a bed in the cave
	while I screamed "Mother! Mother!",
	you, a god, to lie with me,
	with no shame in you,
	doing Aphrodite a favour.
	And I bore you a son, poor wretch that I am,
	and in terror of my mother I threw him
	onto that bed of yours,
	where you had yoked me, miserable,
	in a miserable coupling.
	Oimoi. And now he is gone,
	snatched up as a feast for birds,
	my boy, and yours, poor thing.
	And you play your lyre,
	and sing your songs of healing.
	Ohe.
	You, son of Leto, I am calling you,
	you who deal out your voice from your golden throne,
	your seat at the centre of the earth:
	into your ear I will shout it.
	Io. You were a bad lover.
	You settle a son in my husband's house
	when he has done nothing to earn it,
	and my child, and yours, the poor ignorant thing,
	is gone, torn up by birds,
	stripped of the swaddling clothes his mother wrapped him in.
	Delos hates you now, and the young laurel
	beside the palm with its soft hair,
	where Leto bore you in her holy labour,
	the fruit of Zeus.

Chorus. Oh, what a great storehouse of evils has been opened. Anyone would weep at it.

Old Man. Daughter, I cannot get my fill of looking at your face, and my mind has gone out from under me. I had just bailed one wave of evils out of my thoughts, and another lifts me from astern, from your words. You have flung off the troubles in front of us and gone down some other evil road, into other griefs. What are you saying? What charge are you bringing against Apollo? What child do you say you bore? Where in the city did you lay him down, a tomb for wild beasts to enjoy? Go back over it for me.

Creusa. I am ashamed in front of you, old man. But I will say it all the same.

Old Man. I know how to grieve with the people I love, and grieve properly.

Creusa. Then listen. You know the cave on the north side of Cecrops's rock, the cliffs we call the Long Rocks?

Old Man. I know it. The shrine of Pan is there, and the altars near it.

Creusa. That is where I fought a terrible fight.

Old Man. What fight? My tears are coming out already to meet your words.

Creusa. Apollo forced me. I lay with him against my will.

Old Man. Daughter, was this the thing I noticed at the time?

Creusa. I do not know. If you are telling the truth, I would say yes.

Old Man. When you were groaning in secret over some hidden sickness?

Creusa. That was the time. That was the evil I am showing you plainly now.

Old Man. And then how did you hide what Apollo had done?

Creusa. I gave birth. Bear with me, old man, while you hear this.

Old Man. Where? Who delivered you? Or did you labour through it alone?

Creusa. Alone, in the cave where I was yoked to him.

Old Man. And the child? Where is he, so that you need not be childless any longer?

Creusa. He is dead, old man. I put him out for the wild beasts.

Old Man. Dead? And Apollo, the bad god, gave no help at all?

Creusa. None. My boy is being raised in the house of Hades.

Old Man. Who put him out, then? Surely not you.

Creusa. I did. In the dark, after I had wrapped him in my robes.

Old Man. And nobody at all knew you had left the baby out?

Creusa. Only my misfortune, and the darkness.

Old Man. How did you have the heart to leave your own child in that cave?

Creusa. How? I said a great many pitiful things over him with this mouth—

Old Man. Pheu. You had a hard heart, and the god's was harder than yours.

Creusa. If you had seen the baby stretching out his hands to me.

Old Man. Looking for the breast? Or to fall into your arms?

Creusa. For the place he never got to, where I did him such a wrong.

Old Man. And what put it into your head to throw your child away?

Creusa. I thought the god would save his own son.

Old Man. Oh, what a storm is battering the good fortune of your house.

Creusa. Why have you covered your head, old man? Why are you weeping?

Old Man. Because I see you and your father brought low.

Creusa. That is what it is to be mortal. Nothing stays in the same place.

Old Man. Then let us hold on to our grieving no longer, daughter.

Creusa. What am I supposed to do? To be unlucky is to have no way out.

Old Man. Pay back the god who wronged you first.

Creusa. And how am I, a mortal, going to outrun the powers above me?

Old Man. Set fire to Apollo's holy oracle.

Creusa. I am afraid. I have grief enough already.

Old Man. Then dare what you can. Kill your husband.

Creusa. I respect the bed we shared in the days when he was good.

Old Man. Then at least the boy who has appeared to take your place.

Creusa. How? If only it were possible. How I would love to.

Old Man. Arm your attendants with swords.

Creusa. I would go and do it. But where is it to happen?

Old Man. In the sacred tents, where he is feasting his friends.

Creusa. The murder would be seen by everyone, and slaves are weak.

Old Man. Oh, now you are losing your nerve. Come on then, you think of something.

Creusa. As it happens I do have something. It is a trick, and it works.

Old Man. Then I am your servant for both, the trick and the work.

Creusa. Then listen. You know the battle of the earth-born giants?

Old Man. I know it. At Phlegra, the Giants stood up against the gods.

Creusa. That is where Earth gave birth to the Gorgon, a terrible monster.

Old Man. To fight beside her own children, and make trouble for the gods?

Creusa. Yes. And the goddess Pallas, the daughter of Zeus, killed it.

Old Man. What shape did it have, this wild thing?

Creusa. A breastplate armoured with coils of vipers.

Old Man. Is this the story I heard long ago?

Creusa. That Athena wears its skin over her chest.

Old Man. The thing they call the aegis, Pallas's armour?

Creusa. That is the name it got the day she rushed into the gods' battle.

Old Man. But daughter, how does this hurt your enemies?

Creusa. You know Erichthonius, or— But of course you do, old man.

Old Man. The first of your ancestors, the one Earth sent up?

Creusa. When he was newborn, Pallas gave him—

Old Man. Gave him what? You are slow bringing this word out.

Creusa. Two drops of blood from the Gorgon.

Old Man. And what power do they have over a human body?

Creusa. One kills. The other cures diseases.

Old Man. What did she fasten them in, to hang them round the baby's body?

Creusa. Gold bands. And he gave the thing to my father.

Old Man. And when he died, it came to you?

Creusa. Yes. I wear it here, on my wrist.

Old Man. So how does the goddess's double gift work?

Creusa. The drop that ran from the hollow vein when she killed it—

Old Man. What is that one used for? What power does it carry?

Creusa. It keeps off disease, and it feeds life.

Old Man. And the second one you spoke of, what does that do?

Creusa. It kills. It is the venom of the Gorgon's snakes.

Old Man. And do you carry them mixed into one, or separate?

Creusa. Separate. Good does not mix with evil.

Old Man. My dearest child, you have everything you need.

Creusa. The boy will die by this. And you will be the one who kills him.

Old Man. Where, and how? Yours is to say it, mine is to dare it.

Creusa. In Athens, when he comes to my house.

Old Man. That is not well said. You found fault with my plan, and I find fault with yours.

Creusa. How? Do you suspect the same thing that is coming into my own mind?

Old Man. You will get the blame for the boy's death even if you do not kill him.

Creusa. True. They say stepmothers are jealous of their husbands' children.

Old Man. Then kill him here, where you can deny the murder.

Creusa. And I get the pleasure of it sooner, too.

Old Man. And you will keep your husband in the dark, in exactly the way he is trying to keep you.

Creusa. Then you know what to do? Take this from my hand, this gold thing of Athena's, the old work, and go to where my husband is secretly sacrificing his oxen. When they have finished dinner and are about to pour their libations to the gods, have this ready in the folds of your clothes, and drop it into the young man's cup. His alone, not everyone's. Keep a separate drink for the man who means to be master of my house. And once it is down his throat, he will never reach famous Athens. He will die here, and here he will stay.

Old Man. Now you go inside, to the house of our hosts. I will finish the work I have been set. Come on, old foot, be young in what you do, even if time will not allow you to be young in years. Go with your masters against their enemy, and help to kill him, and help to clear him out of the house. Piety is a fine thing to honour when you are prospering. But when a man wants to hurt his enemies, there is no law that stands in the way.

(Creusa goes into the house of her Delphian hosts. The Old Man goes off toward the feast.)

Chorus.
	Goddess of the crossroads, daughter of Demeter,
	who rule the attacks that walk by night
	and the attacks that walk by day,
	guide the filling of the death-cups
	to where my queen, my queen, is sending them:
	the drops from the cut throat
	of the Gorgon, earth's child,
	for the man who is laying hands
	on the house of Erechtheus's sons.
	Let no one from any other house
	ever rule my city
	except the nobly born sons of Erechtheus.
Chorus.
	And if the death miscarries, and my mistress's efforts,
	and the moment for daring passes,
	the moment where her hope showed itself just now,
	then either a sharpened sword, or a noose
	that fate will knot around her neck.
	She will finish one suffering with another
	and go down to another shape of life.
	Because she would never, while she lived,
	with her eyes open in the bright light,
	put up with strangers from another land
	ruling her house,
	she who was born of the noble houses.
Chorus.
	I am ashamed before the god of the many hymns,
	if this boy is to stand beside the fair-dancing springs
	and watch the torches on the twentieth night,
	sleepless, awake till morning,
	when the starry sky of Zeus
	takes up the dance too,
	and the moon dances,
	and the fifty daughters of Nereus,
	who dance across the sea
	and in the eddies of the ever-flowing rivers,
	in honour of Persephone with her crown of gold
	and her holy mother.
	That is where he hopes to be king,
	dropping onto other men's labour,
	Apollo's vagabond.
Chorus.
	Look at us, all you poets who go
	against us with your ugly music,
	singing of our beds, and our loves,
	Aphrodite's lawless, unholy loves.
	See how far we outdo in decency
	the unjust sowing that men do.
	Let the song turn round.
	Let the ugly music about beds
	go against men now.
	Because this man from the sons of Zeus
	shows how forgetful he is:
	he never fathered on his house
	a child his mistress could share,
	he paid his court to another love instead,
	and got himself a bastard son.

(A Servant of Creusa runs in.)

Servant. Noble women, where can I find my mistress, the daughter of Erechtheus? I have searched every corner of the town for her and I cannot lay hands on her.

Chorus. What is it, fellow slave? Why the hurry in your feet? What news are you carrying?

Servant. We are being hunted. The rulers of this land are looking for her, to put her to death by stoning.

Chorus. Oh. What are you going to tell us? Surely we have not been caught plotting the secret murder of the boy?

Servant. You have guessed it. And you will not be the last to share in the trouble.

Chorus. How were the hidden schemes seen?

Servant. The god found them out. Injustice lost to justice. He would not have his temple polluted.

Chorus. How? I beg you, I go down on my knees to you, tell us. If we have to die anyway, we would die more gladly knowing, or go on looking at the light.

Servant. When Creusa's husband left the god's oracle, he took his new son off to the dinner and the sacrifices he was preparing for the gods. Then Xuthus himself went up to where the god's Bacchic fire leaps, to wet the two rocks of Dionysus with blood, as a thank-offering for the sight of his son. He said, "You stay here, my boy, and have the builders put up the tents, walled in on every side. If I take a long time over the sacrifice to the gods of birth, let the friends who are here begin the feast without me." Then he took the calves and went.

The young man set about the enclosure of the tents, and he did it with ceremony: no walls, upright posts, and he watched the angle of the sun carefully, so that the tent faced neither the burning rays of midday nor the rays of the end of the day. He measured out a square a hundred feet on each side, ten thousand square feet inside it, as the experts put it, as though he were inviting the whole people of Delphi to the feast. Then he took sacred weavings from the treasuries and roofed it with them, and they were a wonder for men to look at.

First he spread over the roof a great wing of woven cloth, the gift of the son of Zeus, the spoils Heracles took from the Amazons and brought to the god. There were pictures woven into it, like this. Heaven, gathering the stars into the circle of the sky. The Sun driving his horses toward the last of the flame, drawing the bright light of the Evening Star behind him. Night in her black robe, driving her chariot with a single pair of horses and no outrunners, and the stars keeping the goddess company. The Pleiades going through the middle of the sky, and Orion with his sword, and above them the Bear, wheeling her golden tail round the pole. The full round moon that cuts the month in half, shooting her light upward, and the Hyades, the clearest sign a sailor has, and Dawn, the light-bringer, chasing the stars away.

On the walls he hung other weavings, barbarian work: ships with fine oars facing Greek ships, and men who were half beast, and huntsmen on horseback chasing deer, and hunts of wild lions. At the entrances, Cecrops, coiling in his serpent spirals, with his daughters beside him, the gift of some Athenian. And in the middle of the dining space he set up gold mixing-bowls.

A herald stood up on tiptoe and announced that any man of the country who wished could come to the feast. When the tent was full, they put on their garlands and filled themselves with good rich food. And when they had had their fill of the pleasure of it, the old man came forward and took his stand in the middle of the floor, and he gave the diners a great deal to laugh at with his busyness. He poured water for their hands from the pitchers, he burned the sweat of the myrrh tree for incense, he put himself in charge of the gold cups, all a job he had assigned to himself. And when they came to the flutes and the shared bowl, the old man said, "Away with these little wine-cups. Bring the big ones, so these gentlemen can get to the pleasures of the mind a little faster." Then there was hard work carrying round the cups of beaten silver and of gold. And he picked out one cup in particular, as though he were doing a favour to his new master, and handed it full, and into the wine he had dropped what they say the mistress gave him, a poison that does its work, so that the new son would leave the light. Nobody knew any of this.

The son that had just been revealed was holding his libation in his hands with the others when one of the household slaves let slip a word of bad omen. And the boy, raised in a temple among good seers, took it as a sign. He ordered a fresh bowl to be filled, and the first libation to the god he gave to the ground, and he told everyone else to pour theirs out. Silence fell. We filled the sacred bowls again with water and with wine from Byblos. And while we were at it, a winged revel of doves came tumbling into the tent, for in Apollo's house they live without fear. When the men had poured out their wine, the doves, thirsty, dipped their beaks into it and drew it up into their fine-feathered throats. For all the others the god's libation was harmless. But the one that settled where the new son had poured his, and tasted the drink: at once she shook her feathered body and went into a frenzy, and screamed out a cry that meant nothing, a wailing, and the whole crowd of diners stared in astonishment at the bird's agony. She died gasping, and her red claws went slack.

Then the son the oracle had given flung his arms bare out of his robes across the table and shouted, "Which of you men was going to kill me? Tell me, old man. The eagerness was all yours. It was from your hand I took the cup." And at once he grabbed the old arm and searched him, to catch the old man red-handed, with the thing on him. He was found out, and forced to it, and slowly, unwillingly, he confessed Creusa's daring and the trick of the cup. Straight away the young man Apollo's oracle had given ran out, taking the diners with him, and stood before the lords of Delphi and said, "Holy Earth, the daughter of Erechtheus, a woman from another country, is killing me with poison." And the lords of Delphi voted, not one vote against, that my mistress should die by being thrown from the rock, for trying to kill the god's own boy, and for planning a murder inside the sanctuary. Now the whole city is hunting her, the wretched woman who rushed so wretchedly down that road. She came to Apollo wanting children, and along with the children she has lost her own life.

Chorus.
	There is no way, no way out of death
	for me. Wretched woman that I am.
	It is plain now, all of it plain:
	the drink-offering from Dionysus,
	the grape mixed with the quick viper's
	drops of blood, for a killing,
	the offering to the dead brought out into the light.
	Disaster for my life,
	and death by stoning for my mistress.
	What flight on wings can I find,
	or what dark hollow under the earth to go down into,
	to escape the ruin of death by stones?
	Should I climb into a chariot
	behind the fastest team of four,
	or up onto the stern of a ship?
Chorus.
	There is no hiding, unless a god
	wants you hidden and steals you away.
	Poor mistress, what is left
