	for your heart to suffer? And we
	who wanted to do our neighbour harm, will we
	be harmed ourselves, the way justice says we should?

Creusa. Women. They are hunting me down to cut my throat. The vote at Delphi has gone against me, and I am handed over to die.

Chorus. We know, poor lady. We know what has happened to you, and where you stand.

Creusa. Then where do I run? I barely got a foot out of the house ahead of them, before they could kill me. I have come this far by slipping past my enemies unseen.

Chorus. Where else but to the altar?

Creusa. And what good does that do me?

Chorus. It is forbidden to kill a suppliant.

Creusa. And it is by the law that I am dying.

Chorus. Only if they take you by force.

Creusa. Well, here they come, the bitter champions of the case, hurrying this way with their swords out.

Chorus. Sit down on the altar, now. If you die there, you fix the guilt of your blood on the men who kill you, and it will hunt them. Whatever comes, you have to bear it.

(Creusa sits down on the altar in front of the temple. Ion comes in with armed men of Delphi.)

Ion. Cephisus, old bull-faced river, this woman's grandfather. What a viper you bred here. What a snake, with fire in it, looking up with murder in its flame. There is no daring she does not have. She is every bit as deadly as the Gorgon's blood she meant to kill me with. Take hold of her. Let the ledges of Parnassus comb out that untouched hair of hers, when she is flung off them and goes bouncing down the rock. I have had good luck, meeting you before I ever got to Athens and fell into a stepmother's hands. I took the measure of your mind here, among friends: how much harm you wished me, how much you hated me. If you had got me inside your walls, you would have shipped me off to the house of Hades whole, with nothing left over. But no altar is going to save you, and no house of Apollo. That pity you are asking for belongs to me, more than to you, and to my mother. She may not be here in body, but her name is never far from me. Look at her, all of you. Look at the schemer, and the trick she has woven out of the last trick. She is cowering at the god's altar so she will not have to pay for what she did.

Creusa. I forbid you to kill me. I say it for myself, and for the god whose altar I am standing at.

Ion. What do you and Apollo have in common?

Creusa. I give my body to the god. It is sacred now. It is his to keep.

Ion. And yet you were poisoning the god's own servant?

Creusa. You were not Apollo's any more. You were your father's.

Ion. But I was his, as good as born to him. That is what I really was, whatever I was called.

Creusa. You were, then. Now I am his, and you are not any more.

Ion. Not with clean hands, you are not. Mine were clean, then.

Creusa. I tried to kill you because you were the enemy of my house.

Ion. I never marched into your country with weapons.

Creusa. You certainly did. And you were setting fire to the house of Erechtheus.

Ion. With what torches? What kind of flame?

Creusa. You were going to live in what is mine, after taking it from me by force.

Ion. When my father was giving me land he had won for himself.

Creusa. And what share did the sons of Aeolus ever have in the land of Pallas Athena?

Ion. He saved it with weapons, not words.

Creusa. A hired ally does not get to settle in the country he was paid to defend.

Ion. So you tried to kill me out of fear of what I might do?

Creusa. So that I would not die myself, when you stopped meaning to and did it.

Ion. You are childless, and jealous, because my father found me.

Creusa. And you? Are you going to snatch the house out of a childless woman's hands?

Ion. Was there no share at all of my father's for me?

Creusa. Whatever his shield and his spear won. That is your whole inheritance.

Ion. Leave the altar. Leave the god's seat.

Creusa. Go and lecture your own mother, wherever she is.

Ion. And you will pay no penalty for trying to kill me?

Creusa. Only if you are willing to butcher me inside this sanctuary.

Ion. What pleasure is there for you in dying among the god's sacred wreaths?

Creusa. I will hurt somebody who has hurt me.

Ion. Ah. It is a terrible thing, how badly the god has made the laws for mortals, with no clever judgement behind them. Criminals should not be allowed to sit at an altar. They should be driven off. It is not right for a dirty hand to touch what belongs to the gods. The just, the people who have been wronged, should have the sacred seats. Not this, where the good man and the bad walk up to the same place and get the same treatment from the gods.

(The Priestess of Apollo comes out of the temple carrying an old wicker cradle.)

Priestess. Stop, my son. I have left the tripod where the oracles are given and stepped across this threshold. I am Apollo's Priestess, the keeper of the tripod's ancient custom, chosen out of all the women of Delphi.

Ion. Welcome, mother. My dear mother, though you never bore me.

Priestess. Well, that is what I am called, and I do not mind the name.

Ion. Did you hear how this woman schemed to kill me?

Priestess. I heard. And you are in the wrong as well, being so savage.

Ion. Should I not kill the people who try to kill me?

Priestess. Wives always hate the children of an earlier marriage.

Ion. And we hate our stepmothers, when they treat us badly.

Priestess. Do not. You are leaving the temple and going home to your own country, and so you should—

Ion. What should I do, then, if I am to be advised?

Priestess. Go to Athens with clean hands, under good omens.

Ion. Anyone who kills his enemies has clean hands.

Priestess. Not you. Take the words I have for you, and listen.

Ion. Say them. You mean me well. Whatever you say will come from that.

Priestess. Do you see this basket I am carrying in the crook of my arm?

Ion. I see an old cradle, with the sacred wool bands still tied round it.

Priestess. This is what I found you in, once, a new-born baby.

Ion. What? That is a new story you are bringing in.

Priestess. I kept it quiet. Now I am showing it.

Ion. Why did you hide it, all those years ago, when you took me in?

Priestess. The god wanted to keep you as his servant in his house.

Ion. And now he does not? How am I supposed to know that?

Priestess. He has told you who your father is. He is sending you out of this country.

Ion. Did he order you to keep this, or how do you come to have it?

Priestess. Apollo put it into my mind, that day—

Ion. To do what? Say it. Finish what you are saying.

Priestess. To keep what I had found, until the time that is here now.

Ion. And what does it hold for me? Gain, or harm?

Priestess. Hidden in here are the baby-clothes you were wrapped in.

Ion. You are bringing me clues to find my mother?

Priestess. Yes, because now the god wants it. Before, he did not.

Ion. This is a day of blessed things to see.

Priestess. Take them, then, and work hard at finding the woman who bore you.

Ion. I will search all of Asia, and to the borders of Europe.

Priestess. You will find that out for yourself. I brought you up for the god's sake, my child, and for his sake I am giving these back to you. He wanted me to take them and keep them safe, without ever telling me to; why he wanted it, I cannot say. No living person knew that we had them, or where they were hidden. Goodbye. I kiss you as your own mother would. Start your search for her where you have to start: first, was it some girl of Delphi who bore you and left you in this temple; and after that, was it any Greek girl at all. That is everything you will get from me, and from Apollo, who has had a share in your fortune.

(The Priestess goes back into the temple, leaving the cradle with Ion.)

Ion. Ah. Ah. The tears are running down my face. My mind has gone back to the day when the woman who bore me, married in secret, sold me off in secret and never gave me her breast. I had no name. I lived a servant's life in the god's house. What came from the god was good; what came from my luck was heavy. The time when I should have been spoilt in a mother's arms, tasting some pleasure in life, I was robbed of the dearest thing there is, a mother's care. And she is wretched too, the woman who bore me. She has suffered the same thing: she lost the joy of a son.

Now I will take this cradle and carry it to the god as an offering, so that I do not find anything in it I do not want to find. If it turns out some slave woman bore me, finding my mother would be worse than leaving her alone in silence. Apollo, I dedicate this to your temple. And yet, what am I doing? I am fighting the god's own wish. He kept my mother's tokens for me. It has to be opened. I have to have the nerve. Whatever is fated, I could never step past it. Sacred bands, what have you been hiding from me? And you, fastenings, that guarded what was mine and dear to me? Look at the lid on this rounded cradle. By some miracle it has not aged. There is no mould on the wickerwork, and yet a long time has gone by over these treasures.

Creusa. What am I seeing? A vision I never hoped for.

Ion. You be quiet. You have known plenty before this that—

Creusa. Silence is not for me. Do not tell me what to do. I can see the basket I once left you in, my child, when you were a baby still, no bigger than that, in the cave of Cecrops under the Long Rocks. I am leaving this altar, even if I have to die for it.

(Creusa comes down from the altar and runs to the cradle.)

Ion. Take hold of her. The god has driven her mad. She has leapt off the altar and left the carved images. Tie her arms.

Creusa. Go on and cut my throat, do not stop. I am going to hold on to this cradle, and to you, and to the things hidden in it that are yours.

Ion. Is this not monstrous? I am being seized and claimed with a story.

Creusa. No. You are being found. Found by the people who love you, as one of their own.

Ion. I am one of yours? And you were trying to murder me behind my back?

Creusa. You are my son, if a son is what parents hold dearest.

Ion. Stop weaving. I will catch you out, properly.

Creusa. Let me come to that. That is the mark I am shooting at, child.

Ion. Is this basket empty, or does it have something in it?

Creusa. Your clothes. The ones I left you in, once.

Ion. And you will name them before you see them?

Creusa. If I cannot describe them, I agree to die.

Ion. Speak. There is something frightening about your nerve.

Creusa. Look. A piece of weaving I made when I was a child—

Ion. What kind? Girls weave plenty of things.

Creusa. Not finished. A first lesson at the shuttle, more like.

Ion. What pattern? You will not catch me that way.

Creusa. A Gorgon, in the middle of the threads of the cloth.

Ion. Zeus. What fate is hunting me down?

Creusa. And the edge is fringed with snakes, like an aegis.

Ion. Look. There it is. The weaving. It is like finding an oracle come true.

Creusa. Oh, the work of my girlhood at the loom, after all this time.

Ion. Is there anything besides this, or does your luck stop at one?

Creusa. Snakes. An old thing, made of solid gold: Athena's gift. She tells us to bring our children up wearing them, copies of the snakes she set to guard Erichthonius, long ago.

Ion. To do what with? What are they for, the golden things? Tell me.

Creusa. Necklaces, for a new-born child to wear, my son.

Ion. Here they are, inside. The third thing. I want to know the third.

Creusa. I put a wreath of olive round you then, from the tree Athena first brought to her rock. If it is there, it has never lost its green. It is flourishing still, because it came from an olive that nothing can touch.

Ion. Mother. My dearest mother. I am so glad to see you, and I am kissing your face, and your face is glad too.

Creusa. My child. My light, brighter to your mother than the sun — the god will forgive me for that — I have you in my arms, found when I had stopped hoping, when I thought you were living under the ground with the dead and with Persephone.

Ion. But here I am, dear mother, in your arms, the one who died and did not die.

Creusa.
	Io, io. Wide bright folds of the sky,
	what voice can I find, what cry
	can I shout? Where did it come from,
	this pleasure I never looked for? Where
	did we get this joy?

Ion. Anything could have happened to me, mother, sooner than this: that I turn out to be yours.

Creusa. I am still trembling with fear.

Ion. That you are holding me and do not have me?

Creusa.
	I had thrown my hopes
	far away from me.
	Io, woman, where, where did you take my baby
	up into your arms?
	Whose hand carried him into the house of Apollo?

Ion. A god did this. But for the rest of our luck, let us be as fortunate as we were unfortunate before.

Creusa.
	Child, you were born in tears,
	and taken from your mother's arms with wailing,
	and now I breathe against your cheek
	and I have found the most blessed happiness there is.
Ion.
	When you say what you feel, you say it for both of us.
Creusa.
	I am not childless any more. No more without a son.
	The house has its hearth again, the land has its kings,
	Erechtheus is young again,
	and the house that was born from the earth no longer looks at night:
	it looks up at the sun's torches.

Ion. Mother, my father is here too. Let him share this happiness I have given the two of you.

Creusa.
	My child,
	what are you saying? How I am found out, how I am found out.
Ion.
	What do you mean?
Creusa.
	You come from somewhere else. Somewhere else.
Ion.
	Oh. Did you bear me as a girl, a bastard?
Creusa.
	No torches, no dancing,
	no wedding song of mine,
	child, when your head came into the world.
Ion.
	Aiai. My birth is shameful. Mother, where am I from?
Creusa.
	Let the Gorgon-killer be my witness—
Ion.
	What are you saying?
Creusa.
	She who sits on my rocks,
	on the hill where the olive grows,
	Athena, on her throne there—
Ion.
	You are speaking in riddles to me, not plainly.
Creusa.
	Beside the rock where the nightingales sing,
	with Apollo—
Ion.
	Why do you name Apollo?
Creusa.
	I lay in a bed he kept secret.
Ion.
	Go on. You are about to tell me something good, something lucky for me.
Creusa.
	And when the tenth month came round,
	I bore you, a hidden labour, to Apollo.
Ion.
	The dearest thing I have ever heard, if it is true.
Creusa.
	And as your baby-clothes I wrapped round you
	this, my girl's work, done in secret from my mother,
	the wanderings of my shuttle.
	I gave you no milk, no breast,
	none of a mother's nursing, no water from my hands to wash you.
	In an empty cave you were thrown out
	to be killed by the beaks of birds, a feast for them,
	thrown out to Hades.
Ion.
	Mother, what a terrible thing you had the heart to do.
Creusa.
	I was bound fast in fear, child,
	and I threw your life away.
	I killed you, and I did not want to.
Ion.
	And I nearly killed you. That would have been unholy.
Creusa.
	Io. Terrible, our fortunes then,
	and terrible these now. We are spun round
	from there to here, from bad luck into good luck again,
	and the winds are shifting.
	Let them hold. What went before was evil enough. Now
	let a fair wind rise out of the evil, my boy.

Chorus. Let no one, ever, think anything is past hoping for, when they look at what is happening now.

Ion. Fortune. You have already changed thousands of lives, into misery and then back into doing well. Look at the line my life came to: killing my mother, and suffering what I never deserved. Ah. Is this the kind of thing you can learn every day, inside the bright circle of the sun? Mother, I have found you, and finding you is dear to me, and as far as I am concerned there is nothing to complain of in my birth. But the rest I want to say to you alone. Come here. I want to say it in your ear and throw a cover of darkness over the whole business. Be careful, mother. Did you slip, the way girls do, into a secret affair, and then pin the blame on the god? Are you saying you bore me to Apollo to escape the shame of my birth, when it was not a god who fathered me?

Creusa. No. By Athena, Victory, who once stood shield to shield with Zeus in his chariot against the giants born from the earth: no mortal man is your father, my son. The one who brought you up is. Lord Apollo.

Ion. Then how could he give his own child to another father, and say I was Xuthus's son by birth?

Creusa. He did not say born. He is giving you, his own son, as a gift. A friend might give his own son to a friend, to be master of his house.

Ion. Whether the god speaks the truth or gives empty oracles, that is what is troubling my mind, mother, and it is a fair thing to be troubled by.

Creusa. Then listen to what has just come to me, child. Apollo is doing you a kindness. He is settling you in a noble house. If you had been called the god's son, you would never have had a house and a whole inheritance, or a father's name. How could you, when I was hiding the marriage myself, and killing you in secret? He is helping you, by handing you over to another father.

Ion. I am not going to chase this so lightly. I will go into the temple and ask Apollo himself whether I am a mortal man's son or his. Ah. Who is that, above the house where the incense burns, showing a face like the sun, a god's face? Run, mother. We should not be looking at the gods' business. Unless it is right that we see it.

(Athena appears above the temple.)

Athena. Do not run. I am not an enemy you are running from. I am well disposed to you in Athens and here alike. I am Pallas Athena, and your country is named after me. I have come at a run, sent by Apollo. He did not think it right to come into your sight himself, in case blame for what happened before came up between you. So he sends me to give you his words. This woman bore you, and Apollo is your father. He gives you to the man he gave you to, who did not beget you, so that you can be counted as belonging to a house of the noblest blood. When the business was uncovered and reported, he was afraid you would die by your mother's plotting and she by your hand, and he saved you both by his devices. The lord meant to keep all this silent and make it known in Athens: that she is your mother, and you were born of her and of Apollo, your father. But to finish the matter, and the god's oracles, which are why I yoked my chariot, listen, both of you.

Creusa, take this boy and go to the land of Cecrops, and set him on the royal throne. He is of Erechtheus's line, and he has the right to rule my country, and he will be famous through all Greece. His sons, four of them from one root, will give their names to the land and to the tribes of the people who live on my rock. Geleon will be the first. Then the second, the Hopletes, and the Argades, and the Aegicores, whose tribe takes its name from my aegis. And their children in turn, when the fated time comes, will settle the island cities of the Cyclades and the coasts of the mainland, which gives my country strength. They will settle the plains on either side of the strait, on the two continents, Asia and Europe, and for this boy's name's sake they will be called Ionians, and they will be famous. To you and Xuthus together a family is coming too: Dorus, from whom the Dorian city will be sung of through the land of Pelops; and the second, Achaeus, who will be king of the coast near Rhium, and a people will be marked out to carry his name. Apollo has done everything well. First, he brought you through childbirth without sickness, so that the people around you never knew. Then, when you had borne this child and put him out in his baby-clothes, he ordered Hermes to snatch the baby up in his arms and ferry him here, and he brought him up, and did not let him breathe out his life. So now, keep silent about this boy being yours, so that Xuthus can enjoy his belief in peace, and you, lady, can go home with your blessings in your hands. And goodbye to you both. After this breathing-space from your troubles, I announce a happy fate for you.

Ion. Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus the greatest, we accept your words without disbelief. I am convinced that I am Apollo's son, and hers. And even before, that was not hard to believe.

Creusa. Now hear from me. I praise Apollo, who I never praised before, because the child he neglected once, he is giving back to me. These gates look beautiful to me now, and the god's oracle too, when they were hateful before. Now I even hang gladly from the knockers on the doors, and I greet the gates.

Athena. I approve of your change, and of your speaking well of the god. What the gods do is always slow, somehow. But in the end it is not weak.

Creusa. My child, let us go home.

Athena. Go. I will follow you.

Creusa. A guide who is worthy of us.

Athena. And one who loves your city.

Creusa. Go and sit on the ancient throne.

Ion. It is a possession worth having.

Chorus. Apollo, son of Zeus and Leto, goodbye. Whoever's house is being driven hard by disaster should honour the gods and keep his courage. In the end the good get what they deserve, and the bad, being what they are, never do well.

Helen (412 BC)

Helen

(Egypt, on the island of Pharos, in front of the royal palace. The tomb of Proteus stands before the doors. Helen is sitting on it.)

Helen. This is the Nile, the river of the lovely nymphs. There is no rain from heaven here; when the white snow melts, it is the Nile that waters the plain of Egypt and its fields. Proteus, while he lived, was king of this land; he lived on the island of Pharos and was lord of Egypt, and he married one of the girls of the sea, Psamathe, after she had left the bed of Aeacus. She bore him two children in this house: a son, Theoclymenus, so called because he honoured the gods all his life, and a noble daughter, her mother's pride, who was called Eido when she was a baby. When she grew up and reached the age for marriage, they called her Theonoe, because she knew everything the gods know, everything that is and everything that is to come. That was an honour handed down to her from her ancestor Nereus.

As for me, my own country is not a nameless one: it is Sparta, and my father is Tyndareus. Though there is a story that Zeus flew to my mother Leda in the shape of a swan, pretending to run from an eagle, and got into her bed by that trick. If the story is true. My name is Helen. And what I have suffered, I will tell you.

Three goddesses came to a hollow on Mount Ida, to Paris, over the question of beauty: Hera, and Aphrodite, and the virgin daughter of Zeus. They wanted a judgement on their looks, and they wanted it settled. Aphrodite held out my beauty as the prize, if a thing that brings such misery can be called beauty: Paris was to have me for his wife. And she won. So Paris of Ida left his cattle stalls and came to Sparta, to take me to bed. But Hera was angry at losing to the other two, and she turned my marriage to Paris into a puff of wind. She gave the son of King Priam not me, but a breathing image, put together out of the sky and made to look like me. He thinks he has me. It is an empty thought. He has nothing.

And on top of these troubles Zeus had plans of his own. He brought a war on the land of the Greeks and on the poor Phrygians, to lighten mother earth of the swarming mass of mortals on her, and to make the strongest man in Greece famous. So I was set up as the prize the Greeks fought for, to test the courage of the Phrygians. Not me. My name. Hermes took me up into the folds of the air and wrapped me in a cloud, because Zeus had not forgotten me, and set me down here in the house of Proteus, whom he had picked out of all mankind as the most self-controlled man alive, so that I could keep my bed untouched for Menelaus. So here I am. And my poor husband gathered an army and went off to the towers of Troy, hunting for the wife who had been snatched from him. Many lives have been lost because of me on the banks of the Scamander. And I, who have endured all of it, am cursed. Everyone thinks I betrayed my husband and started a great war for the Greeks.

Then why am I still alive? Because I heard the god Hermes say that I would live again on the famous plain of Sparta, with my husband, since he knew I never went to Troy, and that I would never lie in another man's bed. Well, as long as Proteus was alive and saw this sunlight, I was safe from marriage. But now he is hidden in the dark of the earth, and the dead man's son is hunting me for his wife. So, for the sake of the husband I married long ago, I have thrown myself down here at Proteus's tomb as a suppliant, so that it will keep my bed safe for my husband. If I carry a filthy name all over Greece, at least my body will not bring me disgrace here.

(Teucer comes in, a bow in his hand. He stares at the palace, then sees Helen.)

Teucer. Who holds the power in this fortress of a house? You could set it beside the house of Wealth himself: the royal walls, the fine cornices on the buildings. Ah. Oh gods, what am I looking at? I see the murderous likeness of the woman I hate most in the world, the woman who destroyed me and every Achaean with me. May the gods spit you out, for how much you look like Helen. If I were not standing on foreign soil, this well-aimed arrow would have killed you by now, as your reward for looking like the daughter of Zeus.

Helen. Poor man. Whoever you are, why turn away from me like that, and hate me for the disasters that woman caused?

Teucer. I was wrong. I gave in to anger more than I should have. All Greece hates the daughter of Zeus. Forgive me for what I said, lady.

Helen. Who are you? Where have you come from, to set foot in this country?

Teucer. One of the Achaeans, lady. One of the unlucky ones.

Helen. Then it is no wonder you hate Helen. But who are you, and where from? Whose son should I call you?

Teucer. My name is Teucer. The father who begot me is Telamon, and Salamis is the land that raised me.

Helen. Then why are you visiting these fields of the Nile?

Teucer. I am an exile. I have been driven out of my father's country.

Helen. That is hard on you. Who threw you out of your homeland?

Teucer. Telamon, my own father. Who could be closer to you than that?

Helen. But why? There is some disaster in this somewhere.

Teucer. My brother Ajax died at Troy, and that destroyed me.

Helen. How? You did not take his life with your own sword, surely?

Teucer. He threw himself on his own sword. That is what killed him.

Helen. Was he mad? Who in his right mind would have the nerve to do that?

Teucer. You know of a certain Achilles, the son of Peleus?

Helen. Yes. He came to Sparta once as a suitor for Helen, so we hear.

Teucer. When he died, he left his allies a quarrel over his armour.

Helen. And how did that turn into harm for Ajax?

Teucer. Somebody else got the armour, and he left his life.

Helen. So you are sick with his sufferings?

Teucer. Yes. Because I did not die along with him.

Helen. So you went to the famous city of Troy, stranger?

Teucer. I did, and I helped to sack it, and I was destroyed in return.

Helen. Has it been set on fire already, and burned to the ground?

Teucer. So that not a trace of the walls can be seen.

Helen. Poor Helen. Because of you the Phrygians are dead.

Teucer. And the Achaeans too. Great evils have been done.

Helen. How long is it since the city fell?

Teucer. Nearly seven years. Seven rounds of harvests.

Helen. And how long were you at Troy before that?

Teucer. Many moons. Ten years' worth of them.

Helen. And did you take the Spartan woman?

Teucer. Menelaus took her. He dragged her off by the hair.

Helen. Did you see the wretched woman yourself? Or is it something you heard?

Teucer. With my own eyes. As plainly as I see you now, no less.

Helen. Consider whether what you saw was an illusion sent by the gods.

Teucer. Talk about something else. Not that woman. Not any more.

Helen. You are that sure your illusion was solid?

Teucer. I saw it with my own eyes. And the mind has eyes too.

Helen. And Menelaus is home already, with his wife?

Teucer. No. He is not in Argos, and not by the streams of the Eurotas.

Helen. Aiai. That is bad news, for anyone it is bad news for.

Teucer. The story is that he vanished, and his wife with him.

Helen. Did all the Argives not sail home the same way?

Teucer. They did. But a storm scattered them, each one somewhere different.

Helen. On what stretch of the salt sea?

Teucer. Crossing the open Aegean, midway over.

Helen. And since then nobody has seen Menelaus come to land?

Teucer. Nobody. All over Greece they say he is dead.

Helen. I am finished. And the daughter of Thestius, is she alive?

Teucer. Leda, you mean? She is dead and gone.

Helen. It was not Helen's shameful name that killed her, surely?

Teucer. They say it was. She tied a noose round her noble neck.

Helen. And the sons of Tyndareus, are they alive or not?

Teucer. Dead, and not dead. There are two stories.

Helen. Which is the stronger? Oh, what a wretched heap of evils I have.

Teucer. They say the two of them have become gods, in the shape of stars.

Helen. That is good to hear. And the other story?

Teucer. That they cut their own throats because of their sister. But enough talk. I do not need to grieve twice over. As for why I came to this royal house: I want to see the prophetess Theonoe. Be my sponsor here and introduce me, so I can get an oracle from her about which way to steer my ship's sail on a fair wind to Cyprus, the island in the sea where Apollo has told me I am to live, and to give the place the island name of Salamis, in memory of the homeland I left behind.

Helen. The voyage will show you the way itself, stranger. But leave this country, get out, before the son of Proteus sees you. He rules this land. He is away just now, out with his hounds, killing wild animals and trusting them to do it. He kills every Greek stranger he catches. Why he does it, do not try to find out, and I will not say. What good would it do you?

Teucer. Well said, lady. May the gods pay you back with good things for your kindness. You have Helen's body, but you do not have her heart. Yours is a very different one. May she die badly, and never reach the streams of the Eurotas. And may you have good luck always, lady.

(Teucer goes.)

Helen.
	Oh. As I lay the foundations of a great lament for great griefs,
	what kind of cry shall I struggle to raise? What Muse shall I go to
	with tears, or dirges, or mourning? Aiai.
Helen.
	Winged girls,
	virgin daughters of the Earth,
	Sirens, come to my crying,
	and bring the Libyan
	flute, or the pipes, or
	the lyre, and tears to match
	my wailing griefs.
	Pain for pain, song for song,
	let Persephone send
	a choir of the dead
	to sing along with my mourning,
	so that under her dark roof
	she may have from me, along with my tears,
	a hymn of thanks
	for the dead who are gone.
Chorus.
	Beside the dark blue water,
	on the curling grass,
	I was spreading purple cloaks
	in the sun's golden rays
	to dry among the young reeds,
	and I heard my mistress
	cry out in misery from where she sat:
	a wail, a song with no lyre in it,
	a shriek of grief, as she groaned
	her cries of Aiai, the way a nymph,
	a Naiad, up in the mountains,
	running, throws out a wailing note,
	and under the hollows of the rocks
	screams that Pan
	has caught her and forced her.
Helen.
	Io, io.
	Girls of Greece, the catch of a barbarian oar,
	a sailor came, an Achaean sailor,
	he came, he came, bringing me tears on top of tears.
	Troy is torn down,
	and it belongs to the enemy's fire,
	because of me, the killer of so many,
	because of my name, the cause of so much pain.
	And Leda died in a noose,
	from the agony of my disgrace.
	And my husband, after all his wandering on the sea,
	is dead and gone,
	and Castor and his brother,
	the twin glory of their homeland,
	have vanished, vanished, and left the plains
	that rang under their horses, and the wrestling grounds
	along the reedy Eurotas,
	where the young men trained.
Chorus.
	Aiai, aiai.
	Lady, what a fate you were dealt, what a destiny of groans.
	A life that is no life
	fell to you, fell to you, when Zeus begot you on your mother,
	flashing through the sky
	on the snow-white wing of a swan.
	What evil have you been spared?
	What life have you not endured?
	Your mother is gone,
	the twin sons of Zeus, your dear brothers,
	have no happiness,
	you cannot see your own country,
	and through the cities runs
	a rumour that hands you over,
	my lady, to a barbarian's bed.
	Your husband has left his life
	in the sea and the waves, and never again
	will you make your father's halls glad,
	or Athena of the Bronze House.
Helen.
	Pheu, pheu. Who was it, a Phrygian
	or someone from the land of Greece,
	who cut the pine
	that brought tears to Troy?
	From it the son of Priam
	built his deadly boat, and rowed
	with barbarian oars
	to my hearth,
	after my beauty, the most unlucky
	beauty there ever was, to take me
	for his bride. And with him came the trickster,
	the killer of so many, Aphrodite,
	bringing death to the sons of Danaus and the sons of Priam.
	Oh, I am wretched in my misfortune.
	And Hera, holy Hera, whom Zeus holds in his arms
	on her golden throne,
	sent the swift-footed son of Maia,
	and he found me gathering fresh rose petals
	into the fold of my dress,
	on my way to Athena of the Bronze House,
	and snatched me up through the sky
	to this luckless land, and made me
	a quarrel, a wretched quarrel
	between Greece and the sons of Priam.
	And my name
	by the streams of the Simois
	carries a story that is a lie.

Chorus. You have pain, I know. But it is best to bear the things life forces on us as lightly as we can.

Helen. Dear friends, what a fate I am yoked to. Did my mother give birth to me as a freak, for people to stare at? No woman, Greek or barbarian, lays a white egg with chicks in it, and they say that is what Leda bore me in, to Zeus. My whole life, everything about me, is a freak, partly because of Hera, and partly because my beauty is to blame. If only I could be wiped out like a painting and drawn again, uglier this time, instead of beautiful, and the Greeks would forget the evil luck I have now and remember what is not evil in me, the way they now remember only the evil.

When someone fixes his eyes on a single misfortune and is ill-treated by the gods, it is heavy, but it can be borne. But I lie under a whole heap of troubles. First: I have done nothing wrong, and my name is filth. And that is worse than the truth would be, to be saddled with evils that are not your own. Second: the gods have taken me out of my own country and set me down among barbarian ways, and stripped of everyone I owe, I have become a slave, though I was born of free people, because among barbarians everyone is a slave except one man. And the one anchor that held my fortunes steady, the hope that my husband would come one day and free me from my troubles: he is dead. He does not exist any more. My mother is dead, and I am her murderer. Unjustly, but the injustice is mine to carry. The child who was born to be the glory of the house and of me, my daughter, is going grey as an unmarried virgin. And the two they call the Dioscuri, the sons of Zeus, are no more. With everything I have gone wrong, I am dead as far as my circumstances go, though not in fact. And this is the last and worst of it: if I ever did get home, they would bar the doors against me, thinking I was that Helen from Troy, coming home at Menelaus's side. If my husband were alive, we could have recognised each other by falling back on the tokens only the two of us know. But now that is gone, and he will never be saved.

Then why am I still alive? What fortune is left for me? Shall I choose marriage as a way out of my troubles, and live with a barbarian man, sitting at his rich table? But when a woman lives with a husband she hates, her own body becomes hateful to her too. Death is best. And how could I die well? Hanging, high in the air, is ugly; even slaves think it is beneath them. The knife has something noble and fine about it, and the moment when the flesh is set free from life is a short one. That is how deep into evil I have come. Other women are lucky because of their beauty. Mine is the very thing that has destroyed me.

Chorus. Helen, whoever that stranger was who came here, do not assume that everything he said was true.

Helen. And yet he said quite clearly that my husband is dead.

Chorus. A great many words can be said that turn out to be lies.

Helen. And the opposite of a lie is plain, and true.

Chorus. You are being carried towards the disaster, instead of the good.

Helen. Yes. Fear has wrapped its arms round me and is leading me straight to the thing I am afraid of.

Chorus. How much goodwill do you have in this house?

Helen. Everyone is my friend, except the one who is hunting me for his bed.

Chorus. Then do you know what you should do? Leave your seat on this tomb and

Helen. And what advice are you creeping towards?

Chorus. Go into the house and ask Theonoe, who knows everything, the daughter of the sea nymph, the child of Nereus's line, about your husband: whether he is still alive or has left the light of day. And when you know for certain, then rejoice or mourn, whichever fits your luck. Before you know anything for sure, what good does it do you to grieve? Listen to me. Leave this tomb and go and join the girl. You have someone in this house who can tell you the whole truth; why look any further? And I want to go in with you, and hear the girl's prophecies with you. Women should share each other's troubles.

Helen.
	Friends, I take your advice.
	Go in, go into the house,
	and inside these walls
	learn how my struggle ends.
Chorus.
	You are calling one who is more than willing.
Helen.
	Io. What a wretched day.
	What word, what tearful word
	am I going to hear, wretched as I am?
Chorus.
	Do not go prophesying pain,
	dear friend, and mourn before the time.
Helen.
	What has my poor husband suffered?
	Does he see the light,
	and the sun's four-horse chariot, and the paths of the stars,
	or down among the dead under the earth
	does he have his lasting fate?
Chorus.
	Put the best face on what is coming,
	whatever it turns out to be.
Helen.
	I call on you, I swear by you,
	Eurotas, green with your watery reeds:
	if this report is true
	that my husband is dead,
	and what was hard to understand in it?
	I will stretch a deadly noose
	round my neck, or drive a sword
	to the kill, a thrust through my throat
	gushing blood, iron forced into flesh,
	a race to the end, a sacrifice
	to the three goddesses and to the son of Priam
	who used to sit in the hollows of Ida
	beside his cattle stalls.
Chorus.
	May the evil be turned away somewhere else,
	and may your luck be good.
Helen.
	Io, poor Troy.
	For things that were never done, you are destroyed,
	and you have suffered pitiably. The gift Aphrodite gave me
	brought forth blood, so much blood,
	and so many tears. Grief on grief,
	tears on tears it took, and pain:
	mothers lost their sons,
	and girls cut off their hair
	for their dead brothers, by the swollen
	Phrygian water of the Scamander.
	And Greece cried out, cried out,
	and broke into wailing,
	and laid her hands on her head,
	and with her nails she drenched her soft cheeks
	in bloody blows.
	Oh, Callisto, girl of Arcadia, blessed once,
	who climbed into the bed of Zeus on four paws,
	how much better your lot was than my mother's:
	you took the shape of a shaggy-limbed beast,
	the form of a lioness with a fierce eye,
	and traded your load of grief for it.
	And the one Artemis once drove out of her dancing,
	the Titan girl, the daughter of Merops,
	as a deer with golden horns, because of her beauty:
	she was blessed too. But my body
	has destroyed, destroyed the towers of Dardanus's city
	and the Achaeans, who are gone.

(Helen and the Chorus go into the house. Menelaus comes in alone, in rags.)

Menelaus. Pelops, you who raced Oenomaus long ago in the four-horse chariot race at Pisa: if only, on the day they talked you into giving the gods a banquet, you had left your life then and there, among the gods, before you ever fathered my father Atreus, who begot Agamemnon and me, Menelaus, from his marriage to Aerope. A famous pair. I believe, and I say it without boasting, that I carried the largest army that ever crossed the sea by oar to Troy, and I was no tyrant driving troops by force; the young men of Greece came because they wanted to, and I led them. Some of them can be counted among the dead now. Others were glad to escape the sea, and brought home the names of the dead. But I have been wandering wretchedly over the swell of the grey salt sea ever since I sacked the towers of Troy, and though I long to reach my own country, the gods do not think I deserve to get there. I have sailed to every desolate, unfriendly landing place in Libya, and whenever I get near my homeland the wind shoves me back again, and never once has a fair breeze filled my sail and let me come home.

And now I am thrown up on this coast, a wretched shipwrecked man who has lost his friends. My ship is smashed against the rocks into more pieces of wreckage than I can count. Out of all its clever joinery only the keel was left, and on it I was saved, barely, by a luck I never hoped for. I, and Helen, whom I tore away from Troy and have with me. What this country is called and what people live here, I do not know. I was ashamed to be seen by a crowd and ask, so I hid these rags of mine, out of shame for my bad luck. When a man of high position does badly, the strangeness of it hits him harder than it hits a man who has been unlucky all along. Need is grinding me down. There is no food, and there are no clothes on my body; you can judge for yourself, what I have on is what the ship threw up. The fine robes and bright cloaks and luxuries I used to wear, the sea has snatched all of them. I have hidden the woman who started every one of my troubles deep in a cave, and I have made the friends I have left guard my wife, and I have come here alone, looking for what those friends of mine over there need, if I can find it by searching. When I saw this house with its cornice running round it, and the grand gates of some prosperous man, I came up to it. Sailors can hope to get something from a wealthy house. From people with no living of their own, they could not help us even if they wanted to.

Hey! Is there a doorkeeper who could come out of the house and take word of my troubles in to the people inside?

(An Old Woman opens the door and stands in it.)

Old Woman. Who is at the door? Get away from the house. Do not stand there at the courtyard gate making a nuisance of yourself to my masters. Or you will die, because you were born a Greek, and Greeks have no business here.

Menelaus. Old woman, you could say all of that in a different tone. I will do what you tell me. Just stop shouting.

Old Woman. Get away from here. That is my one job, stranger: no Greek comes near this house.

Menelaus. Ah. Keep your hands off me. Do not shove.

Old Woman. You will not listen to a word I say. That is your own fault.

Menelaus. Go inside and tell your masters that I am here.

Old Woman. And I would be the one to pay for it, I think, if I carried your message in.

Menelaus. I am a shipwrecked man, a stranger and a guest. People like me are not to be touched.

Old Woman. Then go and find some other house instead of this one.

Menelaus. No. I am going in. Do as I tell you.

Old Woman. You are being a nuisance, I warn you. And you will be thrown out any minute now, by force.

Menelaus. Aiai. Where are my famous armies now?

Old Woman. You were somebody over there, I suppose. You are nobody here.

Menelaus. Oh, my fortune. To be treated with this contempt, and deserve none of it.

Old Woman. Why are you wetting your eyes with tears? Who are you crying to?

Menelaus. To the way things used to be. To my old happiness.

Old Woman. Then go away and give your tears to your friends.

Menelaus. What country is this? Whose palace is this?

Old Woman. Proteus lives in this house. The country is Egypt.

Menelaus. Egypt? Oh, misery. Look where I have sailed to.

Old Woman. And what is wrong with the shining Nile, that you complain of it?

Menelaus. I was not complaining about the Nile. I am groaning at my own luck.

Old Woman. Plenty of people are doing badly. You are not the only one.

Menelaus. So is he in the house, this king you named?

Old Woman. This is his tomb. His son rules the country.

Menelaus. And where would the son be? Out, or in the house?

Old Woman. Not inside. And he is the worst enemy the Greeks have.

Menelaus. What has he got against them? I am the one who has paid for it.

Old Woman. Helen is in this house. The daughter of Zeus.

Menelaus. What did you say? What are you telling me? Say it again.

Old Woman. Tyndareus's daughter, the one who used to live in Sparta.

Menelaus. Where did she come from? What is the story?

Old Woman. She came here from the land of Lacedaemon.

Menelaus. When? I have not had my wife stolen out of the cave, have I?

Old Woman. Before the Achaeans went to Troy, stranger. Now get away from the house. Something is going on inside, a stroke of luck that has the whole house in an uproar. You have come at the worst possible moment. If my master catches you, death is the gift you will get as his guest. I am on the Greeks' side myself, whatever bitter things I said to you. That was fear of my master talking.

(The Old Woman goes back into the palace.)

Menelaus. What can I say? What can I make of this? After everything that went before, what I am hearing now is one more misery to add to the pile. I come here bringing my wife, the wife I took back from Troy, and she is safe in the cave, and some other woman with the same name as my wife is living in this house. The old woman said she was born a daughter of Zeus. Is there some man by the banks of the Nile with the name Zeus? There is only one in the sky. And where on earth is there a Sparta, except the one place, by the streams of the Eurotas with its lovely reeds? Tyndareus is a name one man has, and no other. What country shares a name with Lacedaemon, or with Troy? I do not know what to say.

But then, there are probably many people in the wide world who have the same names, one city with another and one woman with another. There is nothing to be amazed at. And I am not going to run away from a servant's frightening talk, either. No man alive is so barbarian in his heart that he would hear my name and refuse me a meal. The fire of Troy is famous, and so am I, the man who lit it: Menelaus, and not unknown in any country on earth. I will wait for the master of the house. He gives me two things to watch for. If he is a savage sort of man, I will keep myself out of sight and go back to the wreck. If he shows some softness, I will ask him for what my present trouble calls for.

This is the last and worst of the evils that have come on me in my misery, to go begging my living from other kings when I am a king myself. But it has to be. The saying is not mine, but it is a wise one: nothing is stronger than dreadful Necessity.

Chorus.
	I heard the girl who sings the god's answers,
	what she made plain to the royal house:
	that Menelaus is not yet gone
	down into the dark where light goes black,
	hidden in the earth.
	No. He is still out on the salt swell,
	worn to nothing, and has not yet touched
	the harbours of his own country.
	Wandering for his living,
	wretched, with no friend left of all his friends,
	setting his foot on every kind of shore,
	his oar in the sea,
	out of the land of Troy.

(Helen comes back from the palace towards the tomb.)

Helen. Here I am, back again to my seat at this tomb, and I have heard the words I wanted from Theonoe, who knows everything, and knows it truly. She says my husband is alive and in the light, and looking at the sun. She says he has sailed the straits of the sea ten thousand times over, driven this way and that, and that he is no beginner at wandering by now, and that he will come here, when his troubles find their end. One thing she did not say: whether, once he has come, he will get away alive. And I held back from asking her that outright. I was so glad when she told me he was safe. She said he was somewhere near this country, thrown up on the shore, shipwrecked, with a few friends. Oh, when will you come? How I have longed for you to come.

Ah. Who is this? I am not being ambushed, am I, by some scheme of Proteus's godless son? Shall I not run for the tomb like a racing filly, or a Bacchant of the god, and throw my legs at it? There is something wild about the look of this man who is hunting me down.

Menelaus. You there. The woman straining so desperately to reach the base of the tomb and the pillars where the offerings are burned. Stop. Why are you running? You have shown me your body, and the sight has knocked me senseless. I cannot speak.

Helen. Women, I am being wronged. This man is keeping me from the tomb. He wants to catch me and hand me over to the king, whose marriage I have been running from.

Menelaus. I am no thief, and I do not do bad men's dirty work.

Helen. And yet the clothes on your body are ugly enough.

Menelaus. Stop running. Let go of your fear and stand still.

Helen. I am standing still, now that I have my hand on this place.

Menelaus. Who are you? Whose face is this I am looking at, woman?

Helen. And who are you? The same question fits us both.

Menelaus. I have never seen a body so like hers.

Helen. Oh, gods. Recognising the people you love is a god too.

Menelaus. Are you a Greek woman, or from this country?

Helen. Greek. But I want to hear about you too.

Menelaus. You look more like Helen than anyone I have ever seen, woman.

Helen. And you like Menelaus. I do not know what to say.

Menelaus. You have recognised him right. The unluckiest man alive.

Helen. Oh, at last. At last you have come to your wife's arms.

Menelaus. Wife? What wife? Do not touch my clothes.

Helen. The wife Tyndareus, my father, gave you.

Menelaus. Hecate, torch-bearer, send me visions that mean me no harm.

Helen. You are not looking at a ghost of the night, one of the servants of the goddess of the crossroads.

Menelaus. One man cannot be the husband of two women. I am not.

Helen. And what other bed are you master of?

Menelaus. The woman the cave is hiding. The one I am bringing home from the Phrygians.

Helen. There is no other wife of yours. There is only me.

Menelaus. Am I in my right mind, and it is my eyes that are sick?

Helen. When you look at me, do you not think you are looking at your wife?

Menelaus. The body is the same. What I know for certain takes it away again.

Helen. Look. What more do you need? Who knows better than you do?

Menelaus. You are like her. That much I will not deny.

Helen. Then who is going to teach you, if not your own eyes?

Menelaus. That is where I am sick. I have another wife.

Helen. I never went to Troy. That was a phantom.

Menelaus. And who manufactures bodies that can see?

Helen. The air. That is where your wife came from. The gods laboured over her.

Menelaus. Which god shaped her? You are telling me things nobody could hope for.

Helen. Hera. A substitute, so that Paris would not get me.

Menelaus. Then how could you be here and in Troy at the same time?

Helen. A name can be in many places at once. A body cannot.

Menelaus. Let go of me. I came here with grief enough already.

Helen. You are going to leave me? And take away that empty bed?

Menelaus. Yes. And good luck to you, for looking so like Helen.

Helen. I am finished. I found my husband, and I will not have him.

Menelaus. The size of what I went through over there convinces me. You do not.

Helen. Oh, no. Was any woman ever more wretched than I am? The people I love most are leaving me, and I will never reach the Greeks, or my own country. Never.

(Menelaus's old sailor comes in, hurrying.)

Messenger. Menelaus. I have found you at last. I have been searching for you all over this barbarian country. The comrades you left behind sent me.

Menelaus. What is it? You are not being robbed by the barbarians?

Messenger. It is a marvel. And the word is smaller than the thing.

Menelaus. Tell me. Hurrying like that, you are bringing something new.

Messenger. I am telling you that you went through ten thousand labours for nothing.

Menelaus. You are mourning old troubles. What is your news?

Messenger. Your wife is gone. She was lifted up into the folds of the air and vanished. The sky is hiding her. She left the holy cave where we were guarding her, and this is all she said. "Poor Phrygians, and all you Achaeans. It was for me that you kept dying on the banks of the Scamander, by Hera's contriving, thinking Paris had Helen when he did not. And I, now that I have stayed as long as I was meant to stay and kept what fate required, am going away to the sky, to my father. And the poor daughter of Tyndareus has heard evil said of her name for nothing. She was not to blame at all."

(He turns and sees Helen standing there.)

Well. Greetings, daughter of Leda. You were here all the time, were you? I was just announcing that you had gone off to the hidden places of the stars, and I had no idea you were carrying a body with wings on it. I am not going to let you make fools of us like this a second time. You gave your husband and his allies trouble enough at Troy.

Menelaus. That is it. That is the answer. Her words fit together, and they are true. Oh, the day I longed for, that has given you to my arms to hold.

Helen. Menelaus, dearest of men, the time was long, but the joy is here now, at last. I have my husband back, friends, and I am glad, and I have wrapped my loving arms around him, after the long fire of so many days' light.

Menelaus. And I have you. And there is so much to say between us that I do not know where to begin.

Helen.
	I am so happy the hair stands up on my head
	and my tears run down.
	I have thrown my arms round your body,
	husband, to take my joy.
Menelaus.
	Dearest sight. I have no complaint.
	I have the daughter of Zeus and Leda,
	the girl her brothers on their white horses
	blessed, and blessed, under the torches,
	long ago. The god who took you out of my house
	is driving us on now
	to another fortune, better than this one.
	An evil that turned good has brought you together with me, your husband,
	after so long. Still, let me get some good of my luck.

Chorus. Good luck to you. I pray the same thing. When there are two of you, the one cannot suffer and the other not.

Helen.
	Friends, my friends, the old things:
	I do not groan for them any more. It does not hurt.
	I have my husband, I have him, the man I waited for,
	waited for, all those years, to come from Troy.
Menelaus.
	You have me, and I have you. Ten thousand suns
	I barely lived through, and now I understand what the goddess did.
	My tears are tears of joy. There is more
	gladness in them than grief.
Helen.
	What can I say? What mortal ever hoped for this?
	I hold you against my breast, and never thought I would.
Menelaus.
	And I hold you, the woman I thought had gone
	to the city under Ida and the wretched towers of Troy.
	By the gods, how were you taken out of my house?
Helen.
	E, e. That is a bitter beginning you are starting on.
	E, e. That is a bitter story you are asking for.

Menelaus. Tell it. Everything the gods give has to be heard.

Helen. I spit on the story I am about to tell. The very story.

Menelaus. Tell it anyway. It is sweet, hearing about hard times.

Helen.
	Not to the bed of a young barbarian,
	on flying oars,
	on the flying wings of a lust for a lawless marriage.
Menelaus.
	Then what god, or what fate, robbed you from your country?
Helen.
	The son of Zeus, of Zeus, my husband: Hermes.
	He brought me to the Nile.

Menelaus. Astonishing. And who sent him? What a dreadful story.

Helen. I have wept and wept, and my eyes are wet with tears now. The wife of Zeus destroyed me.

Menelaus. Hera? What did she want with heaping evil on the two of us?

Helen.
	Oh, my dreadful story. The baths and the springs
	where the goddesses made their beauty shine,
	and from there the judging came.
Menelaus.
	And the judging. Hera made it the cause of all this for you?
Helen.
	To take me away from Paris.
Menelaus.
	How? Tell me.
Helen.
	The man Aphrodite had promised me to.
Menelaus.
	Oh, poor woman.
Helen.
	Poor, poor. And so she brought me to Egypt.
Menelaus.
	Then she gave him a phantom in your place, from what I hear from you.
Helen.
	And the sufferings in your house, the sufferings,
	mother. Oh, no.

Menelaus. What do you mean?

Helen. My mother is dead. She tied a strangling noose round her neck, for shame of my disgraceful marriage.

Menelaus. Oh. And our daughter Hermione. Is she alive?

Helen.
	Unmarried, childless, husband, she mourns
	my marriage that was no marriage.
Menelaus.
	Paris, who sacked my whole house from top to bottom,
	this destroyed you too, and tens of thousands
	of Greeks in their bronze armour.
Helen.
	And me the god threw out of my country,
	cursed, doomed, out of my city and away from you,
	when I left my house and my bed, and did not leave them,
	for a shameful marriage.

Chorus. If the rest of your luck turns out happy, it might make up for what went before.

Messenger. Menelaus, give me a share of this happiness too. I can see it for myself, but I do not understand it clearly.

Menelaus. Come, old man. You join the conversation too.

Messenger. This woman here is not the one all that trouble at Troy was fought over?

Menelaus. No, she is not. We were tricked by the gods. What we had in our arms was the grim image of a cloud.

Messenger. What are you saying? We went through all that for a cloud? For nothing?

Menelaus. Hera's work. And the quarrel of the three goddesses.

Messenger. And this woman here really is your wife?

Menelaus. She is. Take my word for it.

Messenger. Daughter, what a complicated thing the god is, how hard to make out. Somehow, and for the good, he turns everything over, carrying it this way and that. One man labours. Another never laboured at all, and comes to a bad end just the same, with nothing to hold on to in a fortune that never stops changing. You and your husband have had your share of trouble, you in what people said of you, he in the heat of his fighting. When he pushed, and pushed hard, he got nothing. Now he has the best good fortune there is, and it came to him of its own accord.

So you never disgraced your old father after all, or the twin sons of Zeus, and you never did the things they say you did. I am seeing your wedding all over again now. I remember the torches I carried, running beside the four-horse team, and you in the chariot, a bride, leaving your happy home with this man here. A servant who does not care about his master's affairs, who does not rejoice with him and ache with him when things go wrong, is worthless. I was born a slave, but let me be counted among the noble slaves all the same. I do not have the name of a free man. I have the mind of one. That is better than the double evil of one man carrying a rotten heart and, slave that he is, taking orders from everyone around him too.

Menelaus. Come, old man. You have carried out plenty of hard labour beside my shield, sweating it out for me. Now share my good fortune too. Go and tell the friends I left behind how you found things here, and where our luck stands. Tell them to wait on the shore and keep watch for the struggles that I expect are waiting for me; and if we can find some way to steal this woman out of the country, tell them to stand guard, so that we can throw our luck in together and get away from the barbarians, if we can.

Messenger. It will be done, my lord. But I tell you, I have seen now how worthless the prophets' business is, and how full of lies. There was nothing sound, after all, in the flame of the burnt offering, or in the cries of birds. To think that birds can help human beings is simple-minded. Calchas never said a word, never gave the army a sign, when he saw his friends dying for a cloud. Nor did Helenus. The city was torn down for nothing. You might say: because the god did not want them to. Then why do we consult prophets at all? We should sacrifice to the gods and ask them for good things, and leave prophecy alone. It was invented as a bait, a way of making a living and nothing more, and no one ever got rich from burnt offerings by being lazy. Good judgement and good sense are the best prophets there are.

(The Messenger goes off towards the shore.)

Chorus. My opinion of prophets comes out exactly where this old man's does. Whoever has the gods for friends has the best prophecy there is, at home.

Helen. Well. So far, everything is going well. But how you came out of Troy alive, poor man: there is nothing to gain from knowing it, but people who love you long to hear what the people they love have suffered.

Menelaus. That is a great deal to ask in one question and one breath. Why should I tell you about the wrecks in the Aegean, and Nauplius's false beacons on Euboea, and Crete, and the cities of Libya I put in at, and the lookout of Perseus? I could never fill you up with stories, and telling you the evils I would suffer them all over again, as I did when I was living through them. I would grieve twice over.

Helen. That is a better answer than my question. Leave out all the rest and tell me one thing: how long were you worn down on the back of the sea, wandering the salt water?

Menelaus. On top of the ten years at Troy, I went through seven circling years on board ship.

Helen. Pheu, pheu. That is a long time you name, poor man. And after coming out of that alive, you have come here to be slaughtered.

Menelaus. What do you mean? What are you going to say? You have finished me, woman.

Helen. Run. Get out of this country as fast as you can. The man whose house this is will kill you.

Menelaus. What have I done to deserve that?

Helen. You have turned up, out of nowhere, in the way of my marriage.

Menelaus. What? Someone wants to marry my wife?

Helen. And to do me the outrage I have been putting up with.

Menelaus. Some private strongman, or the man who rules the country?

Helen. The man who is king of this land. The son of Proteus.

Menelaus. That is the riddle I heard from the servant.

Helen. Which of the barbarian's gates were you standing at?

Menelaus. This one. I was being driven off it like a beggar.

Helen. You were not begging for food? Oh, misery.

Menelaus. That is what it was. It just did not have that name.

Helen. Then you know everything about my marriage, it seems.

Menelaus. I know. What I do not know is whether you escaped his bed.

Helen. You can be sure your bed has been kept for you. Untouched.

Menelaus. What proves it? If you are telling the truth, it is sweet to hear.

Helen. Do you see my miserable seat here at this tomb?

Menelaus. I see a wretched bed of straw. What has it got to do with you?

Helen. This is where I have been begging, as a suppliant, to escape his bed.

Menelaus. For lack of an altar? Or is that the barbarians' custom?

Helen. This has protected me as well as the temples of the gods.

Menelaus. So I cannot even sail you home?

Helen. A sword is waiting for you, sooner than my bed.

Menelaus. Then I would be the most wretched of mortals.

Helen. Do not be ashamed now. Run. Get out of this country.

Menelaus. And leave you? I sacked Troy for your sake.

Helen. Yes. Better that than let my marriage kill you.

Menelaus. That is a coward's talk, and unworthy of Troy.

Helen. You could not kill the king, which is what you have in mind, I suppose.

Menelaus. What, has he got a body that iron cannot wound?

Helen. You will find out. But daring the impossible is not what a clever man does.

Menelaus. So I am to hold out my hands and let them be tied, in silence?

Helen. You are at a dead end. We need some contrivance.

Menelaus. Yes. Better to die doing something than doing nothing.

Helen. There is one hope. Only one way we could be saved.

Menelaus. Do we buy it, or dare it, or talk our way to it?

Helen. If the king never found out that you had come.

Menelaus. And who is going to tell him? He will not know who I am.

Helen. He has an ally inside the house, as good as a god.

Menelaus. Some voice, settled in the inner rooms?

Helen. No. His sister. Theonoe, they call her.

Menelaus. The name says she is an oracle. Tell me what she does.

Helen. She knows everything. And she will tell her brother you are here.

Menelaus. Then we die. There is no way I can hide from her.

Helen. Perhaps we could persuade her, if we begged her.

Menelaus. To do what? What hope are you leading me towards?

Helen. Not to tell her brother that you are in the country.

Menelaus. And if we persuade her, could we get our feet out of this land?

Helen. Easily, with her on our side. Behind her back, no.

Menelaus. That is your job. Woman to woman is the fitting way.

Helen. My hands will be on her knees. Count on it.

Menelaus. Right. And if she refuses to hear us?

Helen. You die. And I am married by force. Poor me.

Menelaus. Then you would be a traitor. The force is just your excuse.

Helen. But I have sworn a holy oath, on your head.

Menelaus. What? To die? And never to trade my bed for his?

Helen. By the same sword, yes. And I will lie beside you.

Menelaus. Then on those terms, touch my right hand.

Helen. I touch it. If you die, I leave the light.

Menelaus. And when I have lost you, I will end my own life too.

Helen. Then how do we die so that it does us some credit?

Menelaus. I will kill you on the back of this tomb, and then kill myself. But first I am going to fight a great fight for the right to your bed. Anyone who wants it, let him come and get it. I am not going to disgrace the name I made at Troy, or go home to Greece and take a load of blame with me. I am the man who robbed Thetis of Achilles. I saw Ajax, Telamon's son, cut his own throat. I saw Nestor, Neleus's son, left without his boy. And I am not to think my own wife worth dying for? Of course she is. If the gods have any sense, when a brave man dies at his enemies' hands they cover him in his tomb with a light earth, and the cowards they throw out onto a hard bare ridge of rock.

Chorus. Oh gods, let the family of Tantalus be lucky for once, and step clear of its evils.

Helen. Oh, I am wretched. That is the kind of luck I have. Menelaus, we are finished. The prophetess Theonoe is coming out of the house. I can hear the house ring as the bolts are drawn. Run. But what is the point of running? Whether she is here or not, she knows you have come. Oh, I am lost, I am lost. You came safe out of Troy, out of a barbarian country, and now you have walked onto barbarian swords all over again.

(Theonoe comes out of the house with her attendants. One carries a torch, another a brazier with sulphur burning in it.)

Theonoe. You, lead the way with the torchlight, and burn the sulphur, as the holy rule requires, to cleanse the deep corners of the air, so that I can breathe the pure breath of heaven. And you, if anyone has damaged the path by treading on it with an unholy foot, put the purifying flame to it. Beat the pine torch on the ground ahead of me, so that I can pass through. When you have paid the gods the rite I owe them, carry the fire back inside to the hearth.

Helen. My prophecies. How do they stand now? Your husband Menelaus has come, here he is in plain sight, stripped of his ships and of the copy of you. Poor man. What troubles you have escaped to get here, and you do not know whether you go home or stay where you are. Because there is a quarrel among the gods over you, and a council is sitting beside Zeus, on your account, this very day. Hera, who was your enemy before, is your friend now. She wants to bring you safe home with this woman, so that Greece can learn that the marriage of Paris, Aphrodite's gift to him, was no marriage: he was married to a fake. And Aphrodite wants to wreck your journey home, so that she is never shown up, never proved to have bought the prize for beauty with a marriage to Helen that came to nothing. And the decision is mine. Either I do what Aphrodite wants, and tell my brother you are here, and destroy you. Or I take Hera's side and save your life by hiding you from him, my own brother, who has given me orders to tell him the moment you set foot in this country. One of you go and tell my brother that this man is here, so that I am safe.

Helen. Lady, I fall at your knees and beg you. I take my seat here, at this unhappy station, for myself and for this man, whom I have found at last, after so long, only to see him killed. Do not tell your brother that my husband has come back to my arms, into the hands that love him. Save us. I am begging you. Do not sell your own goodness to your brother, buying favours from him that are wicked and unjust. God hates force. He orders everyone to get what they get without robbery. Wealth that is unjust is wealth to be left alone. The sky is common to all mortals, and so is the earth, and on it people should fill their houses without holding what belongs to somebody else, or taking it by force. Hermes gave me to your father to keep safe for my husband, at the right moment for the gods and the worst possible moment for me. And here is my husband, and he wants me back. How can he take me back if he is dead? And how could your father ever give a living woman back to a dead man? Think now about what the god wants, and what your father wants. Would the god, would the dead man, want a neighbour's property given back to its owner, or would they not? I think they would. So you ought not to give more weight to a foolish brother than to a good father. You are a prophetess. You believe in the things of the gods. If you wreck your father's justice and do a favour to your unjust brother, it is a disgrace: to know everything divine, what is and what is to come, and not know what is right.

Take me out of this, wretched as I am, out of the evils I am sunk in. Give me this, as a little something thrown in on top of my luck. There is not a person alive who does not hate Helen. All over Greece I am known as the woman who betrayed her husband and went to live in the golden houses of the Phrygians. If I get to Greece and set foot in Sparta again, they will hear, they will see with their own eyes, that it was a trick of the gods that destroyed them, and that I was never a traitor to the people I owe. They will bring me back to a good name, and I will find a husband for my daughter, whom nobody will marry now, and I will leave this bitter beggar's life behind and enjoy the property that is sitting in my house. If this man had been killed and burned on a pyre, I would be loving him with my tears from far away. But he is alive, he is safe, and I am to have him taken from me? No, lady. No. I beg you for this one thing. Give me this favour, and copy your father's ways, a just man's ways. Because that is the finest glory children have: the child of a good father, who grows up to match the character of the parents who made him.

Chorus. The words you have laid before us are pitiful, and so are you. But I want to hear what Menelaus will say to save his own life.

Menelaus. I could not bring myself to fall at your knees, or to get tears in my eyes. If we turned coward we would disgrace Troy worse than anything. And yet they say it becomes a well-born man to let the tears fall from his eyes when things go wrong. Well, I will not choose that fine thing, if it is fine, ahead of courage. If you think it right to save a stranger who has come, in justice, to get back his own wife, then give her back and save us into the bargain. If you do not think so, then I am not wretched for the first time, I have been wretched often enough, but you will be shown up as a bad woman. What I think is worthy of me and just, and what will get its grip on your heart most of all, I will say at your father's grave, since I miss him.

Old man, living in this tomb of stone: give her back. I am demanding my wife from you, the wife Zeus sent here for you to keep for me. I know you will never give her back to me yourself, because you are dead. But this woman will not think it right that her father, whom I am calling up from below, once the most honoured of men, should get a bad name. She is the one in charge now. And you, Hades under the ground, I call you as my ally too. You took plenty of bodies for this woman's sake, killed by my sword. You have had your pay. Either give those men back alive, here and now, or make this woman show that she is better than her god-fearing father, and give me back my wife.

And if you two rob me of my wife, I will tell you the thing she left out of her speech. I am bound by an oath, lady, so that you know it. First, to fight your brother, hand to hand. He dies or I do. It is as simple as that. And if he will not put his foot beside mine and fight, but tries to starve us out, two suppliants at this tomb, then I have decided: I kill this woman, and then I drive this two-edged sword into my own liver, on the back of this tomb, so that the streams of blood run down the grave. We will lie there, two corpses side by side on this polished stone, a grief for you that never dies and a reproach to your father. Your brother is not going to marry her, and neither is anybody else. I am taking her away, and if I cannot take her home, I will take her to the dead.

What am I doing? If I went soft and womanish and wept, I would get more pity and less done. Kill me, if you like. You will not be killing people without a name. But better to do what I say. Then you are just, and I get my wife back.

Chorus. It is for you to judge these speeches, young lady. Judge them in a way that pleases everyone.

Theonoe. I was born god-fearing and I want to be. I love myself, and I would not stain my father's good name, or do my brother a favour that would show me up as a disgrace. There is a great sanctuary of justice in my nature. I have it from Nereus, and I will try to keep it, Menelaus. Since Hera wants to do you good, I will cast my vote with her. As for Aphrodite, may she be gracious to me, but she and I have never had anything to do with each other, and I will try to stay a virgin all my life. As for what you say to reproach my father at this tomb, I have the same words to say myself. I would be doing wrong if I did not give her back. Because if he were alive and looking at the light, he would have given her back to you to have, and you to her. There is a reckoning for these things among the dead below and among all of us up here. The mind of the dead does not live, but it keeps its judgement, and that is immortal, once it has fallen into the immortal air.

So, not to make a long sermon of it: I will keep silent about what you have begged me, and I will never be an adviser to my brother's folly. I am doing him good, though he will not think so, if I turn him from godlessness to something holy. You two find some way out yourselves. I will stand aside, out of the way, and say nothing. Begin with the gods. Pray to Aphrodite to let you go home to your country, and pray to Hera that her mind stays where it is, set on saving you and your husband. And you, my dead father: as long as I have the strength, you will never be called godless instead of god-fearing.

(Theonoe goes back into the house with her attendants.)

Chorus. No one who was born lawless has ever prospered. Hope of safety lies in a just cause.

Helen. Menelaus, as far as the lady goes, we are safe. From here on it is for you to put forward the ideas and stitch together a plan of escape for the two of us.

Menelaus. Listen, then. You have been a long time in this house, and you have grown close to the king's servants.

Helen. What do you mean by that? You are dangling hopes in front of me, as if you were about to do something useful for us both.

Menelaus. Could you persuade one of the men who look after the four-horse chariots to give us a chariot?

Helen. I could. But what escape is there for us? We do not know the plains or the roads of this barbarian country.

Menelaus. Impossible, as you say. Well then, what if I hid in the house and killed the king with this two-edged sword?

Helen. His sister would never put up with that, or keep quiet, if you meant to kill her own brother.

Menelaus. And there is no ship, either, to get us away safe. The sea has the one we had.

Helen. Listen to me, in case even a woman can say something clever. Are you willing to be dead in word, without being dead?

Menelaus. A bad omen. But if it gets me something, I am ready to be called dead in word, without being dead.

Helen. And then I would mourn you the way women do, with my hair cut short and my songs of grief, in front of that godless man.

Menelaus. And what cure for our two lives is in that? There is something rather old and worn about the story.

Helen. I will ask the king of this country to let me bury you in an empty tomb, as if you had really died at sea.

Menelaus. Suppose he allows it. Then how do we get away without a ship, once we have put my body in an empty grave?

Helen. I will tell him to give me a boat, so that I can let down the offerings for your tomb into the arms of the sea.

Menelaus. Well said, all but one thing. If he tells you to set up the tomb on dry land, your excuse comes to nothing.

Helen. But I will say that it is not the custom in Greece to bury under the earth people who have died at sea.

Menelaus. You have straightened that one out too. Then I will sail with you, and help let down the offerings, in the same boat.

Helen. You must be there above all, and your sailors too, the ones who escaped from the wreck.

Menelaus. Once I have a ship at anchor, they will stand there, man beside man, each with a sword in his hand.

Helen. You must be in charge of all of it. Only let the winds fill our sail and carry us, and let the ship run fast.

Menelaus. It will. The gods are going to end my troubles. But who will you say you heard of my death from?

Helen. From you. Say that you were the only one who escaped death when you were sailing with the son of Atreus, and that you saw him die.

Menelaus. And these rags I have wrapped round my body will back me up as evidence of a shipwreck.

Helen. They have come in useful now, though losing everything looked so untimely then. That misery may turn out to be luck.

Menelaus. Should I come into the house with you, or sit quietly here at the tomb?

Helen. Stay here. If he tries anything ugly on you, this tomb will protect you, and so will your sword. I will go into the house and cut off my hair, and change my white dress for a black one, and drag my nails down my cheek till the skin bleeds. Because the contest is a great one, and I can see the scale tipping two ways: either I have to die, if I am caught in my scheming, or I go home to my country and bring your body safe out of this.

Lady Hera, you who lie in the bed of Zeus, give two pitiful people a breathing space from their troubles. We ask you, throwing our arms straight up to the sky, where you live among the embroidered stars. And you, who won the prize for beauty at the price of my marriage, Aphrodite, Dione's daughter, do not finish me off. You have done me damage enough already, handing over my name to the barbarians, though not my body. If you want to kill me, let me die in my father's country. Why can you never get enough of evil, working at your loves and your lies, your cunning inventions and your love-charms that bring blood into houses?
