If you only knew where to stop, you would be, in every other way, the sweetest of the gods to human beings. I do not say otherwise.

(Helen goes into the house. Menelaus stays by the tomb.)

Chorus.
	You who sit in your place of song
	under the leafy halls of the trees,
	I call on you, you,
	the most musical bird that sings,
	the nightingale, the bird of tears:
	come, trilling through your brown throat,
	and help me in my mourning,
	as I sing the pains of poor Helen
	and the tearful fate of the women of Troy
	under the spears of the Achaeans.
	When he raced the roaring plains of the sea with his barbarian oar,
	when he came, he came, bringing Priam's sons a misery,
	your bed, Helen, carried out of Sparta,
	Paris, whose marriage was a curse,
	and Aphrodite showed him the way.
Chorus.
	Many of the Achaeans, by the spear and the flung stones,
	breathed out their last, and a wretched Hades holds them now,
	and their unhappy wives have cut off their hair,
	and their houses stand with no bride in them.
	And many more one man destroyed, alone in his one boat,
	lighting a blazing fire on Euboea, the island in the sea,
	and flinging the Achaeans onto the rocks of Caphereus
	and the shores of the Aegean,
	with the treacherous star he lit.
	And the harbourless hills of Malea, in the blast of the storm,
	when he was swept far from his homeland, Menelaus,
	carrying on his ships the prize of a barbarian expedition,
	no prize but a quarrel with the Greeks,
	Hera's holy phantom.
Chorus.
	What is god, what is not god, and what lies between,
	which mortal can say he has searched and found
	the farthest end of it,
	when he sees the gods' business
	leaping this way, and back again that way,
	and round again, in luck
	that contradicts itself and nobody expected?
	You, Helen, were born the daughter of Zeus:
	a winged father begot you in Leda's womb.
	And then you were shouted across Greece
	as traitor, faithless, lawless, godless.
	I do not know what is certain among mortals any more.
	The word of the gods I have found true.
Chorus.
	Fools, all of you who go after honour through war
	and the spear-points of a strong army,
	stupidly putting an end to human troubles that way.
	If a contest of blood is to decide it,
	strife will never leave the cities of men.
	That is how they came by their bedrooms in Priam's earth,
	when they could have settled your quarrel with words,
	Helen.
	And now they are in the keeping of Hades below,
	and fire like the lightning of Zeus has swept over the walls,
	and you bring sufferings on sufferings,
	miseries on miseries, and a song of grief.

(Theoclymenus comes in from hunting, with servants carrying nets and leading dogs. He stops at the tomb.)

Theoclymenus. Greetings, my father's tomb. I buried you here at the doorway, Proteus, so that I could speak to you, and every time I go out of the house and come back in, I, your son Theoclymenus, say a word to you, father. You slaves, take the dogs and the hunting nets into the royal house. I have called myself a fool over and over. Do we not punish criminals with death? And now I hear that some Greek has landed in this country in broad daylight and slipped past the guards, a spy, or a thief on the hunt for Helen. He dies, if I can only catch him.

Ah. It seems I have arrived to find the whole business done. The daughter of Tyndareus has left her seat at the tomb empty and been shipped out of the country. Ho there. Undo the bars. Loose the horses from their stalls, men, and bring out the chariots, so that the wife I want does not get carried off out of this land for want of effort on my part.

Wait. I see the people we are chasing, and they have not run. They are here in the house.

(Helen comes out of the house in a black dress, with her hair cut short.)

You. Why have you put black clothes on your body instead of white? Why have you taken a knife to that noble head and cut off your hair, and why are you wetting your cheeks with fresh tears, and weeping? Is it a dream in the night that has persuaded you to groan like this, or have you heard some rumour from inside the house that has broken your heart with grief?

Helen. My lord, and yes, now I call you by that name, I am destroyed. All that was mine is gone, and I am nothing any more.

Theoclymenus. What disaster are you lying under? What has happened?

Helen. Menelaus, oh, how can I say it, is dead. My husband is dead.

Theoclymenus. I take no pleasure in your words, though they are good luck for me. How do you know? Did Theonoe tell you this?

Helen. She says so, and so does a man who was there when he died.

Theoclymenus. Someone has come who brings this news for certain?

Helen. Someone has come. And may he go where I want him to go.

Theoclymenus. Who is he? Where is he? I want to know this more exactly.

Helen. That man, sitting huddled at the tomb there.

Theoclymenus. Apollo! What a sight he is, in those filthy clothes.

Helen. Oh. I think my husband must have looked like that too.

Theoclymenus. Where is this man from, and from where did he put in to land here?

Helen. He is a Greek, one of the Achaeans who sailed with my husband.

Theoclymenus. What kind of death does he say Menelaus died?

Helen. The most pitiful. In the wet waves of the sea.

Theoclymenus. Where was he sailing, on what barbarian waters?

Helen. He was thrown onto the harbourless rocks of Libya.

Theoclymenus. And how did this man not die, if he shared the same oar?

Helen. Sometimes worse men are luckier than their betters.

Theoclymenus. Where did he leave the wreck of his ship before he came here?

Helen. Where I hope it rots. But not Menelaus.

Theoclymenus. Menelaus is finished. What boat did this man come in?

Helen. Sailors happened on him and picked him up, he says.

Theoclymenus. Then where is the evil thing that was sent to Troy in your place?

Helen. You mean the image made of cloud? It has gone off into the air.

Theoclymenus. Oh Priam, and land of Troy, how you were destroyed for nothing.

Helen. And I had my share in the ruin of Priam's family.

Theoclymenus. Did he leave your husband unburied, or did he put him under the earth?

Helen. Unburied. Oh, the misery of it, on top of all my evils.

Theoclymenus. Is that why you cut the curls of your golden hair?

Helen. Because he is dear to me, whoever he is, and he is here.

Theoclymenus. She is right to weep over this misfortune, if it is true.

Helen. Oh yes, it is so easy to fool your sister.

Theoclymenus. Hardly. Well, what now? Are you going to go on living at this tomb?

Helen. Why do you mock me? Can you not leave the dead man alone?

Theoclymenus. Because you are faithful to your husband, and you keep running from me.

Helen. Not any more. Begin my wedding now.

Theoclymenus. It has been a long time coming, but I am glad of it all the same.

Helen. Do you know what you should do? Let us forget the past.

Theoclymenus. On what terms? One favour deserves another.

Helen. Let us make peace. Be reconciled with me.

Theoclymenus. I let my quarrel with you go. Let it fly away on wings.

Helen. Then by your knees, since you are a friend to me now.

Theoclymenus. What are you hunting, reaching out to me like a suppliant?

Helen. I want to bury my dead husband.

Theoclymenus. What? Is there a tomb for the absent? Are you going to bury a shadow?

Helen. It is the custom among Greeks, when someone dies at sea.

Theoclymenus. To do what? The sons of Pelops are clever at that kind of thing.

Helen. To hold the funeral with empty woven robes.

Theoclymenus. Then hold your funeral. Raise the tomb wherever in the land you like.

Helen. That is not how we bury sailors who have died at sea.

Theoclymenus. How, then? I know nothing of the customs of the Greeks.

Helen. We take everything the dead are owed out to sea, and give it to the water.

Theoclymenus. Then what am I to give you for the dead man?

Helen. This man knows. I do not. I never had to learn, in my lucky days.

Theoclymenus. Stranger, the news you brought was welcome, at least.

Menelaus. Not to me. And not to the dead man.

Theoclymenus. How do you bury men who have died at sea?

Menelaus. Each according to what he can afford.

Theoclymenus. Then never mind the cost. Name what you want, for her sake.

Menelaus. First, blood is shed for the powers below.

Theoclymenus. The blood of what? Tell me, and I will do it.

Menelaus. Decide that yourself. Whatever you give will be enough.

Theoclymenus. Among us barbarians the custom is a horse or a bull.

Menelaus. Whatever you give, give nothing that is low-bred.

Theoclymenus. Our herds are rich. We are not short of those.

Menelaus. Then a bed is carried out, made up and spread, with no body on it.

Theoclymenus. It will be done. What else does custom require?

Menelaus. Weapons of beaten bronze. He loved the spear.

Theoclymenus. What we give will be worthy of the house of Pelops.

Menelaus. And whatever else the earth brings up that is beautiful.

Theoclymenus. And then? How do you let it all down into the swell?

Menelaus. There must be a ship, and men to work the oars.

Theoclymenus. How far from the land does the ship stand off?

Menelaus. Far enough that the wash of the oars can barely be seen from the shore.

Theoclymenus. Why is that? Where did Greece get this custom from?

Menelaus. So the waves cannot throw the pollution back onto the land.

Theoclymenus. You will have a fast Phoenician ship.

Menelaus. That would be good. And it would please Menelaus.

Theoclymenus. Can you not do all this well enough without her?

Menelaus. This is work for a mother, or a wife, or children.

Theoclymenus. So it is her task, you say, to bury her husband.

Menelaus. It is. Piety says the dead are not to be robbed of what is theirs.

Theoclymenus. Let her go, then. It is in my interest to keep a wife who honours the gods. Go into the house and choose the ornaments for the dead man. And I will not send you away from this country empty-handed either, since you have done her this kindness. You brought me good news, and for that you will have clothes instead of the rags you stand in, and food, enough to get you home to your own country. I can see the state you are in.

And you, poor woman, stop wearing yourself out over what cannot be helped. Menelaus has met his fate. A dead husband cannot come back to life.

Menelaus. That is your part now, young woman. You must love the husband you have and let go of the one who no longer exists. That is the best thing for you, as things have turned out. And if I reach Greece and come through alive, I will put an end to the bad name you had before, if you are the kind of wife to your husband that you ought to be.

Helen. I will be. My husband will never have cause to complain of me. You will be close enough to see it for yourself. But go inside now, you poor man, and take a bath and change your clothes. I am not going to put off doing good to you. You will do what is due to my dearest Menelaus with a better heart if you get from me what you deserve.

(Theoclymenus, Helen and Menelaus go into the house.)

Chorus.
	Once the mother of the gods, the mountain mother,
	ran on racing feet
	through the wooded valleys,
	along the running streams of the rivers
	and the deep-thundering waves of the sea,
	aching for her daughter who was gone,
	the girl whose name is not spoken.
	The clattering rattles cried out
	a piercing sound
	when the goddess yoked wild beasts to her chariot
	and two goddesses ran with her, quick as the wind,
	after the girl who had been snatched
	out of the circling dances of the young women:
	Artemis with her bow,
	and the grim-eyed one, Athena,
	in full armour with her spear.
	But Zeus, looking down
	from his seat in heaven,
	was bringing about another fate.
Chorus.
	And when the mother gave up the racing,
	far-wandering labour of hunting
	for her daughter, stolen by a trick,
	she crossed the snow-fed lookouts
	of the nymphs of Mount Ida
	and threw herself down in her grief
	among the rocks and the snowbound thickets.
	And for mortals she would not let the ploughed fields
	of the earth bear crops, and they lay brown and bare,
	and she was killing off the race of men.
	She sent up no fresh pasture,
	no leafy curling shoots for the flocks,
	and the life was going out of the cities.
	There were no sacrifices to the gods,
	and on the altars the cakes lay unburnt.
	She stopped the dewy springs
	from throwing up their clear water,
	in grief for her child,
	an avenger.
Chorus.
	And when she had put an end to the feasts
	for gods and the race of men alike,
	Zeus spoke, softening
	the mother's hateful anger:
	"Go, holy Graces, go,
	and take the grief out of Demeter,
	who is furious over her girl,
	with a great shout of joy,
	and you Muses, with the songs of the dancers."
	Then Aphrodite, most beautiful of the blessed gods,
	first took up the bronze with its deep voice
	and the drums with their tight-stretched hide.
	And the goddess laughed,
	and took into her hands
	the deep-booming pipe,
	delighted with the noise.
Chorus.
	Child, you burned in the gods' inner rooms
	offerings that were not right and not holy,
	and you brought on yourself the anger
	of the great mother
	by not honouring the goddess's rites.
	The dappled fawnskin robes
	have great power,
	and the green ivy wound
	around the sacred wands,
	and the whirling of the bull-roarer
	spinning its circle in the air,
	and hair streaming loose for Dionysus,
	and the goddess's all-night festivals,
	and the moon that rides high
	over those nights.
	You trusted in your beauty alone.

(Helen comes out of the house.)

Helen. Inside the house, friends, everything is going our way. The daughter of Proteus is in the theft with us. When her brother questioned her, she said nothing about my husband being here. For my sake she told him he is dead and under the earth, and does not see the light of day.

And my husband has snatched a piece of luck as fine as any. The weapons he was supposed to let down into the sea, he is carrying himself. He has put his good arm through the shield strap and taken the spear in his right hand, as if he were helping with the honours for the dead. He has fitted his body out with weapons ready for a fight, so that when we step onto the oared ship his one hand can set up trophies over countless barbarians. And I have taken the clothes the shipwreck left him in and dressed him in fresh ones, and given his skin the bath it has waited so long for, in water from the river.

But I must be quiet. The man who thinks he has my wedding safe in his hands is coming out of the house. And I ask you for your good will, and to keep your mouths shut, so that if we save ourselves we may one day save you too.

(Theoclymenus comes out of the house, with slaves carrying the offerings.)

Theoclymenus. Move along in order, slaves, as the stranger told you, carrying the gifts for the burial at sea. And you, Helen, if you do not think I am talking nonsense, listen to me and stay here. You will do the same service to your husband whether you are there or not. I am afraid some sudden longing will come over you and persuade you to throw yourself into the swell of the sea, struck down by love for your first husband. You grieve for him too much, for a man who is not even here.

Helen. My new husband, I cannot help honouring my first marriage bed and the man I lay beside as a bride. Because I loved my husband, I could even die with him. But what thanks would he have from me if I died with him, dead as he is? Let me go myself and give the dead man his funeral gifts. And may the gods give you what I wish for you, and this stranger too, for the help he is giving. And you will have in me the kind of wife you ought to have in your house, since you are doing this good to Menelaus and to me. All this is leading somewhere, to some good fortune. Now, whoever is to give us the ship we will carry these things in, appoint him, so that I have your kindness in full.

(He turns to one of his men.)

Theoclymenus. You. Go and give these people a Sidonian ship with fifty oars, and men to row it.

Helen. And this man, who is arranging the funeral, will be in command of the ship?

Theoclymenus. Certainly. My sailors are to obey him.

Helen. Give the order again, so they understand you clearly.

Theoclymenus. I give it again. And a third time, if you like.

Helen. May it bring you good. And me too, for my plans.

Theoclymenus. Now do not spoil your skin with too much crying.

Helen. This day will show you how grateful I am.

Theoclymenus. The dead are nothing. All this is work for nothing.

Helen. There is something to what I say, both down there and up here.

Theoclymenus. You will find me no worse a husband than Menelaus.

Helen. I have no complaint of you. All I need is luck.

Theoclymenus. That is in your hands, if you give me your good will.

Helen. I do not need lessons now in how to love the people I owe.

Theoclymenus. Do you want me to work alongside you, and see the expedition off myself?

Helen. Certainly not. Do not turn slave to your own slaves, my lord.

Theoclymenus. Well then. I let the customs of the house of Pelops be. My house is clean: Menelaus did not breathe his last here. Let someone go and tell my chieftains to bring wedding gifts to my house. The whole land must ring with songs of blessing for the wedding of Helen and me, so that everyone envies it. And you, stranger, go, and give these things into the arms of the sea for the man who was once her husband, and then hurry back to the house with my wife, so that you can share her wedding feast with me and set out for home, or stay here and live well.

(Theoclymenus goes into the house.)

Menelaus. Zeus, they call you father, and a wise god. Look at us, and turn our troubles aside. We are dragging our fortunes up a cliff of rock. Put your shoulder to it with us. Touch us with only your fingertip and we will reach the place we want to be. We have laboured enough already, in the labours we went through before. Gods, I have called on you many times, and you have heard hard things from me as well as good. I am not owed bad luck for ever. I am owed a straight step forward. Grant me this one favour, and you will make me a lucky man for the rest of my life.

(Menelaus and Helen go out towards the shore.)

Chorus.
	Phoenician ship of Sidon,
	swift oar, mother of the foam the rowers make,
	dear to the beat of the blades,
	leader of the dance
	of the lovely dancing dolphins,
	when the sea lies windless
	and the grey-eyed daughter of the Sea,
	Calm, says this:
	"Let out the sails,
	leave them to the sea breezes,
	and take up your oars of pine,
	sailors, sailors,
	and carry Helen to the good harbours
	and the shores where the house of Perseus stood."
Chorus.
	Perhaps you will find the daughters of Leucippus
	beside the swell of the river,
	or in front of the temple of Athena,
	when at last you join the dances again,
	or the revels for Hyacinthus
	and their night-long joy:
	Hyacinthus, whom Apollo killed
	with the discus, throwing for the longest cast,
	and so the son of Zeus declared
	a day of ox sacrifice in the land of Sparta.
	And you may find the calf
	you left at home, Hermione,
	for no torch has yet been lit
	to light her to her wedding.
Chorus.
	If only we could fly through the air
	the way the cranes, the birds of Libya, go,
	in their long ranks,
	leaving the winter rain behind,
	following the whistle
	of their oldest leader, the shepherd of the flock,
	who cries out as he flies
	over the dry plains and the fields that bear the crops.
	Long-necked birds, winged ones,
	who run with the racing clouds,
	go, under the Pleiades in the middle of the sky
	and Orion of the night,
	and shout the news as you settle
	on the banks of the Eurotas,
	that Menelaus has taken the city of Dardanus
	and is coming home.
Chorus.
	And you, come at last, driving your horses
	down the road through the sky,
	sons of Tyndareus,
	under the whirling of the bright stars,
	you who live in heaven,
	Helen's saviours.
	Come over the grey-green swell and the dark blue waves,
	the white-crested surf of the sea,
	sending the sailors
	fair winds from Zeus.
	And throw off your sister
	the bad name of a barbarian's bed,
	the punishment she was given
	for the quarrel on Ida,
	though she never went to the land of Troy,
	to the towers Apollo built.

(A Messenger, one of the Egyptian sailors, comes running in. Theoclymenus comes out of the house to meet him.)

Messenger. My lord, the worst has happened to this house. You are about to hear strange new troubles from me.

Theoclymenus. What is it?

Messenger. Set to work courting another woman. Helen has left the country.

Theoclymenus. Lifted on wings, or walking on her own feet?

Messenger. Menelaus has carried her off by sea, out of the land. He was the man who came to announce his own death.

Theoclymenus. That is a terrible thing to say. What ship took her away from this country? I cannot believe what you are telling me.

Messenger. The one you gave to the stranger. And he has gone with your own sailors, to put it briefly.

Theoclymenus. How? I want to know. I never dreamed one pair of hands could get the better of all those sailors you were sent out with.

Messenger. When the daughter of Zeus left this royal house and set out for the sea, she stepped along on delicate feet and mourned, very cleverly, for the husband who was right beside her and not dead at all. When we came to the wall of your dockyard, we hauled down the Sidonian ship for her first voyage, fitted with her fifty benches and her full count of oars. Then one job followed another. One man set the mast, another set the oars, the blades in his hands; the white sails were made ready; the steering oars were let down on their straps.

And in the middle of this work, watching for exactly this, it seems, Greeks who had sailed with Menelaus came along the shore, dressed in the rags of shipwrecked men, good-looking men but filthy to look at. The son of Atreus saw them coming and spoke to them, putting on a false show of pity for everyone to hear. "Poor men, how did you get here? What Achaean ship was wrecked under you? Have you come to help bury the son of Atreus, who is lost, and whose empty grave this daughter of Tyndareus is honouring, without a body?" And they shed tears to order, and went on board the ship carrying the offerings that were to go into the sea for Menelaus. We were suspicious, and we said to each other that there were a great many of these extra passengers. But we kept our mouths shut all the same, out of respect for your orders. When you told the stranger to command the ship, you threw the whole thing into confusion.

The rest of the offerings we got aboard easily enough; they were light. But the bull's hoof would not go straight up the gangplank. He bellowed, rolling his eyes round, and arched his back, and glared along his horns, and would not let us touch him. Then Helen's husband called out, "You men who sacked the city of Troy, come on, pick up the bull's body on your young shoulders, the way Greeks do, and heave him into the bow, and have a sword ready to hand at the same time, for the victim's throat, for the dead man." They came at his order, lifted the bull clean off the ground, carried him aboard and set him down on the benches. And Menelaus stroked the horse's neck and forehead, and coaxed him up into the ship.

At last, when the ship had taken everything, Helen climbed the rungs of the ladder with her fine ankles and sat down in the middle, between the rowers' benches, and Menelaus, the man who was dead by all accounts, sat close beside her. The others sat down along the right and the left sides in equal numbers, man beside man, with swords hidden under their clothes, and the water filled with the noise of oars as we heard the voice of the man calling the stroke.

When we were neither very far from the land nor very near, the helmsman asked, "Do we sail farther out, stranger, or is this far enough? The command of the ship is yours." And he said, "This is enough for me." He took his sword in his right hand and went forward to the bow, and stood over the bull for the sacrifice, and with no dead man in his mind at all he cut its throat and prayed. "Poseidon of the sea, who live in the salt water, and you holy daughters of Nereus, bring me and my wife safe out of this country to the shore of Nauplia." And the jets of blood spurted into the swell, a good omen for the stranger.

Then someone said, "There is treachery in this voyage. Row back. You, give the order to the right side. You, turn the steering oar." But the son of Atreus stood up from the bull he had killed and shouted to his friends, "Why are you waiting, you pick of the land of Greece? Cut the barbarians' throats, kill them, throw them off the ship into the sea." And the man calling the stroke shouted the opposite order to your rowers: "Come on, one of you grab a spar from the stern, another break up a bench, another pull an oar out of its socket, and bloody the heads of these foreign enemies." They were all on their feet at once, some with the ship's timbers in their hands, others with swords, and the ship ran with blood. And Helen was cheering them on from the stern: "Where is the glory you won at Troy? Show it to these barbarians." In the rush men fell, and men got up again, and you would have seen others lying there dead. Menelaus in his armour watched for wherever his friends were in trouble, and there he brought his sword in his right hand, so that men dived off the ship, and he swept the benches clean of your rowers. Then he went to the helmsman and told him to steer the ship straight for Greece. They raised the mast, and a fair wind came.

They are gone, out of the country. I escaped the killing by letting myself down into the sea beside the anchor, and when I was at the end of my strength a fisherman with his line pulled me out and put me ashore to bring you this news. There is nothing more useful to human beings than a sensible refusal to believe.

Chorus. I would never have believed, my lord, that Menelaus could be here without your knowing it or ours. But he was, and he stood right in front of us.

Theoclymenus. Caught by a woman's tricks. God help me. My marriage has run away from me. If the ship could be caught by chasing it, I would go to the trouble and have those strangers in my hands soon enough. As it is, I will punish the sister who betrayed me. She saw Menelaus in this house, and she did not tell me. She will never fool another man with her prophecies again.

(He starts towards the house with his sword drawn. A Servant of Theonoe's blocks the doorway and takes hold of his clothes.)

Servant. You. Where are you going, master? What killing are you off to?

Theoclymenus. Where justice tells me. Out of my way.

Servant. I am not letting go of your clothes. You are in a hurry to do something terrible.

Theoclymenus. You are a slave. Are you going to give orders to your masters?

Servant. Yes. Because I am in my right mind.

Theoclymenus. Not to my way of thinking. Not unless you let me...

Servant. No. We will not let you.

Theoclymenus. Kill a sister who is the worst of women...

Servant. The most god-fearing of women, you mean.

Theoclymenus. Who betrayed me...

Servant. A fine betrayal, doing what is right.

Theoclymenus. Giving my bride to another man.

Servant. To the man with the better right to her.

Theoclymenus. And who has a right to what is mine?

Servant. The man who received her from her father.

Theoclymenus. But fortune gave her to me.

Servant. And what had to be took her away.

Theoclymenus. It is not for you to judge my affairs.

Servant. It is, if what I say is better.

Theoclymenus. So I am the one being ruled here. I am not the ruler.

Servant. Ruled when it comes to doing right. Not to doing wrong.

Theoclymenus. You seem to be in love with dying.

Servant. Kill me. You will not kill your sister while I have any say in it. Kill me instead. For a slave of the right kind, dying for his masters is the finest end there is.

(The Dioscuri, Castor and Polydeuces, appear in the air above the house.)

Castor. Hold back the anger that is carrying you where it should not, Theoclymenus, king of this land. We are the two sons of Zeus, and we are calling you: the twins Leda bore, along with Helen, who has fled from your house. You are angry over a marriage that was never fated to be yours. And your sister Theonoe, the daughter of the Nereid goddess, is doing you no wrong when she honours what the gods have ordered and the just commands of her father. It was right that Helen should live in your house up to now, up to this present time. But once the foundations of Troy were torn up, and she had lent her name to the gods for their purposes, it was right no longer. Now she has to be yoked in her own marriage again, go home, and live with her husband.

So keep your black sword away from your sister, and believe that in this she has acted with good sense and kept herself in hand. We would have saved our sister long ago, before all this, since Zeus made us gods. But we were weaker than what was fated, and than the gods, who decided things should go this way.

That is what I have to say to you. To my sister I say this. Sail on with your husband. You will have a fair wind. We, your two brothers, your saviours, will ride the sea beside you and bring you home. And when you round the last turn and come to the end of your life, you will be called a goddess, and share the drink offerings with the Dioscuri, and receive the gifts men give to guests, along with us. That is the will of Zeus. And the place where the son of Maia, Hermes, first set you down on your journey through the sky, when he took you from Sparta and stole your body away so that Paris should not have you, the island that lies like a sentry along the coast of Attica, will be called by your name, Helen, among men from now on, because it took you in when you were stolen from your home. As for Menelaus the wanderer, the gods have fixed it that he will live on the island of the blessed. The gods do not hate the well-born. It is the nameless multitude whose troubles are greater.

Theoclymenus. Sons of Leda and Zeus, I let go my old quarrel over your sister. And my own sister I will not kill now. Let Helen go home, if the gods think it right. Know this, both of you: the same blood that made you made a sister who is the best of women and the most self-controlled. Go, then, and fare well, for the sake of Helen's noble mind, a thing not to be found in many women.

(The Dioscuri disappear into the sky above the house.)

Chorus.
	Many are the shapes of what the gods do,
	and many the things they bring about that no one expected.
	What we counted on did not happen,
	and for what no one counted on, a god found a way.
	That is how this business ended.

The Phoenician Women (c. 410 BC)

The Phoenician Women

(Thebes, in front of the royal house. Jocasta, an old woman dressed in black, comes out of it alone.)

Jocasta. Sun, cutting your road through the stars of the sky, standing in your chariot inlaid with gold, whirling your flame along behind your fast horses: what an unlucky beam you sent down on Thebes the day Cadmus came to this country, leaving Phoenicia and its sea-coast behind him. He married Harmonia, Aphrodite's daughter, and fathered Polydorus, and from Polydorus, they say, came Labdacus, and from Labdacus, Laius. I am known as the daughter of Menoeceus, and Creon is my brother, born of the same mother. They call me Jocasta. That is the name my father gave me. Laius married me. And when he had had me in his bed for years and there were still no children in the house, he went and asked Apollo, and begged him at the same time for sons, for the two of us to share. And the god said, "King of Thebes, city of fine horses, do not sow that furrow for children against the will of the gods. If you father a son, that son will kill you, and your whole house will wade through blood." But he gave in to pleasure one night when the wine had him, and sowed a child in me. And once he had done it, and knew his mistake and what the god had said, he gave the baby to herdsmen to leave out to die in Hera's meadow, on the rocks of Cithaeron, after driving iron spikes through the middle of his ankles. That is why Greece named him Oedipus, the boy with the swollen feet. Polybus's horse-herders found him and carried him home and put him in their mistress's arms. And she put the child I had laboured to bear to her own breast, and persuaded her husband that she had given birth to him.

When my son was a grown man, with a red-gold beard on his cheeks, either he guessed it or somebody told him, and he set out for Apollo's temple, wanting to find out who his parents were. And Laius, my husband, set out too, to ask whether the child he had left out to die was dead by now. And the two of them came together at the same spot, where the road splits in Phocis. Laius's driver called out to him, "Stranger, out of the road for the king." He walked on without a word, proud man. And the colts' hooves bloodied the tendons of his feet. And then, but why should I tell what lies outside our troubles? The son killed the father, and took the chariot and gave it to Polybus, who had raised him.

Then the Sphinx was crushing the city with her raids, and my husband was gone, and my brother Creon put my marriage up as a prize: whoever could solve the clever girl's riddle would have me. And somehow it happened that my son Oedipus understood the Sphinx's song. So he was made king of this land, and took the sceptre of this country as his prize. He married his own mother, poor man, and did not know it, and his mother did not know she was sleeping with her son. I bore my son children: two boys, Eteocles and Polyneices, the strong and the famous, and two girls; one of them her father named Ismene, and the other, the elder, I named Antigone. When Oedipus, who had endured everything, learned that his marriage was a marriage to his mother, he did a terrible slaughter on his own eyes, bloodying the pupils with pins of beaten gold. And when my sons' cheeks darkened with their beards, they hid their father behind locked doors, so that what had happened to him, which took a great deal of cleverness to hide, might be forgotten. He is alive, in the house. And sick with what fate has done to him, he calls down the most unholy curses on his sons: that they should divide this house between them with sharpened iron.

The two of them were afraid the gods would bring those prayers to fulfilment if they went on living together, so they made an agreement: Polyneices, the younger, would leave this country first, an exile of his own free will, and Eteocles would stay and hold the sceptre, and they would change places every year. But once Eteocles was seated on the bench of power he would not get off the throne, and he drove Polyneices out of this land as an exile. Polyneices went to Argos, married into Adrastus's family, gathered a great mass of Argive shields, and is leading them here. He has come against these very walls, the walls with the seven gates, and he is demanding his father's sceptre and his share of the land. And I, to undo their quarrel, have persuaded one son to come to the other under truce, before either of them touches a spear. The messenger I sent says he will come.

Zeus, you who live in the bright folds of the sky, save us. Give my sons an agreement. If you are wise, as they say you are, you must not let the same mortal go on being unlucky for ever.

(Jocasta goes back into the house. The Tutor, an old slave, comes out onto the flat roof above the door, and Antigone climbs after him.)

Tutor. Antigone, glorious child of your father's house. Your mother let you leave the girls' rooms and come up to the top storey of the house because you begged her, to look at the Argive army. But wait a moment, so I can look over the path first and see whether any of the townspeople is in sight on the road. Blame would be a small thing to me, a slave. To you, a princess, it would not. When I have looked at everything, I will tell you what I saw and heard from the Argives, when I carried the terms of the truce from here to your brother over there, and back again from them to here. No. There is nobody from the town anywhere near this house. Come up the old cedar ladder. Look out over the plain, along the streams of Ismenus and the spring of Dirce, and see how big the enemy army is.

Antigone.
	Reach me your hand now, reach it, an old hand to a young one,
	down from the ladder,
	and lift my foot up the last step.

Tutor. There. Take hold of it, girl. You have come at the right moment. The Argive army is just on the move, and they are separating the companies from each other.

Antigone.
	Oh, Lady Hecate, daughter of Leto,
	the whole plain is one sheet of bronze,
	and it flashes like lightning.

Tutor. Polyneices has not come back to this country in any small way. Many horses, weapons by the thousand, and the roar of all of them.

Antigone.
	Are the gates barred? Are the bolts with their bronze bands
	fitted into the stone of the walls Amphion built?

Tutor. Don't worry. Inside, the city is safe. But look at the first one, if you want to know who he is.

Antigone.
	Who is that one with the white plume,
	who marches out in front of the army
	with a shield of solid bronze
	carried light on his arm?
Tutor.
	A captain, mistress.
Antigone.
	Who is he? Where is he from?
	Say it, old man. What is his name?

Tutor. He calls himself a Mycenaean by birth, and he lives by the streams of Lerna. Lord Hippomedon.

Antigone.
	E, e. How proud he is, how frightening to look at,
	like one of the giants born from the earth
	in the paintings, with stars across his shield,
	nothing like the race of men, who live for a day.
Tutor.
	And the one crossing the water of Dirce. Do you see him?
Antigone.
	Different. This one's armour is quite different.
	Who is he?
Tutor.
	He is the son of Oeneus, Tydeus,
	and he carries the war-god of Aetolia in his chest.
Antigone.
	Is this the one, old man, who married
	the sister of Polyneices' wife?
	How foreign his armour looks. Half barbarian.

Tutor. All the Aetolians carry the big shield, child, and there are no surer hands with a throwing spear.

Antigone. And you, old man, how do you know all this so exactly?

Tutor. I saw the devices on their shields then, when I went to your brother carrying the terms of the truce, and I recognised them. I looked at them closely, so I know the men inside the armour.

Antigone.
	And who is this one going past the tomb of Zethus,
	the young one with the long curls
	and the fierce look in his eyes,
	a captain, since a crowd in full armour
	follows at his heels?
Tutor.
	That is Parthenopaeus, Atalanta's son.
Antigone.
	Then may Artemis, who runs the mountains with his mother,
	bring him down with her arrows and destroy him,
	for coming against my city to sack it.

Tutor. May it be so, child. But they have come to this land with justice on their side, and that is what I am afraid of: that the gods will see it the right way.

Antigone.
	And where is the one who was born
	from the same mother as me, to a life of pain?
	Dearest old friend, tell me. Where is Polyneices?

Tutor. He is over there, near the tomb of Niobe's seven unmarried daughters, standing close beside Adrastus. Do you see him?

Antigone.
	I see him. Not clearly. But I see something,
	the shape of a body, the outline of a chest.
	If only I could run the road a cloud runs before the wind,
	on my own feet, through the air,
	to my brother, my own blood, and throw my arms
	round his dear neck at last,
	the poor exile. How he stands out
	in his golden armour, old man,
	blazing like the first rays of the morning sun.
Tutor.
	He will come to this house under truce,
	and fill you with joy.
Antigone.
	And that one, old man. Who is he,
	standing in a chariot, driving white horses?

Tutor. That is the prophet Amphiaraus, mistress. And the animals for the sacrifice are with him, the streams of blood the earth loves to drink.

Antigone.
	Moon, daughter of the Sun with the shining belt,
	circle of golden light,
	how quietly he drives, how steady the goad,
	shifting it from one horse to the other, keeping them straight.
	And where is the one who shouts those terrible insults at this city?

Tutor. Capaneus? That is him, working out the ways up the towers, measuring our walls from top to bottom.

Antigone.
	Io.
	Nemesis, and deep-roaring thunders of Zeus,
	and smoking light of the lightning,
	it is you who put boasts too big for a man to sleep.
	This is the man who says he will give the women of Thebes
	to the women of Mycenae, prisoners of his spear,
	to Lerna's trident and the waters of Amymone
	that Poseidon loves,
	once he has thrown slavery round them.
	Never, never, Lady,
	golden-haired child of Zeus,
	Artemis, let me endure that slavery.

Tutor. Child, go inside the house and stay in your own rooms under the roof, now that you have had what you longed for and seen what you wanted to see. There is a crowd of women coming towards the royal house, now that confusion has got into the city. And women are a fault-finding lot by nature. Give them the smallest opening for talk and they bring in more of it, and there is a kind of pleasure women take in saying nothing good about each other.

(Antigone and the Tutor go down from the roof. The Chorus come in, young women of Phoenicia on their way to Apollo's temple at Delphi, held up at Thebes by the war.)

Chorus.
	I left the swell of the Tyrian sea and came,
	the choicest of offerings for Apollo,
	from the island of Phoenicia,
	to be a slave in Apollo's house,
	where he has settled under the snowy ridges
	of Parnassus. Over the Ionian sea
	I sailed, the oars driving me through the water that rings us round,
	over the plains nobody harvests
	off Sicily, while the west wind
	rode the sky, the loveliest
	music in the heavens.
Chorus.
	Chosen out of my city,
	the finest thing it had to give Apollo,
	I came to the land of Cadmus,
	sent here to the towers of Laius,
	the home of the famous sons of Agenor,
	who are my own blood.
	I have become Apollo's servant,
	like his statues of worked gold.
	But the water of Castalia
	is still waiting for me,
	to drench the girlish glory of my hair
	for the service of Apollo.
Chorus.
	Oh, rock that shines with fire,
	the double-peaked blaze above the heights
	where the women of Dionysus dance,
	and vine that every day
	drips the rich cluster,
	letting the grape-flower loose,
	and holy cave of the serpent,
	and watchtowers of the gods in the hills,
	and sacred mountain under its snow.
	If only I could be whirling in the deathless god's dance
	with nothing to fear,
	in Apollo's valley at the navel of the world,
	with Dirce left behind me.
Chorus.
	But now Ares has come in his fury
	to the front of the walls,
	and he is kindling the blood of war
	against this city. May it never happen.
	The pain of friends is shared,
	and shared too, if this land of seven towers
	suffers anything,
	with the country of Phoenicia. Pheu, pheu.
	One blood, one family of children,
	born from Io, the girl who wore the horns:
	their troubles are mine as well.
Chorus.
	And round the city a thick cloud
	of shields is blazing,
	the shape of bloody battle,
	and Ares will soon know it,
	when he brings down on the sons of Oedipus
	the ruin the Furies have planned.
	Argos, Pelasgian Argos,
	I am afraid of your strength,
	and of what comes from the gods. Because the son
	who comes in arms to claim his house
	is not rushing into an unjust fight.

(Polyneices comes in through the gate, his sword drawn, looking about him.)

Polyneices. The gatekeepers' bolts let me in easily enough, inside the walls. Which is exactly what I am afraid of: that they have me in the net now, and will not let me out again without blood on my skin. So I have to keep my eyes moving everywhere, this way and that, in case there is some trick. With this sword in my hand I can give myself the confidence that comes from daring. Hey. Who is that? Or is it just a noise I am afraid of? Everything looks dangerous to a man who is daring something, once his feet are moving through an enemy's country. I trust my mother, and at the same time I do not trust her, the woman who persuaded me to come here under truce. Still, help is close. The altar hearths are right beside me, and the house is not empty. Come on. Let me put the sword back into its dark sheath and ask these women standing at the house who they are.

Ladies, strangers, tell me: what country do you come from, to be at the door of a Greek house?

Chorus. Phoenicia is my country, the land that raised me. The descendants of Agenor sent me here to Apollo, as the pick of the spoils their spears had won. And the famous son of Oedipus was about to send me on to Apollo's holy oracle and his altars when the Argives marched against the city. Now you answer me in return. Who are you, who have come to the fortress of the Theban land, with its seven gates?

Polyneices. My father is Oedipus, the son of Laius. My mother is Jocasta, the daughter of Menoeceus. And the people of Thebes call me Polyneices.

Chorus. Kinsman of the children of Agenor, my kings, the ones who sent me here.

Chorus. I go down on my knees before you, my lord, honouring the custom of my home. You have come at last to your father's land. Io. Io. Lady, come out to the front of the house. Throw the gates open. Do you hear, mother, you who gave birth to this man? Why are you slow to leave the rooms under your roof and put your arms round your son?

(Jocasta comes out of the house, her white hair cut short.)

Jocasta.
	I heard your Phoenician voices, girls,
	and I am dragging my old foot out here,
	one shaking step at a time. Oh, my child.
	At last, after so many thousand days,
	I see your face. Put your arms round me,
	hold your mother to your chest,
	reach me your cheeks, let the dark curls
	of your hair fall over my neck and shade it.
	Io, io. You have barely appeared,
	beyond all hope, beyond all expecting, in your mother's arms.
	What can I say to you? How can I take it all,
	with my hands and with my words,
	the pleasure that winds round and round,
	dancing this way and that way,
	the delight I had in the old days, the old joy?
	Oh, my child,
	you left your father's house empty
	when you were sent away into exile by your brother's outrage.
	How your friends missed you.
	How Thebes missed you.
	That is why I cut off my white hair
	and let it fall, in tears, for grief,
	and I wear no white clothes now, my child,
	but these dark rags instead,
	black round me, in the dark.
	And the old man in the house, his eyes gone,
	always holding on to his longing, all tears,
	for the pair of you, the matched team
	that was unyoked and driven from the house,
	he rushed at the sword to cut his own throat,
	at the rope over the roof-beams,
	groaning his curses on his sons,
	and now with cry after cry of pain
	he hides himself in the dark.
	And you, my child. I hear you are yoked in marriage,
	and have the pleasure of making children
	in a stranger's house,
	and are tending a stranger's kinship,
	a thing your mother cannot bear,
	that Laius, your ancestor, cannot bear,
	the ruin a marriage brought in from outside.
	I never lit the fire for you,
	the torch a wedding calls for,
	the way a happy mother should.
	Ismenus was never asked to the wedding,
	never asked to bring the water for the bath, the luxury of it,
	and through the city of Thebes there was silence
	when your bride came in.
	Curse them all. Whether iron is to blame,
	or strife, or your father,
	or the god who came dancing drunk
	into the house of Oedipus,
	the pain of all these evils has come to me.

Chorus. Giving birth, with all its pains, is a powerful thing for women. The whole female race is somehow in love with its children.

Polyneices. Mother, whether it was sense or folly, I have come among enemies. But everyone has to love his country; there is no choice about it, and a man who says otherwise enjoys the words, but his mind is somewhere else. I was so frightened, so full of fear that some trick of my brother's would kill me, that I came through the city with my sword in my hand, turning my face in every direction. One thing helps me: the truce, and your promise, which brought me inside my father's walls. And I came in tears. It has been so long since I saw the house and the altars of the gods and the training grounds where I was brought up and the water of Dirce, and I was driven away from them unjustly to live in a foreign city, with a stream of tears running from my eyes. But now, pain on top of pain, I look at you with your head shaved and your black dress. Oh, my troubles. How terrible hatred is, mother, between people of one family, and how hard it makes the making of peace. What is my old father doing in the house, staring at darkness? And what of my two sisters? They must be grieving over my exile, poor things.

Jocasta. Some god is destroying the house of Oedipus out of malice. That is how it began: I gave birth against every law, your father made an evil marriage, and you were born. But what is the use of this? What the gods send has to be borne. I am afraid to ask you what I want to ask, in case I bite into your heart. But I long to.

Polyneices. No. Ask. Leave nothing out. What you want, mother, is what I want.

Jocasta. Then here is the first thing I want to know. What is it, to be robbed of your country? Is it a great evil?

Polyneices. The greatest. And it is worse in the living than in the telling.

Jocasta. What is it like? What is the hard part, for exiles?

Polyneices. One thing above all. You cannot say what you think.

Jocasta. That is a slave's condition you are describing. Not saying what you think.

Polyneices. You have to put up with the stupidity of the people in power.

Jocasta. That is painful too, to play the fool alongside fools.

Polyneices. But for profit you have to be a slave, against your nature.

Jocasta. Hopes feed exiles, they say.

Polyneices. They look at you with lovely eyes. But they keep you waiting.

Jocasta. Doesn't time show them up for the empty things they are?

Polyneices. They have a sweetness of their own for a man in trouble, like love does.

Jocasta. And where did you get your living, before your marriage found you one?

Polyneices. Some days I had enough for the day. Some days I had nothing.

Jocasta. Your father's friends, his guest-friends, did they not help you?

Polyneices. Be prosperous. Friends are nothing once you are down.

Jocasta. Did your good birth not lift you up high?

Polyneices. Having nothing is the evil. My birth did not feed me.

Jocasta. So a man's country, it seems, is the dearest thing he has.

Polyneices. You could not even put into words how dear it is.

Jocasta. How did you come to Argos? What was your idea?

Polyneices. Apollo gave Adrastus an oracle.

Jocasta. What oracle? What are you telling me? I do not follow.

Polyneices. To marry his daughters to a boar and a lion.

Jocasta. And what did you have to do with the names of animals, my child?

Polyneices. I do not know. The god called me to my fate.

Jocasta. Yes, the god is wise. But how did you win your wife?

Polyneices. It was night. I came to Adrastus's porch.

Jocasta. Looking for a bed, wandering, an exile?

Polyneices. That was it. And then another exile came there after me.

Jocasta. Who was that? He was miserable too, then.

Polyneices. Tydeus. They say Oeneus is his father.

Jocasta. And why did Adrastus compare the two of you to wild animals?

Polyneices. Because we came to blows over the bed.

Jocasta. That was when the son of Talaus understood the oracle?

Polyneices. Yes. And he gave the two of us his two daughters.

Jocasta. So are you lucky in your marriage, or unlucky?

Polyneices. I have no complaint against it, so far.

Jocasta. And how did you persuade an army to follow you here?

Polyneices. Adrastus swore this to his two sons-in-law, Tydeus and me, since he is married to my wife's sister: that he would bring us both back home, and me first. Many of the leading men of Argos and of Mycenae are here with me, doing me a favour I hate and cannot do without, because it is my own city I am marching against. I have sworn to the gods that I lifted the spear against the people I love most against my will, when they were willing enough. But the undoing of these evils comes down to you, mother: reconcile the people of one blood, and put an end to the trouble for me and for you and for the whole city. It has been sung a long time, but I will say it anyway: money is what people value most, and of everything in human life it has the most power. That is what I have come here for, with ten thousand spears at my back. A man of good family who is poor is nothing.

Chorus. And here is Eteocles coming to the reconciliation. It is your job, Jocasta, their mother, to say the kind of words that will bring your sons together.

(Eteocles comes in from the city, armed.)

Eteocles. Mother, I am here. I came to do you this favour. What do I have to do? Let somebody start the talking. I broke off posting the citizens in double companies round the walls to come and hear this arbitration of yours between us, the one you persuaded me to admit this man inside the walls under truce for.

Jocasta. Wait. Speed does not carry justice with it. Slow words get the most wisdom done. Loosen that terrible look on your face and the breath of your anger. You are not looking at the severed head of the Gorgon. You are looking at your brother, who has come. And you, Polyneices, turn your face towards your brother. If you look at the same point he is looking at, you will speak better and take in what he says better. I want to give you both one piece of good advice. When a man is angry with a friend and meets him face to face and looks him in the eye, he should consider only what he has come about, and keep no memory of the old evils. Polyneices, my child, your speech comes first, because you have come leading an army of Argives, and you say you have been wronged. May some god be the judge, and reconcile these evils.

Polyneices. The words of truth are simple. What is just does not need elaborate explanations; it carries its own fitness inside it. It is the unjust argument that is sick inside, and needs clever medicines. I looked ahead, for my father's house, to what was mine and what was his. I wanted to escape the curses Oedipus once spoke against us, so I left this country of my own free will, and I let him rule our homeland for the circle of one year, on the understanding that I would take my turn and rule again after him, and not come at him in hatred and envy, and do some harm and suffer some, which is what happens. He agreed to it. He swore it by the gods. And he has done nothing that he promised. He is holding the throne himself, and my share of our house along with it.

And I am ready, even now: give me what is mine, and I will send the army out of this country, and live in my own house for my turn, and hand it back to him for an equal time, turn and turn about. I will not sack my homeland, and I will not bring the fixed ladders up against its towers. Only if I do not get justice will I try to. I call the gods to witness this: that I am acting justly in everything, and it is without justice that I am being robbed of my homeland, the most unholy thing there is. That is the whole of it, mother, point by point. I have not wrapped it in twisted phrases. It is just, to the clever and to the simple alike, or so it seems to me.

Chorus. I was not brought up in the land of the Greeks. But to me, what you say makes sense.

Eteocles. If the same thing were fine and clever to everyone, there would be no disputed quarrels among human beings. As it is, there is nothing alike and nothing equal among mortals, except in the names. The thing itself does not exist. I will hide nothing from you, mother. I would go to where the stars and the sun rise, and under the earth, if I were able to do it, to hold Power, the greatest of the gods. So this good thing, mother, I have no wish to hand to another man rather than keep it for myself. It is cowardice to lose the greater and take the less. And there is this besides: I would be ashamed to let him come with weapons and ravage the land and get what he wants. That would be a disgrace to Thebes, if I gave up my sceptre to him out of fear of a Mycenaean spear. He should not have tried to make terms with weapons, mother. Words can do everything that an enemy's iron could do. Still, if he wants to live in this land on any other footing, he may. But that one thing I will not willingly let go. When I can rule, am I to be his slave? So let the fire come, let the swords come, harness your horses, fill the plains with chariots: I will not hand my power to him. If a man must do wrong, then to do wrong for the sake of power is the finest wrong there is. In everything else, let him be pious.

Chorus. Fine words should not be spent on deeds that are not fine. That is not fine. It is bitter to justice.

Jocasta. My child, Eteocles, not everything about old age is bad. Experience has something to say that is wiser than the young. Why are you reaching for Ambition, the worst of all the gods, my boy? Do not. She is an unjust goddess. She has gone into many homes and many prosperous cities, and come out again, and left the people who dealt with her in ruins. And she is the one you are mad for. It is a finer thing, my child, to honour Equality, who binds friend to friend, city to city, ally to ally, always. Equality is what holds steady among human beings, whereas the less is always the enemy of the more, and that is where the day of hatred begins. It was Equality that laid down measures for men, and the divisions of weights, and marked out numbers. The lightless eye of night and the light of the sun walk their yearly circle as equals, and neither of them is jealous when it has to give way. So the sun and the night are servants of mortals, and you will not put up with holding an equal share of the house and giving the same to him? Then where is justice?

Why do you honour Power so far beyond what she deserves, injustice with luck on its side, and think her such a great thing? Is it worth so much to be stared at? That is empty. Or do you want a great deal of trouble to go with a great deal of property in your house? What is "more"? It is only a name. What is enough is plenty, for people who keep themselves in hand. Mortals do not own their possessions. We hold what belongs to the gods, and look after it, and when they want it, they take it back. Wealth is not sure. It lasts a day.

Come, suppose I put two questions to you at once and ask you: do you want to be king, or do you want to save your city? Will you say, to be king? And what if he beats you, and the Argive spears beat down the spear of Cadmus's men? You will see this city of Thebes broken, and you will see many captive girls forced by enemy men and ravaged. So this wealth you are looking to hold will turn out to be a pain to Thebes. And you, you have your Ambition.

That is what I say to you. And to you, Polyneices, I say this. Adrastus did you a stupid favour, and you were a fool too, coming to lay waste your own city. Come, if you take this land, which may it never happen, then by the gods, how will you set up a trophy to Zeus? How will you begin the sacrifice after conquering your own homeland, and what will you write on the spoils by the streams of Inachus? "Polyneices burned Thebes and dedicated these shields to the gods"? My child, may you never win a name like that from the Greeks. And if instead you are beaten, and his side comes out on top, how will you go back to Argos, leaving ten thousand dead behind you? Someone is sure to say, "Adrastus, that was an evil match you made. For one bride's wedding, we are all destroyed." You are chasing two evils, my child: to lose what you have there, and to fall in the middle of what you are trying here.

Let it go, both of you, this too much. Let it go. When the folly of two men meets in the same place, it is the most hateful evil there is.

Chorus. Gods, turn these evils away, and give the sons of Oedipus some way to come to terms.

Eteocles. Mother, this is no longer a contest of words. The time we spend in between is wasted, and all your good will accomplishes nothing. We will never come to terms on anything but what has been said already: that I hold the sceptre and am king of this land. So spare me your long lectures, and let me be. And you: get outside these walls, or die.

Polyneices. At whose hands? Who is so impossible to wound that he could drive a murderous sword into me and not carry off the same death himself?

Eteocles. He is near. Not far off. Do you see my hands?

Polyneices. I see them. But wealth is a coward, and it loves its own life. That is the evil in it.

Eteocles. Then why did you bring so many men to fight a man who is nothing?

Polyneices. Because a safe general is better than a bold one.

Eteocles. You are a boaster, trusting in the truce that keeps you from dying.

Polyneices. It keeps you alive too. For the second time, I demand the sceptre and my share of the land.

Eteocles. I take no demands. I am going to live in my own house.

Polyneices. Holding more than your share?

Eteocles. I am. Now get out of the country.

Polyneices. Altars of my fathers' gods —

Eteocles. Which you are here to sack.

Polyneices. Hear me —

Eteocles. Who would hear you? You have marched against your homeland.

Polyneices. And temples of the gods who ride white horses —

Eteocles. Who hate you.

Polyneices. I am being driven out of my homeland —

Eteocles. Yes. Because you came to drive us out.

Polyneices. Unjustly, gods.

Eteocles. Call on the gods in Mycenae, not here.

Polyneices. You were born unholy —

Eteocles. But not my homeland's enemy, as you are.

Polyneices. You, who are driving me out with no share.

Eteocles. And I will kill you as well.

Polyneices. Father, do you hear what is being done to me?

Eteocles. Yes. And he hears what you are doing.

Polyneices. And you, mother?

Eteocles. It is forbidden for you to speak the name of your mother.

Polyneices. My city.

Eteocles. Go to Argos, and call on the waters of Lerna.

Polyneices. I am going. Do not trouble yourself. Mother, I thank you.

Eteocles. Get out of the land.

Polyneices. I am going. But let me see my father.

Eteocles. You will not get that.

Polyneices. Then my sisters, the unmarried girls.

Eteocles. You will never see them either.

Polyneices. My sisters.

Eteocles. Why are you calling on them? You are their worst enemy.

Polyneices. Mother, at least you: be well.

Jocasta. Well. Yes, I am doing wonderfully well, child.

Polyneices. I am your son no longer.

Jocasta. I was born to a great deal of misery.

Polyneices. Because this man is treating me with outrage.

Eteocles. And I am being outraged in return.

Polyneices. Where will you take your stand in front of the towers?

Eteocles. Why do you ask me that?

Polyneices. I will set myself opposite you, to kill you.

Eteocles. I have the same desire.

Jocasta. Oh, I am wretched. What are you going to do, my children?

Polyneices. It will show for itself.

Jocasta. Will you not run from your father's Furies?

Eteocles. Let the whole house go to ruin.

Polyneices. Yes. Soon enough my sword will not lie idle any longer. It will be red with blood. I call the land that raised me to witness, and the gods, that I am being driven out of this country dishonoured, suffering pitiful things, like a slave, and not a son of the same father, Oedipus, just as much as he is. And if anything happens to you, my city, do not blame me. Blame him. I did not come willingly, and unwillingly I am driven out of the land. And you, Lord Apollo, guardian of the streets, and these halls, goodbye, and the friends I grew up with, and the statues of the gods where the sheep are offered. I do not know whether I will ever speak to you again. But my hopes are not asleep yet. I trust in them, and in the gods, that I will kill this man and be master of this land of Thebes.

Eteocles. Get out of the country. It was a true name our father gave you, with a god's foresight: Polyneices, the man of many quarrels.

(Jocasta goes into the house. Polyneices goes out toward the Argive camp, and Eteocles into the palace.)

Chorus.
	Cadmus came to this land
	from Tyre, and a four-footed
	heifer, never broken, dropped itself down
	at his feet, and fulfilled the oracle,
	for the god's word had told him
	to settle there, on the plains
	that carry wheat, and make his home
	where the lovely river water
	comes up over the fields,
	the fields of Dirce, green,
	the deep-sown fields.
	There his mother bore Dionysus,
	from her marriage to Zeus,
	and the ivy wound its curling wreath
	round him, still a baby,
	and covered him with its green shoots,
	shade over shade, and blessed him:
	a Bacchic dance for the girls of Thebes
	and the women who cry Euoi.
Chorus.
	There was the murderous dragon
	of Ares, a savage-hearted guard,
	watching the running springs
	and the green streams
	with the wandering pupils of its eyes.
	Cadmus came for water to wash his hands
	and destroyed it with a lump of marble,
	striking the murderous head
	with a throw of his beast-killing arm,
	and at the word of Pallas,
	Zeus's daughter who had no mother,
	he threw the teeth
	into the deep-sown fields, to fall on the ground.
	And out of it the earth sent up
	a sight in full armour, over the topmost
	edge of the soil, and iron-hearted
	slaughter joined them to the dear earth again.
	It wet the ground with their blood, the ground
	that had shown them to the sunlit breath of the air.
Chorus.
	And you, Epaphus, born long ago
	from Io, our first mother,
	child of Zeus:
	I called you, I called you, with a barbarian cry,
	io, with barbarian prayers.
	Come, come to this land.
	Your descendants founded it,
	and the goddesses of the two names,
	Persephone and dear
	Demeter, the goddess who is queen of all,
	Earth, the nurse of all,
	took it for their own. Send the goddesses
	who carry the torches, and defend this land.
	Everything is easy for the gods.

(Eteocles comes out of the palace with a servant.)

Eteocles. You, go and fetch Creon, the son of Menoeceus, my mother Jocasta's brother. Tell him this: that I want to put my head together with his about the city's business, private and public, before we go into battle and set the army in its ranks. But no. He is sparing your feet the trouble. He is here; I can see him walking toward my house.

Creon. I have been a long way round looking for you, my lord Eteocles. I have been all round the gates of Thebes and the guard posts, hunting for you.

Eteocles. And I wanted to see you, Creon. When I went and put it to Polyneices face to face, I found the terms of peace a long way short.

Creon. I hear he has his mind set on more than Thebes, trusting in his marriage tie with Adrastus and in his army. But that we must leave hanging on the gods. What stands most in our way is what I have come to tell you.

Eteocles. What is it? I do not follow you.

Creon. Someone has come in, a prisoner taken from the Argives.

Eteocles. And what does he say is the latest news from there?

Creon. That the Argive army means to wrap the city of Cadmus's people in weapons, right round the towers, at once.

Eteocles. Then the city of Cadmus must carry its weapons out.

Creon. Out where? Are you so young you cannot see what you should see?

Eteocles. Out beyond those trenches, to fight straight away.

Creon. This country's numbers are small. Theirs are endless.

Eteocles. I know those men. They are bold in words.

Creon. Argos carries some weight among the Greeks.

Eteocles. Do not worry. I will soon fill the plain with their dead.

Creon. I would like that. But I see a great deal of hard work in it.

Eteocles. I will not keep my army inside the walls, I tell you.

Creon. And yet winning is all a matter of good planning.

Eteocles. So you want me to turn to some other road?

Creon. Every road, before the whole risk is run at once.

Eteocles. What if we attacked them at night, from ambush?

Creon. Yes, if you can get back here safely when it goes wrong.

Eteocles. Night is even-handed, but it gives more to the man who dares.

Creon. The dark of night is a terrible place to meet disaster.

Eteocles. Then shall I attack them with the spear while they are at their dinner?

Creon. That would give them a fright. But we need to win.

Eteocles. The ford of Dirce is deep, though, if they have to fall back across it.

Creon. Nothing is as good as keeping a good guard.

Eteocles. What if we rode the Argive army down with the cavalry?

Creon. There too the army is fenced all round with chariots.

Eteocles. Then what am I to do? Hand the city to the enemy?

Creon. Certainly not. Think it through. You are a clever man.

Eteocles. And what forethought is cleverer than mine?

Creon. Seven men, they say, or this is what I have heard —

Eteocles. Assigned to do what? Seven is not much strength.

Creon. To command companies, one posted at each of the seven gates.

Eteocles. Then what do we do? I will not sit and wait for the moment when there is nothing left to be done.

Creon. You choose seven men too, to set against them at the gates.

Eteocles. To lead companies, or to fight alone with the spear?

Creon. To lead companies. Pick out the very bravest.

Eteocles. I understand. To stop them scaling the walls.

Creon. And second-in-commands with them. One man does not see everything.

Eteocles. Do I pick them for courage, or for a clear head in planning?

Creon. Both. Either one, left on its own, is nothing.

Eteocles. It will be done. I will go to the city of seven towers and post the captains at the gates, as you say, matching them man for man against the enemy. To tell you each man's name would take a long time, with the enemy camped under our very walls. But I will go, so that my hands do not lie idle. And may I get my brother face to face, stand up to him in battle, take him with my spear, and kill him, for coming to sack my homeland.

The marriage of my sister Antigone and your son Haemon: if I stumble in my luck somehow, that is yours to see to. The promise I made before, I confirm now, as I go out. You are my mother's brother; why make a long speech of it? Look after her in a way that is worthy of you, for your own sake and for mine. As for my father, he has been convicted of folly against himself, blinding his own eyes. I do not have much praise for him. And if he gets the chance, he will kill us with his curses.

One thing we have left undone: to find out from the bird-reader Teiresias whether he has any prophecy to tell. I will send your son Menoeceus, who carries your father's name, to bring Teiresias here, Creon. He will come and talk to you gladly. I have found fault with his prophet's craft before this, to his face, so he has a grievance against me.

And this charge I lay on the city and on you, Creon: if my side wins, the body of Polyneices is never to be buried in this Theban soil, and whoever buries him dies, even if it is one of our own. That is what I have to say to you. And to my servants I say this: bring out my weapons and the armour that goes all round me, so that we can set out now for the contest of the spear that is waiting for us, with Justice on our side to bring the victory. And to Caution, the most useful of the gods, we pray: bring this city safely through.

(Eteocles goes out with his servants. Creon stays.)

Chorus.
	Ares, god of so much suffering, why, why
	are you possessed by blood and death,
	out of tune with the feasts of Dionysus?
	Not for the dances where the young girls
	wear their garlands, in the beauty of their youth,
	do you let your hair fly loose
	and sing to the breath of the pipe
	a song with the Graces in it, who make the dance.
	No. You breathe on the Argive army, armed men,
	with a thirst for the blood of Thebes,
	and lead your revel out in front of them,
	the revel with no flute at all.
	You do not come in the whirl of the fawnskin
	and the madness of the wands. You come
	on chariots, with bridles, four-hooved, uncut horses,
	riding down to the waters of Ismenus,
	breathing into the Argives hatred of the Sown Men,
	dressing an armed troop of shield-bearers in bronze
	to face our walls of stone.
	Strife is a terrible god,
	who planned these sorrows for the kings of this land,
	the sons of Labdacus, who have suffered so much.
Chorus.
	Cithaeron, valley of holy leaves,
	full of wild beasts, the snow-fed eye
	of Artemis: if only you had never
	raised the child put out to die, Jocasta's baby,
	Oedipus, thrown out of his home,
	his ankles marked by gold-bound pins.
	And if only the winged girl had never come,
	that monster from the mountains, a grief to this land,
	the Sphinx with her songs that had no music in them,
	who once came right up to our walls
	and with her four clawed feet carried off
	the sons of Cadmus into the untrodden light of the sky,
	sent up against the people of Cadmus by Hades under the ground.
	And now another strife, god-cursed, is coming into flower
	between the children of Oedipus, in the house and in the city.
	What is not fine can never be fine,
	and neither can children born against the law,
	a mother's labour, a father's pollution.
	She came to the bed of her own blood.
Chorus.
	You bore them, Earth, you bore them once,
	I learned it, I learned it once at home,
	the story told in a barbarian tongue,
	the race grown from the teeth
	of the dragon with the red crest, the eater of beasts:
	the finest disgrace Thebes ever had, its glory and its shame.
	Once the children of heaven came
	to the wedding of Harmonia, and to the lyre,
	to Amphion's lyre, the walls of Thebes rose,
	and its towers stood up
	between the crossing of the two rivers,
	where Dirce waters the green plain
	in front of Ismenus.
	And Io, the horned first mother,
	gave birth to the kings of Cadmus's line.
	And this city, changing from one blessing
	to another, ten thousand of them,
	stands on the heights,
	crowned with the wreaths of Ares.

(Teiresias comes in, old and blind, led by his daughter, with Creon's son Menoeceus beside them. He wears a golden crown.)

Teiresias. Lead the way, daughter. You are the eye for my blind feet, the way a star is to sailors. Set my steps here, on the level ground, and walk ahead, so we do not stumble; your father is weak. And keep the lots safe for me in your girl's hand, the ones I drew when I read the signs of the birds, sitting in the holy seat where I give my prophecies. Menoeceus, my boy, son of Creon, tell me: how much of the road through the city is left, to reach your father? My knees are failing me. I have come a long, hard walk, and I can barely get through it.

Creon. Courage, Teiresias. You are near your friends. You have brought your foot into harbour. Take hold of him, child. Every wagon, and every old man's foot, likes to wait for a hand from outside to lighten the load.

Teiresias. Well, then. Here we are. Why did you send for me in such a hurry, Creon?

Creon. I have not forgotten. But first gather your strength and get your breath back, and shake off the steep climb of the road.

Teiresias. I am worn through with tiredness, I admit it. I was brought here only yesterday from the land of Erechtheus's sons, from Athens. There was a war there too, against the spear of Eumolpus, and I gave the people of Cecrops their glorious victory. And this golden crown, which you can see, I have as the first fruits of the spoils taken from the enemy.

Creon. I take your crown of victory as an omen. We are lying in the surge of a war, as you know, against the spear of the Argives, and it is a great contest for Thebes. Our king, Eteocles, has already gone, dressed in his armour, to fight the strength of Mycenae. He has charged me to learn from you what we should do to have the best chance of saving the city.

Teiresias. For Eteocles' sake I would have shut my mouth and kept my prophecies to myself. But you want to learn, so I will tell you. This land has been sick a long time, Creon, ever since Laius fathered a child in the teeth of the gods, and begot poor Oedipus to be his own mother's husband. The bloody destruction of his eyes was the gods' clever device, and a lesson held up to Greece. The sons of Oedipus wanted to cover it over with time, as if they could outrun the gods, and they made a stupid mistake. They gave their father no honours and no way out of the house, and they turned an unlucky man savage; so he breathed terrible curses at them, in his sickness, and in the disgrace they had added to it. And I, what did I not do, what words did I not say, that I ended up hated by the sons of Oedipus?

Death is close to them, Creon, each at the other's hand. Many dead will fall on top of many dead, Argive weapons mixed with the weapons of Cadmus's men, and they will give the land of Thebes bitter cause for mourning. And you, poor city, you are being dug up by the roots along with them, unless someone listens to what I say. The first thing would have been for none of Oedipus's blood to be a citizen of this land, or its king, since they are possessed by a god and will turn the city over. But since the evil is stronger than the good, there is one other way to save it. But no. It is not safe for me to say it, and it is bitter for the people whose luck it is to supply the city with its saving medicine. I am going. Goodbye. I am one man among many, and what is coming I will suffer, if I have to. What else can I do?

Creon. Stop there, old man.

Teiresias. Do not grab at me.

Creon. Wait. Why are you running away?

Teiresias. It is your luck that is running from you. Not me.

Creon. Tell the citizens and the city how they can be saved.

Teiresias. You want that now. Very soon you will not want it.

Creon. How could I not want to save my father's land?

Teiresias. You really want to hear it, then? You are set on it?

Creon. What should I be more eager about than that?

Teiresias. Then you may hear my prophecies now. But first there is one thing I want to know for certain. Where is Menoeceus, who led me here?

Creon. He is not far off. He is right beside you.

Teiresias. Then let him go away, well out of hearing of my prophecies.

Creon. He is my son. He will keep quiet about what needs keeping quiet.

Teiresias. You want me to tell you with him standing here?

Creon. Yes. He will be glad to hear how the city is going to be saved.

Teiresias. Then hear the road my prophecies take. This is what you must do to save the city of Cadmus. You must cut the throat of Menoeceus here, your own son, for his country. You asked for your luck yourself.

Creon. What are you saying? What is this story you are telling me, old man?

Teiresias. What is so, is so. And you must do it.

Creon. So much evil, said in so short a time.

Teiresias. Evil for you. For your country, great good, and her salvation.

Creon. I did not hear it. I did not listen. Goodbye to the city.

Teiresias. This is not the same man. He is backing away from it.

Creon. Go, and good luck to you. I do not need your prophecies.

Teiresias. Has the truth died, because you have had bad luck?

Creon. By your knees, by your grey hair, I beg you—

Teiresias. Why are you falling at my feet? You are asking for evils that cannot be kept off.

Creon. Be quiet. Do not tell the city any of this.

Teiresias. You are telling me to do wrong. I will not be quiet.

Creon. What are you going to do to me, then? Kill my child?

Teiresias. That will be other people's business. Mine is to speak.
