Creon. And where did this evil come from, on me and on my son?

Teiresias. You are right to ask me that, and to come into the argument. This boy must be killed in the den where the earth-born dragon was born to keep watch over the springs of Dirce, and his throat must give its blood to the ground as a drink-offering to Cadmus's earth. It is because of the old anger of Ares, who is avenging the killing of his earth-born dragon. Do this and you will have Ares as your ally. If the earth takes fruit for fruit and human blood for blood, you will have her kind to you again, the earth who once sent up for us a crop of Sown Men in golden helmets. But one of that race has to die, one who was born from the dragon's jaw. And you are the last of the Sown Men left to us here, pure on both sides, your mother's and your father's, you and your sons. Haemon's marriage keeps him from the knife. He is not unmarried: even if he has not touched the bed yet, he has a wife. But this boy is a colt still loose, and he belongs to this city. If he dies, he can save his father's land. He will make a bitter homecoming for Adrastus and the Argives, throwing a black death over their eyes, and he will make Thebes famous. Choose one of these two fates. Save your son, or save the city.

That is everything I have for you. Lead me home, child. Anyone who practises the art of reading the burnt offerings is a fool. If he happens to see something his clients hate, he is hated by the people he reads the birds for. And if he takes pity on the people consulting him and lies to them, he wrongs the gods. Apollo should have been the only prophet men had. He is afraid of nobody.

(Teiresias goes, led by his daughter.)

Chorus. Creon, why are you silent? Why have you let your voice fall dead? I am no less stunned than you are.

Creon. What is there to say? It is plain enough what my answer is. I will never come to such a pass that I cut my son's throat and hand him to the city. Every human being alive loves his children, and nobody would give his own son to be killed. Let nobody praise me for it while he kills my children. I myself, since I am standing in the ripe part of my life, am ready to die to set my country free.

Come on, boy. Before the whole city hears this, forget the wild prophecies of seers, and run. Get out of this country as fast as you can. He will go to the rulers and the generals and the captains at the seven gates and tell them all of it. If we are ahead of him, you are safe. If you are late, we are finished, and you die.

Menoeceus. Where am I to run to, then? What city? Which of our guest-friends?

Creon. Wherever you will be furthest out of the way of this country.

Menoeceus. Then it is for you to say where, and for me to get there.

Creon. Go past Delphi—

Menoeceus. And where do I go then, father?

Creon. Into the land of Aetolia.

Menoeceus. And from there, where do I cross to?

Creon. The soil of Thesprotia.

Menoeceus. The holy floor of Dodona?

Creon. You have it.

Menoeceus. And what protection will that be for me?

Creon. The god will send you on your way.

Menoeceus. And money? Where does that come from?

Creon. I will send the gold along.

Menoeceus. Good, father. That is a good plan. Go now. I am going to your sister, Jocasta, I mean, the woman whose breast I first sucked when I lost my mother and was left an orphan, unyoked. I will say goodbye to her and then I will save my life. Go on, go. Do not let anything of yours hold me back.

(Creon goes.)

Women, how neatly I took my father's fear away, stealing it with words, so that I get what I want. He is smuggling me out of the country, robbing the city of its luck and handing me over to cowardice. In an old man that is forgivable. In me there is no forgiveness for it: to turn traitor to the country that gave me birth. So that you know, then: I am going to save the city, and I am going to give my life and die for this land. It would be shameful otherwise. Men who are free of any prophecy, who have not come under any necessity laid on them by the gods, stand shield to shield and are not afraid to die, fighting for their country in front of her towers. And I, betraying my father and my brother and my own city, walk out of the country like a coward? Wherever I lived, I would be shown for a bad man. No. By Zeus among the stars, and by Ares the blood-red, who set the Sown Men up as lords of this land when they rose out of the earth, I will go, and I will stand on the top of the battlements, and I will cut my own throat over the dragon's deep black den, where the seer said, and I will set this land free. That is the whole speech. I am going now, to give the city a gift that is nothing to be ashamed of, my death, and to rid this country of its sickness. If every man took whatever good he could do and worked it through to the end and brought it in to the common store for his country, cities would have fewer evils to live through, and they would do well from then on.

(Menoeceus goes.)

Chorus.
	You came, you came,
	winged thing, child of the earth
	and of the snake-woman down below,
	to snatch the sons of Cadmus,
	all death, all groaning,
	half a girl,
	a monster made to kill,
	with wings that never rested
	and claws that ate raw meat.
	From the country round Dirce's stream
	you lifted young men into the air,
	with a song no lyre would play,
	a Fury of destruction,
	and you brought, you brought grief to our country,
	murderous grief. Murderous was the god
	who did this to us.
	Mothers' wailing,
	girls' wailing,
	went groaning through the houses.
	A cry of woe,
	a song of woe,
	one after another took it up
	in turn across the town.
	The groaning, and the echo of it,
	were like thunder
	every time the winged girl
	carried one more man out of the city.
Chorus.
	And in time there came,
	sent out from Delphi,
	Oedipus, the long-suffering man,
	to this land of Thebes.
	We were glad then. Then came the grief.
	He won the riddle, and the prize
	for winning was a marriage,
	an unholy marriage, with his mother,
	poor wretch,
	and he stained the city with it.
	And through blood he passes on
	into a filthy contest, throwing his sons
	down into it with his curses,
	the miserable man. We admire him, we admire him,
	the boy who is going to his death
	for his father's land,
	leaving Creon his tears,
	but making the seven-towered gates of this country
	victorious.
	Let us be mothers like that,
	let us have children like that, dear
	Pallas, you who brought the dragon's blood
	to the ground with a thrown stone,
	when you set Cadmus's mind
	moving to the deed,
	from which some ruin sent by the gods came rushing
	on this land, to snatch and tear.

(A Messenger, one of Eteocles's men, comes in and beats on the door.)

Messenger. Hey. Who is at the gates of the house? Open up. Bring Jocasta out of the house. Hey, again. It is taking a long time, but come out all the same. Listen to me, famous wife of Oedipus. Stop your mourning and your tears of grief.

(Jocasta comes out.)

Jocasta. My dear friend, you have not come with news of disaster, have you? Eteocles dead? You have always marched beside his shield, keeping the enemy's spears off him. What is this new word you have come to bring me? Is my son dead or alive? Tell me.

Messenger. He is alive. Do not be afraid of that. Let me take that fear off you.

Jocasta. Well? How are the walls with the seven towers holding?

Messenger. They stand unbroken. The city has not been taken.

Jocasta. Did they come into danger from the Argive spear?

Messenger. To the very edge of it. But the fighting men of Cadmus proved stronger than the spear of Mycenae.

Jocasta. Tell me one thing, by the gods, if you know anything about Polyneices. That matters to me too, whether he still sees the light.

Messenger. Your sons are alive, the pair of them, as of today.

Jocasta. Bless you. How did you drive the Argive spear back from the gates, shut in behind the towers as you were? Tell me, so that I can go into the house and cheer the old blind man, now that this land is safe.

Messenger. After Creon's son, the boy who died for his country, had stood on the top of the towers and driven a black-hilted sword through his throat to save this land, your son divided the army into seven companies with seven captains and posted them at the seven gates to guard against the Argive spear. He set horsemen in reserve behind horsemen, and armed men behind the shield-bearers, so that wherever the wall was sick, help with the spear would be close at hand. From the high citadel we watched the Argive army with its white shields leave Teumessus, and near the ditch they closed on the town of Cadmus's land at a run. The war-cry and the trumpets rang out together from their side and from our walls.

First to the Neistan gate came Parthenopaeus, the huntress's son, leading a company bristling with close-packed shields. He had his own family emblem in the middle of his shield: Atalanta bringing down the Aetolian boar with a long-range bow. To the Proetid gate went the prophet Amphiaraus, with the animals for sacrifice on his chariot. He carried no boastful emblem. His weapons were modest and plain. To the Ogygian gate marched lord Hippomedon, with an emblem in the middle of his shield: Argus who sees everything, staring out of eyes stippled all over him, some of the eyes open with the rising of the stars and some closing as they set, as we could see afterwards, when he was dead. At the Homoloid gate Tydeus had his post, a lion's skin on his shield with the mane bristling, and in his right hand the Titan Prometheus carried a torch, as if to burn the city. Your own Polyneices brought the fighting to the Crenaean gate. The emblem on his shield was the mares of Potniae, running mad and leaping with fright, turned somehow by pivots on the inside, right under the handgrip, so that they seemed to have really gone mad. And Capaneus, who thinks himself no less than Ares when it comes to a fight, led his company against the Electran gate. On the iron back of his shield was stamped an earth-born giant carrying a whole city on his shoulders, levered up off its foundations with crowbars: a hint to us of what our city was going to suffer. And at the seventh gate was Adrastus, with a hundred snakes painted to fill his shield, the hydra on his left arm, the pride of Argos, and out of the middle of the walls the snakes were carrying off the children of Cadmus in their jaws. I had a view of every one of them, because I was carrying the password along the line to the captains of the companies.

To begin with we fought them with bows and thonged javelins, with long-range slings and crashing stones. And as we were winning the fight, Tydeus and your son suddenly shouted out: "Sons of Danaus, before you are shredded by their missiles, why are you waiting? All of you, together, throw yourselves at the gates, light troops, horsemen, the men on the chariots." When they heard that cry there was not one of them idle. Many fell with their heads streaming blood, and on our side too you could have seen men in front of the walls tumbling to the ground like acrobats, thick on the ground, breathing their last, and wetting the dry earth with streams of blood.

Then the Arcadian, not an Argive, Atalanta's son, threw himself at the gates like a whirlwind and shouted for fire and pickaxes, to dig the city up out of the ground. But Periclymenus, the sea-god's son, stopped him in his frenzy by dropping a stone on his head that would have filled a wagon, a coping-stone off the battlements. It smashed his fair-haired head to powder and burst the seams of the bones of his skull, and the cheek that had only just turned red with youth ran with blood. He will not carry his life home to his mother with the lovely bow, the girl of Maenalus.

When your son saw that this gate was doing well, he went on to the others, and I followed him. I saw Tydeus and a close-packed line of his shield-men hurling their Aetolian spears up into the very mouth of the towers, so that our men left the edge of the battlements and ran. But your son gathered them again, like a huntsman calling in his dogs, and posted them back on the towers. And we hurried on to other gates, once we had stopped the sickness there.

And Capaneus. How can I tell you how mad he was? He came on carrying the climbing-rungs of a long-necked ladder, and this was his boast: that not even the holy fire of Zeus would keep him from taking the city from the top of its citadel. And he was still shouting it as he climbed, under a rain of stones, with his body wound up under his shield, changing his footing rung by smooth rung up the ladder. And just as he was stepping over the coping of the wall, Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt. The earth boomed, so that everyone was afraid, and from the ladder his limbs were slung apart from each other like slingshot, his hair to Olympus and his blood to the ground, and his arms and legs went spinning round like the wheel of Ixion, and the body fell to the earth on fire.

When Adrastus saw that Zeus was his army's enemy, he pulled the Argive force back outside the ditch. But our men had seen the sign from Zeus was on our side, and they drove out the chariots, horsemen and armed men together, and closed their spears with the Argives in the middle of their ranks. And every kind of evil was there at once. Men were dying, men were pitched over chariot-rails, wheels leaped into the air, axles piled on axles, and the dead were heaped on the dead. So we have kept the towers of this land from being dug up, for today. But whether this country will have good luck from now on rests with the gods. Even today it was one of the gods who saved her.

Chorus. Winning is a fine thing. And if the gods have a better judgement in store for us, I would be a lucky woman.

Jocasta. The gods and luck have done well by us. My sons are alive, and the land has escaped. But it is Creon who seems to have got the bitter fruit of my marriage to Oedipus, poor man, and lost his son: good luck for the city, and grief for him alone. But go back over it for me. What do my two sons mean to do next?

Messenger. Leave the rest alone. So far you are lucky.

Jocasta. Now you have made me suspicious. I cannot leave it alone.

Messenger. What more do you want than your sons safe?

Jocasta. To hear whether I am going to be lucky from here on too.

Messenger. Let me go. Your son is out there without his shield-bearer.

Jocasta. You are hiding some evil, and covering it up in the dark.

Messenger. I would not tell you bad news on top of your good news.

Jocasta. You will, unless you sprout wings and fly off into the sky.

Messenger. Aiai. Why did you not let me go after my good news, instead of making me tell the bad? Your two sons mean to do a thing of the most shameful daring: to fight one against one, apart from the whole army. They said this to the Argives and the men of Cadmus together, a speech I wish they had never made. Eteocles began it. He stood up on a high tower, ordered silence to be proclaimed to the army, and said: "Generals of the land of Greece, chiefs of the Danaans who came here, and people of Cadmus, do not sell your lives for Polyneices' sake, or for mine. I am going to take this danger off you myself, and fight my brother alone. If I kill him, I will keep my house alone. If I lose, I will hand it over to him alone. Argives, give up the contest and go home to your country, and do not leave your lives here. And there are enough of the Sown Men lying dead already." That was his speech. Your son Polyneices came running out of the ranks and approved it. And all the Argives roared their approval, and the people of Cadmus too, because they thought it was fair. On those terms they made a truce, and in the ground between the two armies the generals swore oaths to keep it.

And then the two young men, old Oedipus's sons, were covering themselves in bronze armour, and their friends were dressing them: the best of the Sown Men dressing the champion of this land, and the leading Argives dressing the other. There they stood, shining, and their colour did not change, and they were wild to let fly their spears at each other. Their friends came up to them from either side, one after another, and encouraged them with words, and this is what they said: "Polyneices, it rests with you to set up a statue of Zeus as a trophy and to give Argos a glorious name." And to Eteocles: "Now you are fighting for your city. Now, win this and you hold the sceptre." That is what they said, urging them on to the fight. And the prophets were killing sheep, and watching the points of the flames on the fire, and the cracks, and the wet reek that means defeat, and the peak of the flame, which marks two things at once: the sign of victory and the sign of the losers.

So if you have any strength, or any clever words, or any love-spell of a charm, go. Hold your children back from this terrible contest. The danger is very great, and the terrible prize you will win for it is tears, if you are robbed of both your sons on this one day.

(The Messenger goes back the way he came, toward the field.)

Jocasta. Antigone, my child, come out of the house. The way the gods have set things for you now is no time for dancing or the things girls do. There are two brave men, and they are your brothers, and they are swerving toward death, and you and your mother must stop them from dying at each other's hands.

(Antigone comes out of the house.)

Antigone. Mother who bore me, what new terror are you crying out to your friends in front of this house?

Jocasta. Daughter, your brothers' lives are going down.

Antigone. What do you mean?

Jocasta. They have set themselves to fight one spear against one.

Antigone. Oh, no. What are you going to tell me, mother?

Jocasta. Nothing kind. Follow me.

Antigone. Where? Leaving the women's rooms?

Jocasta. Through the army.

Antigone. I am ashamed to face the crowd.

Jocasta. There is no room for shame in your position now.

Antigone. But what am I to do?

Jocasta. You will end your brothers' quarrel.

Antigone. Doing what, mother?

Jocasta. Falling at their knees, with me.

Antigone. Take me to the ground between the armies. We must not wait.

Jocasta. Hurry, hurry, daughter. If I can get to my sons before the spears, my life stays in the light. If they die, I will lie down dead with them.

(Jocasta and Antigone hurry out.)

Chorus.
	Aiai, aiai. My heart is shaking,
	shaking with the cold of fear. Through my flesh
	pity has come, pity
	for the wretched mother.
	Twin sons. Which of them, then,
	will bloody the other,
	io, for the pain of it, io Zeus, io Earth,
	a brother's throat, a brother's life,
	through the shields, through the blood?
	I am wretched, wretched. Which of them
	will I cry over as a corpse when he is gone?
Chorus.
	Pheu, Earth. Pheu, Earth. Twin beasts,
	two murderous souls with spears shaking in their hands,
	in a moment now will bloody
	the enemy fallen, fallen.
	Poor wretches, that it ever came into their heads
	to fight one against one.
	In a foreign voice I will raise the groaning cry
	that is owed to the dead, and weep it through.
	Fortune stands close, close to murder.
	The light of this day will decide it. Doomed,
	doomed is this killing, for the Furies' sake.

(Creon comes in, carrying the body of Menoeceus.)

Chorus. But here is Creon. I see him coming this way to the house, with a cloud on his face, and I will stop the grieving I am in the middle of.

Creon. Oh. What am I going to do? Which do I cry for, myself or the city, which has a cloud round it thick enough to be going through the river of Acheron? My son is dead. He died for this land, and he won a noble name for it, and a painful one for me. I have just taken him from the dragon's cliffs, where he cut his own throat, and I carried him here in my own arms, wretched as I am, and the whole house is crying out. And now I have come, an old man, for my old sister, for Jocasta, so that she can wash my boy and lay him out. He is gone now. Those who are not yet dead have to pay the dead their honours. It is how we show respect to the god under the ground.

Chorus. Your sister has left the house, Creon, and her daughter Antigone went out with her, the two of them together.

Creon. Where to? What has happened? Tell me.

Chorus. She heard that her sons were about to meet shield to shield, in single combat, for the royal house.

Creon. What are you saying? I was cradling the body of my own boy. I never got as far as hearing this too.

Chorus. Your sister has been gone a long while, Creon. I think the fight for life and death between the sons of Oedipus has already been fought.

Creon. Oh. And there is the sign of it, I can see it: the dark look on the face of a messenger, coming this way. He will tell us everything that has been done.

(A Messenger comes in from the battlefield.)

Messenger. God help me, what story do I tell? What grief do I cry out first?

Creon. We are finished. That is no fair face to put on the start of a speech.

Messenger. God help me, I say it twice. What I am carrying is a great evil.

Creon. On top of the evils already done. What is it? Say it.

Messenger. Your sister's sons are no longer in the light, Creon.

Creon. Aiai. That is a great grief you are crying out, for me and for the city. House of Oedipus, did you hear this? Both sons dead, and dead the same way?

Chorus. Enough to make it weep, if it happened to have feelings.

Creon. Oh, the heaviest blow fortune ever struck. Oh, the evils. I am a wretched man. God help me.

Messenger. You would say so, if you knew the evils on top of these.

Creon. How could anything be worse fortune than this?

Messenger. Your sister is dead. She died with her two sons.

Chorus.
	Raise it, raise the cry of mourning,
	and beat your heads with your white arms.

Creon. Jocasta, poor woman, what an end you came to. Your life and your marriage together, the whole of what you had to bear from the Sphinx and her riddles, over. And how was it done, the killing of the two boys, the curse of Oedipus fighting itself out? Tell me.

Messenger. You know how the fighting in front of the towers went for us. The circuit of the walls is not far off, so none of that was hidden from you. But once the young sons of old Oedipus had fitted their bodies with bronze armour, they came out and took their stand in the middle ground between the two armies, two captains, two generals, ready for the contest, ready to settle it with the strength of one spear each.

Polyneices looked towards Argos and made his prayer. "Lady Hera. I am your man, since I married the daughter of Adrastus and live in your country. Grant me this: let me kill my brother, and let my right hand, raised against his, come home red with his blood and victorious." He was asking for the most shameful crown there is, to kill his own blood. Tears came to many eyes at the size of the misfortune, and men looked at one another, passing the glance from face to face.

Eteocles looked towards the temple of Athena with the golden shield and prayed. "Daughter of Zeus, grant that this arm of mine throws the winning spear from my hand into my brother's chest, and kills the man who came to sack my country."

Then the call of the Tuscan trumpet was let loose like a torch, the signal for the bloody fight, and they went at each other at a terrible run. Like two boars whetting their savage jaws they closed, beards soaked with foam. They lunged with their spears, but each crouched down under the circle of his shield, so the iron would slide off and find nothing. If either saw the other's eye showing above the rim, he worked his lance towards it, hoping to get in first with the point. But they both kept their eyes so close to the spy-holes of their shields that the spears had nothing to do. More sweat ran off the men watching than off the men fighting, out of fear for the friends they loved.

Then Eteocles kicked aside a stone that had rolled under his foot, and in doing it he put his leg out beyond his shield. Polyneices saw a blow offered to his iron and met it with his spear, and the Argive point went through the shin. The whole army of the Danaids roared. But in the same effort the man who had been wounded first saw a shoulder left bare, and drove his lance with all his weight into Polyneices' chest, and gave the citizens of Cadmus their joy back, and snapped the head off his spear doing it. Left without a weapon he backed away step by step, then snatched up a lump of marble and threw it and broke the other's javelin in the middle. Now Ares had made it even. Both of them had lost the shaft out of their hand.

So they grabbed the hilts of their swords and came together, and their shields clashed, and they set up a great turmoil of fighting, round and round each other. Then Eteocles somehow thought of the Thessalian trick, and brought it in; he knew it from time spent in that country. He broke off from the struggle in front of him and drew his left foot back, watching the hollow of the other man's belly from a distance, then stepped in on his right leg and drove the sword through the navel and lodged it in the spine. Ribs and belly folded together, and Polyneices went down, poor man, in a spray of blood.

And the other, as if he had won now, as if the fight were over, threw his sword down on the ground and started stripping him, with his whole mind on that and none of it on himself. And that was what brought him down. Polyneices was still breathing, a little, and he had kept hold of his iron through his miserable fall, and with difficulty, but he did it, he pushed the sword up into Eteocles' liver: Polyneices, the one who had fallen first. And they lie there, both, biting the earth, close beside each other, and they have not decided who was the stronger.

Chorus. Ah. Ah. Oedipus, how I groan for your evils. It looks as if a god has filled your curses to the brim.

Messenger. Now hear the evils that came on top of these. When the two sons had fallen and were letting go of life, at that moment their wretched mother came rushing up, with the girl beside her, as fast as her feet would take her. She saw them, wounded, the wounds that kill, and she wailed: "Children, I have come to help you and I have come too late." She threw herself on each of her children in turn and wept and keened, groaning over all the long labour of the breasts that fed them, and their sister, standing at her side like a shield-bearer, cried with her: "You two were meant to keep our mother in her old age. My dearest brothers, you have thrown my marriage away."

Then lord Eteocles let a hard dying breath out of his chest, and heard his mother, and laid a wet hand on her. He sent no voice out, but he spoke to her with tears, from his eyes, so as to show that he loved her. And the other was still breathing, and Polyneices looked at his sister and his old mother and said this: "We are finished, mother. I pity you, and this sister of mine, and my brother lying dead. The one I loved became my enemy, but I loved him all the same. Bury me, mother, mother who bore me, and you too, sister, in the land of my fathers, and talk the city out of its anger, so that I get at least this much of my father's country, even if I have lost the house. Close my eyelids with your hand, mother" (and he put her hand on his eyes himself) "and goodbye. The dark is closing round me already." Then both of them, at the same moment, breathed out their wretched lives.

And the mother, when she saw what had happened, was past bearing it. She snatched a sword from the dead and did a terrible thing. She drove the iron straight through the middle of her throat, and she lies there dead among the people she loved most, with an arm thrown round each of them.

Then the whole crowd of soldiers leapt to their feet and fell to arguing: we said my master had won, they said theirs had. And the generals quarrelled too, some saying Polyneices had struck first with the spear, others that since both were dead there was no victory anywhere. In the middle of it Antigone slipped away from the army. Then they ran for their weapons. But by some good forethought the people of Cadmus had stayed sitting under their shields, and we got in first, and fell on the Argive army before it had got itself fenced in armour. Not a man stood his ground. They filled the plain, running, and the blood ran from the countless dead going down under our spears. And when we had won the battle, some set up an image of Zeus as a trophy, and some stripped the shields off the Argive dead and sent the spoils inside the walls. And others are coming here now with Antigone, carrying the dead, for the people who loved them to mourn over. So for the city these contests came out two ways: the luckiest that could be, and the unluckiest.

(The Messenger goes. The bodies of Eteocles, Polyneices and Jocasta are carried in, with Antigone walking beside them.)

Chorus.
	The bad luck of this house
	no longer reaches us as a rumour. Look, you can see it:
	three bodies of the dead, here already,
	at the palace door, who drew one death between them
	and a lifetime in the dark.
Antigone.
	I am not veiling the soft cheek
	with its curls. I am not hiding, like a modest girl,
	the crimson under my eyes, the blush on my face.
	I am carried along, a bacchant of the dead,
	throwing the veil off my hair,
	letting the fine saffron of my dress fall loose,
	an escort for the dead, full of groaning. Aiai. Io moi.
	Polyneices, Man of Many Quarrels, your name came true. Omoi moi, Thebes.
	Your quarrel, no, not a quarrel, murder on top of murder,
	has destroyed the house of Oedipus,
	finished it in terrible blood, in grievous blood.
	What singer,
	what music-maker's groan over tears
	and more tears, house, oh house,
	shall I call in,
	carrying these three bodies of my own blood,
	a mother and her children, the Fury's delight?
	She wrecked the house of Oedipus from top to bottom,
	the day he understood
	the song nobody understood, the song of the wild Sphinx,
	and killed the singer where she sat.
	Io moi moi, father.
	What Greek, what barbarian,
	what nobleman of the old days
	ever bore such evils
	of a single day's blood,
	such griefs laid out in plain sight?
	Poor girl, how I cry.
	What bird, sitting up in the high-leaved
	branches of an oak or a fir,
	will sing along with my grief,
	a girl mourning a mother who is gone?
	Ailinon, with these wails
	I cry out ahead of time for the solitary life
	I will lead for the rest of time,
	in tears that never stop dripping.
	On whom shall I throw the first
	offerings torn out of my hair?
	On the two breasts of my mother
	that gave me milk,
	or on my brothers'
	bodies, on the ruin of their wounds?
	Ototototoi. Come out of your
	house, carrying your blind eyes,
	old father, show yourself,
	Oedipus, show your wretched life, you who threw
	a misty darkness over your own eyes inside that house
	and go on dragging out a long-drawn breath of living.
	Do you hear, you wandering the courtyard
	on your old feet,
	or lying wretched
	in your bed?

(Oedipus comes out of the palace, feeling his way with a staff.)

Oedipus.
	Girl, why have you brought me out into the light,
	me, a blind man and his stick,
	out of my bed in the dark rooms,
	with these most pitiful tears of yours,
	a grey unseen phantom of air, or
	a corpse from under the earth, or
	a dream with wings?
Antigone.
	It is bad news you are going to hear, father.
	Your children no longer look at the light,
	and neither does your wife, who worked
	for ever at your side like a second staff, tending your blind feet.
	Father. Omoi.
Oedipus.
	Omoi for what I suffer. I have cause to groan at this, to cry out.
	Three lives. By what fate,
	how, did they leave the light? Child, tell me.
Antigone.
	I do not say it to reproach you or to mock you,
	I say it in pain: your own avenging spirit,
	heavy with swords
	and fire and pitiless fighting, came down on your sons.
	Father. O moi.
Oedipus.
	Aiai.
Antigone.
	Why do you groan at that,
Oedipus.
	My children.
Antigone.
	You have gone through pain.
	But if you could still see the sun's four-horse chariot
	and turn the light of your eyes
	onto these dead bodies here...
Oedipus.
	What happened to my children is plain enough.
	But my poor wife, child, by what fate did she die on me?
Antigone.
	Weeping, wailing,
	where everyone could see,
	she carried her breast to her children, carried it,
	a suppliant running to beg them.
	She found her children at the Electran gate,
	in the meadow where the lotus grows, at spear-point,
	at war with each other,
	the mother did, like lions in a den,
	fighting on over their wounds, their blood
	already a cold murderous offering
	that Hades took and Ares poured.
	And she took a beaten-bronze sword from the dead men and dipped it
	into her flesh, and in grief for her children she fell across her children.
	All of it, father, in this one day,
	the god who is finishing this has heaped up
	the griefs on our house.

Chorus. This day has been the beginning of many evils for the house of Oedipus. May the life that is left be luckier.

Creon. Stop the mourning now. It is time to think about burial. And you, Oedipus, hear this. Your son Eteocles gave me the rule of this land when he gave it as a dowry to Haemon, along with your daughter Antigone's hand in marriage. So I will not let you live in this country any longer. Teiresias said it in plain words: this city will never do well while you are living in it. So get out. And I say this without any outrage, and not as your enemy. It is those avenging spirits of yours. I am afraid the land will suffer some evil from them.

Oedipus. Fate, how you made me from the very start, wretched and miserable, if ever a man was born so. Before I had even come out of my mother's womb into the light, when I was not yet born, Apollo told Laius that I would be my father's killer. God help me. Then, once I was born, the father who begot me tried to kill me, in his turn, because he took me for his enemy, since he was fated to die at my hands. So he sent me out, still crying for the breast, to be a wretched meal for wild animals. And I was saved from that. I wish Cithaeron had sunk into the bottomless gulf of Tartarus for not finishing me off there, and instead my fate handed me over to a life in another man's house, with Polybus for a master.

And I killed my own father, I, the man the god hates, and went into the bed of my poor mother, and fathered sons who were my brothers, and I have destroyed them, by taking over the curses of Laius and handing them on to my children. I was not born such a fool that I could have devised all this against my own eyes and my own children's lives without some god being in it.

Well, then. What am I to do now, the man the god hates? Who will walk beside me and guide my blind feet? This woman lying dead? If she were alive, I know very well she would. My fine pair of sons? I have none. Am I still young enough to find my own living? Where would I find it? Why are you killing me outright like this, Creon? You will be killing me, if you throw me out of the country. But I will not wrap my arms round your knees and show myself a coward. I would not betray what I once was, a man of good birth, even now that I am doing badly.

Creon. Well said, on your side, that you will not touch my knees. And on mine, I could not let you go on living in this land. As for these dead, one of them must be taken into the house now. The other, the one who came with strangers to sack the city of his fathers, Polyneices: throw his body out unburied, beyond the borders of this country. And this will be proclaimed to every man of Thebes: whoever is caught laying wreaths on this corpse, or covering it with earth, will pay for it with his death. Leave him unwept, unburied, food for birds. And you, Antigone, leave off your keening for these three dead and take yourself indoors, and live as a girl should until the day that is coming, the day the bed of Haemon waits for you.

Antigone. Father, what evils we lie in, the two of us, wretched as we are. How I groan for you, more than for the dead. It is not as if one of your evils weighs heavy and another does not. You were born unlucky in everything, father. But I have a question for you, our brand-new ruler. Why are you outraging my father here by sending him out of the country? Why are you making laws over a poor dead body?

Creon. This was Eteocles' decision. Not ours.

Antigone. A senseless one, and you are a fool to obey it.

Creon. How so? Is it not right to carry out what you have been ordered to do?

Antigone. Not if the orders are wicked, and wickedly given.

Creon. What? Is it not justice for this man to be given to the dogs?

Antigone. No. The justice you are taking from him is against the law.

Creon. Not if he was an enemy of his city, when he was not born one.

Antigone. And so he has paid his fate over to fortune. He is dead.

Creon. Then let him pay the penalty in his burial too.

Antigone. What did he do wrong, if he came for his share of the land?

Creon. This man will go unburied. You may as well learn that now.

Antigone. I will bury him, even if the city forbids it.

Creon. Then you will be burying yourself beside him.

Antigone. It is an honour, for two people who love each other to lie side by side.

Creon. Take hold of her and bring her into the house.

Antigone. No. I will not let go of this body.

Creon. The god has decided this, girl. Not you.

Antigone. And this has been decided too: that the dead are not to be outraged.

Creon. Nobody is going to put damp earth round this man.

Antigone. Yes, they are. I beg you, Creon, by my mother Jocasta lying here.

Creon. You are wasting your effort. You will not get it.

Antigone. Then at least let me wash the body.

Creon. That would be one of the things forbidden to the city.

Antigone. Then let me put bandages round his terrible wounds.

Creon. There is no way you are going to pay this corpse any honour.

Antigone. My dearest. Then I will kiss your mouth, at least.

Creon. Do not go buying yourself a disaster for your wedding with all this grieving.

Antigone. Do you really think I will marry your son while I am alive?

Creon. You will have to. Where would you run away from the marriage bed?

Antigone. Then that wedding night will make me one of the daughters of Danaus, who killed their husbands in the dark.

Creon. Did you hear the nerve of that? Did you hear the insult?

Antigone. Let the iron witness it. Let the sword be my oath.

Creon. Why are you so anxious to be out of this marriage?

Antigone. I am going into exile with him. With my father, the most wretched man alive.

Creon. There is nobility in you. And there is some foolishness too.

Antigone. And I will die with him, so that you learn the rest of it.

Creon. Go, then. You will not murder my son. Leave the country.

(Creon goes into the palace.)

Oedipus. Daughter, I honour you for your loyalty.

Antigone. And what should I do, father, get married while you go into exile alone?

Oedipus. Stay, and be happy. I will put up with my own evils.

Antigone. And who will look after you, father, blind as you are?

Oedipus. I will fall where my fate decides, and lie on the ground.

Antigone. And where is Oedipus then, and the famous riddle?

Oedipus. Gone. One day made me rich, and one day destroyed me.

Antigone. Then should I not share in your evils too?

Oedipus. It is a shameful thing, a daughter in exile with a blind father.

Antigone. Not if she keeps herself in hand. Then it is a noble thing, father.

Oedipus. Lead me over, then, so I can touch your mother.

Antigone. There. Put your hand on her. The old woman you loved most.

Oedipus. Mother. Wife. The most wretched woman alive.

Antigone. She lies there pitifully, with every evil on her at once.

Oedipus. And where are they, the fallen bodies of Eteocles and Polyneices?

Antigone. The two of them lie stretched out here, close together.

Oedipus. Put my blind hand on their unlucky faces.

Antigone. There. Touch your dead children with your hand.

Oedipus. Dear fallen bodies. Wretched sons of a wretched father.

Antigone. And you, Polyneices, the dearest name of all to me.

Oedipus. Now Apollo's prophecy is coming true, child.

Antigone. Which one? Do you have more evils to tell me, on top of these?

Oedipus. That I would die in Athens, a wanderer.

Antigone. Where? What walled town in Attica will take you in?

Oedipus. Holy Colonus, the home of the god of horses. But come, be a servant to your blind father here, since you are so eager to share this exile.

Antigone.
	Go, then, into wretched exile. Stretch out your dear hand,
	old father. I will carry you along
	the way a wind carries a ship.
Oedipus.
	Look, look, I am walking.
	Child, be the guide for my feet, poor girl.
Antigone.
	I am, I am. Poor girl, yes,
	the poorest of all the girls in Thebes.
Oedipus.
	Where do I put my old feet down?
	Hand me my staff, child.
Antigone.
	This way, this way, step to me,
	this way, this way, put your foot here,
	with a strength like a dream's.
Oedipus.
	Io, io. Driving an old man out of his country
	into the most miserable exile there is.
	Io, io. Terrible, terrible, what I have endured.
Antigone.
	Endured? Endured? Justice does not see the wicked,
	and does not pay mortals back for their folly.
Oedipus.
	I am the man who rose up to the song
	of victory that reached the sky,
	when I solved the riddle nobody could solve,
	the riddle of the girl who was half a girl.
Antigone.
	You are bringing up the Sphinx again, that old reproach.
	Enough talk of the good luck you used to have.
	This was what was waiting for you all along, this misery:
	to become an exile from your own country,
	father, and die somewhere or other.
	I leave my dear friends, the girls I grew up with, tears and longing,
	and go away, far from the land of my fathers,
	to wander as no girl should.
	Ah, this dutiful heart of mine,
	in my father's misfortunes,
	will make me famous.
	Poor me, for the outrages done to you and to my brother,
	who goes out from the house a corpse, unburied,
	poor boy. And him, even if I have to die for it, father,
	I will cover with earth in the dark.
Oedipus.
	Go and show yourself to the girls your own age.
Antigone.
	I have had enough of my own laments.
Oedipus.
	Then the prayers at the altars...
Antigone.
	They have had their fill of my evils.
Oedipus.
	Then go at least to Dionysus, and his sanctuary
	that no foot may enter, in the mountains of the maenads.
Antigone.
	Dionysus, for whom I once tied on
	the Theban fawnskin and danced, up in the mountains,
	in the holy company of Semele's son?
	And give the gods a thanks that is no thanks?

Oedipus. Citizens of a famous country, look at me. This is Oedipus, who solved the famous riddles and was the greatest of men, who alone put down the power of the murdering Sphinx. And now I am driven from the land, myself, stripped of honour, a pitiful thing. But why am I keening over this, and mourning for nothing? A man is mortal, and what the gods make necessary he has to bear.

(Oedipus and Antigone go out together, towards the road out of Thebes.)

Chorus.
	Great Victory, holy one,
	stay with me all my life,
	and never stop crowning me.

Orestes (408 BC)

Orestes

(Argos, in front of the palace of Agamemnon. Orestes lies asleep on a bed that has been carried out of the house, wrapped in his cloak. Electra sits beside him.)

Electra. There is nothing so terrible you could put it into words, no suffering, no disaster the gods send down, that human nature cannot take the weight of. Take Tantalus, the blessed one, and I am not mocking his bad luck. He was born from Zeus, they say, and now he floats in the air with a rock hanging over his head, in terror of it. That is the price he pays, and the reason, they say, is this: he was a man, and the gods let him sit at their table as an equal, and he could not keep his tongue under control. The most shameful sickness there is. Tantalus was the father of Pelops, and Pelops of Atreus, and for Atreus the goddess carded her wool and spun out strife: a war with his own brother, Thyestes. Why should I go back over things that are better not said? Atreus killed Thyestes's children and served them to him at dinner. And from Atreus, passing over what came in between, came Agamemnon the famous, if he really was famous, and Menelaus, and their mother was Aerope, from Crete. Menelaus married Helen, whom the gods hate, and lord Agamemnon married Clytemnestra, a marriage all Greece knew about. And she bore him three daughters, Chrysothemis, Iphigenia, and me, Electra, and one son, Orestes. All from one mother, and no mother was ever less holy. She wrapped her husband in a robe he could not find his way out of, and killed him. Why she did it is not a thing an unmarried girl should say. I leave it unclear, for people to work out for themselves.

And Apollo. What is the point of accusing Apollo of injustice? But he did persuade Orestes to kill the mother who gave birth to him, and not everyone thinks that a glorious thing to have done. Still, he killed her, because he would not disobey the god. And I had a share in the killing, as much as a woman can. And Pylades, who did the work with us. Since then poor Orestes here has been melting away in a savage sickness. He fell on this bed and he lies there, and his mother's blood drives him round and round in fits of madness. I am ashamed to name the goddesses who are racing him to death with terror. The Kindly Ones, people call them. This is the sixth day since our mother's throat was cut and her body was purified with fire, and in all that time he has not let a mouthful of food down his throat or put water on his skin. He hides inside his cloak, and when his body gets some relief from the sickness he comes to his senses and cries, and then at other times he leaps off the bed and runs, like a colt getting out from under the yoke.

And this city of Argos has decreed that no one is to take us in under a roof or at a fire, and no one is to speak to us. We killed our mother. And today is the day that decides it. Today the city of Argos votes on whether the two of us must die, under a pile of stones, or by sharpening a sword and driving it into our necks. There is one hope we have of not dying. Menelaus has landed here from Troy. His oars fill the harbour at Nauplia and he is riding at anchor off the shore, after wandering a long time on his way home from Troy. As for Helen, the woman so many people have groaned over, he waited for night and sent her on ahead to our house, in case somebody whose sons died at Troy saw her walking about in daylight and started throwing stones. She is inside, crying for her sister and for the ruin of the house. She does have one comfort in her grief. The daughter she left at home when she sailed for Troy, Hermione, whom Menelaus brought from Sparta and gave to my mother to bring up, is here. Helen is happy in her, and forgets her troubles.

So I am watching every road, for the moment I see Menelaus coming. Because otherwise we are riding on very little strength, unless he is the one who saves us. A house that has run out of luck has run out of everything.

(Helen comes out of the house.)

Helen. Daughter of Clytemnestra and Agamemnon. Electra. Still unmarried, after all this time. How are you, you poor thing, you and your brother, poor Orestes here, who killed his mother? I am not polluted by speaking to you, because I put the blame for the sin on Apollo. And yet I do grieve for the death of Clytemnestra, my sister. I never saw her again after I sailed for Troy, the way I did sail, because a god had driven me out of my mind. And now I am left behind without her, and I weep for what has happened to us.

Electra. Helen, why should I tell you what you can see for yourself, standing here? The house of Agamemnon in ruins. I sit up all night beside a miserable corpse, because a corpse is what he is, for all the little breath that is in him. I am not blaming him for his troubles. But you are blessed, and your husband is blessed, and the two of you have come to us when we are as badly off as we could be.

Helen. How long has he been lying on that bed?

Electra. Ever since he shed the blood he was born from.

Helen. Oh, poor man. And his mother. What a way to die.

Electra. That is how it is. He has given in to his troubles.

Helen. By the gods, would you do something for me, girl?

Electra. As far as I have time, sitting here with my brother.

Helen. Will you go to my sister's tomb for me?

Electra. To my mother's tomb, you mean? What for?

Helen. To take her a lock of my hair, and my offerings to pour.

Electra. Is it not allowed for you to go to the tomb of your own family yourself?

Helen. I would be ashamed to show my face to the Argives.

Electra. A little late to be thinking straight, when you left your home in such a shameful way back then.

Helen. That is true. But it is not kind of you to say it.

Electra. What is this shame that comes over you in front of the people of Mycenae?

Helen. I am afraid of the fathers of the men who died at Troy.

Electra. And you should be. In Argos your name is shouted from every mouth.

Helen. Then do me this favour and set me free from my fear.

Electra. I could not bring myself to look at my mother's tomb.

Helen. But it would be a disgrace to have slaves carry these things.

Electra. Then why not send your daughter Hermione?

Helen. It is not nice for an unmarried girl to go creeping into a crowd.

Electra. And yet she would be paying the dead woman back for bringing her up.

Helen. That is true, and you have convinced me, girl. Yes, I will send my daughter. You are quite right. Hermione, child, come out here in front of the house.

(Hermione comes out.)

Take these offerings in your hands, and this hair of mine, and go to Clytemnestra's tomb, and pour round it a mixture of honey and milk, and the foam of wine, and stand on the top of the mound and say this: "Your sister Helen sends you these offerings as a gift. She is afraid to come to your grave herself, because she is frightened of the Argive crowd." And ask her to keep kind thoughts towards me, and towards you, and towards my husband, and towards these two poor things, whom a god has destroyed. And whatever it is right for me to do for a sister, promise it all, every gift that is owed to the dead. Go on, my child, hurry. Give the offerings at the tomb, and then remember the road back as fast as you can.

(Hermione goes off with the offerings. Helen goes back into the house.)

Electra. Nature. What a great evil you are among human beings, and what a salvation, to the people who were born with a good one. Did you see how she cut her hair just at the very tips, to keep it beautiful? She is the same woman she always was. May the gods hate you, for what you have done to me, and to him, and to the whole of Greece. Oh, I am so tired of this. And here they are again, my friends, the women who sing my laments with me. They will shake him out of his sleep in a moment, this quiet man lying here, and melt my eyes with tears, when I see my brother mad. Dearest women, walk softly. Make no noise. Not a sound. Your friendship is kind, I know, but if you wake him it will be a disaster for me.

(The Chorus, women of Argos, come in on tiptoe.)

Chorus.
	Quiet. Quiet. Set the soles of your shoes down
	lightly. Not a sound.
Electra.
	Further off. Over there. Away from the bed, I beg you.
Chorus.
	There. I am doing as you say.
Electra.
	Ah. Ah. Like the breath through a pipe
	of thin reed, my dear. Speak to me like that.
Chorus.
	Listen. I am bringing my voice down,
	low as a whisper under a roof.
Electra.
	Yes. Like that.
	Down, keep it down. Come close, gently. Gently, come.
	Now tell me what it is you have come here for.
	Because at last, after so long, he has fallen down and is asleep.
Chorus.
	How is he? Tell me, my dear.
	What am I to say has happened? What disaster?
Electra.
	He is still breathing. But his groans are getting faint.
Chorus.
	What are you saying? Oh, the poor man.
Electra.
	You will kill him, if you make his eyelids move
	while he is being carried on the sweetest grace sleep gives.
Chorus.
	Poor man. For the most hateful deeds,
	and a god behind them. Poor man.
Electra.
	Ah, the pain of it.
	Unjust. It was an unjust thing he cried out then, cried out,
	when Apollo sat on the tripod at Delphi that was Themis's once
	and decreed it: the killing of my mother. A killing against nature.
Chorus.
	Do you see? He is moving under his clothes.
Electra.
	That was you, you poor fool.
	You shouted, and threw him out of his sleep.
Chorus.
	No. I think he is sleeping.
Electra.
	Will you not go away from us, away from the house,
	turn round on your heel and go back,
	and stop that noise?
Chorus.
	He is dozing.
Electra.
	You are right.
	Lady. Lady Night,
	who gives sleep to human beings who labour so hard,
	come up from Erebus, from the dark below, come, come on your wings
	to the house of Agamemnon.
	Because under our griefs, under our disaster,
	we are going, we are gone. You made a noise. Will you not be quiet,
	quiet, keep a guard on your mouth,
	keep your clatter away from his bed,
	and let him have the quiet grace of sleep, my dear?
Chorus.
	Tell me. What end is waiting for his troubles?
Electra.
	Death. Death, what else?
	He does not even want food any more.
Chorus.
	Then his end is plain to see.
Electra.
	Apollo sacrificed us,
	when he handed us the blood of a mother who killed our father.
	Pitiful blood. Blood against nature.
Chorus.
	It was just.
Electra.
	But it was not well done.
	You killed, and you died, mother
	who gave birth to me, and you destroyed
	a father, and these children of your own blood.
	We are gone, as good as corpses, gone.
	You are among the dead, and the greater part
	of my life is gone too, in groaning and wailing
	and tears in the night, unmarried,
	childless, dragging out a miserable life
	for ever and ever.

Chorus. Electra, you are close to him. Look and make sure your brother has not died without your noticing. I do not like how limp he has gone.

Orestes. Sweet spell of sleep, the sick man's helper, how sweetly you came to me, and just when I needed you. Lady Forgetfulness, who takes away our troubles, what a clever goddess you are, and how the unlucky pray to you. Where did I come here from? How did I get here? I cannot remember. The mind I had before has gone from me.

Electra. My dearest, how happy you made me when you fell asleep. Do you want me to take hold of you and lift you up?

Orestes. Yes, take hold of me, take hold, and wipe the crust of foam off my poor mouth, and off my eyes.

Electra. There. It is a sweet service. I do not mind nursing a brother's body with a sister's hand.

Orestes. Put your side under mine, and get this filthy hair off my face. I can hardly see.

Electra. Oh, your poor head, your hair all matted and dirty. How wild you look, after so long without washing.

Orestes. Lay me back on the bed again. When the fit of madness lets go of me there is no strength in my joints and my limbs go weak.

Electra. There. A sick man loves his bed. It is a painful thing to own, but he cannot do without it.

Orestes. Sit me upright again. Turn my body round. Sick people are hard to please. It is because they cannot help themselves.

Electra. Do you want to set your feet on the ground and take a step, after all this time? Any change is sweet.

Orestes. Yes, very much. It has the look of health about it. And looking well is better than being well, even if the truth is nowhere near.

Electra. Then listen to me now, brother, while the Furies are letting you think straight.

Orestes. You have some news. If it is good, I will thank you for it. If it is going to hurt, I have had enough of bad luck.

Electra. Menelaus has come. Your father's brother. His ships are moored at Nauplia.

Orestes. What did you say? He has come, a light in my troubles and yours, a man of our own blood, who owes our father his thanks?

Electra. He has come, and here is your proof that I am telling the truth: he is bringing Helen with him, from the walls of Troy.

Orestes. If he had come home safe by himself, he would be more to be envied. If he is bringing his wife, he has come home with a great evil in his luggage.

Electra. Tyndareus fathered a brood of daughters marked out for blame, and infamous all through Greece.

Orestes. Then you be different from the bad ones. You can. And do not just say it. Think it.

Electra. Oh, no. Brother, your eyes are going strange. You were sane a moment ago, and now you are turning back into madness so fast.

Orestes. Mother, I beg you, do not shake them at me, those girls with the blood in their faces and the snakes in their hair. There they are. There, right beside me, jumping at me.

Electra. Stay where you are, you poor man. Lie still on your bed. You are seeing nothing of what you think you see so clearly.

Orestes. Apollo. They are going to kill me, the dog-faced ones, with the Gorgon's stare, the priestesses of the dead. The terrible goddesses.

Electra. I will not let you go. I am going to wind my arm round you and stop you making these miserable leaps.

Orestes. Let go of me. You are one of my Furies. You have got me round the middle to throw me into Tartarus, into the pit.

Electra. Oh, what am I going to do? Where can I turn for help, when it is the gods themselves we have against us?

Orestes. Give me the bow, the horn-tipped bow Apollo gave me. He told me to fight the goddesses off with it if they tried to frighten me out of my mind with their raving. One of the gods is going to be shot by a mortal hand, if she does not get out of my sight. Do you not hear me? Do you not see the feathered notches of the arrows springing out from my bow, the bow that shoots so far? Ah. Ah. What are you waiting for? Up. Skim the sky on your wings, and take it up with Apollo's oracles.

Ah. What is this? What am I raving about, gasping the breath out of my lungs? Where, where did I jump to, off my bed? The waves have gone down. I can see calm water again. Sister, why are you crying with your head inside your dress? I am ashamed in front of you, giving you a share in my troubles, making a girl who has never married carry the weight of my sickness. Do not waste away because of my troubles. You nodded yes to it, but the blood of our mother was shed by me. And I blame Apollo. He set me on to the most unholy deed there is, and he cheered me on with words, and with deeds he has done nothing. I believe that if I had asked my father to his face whether I had to kill my mother, he would have begged me, over and over, by this chin of mine, never to push a sword into the throat of the woman who bore me. Because he was never going to get back into the light either way, and I, poor fool, would be filling myself up with evils like these.

So now, sister, uncover your head, and come away from the tears, however badly off we are. And when you see me lose heart, it is your job to calm down the terrible broken part of my mind and soothe it, and when you are the one groaning, I have to be there and talk you kindly out of it. That is the kind of help that is good between people who belong to each other. Now, my poor sister, go into the house. Lie down and give your sleepless eyes some sleep. Reach for some food, and put some water on your skin. Because if you leave me before the end, or catch some sickness from sitting up with me, we are finished. You are the only helper I have. Everyone else has left me, as you can see.

Electra. No. I am not going. I will choose to die with you, and to live with you, because it comes to the same thing. If you die, what am I going to do, a woman? How will I survive on my own, with no brother, no father, no friends? But if you think it is right, I must do as you say. But lie down on the bed, and do not take the thing that terrifies you and scares you up off your bed so seriously. Stay on your bed where it is made up. Because even if you are not sick, and only think you are sick, that alone wears a person out and leaves them helpless.

(Electra goes into the house.)

Chorus.
	Aiai.
	Running goddesses, wings on your backs,
	goddesses of frenzy,
	whose company is a company that has nothing to do with Dionysus,
	a company of tears and groans,
	black-skinned Kindly Ones, who go bounding
	across the long stretch of the sky, exacting
	the price of blood, exacting the price of murder,
	I beg you, I beg you,
	let the son of Agamemnon
	forget the madness that hunts him,
	the raving and the wandering. Ah, the pain,
	what pains you reached for, poor man, and are lost,
	when you took the word from the tripod that Apollo cried out
	on the floor of his house at Delphi,
	where they say the hollows are, at the navel of the earth.
Chorus.
	Io, Zeus.
	What pity is this, what struggle
	for blood is this coming on,
	driving you, poor man, on whom some avenging spirit
	is heaping tears on tears,
	carrying into the house your mother's blood,
	and the blood is what sends you raving?
	Great good fortune does not stay put among human beings.
	I mourn for it, I mourn for it.
	Some god shook it like the sail of a fast boat
	and sank it under terrible labours,
	as the sea sinks a boat
	under its wild and deadly waves.
	Because what other house should I honour above this one,
	the house that came from a marriage with a god,
	the house of Tantalus?
Chorus.
	And look, here comes the king,
	Menelaus the king, and anyone can see
	from all that luxury
	that he is of the blood of Tantalus.
	You who launched an army in a thousand ships
	against the land of Asia,
	welcome. Good fortune is your companion.
	The gods have given you everything you prayed for.

(Menelaus comes in, with his attendants.)

Menelaus. My house. In one way I am glad to look at you, coming home from Troy. In another I look at you and groan. Because I have never seen another hearth so wretchedly wrapped round with evils. I knew what had happened to Agamemnon, and how he died, at his wife's hands, as I was bringing my prow in to Cape Malea. The sailors' prophet told me it out of the waves, Glaucus, the seer of Nereus, a god who does not lie. He stood up in plain view and said this to me: "Menelaus, your brother is lying dead. His wife gave him his last bath, and he fell into it." He filled me and my sailors with a great many tears. And when I touched land at Nauplia, with my wife already setting out for this house, I was expecting to throw my arms round Orestes, Agamemnon's son, and round his mother, and find them doing well, when I heard from one of the fishermen about the unholy murder of Tyndareus's daughter. So now tell me where he is, young women, Agamemnon's son, the one who had the nerve to do these terrible things. He was a baby in Clytemnestra's arms when I left the house on my way to Troy, so I would not know him if I saw him.

Orestes. Here he is, Menelaus. I am Orestes, the one you are asking about. I will tell you my troubles myself, and willingly. But first, before anything else, I touch your knees as a suppliant, and I hang my prayers from a mouth that has no olive branch to hold. Save me. You have come, in person, at the crisis of my troubles.

Menelaus. Gods, what am I looking at? Which of the dead is this I see?

Orestes. Well said. I am not alive, for all my troubles. But I see the light.

Menelaus. How wild you look, poor man, with your hair all dry and filthy.

Orestes. It is not my looks that torture me. It is what I did.

Menelaus. That is a terrible stare, out of eyes with no tears in them.

Orestes. The body is gone. The name has not left me yet.

Menelaus. I never expected you to look like this. What a ruin.

Orestes. Here I am, the man who killed his poor mother.

Menelaus. I have heard. Spare me. Evils should be spoken of as little as possible.

Orestes. I will spare you. But the god who has me is rich in evils, and spends them on me.

Menelaus. What is wrong with you? What is this sickness that is destroying you?

Orestes. Understanding. I understand what I have done, and it was terrible.

Menelaus. What do you mean? Being clear is clever. Being unclear is not.

Orestes. Grief, mostly. That is what is destroying me.

Menelaus. Grief is a terrible goddess. But she can be cured, all the same.

Orestes. And fits of madness. My mother's blood, taking its revenge.

Menelaus. When did the madness begin? What day was it?

Orestes. The day I was heaping up the earth on my poor mother's grave.

Menelaus. In the house, or sitting up by the pyre?

Orestes. At night. Waiting to gather up her bones.

Menelaus. Was anyone else there, to hold you up?

Orestes. Pylades. He did the blood with me. My mother's murder.

Menelaus. So it is visions that make you sick. What kind?

Orestes. I thought I saw three girls, as dark as night.

Menelaus. I know the ones you mean. I would rather not name them.

Orestes. No. They are holy. You were well brought up, to turn away from saying it.

Menelaus. And these are what drive you mad, over the blood of your own family?

Orestes. Oh, the hunting. The way they hunt me, and drive me. Poor fool that I am.

Menelaus. It is not strange for people who have done terrible things to suffer terrible things.

Orestes. But there is somewhere I can shift this disaster.

Menelaus. Do not say death. That is not clever.

Orestes. Apollo. He ordered me to carry out my mother's murder.

Menelaus. Then he knew less than he should about what is right and what is just.

Orestes. We are slaves to the gods. Whatever the gods are.

Menelaus. And then Apollo does nothing to defend you in your troubles?

Orestes. He is taking his time. That is what the divine is like, by nature.

Menelaus. How long is it since your mother stopped breathing?

Orestes. This is the sixth day. The pyre at her grave is still warm.

Menelaus. How fast the goddesses came after you for your mother's blood.

Orestes. I am not clever. But I was born a true friend to the people I owe.

Menelaus. And your father? Does it do you any good that you avenged him?

Orestes. Not yet. And I call what is still to come the same thing as nothing.

Menelaus. And the city? How do you stand with it, after doing this?

Orestes. They hate us so much that nobody will speak to us.

Menelaus. You have not even washed the blood off your hands, as the custom is?

Orestes. Wherever I go, the door is shut in my face.

Menelaus. Which of the citizens are pushing to have you driven out of the country?

Orestes. Oeax. He has a grudge from Troy, and he lays it on my father.

Menelaus. I understand. He is making you pay for his brother Palamedes, who was killed there.

Orestes. Which I had nothing to do with. But there are three things destroying me.

Menelaus. Who else? Some of Aegisthus's friends, I suppose?

Orestes. Those are the ones. They are treating me with outrage, and it is them the city listens to now.

Menelaus. And will the city let you hold Agamemnon's sceptre?

Orestes. How would it, when they will not even let us go on living?

Menelaus. What are they doing? Is there anything you can tell me plainly?

Orestes. There is a vote being taken against us. Today.

Menelaus. On what? Banishment from the city? Or whether you live or die?

Orestes. Whether I die. At the hands of the citizens, under a heap of stones.

Menelaus. Then why not get over the border and run for it?

Orestes. Because we are ringed round with men in bronze armour.

Menelaus. Your own private enemies, or the armed force of Argos?

Orestes. Every citizen in the place, so that I die. It is a short story.

Menelaus. Poor man. You have come to the very end of misfortune.

Orestes. You are the hope I have left. You are where I run to, out of all this. You have come home lucky, and you find us in misery. Share your good fortune with the people you owe. Do not take the good thing you have got and keep it to yourself. Take your turn at carrying the trouble too, and pay back what my father did for you to the people you owe it to. Friends who are not friends when the trouble comes have the name of friends and nothing else.

Chorus. And here is Tyndareus the Spartan, hurrying this way as fast as an old man's legs will carry him, dressed in black, his hair cropped in mourning for his daughter.

Orestes. I am finished, Menelaus. This is Tyndareus coming towards us, and of all men alive he is the one I am most ashamed to look in the face, after what I have done. He brought me up when I was small. He covered me with kisses, carrying Agamemnon's boy round in his arms, and Leda did the same, and the two of them made as much of me as they did of their own sons, Castor and Polydeuces. And I have paid them back, oh my wretched heart, my wretched soul, with this. Where is there a darkness I can pull over my face? What cloud can I put between me and him, so that I get away from the old man's eyes?

(Tyndareus comes in, an old man in black with his hair cut short, led by his attendants.)

Tyndareus. Where is he, where is my daughter's husband? Where can I see Menelaus? I was pouring the offerings on Clytemnestra's grave when I heard that he had put in at Nauplia, with his wife, safe after all these years. Take me to him. I want to stand at his right hand and greet him. It is a long time since I set eyes on a friend.

Menelaus. Greetings, old man. You shared a wife with Zeus.

Tyndareus. Greetings to you too, Menelaus, my daughter's husband. Ah. What an evil thing it is, not to know the future. There he is, the mother-killer, in front of the house, a snake, flashing the sick light out of his eyes. I loathe him. Menelaus, are you speaking to him? To that godless thing?

Menelaus. Why not? He is the son of a man I loved.

Tyndareus. That is Agamemnon's son? This thing here?

Menelaus. It is. And when he is down on his luck, he is owed respect.

Tyndareus. You have been too long among barbarians. You have turned into one yourself.

Menelaus. It is the Greek way, surely, always to honour your own blood.

Tyndareus. And it is the Greek way not to want to put yourself above the laws.

Menelaus. The wise say that anything done under necessity is a slave to it.

Tyndareus. Then you keep that piece of wisdom. I will not have it.

Menelaus. No, because you are angry, and old age and anger together are not wise.

Tyndareus. An argument about wisdom, with him standing there? If everyone can see what is right and what is not, was there ever a man more senseless than this one? He never once looked at what justice required. He never went to the law that all Greeks share. When Agamemnon breathed out his life, struck over the head by my daughter, a filthy deed, and I will never defend it, he should have brought a charge for the blood, a holy prosecution, and thrown his mother out of the house. That would have been the disciplined course, instead of a disaster: he would have kept to the law, and he would have kept his hands clean before the gods. As it is, he has walked into the same fate as his mother. He was right to think her wicked. He became more wicked than she was, by killing her.

Let me ask you one thing, Menelaus, just this. Suppose this man's wife kills him. And his son kills his mother to pay for it. And then that man's son wipes out killing with another killing. Where does it end? Where is the last of the evil? Our fathers long ago settled this the right way. A man with blood on his hands was not allowed into their sight, was not allowed to cross their path; they made him clean by exile. They did not kill him back. Otherwise there is always going to be one more man liable for a killing, the one who took the last stain onto his hands.

Now, I hate godless women, and my own daughter first of all, who killed her husband. And Helen, your wife: I will never say a good word for her, and I would not so much as speak to her, and I do not envy you your trip to Troy for a worthless woman. But the law I will defend with everything I have, to put a stop to this savagery, this bloodlust, which is always the ruin of countries and of cities.

(Tyndareus turns away from Menelaus and speaks to Orestes directly.)

What kind of heart did you have in you, you wretched man, when your mother bared her breast and begged you? I was not there, I did not see the horror of it, and it still melts these old eyes of mine with tears. And here is one thing that agrees with what I say: the gods hate you. You are paying for your mother, wandering about in fits of madness and terror. What do I need other witnesses for, when I can see it for myself?

So understand this, Menelaus. Do not set yourself against the gods by wanting to help this man. Leave him to the citizens, to be stoned to death, or never set foot on Spartan soil again. My daughter died, and she deserved to die. But it should not have been by his hand. In everything else I have been a happy man. Except in my daughters. There I have had no luck at all.

Chorus. The one to envy is the man who has been lucky in his children and has never had a famous disaster in his house.

Orestes. Old man, I am afraid to speak to you, because whatever I say I am going to hurt you, and hurt your heart. I know: I am unholy, because I killed my mother. But there is another name for me too, and it is holy: I avenged my father. Let your old age get out of the way of my argument. It is your years that knock the words out of me. If they were not standing there I would go straight down the road; as it is, I am afraid of your grey hair.

What should I have done? Set one thing against the other. My father planted me. Your daughter bore me: she was the field that took the seed from someone else. Without a father there would never be a child. So I reasoned it out: I owed more to the founder of my line than to the woman who took on the job of feeding me. And your daughter, I am ashamed to call her my mother, went to a man's bed in a private wedding of her own, and not a decent one. I speak against myself when I speak badly of her. I know that. I will say it anyway. Aegisthus was the husband hidden in the house. I killed him. And on top of that I sacrificed my mother. An unholy thing to do, yes. But I was avenging my father.

And now, as to the reason you say I should be stoned, hear how I am doing every Greek a service. If women get the nerve to go this far, to murder their husbands, and then run to their children for shelter and hunt for pity with their bared breasts, then killing a husband would be nothing to them. Any charge that came to hand would do. I did a terrible thing, as you keep announcing, and I put a stop to that custom. I hated my mother and I destroyed her, and I was within my rights. While her husband was away from home under arms, leading the army for the whole of Greece, she betrayed him. She did not keep his bed clean. And when she realised she had been caught out, she did not punish herself. No. To keep from being punished by her husband, she punished my father. She killed him.

By the gods, and this is not the moment to be bringing up the gods, when I am arguing a case of murder, but if I had kept my mouth shut and gone along with what my mother did, what would the dead man have done to me? Would he not have hated me, and set the Furies dancing round me? Or are there goddesses on my mother's side and none on his, when he was wronged far worse than she was? You are the one, old man. You fathered a wicked daughter, and you destroyed me. It was her nerve that took my father from me, and made me my mother's killer.

Look at Telemachus. He did not kill the wife of Odysseus, because she did not marry a second husband on top of the first. The bed in her house stayed sound. And look at Apollo, who lives at the navel of the earth and gives mortals the clearest word there is, the god we obey in everything he says. I obeyed him, and I killed the woman who bore me. Call him the unholy one. Kill him. It was his mistake, not mine. What should I have done? Or is the god not good enough to take the pollution off me when I hand it over to him? Where is anyone supposed to run, then, if the one who gave the order will not save me from death? So do not say that what was done was done badly. Say that for the ones who did it, it has turned out unhappily. When people's marriages are well made, their life is blessed. When they fall out badly, everything goes wrong for them, at home and outside it.

Chorus. Women are always getting in the way of what men do, and always to make things worse.

Tyndareus. Since you are so bold about it, since you will not tone down a word, and you answer me in a way that is meant to hurt, you are making me all the more eager to go and see to your death. And I will count it a fine extra piece of work on top of the business I came here for, which was to dress my daughter's grave. I am going to the assembly of the Argives, and I will set the city on you, willing or not, on you and on your sister, to pay the penalty of stoning. She deserves to die more than you do. She is the one who made you savage against your mother, always dripping stories into your ear to make you hate her more, telling you about dreams sent by Agamemnon, and about Aegisthus's bed, may the gods below loathe it, because it was bitter enough up here, until she set the house on fire with a fire no forge ever lit.

Menelaus, I say this to you, and I will do it as well. If you count my hatred for anything, or the marriage that binds us, do not defend this man from death against the gods. Leave him to the citizens to be stoned to death, or never set foot on Spartan soil. You have heard it. Now you know it. And do not choose godless friends and push the god-fearing ones aside. Take me away from this house, servants.

(Tyndareus goes, led away by his attendants.)

Orestes. Go, then. Let the rest of what I have to say reach this man without a disturbance, and without your old age in the way. Menelaus, why are you pacing round in circles, thinking, going up one road and back down the other, with two cares pulling at you?

Menelaus. Leave me alone. I am turning something over in my mind, and I cannot see which way to turn, the way things stand.

Orestes. Do not finish deciding yet. Hear what I have to say first, and then make up your mind.

Menelaus. Speak, then. You are right. There are times when silence is better than talk, and times when talk is better than silence.

Orestes. Then I will speak now. A long speech has the advantage over a short one, and is clearer to listen to. Give me nothing of your own, Menelaus. Pay back what you took from my father. I am not talking about money. Or rather, money is exactly what it is, if you save my life, because my life is the dearest thing I own.

I did wrong. And I need to get a little wrong from you in return for that evil. Because my father Agamemnon did wrong too, when he gathered Greece together and went to Troy. Not a fault of his own. He was trying to heal your wife's fault, and your wife's wrong. That is one thing, and you owe me one thing back for it. And he gave up his body, truly, as friends should for friends, slogging beside your shield so that you could get your wife back. So pay me back the very thing you got there. Work hard for one day, standing up as my saviour, not ten full years. And what Aulis took, my sister's blood: I let you keep that. Do not kill Hermione. When I am doing as badly as I am doing now, you have to come out ahead, and I have to let it pass.

But give my life to my poor father, and my sister's life, a girl who has gone unmarried too long. If I die I leave my father's house with no one in it. You will say it is impossible. That is just it.
