It is when things are bad that friends have to help friends. When the god gives freely, what do you need friends for? The god is enough by himself, when he is willing to help.

Every Greek believes you love your wife, and I do not say that to crawl to you or to flatter you. By her, I beg you. Oh, the misery of my troubles, and where I have come to. What of it? I have to suffer this. I am begging for the whole house. Uncle, my father's own brother, imagine that the dead man under the ground can hear this, that his spirit is hovering over you and saying what I am saying, the same words, for tears and groans and disasters. I have spoken. I have asked for my life. I am hunting what everybody hunts, not only me.

Chorus. And I beg you too, a woman though I am, to help people who need it. And you can.

Menelaus. Orestes, I do respect you, and I want to share the labour of your troubles. And that is what you are supposed to do: carry the evils of your own blood together, when a god gives you the power for it, dying and killing the other side. But the power is what I would need to get from the gods. I have come home with a spear and no allies behind it, worn down by ten thousand troubles, with the small strength of the friends I have left. In a battle, then, we could never beat Pelasgian Argos. If we could win with soft words, that is where our hope comes in. How does anyone take a great thing with small means? By hard work? It is stupid even to want it.

When the people are in the flush of their anger, it is like trying to put out a raging fire. But if a man goes quietly, slackens off and gives way while they are pulling hard, and watches for his moment, they might blow themselves out. And once they let their breath go, you can easily get whatever you want from them. There is pity in them, and there is a great temper in them too, and to a man who watches and waits that is the most valuable possession there is. I will go and try to persuade Tyndareus and the city for you, to use their excess well. A ship dips too, when the sheet is hauled hard against the wind, and rights itself again when the sheet is let go. The god hates too much eagerness, and so do the citizens. I have to save you, and I say it straight out, by cleverness, not by force against people who are stronger than we are. By strength I could not save you, whatever you may imagine. It is not easy for one spear to set up a trophy over the troubles you are in. We never approached the land of Argos with softness before. But now it has to be done. The wise are slaves to fortune.

(Menelaus goes out, in the direction of the town.)

Orestes. You are no use for anything except leading an army for a woman's sake. You worst of men at defending your friends. You turn your back on me and run, and what Agamemnon did for you is gone with the wind? So you had no friends after all, father, when things went badly. Oh. I am betrayed. There is no hope left, nowhere to turn to get away from the Argives' death sentence. He was my refuge. He was my safety. But look: here is the man I love best in the world, Pylades, running this way from Phocis. A sweet sight. A man you can trust when things are bad is a better sight than a calm sea is to sailors.

(Pylades comes in on foot, out of breath from running.)

Pylades. I came through the town faster than I should have. I heard the city was gathering, and then I saw it for myself, plainly: it is against you and your sister, to kill you at once. What is this? How are you? What is happening to you, dearest of all the friends my age, dearest of my friends and my kin? Because you are all of those things to me.

Orestes. We are finished. That is my trouble for you, in short.

Pylades. Then you would be pulling me down with you. Friends have everything in common.

Orestes. Menelaus is the worst of men, to me and to my sister.

Pylades. Naturally. A bad woman's husband turns into a bad man.

Orestes. He came, and he paid me back exactly as if he had never come.

Pylades. So he really has arrived in this country?

Orestes. After a long time. But he was found out very quickly as a bad friend.

Pylades. And did he sail here with that wife of his, the worst of women?

Orestes. He did not bring her here. She brought him.

Pylades. Where is she, the one woman who destroyed more Achaeans than anyone?

Orestes. In my house. If I am supposed to call this house mine.

Pylades. And what did you say to your father's brother?

Orestes. Not to stand there and watch me and my sister killed by the citizens.

Pylades. By the gods, what did he say to that? That is what I want to know.

Orestes. He was careful. That is what bad friends do to their friends.

Pylades. And what excuse did he take cover behind? Once I know that, I know everything.

Orestes. He arrived. The father who sowed those excellent daughters.

Pylades. You mean Tyndareus. Angry with you, I suppose, over his daughter?

Orestes. You have got it. And Menelaus chose the marriage tie to him over the one to my father.

Pylades. He did not have the nerve to take up a share of your troubles, when he was standing right here?

Orestes. No. He was not born a fighter. He is brave among women.

Pylades. Then you are in the worst trouble there is. And you have to die?

Orestes. The citizens have to cast their vote on us, about the killing.

Pylades. And what does the vote decide? Tell me. I am frightened.

Orestes. Death or life. A short speech about a long matter.

Pylades. Then leave the house with your sister and run.

Orestes. Can you not see? There are guards on us in every direction.

Pylades. I saw the streets of the town blocked with armed men.

Orestes. We are besieged, like a city with the enemy round its walls.

Pylades. Now ask me what is happening to me. I am finished too.

Orestes. Who did it? That would be a new evil on top of mine.

Pylades. Strophius, my father. He lost his temper and drove me out of the house, into exile.

Orestes. On a charge of his own, or one the citizens share?

Pylades. That I helped you kill your mother. He calls it unholy.

Orestes. You poor man. It looks as if my troubles are going to hurt you as well.

Pylades. I do not go about things the way Menelaus does. This has to be borne.

Orestes. Are you not afraid Argos will want to kill you too, as well as me?

Pylades. It is not their place to punish me. I belong to the land of Phocis.

Orestes. The mob is a terrible thing, when it has villains for leaders.

Pylades. But when it gets honest ones, its decisions are always honest.

Orestes. Right. We need to talk this through together.

Pylades. What is it we have to decide?

Orestes. Suppose I went to the citizens and told them —

Pylades. That what you did was just?

Orestes. Avenging my own father?

Pylades. They might be only too glad to lay hands on you.

Orestes. So I cower here in silence and die?

Pylades. That is cowardly.

Orestes. Then what should I do?

Pylades. If you stay here, have you any way of saving yourself?

Orestes. I have none.

Pylades. And if you go, is there any hope of coming out of this alive?

Orestes. With luck, there might be.

Pylades. Then that is better than staying.

Orestes. Then I will go.

Pylades. At least if you die that way, you die better.

Orestes. You are right. That way I get clear of cowardice.

Pylades. More than by staying.

Orestes. And what I did was just.

Pylades. Just pray it looks that way to them.

Orestes. And somebody might pity me —

Pylades. Yes. Your birth counts for a great deal.

Orestes. — someone angry about my father's death.

Pylades. All of that is plain to see.

Orestes. I have to go. To die without honour is not a man's death.

Pylades. I agree.

Orestes. Then shall we tell my sister?

Pylades. No. By the gods, no.

Orestes. There would be tears, certainly.

Pylades. And that is a bad omen. A big one.

Orestes. Clearly better to keep quiet.

Pylades. And you will gain time.

Orestes. There is only one thing in my way.

Pylades. What is this new thing now?

Orestes. That the goddesses might take hold of me and drive me mad.

Pylades. But I will take care of you.

Orestes. It is an unpleasant business, handling a sick man.

Pylades. Not for me. Not when it is you.

Orestes. Be careful. You could catch my madness.

Pylades. Let that go.

Orestes. Then you will not hesitate?

Pylades. No. Hesitation is a great evil between friends.

Orestes. Then walk on, and steer my feet.

Pylades. Gladly, when the man I am caring for is a friend.

Orestes. And take me to my father's tomb.

Pylades. Whatever for?

Orestes. So that I can beg him to save me.

Pylades. Yes. That is right and proper.

Orestes. But my mother's grave: I do not even want to see it.

Pylades. No. She was your enemy. But hurry, or the vote of the Argives will get to you first. Put your side against my side, slow as it is with the sickness. I will carry you through the town, and think very little of the crowd, and not be ashamed of it. Where would I ever show myself a friend, if I did not stand by you when you are in terrible trouble?

Orestes. That is the old saying exactly: get yourself friends, not only relations. A man whose ways are melted into yours, even if he is from outside the house, is a better friend for a man to have than ten thousand of his own blood.

(Orestes and Pylades go out together, Orestes leaning on his friend.)

Chorus.
	The great wealth and the courage
	that held its head high through Greece
	and by the streams of the Simois
	turned back, for the sons of Atreus, out of good fortune,
	long ago, from an old disaster in the house,
	when the quarrel over a golden lamb
	came to the sons of Tantalus:
	the most pitiful feasts,
	and the slaughter of high-born children.
	And from that day killing pays for killing
	through blood, and does not let go
	of the two sons of Atreus.
Chorus.
	The fine thing was not fine:
	to cut a parent's flesh with a hand and a forged blade,
	and hold the sword up black with blood
	to the rays of the sun.
	Doing evil well is a many-coloured impiety,
	the madness of men whose minds have gone wrong.
	In her terror of death
	the poor daughter of Tyndareus screamed:
	"Child, this is not holy, what you dare,
	killing your own mother. Do not, for honouring
	your father, fasten a disgrace
	on yourself for ever."
Chorus.
	What sickness, what tears,
	what pity is greater anywhere on earth
	than to take a mother's blood on your hands?
	Look at what he did,
	and now he is raving in fits of madness,
	the Furies' prey, whirling murder
	in his racing eyes,
	Agamemnon's son.
	Poor man. When he saw his mother's breast
	rising out of her gold-threaded dress,
	he saw it, and he made his mother
	the sacrifice, to pay back
	what was done to his father.

Electra. Women, has poor Orestes gone out of the house? Has the madness the gods sent got the better of him?

Chorus. Not at all. He has gone to the people of Argos, to stand the trial that has been set for his life, the one where you and he must live or die.

Electra. Oh. What has he done? Who talked him into it?

Chorus. Pylades. But here is a messenger, and it looks as if he will soon be telling us what happened there to your brother.

(An old man comes in from the direction of the town.)

Messenger. Poor girl. Unhappy daughter of Agamemnon the general, my lady Electra, listen to the news I have come to bring you. It is bad.

Electra. Aiai. Then we are finished. Your words make it plain. You have come with bad news, by the look of you.

Messenger. The Argives have voted. Your brother is to die, and you too, poor girl, this very day.

Electra. Oh. So it has come, the thing I expected. I have been afraid of it for so long, wasting away with weeping for what was going to happen. But what was the trial like? What did the Argives say that brought us down and confirmed our deaths? Tell me, old friend. Is it stones that will knock the breath out of me, or the knife? Since I share my brother's misfortunes, whatever they are.

Messenger. I happened to be coming in from the country, through the gates, wanting to find out how things stood with you and with Orestes. I was always well disposed to your father, and your house fed me: a poor man, but a loyal one where his friends were concerned. And I saw a crowd on the move, going up to sit on the hill where they say Danaus first gathered the people into a public assembly, when he was on trial against Aegyptus. When I saw the crowd I asked one of the townsmen, "What is happening in Argos? Has some news from the enemy got the city of Danaus all in a flutter?" And he said, "Don't you see Orestes there, coming this way, on his way to a race where the prize is his life?" And then I saw a sight I never expected, and wish I had never seen: Pylades and your brother coming along together, the one with his head hanging, slack with sickness, and the other grieving for his friend as if he were his own brother, nursing him along like a tutor with a child.

When the crowd of Argives was complete, a herald stood up and said, "Who wishes to speak on the question, whether Orestes should be put to death or not, for killing his mother?" And at that Talthybius got up, the man who was with your father when he sacked the Phrygians. He is always on the side of whoever holds the power, and he spoke to face both ways. He was full of admiration for your father, and then he had nothing good to say about your brother, winding fine words and foul words together: that Orestes was setting up a bad precedent about how to treat parents. And the whole time his eye kept flicking, bright and friendly, towards the friends of Aegisthus. That is what the breed is like. Heralds are always jumping across to whoever is on top. Their friend is the man who has the power in the city and the office to go with it.

After him lord Diomedes spoke. He said they should kill neither you nor your brother, but punish you with exile and keep themselves clean before the gods. Some shouted that this was well said, and others did not like it. And then up gets a man with no door on his mouth, a man whose strength is his cheek. An Argive, but no Argive, a man they had been forced to take in. He trusts in noise and in the ignorant freedom of his own tongue, and he is just persuasive enough to get them into some serious trouble one of these days. Because when a man who talks pleasantly and thinks badly persuades the crowd, it is a great evil for the city, whereas the men who give good advice with their brains switched on may not look useful at the moment, but are useful to the city later. That is how you should judge a leader, if you have your eyes open, because the same thing happens to a man who makes speeches as to a man in office. He said that they should stone you and Orestes to death. And it was Tyndareus who kept feeding him his lines, the arguments the man used to get you both killed.

Then another man stood up and said the opposite. Not much to look at, but a man. He does not often come near the town or the round of the marketplace. A farmer, one of the men who work their own land, and they are the only ones who keep this country alive. But he had his wits about him, and he wanted to close with the arguments and fight them. A clean man, who had lived a life nobody could point a finger at. He said they ought to put a crown on Orestes, the son of Agamemnon, for being willing to avenge his father by killing a wicked, godless woman, one who would have put a stop to men ever arming themselves and leaving home to go on campaign, if the men left behind at home were going to ruin the household and seduce the soldiers' wives. And the decent people, at least, thought he spoke well.

Nobody spoke after him. Then your brother came forward and said, "You who hold the land of Inachus, Pelasgians in the old days and Danaids after, it was in your defence as much as my father's that I killed my mother. Because if killing men is going to be a holy act for women, you had better hurry up and die, all of you, or else be the slaves of your wives. And that is the opposite of what you ought to do. As things stand, the woman who betrayed my father's bed is dead. But if you kill me, the law goes slack, and none of you can die too soon, because there will be no shortage of women with the nerve for it." He seemed to speak well, but he did not persuade the crowd. The other one won, that bad man who spoke to the mob, who called for the death of you and your brother.

Poor Orestes only just talked them out of stoning. He promised that he would leave life today, by his own hand, and you with him. Pylades is bringing him home from the assembly now, in tears, and their friends are walking with them, weeping and pitying them. So he is coming to you, a bitter thing to look at, a wretched sight. Get the sword ready, or the noose for your neck, because you have to leave the light. Your noble blood was no use to you, and neither was Apollo, sitting on his tripod at Delphi. He destroyed you.

(The old man goes.)

Chorus. Poor girl. You have hidden your face and bent it to the ground and you have gone silent, as if you were about to break into groans and weeping.

Electra.
	I begin the groaning, Pelasgian land.
	I set my white nails to my cheeks,
	bloody ruin,
	and beat my head, the beating that falls to the share
	of the goddess under the earth, Persephone, lovely child of the dead.
	Let the land the Cyclopes built cry out too,
	and set the iron to its head and crop the hair,
	for the ruin of our house.
	Pity, pity: this is what comes
	for those who are about to die,
	who were once the generals of Greece.
Electra.
	It is gone, gone, it has vanished,
	the whole line of the children of Pelops, and the glory
	that once made the house a thing to envy.
	The jealousy of the gods took hold of it, and the hateful
	bloody vote of the citizens.
	Io, io, you tribes of creatures who live for a day,
	full of tears and full of trouble, look how fate
	walks past all your hopes.
	Each of you takes his turn
	of different sorrows, in the long run of time,
	and nothing in the whole life of mortals stands still.
Electra.
	Let me go to the rock
	that hangs stretched out between sky and earth,
	swinging on its chains,
	a lump broken off Olympus, carried round on golden links,
	so that I can shout out my lament
	to the old man, my father's father, Tantalus,
	who fathered, fathered the founders of my house,
	who saw ruin come.
	The winged flight of horses,
	when Pelops in his four-horse chariot
	drove across the sea, and threw the body of murdered Myrtilus
	into the swell of the deep,
	racing his chariot
	along the shore at Geraestus,
	where the white waves
	of the sea come rolling in.
	From that came the curse on my house,
	the curse of many groans,
	when a lamb was born among the flocks, by the doing of Hermes,
	a lamb with a golden fleece,
	a portent of destruction, destruction,
	for Atreus, the breeder of horses.
	From that came Strife, who turned round
	the winged chariot of the sun
	and fitted the westward road of the sky
	to the single horse
	of the Dawn.
	And Zeus turned the seven Pleiades
	off their course onto another road,
	and after that he hands out death for death,
	the feast that carries the name of Thyestes,
	and the bed of Aerope of Crete,
	who was false, false to her marriage. And at the very last
	it has come to me and to my father,
	by the pitiless necessity of our house.
Chorus.
	And look, here comes your brother,
	condemned to death by the vote,
	and with him Pylades, the most faithful man alive,
	as good as a brother, steadying
	the sick limbs of Orestes,
	yoked beside him, and setting his feet with care.

(Orestes comes in, supported by Pylades.)

Electra. Oh, no. I am groaning because I see you standing at your grave, brother, in front of the pyre of the dead. Oh, no, again. I have looked at you for the very last time, and I am out of my mind.

Orestes. Will you not be quiet, and drop this women's wailing, and put up with what has been decided? It is pitiful, yes. But all the same you have to bear the luck we have.

Electra. And how am I supposed to keep quiet? We are not going to look at this light of the sun any more, we two poor wretches.

Orestes. Do not you kill me too. It is enough that the hand of Argos has killed me already. Leave what we have now alone.

Electra. Oh, your youth, Orestes, and your fate, and your death before its time. You ought to have been living, and now you are gone.

Orestes. By the gods, do not wrap me in cowardice, ferrying me over into tears by reminding me of everything that has gone wrong.

Electra. We are going to die. I cannot help groaning about it. Everyone alive finds it pitiful to lose his own dear life.

Orestes. This is our appointed day. We have to fasten a noose to hang from, or sharpen a sword for our hands.

Electra. Then you kill me, brother. Do not let some Argive kill me and make an outrage of the child of Agamemnon.

Orestes. I have enough of my mother's blood on me. I will not kill you. Die by your own hand, whichever way you like.

Electra. So be it. I will not be a step behind your sword. But I want to put my arms round your neck.

Orestes. Enjoy the empty pleasure, if there is any pleasure in putting your arms round someone when you are this close to death.

Electra. My dearest, the one who has the name that is sweetest to your sister and the one she misses most, and one soul with her.

Orestes. You will melt me. And I want to give you back the love of my arms. Why should a wretch like me be ashamed any more?

(He takes her in his arms.)

Oh, my sister's breast, how dear it is to hold you. This is what the two of us have, poor wretches, instead of children and a marriage bed: these words of greeting.

Electra. Ah. If only the same sword could kill us both, if it is allowed, and one tomb receive us, a coffin made of cedar wood.

Orestes. That would be the sweetest thing of all. But you can see how short of friends we are, when we cannot even share a grave.

Electra. Did he not even speak for you, or make any effort to save your life, Menelaus, that bad man, the traitor to my father?

Orestes. He never showed his face. He has his hopes set on the throne, and he was careful not to save his friends. Well then, let us see that we do something noble, something worthy of Agamemnon, and die doing it. I will show the city what my blood is worth, driving the sword into my liver. And you must match my daring with your own. Pylades, you be the umpire of our deaths. When we are both dead, lay our bodies out properly, and carry us to our father's tomb and bury us there together. And goodbye. I am going to the work, as you see.

Pylades. Stop. First there is one thing I have to blame you for. Did you think I would want to go on living when you were dead?

Orestes. Why? What is it to you to die with me?

Pylades. You ask? What is life to me without your company?

Orestes. You did not kill your mother. I did, poor wretch.

Pylades. With you, together. So I have to suffer the same as you.

Orestes. Give your body back to your father. Do not die with me. You have a city. I do not, not any more. You have your father's house, and a great harbour of wealth. You have lost your marriage to this unlucky sister of mine, whom I promised to you out of respect for your friendship. So take another bride and have children with her. The tie between my house and yours does not exist any more. Goodbye, dearest face of my company. That word is not for us, but it is still for you. The dead are robbed of joys.

Pylades. You are a long way from understanding what I mean. May the fruitful earth refuse to take my blood, and the bright sky too, if I ever betray you: if I ever get myself free and leave you behind. I helped with the killing, I will not deny it, and I planned the whole thing you are now paying for. So I have to die with you, and with her. Because I count her as my wife, the woman whose bed I agreed to. What am I going to say one day, when I come home to Delphi, the citadel of the Phocians? That I was your friend before your troubles, and now that you are in trouble I am your friend no longer? It is not possible. No. This is my business too. But since we are going to die, let us put our heads together and see how Menelaus can share our bad luck.

Orestes. Dearest friend. If only I could see that before I die.

Pylades. Then listen to me, and put off the stroke of the sword.

Orestes. I will, if there is any way to get back at my enemy.

Pylades. Quiet, now. I have very little trust in women.

Orestes. Do not be afraid of these. They are our friends.

Pylades. Let us kill Helen. A bitter grief for Menelaus.

Orestes. How? I am ready, if there is a chance of it coming off.

Pylades. Cut her throat. She is hiding in your house.

Orestes. She certainly is. And she is already putting her seal on everything in it.

Pylades. Not any more, once she has Hades for a bridegroom.

Orestes. But how? She has barbarian slaves around her.

Pylades. Who? I would not be afraid of any Phrygian alive.

Orestes. The kind who are in charge of mirrors and perfume.

Pylades. So she has come here with her Trojan luxuries?

Orestes. So much of it that Greece is too small a house for her.

Pylades. A race of slaves is nothing against men who are not slaves.

Orestes. If I can do this, I am not afraid to die twice over.

Pylades. Nor am I, if it is you I am avenging.

Orestes. Then lay the thing out for me, and go on to the end of it.

Pylades. We go into the house, as if we were going in to die.

Orestes. I have that much. The rest I do not.

Pylades. We pour out our sorrows to her, everything we are suffering.

Orestes. So that she cries for us, while inside she is delighted.

Pylades. And we will be doing exactly what she is doing, at the same time.

Orestes. And then how do we fight the fight?

Pylades. We will have swords hidden in these cloaks.

Orestes. But before that, how do we get rid of her attendants?

Pylades. We shut them out, one here, one there, in different parts of the house.

Orestes. And any one of them who will not keep quiet, we have to kill.

Pylades. And then the work itself shows us where to aim.

Orestes. At Helen. Kill Helen. I understand the signal.

Pylades. You have it. Now hear how good my plan is. If we drew the sword on a woman with more decency in her, the killing would be a disgrace. But as it is, she is going to pay the penalty on behalf of all Greece, for the fathers she killed and the children she destroyed, and the brides she made widows of their husbands. There will be shouts of joy. They will light fires to the gods, and pray for every blessing on your head and mine, because we took a wicked woman's blood. And when you have killed her you will not be called the man who killed his mother. You will leave that name behind you and rise to a better one: the man who killed Helen, the killer of so many. It is not right, it can never be right, that Menelaus should do well while your father and you and your sister die, and your mother, but I let that pass, it is not a fitting thing to say, and that he should hold your house, when it was Agamemnon's spear that won him back his bride. Let me not live another day if I do not draw the sword on her. And if we do not manage to kill Helen, then we set fire to this house and die. One of two things we will not fail to get, and either one is glory: to die well, or to be saved well.

Chorus. The daughter of Tyndareus has earned the hatred of every woman alive. She has shamed her whole sex.

Orestes. Ah. There is nothing better than a friend you can be sure of. Not wealth, not a throne. And the crowd is a stupid thing to trade for one noble friend. You were the one who worked out what we did to Aegisthus, and you stood next to me in the danger, and now once again you are handing me my revenge on my enemies and you are not stepping out of the way. But I will stop praising you. There is something heavy about it, being praised too much. Now I am going to breathe out my life whatever happens, and I want to do something to my enemies before I die, so that I can pay back the people who betrayed me with ruin of their own, and so that the ones who made me miserable will have something to groan about. I am the son of Agamemnon, who was judged worthy to rule Greece, no tyrant, but a man who had something like a god's strength in him. I will not shame him by dying a slave's death. I will let go of my life like a free man, and I will make Menelaus pay. Because if we could get hold of one thing, we would be lucky men: if rescue fell into our lap from somewhere, unlooked for, and we turned out the killers and not the killed. That is my prayer. And what I want is a pleasant thing to say, it costs nothing, and it cheers the heart with words that fly out of the mouth.

Electra. Brother, I think I have it. That very thing. A rescue for you, and for him, and thirdly for me.

Orestes. You are talking about the foresight of a god. But where is it? Since I know the good sense you carry in that soul of yours.

Electra. Listen to me, then. And you, over here. Pay attention.

Orestes. Say it. There is a certain pleasure in waiting for good news.

Electra. You know Helen's daughter? Of course you do. I am asking a man who knows.

Orestes. I know her. Hermione. My mother brought her up.

Electra. She has gone to the tomb of Clytemnestra.

Orestes. To do what? What hope are you putting in front of me?

Electra. To pour drink-offerings on our mother's grave.

Orestes. Well, and how does what you have just said get us to safety?

Electra. Seize her as a hostage, when she comes back.

Orestes. What sort of cure is that, for the three of us?

Electra. Once Helen is dead, if Menelaus tries to do anything to you, or to Pylades, or to me, because the three of us are one friend now, tell him you will kill Hermione. You have to draw your sword and hold it right against the girl's throat. And if Menelaus, when he sees Helen lying in her blood, wants the girl to live and offers to save you, then let her father have his daughter's body back. But if he cannot hold his hot temper in hand and tries to kill you, then you cut the girl's throat. And I think that if he blusters a great deal at first, he will soften in time. He was not born bold, and he was not born brave. That is the rampart I have for our safety. My speech is finished.

Orestes. You have the mind of a man, and the body that belongs among women. How much more you deserved to live than to die. Pylades, this is the woman you will lose, poor man. Or else you will live, and have a blessed marriage.

Pylades. If only it could be so, and she could come to the city of the Phocians with a fine wedding song, and the honour she deserves.

Orestes. How soon will Hermione get back to the house? Because everything else you said was perfect, if our luck holds, and we catch the cub of that unholy father.

Electra. I think she must be near the house by now. The time it would take matches exactly.

Orestes. Good. Then you, Electra, my sister, stay here in front of the house and wait for the girl to arrive. And keep watch, in case anyone, some ally of his, or our father's brother himself, gets into the house before the killing is finished. If so, shout into the house, or bang on the door, or send word in to us. We are going inside, Pylades, to arm our hands with swords for the last fight. Because you are sharing this labour with me.

Father, you who live in the house of the dark night, your son Orestes is calling you to come and help the people who need you. It is because of you that I am suffering this, wretched and wrongly. I have been betrayed by your brother for doing what was right. I want to take his wife and kill her. Be our partner in it.

Electra. Father, come. Come, if you can hear under the ground your children calling, who are dying for your sake.

Pylades. Agamemnon, kinsman of my father, hear my prayers too. Save your children.

Orestes. I killed my mother —

Electra. And I put my hand to the sword —

Pylades. And I made the plan, and cut them loose from their fear —

Orestes. For you, father. To help you.

Electra. And I did not betray you either.

Pylades. Will you hear these reproaches and not rescue your children?

Orestes. I pour you a drink-offering of tears.

Electra. And I pour you one of laments.

Pylades. Stop now, and let us get on with the work. If prayers can pierce the ground like spears, he hears. And you, Zeus, our ancestor, and you, holy Justice, give good luck to him, and to me, and to her. One fight for three friends, one judgement: either all of us live, or we pay the debt of death.

(Orestes and Pylades go into the house.)

Electra.
	Women of Mycenae, my friends,
	first in rank in Argos, where the Pelasgians made their home.

Chorus. What are you calling out to us, mistress? That name is still yours, in the city of the Danaids.

Electra. Stand there, some of you on this cart road, and the rest of you over here on the other path, to keep watch over the house.

(The Chorus divides. Half of them go to watch each road.)

Chorus.
	Why are you calling on me for this duty?
	Tell me, my dear.
Electra.
	I am afraid that someone will come to the house
	and stand over the fresh blood
	and find trouble on top of trouble.

First Half-Chorus. Go on, hurry. I will keep guard on this road, the one toward the rising sun.

Second Half-Chorus. And I on this one, the one that leads toward the west.

Electra. Now turn your eyes sideways, this way and that.

Chorus.
	From there to here, and then back again
	we turn to look, as you tell us.
Electra.
	Roll your eyes about now,
	look at everything, through your hair.

First Half-Chorus. Someone is coming along the road. Who is this country man wandering about your house?

Electra. Then we are finished, friends. Any moment now he will show our enemies the armed beasts we have hidden.

First Half-Chorus.
	Do not be afraid. The path is empty, my dear.
	It is not what you think.
Electra.
	And you? Is your side still safe for me?
	Give me some good news,
	tell me the ground in front of the courtyard is deserted.

Second Half-Chorus. All is well on this side. But watch your own. Not one of the Argives is coming near us.

First Half-Chorus. Same here. There is no crowd on this side either.

Electra. Well then, let me put my ear to the gates.

Chorus.
	You inside the house, why are you so slow
	to redden the blade with the victim's blood, while all is quiet?

Electra. They do not hear me. Oh, I am wretched. Has her beauty blunted their swords? Any moment now some Argive will come running in full armour to the rescue and close in on the house. Watch more carefully. This is no contest for sitting still. Turn about, some of you this way, the rest of you that way.

Chorus. I am going up and down the road, watching everywhere.

(Helen screams from inside the house.)

Helen. Io, Pelasgian Argos! I am being murdered, foully murdered.

Chorus. Did you hear? The men have their hands in the killing. That is Helen screaming, if I can judge.

Electra. Zeus, oh Zeus, power that never runs dry, come and help the people I love, whatever it takes.

Helen. Menelaus, I am dying, and you are right here and do nothing for me.

Electra.
	Murder her, kill her,
	destroy her, drive the two double-edged swords
	out of your hands
	into the woman who left her father, left her husband,
	who killed so many Greeks
	by the spear, dead beside the river,
	where tears fell on tears
	from the iron arrows
	around the eddies of Scamander.

Chorus. Quiet, quiet. I heard a footstep. Someone is coming down the road to the house.

Electra. Dearest women, it is Hermione, walking right into the middle of the killing. Let us stop shouting. She is stepping into the meshes of the net. A fine catch she will make, if she is taken. Back to your places, with calm eyes, and nothing in your faces to show what has been done. I will keep my own eyes down and gloomy, as if I knew nothing of what has happened here.

(Hermione comes in from the direction of Clytemnestra's tomb.)

Girl, are you back from wreathing Clytemnestra's grave and pouring drink-offerings to the dead below?

Hermione. I am back. I won her goodwill. But a kind of fear has come over me. I heard a cry from the house while I was still a long way off.

Electra. Why not? What is happening to us deserves groans.

Hermione. Say something better than that. What is the news?

Electra. This country has voted that Orestes and I must die.

Hermione. No. Not my own kin.

Electra. It is fixed. We are standing under the yoke of necessity.

Hermione. Is that the reason for the cry inside the house?

Electra. Yes. A suppliant fell at Helen's knees and was crying out—

Hermione. Who? I know nothing more unless you tell me.

Electra. Poor Orestes. Begging not to die, and for me too.

Hermione. Then the house has good reason to be shouting.

Electra. What else would anyone cry out about, if not that? But come and join your friends in begging. Fall at your mother's feet, blessed as she is, so that Menelaus does not have to watch us die. You were nursed in my mother's arms. Pity us, and lift some of this evil off us. Come here, into the struggle, and I will lead the way. You alone hold the end of our safety in your hands.

Hermione. Look, I am hurrying my feet into the house. As far as it lies with me, count yourselves saved.

Electra. You inside the house, friends with your swords, will you not seize the prey?

Hermione. Oh, no. Who are these men I see?

(Armed men seize Hermione at the door. Orestes speaks from inside.)

Orestes. Quiet. You have come here for our safety, not for yours.

Electra. Hold her, hold her. Put a sword to her throat and then keep quiet, so that Menelaus learns he has found men here, not Phrygian cowards, and has been treated the way cowards deserve.

(They drag Hermione into the house. Electra goes in after them, and the doors are shut.)

Chorus.
	Io, io, friends,
	raise a noise, a noise and a shout
	in front of the house, so that the murder that has been done
	does not throw the Argives into a terrible panic
	and bring them running to the royal house,
	before I see for certain that Helen lies
	murdered and bloody in the house,
	or hear the story from one of her servants.
	Part of what has happened I know. The rest I do not know for sure.
	Through justice the vengeance of the gods
	has come to Helen.
	She filled all Greece with tears
	because of that cursed, cursed Paris of Ida,
	who brought Greece to Troy.

Chorus. But the bolts of the royal doors are rattling. Be quiet. One of the Phrygians is coming out. We can ask him how things stand inside.

(A Phrygian slave scrambles down from the roof of the porch and tumbles out in front of the house.)

Phrygian.
	I have escaped the Argive sword, out of death,
	in my barbarian slippers,
	over the cedar beams that roof the porch,
	over the Doric triglyphs,
	gone, gone, oh Earth, Earth,
	a barbarian's flight.
	Aiai.
	Where can I run, strangers? Into the grey air,
	fly up, or into the sea, that the Ocean
	with the bull's head
	winds round the earth in his arms?
Chorus.
	What is it, Helen's servant, you head from Ida?
Phrygian.
	Ilium, Ilium, oh, oh,
	city of Phrygia, and holy Ida
	with your rich soil, how I groan for your ruin,
	a chariot-song, a chariot-song of grief
	in my barbarian cry, over the beauty born of a bird,
	the swan-feathered face, Leda's
	cub, Helen the ruin,
	Helen the ruin,
	a Fury for Apollo's towers of polished stone.
	Ottotoi.
	Wailing, wailing,
	poor Dardania, for Ganymede
	and his horses, the boy who shared the bed of Zeus.

Chorus. Tell us clearly, one thing after another, what happened in the house. Up to now I have only been guessing, and I cannot make it out.

Phrygian.
	Ailinon, ailinon: that is how the barbarians
	begin a death, aiai,
	in the tongue of Asia, whenever
	the blood of kings is poured on the ground
	by the iron swords of Hades.
	They came into the house, to tell you
	one thing after another, two twin lions
	of Greece.
	One of them, they said, had the general for his father.
	The other was the son of Strophius, a man of evil cunning,
	like Odysseus, treacherous in his silence,
	but true to his friends, bold in a fight,
	clever in war, and a deadly snake.
	Curse him for his quiet
	planning, the villain.
	They went in to the throne
	of the woman Paris the archer married,
	their eyes smeared with tears,
	and sat down, humble,
	one on this side, one on that,
	each guarding his own flank.
	And they threw, they threw their suppliant hands
	round Helen's knees, both of them.
	And up leapt the Phrygian slaves,
	leapt running,
	and each one said to the next, dropping in fear,
	that this might be a trick.
	Some thought not,
	but others thought the snake who killed his mother
	was tangling the daughter of Tyndareus
	in the meshes of a trap.
Chorus.
	And where were you then? Or had you already run away in fear?
Phrygian.
	It happened I was, in the Phrygian way, the Phrygian way,
	stirring the air, the air beside Helen's curl,
	Helen's, with a round fan
	of feathers, well made, in front of her cheek,
	waving it, the way barbarians do.
	And she was twisting flax on her spindle
	with her fingers,
	letting the thread fall to the floor,
	because she wanted to stitch ornaments for the tomb
	out of the Phrygian spoils, with her flax,
	purple robes, a gift for Clytemnestra.
	Orestes spoke to the Spartan girl:
	"Daughter of Zeus, set your foot
	on the floor here, get up off your chair,
	and come to the seat of Pelops our forefather,
	the old hearth,
	so that you can hear what I have to say."
	And he led her, led her, and she followed,
	no prophet of what was coming.
	And his partner in the work was busy elsewhere,
	the evil Phocian, going about:
	"Out of the way! Phrygians. Cowards, always."
	And he locked us up, one here and one there,
	all over the house: some in the horse
	stables, some in the outer rooms,
	one this way and another that,
	posting each of us far away from our mistress.
Chorus.
	And what came next, in this disaster?
Phrygian.
	Mother of Ida,
	mother, mighty, mighty,
	aiai, the bloody sufferings, the lawless
	evils I saw, I saw
	in the house of kings.
	From under the shadow of their purple-bordered cloaks
	they pulled their swords,
	and each one spun his eye
	a different way, in case anyone was near.
	Like boars of the mountain
	they stood facing the woman
	and said: "You will die,
	you will die.
	Your coward husband is killing you,
	because he betrayed his brother's son
	to die in Argos."
	And she screamed, she
	screamed: "Oh, oh."
	She struck her white arm on her breast
	and beat her poor head with the blow,
	and turned her gold-sandalled foot
	to flight, to flight. But Orestes
	stepped after her in his Mycenaean boot,
	threw his fingers into her hair,
	bent her neck back over her left shoulder,
	and was about to drive the black sword
	into her throat.
Chorus.
	And where were you Phrygians in the house, to defend her?
Phrygian.
	With a scream
	we broke out the doors and doorposts
	with bars, from the rooms where we were waiting,
	and came running to help from every corner of the house,
	one with stones, one with javelins,
	one with a sword drawn in his hands.
	And against us came Pylades,
	unflinching, like, like Hector
	the Phrygian, or Ajax of the triple crest,
	whom I saw, I saw at the gates
	of Priam. And we met, point to point
	of our swords.
	And then, then it was very plain what Phrygians are,
	how much less than Greek spears
	we were in the strength of Ares:
	one gone, running; one a corpse;
	one carrying a wound; one begging,
	holding that up against death.
	We ran for cover in the dark.
	Corpses were falling, others were about to fall, others lay still.
	And poor Hermione came into the house
	just as her mother fell to the floor, murdered,
	the poor woman who bore her.
	And like Bacchants without their wands,
	the two of them ran at her and caught her up,
	a mountain cub in their hands,
	and turned back to the daughter of Zeus
	to slaughter her. But she,
	out of the bedroom,
	straight through the house, she
	vanished, oh Zeus and Earth
	and light and night,
	by drugs, or the arts
	of magicians, or the gods stealing her away.
	What came after I no longer know.
	I stole my runaway foot out of the house.
	So Menelaus, after all his troubles, all his troubles,
	took his wife Helen back from Troy
	and got nothing for it.

Chorus. And here is a new thing on top of new things. I see Orestes coming out in front of the house with a sword in his hand, walking with a wild step.

(Orestes comes out of the house with a drawn sword.)

Orestes. Where is the man who ran out of the house to get away from my sword?

Phrygian. I bow down to you, my lord, falling at your feet the way barbarians do.

Orestes. This is not Ilium. This is the land of Argos.

Phrygian. Everywhere, a man with sense finds living sweeter than dying.

Orestes. You did not by any chance raise that shout for Menelaus to come running?

Phrygian. No, for you. To help you. You deserve it more.

Orestes. So the daughter of Tyndareus died justly?

Phrygian. Most justly. Even if she had three throats to die with.

Orestes. It is cowardice that makes your tongue so obliging. You do not think so inside.

Phrygian. Don't I? The woman who ruined Greece, and the Phrygians along with it?

Orestes. Swear it, or I kill you. Swear you are not saying it to please me.

Phrygian. I swear by my life. That is an oath I would keep.

Orestes. Was it like this at Troy too? Were all the Phrygians this afraid of iron?

Phrygian. Take the sword away. This close, it flashes back a terrible death.

Orestes. Afraid you will turn to stone, as if you had looked at a Gorgon?

Phrygian. Into a corpse, more likely. I do not know anything about the Gorgon's head.

Orestes. You are a slave, and you are afraid of Hades, who would set you free from your troubles?

Phrygian. Every man, even a slave, likes looking at the light.

Orestes. Well said. Your good sense saves you. Go inside the house.

Phrygian. You are not going to kill me, then?

Orestes. You are let off.

Phrygian. That is a fine thing to say.

Orestes. But we may change our minds.

Phrygian. That is not a fine thing to say.

Orestes. Fool. Do you think I could bring myself to bloody your throat? You were not born a woman, and you do not count among men either. I came out of the house to stop your shouting, and for nothing else. Argos wakes up fast when it hears a cry for help. As for Menelaus, I am not afraid to take him on within reach of my sword. Let him come, proud of the yellow curls on his shoulders. If he gathers the Argives and brings them against this house to avenge Helen's murder, and refuses to save me, and my sister, and Pylades who did this with me, he will have two corpses to look at, his daughter's and his wife's.

(Orestes drives the Phrygian into the house ahead of him. The doors are shut.)

Chorus.
	Io, io, fortune.
	Into another struggle, another one, the house
	is falling, a fearful one, around the sons of Atreus.
	What do we do? Report this to the city?
	Or keep quiet? That is safer, friends.
	Look, in front of the house, look, smoke
	is rushing up into the air. It is telling the story already.
	They are lighting torches to burn the house
	of Tantalus, and they do not hold back from murder.
	A god holds the end for mortals,
	the end where he wants it.
	Great is the power. Through avenging spirits
	this house has fallen, fallen, through blood,
	ever since Myrtilus was thrown from the chariot.

Chorus. But here comes Menelaus too. I see him near the house, moving fast. He has heard, I suppose, about the luck that stands here now. You sons of Atreus inside, you had better hurry and fix the bolts across the doors. A man who is doing well is a terrible thing to men who are doing badly, and you are doing badly now, Orestes.

(Menelaus comes in with armed servants.)

Menelaus. I have come because I heard of the terrible, violent deeds of a pair of lions. I will not call them men. What I heard was that my wife is not dead but has vanished, gone out of sight. An empty rumour, that. Someone brought it to me who had lost his head from fear. No, this is one of the mother-killer's tricks, and a great joke. Someone open the house. I am telling my servants: force these gates, so that at least we can rescue my daughter out of the hands of these blood-stained men, and take up my poor, wretched wife, and the men who destroyed her can die alongside her, by my hand.

(Orestes appears on the roof of the house, holding Hermione with a sword at her throat. Pylades and Electra are beside him with torches.)

Orestes. You there. Keep your hand off those bolts. I mean you, Menelaus, towering up there in your nerve. Or I will smash your skull with this coping-stone, tearing off the old cornice, the masons' work. The doors are fixed fast with bars, which will keep your rescuing zeal locked out and stop you getting inside the house.

Menelaus. Ah. What is this? I see the glare of torches, and men on top of the house, standing at bay as if it were a fort, and a sword guarding my daughter's throat.

Orestes. Do you want to ask questions, or to hear me?

Menelaus. Neither. But I have to hear you, it seems.

Orestes. I am going to kill your daughter, if you want to know.

Menelaus. You murdered Helen, and now you are adding murder to murder?

Orestes. If only I had done it, instead of being robbed by the gods.

Menelaus. You deny killing her? You say this to outrage me?

Orestes. It is a painful denial. If only I had—

Menelaus. Had done what? You are frightening me.

Orestes. Thrown the polluter of Greece down into Hades.

Menelaus. Give me my wife's body back, so I can heap a tomb over her.

Orestes. Ask the gods for it. But I will kill your daughter.

Menelaus. The mother-killer adds murder to murder?

Orestes. The man who avenged his father, whom you betrayed to death.

Menelaus. Was your mother's blood not enough for you, the blood you have on you already?

Orestes. I would never get tired of killing evil women.

Menelaus. And you, Pylades, are you a partner in this killing too?

Orestes. He says yes by his silence. I will do the talking, and that will be enough.

Menelaus. You will not enjoy it, unless you can fly away on wings.

Orestes. We will not run. We will set the house on fire.

Menelaus. What, you will destroy your father's house?

Orestes. So that you cannot have it. And I will cut her throat over the fire.

Menelaus. Kill her, then. Kill her, and you will pay me for it.

Orestes. So be it.

Menelaus. Ah, ah. No. Do not do it.

Orestes. Be quiet, then, and bear it. You are suffering justly.

Menelaus. Is it just that you should live?

Orestes. Yes, and rule a country.

Menelaus. Which country?

Orestes. This one. Pelasgian Argos.

Menelaus. You would be a fine one to touch the holy water—

Orestes. Why ever not?

Menelaus. And to kill the victims before a battle.

Orestes. And you would be fit for it?

Menelaus. My hands are clean.

Orestes. But not your mind.

Menelaus. Who would speak to you?

Orestes. Anyone who loves his father.

Menelaus. And anyone who honours his mother?

Orestes. Was born lucky.

Menelaus. Not you, then.

Orestes. No. I do not like evil women.

Menelaus. Take that sword away from my daughter.

Orestes. You were born a liar.

Menelaus. So you will kill my daughter?

Orestes. Now you are not lying.

Menelaus. Oh, what am I to do?

Orestes. Go to the Argives and persuade them—

Menelaus. Persuade them of what?

Orestes. Not to kill us. Beg the city.

Menelaus. Or you will murder my child?

Orestes. That is how it is.

Menelaus. Poor Helen—

Orestes. And I am not poor?

Menelaus. I brought you back from Phrygia to be a victim—

Orestes. If only that were true.

Menelaus. After a thousand labours.

Orestes. Except for me. Not one on my account.

Menelaus. I have suffered terribly.

Orestes. Yes. Because back then you were no use.

Menelaus. You have me.

Orestes. You caught yourself, by being a coward. Come on, Electra, set fire to the house from below. And you, Pylades, the truest friend I have, burn the cornice of these walls.

Menelaus. Land of the Danaans, you who founded Argos, city of horses, come on, will you not come running in arms to help? This man is forcing your whole city to let him live, when he has shed his mother's polluted blood.

(Apollo appears above the house, with Helen beside him.)

Apollo. Menelaus, stop. Put away that sharpened temper. I am Apollo, the son of Leto, here close beside you, and I am calling you by name. And you, Orestes, standing over this girl with your sword, listen, so that you know what words I have brought. Helen, whom you were so eager to destroy, to make Menelaus angry, and failed: here she is, the woman you see in the folds of the sky, saved, and not killed by you. I rescued her. I snatched her from under your sword at the order of Zeus my father. She is Zeus's child, and she must live and never die. She will sit with Castor and Polydeuces in the folds of the sky, a saviour to sailors. Take another bride into your house, Menelaus. The gods used her beauty to bring Greeks and Phrygians together in one place and set deaths going, to drain off from the earth the outrage of mortals swarming in numbers without end.

That is how it stands with Helen. As for you, Orestes, you must cross the borders of this land and live on the soil of Parrhasia for the circle of one year. The Azanians and the Arcadians will name it after your exile and call it Oresteion. From there go to the city of the Athenians and stand trial for your mother's blood before the three Kindly Ones, the Furies. The gods will be the judges of your trial, on the hill of Ares, and they will cast a most righteous vote, and there you must win. And the girl at whose throat you are holding the sword, Orestes, Hermione: it is fated that you will marry her. Neoptolemus thinks he will marry her; he never will. It is his fate to die by a Delphian sword when he comes to demand satisfaction from me for his father Achilles. Give your sister to Pylades in marriage, as you once promised. A happy life waits for him. Menelaus, let Orestes rule Argos. Go and be king in the land of Sparta, and keep it as the dowry of a wife who never stopped handing you troubles by the thousand, until this very day. I will set things right between him and the city. It was I who forced him to murder his mother.

Orestes. Apollo, prophet, your oracles. You were no lying prophet after all, but a true one. And yet a fear had crept into me, that I was listening to some avenging spirit and only thought I heard your voice. But it is ending well, and I will obey your words. Look: I release Hermione from the slaughter, and I agree to the marriage, whenever her father gives her.

Menelaus. I greet you, Helen, daughter of Zeus, and I envy you your home in the blessed house of the gods. Orestes, I pledge my daughter to you, since Apollo says so. Well born yourself, marrying a well-born wife, may you have joy of her, and I too, who give her.

Apollo. Go now, each of you, where I have ordered, and let your quarrels dissolve.

Menelaus. We must obey.

Orestes. I am of the same mind. I make my peace with what has happened, Menelaus, and with your oracles, Apollo.

Apollo.
	Go your ways now, and honour Peace,
	the most beautiful of the gods. And I
	will bring Helen to the halls of Zeus,
	when I have crossed the vault of the bright stars.
	There, beside Hera and Hebe,
	the wife of Heracles, she will sit enthroned, a goddess
	to men, honoured with drink-offerings forever,
	with the sons of Tyndareus, the sons of Zeus,
	keeping watch over the sea for sailors.

(Apollo and Helen vanish above. The others go their separate ways.)

Chorus.
	Great Victory, holy one,
	stay with me all my life,
	and never stop crowning me.

The Bacchae (405 BC)

The Bacchae

(Thebes, in front of the royal house of Pentheus. To one side is the tomb of Semele, fenced off, still smoking, with vines trained over it. Dionysus comes in, in the shape of a young man with long hair, a fawnskin over his shoulders and an ivy wand in his hand.)

Dionysus. I have come to this land of Thebes, and I am the son of Zeus. I am Dionysus. Semele, Cadmus's daughter, gave birth to me once, in a labour brought on by a flash of lightning. I have changed my shape from a god's to a man's, and here I am, at the springs of Dirce and the waters of the Ismenus. And I can see my mother's tomb, the mother the thunderbolt struck, right here beside the house, and the ruins of her home, still smoking with the living flame of Zeus's fire: Hera's outrage against my mother, and it never dies. I give Cadmus credit. He has made this ground off limits, a shrine for his daughter, and I have covered it over with the green of the vine and its clustering grapes.

I left the gold-rich fields of Lydia and Phrygia behind me, and the sun-beaten plains of Persia, and the walled towns of Bactria, and the bitter winter country of the Medes, and Arabia the blessed, and all of Asia that lies along the salt sea with its fine-towered cities full of Greeks and barbarians living side by side. I set every one of those places dancing and established my rites there, so that mortals could see me for the god I am. And then I came to this city, the first in Greece. Thebes was the first town in this Greek land that I made shriek my cry. I tied the fawnskin on their bodies and put the thyrsus in their hands, the ivy-tipped wand that is my weapon. Because my mother's sisters, the last women on earth who should have said it, said that I, Dionysus, was no son of Zeus at all. They said Semele had been to bed with some mortal man and was laying the blame for it on Zeus, and that the whole story was a clever invention of Cadmus's. That was why Zeus killed her, they crowed: for lying about who was in her bed.

So I have driven those same women stinging mad out of their houses. They are living on the mountain, out of their minds, and I have made them wear the dress of my rites. Every woman of the seed of Cadmus, every one of them, I have sent raving out of her home. They are sitting up there with the daughters of Cadmus among them, under the green firs, on rocks with no roof over them. Because this city has to learn, whether it likes it or not, what it means to be left outside my rites, and I have to speak up for my mother Semele by showing myself to mortals as the god she bore to Zeus.

Now Cadmus has handed his honours and his throne to Pentheus, his daughter's son. And Pentheus is fighting a god, where I am concerned. He shoves me away from his sacrifices, and there is no mention of me anywhere in his prayers. So I am going to show him, and every Theban with him, that I was born a god. And when I have put things right here, I will move on to another country and reveal myself there. But if the city of Thebes loses its temper and tries to bring the Bacchants down off the mountain by force of arms, I will take the field against it with the Maenads as my army. That is why I have taken on a mortal appearance and changed my shape into a man's.

But you, women who left Tmolus behind, the mountain fortress of Lydia. My own company. I brought you from among the barbarians to sit at my side and travel with me. Take up the drums, the drums that belong to the Phrygian towns, that Mother Rhea and I invented between us, and come round this royal house of Pentheus and beat them, so that Cadmus's city can see. As for me, I am going to the folds of Mount Cithaeron, where the Bacchants are, to join in their dances.

(Dionysus goes. The Chorus come in, Asian women in fawnskins, carrying ivy wands and drums.)

Chorus.
	From the land of Asia,
	leaving holy Tmolus behind, I hurry
	to do sweet work for Bromius, the Roarer,
	which is one of the names of Dionysus,
	labour that is no labour at all,
	crying his cry, Euoi.
	Who is in the road? Who is in the road? Who?
	Get indoors, out of the way. Let every mouth
	keep itself clean and holy,
	because I am going to sing the hymn to Dionysus
	the way it has always been sung.
Chorus.
	Oh, happy is the man who is blessed,
	who knows the rites of the gods,
	who keeps his life pure
	and gives his soul to the company,
	dancing for Dionysus on the mountains
	in holy purifications,
	who keeps the mysteries of Cybele,
	the Great Mother, as they should be kept,
	shaking the thyrsus high,
	crowned with ivy,
	serving Dionysus.
	Go, Bacchants, go, Bacchants,
	bring Dionysus home, the god who is a god's son,
	down from the mountains of Phrygia
	into the wide streets of Greece,
	the god who roars.
Chorus.
	Once his mother carried him,
	and her time came on her,
	the pains of birth forced on her early
	by the thunder of Zeus flying at her,
	and she pushed him out of her womb
	and left her life behind under the stroke of the lightning.
	And at once Zeus, the son of Cronus,
	took him into a birth-chamber of his own.
	He hid him in his thigh
	and pinned him in with golden clasps,
	out of Hera's sight.
	And when the Fates had brought him to his term,
	Zeus gave birth to him, the god with the horns of a bull,
	and crowned him with crowns of snakes.
	That is why the Maenads catch wild snakes
	and twist them into their hair.
Chorus.
	Thebes, you who nursed Semele,
	crown yourself with ivy.
	Burst into leaf, burst into leaf, with green
	bryony and its lovely berries,
	and go mad for Dionysus with branches
	of oak or fir.
	Trim your spotted fawnskins
	with tufts of white wool,
	and make yourselves holy with the wild fennel wands.
	In a moment the whole earth will be dancing,
	and whoever leads the dance is Dionysus himself,
	to the mountain, to the mountain, where the crowd of women waits,
	driven from their looms and their shuttles,
	stung mad by Dionysus.
Chorus.
	Cave where the Curetes hid the child,
	holy caverns of Crete
	where Zeus was born:
	there, in their caves, the Corybantes in their triple helmets
	invented this for me,
	this circle of stretched hide, the drum.
	And in the strain of their Bacchic dance
	they blended its beat with the sweet-voiced breath
	of Phrygian pipes, and put it in the hand
	of Mother Rhea, to pound out time for the Bacchants' cries.
	And the Satyrs in their madness
	got it from the Mother goddess,
	and joined it to the dances
	of the festival that comes every second year,
	the festival Dionysus loves.
Chorus.
	He is sweet on the mountains, when he drops to the ground
	out of the running companies,
	wearing the holy fawnskin,
	hunting the blood of the slaughtered goat,
	the joy of raw flesh,
	racing for the mountains of Phrygia, of Lydia,
	and the leader of the dance is Dionysus.
	Euoi.
	The ground runs with milk, it runs with wine,
	it runs with the nectar of bees.
	And the god of the Bacchants lifts high
	the blazing flame of the pine torch on his wand,
	like the smoke of Syrian frankincense,
	and he darts, running and dancing,
	stirring up the stragglers,
	tossing them with his shouts,
	flinging his soft hair into the air.
	And over the cries he roars out this:
	"Oh, go, Bacchants,
	go, Bacchants,
	pride of Tmolus where the river runs gold,
	sing Dionysus
	to the deep growl of the drums,
	Euoi, glorying in the god of Euoi
	with Phrygian shouts and calls,
	when the holy pipe, sweet-sounding,
	sounds its holy games,
	keeping time with the women who wander to the mountain,
	to the mountain." And then she is glad,
	like a foal at pasture beside its mother,
	and the Bacchant throws her quick feet into leaps.

(Teiresias comes in, blind, very old, dressed in a fawnskin with ivy on his head and a wand in his hand.)

Teiresias. Who is at the gates? Call Cadmus out of the house, Agenor's son, the man who left the city of Sidon and built this towered town of Thebes. Somebody go. Tell him Teiresias is looking for him. He knows what I have come about, and what I agreed with him, one old man with an older one: to wind the ivy on the thyrsus, to wear the skins of fawns, and to crown our heads with sprigs of ivy.

(Cadmus comes out of the house, dressed the same way.)

Cadmus. My dear old friend. I was inside, and I heard your voice and knew it, a clever voice from a clever man. And here I am, ready, with the god's outfit on. He is my daughter's son, this Dionysus who has shown himself to mankind as a god, and we have to make him as great as we possibly can. Where do we dance? Where do I put my feet and shake this grey head? You show me, Teiresias, one old man leading another. You are the clever one. I could keep this up all night and all day and never get tired, beating the ground with the thyrsus. It is a pleasure to forget how old we are.

Teiresias. Then you feel exactly what I feel. I am young again too, and I am going to try the dancing.

Cadmus. So shall we go up the mountain in a carriage?

Teiresias. No. The god would not get the same honour from that.

Cadmus. One old man leading another by the hand like a schoolboy. That will be me, leading you.

Teiresias. The god will lead us both up there, and it will cost us nothing.

Cadmus. Are we the only men in the city who are going to dance for Dionysus?

Teiresias. Yes. We are the only ones thinking straight. The rest are thinking wrong.

Cadmus. We are wasting time. Here, take my hand.

Teiresias. There. Take hold, and yoke your hand to mine.

Cadmus. I was born a mortal. I do not look down on the gods.

Teiresias. We do not play clever with the gods. The traditions our fathers handed down to us, as old as time itself, no argument is going to knock down, not even if some brilliant mind has thought its way to the very top of cleverness. Will somebody say I have no shame about my old age, going out to dance with ivy on my head? Let him. The god drew no line. He did not say the young should dance and the old should not. He wants his honours from everybody alike. He wants to be made great, and he counts nobody out.

Cadmus. Since you cannot see this daylight, Teiresias, I will be your prophet and tell you what is happening. Here comes Pentheus, hurrying to the house, Echion's son, the man I gave the rule of this land to. Look how worked up he is. What is the news this time?

(Pentheus comes in with his attendants. At first he does not notice the two old men.)

Pentheus. I happened to be out of the country, and I hear there is new trouble in this city. The women have left our homes for a Bacchic worship they have made up themselves, and they are running about in the shadowy mountains, honouring this new god with dances, this Dionysus, whoever he is. They set up mixing bowls full of wine in the middle of their gatherings, so I hear, and then they slink off one by one to some lonely spot to serve a man in bed. Maenads at their sacrifices, that is the story. Aphrodite comes before Dionysus with them.

Every one I have caught, my servants are holding in the public prison with her hands tied. The ones still out I will hunt down off the mountain. Ino, and Agave, who bore me to Echion, and Actaeon's mother, I mean Autonoe. I will clamp them in iron nets, and that will put a quick stop to this vicious Bacchic business.

And they say some stranger has come, a sorcerer, a chanter of spells from the land of Lydia, with golden curls and scented hair and the wine-dark charms of Aphrodite in his eyes, who spends his days and his nights with young girls, dangling his rites of joy in front of them. If I catch him inside this house, I will stop him banging his thyrsus and tossing his hair. I will cut his head off his neck. This is the man who says Dionysus is a god. He says he was once stitched into the thigh of Zeus. Dionysus, who was burnt to nothing by the lightning along with his mother, because she lied about being Zeus's bride. Does that not deserve a hanging, and a hard one, whoever this stranger is? Outrage on top of outrage.

But here is another wonder. I see the prophet Teiresias in a spotted fawnskin, and my own mother's father, and this is too funny, playing the Bacchant with a fennel wand. Father, I am ashamed to look at you. Two old men, and no sense between you. Shake that ivy off. Let go of the thyrsus, grandfather. Empty your hand.

You talked him into this, Teiresias. You want to bring in one more new god for mankind so that you can watch more birds and rake in more fees from burnt offerings. If your grey hairs were not protecting you, you would be sitting in chains among the Bacchants for importing these vicious rites. Because when women get the gleam of the grape at a feast, I say there is nothing healthy left in any of their worship.

Chorus. What blasphemy. Stranger, have you no respect for the gods, or for Cadmus, who sowed the crop of men that grew out of the earth? You are Echion's son, and you are shaming your own family.

Teiresias. When a clever man has a good case to argue, it is no great feat to speak well. You have a tongue that runs smoothly, as if you had sense, but there is no sense in what it says. A man who is strong in nerve and knows how to speak, and has no judgement, makes a bad citizen.

This new god you are laughing at: I could not begin to tell you how great he is going to be all over Greece. Two things, young man, come first for human beings. The goddess Demeter, and she is the earth, call her by whichever name you like, feeds mortals on dry food. And then the one who came after her, Semele's son, found the match to it, the wet drink of the grape, and brought it to mortals. It puts an end to grief for poor suffering men, when they are filled with the stream of the vine, and it gives them sleep, and forgetfulness of the day's troubles, and there is no other medicine for hardship. He is a god, and he is poured out in offering to the gods, so that through him mankind gets its good things.

And you laugh at him for being stitched into Zeus's thigh? I will teach you how that story makes good sense. When Zeus snatched him out of the lightning-fire and carried the baby up to Olympus as a god, Hera wanted to throw him out of heaven. Zeus made a counter-plan, the way a god does. He tore off a piece of the sky that wraps round the earth and gave that to Hera as a hostage, a Dionysus for her to quarrel with, and kept the real one safe. And in time people said he had been stitched into Zeus's thigh. They changed a word. The god had been a hostage, a homeros, to the goddess Hera, and the word for a thigh is meros, and the one slid into the other and they made a story out of it.

And this god is a prophet. Bacchic frenzy and madness have a great deal of prophecy in them. When the god comes into a body in full force, he makes the people he has maddened tell the future. He has taken over a share of Ares's business too. An army standing armed and in its ranks has been scattered by panic before a spear was touched, and that is madness too, and it comes from Dionysus. One day you will see him on the rocks of Delphi as well, leaping across the plateau between the two peaks with pine torches, whirling and shaking the Bacchic branch, great all over Greece.

Listen to me, Pentheus. Do not go boasting that power is what counts among men, and do not imagine you are thinking straight when your thinking is sick. Take the god into your land. Pour him wine, be a Bacchant, crown your head. It is not Dionysus who will force women to keep themselves in hand where Aphrodite is concerned. That lives in a woman's nature, always, in everything she does, and that is where you have to look. Even in the middle of a Bacchic revel, a woman who keeps herself in hand will not be ruined.

You see? You enjoy it when a crowd stands at your gates and the city makes the name of Pentheus great. Well, he enjoys being honoured too, I imagine. So Cadmus, whom you are laughing at, and I are going to put ivy on our heads and dance, a grey team in harness, but dance we must. And I will not fight a god because you talked me into it. You are mad, in the most painful way there is. No drug will cure you, and yet it is a kind of drug that has made you ill.

Chorus. Old man, you do no shame to Apollo with those words, and when you honour Dionysus you are keeping yourself in hand. He is a great god.

Cadmus. My boy, Teiresias has given you good advice. Live with us, inside the laws, not outside them. Right now you are all up in the air. You think you are thinking, and you are thinking nothing. Even if this god is no god, as you say, tell people he is. Tell the lie, and tell it well, so that Semele can be said to have given birth to a god, and the honour comes to our whole family. You know how Actaeon died, poor man, torn to pieces in the meadows by the flesh-eating hounds he had raised himself, because he boasted he was a better hunter than Artemis. Do not let that happen to you. Come here, let me crown your head with ivy. Give the god his honour, along with us.

Pentheus. Do not lay a hand on me. Go and play the Bacchant, and do not wipe your idiocy off on me. As for the man who taught you this folly, I am going to make him pay. Somebody go, quickly, to the seat where he sits and watches his birds. Lever it up with crowbars, tip it over, turn the whole place upside down, everything in a heap, and throw his holy ribbons to the winds and the storms. That is where I can hurt him most. And the rest of you, go through the city and track down this womanish stranger who is bringing a new disease to our women and fouling our beds. If you catch him, tie him up and bring him here, so that he can be sentenced to death by stoning and die that way. He will find his Bacchic revels in Thebes a bitter business.

(Pentheus's men go off in different directions. Pentheus goes into the house.)

Teiresias. You poor fool, you have no idea what you are saying. You are mad now, and you were out of your mind before. Let us go, Cadmus, and pray to the god for this man, savage as he is, and for the city, that he does nothing terrible. Follow me, with your ivy staff. Try to hold me up, and I will hold you up. It would be a disgrace if two old men fell over. But never mind that. We have to serve Dionysus, the son of Zeus. And Cadmus, watch that Pentheus does not bring grief into your house. His name means grief. I am not saying that as a prophet. I am looking at the facts. A fool talks folly.

(The two old men go off together, slowly, holding each other up.)

Chorus.
	Holiness, queen among the gods,
	Holiness, who carry your golden wing
	low over the earth,
	do you hear what Pentheus is saying?
	Do you hear his unholy outrage
	against Dionysus, Semele's son,
	the god who comes first among the blessed
	at the feast where the garlands are lovely?
	This is his office:
	to dance with the company,
	to laugh with the pipe,
	to put an end to worry,
	whenever the gleam of the grape comes
	to the feast of the gods,
	and at the ivy-wearing banquets
	the wine bowl wraps men in sleep.
Chorus.
	Mouths without a bridle
	and folly without a law
	end in disaster.
	But the quiet life
	and good sense
	stay unshaken, and hold a house together.
	The gods live far off in the sky,
	but they still see what mortals do.
	Being clever is not being wise,
	and neither is thinking thoughts too big for a mortal.
	Life is short. A man who chases
	great things on that short lease
	loses what is in his hands.
	That is how madmen behave,
	people whose judgement is bad,
	if you ask me.
Chorus.
	Let me go to Cyprus,
	Aphrodite's island,
	where the Loves live
	who charm the hearts of mortals,
	and to Paphos, where no rain falls
	and the hundred mouths of a foreign river
	make the land fruitful.
	And where Pieria is, the loveliest,
	the seat of the Muses,
	the holy slope of Olympus:
	take me there, Dionysus, Dionysus,
	leader of the Bacchants, god of the cry.
	There are the Graces,
	there is Desire, and there
	the Bacchants are allowed their rites.
Chorus.
	The god, the son of Zeus,
	is glad at the feast,
	and he loves Peace, the giver of riches,
	the goddess who rears the young.
	To the rich man and to the poorer one alike
	he gives the joy of wine, that has no grief in it.
	And he hates the man who does not care for this:
	to live a life of happiness, by daylight
	and through the dear nights,
	and to keep a wise heart and mind
	clear of men who want too much.
	Whatever the ordinary crowd
	believes and lives by,
	that is good enough for me.

(Pentheus comes out of the house. A Servant arrives with other guards, leading the stranger, whose hands are bound.)

Servant. Pentheus, here we are. We have caught the prey you sent us after, and we did not go out for nothing. But this animal was gentle with us. He did not pull his foot back and run. He held out his hands, and not unwillingly either. He did not go pale. He did not lose the wine colour in his cheeks. He laughed, and told us to tie him up and take him away, and he stood still and made my job easy. I felt ashamed, and I said to him, "Stranger, I am not doing this by choice. Pentheus sent me. These are his orders."

And the Bacchants you locked up, the ones you rounded up and chained in the public prison: they are gone. They are loose, and they are skipping off to the meadows calling on their god Dionysus. The chains fell off their feet by themselves, and the keys turned in the doors without a mortal hand touching them. This man has come to Thebes full of wonders. What happens next is your business.

Pentheus. Let go of his hands. He is in my net now, and he is not so quick that he can get away from me. Well. You are not bad-looking, stranger, not to a woman's eye, which is what you came to Thebes for. That long hair, for one thing, and no wrestler's crop either, spilling down along your cheek, full of longing. And the white skin, carefully kept. You have stayed out of the sun, in the shade, hunting Aphrodite with your good looks. First of all, then, tell me who your people are.

Dionysus. No boasting about it. It is easy to say. You have heard of Tmolus, I expect, the mountain covered in flowers.

Pentheus. I know it. It circles the city of Sardis.

Dionysus. That is where I am from. Lydia is my country.

Pentheus. And why are you bringing these rites into Greece?

Dionysus. Dionysus sent us on our way. The son of Zeus.

Pentheus. Is there some Zeus over there who breeds new gods?

Dionysus. No. The same one who married Semele here.

Pentheus. And did he force this on you at night, in a dream, or with your eyes open?

Dionysus. Face to face. He saw me and I saw him, and he gave me the rites.

Pentheus. These rites of yours. What form do they take?

Dionysus. That may not be spoken to any mortal who is not a Bacchant.

Pentheus. And what good do they do the people who hold them?

Dionysus. It is not lawful for you to hear it. But it is worth knowing.

Pentheus. Nicely faked. Now I want to hear it.

Dionysus. The god's rites hate a man who practises impiety.

Pentheus. You say you saw the god plainly. What was he like?

Dionysus. Whatever he wanted to be like. I did not give the orders.

Pentheus. You have channelled that one round me too, very neatly, and said nothing.

Dionysus. Talk wisdom to an ignorant man, and he will think you a fool.

Pentheus. Is this the first place you have come to, bringing your god?

Dionysus. Every barbarian is dancing these rites already.

Pentheus. Because they have far less sense than Greeks.

Dionysus. In this they have more. Their customs are different, that is all.

Pentheus. These rites of yours. Do you hold them at night, or by day?

Dionysus. At night, mostly. Darkness has a solemnity to it.

Pentheus. Where women are concerned, that is a trick, and a rotten one.

Dionysus. Anyone who wants something shameful can find it in daylight too.

Pentheus. You are going to pay for these dirty clever tricks of yours.

Dionysus. And you for your ignorance, and for insulting the god.
