Pentheus. How bold the Bacchant is. And not out of practice at talking, either.

Dionysus. Tell me what I have to suffer. What is this terrible thing you are going to do to me?

Pentheus. First, I will cut off that soft curl of yours.

Dionysus. The hair is holy. I grow it for the god.

Pentheus. Next, hand over that thyrsus.

Dionysus. Take it from me yourself. It is Dionysus's wand, and I carry it.

Pentheus. And we will keep your body inside, in a cell.

Dionysus. The god himself will set me free, whenever I want.

Pentheus. Yes. When you stand among your Bacchants and call him.

Dionysus. He is close by right now, and he sees what is being done to me.

Pentheus. And where is he? He is not visible to my eyes.

Dionysus. Here, with me. You are godless yourself, so you cannot see him.

Pentheus. Seize him. This man is sneering at me, and at Thebes.

Dionysus. I tell you not to bind me. I have myself in hand, and you do not.

Pentheus. And I say bind him. I have more authority here than you.

Dionysus. You do not know what your life is, or what you are doing, or who you are.

Pentheus. Pentheus, the son of Agave, and my father is Echion.

Dionysus. Pentheus. Grief. You have a name that fits a man about to come to grief.

Pentheus. Go. Lock him up near the horses' stalls, where he can look at nothing but darkness. Dance in there. As for these women you have brought with you, your partners in crime, either we will sell them off, or I will stop their hands from this thumping and this beating on drumskins and keep them as slaves at my looms.

Dionysus. I will go. What is not going to happen, I do not have to suffer. But Dionysus, the god you say does not exist, will come after you to make you pay for these outrages. When you wrong me, it is him you are putting in chains.

(The guards take Dionysus into the house. Pentheus follows.)

Chorus.
	Daughter of Achelous,
	lady Dirce, lovely girl of a river,
	it was in your springs, once,
	that you took the baby of Zeus,
	when Zeus his father snatched him
	out of the deathless fire and hid him in his thigh,
	and shouted this:
	Come, Dithyrambus, child of the double door,
	come into this male womb of mine.
	I show you to Thebes, Bacchic one,
	so that they will call you by this name.
	And you, blessed Dirce,
	you push me away,
	when I come to your banks with my worshippers in garlands.
	Why do you refuse me? Why do you run from me?
	A day is coming, I swear it by the clustered grapes,
	the grace of Dionysus's vine,
	a day is coming when you will care about Dionysus.
Chorus.
	What rage, what rage he shows,
	the breed that came out of the earth,
	Pentheus, sprung from the snake
	that Echion planted, Echion the earth-born,
	a wild-faced monster, not a mortal man,
	a killer, like one of the giants
	who fought the gods.
	He will have me in ropes soon,
	me, who belong to Dionysus,
	and he already has my fellow-worshipper
	inside his house,
	hidden in a dark cell.
	Do you see this, Dionysus, son of Zeus,
	your prophets wrestling with force?
	Come, lord, down from Olympus,
	shaking your gold-faced thyrsus,
	and put a stop to the outrage of a murderous man.
Chorus.
	Where are you, Dionysus? On Nysa,
	that nurses the wild beasts,
	leading your worshippers with the thyrsus,
	or on the Corycian peaks?
	Or perhaps in the deep-wooded
	hollows of Olympus, where once
	Orpheus played his lyre
	and drew the trees together with his music,
	drew the wild beasts of the fields to him.
	Blessed Pieria,
	the god of the cry honours you: he will come
	to dance his revels there,
	and cross the fast-running Axius
	and bring his whirling Maenads,
	and cross the Lydias too,
	the father who gives mortals their wealth,
	the river I have heard
	makes a country of fine horses rich
	with the loveliest of waters.

(The voice of Dionysus is heard from inside the house.)

Dionysus.
	Io.
	Hear my voice, hear it,
	io, Bacchants, io, Bacchants.
Chorus.
	Who is that? Who? Where did it come from,
	the shout that called me up, the shout of the god of the cry?
Dionysus.
	Io, io, I call again,
	the son of Semele, the son of Zeus.
Chorus.
	Io, io, master, master,
	come to us now, to your worshippers,
	Dionysus, Dionysus.
Dionysus.
	Shake the floor of the earth, Lady Earthquake.
Chorus.
	Ah. Ah.
	Soon the house of Pentheus
	will be shaken down in ruins.
	Dionysus is in the house.
	Worship him. We worship him, oh.
	Did you see the stone lintels
	on the pillars there, splitting apart?
	Dionysus is shouting his victory inside the roof.

Dionysus. Light the blazing torch of the lightning. Burn, burn down the house of Pentheus.

Chorus.
	Ah. Ah.
	Do you not see the fire? Do you not see it,
	round the holy tomb of Semele,
	the flame the thunderbolt of Zeus
	left there when it struck her?
	Throw your trembling bodies on the ground,
	throw them down, Maenads. The lord
	is coming against this house
	and turning it upside down,
	the son of Zeus.

(The women fall to the ground. Dionysus comes out of the ruined house, unbound.)

Dionysus. Barbarian women, are you so struck with fear that you have fallen to the ground? You felt Dionysus shake the house of Pentheus, it seems. Get up. Lift yourselves and take heart, and let the trembling go out of your flesh.

Chorus. Greatest light of our joyful worship, how glad I am to see you. I was alone, and I had nobody.

Dionysus. Did you lose heart when I was taken inside, on my way to fall into Pentheus's dark cells?

Chorus. How could I not? Who was there to protect me if something happened to you? But how did you get free, after falling into that godless man's hands?

Dionysus. I saved myself. Easily. No trouble at all.

Chorus. Did he not tie your hands together in knotted ropes?

Dionysus. That was exactly where I made a fool of him. He thought he was tying me up, and he never touched me, never laid a hand on me. He was feeding on hope. He found a bull by the stalls where he had taken me to lock me up, and it was the bull he threw his ropes round, knees and hooves, panting out his rage, sweat dripping off his body, biting his lips with his teeth. And I sat quietly close by and watched.

In the middle of this Dionysus came and shook the house and lit a fire on his mother's tomb. When Pentheus saw it, he thought the house was burning, and he ran this way and that, shouting to the slaves to bring water, and every slave in the place was hard at work, and all for nothing. Then he dropped that job, since I had escaped, snatched up a dark sword and rushed into the house. And then Dionysus, this is how it looked to me, I am only giving you my opinion, made a phantom of me in the courtyard. Pentheus went for it. He charged and stabbed at the bright air, as if he were cutting my throat. And on top of this, Dionysus did him other damage. He brought the house down to the ground. It lies in ruins, all of it. Pentheus has seen what my chains cost: they turned out very bitter for him. Worn out, he has dropped his sword and gone limp. He is a man, and he had the nerve to go into battle against a god.

I walked quietly out of the house and here I am with you, and Pentheus does not worry me at all. I think, I can hear a boot inside the house, anyway, that he will be out at the front any moment. What on earth is he going to say after all this? I will take him easily, even if he comes out breathing hard. A clever man keeps his temper in hand.

(Pentheus comes out of the house.)

Pentheus. Something terrible has happened to me. The stranger has got away, the one I had in chains a minute ago. Ah. Ah. There he is. What is this? How are you out here, standing in front of my house? How did you get outside?

Dionysus. Stand still. Set your anger down and walk quietly.

Pentheus. How did you slip your chains and get out here?

Dionysus. Did I not say, or were you not listening, that someone would set me free?

Pentheus. Who? You keep bringing in new stories.

Dionysus. The one who grows the clustering vine for mortals.

Dionysus. You meant that as an insult. It is Dionysus's glory.

Pentheus. I order every tower in the wall shut fast, all the way round.

Dionysus. What for? Do gods not climb over walls too?

Pentheus. Clever. You are very clever, except in the one thing you ought to be clever in.

Dionysus. In the thing that matters most, I was born clever. But first listen to this man and hear what he has to say. He has come from the mountain with news for you. I will wait for you. I am not going to run.

(A Messenger comes in, a herdsman down from the mountain.)

Messenger. Pentheus, ruler of this land of Thebes, I have come from Cithaeron, where the bright falls of white snow never let go.

Pentheus. And what is this urgent news you have come to bring?

Messenger. I have seen the holy Bacchants, the women who shot out of this country like arrows, white legs flying, stung mad, and I have come to tell you and the city, my lord, that they are doing terrible things, things beyond wonder. But I want to hear first whether I should tell you freely what is happening up there, or trim my story. I am afraid of the quickness of your mind, my lord, and your sharp temper, and too much of the king in you.

Pentheus. Speak. Whatever you say, you will go unpunished by me. It is wrong to be angry with people who do right. And the more terrible the things you tell me about the Bacchants, the harder I will make this man pay, the one who taught the women their tricks.

Messenger. The herds of grazing cattle were just climbing up towards the high ground, the calves with them, at the hour when the sun sends out its rays and warms the earth. And I see three companies of women dancers. Autonoe led one, your mother Agave the second, and Ino the third. They were all asleep, their bodies gone slack, some leaning their backs against the foliage of a pine, others with their heads dropped anyhow on the oak leaves on the ground. Decently. Not as you say: drunk on the wine-bowl and the noise of the pipe, hunting Aphrodite alone through the woods.

Your mother heard the lowing of the horned cattle, and she stood up in the middle of the Bacchants and gave the cry, to get their bodies moving out of sleep. And they threw the fresh sleep off their eyes and sprang upright, a marvel of good order to look at: young women, old women, and girls still unyoked, unmarried. First they let their hair down over their shoulders, and those whose fawnskins had come loose at the knots fastened them up again, and belted the dappled hides with snakes that licked their cheeks. Some of them held a fawn, or the wild cubs of wolves, in their arms and gave them white milk: the ones who had left new babies at home and whose breasts were still swollen. They put on garlands of ivy and oak and flowering bryony. One took a thyrsus and struck it against a rock, and a dewy stream of water leapt out of it. Another set her wand down against the ground, and there the god sent up a spring of wine for her. Whoever wanted the white drink scraped the earth with the tips of her fingers and had milk in streams; and from the ivy on the thyrsus-wands sweet rivers of honey dripped. If you had been there and seen this, the god you are abusing now, you would have gone to him with prayers.

We herdsmen and shepherds came together to argue about it, trading talk about the terrible, wonderful things they were doing. And one man, a wanderer about the town with a practised tongue, said to all of us: "You who live on the holy uplands of the mountains, what do you say? Shall we hunt Agave, Pentheus's mother, out of her revels, and do the king a favour?" We thought he talked sense, and we lay in ambush, hiding ourselves in the leaves of the bushes. At the appointed hour they began to shake the thyrsus for the revels, calling with one voice on the son of Zeus, calling him Iacchus, calling him Dionysus, and the whole mountain went mad along with them, and the wild animals with it, and nothing stood still: everything was running. Agave happened to come leaping past close to me, and I jumped out, wanting to grab her, and left the thicket where I had hidden myself empty. And she screamed: "My running hounds! We are being hunted, by these men. Follow me, follow me, with your thyrsus-wands for weapons in your hands."

We ran, and we got away from being torn to pieces by the Bacchants. But they went for the heifers that were grazing the grass, with no iron in their hands. You could have seen one woman holding a young cow, fat with milk, bellowing, and tearing it in two with her bare hands. Others were ripping full-grown cows apart, piece from piece. You would have seen ribs, or a cloven hoof, flung up and down; they hung in the pine branches, dripping, smeared with blood. Bulls, the arrogant ones who had done all their fighting with their horns before, stumbled forward onto the ground, dragged down by ten thousand girls' hands. The coat of flesh was pulled off them faster than you could close your royal eyes.

Then they were off, like birds rising into flight, over the low plains that grow the fine Theban corn along the streams of the Asopus; and they fell on Hysiae and Erythrae, the towns that lie down below the crag of Cithaeron, like an enemy army, and turned everything upside down. They snatched children out of the houses. Whatever they put on their shoulders stayed there without being tied and did not fall to the black ground, not bronze, not iron. They carried fire in their hair and it did not burn them. The townspeople, in a rage at being plundered by Bacchants, ran for their weapons, and that, my lord, was the terrible thing to see. The men's pointed spears drew no blood, but the women threw their thyrsus-wands from their hands and wounded them, and turned them, and put them to flight. Women did that to men. Not without some god's help. Then they went back to where they had started from, to the very springs the god had sent up for them, and washed off the blood, and snakes licked the drops off their cheeks with their tongues and made their skin clean.

So whoever this god is, master, receive him into this city. He is great in other ways, and they say this too of him, as I hear it: that he gave mortals the vine that puts an end to grief. And where there is no wine there is no Aphrodite either, and nothing else that gives human beings any pleasure.

Chorus. I am afraid to speak freely in front of the king, but it will be said all the same: Dionysus is second to none of the gods.

Pentheus. It is close now, this outrage of the Bacchants, catching like fire, a great disgrace to us in the eyes of the Greeks. No time for hesitating. Go to the Electran gates. Order out every man who carries a shield, and the riders of the fast horses, and everyone who swings a light shield and plucks a bowstring with his hand. We are marching against the Bacchants. It is past all bearing, if we are to suffer what we are suffering at the hands of women.

Dionysus. You hear my words, Pentheus, and you take in none of them. You have treated me badly, and still I say it: you should not take up arms against a god. Keep still. Dionysus will not stand for you driving his Bacchants off the mountains where they cry his name.

Pentheus. Do not lecture me. You escaped your chains; be content with that. Or shall I turn the punishment back on you?

Dionysus. I would sacrifice to him, rather than kick against the goad in a temper, a mortal against a god.

Pentheus. Sacrifice? I will. A slaughter of women, which is what they deserve, and plenty of it, in the folds of Cithaeron.

Dionysus. You will all run. And it will be a disgrace, bronze shields turning tail from the thyrsus-wands of Bacchants.

Pentheus. There is no getting anywhere with this stranger I am tangled up with. Whatever is done to him, whatever he does, he will not be quiet.

Dionysus. My friend, there is still a way to set all this right.

Pentheus. Doing what? Being a slave to my own slaves?

Dionysus. I will bring the women here, without any weapons.

Pentheus. Oh. Now you are working some trick against me.

Dionysus. What kind of trick, if I want to save you with my skills?

Pentheus. You made this agreement together, so you can go on with your revels forever.

Dionysus. I did make an agreement, that is true. With the god.

Pentheus. Bring my armour out here. And you, stop talking.

Dionysus. Ah. Would you like to see them, sitting together up in the mountains?

Pentheus. Very much. I would give a great weight of gold for it.

Dionysus. Why have you fallen into such a passion for that?

Pentheus. It would pain me to see them drunk.

Dionysus. And yet you would gladly see what pains you?

Pentheus. Yes. Be sure of it. Sitting quietly under the pines.

Dionysus. But they will track you down, even if you come secretly.

Pentheus. Then openly. You are right about that.

Dionysus. Shall I lead you, then? Will you take the road?

Pentheus. Lead me. As fast as you can. I resent every minute you waste.

Dionysus. Then put on a dress of fine linen.

Pentheus. What? Am I to stop being a man and be counted among the women?

Dionysus. So they do not kill you, if you are seen there as a man.

Pentheus. Right again. You have been clever all along.

Dionysus. Dionysus taught me all of it.

Pentheus. So how is this good advice of yours to be carried out?

Dionysus. I will go inside the house and dress you.

Pentheus. Dress me in what? A woman's dress? No. Shame stops me.

Dionysus. Then you are not so eager to watch the Maenads any more.

Pentheus. What dress is it you say you would put on my body?

Dionysus. I will spread long hair over your head.

Pentheus. And the second piece of my outfit?

Dionysus. A robe down to your feet, and a headband round your hair.

Pentheus. And will you add anything else to these?

Dionysus. A thyrsus for your hand, and a spotted fawnskin.

Pentheus. I could not put on a woman's dress.

Dionysus. Then you will shed blood, if you fight the Bacchants.

Pentheus. True. First I must go and spy.

Dionysus. Cleverer, anyway, than hunting evil with evil.

Pentheus. And how will I get through the city without the Thebans seeing me?

Dionysus. We will go by empty roads. I will lead you.

Pentheus. Anything is better than having the Bacchants laugh at me. We will go into the house, and I will decide what seems best.

Dionysus. You may. Whatever you decide, I am ready for it.

Pentheus. I will go in. Either I march with my armour on, or I follow your advice.

(Pentheus goes into the house.)

Dionysus. Women, the man is walking into the net. He will go to the Bacchants, and there he will pay the penalty with his death. Dionysus, now it is your work. You are not far off. Let us punish him. First, drive him out of his mind: put a light madness into him. In his right mind he will never agree to put on a woman's dress; driven out of his senses, he will put it on. And I want him laughed at by the Thebans, led through the city in a woman's shape, after those threats of his that made him so terrible before. Now I am going in to dress Pentheus in the costume he will wear down to Hades, slaughtered by his mother's hands. He will come to know the son of Zeus, Dionysus, who is a god in the fullest sense: most terrible, and to human beings most gentle.

(Dionysus goes into the house after him.)

Chorus.
	Will I ever, in the all-night dances,
	set my white foot
	to the beat of the god, and throw back
	my throat to the dewy air,
	like a fawn playing
	in the green joys of a meadow
	when it has escaped the terror of the hunt,
	clear of the watchers,
	over the well-woven nets,
	and the huntsman shouting
	drives his hounds to run harder,
	and she, straining, fast as a gale,
	leaps along the plain
	beside the river, glad
	of the places empty of men
	and the young shoots of the shadowy wood?
	What is cleverness? What finer gift
	do the gods give to mortals
	than to hold a hand that is stronger
	over the heads of your enemies?
	What is fine is loved forever.
Chorus.
	The strength of the gods moves slowly,
	but it is sure, all the same.
	It straightens out those mortals
	who honour their own stupidity
	and do not, in their mad conceit,
	make the things of the gods greater.
	The gods have many ways of hiding
	the long foot of time,
	and they hunt the godless man down.
	Never know, never practise
	anything stronger than the laws.
	It costs little to believe
	that whatever the divine is, it has power,
	and that what has been law through long time
	is law forever, and rooted in nature.
	What is cleverness? What finer gift
	do the gods give to mortals
	than to hold a hand that is stronger
	over the heads of your enemies?
	What is fine is loved forever.
Chorus.
	Happy the man who has run from a storm at sea
	and reached the harbour.
	Happy the man who has got above his troubles.
	In one way or another each man
	passes another in wealth or power.
	And there are hopes, ten thousand of them,
	for ten thousand men: some of them
	end in wealth for mortals,
	and some go nowhere.
	But the man whose life is happy
	day by day: that man I call blessed.

(Dionysus comes out of the house.)

Dionysus. You there, the man so eager to see what he should not see, so hot for what nobody should chase, I mean you, Pentheus: come out in front of the house. Let me look at you, in the costume of a woman, a Maenad, a Bacchant, a spy on your mother and her company.

(Pentheus comes out of the house, dressed as a woman.)

You look exactly like one of Cadmus's daughters.

Pentheus. Look. I think I see two suns, and two Thebes, two cities with seven gates. And you seem to be a bull walking ahead of me, and horns seem to have grown on your head. Were you an animal before? You certainly are a bull now.

Dionysus. The god is walking with us. He was not kind before; now he is on our side. Now you see what you should see.

Pentheus. So how do I look? Do I not stand just the way Ino stands, or Agave, my own mother?

Dionysus. Looking at you, I think I am seeing them. But this curl of yours has slipped out of place, not the way I set it under your headband.

Pentheus. Inside, I was tossing it forward and back, shaking my head and playing the Bacchant, and I shook it out of its place.

Dionysus. Then I will put it back in place. Looking after you is my business now. Hold your head up.

Pentheus. There. You dress me. I have handed myself over to you.

Dionysus. Your belt has come loose, and the pleats of your gown are not hanging straight all the way down to your ankles.

Pentheus. I think so too, at least by my right foot. On this side the robe sits properly along the back of my heel.

Dionysus. You will count me the first of your friends, I think, when you see the Bacchants behaving decently, against everything you expected.

Pentheus. Should I take the thyrsus in my right hand, or this one, to look more like a Bacchant?

Dionysus. In the right hand, and you lift it at the same moment as your right foot. I am glad your mind has changed.

Pentheus. Could I carry the glens of Cithaeron on my shoulders, Bacchants and all?

Dionysus. You could, if you wanted to. The mind you had before was not sound. Now you have the mind you ought to have.

Pentheus. Shall we bring levers? Or shall I tear them up with my hands, putting a shoulder or an arm under the peaks?

Dionysus. Do not wreck the shrines of the Nymphs, or the places where Pan sits and plays his pipes.

Pentheus. Well said. Women are not to be beaten by strength. I will hide myself in the pines.

Dionysus. You will be hidden in the hiding place you have earned, coming as a treacherous spy on the Maenads.

Pentheus. Yes. I imagine them in the thickets like birds, held in the sweetest grip of their lovemaking.

Dionysus. And that is exactly what you are being sent out to watch for. Perhaps you will catch them. If you are not caught first.

Pentheus. Take me through the middle of Thebes. I am the only man of them with the nerve for this.

Dionysus. You alone wear yourself out for this city, you alone. So the struggle waiting for you is the one you had coming. Follow me. I am your escort and I will bring you there safely. Someone else will bring you back.

Pentheus. My mother, you mean.

Dionysus. And every eye will be on you.

Pentheus. That is what I am going for.

Dionysus. You will come home carried.

Pentheus. You are promising me luxury.

Dionysus. In your mother's arms.

Pentheus. You will force me to be spoiled.

Dionysus. Spoiling of a kind.

Pentheus. I am laying my hands on what I deserve.

Dionysus. You are terrible. Terrible, and the suffering you are walking into is terrible, and out of it you will find a fame that stands up as high as heaven. Reach out your hands, Agave, and you too, her sisters, the daughters of Cadmus. I am taking this young man to a great contest, and the winner will be me, and Dionysus. The rest the thing itself will show.

(Dionysus leads Pentheus away towards the mountain.)

Chorus.
	Go, fast hounds of Madness, go to the mountain,
	where the daughters of Cadmus hold their company,
	and sting them into a rage
	against the man in a woman's dress,
	the raving spy on the Maenads.
	His mother will be the first to see him,
	from a smooth rock or a broken stump,
	watching them, and she will call out to the Maenads:
	Who is this who has come to the mountain,
	to the mountain, Bacchants, hunting for
	the mountain-running women of Thebes? Who bore him?
	He was not born out of a woman's
	blood. He is the offspring of some lioness,
	or of the Gorgons of Libya.
	Let Justice go out where all can see her, let her go with a sword,
	killing him straight through the throat,
	the godless, lawless, unjust son
	of Echion, born out of the earth.
Chorus.
	The man who with an unjust mind and a lawless temper
	sets out against your rites, Dionysus,
	and your mother's, with a maddened heart
	and a wrecked purpose,
	meaning to master by force what cannot be mastered:
	death takes those plans in hand
	and listens to no excuses,
	where the business of the gods is concerned.
	To live the way a mortal lives is a life without pain.
	I do not grudge anyone cleverness.
	I am glad to go hunting the other things,
	the great ones, the plain ones: to let a life run
	towards what is fine, to be clean
	and worship, day and night,
	to throw out the customs that lie outside justice,
	and to honour the gods.
	Let Justice go out where all can see her, let her go with a sword,
	killing him straight through the throat,
	the godless, lawless, unjust son
	of Echion, born out of the earth.
Chorus.
	Show yourself as a bull, or a snake with many heads
	to look at, or a lion breathing fire.
	Come, Dionysus, with a laughing face
	throw the noose of death
	round the hunter of the Bacchants
	as he goes down under the herd of Maenads.

(A Second Messenger comes down from the mountain.)

Second Messenger. House that was fortunate once in all Greece, house of the old man from Sidon, who sowed the earth-born crop of the snake in this ground: how I groan for you. I am a slave, but even so, a good slave takes his masters' troubles for his own.

Chorus. What is it? Do you have news from the Bacchants?

Second Messenger. Pentheus is dead. Echion's son.

Chorus. Lord Dionysus, you are showing yourself a great god.

Second Messenger. What are you saying? What was that? Are you glad, woman, when things go badly for my masters?

Chorus.
	I am a stranger here and I shout for joy in a foreign song.
	I do not cower in fear of chains any more.
Second Messenger.
	And do you think Thebes is so short of men?
Chorus.
	Dionysus, Dionysus, not Thebes,
	has the power over me.

Second Messenger. You can be forgiven. But it is not right, women, to be glad about things as evil as this, once they have actually been done.

Chorus. Tell me. Say it. What kind of death did he die, the unjust man who did unjust things?

Second Messenger. We left the farms of Theban country behind and crossed the streams of the Asopus, and started up the crags of Cithaeron, Pentheus and I, for I was following my master, and the stranger who was guiding us to the show. First we sat down in a grassy hollow, keeping our feet quiet and our tongues quiet, so that we could see without being seen. There was a gorge with cliffs on both sides of it, running with water, shaded over with pines, and there the Maenads were sitting with their hands busy at work they enjoyed. Some of them were binding a worn-out thyrsus and making it leafy with ivy again. Others, like colts let out of the painted yoke, were singing Bacchic music back and forth to each other. And poor Pentheus, who could not see the crowd of women, said this: "Stranger, from where we are standing I cannot reach these fake Maenads with my eyes. But up on the bank, if I climbed a pine with a high neck to it, I could see the Maenads and their filthy business properly."

And then I saw the stranger do a marvellous thing. He took hold of the topmost branch of a pine, high up in the sky, and pulled it down, and down, and down to the black ground. It curved like a bow, or like a wheel whose curve a compass draws round in a circle. That is how the stranger dragged the mountain branch down with his hands and bent it to the earth, doing work that is no mortal's work. He set Pentheus on the pine boughs, and let the trunk go straight back up through his hands, steadily, taking care not to throw him off, and it stood upright into the upright sky with my master sitting on its back.

He was seen more than he saw. He had hardly come into view up there when the stranger was nowhere to be seen at all, and out of the sky a voice, Dionysus, I suppose, shouted: "Young women, I bring you the man who made a laughing-stock of you, and of me, and of my rites. Punish him." And as he was saying it, a light of holy fire stood fixed between the sky and the ground. The air went silent. The wooded glen held its leaves silent. You would not have heard an animal's voice. The women had not caught the sound clearly with their ears, and they stood up straight and turned their eyes this way and that. He called again. And when the daughters of Cadmus recognised the clear command of Dionysus, they shot forward, as fast as doves, running on straining feet: his mother Agave, her sisters born of the same womb, and all the Bacchants. Through the torrent gorge, over the broken rocks, they went leaping, mad with the god's breath in them.

When they saw my master sitting up in the pine, first they climbed a rock that stood opposite it like a tower and began throwing stones at him, hard enough to smash him, and they threw pine branches at him like javelins, and others sent their thyrsus-wands flying through the air at Pentheus, a miserable target. But they were not getting there. The poor man was sitting at a height above their eagerness, trapped, with nothing he could do. In the end they smashed oak branches down like lightning and began to prise the roots up with levers that were not iron. When all that work came to nothing, Agave said: "Come, Maenads, stand round in a circle and take hold of the trunk, so we can catch the beast that has climbed up there, and stop him telling anyone about the god's secret dances." They put ten thousand hands on the pine and tore it up out of the earth, and down from his high seat, all that way to the ground, Pentheus fell, with ten thousand cries out of him, because he was close enough to the evil now to understand it.

His mother began the killing, as the priestess of it, and fell on him. He threw the headband off his hair, so that poor Agave might recognise him and not kill him, and he touched her cheek and said: "It is me, mother. I am your son. Pentheus. The one you bore in Echion's house. Pity me, mother. Do not kill your own child because of my mistakes." But she was foaming at the mouth, rolling her eyes round in her head, not thinking what she ought to have thought, and Dionysus had hold of her, and Pentheus did not persuade her. She took his left arm at the wrist, and set her foot against the wretched man's ribs, and tore his shoulder out. Not by her own strength: the god put the ease into her hands. Ino was working on the other side of him, ripping the flesh open, and Autonoe, and the whole crowd of Bacchants were pressing in. Every kind of noise at once: Pentheus groaning for as long as he had breath left in him, the women shrieking in triumph. One of them was carrying an arm. Another had a foot with the boot still on it. His ribs were stripped bare by the tearing. And every one of them, with blood all over her hands, was tossing Pentheus's flesh about like a ball.

His body lies in pieces in different places, some of it under the hard rocks, some in the deep leaves of the wood, and it will not be an easy thing to look for. His poor head: his mother happened to take that in her hands, and she has fixed it on the point of a thyrsus, and she is carrying it through the middle of Cithaeron like the head of a mountain lion, leaving her sisters behind in the Maenads' dances. She is coming inside these walls, glorying in her disastrous hunt, calling on Dionysus, her fellow huntsman, her partner in the chase, the winner, the beautiful winner. And the victory she wins in his service is tears.

As for me, I am getting out of the way of this disaster before Agave reaches the house. To keep yourself in hand, and to reverence what belongs to the gods, is the finest thing there is; and I think it is the cleverest thing a mortal can own, for anyone who uses it.

(The Second Messenger goes back towards the mountain, away from the house.)

Chorus.
	Let us dance for Dionysus,
	let us shout out what has happened
	to Pentheus, the snake's descendant,
	who put on a woman's clothes
	and took up the fennel wand, the fine thyrsus,
	which was death, and could be trusted to be death,
	with a bull walking ahead of him into disaster.
	Bacchants of Thebes,
	you have made your famous victory
	end in groaning, and in tears.
	A fine contest: to close a hand
	dripping with blood round your own son.

Chorus. But I can see Pentheus's mother Agave hurrying towards the house, with her eyes rolling in her head. Welcome the reveller of the god of the cry.

(Agave comes in, carrying the head of Pentheus on a thyrsus.)

Agave. Bacchants of Asia.

Chorus. Why do you call me out? Oh.

Agave.
	I am bringing home from the mountain
	a fresh-cut tendril to the house.
	A blessed catch.
Chorus.
	I see it. I will take you in as a fellow reveller.
Agave.
	I caught him without any snares:
	the young cub of a wild lion.
	Look at him.
Chorus.
	Out of what wilderness?
Agave.
	Cithaeron.
Chorus.
	Cithaeron?
Agave.
	Killed him.
Chorus.
	Who struck him first?
Agave.
	Mine was the first honour.
	Blessed Agave, they call me in the company.
Chorus.
	Who else?
Agave.
	Cadmus's.
Chorus.
	Cadmus's what?
Agave.
	Children. After me, after me,
	they got their hands on this animal.
	This was a lucky hunt.
Agave.
	Take your share of the feast, then.
Chorus.
	Share it? Share it, you poor woman?
Agave.
	The bull is young. The down
	is only just coming up on his cheek
	under the soft-haired crest of his head.
Chorus.
	Yes, the hair is like a wild animal's.
Agave.
	Dionysus, the clever huntsman,
	cleverly set the Maenads on
	to this beast.
Chorus.
	Our lord is a hunter.
Agave.
	Do you praise me?
Chorus.
	I praise you.
Agave.
	And soon the Thebans.
Chorus.
	And your son Pentheus too.
Agave.
	Will praise his mother
	for taking this lion of a catch.
Chorus.
	Extraordinary.
Agave.
	Extraordinarily taken.
Chorus.
	Are you proud of it?
Agave.
	I am delighted.
	Great things, great things,
	and plain for anyone to see, done in this hunt.

Chorus. Then show the citizens, poor woman, the prize you have brought home in victory.

Agave. You who live in the fine-towered city of Thebes, come and see this catch, the animal we hunted down, we the daughters of Cadmus. Not with the looped javelins of Thessaly, not with nets, but with the sharp tips of our own white arms. And after that, why should men boast, and buy the spear-makers' tools for nothing? We took him with our own bare hands, and we pulled the beast's joints apart. Where is my old father? Let him come here. And where is my son Pentheus? Let him take a ladder, and put it up against the house, and climb it, so he can nail this lion's head to the beam, the head I have come home from hunting.

(Cadmus comes in. Slaves follow him, carrying the pieces of Pentheus's body on a bier.)

Cadmus. Follow me. Carry the miserable weight that is Pentheus, follow me, slaves, and set it down in front of the house. I am bringing his body here, worn out with searching a thousand times over. I found it in the folds of Cithaeron, torn to pieces, no two parts of it in the same place, lying in woodland where nothing is easy to find. I heard what my daughters had dared to do when I was already back inside the city walls with old Teiresias, coming home from the Bacchants. So I turned round and went back up the mountain, and here I am bringing home my child, killed by Maenads. I saw Autonoe, the woman who once bore Actaeon to Aristaeus, and Ino with her, still in the thickets, still stung out of their minds, poor creatures. And somebody told me Agave was coming this way with her Bacchic step. What I heard was true. I can see her, and it is not a happy sight.

Agave. Father, you have the greatest boast in the world to make: that you fathered daughters who are by a long way the best of all mortal women. I mean all of us, and myself most of all. I left my shuttle at the loom and went on to greater things: catching wild animals with my two hands. And here in my arms, as you can see, I am carrying the prize I won, to be hung up on your house. Take it, father, take it in your hands. Be proud of what I hunted, and call your friends to a feast, because you are blessed. Blessed, now that we have done this.

Cadmus. Grief past all measuring, and I cannot bear to look at it: a murder, done by miserable hands. This is the fine victim you have brought down for the gods, and it is on this that you are inviting Thebes and me to a banquet. Oh. Your trouble first, and then my own. The god has destroyed us justly, and much too far: Lord Dionysus, who was born into our own family.

Agave. How bad-tempered old age is in a man, and how sour in the face. I hope my son turns out a good hunter, and takes after his mother's ways, when he goes after wild animals with the young men of Thebes. But all he can do is fight with the gods. You must have a word with him, father. Somebody call him here where I can see him, so he can see how lucky I am.

Cadmus. Ah. Ah. When you understand what you have done, you will suffer a terrible pain. If you stayed in the state you are in now, right through to the end, you would not be fortunate, but you would not think you were unfortunate either.

Agave. What is wrong with any of this? What is there in it to be sad about?

Cadmus. First lift your eyes up to this sky.

Agave. There. Why did you tell me to look at it?

Cadmus. Is it still the same, or does it seem to you to have changed?

Agave. It is brighter than it was before, and clearer.

Cadmus. And that fluttering in your mind. Is it still there?

Agave. I do not know that word of yours. But somehow I am coming to my senses. Something has shifted out of the mind I had before.

Cadmus. Can you hear me, then, and answer me clearly?

Agave. Yes. I have forgotten what we said before, father.

Cadmus. Whose house did you come to when you married?

Agave. You gave me to Echion, they say. One of the Sown Men.

Cadmus. And what son was born in that house to your husband?

Agave. Pentheus. From me and his father together.

Cadmus. Then whose face is it you are holding in your arms?

Agave. A lion's. That is what the women who hunted him said.

Cadmus. Look at it properly, then. It takes very little effort to see.

Agave. Ah. What am I looking at? What is this I am carrying in my hands?

Cadmus. Look hard at it. Learn it more clearly.

Agave. I see the greatest grief there is. I am ruined.

Cadmus. Does it still look like a lion to you?

Agave. No. It is Pentheus's head I am holding, and I am the most miserable woman alive.

Cadmus. Yes, and it was mourned over before ever you recognised it.

Agave. Who killed him? How did he come into my hands?

Cadmus. Miserable truth, what a moment you have picked to arrive.

Agave. Say it. My heart is jumping at what is coming.

Cadmus. You killed him. You and your sisters.

Agave. Where did he die? At home? In what place?

Cadmus. Where the dogs once shared Actaeon out between them.

Agave. And why did the poor man go to Cithaeron?

Cadmus. He went to mock the god, and to mock your worship.

Agave. And how did we come to be up there?

Cadmus. You went mad. The whole city was raving with the god.

Agave. Dionysus destroyed us. I understand it now.

Cadmus. Outrage was done to him. You would not count him a god.

Agave. And my child's body, father, the dearest body there is. Where is it?

Cadmus. I hunted it out. It was hard. I have brought it here.

Agave. Is all of it fitted properly together, joint into joint?

Agave. And what part did Pentheus have in my foolishness?

Cadmus. He was the same as you. He would not reverence the god. And so the god joined us all together in one ruin, you and him alike, and destroyed this house, and me with it. I had no sons of my own, and now I see this shoot of your womb, poor woman, killed in the most shameful and the ugliest way there is. You were the eye the house looked out of. You held my roof together, child, my daughter's son, and the city was afraid of you. Nobody who saw your face wanted to insult the old man, because you would have given him the punishment he deserved. And now I will be thrown out of my own house without honour: Cadmus the great, who sowed the people of Thebes and reaped the finest crop there ever was. Dearest of men, and even now you are gone I still count you among the dearest, child, you will never again put your hand to my chin and hold me and call me your mother's father and say: "Who is wronging you, old man? Who is dishonouring you? Who is upsetting your heart and giving you trouble? Tell me, father, so that I can punish the man who wrongs you." Now I am wretched, and you have suffered, and your mother is pitiful, and your aunts have suffered too. If there is anybody who looks down on the gods, let him look at this man's death and believe in them.

Chorus. I am sorry for your part in it, Cadmus. Your daughter's son has the punishment he deserved, and it is a hard one for you.

Agave. Father, you can see for yourself how far everything of mine has been turned upside down.

(Dionysus appears above the ruined house, no longer disguised.)

Dionysus. Cadmus, hear what is left for you. You will change your shape and become a snake, and your wife will be turned into an animal and take the form of a serpent: Harmonia, the daughter of Ares, whom you married while you were a mortal man. You will drive a wagon of oxen, with your wife beside you, at the head of a barbarian army. That is what the oracle of Zeus says. You will sack many cities with a force nobody can count. And when they plunder the oracle of Apollo, they will have a miserable journey home. But Ares will rescue you and Harmonia, and settle your life in the land of the blessed. I say this as Dionysus, and my father was no mortal. I was born from Zeus. If you had learned to keep yourselves in hand when you refused to, you would have had the son of Zeus for an ally, and you would be happy now.

Cadmus. Dionysus, we beg you. We were wrong.

Dionysus. You learned what I am too late. When you should have known it, you did not.

Cadmus. We understand that now. But you are coming after us too hard.

Dionysus. I am a god by birth, and you did me outrage.

Cadmus. Gods should not be like mortals in their anger.

Dionysus. My father Zeus nodded to all this long ago.

Agave. Aiai. It is decided, old man. Exile, and misery in it.

Dionysus. Then why put off what has to happen?

Cadmus. Child, what a terrible evil we have all come to: you, poor girl, and your sisters, and me. I will go to a foreign country, an old man living among strangers. And there is more foretold for me: that I will bring a mixed barbarian army into Greece. I will lead them under arms, with Harmonia beside me, the daughter of Ares, my wife, with the wild nature of a serpent on her, and I a serpent myself, against the altars and the tombs of Greece. I will never have any rest from my troubles. Not even when I have sailed down the Acheron will I be at peace.

Agave. Father, and I will go into exile without you.

Cadmus. Why do you put your arms round me, poor child, like a young swan round its useless grey-feathered parent?

Agave. Where am I to turn, thrown out of my own country?

Cadmus. I do not know, child. Your father is a poor ally.

Agave.
	Goodbye, house. Goodbye, city
	of my fathers. I am leaving you in disaster,
	an exile out of my own room.
Cadmus.
	Go now, child, to the country of Aristaeus.
Agave.
	I grieve for you, father.
Cadmus.
	And I for you, child,
	and I have wept for your sisters.
Agave.
	Terribly, terribly has lord Dionysus
	carried this humiliation
	into your house.
Dionysus.
	Yes, because I suffered terribly at your hands.
	My name had no honour in Thebes.
Agave.
	Goodbye, father.
Cadmus.
	Goodbye, my miserable
	daughter. You will not easily come to any good.
Agave.
	Take me, escorts, to where I can find
	my sisters, my pitiable companions in exile.
	Let me come somewhere
	where filthy Cithaeron cannot see me,
	and my eyes cannot see Cithaeron,
	and where no thyrsus stands as a memorial.
	Let those be some other Bacchant's business.

(Agave goes out one way, Cadmus the other. Dionysus is gone from above the house.)

Chorus.
	Many are the shapes of what the gods do,
	and many the things they bring about that no one expected.
	What we counted on did not happen,
	and for what no one counted on, a god found a way.
	That is how this business ended.

Iphigenia at Aulis (405 BC)

Iphigenia at Aulis

(Night, on the beach at Aulis, in front of Agamemnon's tent. The Greek fleet lies drawn up along the shore. Agamemnon comes out carrying a folding writing tablet and a lamp.)

Agamemnon. Leda, the daughter of Thestius, had three girls: Phoebe, and Clytemnestra, who is my wife, and Helen. And it was Helen the young men of Greece came courting, the ones who had had the best of life so far. There were terrible threats between them, and blood, each one of them ready to kill the rest if he did not get the girl. Her father Tyndareus could see no way through it. Give her, do not give her, how to take hold of his luck and come off best. And then this came to him. The suitors should swear oaths to one another, and clasp right hands, and pour offerings over a burnt sacrifice, and bind themselves with this curse: whichever of them got Tyndareus's daughter for a wife, they would all stand by that man, if anybody ever took her out of his house and went off with her and pushed the husband out of his own bed. They would march against that man in armour and level his city to the ground, Greek or barbarian, it would make no difference. And once they had given their word — and the old man had come at them well, and worked round them with a shrewd mind — he let his daughter choose one of the suitors for herself, whichever one the sweet breezes of Aphrodite carried her toward.

And she chose. I wish to god he had never taken her. She chose Menelaus. And then out of Phrygia came the man who judged between the goddesses, Paris, the way the story runs among the Argives, and he came to Sparta: flowering in his clothes, a blaze of gold on him, barbarian luxury. He was in love with her and she was in love with him, and he snatched her up and was gone with her to the cattle pens of Ida, and he took his moment while Menelaus was away from home. And Menelaus went running the length of Greece like a beast with a sting in it, calling Tyndareus's old oath to witness, saying they were bound to help a man who had been wronged.

So the Greeks came at it with the spear. They took up their armour and came here, to the narrow water at Aulis, with ships and shields together, with plenty of horses and chariots. And they picked me to be general, and they did it for Menelaus's sake, because I am his brother. I wish somebody else had picked up that honour instead of me.

Then, with the army gathered and standing together, we sat here at Aulis and could not sail. We were at a loss, and Calchas the prophet told us this: sacrifice Iphigenia, my own daughter, to Artemis, who lives in this country. If we sacrificed her, we would sail and we would tear the Phrygians' city down; if we did not sacrifice her, none of it would happen. And when I heard it, I told Talthybius to give the order out at the top of his voice and let the whole army go home, because I would never have the nerve to kill my daughter. And then my brother came at me with every argument there is, and talked me into daring a terrible thing. So I wrote it in the folds of a tablet and sent it to my wife: send our daughter here to be married to Achilles. I made a great deal of the man's standing, and I said he refused to sail with the Achaeans unless a bride out of our house went home with him to Phthia. That was the persuasion I used on my wife. I put a marriage together for the girl out of nothing.

Of all the Achaeans, only we know how it really stands: Calchas, Odysseus, Menelaus, and I. And what I decided badly then, I have now written out again, and written it well, in this tablet here — the one you saw me untying and tying up again in the shadow of the night, old man. Come on, take these letters and go to Argos. And what the tablet keeps hidden in its folds, I will tell you out loud, all of it, every word that is written there. You are loyal to my wife and to my house.

Agamemnon.
	Old man, come out here, out in front of the tent.
Old Man.
	I am coming. What is the new plan,
	Agamemnon, my lord?
Agamemnon.
	Will you hurry?
Old Man.
	I am hurrying.
	Old age gets very little sleep,
	and it keeps a sharp watch on my eyes.
Agamemnon.
	What star is that, the one steering across up there?
Old Man.
	Sirius, running close to the seven roads
	of the Pleiades, still high at the middle of the sky.
Agamemnon.
	No sound of birds, then, and no sound
	from the sea. The winds are keeping their silence
	over this water, over the Euripus.
Old Man.
	Then why are you rushing about outside the tent,
	Agamemnon, my lord?
	It is still quiet here in Aulis
	and the guard on the walls has not stirred.
	Let us go inside.
Agamemnon.
	I envy you, old man.
	I envy any man who comes to the end of a life
	with no danger in it, unknown, with no fame.
	The ones with honours I envy less.
Old Man.
	And yet that is where the beauty of a life is.
Agamemnon.
	That beauty is a thing a man slips on,
	and being honoured above other men
	is sweet, and it hurts when it stands close to you.
	Sometimes it is the gods' business, not set straight,
	that turns a life over; sometimes it is people,
	their many opinions,
	hard to please, grinding you away.
Old Man.
	I do not admire this in a man who is the best of us.
	Atreus did not father you, Agamemnon,
	for nothing but good things.
	You have to feel joy and you have to feel pain.
	You were born mortal. Even if you do not want it,
	that is what the gods want, and that is how it will be.
	And you have opened out the light of the lamp
	and you are writing that tablet,
	the one you are still carrying there in your hands,
	and then you smear out the same letters again,
	and seal it, and untie it again afterwards,
	and throw the pinewood down on the ground,
	crying, the tears coming thick,
	and there is nothing in the whole list of helpless things
	that you are leaving out. You look like a madman.
	What is the trouble? What is new with you, king?
	Come on, share the story with me.
	You will be telling it to a good man, and a loyal one.
	Tyndareus sent me along with your wife once,
	as part of her dowry,
	to look after the bride, and to do it honestly.
Agamemnon.
	I am sending you word, on top of the letters
	I sent before, daughter of Leda —
Old Man.
	Say it, spell it out, so that my tongue
	can say the same thing your writing says.
Agamemnon.
	Do not send your girl to the
	deep-bayed wing of Euboea,
	to Aulis, where no wave comes.
	We will hold our child's wedding feast
	in some other season.
Old Man.
	And Achilles, cheated of his bride —
	how will he not swell up with a huge anger
	against you and against your wife?
	That is dangerous too. Tell me what you mean.
Agamemnon.
	Achilles is lending a name, not a deed.
	He knows nothing about a wedding, or about what we are doing,
	or that I promised the girl to him,
	that I would give her over to a bridegroom's arms
	and a bridegroom's bed.
Old Man.
	That was a terrible thing to dare, Agamemnon, my lord.
	You said your daughter was a wife for the goddess's son
	and you were bringing her here as a throat to cut for the Greeks.
Agamemnon.
	Oh. I have gone out of my mind.
	Aiai. I am falling into ruin.
	Go on now, row your feet along,
	and give nothing away to your age.
Old Man.
	I am hurrying, king.
Agamemnon.
	Do not sit down beside the springs in the woods
	and do not let sleep charm you.
Old Man.
	Do not say such things.
Agamemnon.
	And wherever the road splits, cross it
	looking hard, keeping watch that no wagon
	slips by you on its rolling wheels
	and gets past, bringing my child here
	to the ships of the Greeks.
Old Man.
	It will be done.
Agamemnon.
	And if you meet her with her escort
	already out through the gates,
	turn them back, shake the reins,
	send them off to the walls the Cyclopes built.
Old Man.
	Tell me, when I say all this,
	how am I to be believed by your daughter and your wife?
Agamemnon.
	Keep the seal, the one on the tablet
	you are carrying. Go. The dawn
	is whitening this light already, burning,
	and so is the fire of the Sun's four horses.
	Take some of this labour off me.
	No mortal is fortunate all the way to the end.
	Nobody is happy.
	No one was ever born without pain.

(The Old Man hurries away. Agamemnon goes into the tent. It is daylight. A group of young women from Chalcis come along the shore, looking at the ships.)

Chorus.
	I came down to the sandy beach
	beside the sea at Aulis,
	sailing across the currents
	of the narrow Euripus,
	leaving Chalcis behind me, my own city,
	that feeds the waters of Arethusa,
	the famous spring beside the sea,
	so that I could see the army of the Achaeans
	and the oared ships of the Achaeans
	that carry the half-gods across,
	the ones our husbands say
	fair-haired Menelaus
	and high-born Agamemnon
	are leading to Troy
	in a thousand ships of fir,
	after Helen, whom Paris the herdsman
	took from the reedy banks of the Eurotas,
	a gift to him from Aphrodite,
	when beside the dripping spring
	she stood up against Hera and Pallas
	in a quarrel, a quarrel about beauty.
Chorus.
	I came through the grove of Artemis,
	where so much is killed on the altars,
	running, and my cheek went red
	with a shame that was new to me,
	because I wanted to see the wall of shields
	and the tents of the Greeks under arms
	and the crowd of their horses.
	I saw the two Ajaxes sitting together,
	the son of Oileus and the son of Telamon,
	the crown of Salamis; and Protesilaus
	and Palamedes, whose father was Poseidon's son,
	enjoying themselves over a board
	at a game of counters with complicated shapes;
	and Diomedes, taking his pleasure
	in the throwing of the discus;
	and beside him Meriones,
	a shoot of the war god, a wonder to look at;
	and the son of Laertes, Odysseus,
	down from his island hills,
	and with him Nireus,
	the best-looking man among the Achaeans.
Chorus.
	And Achilles, quick as the wind on his feet,
	the light-running one,
	whom Thetis bore and Chiron finished,
	I saw him along the beach,
	down on the shingle,
	running a race in his armour.
	He was working his feet against
	a four-horse chariot,
	wheeling round the turn for the win.
	And the driver was shouting,
	Eumelus, the grandson of Pheres,
	and I saw his horses, the loveliest,
	their bits worked in gold,
	taking the goad:
	the middle pair, the yoke-horses,
	dappled, with white flecks in their coats,
	and the outside pair, the trace-horses,
	leaning into the bends of the course,
	fire-red, with spotted skin
	above their single hooves. And beside them
	the son of Peleus was springing along in his armour,
	level with the rail and the axle-box of the car.
Chorus.
	And I came to count the ships,
	a sight there are no words for,
	to fill a girl's eyes with looking,
	a sweet pleasure, like honey.
	The right wing was held
	by the war of the Myrmidons out of Phthia,
	fifty ships that come on hard,
	and high on the sterns stood
	Nereid goddesses in gold,
	the badge of Achilles' fleet.
Chorus.
	Next to them the Argive ships lay,
	with as many oars as those,
	and the son of Mecisteus commanded them,
	whom his grandfather Talaus brought up,
	and Sthenelus, the son of Capaneus.
	And next in the line, with sixty ships
	out of Attica, the son of Theseus
	was anchored, and he had the goddess
	Pallas set on a winged chariot
	drawn by whole-hoofed horses:
	a lucky sign for men at sea.
Chorus.
	And I saw the sea-armour of the Boeotians,
	fifty ships dressed out with their signs.
	Theirs was Cadmus, holding a snake of gold,
	up at the beaks of the ships,
	and Leitus, who was born out of the earth,
	was in command of that fleet.
	And from the land of Phocis,
	and from Locris, with as many ships as those,
	came the son of Oileus,
	who had left the famous town of Thronium.
Chorus.
	And from Mycenae, the city the Cyclopes built,
	the son of Atreus sent his crews,
	a hundred ships gathered together,
	and Adrastus was with him
	as a leader, friend beside friend,
	so that Greece could take payment
	for the woman who ran out of her house
	for the sake of a barbarian marriage.
	And out of Pylos I saw, on the sterns
	of Nestor of Gerenia,
	the sign of his neighbour the Alpheus,
	a river drawn with a bull's feet.
Chorus.
	And there was a squadron of twelve
	Aenianian ships, with lord Gouneus
	in command of them. And near those,
	the rulers of Elis,
	whom all the people call the Epeians,
	and Eurytus was their master.
	And he led the white-oared war of Taphos,
	whose lord was Meges, the child of Phyleus,
	who had left the Echinae behind,
	islands where a sailor cannot put in.
Chorus.
	And Ajax, brought up in Salamis,
	was joining his right wing to the left
	of the fleet he was moored nearest to,
	locking them in with his outermost oars,
	twelve ships, the handiest that turn.
	That is what I heard, and I saw
	the men who row them.
	If anyone brings barbarian boats up
	to grapple with that,
	he will carry no homecoming away.
	Such was the fleet under sail
	that I looked at here,
	and the rest I heard at home,
	about the gathered army, and I hold it in my memory.

(The Old Man comes back along the shore, struggling with Menelaus, who has the tablet in his hand.)

Old Man. Menelaus, you have the nerve for terrible things, and no right to them.

Menelaus. Get away. You are far too loyal to your masters.

Old Man. That is a fine insult you have insulted me with.

Menelaus. You will be sorry, if you do what is not yours to do.

Old Man. You had no business breaking open a letter I was carrying.

Menelaus. And you had no business carrying misery to every Greek alive.

Old Man. Argue that out with somebody else. Let go of this and give it to me.

Menelaus. I will not let go.

Old Man. And I will not let go either.

Menelaus. Then this staff will have your head bloody in a moment.

Old Man. It is a fine thing to die for one's masters.

Menelaus. Let go. For a slave you make long speeches.

Old Man. Master, I am being wronged. He tore your letter out of my hands by force, Agamemnon, and he will have nothing to do with what is right.

(Agamemnon comes out of the tent.)

Agamemnon. Ah. What is this uproar at my door, this disorderly shouting?

Menelaus. It is my story that has the right to speak first, not his.

Agamemnon. And you, Menelaus, why have you come to a quarrel with this man, and why are you dragging him about?

Menelaus. Look at me. Let that be where my story starts.

Agamemnon. Do you think I am afraid to lift my eyes? I am a son of Atreus.

Menelaus. Do you see this tablet? The servant of the worst kind of writing?

Agamemnon. I see it. And before anything else, get it out of your hands.

Menelaus. No. Not until I have shown what is written in it to every Greek here.

Agamemnon. So you broke the seals, and you know what it was no business of yours to know?

Menelaus. I opened it, yes. And I know what you have been doing behind our backs, and it will hurt you.

Agamemnon. And where did you get hold of it? Gods, what a shameless mind you have.

Menelaus. I was waiting for your daughter to come from Argos to the camp.

Agamemnon. And what business have you keeping watch on what is mine? Is that not shamelessness?

Menelaus. The itch to do it. That is why. I was not born your slave.

Agamemnon. Is that not outrageous? Am I not to be allowed to run my own house?

Menelaus. No, because your mind runs crooked. One thing now, another thing a while ago, another in a moment.

Agamemnon. Very pretty polish on a nasty argument. A clever tongue is a hateful thing.

Menelaus. And a mind that will not stay put is a dishonest possession, and no use to the people you owe. I want to put you to the test, and you must not turn away from the truth out of anger, and I will not strain the case too hard either.

You remember when you were straining every muscle to lead the Greeks against Troy — pretending you did not want it, wanting it badly all the same — how humble you were then? Taking every man by the right hand, keeping your doors unbolted for any citizen who felt like walking in, giving every man in turn a chance to speak with you, even the ones who did not want it, trying with your manners to buy popularity off the open market? And then, when you had the command in your hands, you changed your ways. You were no longer the friend to your old friends that you used to be. You were hard to get at, and hardly ever inside your own doors. A good man who comes into a great position ought not to change his manners. That is exactly the moment when he ought to be steadiest with the people he owes: when his own luck is good and he has the most power to help them.

That is the first thing I went through, because that is where I first found you out to be bad.

And then, when you came here to Aulis with the whole army of Greece, you were nothing. The luck the gods dealt you knocked you off your feet, and there was no wind to carry us. And the Greeks began saying you should let the ships go and stop labouring at Aulis for nothing. And what a wretched, confused look you had on your face, at the thought that you commanded a thousand ships and were not going to fill Priam's plain with spears. And you kept calling me in. "What am I to do? What way out can I find, and where?" So that you would not be stripped of the command and lose your fine name.

And then, when Calchas said in the middle of the rites that you should sacrifice your daughter to Artemis, and that the Greeks would sail, you were delighted in your heart. You gladly promised to sacrifice the child. And you send word to your wife — willingly, nobody forced you, do not tell me that — to send your daughter here, on the excuse of a marriage to Achilles. And then you turn round, and you get caught changing the writing to something else: that you will not be your daughter's murderer after all. Exactly. And this is the same air that heard you say the first thing.

Thousands of men have had this happen to them. They work hard at power while they hold it, and then they get out of it badly, sometimes because the citizens have no sense, and sometimes justly, because they were not able themselves to keep a city safe.

It is Greece I groan for most, poor Greece. She wanted to do something worth doing, and now she is going to let these barbarian nobodies get away laughing at her, because of you and because of your daughter. I would never put a man in charge of a country for his courage, or make him commander of an army. A general has to have a mind on him. Any man at all can rule a city, so long as he happens to have some understanding.

Chorus. It is a terrible thing when brothers come to words and to blows, once they have fallen into a quarrel.

Agamemnon. I want to say hard things to you, and say them well: briefly, and without lifting my eyelids too high into a shameless stare, but keeping myself in hand, as one brother should. A decent man knows how to feel shame.

Tell me. Why are you breathing so hard, with blood in your eyes? Who is wronging you? What is it you want? A good wife? I cannot supply you with one. The one you did get, you ruled badly. Am I to pay the penalty for your troubles, when I never made the mistake? Is it my ambition that bites you? No. What you want is a good-looking woman in your arms, and you have thrown reason and decency away to get her. A bad man's pleasures are bad.

And if I judged wrongly before and have now changed to a better plan, am I mad? You are the madder one. You lost a worthless wife and you want her back, when a god handed you good luck by taking her away. It was the suitors who swore Tyndareus's oath, out of bad judgement, because they were all in love with the wedding. Hope is a god, I think, and it was Hope that brought the thing about, rather than you and your strength. Take them and go to war. They are ready enough, in the folly of their minds. But the divine is not without understanding. It can tell an oath that was badly fixed and forced out of a man.

I will not kill my own children. It is not going to happen that your affairs come out well, against all justice, in a revenge for the worst of wives, while the nights and the days grind me down in tears for doing a lawless and unjust thing to children I fathered myself.

There. That is said to you briefly, and it is clear, and it is easy to follow. If you will not think straight, I will set my own affairs in order.

Chorus. This is different from what was said before. But it is good, this: sparing the children.

Menelaus. Aiai. So I have no friends after all, wretched man that I am.

Agamemnon. You have friends, if you are not trying to destroy them.

Menelaus. And where will you show me that you were born from the same father as I was?

Agamemnon. I want to keep myself in hand along with you. I do not want to be sick along with you.

Menelaus. The people you owe should hurt along with the people they owe.

Agamemnon. Call me in by doing me good, not by giving me pain.

Menelaus. So you do not mean to take on this labour along with Greece?

Agamemnon. Greece is sick, and so are you, by some god's doing.

Menelaus. Go on, boast about your sceptre, now that you have betrayed your own brother. I will go and look for other devices, and other friends—

(A Messenger comes running along the shore.)

Messenger. Lord of all the Greeks, Agamemnon. I am here, and I have brought your daughter, the one you called Iphigenia at home. Her mother is with her, Clytemnestra your wife herself, and the child Orestes, so that you might have some pleasure in seeing him, after being away from home so long. But the road was long, and they are cooling their soft feet now at a spring with a good flow of water, they and the horses; we turned those loose in the green of the meadow to get a taste of grass. I have come running ahead so that you could get ready for them.

The army knows already that your daughter has arrived. Rumour went through it fast. The whole crowd is coming down to the beach at a run to get a look at your child. People who are fortunate are famous everywhere, and everyone stares at them. And they are saying: "Is it a wedding? What is going on? Or has King Agamemnon been missing his daughter and brought the girl here?" And from others you would have heard this: "They are giving the girl her wedding-eve rites for Artemis, the queen of Aulis. Who is going to marry her?"

Come on, then. Start the baskets for what comes next, and put wreaths on your heads. And you, lord Menelaus, get the wedding song ready. Let the pipe sound through the tents and let there be a stamping of feet. This is a blessed day that has come for the girl.

Agamemnon. Thank you. Now go inside. The rest will be well enough, as fortune takes its course.

(The Messenger goes into the tent.)

Oh. What am I to say? Where do I begin? What a yoke of necessity I have fallen under. A god has come at me from underneath and turned out to be a great deal cleverer than all my cleverness.

Low birth has something useful about it. Those men can cry easily and say everything they feel. The well-born man has the same troubles and none of that comfort. We have our dignity standing over our lives like a master, and we are slaves to the crowd. I am ashamed to let a tear fall, and then, wretched man, I am ashamed not to cry, when I have come into the greatest disasters there are.

Well. What am I going to say to my wife? How will I receive her? What sort of face will I meet her with? She has ruined me, coming when I did not call for her, on top of everything else. And of course she came, with her daughter, to give the bride away, to hand over what she loves most — and she is going to find out what kind of men we are.

And the poor girl. Girl? What girl? It looks as though Hades is going to marry her soon. How I pity her. I think she will beg me like this. "Father, are you going to kill me? Then I hope you make a marriage like this yourself, and everyone who is a friend to you." And Orestes will be standing there beside her, shouting things that make no sense and make all the sense in the world, because he is still a baby.

Aiai. Priam's son Paris destroyed me when he married Helen. He is the one who has done all this.

Chorus. I pity her myself, as far as a woman from another country can grieve over the troubles of kings.

Menelaus. Brother. Give me your right hand to hold.

Agamemnon. Take it. You have won, and I am the wretched one.

Menelaus. I swear by Pelops, who was called my father's father and yours, and by Atreus who fathered us both, that I will tell you what is in my heart, plainly, nothing said for effect, only what I think.

When I saw you letting a tear fall out of your eyes, I pitied you, and I let one fall for you in return. I take back what I said before. I am not going to be a terror to you. I stand where you are standing now. And this is my advice: do not kill your child, and do not choose my business ahead of your own. It is not just that you should be groaning while my affairs go pleasantly, that your children should die while mine look at the light.

What is it I want, after all? If it is a marriage I am longing for, could I not get another bride, and a fine one? Was I to destroy my brother — the last man on earth I ought to destroy — and take Helen, getting the bad thing in place of the good one? I was out of my mind. I was young about it. Then I looked at the business from close up and saw what killing children means.

And besides that, pity for the poor girl came over me, when I thought about the blood between us. She is going to have her throat cut for the sake of my marriage. What has your girl to do with Helen?

Let the army break up and go from Aulis. And you, brother, stop soaking your eyes with tears, and stop calling me into tears with you. Whatever share you have in the oracles about your daughter, let me have none of it. I hand over my part to you.

A sudden turn, you will say, after all those terrible words of mine? What has happened to me is natural. I loved the man born from the same blood as me, and I changed. These are the turns a man makes who is not a bad one: to take whatever is best, every time.

Chorus. That was nobly said, and worthy of Tantalus, the son of Zeus. You do not shame your ancestors.

Agamemnon. I praise you, Menelaus, for putting the argument down in the right place, against everything I expected of you, and worthily of yourself. Brothers fall into confusion over love, and over greed for the family property. I spit on a family tie like that, bitter for both of them. But we have come to a hard necessity: to carry out the bloody murder of my daughter.

Menelaus. How? Who is going to force you to kill your own child?

Agamemnon. The whole gathered assembly of the Achaean army.

Menelaus. Not if you send her back to Argos.

Agamemnon. I could do that without being noticed. There is another thing I will not get away with.

Menelaus. What thing? You must not be too frightened of a crowd.

Agamemnon. Calchas will tell his prophecies to the Argive army.

Menelaus. Not if he dies first. That is easily done.

Agamemnon. The whole breed of prophets is a bad thing, chasing honour.

Menelaus. And no use at all, and no good to anybody when they are among us.

Agamemnon. And the other thing that is coming over me: does that not frighten you?

Menelaus. How can I take up an argument you do not tell me?

Agamemnon. The seed of Sisyphus knows all of it.

Menelaus. Odysseus is not the man to do you or me any harm.

Agamemnon. He was born shifty, always was, and he goes with the crowd.

Menelaus. He is held fast by the love of honour. That is a terrible evil.

Agamemnon. Then do you not think he will stand up in the middle of the Argives and tell them the prophecies Calchas gave out, and how I promised the goddess a victim and then broke my word? That I would sacrifice to Artemis? And that he will carry the whole army away with him, and tell the Argives to kill you and me and cut the girl's throat? And if I run for Argos, they will come and take the place and tear it down to the ground, walls and all, and the Cyclopes built those walls. That is what my troubles are.

I am wretched. What a helpless place the gods have put me in now.

Do one thing for me, Menelaus, when you go through the army. See that Clytemnestra does not learn about this, until I have taken my child and handed her to Hades. Let me do this badly with the fewest tears possible.

And you, women from abroad, keep silence.

(Menelaus goes off along the shore. Agamemnon goes into the tent.)

Chorus.
	Blessed are the ones who share
	the bed of Aphrodite
	with the goddess in her measure,
	and with themselves in hand,
	who get a calm sea
	instead of the maddening sting,
	there where Love with the golden hair
	draws two arrows of delight:
	one of them for a life of good days,
	one to throw a life into confusion.
	Aphrodite, most beautiful,
	I forbid that arrow my bedroom.
	Let my pleasure be measured,
	and my longings holy,
	and let me have my share of her,
	and put the great share away.
Chorus.
	People's natures are different,
	and their ways of living are different,
	but what is truly good is always plain.
	And a rearing that has been taught
	carries a person a long way toward being good.
	Knowing how to feel shame is wisdom,
	and it has this rare grace with it,
	that judgement lets you see
	what has to be done, and reputation
	sheds a glory over a life
	that never grows old.
	It is a great thing to hunt goodness down:
	for women, in a love kept out of sight,
	and among men, an order inside them,
	present in a thousand ways,
	which makes a city greater.
Chorus.
	You came, Paris, to the place where you were reared
	as a herdsman among the white heifers of Ida,
	piping in a foreign scale,
	breathing into your reeds
	an imitation of the Phrygian pipes of Olympus.
	The cows were grazing with their udders full
	when the judging of the goddesses drove you mad,
	the judging that sends you to Greece.
	And you stood in front of the ivory-inlaid house
	and put love into Helen's eyes
	as they looked back into yours,
	and you were shaken with love yourself.
	And out of that, quarrel brings quarrel
	and brings Greece with her spears and her ships
	against the towers of Troy.

(A carriage comes along the shore, with Clytemnestra and Iphigenia in it, and an escort of soldiers.)

Argive Soldiers.
	Io, io. Great is the good fortune
	of great people. Look at Iphigenia,
	the king's child, my queen,
	and Clytemnestra, the daughter of Tyndareus.
	See what great stock they grew from,
	and how high a fortune they have come to.
	The powerful, the ones who carry riches,
	are gods to those mortals who have no luck.
Chorus.
	Let us stand here, we children of Chalcis,
	and take the queen down out of her carriage
	to the ground without a stumble,
	gently, with our hands, with a soft strength,
	so that Agamemnon's famous daughter,
	just come to me now, will not be frightened,
	and so that we, strangers to the women of Argos,
	give strangers no confusion and no shock.

(The carriage has drawn up in front of the tent. Clytemnestra is in it with Iphigenia, the baby Orestes and their attendants. Agamemnon stands at the door.)

Clytemnestra. I take that as a good omen: your kindness, and the good words you have for us. I have some hope that the wedding I am here to lead a bride to is a fine one. Now, take the dowry I have brought for the girl out of the carriages and carry it into the tent, and be careful with it. And you, my child, get down from the carriage. Put your foot down gently; it is a delicate foot, and not strong. You girls, take her in your arms and help her down. And somebody give me a hand to lean on, so I can get out of the carriage seat without making a spectacle of myself. Some of you stand in front of the horses, by the yoke. A horse's eye is a nervous thing, and there is no reasoning with it. And take this boy, Agamemnon's son, Orestes. He is still only a baby. Child, are you asleep? Did the carriage rock you off? Wake up. It is your sister's wedding day, and a lucky one. You are a good man's son and you are going to have a good man for a brother-in-law: the child of the Nereid's daughter, a family that is very nearly gods. Sit here by my feet, child. Iphigenia, come and stand close to your mother, and let these foreign women see what a happy woman I am. And here he is. Go and greet your father. You love him.

Iphigenia. Mother, I am going to run on ahead of you. Do not be angry. I want to throw my arms round my father's chest, and hold him.

Clytemnestra. Agamemnon, my lord, the man I honour above everyone. We have come. You gave your orders and we did not doubt them.

Iphigenia. I want to run to you, father, and throw myself against your chest. It has been so long. I have missed your face. Do not be angry.

Clytemnestra. Go on, child, you should. Of all the children I have given him you were always the one who loved her father most.

Iphigenia. Father. It is so good to see you. It has been so long.

Agamemnon. And your father is glad to see you. What you said goes for both of us.

Iphigenia. Hello, father. You did a good thing, bringing me here to you.

Agamemnon. I do not know how to say yes to that, child, and I do not know how to say no.

Iphigenia. Ah. You are glad to see me, and you do not look it. You look troubled.

Agamemnon. A king and a general has a great deal on his mind.

Iphigenia. Be with me now. Do not go off into your worries.

Agamemnon. But I am with you now. All of me. I am nowhere else.

Iphigenia. Then let go of that frown, and look at me the way you love me.

Agamemnon. There. I am glad to see you. Exactly as glad as I am, child.

Iphigenia. And then you have tears running down your face?

Agamemnon. Yes. Because we are going to be apart a long time.

Iphigenia. I do not know what you mean. I do not know, father, my dearest father.
