Agamemnon. The more sense you talk, the more you make me pity you.

Iphigenia. Then I will talk nonsense, if that will cheer you up.

Agamemnon. Papai. I have not got the strength to keep this in. Good girl.

Iphigenia. Stay at home, father, with your children.

Agamemnon. I want to. And I cannot have what I want, and it hurts.

Iphigenia. Curse the spears, and Menelaus and his troubles.

Agamemnon. They will destroy other people first. They have already destroyed me.

Iphigenia. You have been away so long, tucked into this bay at Aulis.

Agamemnon. And even now there is something holding me back from sending the army out.

Iphigenia. Where do they say the Phrygians live, father?

Agamemnon. Somewhere Priam's son Paris should never have lived at all.

Iphigenia. You are going a long way, father, and leaving me behind.

Agamemnon. You have come to the same place as your father, daughter.

Iphigenia. Pheu. If only it were proper for you to take me on the voyage with you.

Agamemnon. There is a voyage ahead of you too. And on it you will remember your father.

Iphigenia. Do I sail with my mother, or do I make the journey alone?

Agamemnon. Alone. On your own, without your father and without your mother.

Iphigenia. You are not settling me in some other house, are you, father?

Agamemnon. Enough. Girls should not know about such things.

Iphigenia. Hurry back from the Phrygians for me, father, once you have settled everything there.

Agamemnon. First I have a certain sacrifice to make here.

Iphigenia. Yes. You have to see to what is holy, with the proper rites.

Agamemnon. You will know all about it. You will be standing right beside the holy water.

Iphigenia. Then are we going to have dances round the altar, father?

Agamemnon. I envy you. I envy you more than I do myself, for knowing nothing. Go inside the tent now; it is not good for girls to be looked at. Give me a kiss first, and your right hand, because you are going to live a long time away from your father. Oh, this chest, and these cheeks, and this golden hair. What a weight the Phrygians' city has turned out to be for you, and Helen. I will stop talking. The moment I touch you the tears come too fast for me. Go into the tent.

(Iphigenia goes into the tent.)

And you, daughter of Leda, forgive me if I was too full of pity just now, when I am about to give my daughter to Achilles. Sending a daughter off is a happy thing, and all the same it bites the parents, when a father who has laboured so long over his children hands them over to another house.

Clytemnestra. I am not so stupid. Count on it, I will feel exactly the same, so I am not going to lecture you, when I lead the girl out to the wedding songs. But it is what people do, and time wears it down. Now, the man you have promised our child to: I know his name. I want to hear about his family and where he comes from.

Agamemnon. There was a girl called Aegina, and her father was the river Asopus.

Clytemnestra. And who married her? A mortal, or a god?

Agamemnon. Zeus. Their son was Aeacus, the lord of the island of Oenone.

Clytemnestra. And which of Aeacus's sons took over his house?

Agamemnon. Peleus. And Peleus got the daughter of Nereus for a wife.

Clytemnestra. With a god's blessing? Or did he take her by force, against the gods?

Agamemnon. Zeus made the match, and her father, who had the right to, gave her away.

Clytemnestra. And where did he marry her? Under the swell of the sea?

Agamemnon. Where Chiron lives, at the holy foot of Mount Pelion.

Clytemnestra. Where they say the race of Centaurs has its home?

Agamemnon. That is where the gods held the wedding feast for Peleus.

Clytemnestra. And who brought Achilles up? Thetis, or his father?

Agamemnon. Chiron. So he would not pick up the habits of bad men.

Clytemnestra. Pheu. A wise man, the one who raised him. And wiser still the one who gave him to be raised.

Agamemnon. That is the kind of man your daughter is going to have for a husband.

Clytemnestra. No fault to find there. And what city in Greece does he live in?

Agamemnon. By the river Apidanus, inside the borders of Phthia.

Clytemnestra. And that is where he will take your girl and mine?

Agamemnon. That will be his business. She will belong to him.

Clytemnestra. Well, good luck to them both. What day does he marry her?

Agamemnon. When the circle of the moon comes round full, and lucky.

Clytemnestra. And have you already killed the first offerings to the goddess, for the girl's wedding?

Agamemnon. I am about to. That is exactly the business we are standing in the middle of.

Clytemnestra. And then you will hold the wedding feast afterwards?

Agamemnon. Yes. Once I have made the sacrifice I have to make to the gods.

Clytemnestra. And where am I to lay out the feast for the women?

Agamemnon. Here. Beside the fine sterns of the Argive ships.

Clytemnestra. Fine. Since it has to be. Well, may it turn out for the best all the same.

Agamemnon. Do you know what you should do, wife? Do as I say.

Clytemnestra. What is it? I am used to doing as you say.

Agamemnon. I will stay here, where the bridegroom is, and I will—

Clytemnestra. You will do what, without her mother? What is mine to do?

Agamemnon. Give your child away, with the Greeks looking on.

Clytemnestra. And where am I supposed to be while that happens?

Agamemnon. Go to Argos and look after your other girls.

Clytemnestra. And leave my child? Then who is going to hold up the torch?

Agamemnon. I will provide whatever light a wedding needs.

Clytemnestra. That is not the custom. And these are not small things, to be brushed aside.

Agamemnon. It is not right for you to be mixing with a mob of soldiers.

Clytemnestra. It is right for me to give my own children away. I bore them.

Agamemnon. And right for the girls at home not to be left on their own.

Clytemnestra. They are well guarded, behind strong walls, in the women's rooms.

Agamemnon. Do as I say.

Clytemnestra.
	No. By the queen of heaven, the goddess of Argos, no.
	Go and manage what is outside. What is inside the house is mine,
	and a girl on her wedding day needs her mother there.

(Clytemnestra goes into the tent.)

Agamemnon. Oh. I rushed at that and got nowhere. My hope has slipped through my fingers. I wanted my wife out of my sight. I make clever plans, I devise tricks, against the people I love most in the world, and I am beaten at every turn. All the same, I will go and find Calchas the priest, and together we will work out what the goddess wants, which is no good luck for me, and is the labour of all Greece. A clever man should keep a good and useful wife in his house, or no wife at all.

(Agamemnon goes out.)

Chorus.
	So they will come to the Simois
	and its silver-flashing eddies,
	the gathered army of the Greeks,
	in ships and in armour,
	to Ilium, to the plain of Troy
	that belongs to Apollo,
	where I hear Cassandra
	tosses her golden hair,
	crowned with a wreath of green laurel,
	whenever the god's prophecy
	comes on her, and she cannot fight it.
Chorus.
	And the Trojans will stand on the citadel,
	on the towers of Troy and all round the walls,
	when Ares in his bronze shield comes up from the sea,
	rowed in on the oars of fine-prowed ships,
	to the channels of the Simois,
	wanting to take Helen back from Priam,
	Helen, whose brothers are the twin Dioscuri,
	the stars in the sky,
	and carry her home to the land of Greece
	by the toil of Achaean shields
	and Achaean spears.
Chorus.
	And Pergamum, the Phrygians' city,
	he will ring round with murdering war,
	its walls and its stone towers,
	the son of Atreus, and drag back Paris's head
	and cut his throat,
	and sack the city from the top down,
	and leave the girls weeping,
	and Priam's wife weeping.
	And Helen, the daughter of Zeus,
	will sit and weep and weep
	for leaving her husband.
	Never on me,
	never on my children's children
	may that expectation fall,
	the one the Lydian women, heavy with gold,
	and the wives of the Phrygians
	will stand at their looms
	and talk over with each other:
	Who is the man who will wind my lovely hair
	round his fist and drag me off in tears,
	and pluck me like a flower from my country as it dies?
	Because of you, child of the long-necked swan,
	if the story is true
	that Leda lay with a bird on the wing
	when Zeus had changed his body,
	or whether it is all in the poets' tablets,
	tales carried to men
	for nothing, out of season.

(Achilles comes in.)

Achilles. Where is the general of the Achaeans? Which of his servants will tell him that Achilles, the son of Peleus, is at his gates looking for him? Because this waiting beside the Euripus is not the same for all of us. Some of us are not married, and have left empty houses behind to sit here on the beach. Others have wives, and no children yet. That is how fierce the passion for this expedition is that has fallen on Greece, and the gods had a hand in it. I have a just claim of my own, and I am the one who has to state it; anyone else who wants to can speak for himself. I left my country, Pharsalus, and I left Peleus, and I am waiting here for these thin breezes on the Euripus, holding my Myrmidons back. And they are at me the whole time. "Achilles, what are we waiting for? How much longer do we have to count off the days before the fleet sails for Ilium? Do something, if you are going to do anything, or take the army home, and stop waiting on the sons of Atreus and their dithering."

(Clytemnestra comes out of the tent.)

Clytemnestra. Son of the Nereid goddess. I heard you talking from inside, and I have come out in front of the tent.

Achilles. Holy Modesty. Who is this woman I am looking at? And such a beautiful woman.

Clytemnestra. No wonder you do not know me. You never had anything to do with me before. And I like that in you, that you honour a proper reserve.

Achilles. Who are you? And why have you come to the muster of the Greeks? A woman, among men fenced in with shields.

Clytemnestra. I am Leda's daughter. My name is Clytemnestra. And my husband is Agamemnon, the king.

Achilles. Well said. Short, and everything that matters. But it is shameful for me to stand here talking with women.

Clytemnestra. Stay. Why are you running away? Put your right hand in mine. It is the happy beginning of a marriage.

Achilles. What are you saying? I, give you my hand? I would be ashamed to face Agamemnon, if I touched what I have no right to touch.

Clytemnestra. Every right. You are marrying my child, son of the sea-goddess, the daughter of Nereus.

Achilles. What marriage are you talking about? I am speechless, lady. Unless you have lost your mind, and are making up a story?

Clytemnestra. Everyone is like this. They go shy when they meet their new relations and someone mentions the wedding.

Achilles. I have never once courted your daughter, lady. And no word about any marriage has ever come to me from the sons of Atreus.

Clytemnestra. Then what can this be? You wonder at what I say. Well, it is my turn. What you say is a wonder to me.

Achilles. Guess. We can both guess at this. It may be neither of us is lying.

Clytemnestra. Then something dreadful has been done to me. I am courting a marriage that does not exist, by the look of it. I am ashamed.

Achilles. Perhaps somebody has made fools of both of us, you and me. Pay no attention to it. Take it lightly.

Clytemnestra. Goodbye. I cannot look you in the eye any longer. I have been made a liar, and I have been treated as I do not deserve.

Achilles. And goodbye to you, from me. I am going into the tent to look for your husband.

(The Old Man opens the door of the tent a little and calls out.)

Old Man. Stranger, descendant of Aeacus, wait. You, yes, you, I am talking to you, the goddess's son. And you, Leda's daughter.

Achilles. Who is that calling, with the door half open? How frightened he sounds.

Old Man. A slave. I am not proud of it, but my luck does not allow me to be anything else.

Achilles. Whose slave? Not mine. What is mine and what is Agamemnon's are two separate things.

Old Man. This lady's, standing in front of the tent. Her father Tyndareus gave me to her.

Achilles. We are standing still. Say what you want, if you want something. Tell me what you stopped me for.

Old Man. Is it really just the two of you here at the doors?

Achilles. You can talk as if it were just the two of us. Come out of the king's tent.

(The Old Man comes out of the tent, looking around him.)

Old Man. Fortune, and my own foresight. Save the people I want saved.

Achilles. That is a speech that is putting something off. It sounds important, though.

Clytemnestra. Never mind kissing my hand. Do not waste time, if you have something to tell me.

Old Man. You do know me, do you not? Who I am, and that I have always been loyal to you and your children?

Clytemnestra. I know you. You are an old servant of my house.

Old Man. And that King Agamemnon got me as part of your dowry?

Clytemnestra. You came to Argos with us, and you have always been mine.

Old Man. That is right. And I am loyal to you. Less so to your husband.

Clytemnestra. Then out with it, at last. Whatever it is you have to tell us.

Old Man. Your child. Her father, the man who gave her life, is going to kill her with his own hand.

Clytemnestra. What? I spit that story out, old man. You are out of your mind.

Old Man. With a sword. Cutting the poor girl's white throat.

Clytemnestra. Oh, no. Oh, no. Has my husband gone mad, then?

Old Man. He is in his right mind, except where you and your daughter are concerned. There he has lost it.

Clytemnestra. On what grounds? What avenging spirit is driving him to it?

Old Man. Oracles. So Calchas says, anyway. So the army can sail.

Clytemnestra. Sail where? Oh, this is misery, for me, and for the girl her father is going to kill.

Old Man. To the house of Dardanus. So that Menelaus can get Helen back.

Clytemnestra. So Helen's homecoming was fated to cost Iphigenia?

Old Man. You have the whole of it. Her father is going to sacrifice your child to Artemis.

Clytemnestra. And the marriage? What was that for? The excuse that brought me from home?

Old Man. So that you would come gladly, bringing your daughter to marry Achilles.

Clytemnestra. Daughter, you have come here to be destroyed. You, and your mother with you.

Old Man. It is pitiful, what the two of you are suffering. And Agamemnon has dared a terrible thing.

Clytemnestra. I am finished. My eyes cannot hold the tears back any more.

Old Man. If losing a child hurts, then cry.

Clytemnestra. And you, old man. Where did you hear this? How do you come to know it?

Old Man. I was on my way to you, carrying a letter about what he had written before.

Clytemnestra. Telling me not to bring the child to her death, or telling me again to bring her?

Old Man. Telling you not to bring her. Your husband was in his right mind then.

Clytemnestra. Then if you were carrying a letter, how is it you are not giving it to me?

Old Man. Menelaus took it off me. He is the cause of all this.

Clytemnestra. Child of the Nereid, son of Peleus. Do you hear this?

Achilles. I hear that you are a wretched woman. And I do not take my own part in it lightly.

Clytemnestra. They are going to kill my child. They tricked her here with a marriage to you.

Achilles. I blame your husband too. And I do not simply let it go at that.

Clytemnestra. I will not be ashamed to fall at your knees, a mortal at the knees of a goddess's son. Why should I stand on my dignity? Whose business should I work harder for than my own child's?

(She kneels and clasps his knees.)

Defend me, son of the goddess, in my misfortune. And defend her, the girl who was called your wife. Falsely, yes, but called it all the same. For you I put the wreath on her head and brought her here to be married, and now I am bringing her to have her throat cut. And the disgrace will fall on you, if you do not defend her. You were never yoked to her in marriage, but you were called the poor girl's loving husband all the same. By your beard I beg you, by your right hand, by your mother. Your name destroyed me, and your name is what has to save me. I have no altar to run to but your knee. I have no friend to smile on me. You have heard what Agamemnon has done: savage, and stopping at nothing. And I have come, as you can see, a woman, into a camp of sailors with no one in charge of them, bold for any mischief, though useful enough when they want to be. If you have the nerve to stretch out your hand over me, we are saved. If you do not, we are not saved.

Chorus. Motherhood is a strange thing. It carries a great love-charm with it, and every woman shares it: they will go through anything for their children.

Achilles. My spirit is a proud one, and it is rising in me now. But I have learned to grieve at bad fortune in moderation, and to take joy in good fortune in moderation too. Men like that are the ones who have thought their lives through, and live them rightly, with judgement. There are times when it is pleasant not to think too much, and there are times when it is useful to have some judgement. I was brought up in the house of the most god-fearing man alive, Chiron, and I learned to keep my ways simple. As for the sons of Atreus: when they lead well, I will follow them, and when they lead badly, I will not. Here, and in Troy, I will show what a free nature is, and honour Ares with my spear as far as it is in me to do it.

And you, who have suffered so monstrously at the hands of the people closest to you: as far as a young man can, I will wrap you round in my pity and set you right. Your daughter was called mine, and she will never have her throat cut by her father. I am not going to lend your husband my body to weave his plots with. Because it is my name that will kill your child, even if it never lifts the iron. The cause is your husband. But my body is no longer clean, if because of me, because of my marriage, this girl dies, who has suffered terribly, unbearably, who has been dishonoured so astonishingly and so undeservedly. Then I would be the worst man in the Argive army. I would be nothing, and Menelaus would count as a man. I would be no son of Peleus but the son of some avenging fiend, if my name does your husband's murdering for him.

By Nereus, who was bred in the wet waves, the father of Thetis, who bore me: King Agamemnon will not lay a hand on your daughter. Not a fingertip. Not so much as to brush her dress. Or else Sipylus will be a real city, that barbarian outpost these generals' family comes from, and the name of Phthia will never be spoken anywhere again. Calchas the prophet will find his barley and his holy water bitter when he lifts them. And what is a prophet? A man who says a few true things and a great many false ones when his luck is in, and when his luck is out, he is finished.

It is not for the sake of the marriage that I say this. There are ten thousand girls hunting for a place in my bed. No. King Agamemnon has committed an outrage against me. He should have asked me for the use of my name, if he wanted bait for his child. It was mostly on my account that Clytemnestra was persuaded to give her daughter away to a husband. I would have given it to the Greeks, if that was where the voyage to Ilium was breaking down. I would not have refused to build up the common cause of the men I marched with. But as it is, I am nothing. To the generals it is all one whether they treat me well or badly. My sword will soon know the answer. Before it ever gets to the Phrygians I will stain it with the marks of slaughter, with blood, if anyone tries to take your daughter away from me. Now calm yourself. I have appeared to you as a very great god. I am not one. But I will become one, all the same.

Chorus. Son of Peleus, you have spoken as you should, worthy of yourself and of the goddess of the sea, your holy mother.

Clytemnestra. Pheu. How can I praise you without overdoing it in words, and yet not fall short and lose your goodwill? When good men are praised, they somehow come to hate the people praising them, if the praise goes too far. And I am ashamed to be bringing in my pitiful story, when the sickness is mine alone and you are untouched by my troubles. But still, it looks well when a good man, even from a distance, helps people in trouble. Pity us. What we are suffering is pitiable. First I thought I had you for a son-in-law, and the hope I held was empty. And then, perhaps, if my child dies it might turn into a bad omen for your own marriage, when it comes; you should guard against that. But you have spoken well from the beginning, and well at the end. If you are willing, my child will be saved.

Do you want her to come and clasp your knee as a suppliant? It is not what a girl should do. But if you think she should, she will come, with the modest look of a free-born girl. And if I can get the same from you without her here, then let her stay inside. She has a proud sense of her own dignity. Still, modesty only goes as far as it can.

Achilles. Do not bring your daughter out where I can see her, lady. Let us not come in for the reproach of ignorant men. An army massed together, idle and away from home, loves nasty, foul-mouthed gossip. In any case, you will get the same from me whether the two of you beg me or nobody begs me at all. I have one great contest in front of me: to get you out of your troubles. Hear one thing and know it. I will not lie to you. If I am lying to you, or mocking you for nothing, let me die. And let me not die, if I save the girl.

Clytemnestra. Bless you, for always helping people in trouble.

Achilles. Then listen to me now, so that the thing goes well.

Clytemnestra. What do you mean? I certainly have to listen to you.

Achilles. Let us try again to persuade her father to think better of it.

Clytemnestra. He is a coward, and he is far too afraid of the army.

Achilles. But arguments wrestle arguments down.

Clytemnestra. Cold hope. But tell me what I have to do.

Achilles. Beg him first not to kill his children. If he resists, then you come to me. Because if he does what you ask, there is no need for my part in this to move at all: his consent is the rescue by itself. And I will be on better terms with a friend, and the army will have nothing to blame me for, if I settle things by reasoning rather than by force. And if it turns out well, it would come out to the liking of your family and you, even without me.

Clytemnestra. How sensibly you talk. We must do what you think best. But if we do not get what I want, then where do I see you again? Where? Where do I have to go, poor woman that I am, to find your hand to help me?

Achilles. I will keep watch to guard you, where you need guarding, so that nobody sees you rushing in a panic through the crowd of Greeks. Do not shame your father's house. Tyndareus does not deserve to be spoken of badly. He is a great man among the Greeks.

Clytemnestra. So be it. Give the orders. I have to be your slave now. If there are gods, then you are a just man, and you will find the gods good to you. And if there are none, why should anyone take the trouble?

(Achilles goes out. Clytemnestra goes into the tent.)

Chorus.
	What was the wedding cry Hymen raised
	to the Libyan flute,
	and the lyre that loves the dance,
	and the pipes of reed,
	when over Pelion the Muses,
	the lovely-haired daughters of Pieria,
	came to the feast of the gods,
	striking the ground with their golden sandals,
	came to the wedding of Peleus,
	and sang Thetis and the son of Aeacus in their music
	across the Centaurs' mountains,
	down through the woods of Pelion?
	And the Dardanian boy,
	the darling of the bed of Zeus,
	drew off the wine in the golden hollows
	of the mixing bowls,
	Ganymede the Phrygian.
	And along the white-shining sand
	the fifty daughters of Nereus
	wheeled in their circles
	and danced the wedding.
Chorus.
	And up through the firs and the green of their wreaths
	came the troop of Centaurs on their horse-feet,
	to the feast of the gods
	and the mixing bowl of Dionysus.
	And they shouted out loud: Daughter of Nereus,
	the prophet who knows Apollo's music,
	Chiron, has named the son you will bear,
	a great light for Thessaly,
	who will come to the famous land of Priam
	with Myrmidon spearmen and Myrmidon shields
	to burn it to the ground,
	his body cased in golden armour,
	the work of Hephaestus,
	a gift from his goddess mother,
	from Thetis, who bore him.
	That was the day the gods made blessed
	the marriage of the high-born bride,
	the first of the daughters of Nereus,
	and the wedding of Peleus.
Chorus.
	But you. The Argives will crown your head,
	crown your lovely hair,
	like a dappled heifer brought down
	unblemished from the mountains,
	from the rocky caves,
	and they will bloody your throat, a human throat,
	you who were never raised to the pipe
	or the whistling of herdsmen,
	but at your mother's side,
	dressed for a bride's wedding to a son of Inachus.
	Where does the face of Modesty
	or the face of Virtue
	have any strength now,
	when what is unholy has the power
	and Virtue is left behind
	and mortals take no notice of her,
	and Lawlessness rules over the laws,
	and mortals no longer stand together
	to keep the anger of the gods away?

(Clytemnestra comes out of the tent.)

Clytemnestra. I have come out of the tent to look for my husband. He went off a long while ago and left the place empty. And my poor child is in there in tears, pouring out one lament after another, since she heard about the death her father is planning for her. It seems I was talking about a man who was not far away. Here is Agamemnon now, and in a moment he is going to be caught in the act, doing something unholy to his own children.

(Agamemnon comes in.)

Agamemnon. Daughter of Leda. Good, I have found you outside the tent, so I can say some things away from the girl, things a bride should not hear.

Clytemnestra. And what is it? What is so pressing that the moment has caught you?

Agamemnon. Send the child out of the tent, to be with her father. The holy water is standing ready, and the barley to throw with our own hands onto the cleansing fire, and the heifers that have to fall to the goddess before a wedding. To Artemis. With the black blood spurting out of them.

Clytemnestra. In words, you speak well. It is your deeds I do not know how to find a good name for. Come outside, daughter. You know everything your father means to do. And bring Orestes with you, your brother, carried under your dress, child. There. Here she is, doing as you told her. The rest I will say myself, for her and for me.

Agamemnon. Child, why are you crying? Why do you not look at me gladly any more? Why are you staring at the ground, with your dress held up in front of your eyes?

Clytemnestra. Pheu. Where do I take hold of my troubles and begin? Any one of them could come first, or last, or in the middle. They fit anywhere.

Agamemnon. What is it? All of you have come at me together, with the same confusion in your faces and the same trouble in your eyes.

Clytemnestra. Answer what I ask you honestly, husband.

Agamemnon. You do not need to order me. I am willing to be asked.

Clytemnestra. Your child, and mine. Are you going to kill her?

Agamemnon. Ah. That is a cruel thing to say. You are suspecting what you have no business suspecting.

Clytemnestra. Keep calm. Just answer the first question again.

Agamemnon. Ask me a fair question and you will get a fair answer.

Clytemnestra. I have no other question, and do not give me any other answer.

Agamemnon. Fate, my lady. Luck. The spirit that has charge of my life.

Clytemnestra. And of mine, and of hers. One spirit for three people, and unlucky for all three.

Agamemnon. What wrong have I done you?

Clytemnestra. You ask me that? That mind of yours has lost its mind.

Agamemnon. I am finished. My secret is out.

Clytemnestra. I know all of it. I have found out what you mean to do to me. The silence itself is your confession, and so is the groaning. Do not wear yourself out with a long speech.

Agamemnon. There. I am silent. Why should I add shamelessness to disaster by telling lies on top of it?

Clytemnestra. Then listen. I am going to uncover what I mean, and there will be no more talking in riddles and hints. First, and I put this first so that it is the first thing I throw in your face: you married me against my will. You took me by force, after you had killed Tantalus, the husband I had before you. And my baby, you tore him from my breast and dashed him on the ground. Then the two sons of Zeus, my brothers, came riding against you with the sun flashing off their horses, and my old father Tyndareus saved you, because you went down on your knees to him and begged. And so you had my bed after all.

I made my peace with you on those terms, and you will be my witness that from then on I was a wife nobody could fault, to you and to your house. I kept myself in hand where Aphrodite was concerned, and I made your household grow, so that coming in at your door was a joy to you and going out of it was good fortune. That is a rare catch for a man, a wife like that. There is no shortage of the worthless kind. And I bore you three girls, and then this boy, and now, of the girls, you are taking one away from me. Heartlessly. If anyone asks you why you are killing her, tell me, what will you say? Or shall I say it for you? So that Menelaus can have Helen back. A fine bargain. Pay for a bad woman with your children. We are buying what we hate most with what we love best.

Come on, then. Suppose you go off to the war and leave me in the house, and you are away at Troy for years. What do you think my heart will be like at home? When I look at her chair, and every chair of hers is empty, and her room is empty, and I sit by myself in tears, singing the same lament for her over and over: "The father who made you has destroyed you, child. He killed you himself. Not another man, not another man's hand. And this is the homecoming he has left waiting for himself." Because after that it will only take a small excuse for me and the daughters you have left me to give you the welcome you deserve to get. By the gods, do not force me to become an evil woman for your sake. And do not become an evil man yourself.

Well, then. You will sacrifice the child. And what prayers will you say over her, while you do it? What good thing will you ask for yourself, with your daughter's throat under the knife? A wretched homecoming, to match the shameful way you went out? Or is it my job to pray for something good for you? We would have to think the gods were fools if we wished murderers well. And when you come home to Argos, will you throw your arms round your children? You have no right to. Which of them will so much as look you in the face, once you have called one of them to you and killed her? Have you even got as far as thinking about this? Or is your only concern to carry a sceptre about and command an army?

Here is the fair proposal you should have put to the Argives. "Achaeans, do you want to sail for the land of the Phrygians? Then draw lots for whose child has to die." That would have been even-handed. Instead you pick out your own daughter as the one special victim and hand her to the Greeks. Or Menelaus could have killed Hermione for her mother's sake, since it was his business in the first place. As it is, I, who kept your bed faithfully, am to lose my child, and the woman who did the wrong will bring her girl home to Sparta safe and grown, and be happy. Answer me, if anything I have said is wrong. But if I have put it well, then do not kill her, your child and mine. Then you will be a man who keeps himself in hand.

Chorus. Do what she says. Joining together to save your children is a fine thing, Agamemnon. No one alive will argue with that.

Iphigenia. If I had the voice of Orpheus, father, so that I could sing a spell and make the rocks get up and follow me, and charm anyone I liked with words, I would have gone that way. But the only cleverness I have is tears, and I will give you those. Tears I can manage. I press my body against your knees like a suppliant's branch, this body your wife here bore you. Do not destroy me before my time. It is sweet to look at the light. Do not force me to see what is under the ground.

I was the first to call you father, and you were the first to call me your child. I was the first to climb into your lap and give you a child's kisses and take yours back. And this is what you used to say: "Shall I see you one day, my girl, happy in a husband's house, living and flowering, the way a daughter of mine should?" And I would answer, hanging from your beard, the way I am holding it now with my hand: "And what will I do for you, father? When you are old, shall I have you in my house and look after you, and pay you back for all the work it took to raise me?" I remember every word of it. You have forgotten, and you want to kill me.

No. By Pelops, and by your father Atreus, and by my mother here, who went through labour for me once already and is going through this second labour now. What have I got to do with Paris and Helen and their marriage? Where did he come from, father, to be my ruin? Look at me. Give me one look, and a kiss, so that at least I have that to take with me when I die, something of yours to remember, if you will not do what I ask.

(She holds the baby up toward him.)

Brother, you are a small helper for the people you love. But cry with me all the same, and beg our father not to let your sister die. Even babies have some feeling for evil when it comes. Look, father. He is begging you without a word. Have some respect for me. Pity my life. Yes, by your beard, we two who love you are pleading with you, one a nestling and the other grown. I will cut it all down to one thing and win the whole argument with it. This light is the sweetest thing human beings can look at, and what is under the ground is nothing. Anyone who prays to die is mad. A bad life is better than a fine death.

Chorus. Miserable Helen. Because of you and your marriages a great struggle has come on the sons of Atreus and their children.

Agamemnon. I understand what deserves pity and what does not. And I love my children. I would be mad if I did not. It is a terrible thing for me to bring myself to do this, wife, and a terrible thing not to. Because I have to do it. Look at the size of this army, and the fleet drawn up round it like a wall. Look at all these lords of Greece in their bronze armour. There is no sailing to the towers of Troy for them, and no tearing out the famous foundations of Troy, unless I sacrifice you, as the prophet Calchas says. Some Aphrodite has driven the Greek army mad to sail for the barbarians' country as fast as it can and put an end to the stealing of Greek wives. And they will kill my girls in Argos, and you, and me, if I break the goddess's oracle. It is not Menelaus who has made a slave of me, child. I have not come here to do what he wants. It is Greece. Whether I want it or not, I have to sacrifice you for her, and against that we are the weaker side. She has to be free, child, as far as it lies in you and in me to make her free, and Greeks must not have their wives dragged out of their beds by barbarians.

(Agamemnon goes out toward the camp.)

Clytemnestra.
	Child. Foreign women.
	Oh, I am wretched. Your death.
	Your father is running from you. He has handed you to Hades.
Iphigenia.
	Oh, mother. The same song
	of the same bad luck has fallen on us both,
	and there is no more light for me,
	no more of this blaze of the sun.
	Io. Io.
	Snow-beaten valley of the Phrygians, mountains of Ida,
	where Priam once threw out a soft baby
	he had taken from its mother, to die,
	and the baby was Paris, who was called
	Idaean, Idaean, in the city of the Phrygians.
	If only Priam had never
	brought that cowherd, raised among his cattle,
	Paris, Alexander, to live
	by the white water, where the springs
	of the Nymphs lie,
	and the meadow, green with young shoots,
	and roses
	and hyacinths for goddesses to pick. Because there one day
	came Pallas Athena, and Aphrodite with her scheming heart,
	and Hera, and Hermes, the messenger of Zeus:
	Aphrodite preening in the desire she causes,
	Athena in her spear,
	Hera in the royal bed
	of Zeus the king,
	to a hateful judgement, a contest
	over beauty. And for me it meant death,
	a death that brings the Greeks
	a name, girls, but it is my death
	Artemis took as the first offering on the road to Troy.
	And the man who fathered me, wretched me,
	mother, oh mother,
	is gone. He has betrayed me and left me alone.
	Oh, I am the unluckiest of all. I have seen
	bitter, bitter Helen, Helen my ruin,
	and I am murdered, I am destroyed,
	cut down in an unholy killing by an unholy father.
	I wish this Aulis had never
	taken the bronze-beaked ships
	into these harbours, sterns first,
	the pine fleet bound for Troy,
	and that Zeus had never breathed a wind
	against them on the Euripus. He tempers
	one breeze for one man's sails and another for another's,
	so that some rejoice,
	and some grieve, and some are forced,
	some put out to sea, some make ready,
	some wait.
	Full of trouble, then, full of trouble
	is the race of us who live a day at a time, and what has to be
	is a hard thing for people to find out.
	Io. Io.
	Great suffering, great grief,
	the daughter of Tyndareus has laid on the Greeks.

Chorus. I pity you. This is bad luck you have met, the kind you should never have met.

Iphigenia. Mother, mother who bore me, I can see a crowd of men close by.

Clytemnestra. It is the goddess's son, child. The one you came here for.

Iphigenia. Open the tent for me, slaves. Let me hide myself.

Clytemnestra. Why run away, child?

Iphigenia. I am ashamed to look at Achilles.

Clytemnestra. Why?

Iphigenia. My marriage went so badly. It makes me ashamed.

Clytemnestra. This is no time to be delicate, with things the way they have fallen. Stay. There is no room for pride, if it can help us.

Achilles. Unhappy woman, daughter of Leda—

Clytemnestra. That is no lie.

Achilles. There is terrible shouting among the Argives—

Clytemnestra. What shouting? Tell me.

Achilles. About your daughter—

Clytemnestra. That is a bad omen, that word.

Achilles. That she has to be sacrificed.

Clytemnestra. And no one speaks against them?

Achilles. I got into some trouble myself—

Clytemnestra. What trouble, stranger?

Achilles. Of being stoned to death.

Clytemnestra. For trying to save my girl?

Achilles. Exactly that.

Clytemnestra. Who would have the nerve to lay a hand on you?

Achilles. Every Greek there.

Clytemnestra. Were your Myrmidons not there with you?

Achilles. They were the first to turn on me.

Clytemnestra. Then we are finished, child.

Achilles. They called me the man a marriage had beaten.

Clytemnestra. And what did you answer?

Achilles. Not to kill the woman who was going to be my wife—

Clytemnestra. Quite right.

Achilles. The wife her father promised me.

Clytemnestra. And sent for from Argos.

Achilles. But I was beaten by the shouting.

Clytemnestra. A mob is a terrible thing.

Achilles. But I will help you all the same.

Clytemnestra. And fight so many, one man alone?

Achilles. Do you see these men, carrying my armour?

Clytemnestra. Bless you for your good heart.

Achilles. Then I will be blessed.

Clytemnestra. So the child is not going to be slaughtered after all?

Achilles. Not with my consent.

Clytemnestra. But will someone come to lay hands on the girl?

Achilles. Thousands of them. And Odysseus will lead them.

Clytemnestra. The son of Sisyphus?

Achilles. The very man.

Clytemnestra. Acting on his own, or under the army's orders?

Achilles. Chosen, and willing.

Clytemnestra. A wicked thing to choose. Blood on his hands.

Achilles. But I will hold him off.

Clytemnestra. Will he drag her away by force, if she will not go?

Achilles. Certainly. By her yellow hair.

Clytemnestra. And what should I do, when it comes to that?

Achilles. Hold on to your daughter.

Clytemnestra. If that is all it takes, she will not be slaughtered.

Achilles. It will come to that. Be sure of it.

Iphigenia. Mother, listen to me, both of you. I can see you are angry with your husband, and it is for nothing. It is not easy for us to hold out against what cannot be helped. The stranger deserves our thanks for his good will, but you have to see this too: he must not be put in the wrong with the army, so that we gain nothing and he comes to grief. Now listen, mother, to what has come into my mind as I thought about it.

I have decided to die. And I want to do it well, with a good name, putting anything low or mean out of my way. Come and look at it with me, mother, and see how right I am. The whole of Greece, all of great Greece, is looking at me now. On me depends the fleet's crossing and the destruction of the Phrygians, and whether barbarians are ever again allowed to steal women from happy Greece, if they try anything, once they have paid for the ruin of Helen, whom Paris carried off. All of that I will save by dying, and my fame, as the girl who set Greece free, will be a blessed one.

And after all, I have no right to cling too hard to my life. You bore me for all the Greeks together, not for yourself alone. Thousands of men have armed themselves with shields, and thousands have taken up oars, because their country has been wronged, and they will have the nerve to go at the enemy and die for Greece. And my one life is to stand in the way of all that? What kind of justice would that be? Could I find one word to answer it? And here is the other point. This man should not have to fight the whole of Argos for a woman's sake, or die for one. One man is worth more than ten thousand women, when it comes to seeing the light of day. And if Artemis has decided to take my body, am I, a mortal, going to stand in a goddess's way? It cannot be done. I give my body to Greece. Sacrifice it, and go and sack Troy. That will be my monument for a long time to come. That will be my children, and my marriage, and my good name. It is right, mother, for Greeks to rule barbarians, and not for barbarians to rule Greeks. They are slaves, and we are free.

Chorus. Your part in this, young woman, is a noble one. It is the part played by luck and by the goddess that is sick.

Achilles. Daughter of Agamemnon, some god was going to make me a happy man, if I had won you for my wife. I envy Greece for having you, and I envy you for having Greece. What you have said is good, and worthy of your country. You have given up fighting the gods, who are stronger than you, and you have worked out what is best and what has to be. And now that I have looked at your nature and seen what it is, I want you for my wife more than ever. You are a noble woman. Think about it. I want to do you good, and take you home to my house, and it hurts me, Thetis be my witness, if I cannot save you by fighting my way through the Greeks. Look at it squarely. Death is a terrible thing.

Iphigenia. I say this with no fear of anyone. The daughter of Tyndareus is already causing enough fighting and killing among men with her beauty. You, stranger, do not die for me, and do not kill anyone. Let me save Greece, if I can.

Achilles. What a spirit. There is nothing more I can say against that, since this is what you have decided. It is a noble way to think, and why should anyone not say so, when it is true? All the same, you may change your mind about this. So that you know exactly where I stand, I will go and set this armour down beside the altar, ready to stop you dying, not to let it happen. You may want to take up my offer soon enough, when you see the knife close to your throat. I will not let you die through rashness of your own. I am going to the goddess's temple with these weapons, and I will be watching for you to arrive.

(Achilles goes out with his men.)

Iphigenia. Mother, why are you crying without a word, wetting your eyes?

Clytemnestra. I have reason enough for a heart that hurts. I am wretched.

Iphigenia. Stop. Do not make a coward of me. Do this one thing I ask.

Clytemnestra. Say it. You will get no wrong from me, child.

Iphigenia. Then do not cut off a lock of your hair for me, and do not wrap your body in black clothes.

Clytemnestra. What are you saying, child? When I have lost you?

Iphigenia. You have not. I am saved, and through me you will have a good name.

Clytemnestra. What do you mean? Am I not to mourn your life?

Iphigenia. No. Because no grave will be heaped up over me.

Clytemnestra. What of that? It is the dying we mourn, not the grave.

Iphigenia. The altar of the goddess, the daughter of Zeus, will be my memorial.

Clytemnestra. Well, child. I will do as you say. You put it well.

Iphigenia. Yes. As a woman who is fortunate, and who has done Greece a service.

Clytemnestra. What message shall I take to your sisters from you?

Iphigenia. Do not put black clothes on them either.

Clytemnestra. But is there some loving word I can give the girls from you?

Iphigenia. Goodbye. And raise Orestes here to be a man, for me.

Clytemnestra. Hold him close. You are looking at him for the last time.

Iphigenia. My darling. You helped the people you love as much as you could.

Clytemnestra. Is there anything I can do in Argos that would please you?

Iphigenia. Do not hate my father. He is your husband.

Clytemnestra. He has terrible races to run because of you.

Iphigenia. He destroyed me against his will, for the land of Greece.

Clytemnestra. By a trick. Basely. Not the way a son of Atreus should.

Iphigenia. Who will come and lead me there, before I am dragged by the hair?

Clytemnestra. I will. I will go with you—

Iphigenia. Not you. That is not right.

Clytemnestra. Holding on to your dress.

Iphigenia. Mother, do as I ask. Stay here. It is better this way, for me and for you. Let one of these attendants of my father's take me to the meadow of Artemis, where I am going to be slaughtered.

Clytemnestra. Child, are you going?

Iphigenia. Yes. And I will never come back.

Clytemnestra. Leaving your mother?

Iphigenia. As you see. And not deserving it.

Clytemnestra. Wait. Do not leave me.

Iphigenia. I will not let you shed a tear. And you, young women, sing a hymn of good omen over what is happening to me, a healing song to the daughter of Zeus, to Artemis. Let the word go out to the Greeks to keep a holy silence. Let someone begin the rite with the baskets. Let the fire blaze up for the barley we scatter to make it clean, and let my father go round the altar from left to right. Because I am coming to give the Greeks their safety, and their victory with it.

Iphigenia.
	Lead me away, the girl who takes the cities
	of Troy and the Phrygians.
	Give me wreaths to wind round me, bring them here,
	here is my hair to crown,
	and bring the streams of holy water.
	Dance round the temple,
	round the altar, for Artemis,
	Artemis the queen,
	Artemis the blessed. Because with my blood
	and my sacrifice, if it has to be,
	I am going to wipe the oracle clean.
	Mother, my lady, my lady mother, I will not
	give you my tears.
	They are out of place at the holy rites.
	Io, io, young women,
	sing with me to Artemis,
	whose temple looks across the water at Chalcis,
	where the spears are mad for war
	because of my name, here in the narrow
	harbours of Aulis.
	Io, Pelasgian earth, my mother,
	and Mycenae, where I was brought up—
Chorus.
	Are you calling on the city of Perseus,
	the walls the Cyclopes built with their hands?
Iphigenia.
	You raised me to be a light for Greece.
	I am dying, and I do not say no.
Chorus.
	No. Your fame will never leave you.
Iphigenia.
	Io. Io.
	Day that carries the torch,
	and light of Zeus, another, another
	life and another fate will be my home now.
	Goodbye, dear light.

(Iphigenia goes out toward the altar, and the crowd of men with her.)

Chorus.
	Io. Io.
	Look at her, the girl who takes the cities
	of Troy and the Phrygians,
	walking away, with the wreaths
	to be set on her head, and the streams of holy water,
	to stain the altar of the goddess, that spirit,
	with drops of running blood
	when the lovely neck of her body
	is cut. The dewy streams
	her father pours are waiting for you, and the holy water,
	and the army of the Achaeans, wanting
	to reach the city of Troy.
	But let us call on the daughter of Zeus,
	on Artemis,
	the queen of the gods, as if for a fortunate end.
	Lady, lady, who takes pleasure
	in human sacrifice, send the army of the Greeks
	into the land of the Phrygians,
	to the treacherous seats of Troy,
	and grant that Agamemnon, with his spears,
	sets round his own head the most glorious crown
	Greece ever gave,
	a fame that will never be forgotten.

(The Chorus waits. A Messenger comes running from the direction of the altar.)

Messenger. Daughter of Tyndareus, Clytemnestra, come out of the tent and hear what I have to say.

Clytemnestra. I heard your voice and I have come. I am wretched, and I am shaking, struck stupid with fear. Have you come bringing me some new disaster, on top of the one I have?

Messenger. No. About your child I want to tell you something wonderful, and terrible.

Clytemnestra. Then do not wait. Say it, as fast as you can.

Messenger. Dear mistress, you will hear all of it plainly. I will tell it from the beginning, unless my mind stumbles somewhere and trips up my tongue as I go. When we reached the grove of Artemis, the daughter of Zeus, and the meadows full of flowers where the Achaean army was assembled, bringing your daughter with us, the crowd of Argives gathered at once. And when King Agamemnon saw the girl walking into the grove to be slaughtered, he groaned aloud and turned his head away and wept, with his cloak held up in front of his eyes.

But she stood close to the man who fathered her and said this: "Father, here I am. I give my body, of my own free will, for my country and for the whole land of Greece, for them to lead to the goddess's altar and sacrifice, if that is what the oracle demands. And for my part, I wish you good fortune. May you win the gift of victory and come home to your fathers' land. And so let none of the Argives lay a hand on me. I will offer my neck in silence, with a good heart."

That is what she said, and every man who heard it was amazed at the courage and the goodness of the girl. Then Talthybius, whose business it was, stood up in the middle of them and called for a holy silence, with not a word from the army. And Calchas the prophet drew a sharp knife from its sheath and laid it in a basket of beaten gold, and put the wreath on the girl's head. Then the son of Peleus took the basket and the holy water together, and ran in a circle round the goddess's altar sprinkling it, and said: "Daughter of Zeus, killer of wild animals, who wheel your bright light through the darkness, accept this offering, which the army of the Achaeans and King Agamemnon give you together: the pure blood from a beautiful girl's neck. And grant our ships a voyage without harm, and grant that our spears tear the towers of Troy to the ground."

The sons of Atreus and the whole army stood looking at the ground. The priest took the knife and said his prayer, and studied her throat for the place to strike. And no small pain went into my heart, and I stood there with my head down. And then, all at once, there was a wonder to see. Everyone heard the sound of the blow, clearly. But nobody saw where in the earth the girl had gone. The priest shouted, and the whole army shouted back, at the sight of a thing no one had hoped for, sent by some god, a thing you could not believe even with your eyes on it. Because there on the ground lay a deer, gasping, huge to look at and magnificent, and the goddess's altar was soaked from end to end with its blood.

At that, you can imagine how happily Calchas spoke. "Captains of this united army of the Achaeans, do you see this sacrifice, the one the goddess has set before her altar, a deer that runs the mountains? She welcomes this far more than the girl, so that her altar is not stained with noble blood. She has accepted it gladly, and she is giving us a following wind and a landing at Troy. So take heart, every sailor here, and go to your ships. Because today we must leave the hollow bays of Aulis and cross the swell of the Aegean."

And when the whole offering had been burned to ash in the fire of Hephaestus, he prayed the fitting prayers, that the army might have its homecoming. Agamemnon sends me to tell you this, and to say what share the gods have given him, and that he has won a fame that will never die throughout Greece. And I was there, I saw the thing happen, and I am telling you: your child has plainly flown away to the gods. So let go of your grief, and let go of your anger at your husband. What the gods do is not what mortals expect, and the people they love, they keep safe. This day has seen your daughter dead and alive.

Chorus. I am so glad to hear this from the messenger. He says your child is alive and living among the gods.

Clytemnestra.
	Child, which of the gods has stolen you?
	What am I to call you now? How can I help saying
	that this is a story made up to comfort me, and all for nothing,
	so that I would stop my bitter grieving for you?
Chorus.
	And look, here comes King Agamemnon,
	with the same story to tell you himself.

Agamemnon. Wife, as far as our daughter goes we can count ourselves blessed. She really is in the company of the gods. Now you must take this young calf of ours and go home, because the army has its eyes on the sea. And goodbye. It will be a long time before I greet you again, from Troy. May it go well with you.

Chorus.
	Go gladly, son of Atreus, to the land of Phrygia,
	and gladly come back,
	with the finest spoils of Troy in your hands, for me.

Cyclops (date unknown)

Cyclops

(Sicily, at the foot of Mount Etna, in front of a great cave. It is the home of the Cyclops Polyphemus. Old Silenus comes out of it, bald and pot-bellied, dragging an iron rake behind him.)

Silenus. Dionysus. The troubles I have had because of you. Thousands of them, now, and back when I was young and my body was still good for something. First there was the time Hera drove you mad and you ran off from the mountain nymphs who were bringing you up. Then there was the war with the Giants, the sons of Earth: I stood at your right hand with my shield, and I killed Enceladus, put my spear straight through the middle of his shield and killed him. Hold on. Let me think. Am I telling you something I saw in a dream? No, by Zeus, because I showed you the trophies afterwards, so it must have happened.

And now I am bailing out a worse trouble than any of those. When Hera set that gang of Tyrrhenian pirates on you, to have you carried off and sold somewhere a long way away, I heard about it, and I put to sea with my boys to look for you. I stood right up at the stern and took the two steering oars myself and held her straight, and my sons sat at the benches and whipped the grey sea white with their rowing, hunting for you, my lord. We had got as far as Cape Malea when an east wind blew into the ship and threw us up here, on this rock of Etna, where the one-eyed sons of the sea god live, the Cyclopes, in their lonely caves, killing men.

One of them caught us, and now we are slaves in his house. The one we work for is called Polyphemus. Instead of dancing and shouting for Dionysus, we herd the sheep of a Cyclops who has no use for the gods. My boys, being young, graze the young sheep out on the far edges of the hills. My orders are to stay here, fill the water troughs and sweep out the house: the waiter to this godless Cyclops at his godless dinners. And right now orders are orders, and I have to sweep the place out with this iron rake, so that when my master the Cyclops gets back we can welcome him and his sheep into a clean cave.

And here come my boys already, driving the flocks in. What is this now? Is that the stamp of the satyr dance I hear? The same as it was when you were the god's escort at his parties, swaggering up to Althaea's front door to the sound of lyres?

(The Chorus of satyrs come in, driving sheep and goats in front of them, and dancing as they come.)

Chorus.
	Son of a fine father
	and a fine mother too,
	where are you off to, up the crags?
	Isn't the breeze soft here, out of the wind,
	and isn't the grass thick?
	Isn't there river water, fresh from the eddies,
	lying in the troughs beside the cave?
	Can't you hear your lambs crying for you?
Chorus.
	Psst. Not here? No? Won't you graze
	here on the wet slope?
	Hey. I'll throw a stone at you in a minute.
	Get along, get along, horn-head,
	back to the pens, where the herdsman
	of the wild Cyclops keeps his watch.
Chorus.
	Let down those swollen udders.
	Take to your teats the babies
	you left behind in the lambing pens.
	They miss you, the little ones,
	asleep all day and bleating.
	When are you going to come inside the yard,
	leave the grassy pastures,
	and get in among the rocks of Etna?
Chorus.
	Psst. Not here? No? Won't you graze
	here on the wet slope?
	Hey. I'll throw a stone at you in a minute.
	Get along, get along, horn-head,
	back to the pens, where the herdsman
	of the wild Cyclops keeps his watch.
Chorus.
	There is no Dionysus here. No dancing here,
	no women of the god with their ivy wands,
	no rattle of drums
	beside the springs pouring out their water,
	no fresh bright drops of wine.
	I am not on Nysa with the nymphs
	singing Iacchus, Iacchus,
	the song for Aphrodite,
	the goddess I used to fly after
	with the white-footed women of the god.
	Oh, my friend.
	Dear Dionysus, where are you wandering, all alone?
	Where are you tossing that yellow hair?
	And here am I, your own attendant,
	working for the Cyclops,
	the one-eyed thing, a slave, a stray,
	in this miserable goat-skin coat,
	without your love.

Silenus. Quiet, boys. Tell the men to round up the flocks and get them into the cave under the rock.

Chorus. Go on, get them in. But what's the hurry, father?

Silenus. I can see the hull of a Greek ship down at the shore, and the lords of the oar coming up to this cave with some captain or other. They have empty pots slung round their necks, and water jars. They want food. Poor strangers. Who can they be? They don't know what sort of a man our master Polyphemus is. They have walked into a house where no guest is welcome, and they have come, worse luck for them, straight to the Cyclops's jaw, the jaw that eats men. Hush, though. Let's find out where they have come from, to the Sicilian rock of Etna.

(Odysseus comes up from the shore with his men.)

Odysseus. Strangers, could you tell us where there's a running stream we could drink from and take the edge off our thirst? And is there anyone who would sell food to sailors who need it? What's this? We seem to have landed in a town that belongs to Dionysus. That's a crowd of satyrs I can see by the caves. I'll greet the oldest first. Good day to you.

Silenus. Good day to you, stranger. Who are you, and where are you from?

Odysseus. Odysseus of Ithaca, king of the land of the Cephallenians.

Silenus. I know the man. Sharp as a rattle and twice as noisy. Sisyphus's boy.

Odysseus. That's who I am. And you can stop insulting me.

Silenus. Where have you sailed from, to get here to Sicily?

Odysseus. From Ilium. From the war at Troy.

Silenus. How? Didn't you know the way home to your own country?

Odysseus. Storm winds snatched me and carried me here by force.

Silenus. Papai. You're bailing out the same bad luck I am.

Odysseus. You were driven here by force too?

Silenus. Chasing the pirates who carried off Dionysus.

Odysseus. What country is this, and who lives here?

Silenus. This is Etna, the highest hill in Sicily.

Odysseus. And where are the walls? Where are the city towers?

Silenus. There aren't any. These headlands are empty of men, stranger.

Odysseus. Then who holds the land? Wild animals?

Silenus. The Cyclopes. They live in caves, not houses with roofs.

Odysseus. Who do they obey? Or does the power belong to the people?

Silenus. They're nomads. Nobody listens to anybody about anything.

Odysseus. Do they sow grain, Demeter's crop? Or what do they live on?

Silenus. Milk and cheese, and the meat of sheep.

Odysseus. Do they have the drink of Dionysus, what flows from the vine?

Silenus. Not a drop. Which is why there's no dancing in the country they live in.

Odysseus. Are they kind to strangers? Do they respect the rights of a guest?

Silenus. They say strangers make the sweetest meat.

Odysseus. What did you say? They enjoy eating human beings?

Silenus. Nobody has ever come here without getting his throat cut.

Odysseus. And the Cyclops himself, where is he? Inside?

Silenus. Gone off on Etna, hunting animals with his dogs.

Odysseus. Then do you know what to do, so we can get away from this land?

Silenus. I don't, Odysseus. But we'd do anything for you.

Odysseus. Sell us bread. We've run out.

Silenus. There isn't any, as I said. There's nothing but meat.

Odysseus. That's sweet enough. It stops the hunger.

Silenus. And there's cheese set with fig juice, and cow's milk.

Odysseus. Bring them out. A man should see what he's buying, in daylight.

Silenus. And what will you give me for them? How much gold, tell me?

Odysseus. No gold. What I have is the drink of Dionysus.

Silenus. Oh, the sweetest words. That's what we've been short of for so long.

Odysseus. And it was Maron who gave it to me. The god's own son.

Silenus. Maron? The one I brought up in these arms?

Odysseus. The son of Dionysus, to make it perfectly clear.

Silenus. Is it on board the ship, or have you brought it with you?

Odysseus. This skin here is what holds it. As you can see, old man.

Silenus. That? That wouldn't so much as fill my cheek.

Odysseus. Oh yes it would. For every drop that runs out of the skin, it gives twice as much again.

Silenus. That's a lovely spring you're describing. Music to my ears.

Odysseus. Would you like a taste first? Neat, no water?

Silenus. Only fair. A taste is what brings on the sale.

Odysseus. And look, I carry a cup along with the skin.

Silenus. Go on, then. Knock it out into the cup, so I can drink and remember what it was like.

Odysseus. There.

Silenus. Papaiax. What a beautiful smell it has.

Odysseus. You can see the smell, can you?

Silenus. No, by Zeus. But I can sniff it.

Odysseus. Taste it, then, so you're not praising it in words alone.

Silenus. Babai. Dionysus is asking me to dance. Ah, ah, ah.

Odysseus. Did it gurgle down your throat nicely?

Silenus. Right down to the ends of my toenails.

Odysseus. And we'll give you money as well, on top.

Silenus. Just loosen the skin. Never mind the gold.

Odysseus. Bring out the cheeses, then, or a lamb from the flock.

Silenus. I will. And I'll spare very little thought for my masters while I do it. For one cup of that I'd go out of my mind. I'd hand over the flocks of every Cyclops there is for it, and throw myself into the sea off the white cliff of Leucas, once I'd got well drunk and smoothed the frown off my face. The man who doesn't enjoy his drinking is mad. Drinking is what makes this thing here stand up straight, and gets you a handful of breast, and puts a meadow all ready for you under both your hands, and there's dancing, and forgetting your troubles. And I'm not going to kiss a drink like that? Not tell the Cyclops and his stupidity to go and cry about it, and his eye, the one in the middle, along with him?

(Silenus goes into the cave.)

Chorus. Listen, Odysseus. We'd like a little chat with you.

Odysseus. Go ahead. Friends talking to a friend.

Chorus. Did you take Troy? Did you get Helen into your hands?

Odysseus. Yes. And we sacked the whole house of Priam, every one of them.

Chorus. Well then, once you'd caught the young lady, did you all take turns with her, one after another? Since she does like being married to a lot of men. The traitor. She took one look at a man in fancy embroidered trousers, with a gold collar round the middle of his neck, and her heart went flutter, and off she went and left Menelaus, the best little man there is. I wish the whole race of women had never been born anywhere at all. Except for me. I'd keep them for me.

(Silenus comes back out of the cave, carrying cheeses and leading lambs.)

Silenus. Here you are. The shepherds' stock, King Odysseus: the young of the bleating sheep, and cheeses of pressed milk, and plenty of them. Take them, and get away from the cave as fast as you can, and give me the drink of the joyful grape in exchange. Oh. Oh no. Here comes the Cyclops. What do we do?

Odysseus. Then we're finished, old man. Where can we run?

Silenus. Inside this rock. You could hide in there, at least.

Odysseus. That is a dreadful thing to suggest. Walk into the net?

Silenus. Nothing dreadful about it. There are plenty of hiding places in the rock.

Odysseus. No. I will not. Troy would groan aloud if I ran from one man, when I stood up to ten thousand Phrygians at a time, with my shield, over and over again. If we have to die, we'll die like men of good birth. Or we live, and keep the good name we had before.

(The Cyclops comes in from the hills, carrying a club.)

Cyclops. Out of the way. Stand back. What's all this? What's this idling? Why are you carrying on like Bacchants? There's no Dionysus here. No bronze rattles, no banging on drums. How are my new-born lambs doing in the cave? Are they at the teat, running along beside their mothers? Are the rush baskets full of milk, squeezed out ready for the cheese? What do you say? What are you saying? One of you is going to be weeping soon, from this club. Look up, not down.

Chorus. There. We've tipped our heads back till we can see Zeus himself. I can see the stars. I can see Orion.

Cyclops. Is my breakfast ready? Properly done?

Chorus. It's ready. Just make sure your throat is.

Cyclops. And are the bowls full of milk as well?

Chorus. Enough to drink off a whole cask, if you want to.

Cyclops. Sheep's milk, or cow's, or mixed?

Chorus. Whichever you like. Just don't swallow me.

Cyclops. Not likely. You'd start jumping about in the middle of my stomach and kill me with your dance steps. Ah. What's this crowd I see by the pens? Have pirates put in here, or thieves? I can see lambs from my caves with their bodies tied up in twisted willow, and cheese baskets jumbled about, and an old man with his bald face all swollen up from a beating.

Silenus. Oh. Oh. I'm running a fever, poor me. Beaten to a pulp.

Cyclops. By who? Who's been punching your head, old man?

Silenus. These men, Cyclops. Because I wouldn't let them carry off what's yours.

Cyclops. Didn't they know that I'm a god, and come from gods?

Silenus. I told them. But they carried off your things anyway, and they ate the cheese, when I told them not to, and they were carrying out the lambs. And they said they'd tie you up in a collar three cubits long, and rip your guts out through your eye, the one in the middle, by force, and flog your back raw with a whip, and then tie you up hand and foot and throw you down among the rowing benches of their ship, and sell you to somebody for levering rocks, or throw you into a mill to grind.

Cyclops. Is that so? Then off you go and sharpen the cleavers and the knives, quick as you can, and pile a great bundle of wood on the fire and get it lit. They'll be slaughtered straight away, and fill this belly of mine: a hot dinner straight off the coals for the carver to eat, and the rest boiled soft and tender from the cauldron. I've had my fill of mountain food. I've feasted on lions and deer enough. It's a long time since I ate a man.

Silenus. A change from the usual is all the sweeter, master. It's not as if you've had any other strangers turning up at your cave lately.

Odysseus. Cyclops, hear the strangers' side too, in turn. We needed food, and we came up from our ship to your cave to buy some. This man sold us the lambs for a cup of wine. He handed them over, and he took a drink for them: a willing seller and willing buyers, and there was no force in any of it. There isn't a sound word in anything he says. He's been caught selling your property behind your back, that's all.

Silenus. Me? I hope you die a horrible death.

Odysseus. If I'm lying, yes.

Silenus. By Poseidon who fathered you, Cyclops, by great Triton and by Nereus, by Calypso and the daughters of Nereus, by the holy waves and every kind of fish in the sea, I swear, my beautiful one, my dear little Cyclops, my own dear little master, that I did not sell your property to the strangers. Or may these bad boys of mine come to a bad end. The boys I love best in the world.

Chorus. Keep that for yourself. I saw you selling the goods to the strangers. I saw you with my own eyes. And if I'm lying, may my father drop dead. Don't do the strangers any wrong.

Cyclops. You're lying. I'd trust this man before I trusted Rhadamanthus, the judge of the dead himself, and I say he's the more honest. But I have some questions. Where did you sail from, strangers? Where are you from? What city brought you up?

Odysseus. Ithacans by birth. We're from Ilium, where we sacked the city, and the sea winds drove us off course onto your land, Cyclops.

Cyclops. You're the ones who went to Ilium, the city by the Scamander, to get back that worst of women, Helen, after she was carried off?

Odysseus. That's us. We drained that dreadful labour to the bottom.

Cyclops. A shameful expedition. Sailing to the land of the Phrygians for the sake of one woman.

Odysseus. A god did that. Don't blame any mortal for it. But we are begging you, noble son of the sea god, and we are speaking to you as free men. Do not have the heart to kill friends who have come to your cave and make a godless meal of them for your jaws. It was we who kept your father's temple seats safe for him in the corners of Greece, my lord. The holy harbour at Taenarus stands unbroken, and the high coves of Malea, and Sunium's rock with the silver in it, sacred to Athena, daughter of Zeus, is safe, and so are the harbours of refuge at Geraestus. We did not let the Phrygians put their heavy shame on Greece. And you have a share in that, because you live in a corner of the Greek world, under Etna, the rock that drips fire.

And if you turn your back on arguments, there is still a law among mortals: to take in shipwrecked men who come begging, and give them the gifts a guest is owed, and help them to clothes. Not to spit their limbs on the skewers you use for oxen and fill your belly and your jaw with them. The land of Priam has widowed Greece enough. It has drunk the blood of many dead men, fallen to the spear, and it has destroyed wives with no husbands, old women with no children, grey-haired fathers. If you roast the ones who are left and use them up in one bitter meal, where is anyone to turn? Listen to me, Cyclops. Let go of the greed in your jaw. Choose reverence over its opposite. For a great many men, a wicked profit has turned into a punishment.

Silenus. I'd like to offer some advice. Don't leave a scrap of this one's meat. And if you bite into his tongue, Cyclops, you'll turn out smart, and a great talker.

Cyclops. Wealth, little man, is the clever man's god. The rest is boasting and pretty words. As for the headlands by the sea where my father has his seat, I bid them goodbye. Why did you drag them into your speech? I don't shiver at Zeus's thunderbolt, stranger, and I don't know of any way in which Zeus is a stronger god than me. I don't care about him, either way. And since I don't care, listen to why.

When he pours rain down from above, I've a snug dry lodging in this rock. I dine on roast calf, or some wild beast, and I give my belly a good soaking, lying on my back, and drink off a jar of milk on top of it, and then I let off a thunderclap under my cloak to compete with the thunder of Zeus. And when the north wind blows out of Thrace and pours down snow, I wrap my body in animal hides and build the fire up, and the snow is nothing to me. And the earth, whether she likes it or not, has to grow grass and fatten my flocks, and I sacrifice them to nobody but myself, never to the gods, and to the greatest divinity of them all, this belly here. Because to drink and eat your fill, day after day, and never give yourself a moment's grief: that is Zeus, for people with any sense. The men who made the laws and tangled up human life with them can go and cry. I'm not going to stop doing my soul good. By eating you. And you'll get your guest-gifts too, so nobody can find fault with me: fire, and this cauldron here that was my father's, which will boil up nicely and hold your flesh in pieces. So crawl inside, and stand round the altar of the god of this yard, and make him a feast. That god is me.

(He drives Odysseus's men into the cave ahead of him.)

Odysseus. Aiai. I got out of the troubles at Troy, and the troubles of the sea, and now I have run aground on the judgement of a godless man, a heart with no harbour in it. Pallas, my lady, goddess born of Zeus, help me now. Now. I have come to a worse labour than Ilium, and to the very edge of the drop. And you who live where the bright stars have their seats, Zeus who protects strangers, look at this. Because if you don't see it, then you're called Zeus for nothing. A god who is nothing at all.

(He goes into the cave after his men.)

Chorus.
	Open up that wide throat of yours, Cyclops,
	stretch your lips. It is all ready for you,
	boiled and roasted and hot off the coals,
	to gnaw, to crunch,
	to carve the limbs of strangers,
	lying back on your shaggy goatskin.
Chorus.
	No. None for me, thank you.
	Fill the hold of that boat of yours alone, by yourself.
	Goodbye to this cave.
	Goodbye to the sacrifice
	with no altar, the slaughter
	the Cyclops of Etna keeps,
	gloating over a dinner of strangers' meat.
Chorus.
	Pitiless. Wretched man, to kill the strangers
	who came begging at his hearth, and butcher them in his own house,
	and feast on them boiled, and with his filthy teeth
	chop and crunch
	men's flesh, hot from the coals.
Chorus.
	No. None for me, thank you.
	Fill the hold of that boat of yours alone, by yourself.
	Goodbye to this cave.
	Goodbye to the sacrifice
	with no altar, the slaughter
	the Cyclops of Etna keeps,
	gloating over a dinner of strangers' meat.

(Odysseus comes out of the cave, white-faced.)

Odysseus. Zeus, what am I going to say? I have seen things inside that cave that are terrible, and past believing, things out of the stories people tell, not out of anything human beings do.

Chorus. What is it, Odysseus? Has that godless Cyclops been feasting on your dear companions?

Odysseus. Two of them. He looked them over and weighed them in his hands, and picked the two with the fattest, best-fed flesh on them.

Chorus. Poor man. How did you stand it, while it was happening?

Odysseus. When we had gone into this rocky place, first he lit a fire. He threw the trunks of a tall oak onto his broad hearth, a load heavy enough for three wagons. Then he spread a bed of fir branches on the ground, close to the flame. He milked his heifers and filled a mixing bowl with white milk, a bowl that would hold ten jars. He set a cup of ivy-wood beside it, three cubits across and, as far as I could see, four deep. He set a bronze cauldron boiling on the fire, and laid out spits, buckthorn branches with their points hardened in the fire and the rest trimmed smooth with a sickle, and the Etna butchers' bowls that catch the blood under the axe.

And when everything was ready for that god-hated cook from hell, he snatched up two of my companions and killed them, with one steady movement each. One he cut over the beaten-bronze belly of the cauldron. The other he took by the tendon at the heel and swung against the sharp edge of a rock, and spattered his brains out. Then he hacked the flesh off with a greedy knife and roasted it over the fire, and the limbs he threw into the cauldron to boil. And I, God help me, with the tears running out of my eyes, stayed close to the Cyclops and waited on him. The others were crouched in the crannies of the rock like birds, and there was no blood left in their skin.

When he had eaten his fill of my companions and fell back, letting out a heavy breath from his throat, something came to me from a god. I filled a cup with this wine of Maron's and held it out to him and said, "Cyclops, son of the sea god, look at this. This is the divine drink that Greece makes from the vine, the bright joy of Dionysus." And he, stuffed with his shameless dinner, took it and pulled the whole cup down in one draught, and raised his hand and thanked me. "Dearest of all my guests," he said, "a fine drink you have given me, on top of a fine dinner." When I saw how much he liked it, I gave him another cup, knowing the wine would wound him and he would soon be paying for what he did. And sure enough he slid into singing. I kept pouring, one cup after another, and warming his insides with the drink. So there he is now, singing tunelessly beside my weeping shipmates, and the cave rings with it. And I have crept out without a sound.

I want to save you, and myself, if you are willing. So tell me: do you want to get away from this man nobody can live with, or not, and go and live in the house of Dionysus with the water-nymphs? Your father inside has already said yes. But he is weak, and he is making the most of the drink. He is stuck to that cup like a bird on a limed twig, flapping his wings. But you are young. Save yourself, with me, and get back your old friend Dionysus. He is nothing like the Cyclops.

Chorus. Dearest of friends, if only we could see that day, and be out from under the godless head of the Cyclops. It has been a long, long time since we had our dear old spout to suckle at. And there is nowhere we can run to get away from him.

Odysseus. Then listen to the revenge I have in mind for this beast of a villain, and the way out of your slavery.

Chorus. Tell us. We would not rather hear the sweetest lyre in Asia than hear that the Cyclops is dead.

Odysseus. He is so pleased with this drink of Dionysus that he wants to go off partying with his brother Cyclopes.

Chorus. I understand. You are going to catch him alone in the woods and cut his throat, or push him off a cliff.

Odysseus. Nothing of the kind. What I have in mind is a trick.

Chorus. What, then? We have been hearing for years how clever you are.

Odysseus. First, to keep him away from this party. I will tell him he should not give this drink to the other Cyclopes, but keep it for himself and enjoy life. Then, when he falls asleep, beaten by Dionysus, there is an olive branch inside the cave. I will sharpen the end of it with this sword and put it in the fire. And then, when I see it burning, I will lift it, red-hot, and drive it into the middle of the Cyclops' face, and melt his eye out with fire. And the way a shipwright fitting timbers works his drill back and forth with a strap wound twice round it, that is how I will spin the brand in the eye that gives the Cyclops his light, and shrivel up the pupil.

Chorus. Iou, iou. I am delighted. We are mad with joy at what you have thought of.

Odysseus. And then I will put you and your friends and the old man into the hollow hull of my black ship, and with two banks of oars I will carry you away out of this land.

Chorus. Is there any way I could take hold of the brand that blinds him too, as if I were pouring a libation to a god? I want a share in this killing.

Odysseus. You will have to. The brand is big, and it will take more than one pair of hands.
