Chorus. I would lift the weight of a hundred wagons, if it means we smoke out the eye of that Cyclops, damn him, like a wasps' nest.

Odysseus. Quiet now. You know the whole trick. When I give the order, do what the architects tell you. I am not going to abandon the friends I have inside and save my own skin. And yet I could run. I am out of the depths of the cave already. But it is not right to leave the friends I came here with and be saved alone.

(He goes back into the cave.)

Chorus.
	Come on, who is first, and who is second
	behind him, to grip the handle of the brand,
	drive it in under the Cyclops' eyelids
	and grind out that bright eye?
	Quiet. Quiet. Here he comes,
	drunk, making a noise he thinks is music,
	a clumsy off-key singer who will be crying soon,
	out of his house of stone.
	Come on, let us teach this lout
	how a party is done.
	He is going to be blind either way.
Half-Chorus.
	Happy the man who shouts for the god
	with the sweet streams of the grape,
	stretched out for a party,
	his arm round a friend he loves,
	and on the couch, the yellow hair
	of some soft, expensive girl,
	his own glossy curls shining with perfume,
	and he calls out, "Who is going to open the door for me?"

(The Cyclops comes out of the cave, garlanded and reeling, with Silenus behind him.)

Cyclops.
	Papapa. I am full of wine,
	and I am loving the freshness of that feast,
	loaded like a cargo ship
	right up to the top deck of my belly.
	This nice soft grass is tempting me out
	to a spring party
	with my brother Cyclopes.
	Come on, stranger, come on, hand me the wineskin.
Chorus.
	Here comes the handsome one, out of his house,
	casting his handsome eye around.
	Papapa. Somebody loves us.
	There is a torch waiting for you, to light your skin,
	like a torch for a tender bride
	deep in a dewy cave.
	And a garland of more than one colour
	will soon be wound close round your head.

Odysseus. Cyclops, listen. I know this Dionysus I gave you to drink very well.

Cyclops. And this Dionysus, what sort of god is he supposed to be?

Odysseus. The greatest there is, for the pleasure human beings take in life.

Cyclops. Well, he tastes good coming back up, I will say that.

Odysseus. That is the kind of god he is. He never hurts anybody.

Cyclops. But how does a god enjoy living in a wineskin?

Odysseus. Wherever you put him, he is comfortable.

Cyclops. Gods should not keep their bodies in leather.

Odysseus. What does it matter, if he gives you pleasure? Or does the leather taste bitter?

Cyclops. I hate the skin. The drink, I love.

Odysseus. Then stay right here and drink, Cyclops, and enjoy yourself.

Cyclops. Should I not give my brothers a share of this drink?

Odysseus. Keep it yourself and you will look more important.

Cyclops. Give it to my friends and I will look more useful.

Odysseus. Parties love fists, and insults, and fights.

Cyclops. I may be drunk, but nobody is going to lay a hand on me.

Odysseus. My good man, a man who has been drinking should stay at home.

Cyclops. Anyone who drinks and does not go partying is an idiot.

Odysseus. And anyone who gets drunk and stays at home is wise.

Cyclops. What do we do, Silenus? Do you think we should stay?

Silenus. I do. Who needs other people at the drinking, Cyclops?

Cyclops. And the ground here is soft, come to think of it, all thick with flowering grass...

Silenus. And it is lovely to drink in the warm sun. Lie down for me, now. Put your side on the ground.

(The Cyclops lies down on the grass. Silenus sets the mixing bowl behind his back.)

Cyclops. There. Now why are you putting the mixing bowl behind me?

Silenus. So nobody passing by knocks it over.

Cyclops. No. You want to steal drinks out of it. Put it down in the middle. And you, stranger, tell me your name. What am I to call you?

Odysseus. Nobody. And what favour am I going to get from you, to thank you for?

Cyclops. I will eat you last, after all your companions.

Silenus. That is a fine prize you are giving the stranger, Cyclops.

Cyclops. You. What are you doing? Drinking the wine behind my back?

Silenus. No. It kissed me. Because of my good looks.

Cyclops. You will be sorry, kissing the wine when the wine does not kiss you.

Silenus. Yes it does, by Zeus. It says it is in love with me. I am so handsome.

Cyclops. Pour, and fill the cup. Just give it to me.

Silenus. How is it mixed, though? Come on, let us have a look.

(He drinks.)

Cyclops. You are killing me. Give it here as it is.

Silenus. No, by Zeus. Not until I have seen you put a garland on, and had one more little taste...

Cyclops. This wine-waiter is a cheat.

Silenus. No, by Zeus. This wine is sweet. And you need to wipe your nose before you get a drink.

Cyclops. There. My lip is clean, and so is my beard.

Silenus. Now set your elbow nicely, like this, and drink it down, the way you see me drinking. And the way you do not see me.

(He buries his face in the cup and drains it.)

Cyclops. Ah. Ah. What are you doing?

Silenus. Down in one. That was delicious.

Cyclops. Stranger, take it. You be my wine-waiter yourself.

Odysseus. Well, the vine and my hand are old acquaintances.

Cyclops. Come on, pour.

Odysseus. I am pouring. Just be quiet.

Cyclops. That is a hard thing to ask of a man who drinks a lot.

Odysseus. There. Take it and drink it off, and do not leave a drop. A man drinking should die at the same moment as the drink.

Cyclops. Papai. What a clever piece of wood the vine is.

Odysseus. And if you drink a lot on top of a big dinner, and soak your belly until it has no thirst left, it will throw you into sleep. But leave any behind, and Dionysus will dry you out.

Cyclops. Iou, iou. I only just swam out of that one. Pure pleasure, and neat. The sky looks to me as if it is all mixed up with the earth and carried round with it. I can see the throne of Zeus, and the whole holy majesty of the gods. No, I will not kiss you. The Graces are trying to tempt me. Enough. I have my Ganymede here, and I will go and lie down with him, and that is the finest thing of all, by the Graces. Somehow I have always liked boys better than women.

Silenus. What? Am I Zeus's Ganymede, Cyclops?

Cyclops. Yes, by Zeus. And I am carrying you off from the house of Dardanus.

Silenus. I am done for, boys. Something dreadful is going to happen to me.

Cyclops. Finding fault with your lover? Playing hard to get, because he has been drinking?

Silenus. Oh. This is a very bitter wine I am going to be tasting in a minute.

(The Cyclops hauls Silenus into the cave.)

Odysseus. Now then, children of Dionysus, sons of a noble father. The man is inside. Any moment now, gone slack with sleep, he will be pushing meat back out of that shameless throat. The brand inside the cave is sending up smoke. It is ready. There is nothing left to do but burn out the Cyclops' eye. So see that you act like a man.

Chorus. We will have hearts of rock and iron. Get inside, before something unspeakable happens to my father. Out here, everything is ready for you.

Odysseus. Hephaestus, lord of Etna, burn the bright eye out of your evil neighbour and be rid of him once and for all. And you, Sleep, child of black Night, come down at full strength on this beast the gods hate. After the glorious work at Troy, do not let Odysseus and his sailors be destroyed by a man who cares nothing for gods or men. If you do, then we will have to count Chance as a god, and the gods as weaker than Chance.

(He goes into the cave.)

Chorus.
	The pincers are going to grip the neck
	of the man who eats his guests,
	and grip it hard. Soon, by fire,
	he loses the eyes that give him light.
	Already
	the brand is charred through
	and hidden in the ash, a huge
	limb of oak. Let Maron's wine come on.
	Let it do its work.
	Let it take out the eye of the raving Cyclops,
	so that his drinking ends badly.
	And I
	want to see Dionysus, the roaring god
	who loves his ivy, the god I long for,
	and leave
	the Cyclops' lonely country behind.
	Will I ever get that far?

(Odysseus comes back out of the cave.)

Odysseus. Quiet, by the gods, you animals. Be still. Shut the hinges of your mouths. I will not have anyone so much as breathe, or blink, or clear his throat, in case the thing wakes up, until the sight in the Cyclops' eye has had its fight with the fire.

Chorus. We are quiet. We have swallowed the air with our jaws.

Odysseus. Come on, then. Get your hands on the brand and come inside. It is beautifully red-hot.

Chorus. Should you not tell us which of us has to go first, and take the burning bar and burn out the Cyclops' light, so we all share the luck?

First Satyr. We are standing too far away from the doors to push the fire into his eye.

Second Satyr. And we have just gone lame.

Third Satyr. Then the same thing has happened to you as to me. We were standing here and we sprained our feet, I do not know how.

Odysseus. You sprained your feet standing still?

Fourth Satyr.
	And our eyes are full
	of dust, or ash, from somewhere.

Odysseus. Cowards. These men are no allies at all.

Chorus. Because I feel sorry for my back and my spine, and would rather not have my teeth knocked out with a beating, that makes me a coward? But I know a spell of Orpheus, a very good one, that will make the brand walk into his skull all by itself and set fire to the one-eyed son of Earth.

Odysseus. I knew long ago what you were made of. Now I know it better. I will have to use my own friends. But if there is no strength in your hands, at least cheer us on, so that my friends can get some courage from your shouting.

Chorus. I will do that. Let the hired man run the risks. As far as cheering goes, let the Cyclops go up in smoke.

(He goes in. The satyrs shout toward the cave.)

Chorus.
	Io, io. Push, like heroes,
	hurry, burn out the brow
	of the beast who eats his guests.
	Let him smoke, let him burn,
	the shepherd of Etna.
	Twist it, pull it, and mind he does not
	do something wild to you in his pain.

Cyclops. Oh. The light of my eye is burnt to charcoal.

Chorus. A lovely victory song. Sing it again for me, Cyclops.

Cyclops. Oh, and oh again. What an outrage. I am finished. But you will not get out of this rock and laugh about it, you nothings. I am going to stand in the mouth of this cave and fit my hands across it.

(The Cyclops gropes his way out of the cave, blind, his face blackened.)

Chorus. What are you shouting about, Cyclops?

Cyclops. I am destroyed.

Chorus. You do look a sight.

Cyclops. And a miserable one, on top of it.

Chorus. Did you fall into the middle of the coals, drunk?

Cyclops. Nobody has destroyed me.

Chorus. Then no one has done you any harm.

Cyclops. Nobody is blinding my eye.

Chorus. Then you are not blind.

Cyclops. I wish you were as blind as—

Chorus. But how could nobody make you blind?

Cyclops. You are making fun of me. Where is this Nobody?

Chorus. Nowhere, Cyclops.

Cyclops. It was the stranger, if you want to get it right. The stranger destroyed me, the filthy thing. He gave me the drink and drowned me in it.

Chorus. Wine is a terrible thing. A heavy wrestler.

Cyclops. By the gods, have they run, or are they still inside the cave?

Chorus.
	They are standing right here, in silence,
	with the overhang of the rock for cover.
Cyclops.
	Which hand?
Chorus.
	On your right.
Cyclops.
	Where?
Chorus.
	Right up against the rock.
	Have you got them?
Cyclops.
	Trouble on top of trouble. I have hit my head
	on the rock and cracked it.
Chorus.
	And they are getting away from you.
Cyclops.
	Not this way? You said this way.
Chorus.
	No. This way, I am telling you.
Cyclops.
	Which way, then?
Chorus.
	Turn round. Over there. To your left.
Cyclops.
	Oh, they are laughing at me. You are mocking me in my misery.
Chorus.
	Not any more. He is right in front of you.
Cyclops.
	You total villain, where are you?
Odysseus.
	A long way from you,
	standing guard over this body, which belongs to Odysseus.

Cyclops. What did you say? You have changed your name. That is a new one.

Odysseus. It is the one my father gave me. Odysseus. And you were always going to pay for that unholy dinner. I would have burned Troy for nothing if I had not made you pay for murdering my companions.

Cyclops. Aiai. An old prophecy is coming true. It said I would lose my sight at your hands, on your way home from Troy. But it also said that you would pay for it, that you would be tossed about on the sea for a long, long time.

Odysseus. Go and cry about it. I have done exactly what you say. And now I am going down to the shore, and I will launch my ship on the Sicilian sea and sail her home.

Cyclops. Oh no you will not. I am going to break a piece off this rock and throw it, and crush you, and your shipmates with you. Blind or not, I am going up onto the hill. I know the way through this tunnel.

(He feels his way back into the cave. Odysseus goes down toward the shore.)

Chorus. And we are shipmates of this Odysseus now. From here on, we are the slaves of Dionysus.

Rhesus (date unknown)

Rhesus

(The Trojan camp on the plain in front of Troy, in the middle of the night. Hector is asleep on a bed of leaves. The sentries of the night watch come in quietly and stand over him.)

Chorus.
	Go to Hector's bed.
	Which of the king's shield-bearers is awake,
	or of the men in armour?
	Let him take the news we bring,
	we who keep the fourth watch of the night
	on guard in front of the whole army.
	Lift your head. Prop it on your elbow.
	Open that fierce eye of yours.
	Get up off the leaves you are lying on,
	Hector. It is time to listen.
Hector.
	Who is that? A friend's voice? Who is the man?
	What is the password? Speak.
	Who is coming near our beds
	out of the night? You have to tell me.
Chorus.
	Sentries of the army.
Hector.
	What is this noise you bring?
Chorus.
	Steady.
Hector.
	I am steady.
	Is there an ambush out there in the dark?
Chorus.
	There is not.
Hector.
	Then why leave your post
	and stir the army up,
	unless you have some news out of the night?
	Do you not know that we lie down
	close to the Argive spears,
	in full armour, to sleep?
Chorus.
	Arm your hand. Hector,
	go to the beds of the allies,
	tell them to lift the spear. Wake them up.
	Send friends to your own company.
	Get the bits into the horses' mouths.
	Who will go to the son of Panthus,
	or to Europa's son, the captain of the Lycians?
	Where are the men who watch the sacrifices?
	Where are the leaders of the light-armed troops,
	and the Phrygian bowmen?
	String the horn-tipped bows.
Hector.
	Some of your news is frightening to hear
	and some of it is meant to steady me, and none of it is clear.
	Has Pan, the son of Cronus, cracked
	his whip and set you shaking? You leave the watch
	and stir the army up. What are you shouting?
	What am I to say your news is? You have said a great deal
	and shown me nothing plainly.
Chorus.
	The Argive army is burning fires,
	Hector, all through the dark,
	and the ships' moorings are lit up with torches.
	The whole army has gone to Agamemnon's tent
	in the night, in an uproar,
	wanting some new
	word. That sea-going army has never
	been frightened like this before.
	And I, suspecting what is coming,
	came to you as a messenger,
	so you can never lay any blame on me.

Hector. You have come at the right moment, even if the news is frightening. The men mean to slip away from this land by night, under oars, without my seeing them. Those fires burning out there in the dark please me. You god, whoever you are, you robbed me in the middle of my luck. You took the meat out of a lion's mouth, before this spear had swept the whole Argive army away in one stroke. If the sun's bright lamps had not gone out on me, I would never have held my winning spear back until I had burned their ships and gone from tent to tent killing Achaeans with this hand that has killed so many. I was ready to throw the spear that night and use the good luck a god had sent me. But my clever prophets, the men who know the will of heaven, talked me into waiting for daylight, and then leaving not one Achaean alive on dry land. Well, the enemy is not waiting for my sacrificers' advice. A runaway is strong in the dark. So the word has to go through the army at once: pick up your weapons, stop sleeping. Then when one of them jumps aboard a ship he will get a gash across the back and splash the boarding ladders with blood, and others will be caught in the ropes and tied up and learn to farm the fields of Phrygia.

Chorus. Hector, you are moving fast, before you know what is happening. We do not know for certain that the men are running.

Hector. What other reason would the Argive army have to burn fires?

Chorus. I do not know. But my mind is very suspicious of it.

Hector. If this frightens you, then you may as well be frightened of anything.

Chorus. The enemy never lit that much light before.

Hector. And they were never beaten and routed as shamefully before.

Chorus. You did that. Now look at what is left to do.

Hector. There is one simple thing to say about an enemy: arm.

Chorus. Look, here comes Aeneas, and in a great hurry, with something new to tell his friends.

Aeneas. Hector, why have the sentries come through the camp at night in a panic, to your bed? Why the conference in the dark, and why is the army on the move?

Hector. Aeneas, get your body into your armour.

Aeneas. What is it? Is there word of some hidden trick from the enemy, set up in the night?

Hector. The men are running. They are going aboard their ships.

Aeneas. What solid proof of that can you give me?

Hector. They are burning torches all night long. I do not think they will wait for tomorrow. They have lit fires on their well-benched ships and they mean to run for home and leave this country.

Aeneas. And you are arming for this. To do what?

Hector. I will catch them with my spear as they run and jump aboard, and I will come down on them hard. It would be shameful for us, and worse than shameful, it would be cowardice, to let our enemies get away without a fight when a god is handing them over, after all the harm they have done us.

Aeneas. I wish you were as good at planning as you are with your hands. But no one man is born knowing everything. Each of us is given his own gift: yours is fighting, and another man's is thinking well. You heard that the Achaeans are burning torches, you were lifted right off the ground by it, and now you mean to take the army over the ditches in the dead of the night. Suppose you get across that deep hollow trench and find the enemy is not running from this land at all but standing and looking straight at your spear. If you lose, you will never get back. How does an army get through the stakes in a rout? How do the chariot drivers cross the causeways without smashing the axle-boxes of their wheels? And if you win, you still have Peleus' son sitting fresh behind them, and he will not let you throw fire on the ships or snatch the Achaeans away, whatever you imagine. The man burns, and his arm is a tower. No. Let the army sleep quietly beside their shields and rest from the killing work. My advice is to send a spy in against the enemy, whoever is willing to go. If they really are taking to flight, we march out and fall on the Argive army. If those fires are drawing us into a trap, the spy will tell us what the enemy has built, and we can decide then. That is my opinion, my lord.

Chorus.
	That is what we think. Change your mind and think it too.
	I have no love for a general's power when it slips.
	What could be better
	than a fast runner going down close to the ships
	to see what it is
	that keeps the enemy burning fires in front of their moorings?

Hector. You win, since it pleases everyone. Go and settle the allies down. The army may start moving when it hears there are meetings in the night. I will send a man to spy on the enemy. If we find out they have some scheme, you will hear the whole of it and be there to know what was said. But if they are pulling out and starting to run, keep your ear open for the trumpet, because I will not be waiting. I will be at the hauling-ground where the ships lie, tonight, on top of the Argive army.

Aeneas. Send him quickly. Your thinking is safe now. And when the moment comes, you will see me standing beside you and holding.

Hector. Which of the Trojans here in council is willing to go and spy on the Argive ships? Who will do this country that service? Who says he will? I cannot do everything myself for my father's city and for our allies.

Dolon. I will throw myself into this danger for the country. I will go and spy on the Argive ships, learn every plan the Achaeans have, and come back. Those are my terms for taking the work on.

Hector. Your name is a word for a trick, Dolon, and it fits you, and so does your love for this city. Your father's house had a name before this. Now you have made it twice the name it was.

Dolon. Then a man has to work. But when he works he ought to carry off a wage worth having. Put a profit on top of any job and it doubles the good will in it.

Hector. Yes. That is fair, and I do not say otherwise. Name your wage. Anything but my kingship.

Dolon. I do not want your kingship, with a city on its back.

Hector. Then marry one of Priam's daughters and become one of the family.

Dolon. I do not want to marry above myself either.

Hector. There is gold, if that is the prize you will ask for.

Dolon. I have gold at home. I am not short of a living.

Hector. Then what do you want out of everything Troy has stored up?

Dolon. Promise me a gift for when you have taken the Achaeans.

Hector. I will give it. Ask for anyone except the commanders of the fleet.

Dolon. Kill them. I am not asking you to keep your hand off Menelaus.

Hector. It is not the son of Oileus you are asking me for?

Dolon. Hands that have been brought up well are no good at farming.

Hector. Then which of the Achaeans do you want alive, to hold for ransom?

Dolon. I told you before. There is gold in my house.

Hector. Well then, you will be there yourself and take your pick of the plunder.

Dolon. Nail the plunder up for the gods on their temples.

Hector. Then what greater prize than any of these are you going to ask me for?

Dolon. The horses of Achilles. A man throwing his life onto the dice a god shakes should be working for something worth having.

Hector. Then we are rivals, because I am in love with those horses too. They are immortal, born from immortals, and they carry the raging son of Peleus. Poseidon, the lord of the sea, broke them in and gave them to Peleus, so the story goes. All the same, I urged you into this and I will not cheat you. I will give them to you: Achilles' team, the finest thing your house will ever hold.

Dolon. Thank you. And taking it, I say I am taking the finest gift any Phrygian ever had for his courage. You have no reason to be jealous. There are ten thousand other things to please you, being the best man in this land.

Chorus.
	The contest is great, and what you plan to win is great.
	You will be a blessed man if you get it.
	This work will bring you glory.
	It is a great thing, too, to marry into a king's house.
	Let Justice keep her eye on what comes from the gods.
	What men can give looks to be yours already.

Dolon. I will go. First to my house and my own hearth, and I will put the right gear on my body, and from there I will run for the Argive ships.

Chorus. And what will you put on instead of the clothes you have?

Dolon. Something that suits the job and a thief's footsteps.

Chorus. A clever man is the one to learn something clever from. Tell us: what is the harness going to be?

Dolon. I will fasten a wolf's skin over my back and put the animal's open jaws over my head. I will fit its front feet to my hands and its legs to my legs, and I will copy a wolf's four-footed walk, so that the enemy cannot make me out, as I come up to the ditches and the barricades in front of the ships. And when I reach empty ground I will go on two feet. That is how the trick is put together.

Chorus. Then may Hermes, the son of Maia, send you there and back safely, since he is the lord of thieves. You know the job. All you need now is luck.

Dolon. I will come through safely. And I will kill Odysseus and bring you his head. You will have a clear token, and you will say that Dolon went to the Argive ships. Or the son of Tydeus. My hand will not be clean of blood when I come home, and I will be home before the light reaches the ground.

(Dolon goes out into the dark, toward the Greek camp.)

Chorus.
	Lord of Thymbra, lord of Delos,
	you who walk in your temple in Lycia,
	Apollo, holy head, come with your bow,
	come tonight,
	be the man's rescue and the guide
	who leads him, and take the side of the sons of Dardanus,
	you who can do anything, you who built
	the old walls of Troy.
Chorus.
	Let him reach the moorings, let him come
	and see the Greek army with his own eyes,
	and let him turn back again to the altars
	of his father's house in Troy.
	And one day let him ride behind the horses of Phthia,
	when our master has broken the Achaean war,
	the horses the sea god gave
	to Peleus, the son of Aeacus.
Chorus.
	He alone had the heart, for his house and his land,
	to go down and look at the moorings. I admire
	his nerve. Good men are rare
	when the sun goes out
	over the water
	and the city
	is rolling. There is a brave man among the Phrygians. There is.
	There is daring in the
	spear here. Where are the Mysians
	who think our alliance is worth nothing?
Chorus.
	Which of the Achaeans will the killer on the ground
	stab in his hut, going on four feet
	in the shape of an animal
	of the earth? Let him take Menelaus,
	and kill Agamemnon and carry
	the head
	to Helen's hands, a grief for the marriage she made,
	the man who came against my city,
	against the land of Troy,
	with an army of a thousand ships.

(A herdsman comes down from the slopes of Mount Ida.)

Shepherd. My lord, I hope that for the rest of my life I bring my masters news like the news I am bringing you now.

Hector. There is a great deal of thickheadedness in country people. Here you are, coming to men in armour with news about sheep, and this is not the place for it. Do you not know where my house is, or my father's throne? That is where you should have gone shouting about how well your flocks are doing.

Messenger. We herdsmen are thick. I will not argue about that. But I have good news for you all the same.

Hector. Stop telling me how things are around the sheepfold. We have fighting in front of us and spears in our hands.

Messenger. Those are exactly the things I came to tell you about. A man is on his way here at the head of an army beyond counting, a friend to you and an ally to this land.

Hector. And what country did he leave empty behind him?

Messenger. Thrace. His father is called Strymon.

Hector. Are you telling me Rhesus is setting foot in Troy?

Messenger. You have it. And you have taken half my speech off me.

Hector. And how does he come to be up in the pastures of Ida, off the broad wagon road across the plain?

Messenger. I do not know exactly, though I can guess. It is no light thing to bring an army in at night, when you have heard the plains are packed with enemy troops. He gave us country people a fright, we who live on the rock of Ida, where the first hearth in this land was rooted, coming through the wood in the dark with the wild animals in it. The Thracian army came pouring on with a huge noise, and we were knocked out of our senses and drove the flocks up to the high ground, in case some of the Argives were coming to lift the cattle and strip your steadings. Then the sound that reached our ears was not Greek, and our fear went away. I went and stopped the men who were scouting the road ahead of their king, and asked them in Thracian: who is the general, and whose son is he called, this man coming to the city as an ally to the sons of Priam? And when I had heard everything I wanted to know, I stood still. And I could see Rhesus, standing in his chariot behind Thracian horses, like a god. There was a plate of gold holding the yoke on the necks of the colts, and the colts were whiter than snow. On his shoulders the light shield flashed with figures welded into it in gold. A bronze Gorgon, like the one on the goddess's shield, was strapped to the horses' foreheads, and it rang out fear with all its bells. As for the size of that army, I could not put a number on it however I counted; it was too much to take in with the eye. Many horsemen, many companies of shield-men, many archers with their shafts, and a great crowd of light-armed men running along with them, all of them in Thracian gear. That is the man who has come to Troy as an ally. Peleus' son will not be able to get away from him, either by running or by standing up to him with the spear.

Chorus. When the gods are standing steady on the citizens' side, the whole thing runs downhill toward the good.

Hector. Now that my spear is winning and Zeus is on our side, I will find plenty of friends. But we have no need of any of them, the ones who did not work beside us long ago, when Ares was blowing hard and tearing this country's sails to pieces. Rhesus has shown what kind of friend he was to Troy. He is coming to the feast, and he was not out with the hunters who took the game, and he never wore out a spear beside us.

Chorus. You are right to think little of them, and right to blame friends like that. But take the ones who are willing to help the city.

Hector. We who have kept Troy safe all this time are enough.

Chorus. Are you so sure you have already caught the enemy?

Hector. I am sure. The god's light tomorrow will show it.

Chorus. Watch what is coming. A god turns a great many things over.

Hector. I hate a man who comes running to help his friends late. Well then: since he has come, let him come to our table not as an ally but as a guest, one stranger among strangers. As far as he is concerned, the gratitude of Priam's sons is gone.

Chorus. My lord, pushing allies away earns ill will.

Messenger. The sight of him alone would frighten the enemy.

Hector. Your advice is good, and you see the moment. So let Rhesus in his golden armour come and join the allies of this land, on the strength of the messenger's report.

(The herdsman goes back up toward the hills. Trumpets sound out on the plain as the Thracian army comes in.)

Chorus.
	Let Adrasteia, the daughter of Zeus,
	who punishes a boast, keep the ill will off my mouth.
	I am going to say all of it,
	everything my heart loves to say.
	You have come, son of the river,
	you have come, you are at the courtyard of the god of friendship,
	and you are welcome, because at last
	your mother, the Muse of Pieria, and the river
	with the beautiful bridges are bringing you here.
Chorus.
	Strymon, who whirled once
	as running water through the clean
	folds of the singing Muse
	and planted your young life in her.
	You are Zeus to me, Zeus of the daylight,
	coming here driving your dappled colts.
	Now, my country, my Phrygia,
	now with a god's help you can say the name
	of Zeus who sets us free.
Chorus.
	Will old Troy ever again
	spend a whole day
	in the drinking, in the companies
	of love, with the harps
	and the cups
	going round in wandering contests,
	while the sons of Atreus go over the sea
	to Sparta,
	away from the shore of Troy?
	Friend, I wish you would do this for me
	with your hand and your spear, and then go home.
Chorus.
	Come, show yourself, hold that shield
	heavy with gold up in the face
	of Peleus' son, tilt it sideways
	along the chariot's split rail, work
	the colts up, shake
	the double-pointed javelin. Nobody who stands
	against you will ever dance again
	on the floor of Argive Hera's ground.
	No. This land will carry him
	as the dearest weight it ever took,
	killed by a Thracian death.
Chorus.
	Io, io, great king.
	Thrace, what a fine
	cub you raised, a ruler to look at.
	Look at the strength of that body bound in gold,
	listen to the boasting of the bells
	clattering at the shield-straps.
	A god, Troy, a god. Ares himself,
	the colt of Strymon and of the singing
	Muse, has come and is breathing on you.

Rhesus. Greetings, brave son of a brave father, king of this land, Hector. It is a long-delayed day, and I greet you on it. I am glad to see you winning, and camped up against the enemy's towers. I am here to help you dig their walls down and burn their ships.

Hector. Son of the singing mother, one of the Muses, and of Strymon, the Thracian river: I like to say what is true, always, and I am not a double man. You should have come long ago, long ago, and taken your share of this country's work, and not left Troy, as far as you were concerned, to fall to the enemy spear under the Argives. You cannot say that nobody called you, and that is why you never came to your friends, never defended them, never even turned your head. What herald, what council of Phrygian elders did not go to you and beg you to defend the city? What set of gifts did we not send you? And you, a man of our own blood, a barbarian yourself, drank us away to the Greeks: your own barbarians, toasted off for your share of the wine. And it was this arm that took you out of a small kingship and made you the great lord of Thrace, when I went at the best men of Thrace face to face around Pangaeum and the country of the Paeonians and broke their shields, and enslaved their people and handed them to you. You kicked that great favour aside, and now you come running to help your friends late, when they are sick. And men with no blood tie to us at all have been here a long time. Some of them lie fallen in heaped-up graves, which is no small proof of loyalty to a city. Others stand it out in their armour beside their horses and chariots, holding on through the cold blast and the god's thirsty fire, and not lying on couches draining cup after cup the way you do. That is my charge against you, and I am saying it to your face, so you know Hector is a free man.

Rhesus. I am the same kind of man myself. I cut a straight road through what I say, and I am not a double man either. Being away from this country hurt me more than it hurt you. It wore at my liver and I could hardly carry it. But the land on my border, the Scythian people, made war on me just as I was setting out to cross over to Troy. I had already reached the shores of the Friendly Sea, to ferry the Thracian army across. That was where Scythian blood was poured out on the ground by my spear, with Thracian blood mixed into it. That was the accident that kept me from reaching the plain of Troy and coming to you as an ally. And when I had destroyed them, and taken their children as hostages, and set the yearly tribute they must bring to my house, then I came. I crossed the mouth of the sea in ships and did the rest of it on foot, across the boundaries of countries. Not the way you jeer at me, tipping back my cupfuls, not sleeping in houses stuffed with gold, but out in the frozen squalls that batter the Thracian sea and press down on the Paeonians, and I know what it is to lie awake in nothing but this cloak. I came late, but I came at the right moment. You have been fighting for ten years now and finishing nothing, throwing the dice against the Argives day after day and losing. One day's light will be enough for me. I will break their towers, fall on their moorings, and kill the Achaeans. The next day I will go home from Troy, having cut your labour short. Let none of you lift a shield. I will take the Achaeans who boast so loudly and break them with my spear, late as I have come.

Chorus.
	Io, io.
	What you say is dear to us, and you are dear, and you come from Zeus.
	Only let Zeus on high be willing
	to keep the unbeatable ill will away from your words.
	The seafaring spear out of Argos
	never brought,
	not before and not now, a man greater than you. How could
	Achilles stand up to your spear,
	how could Ajax?
	If only I could see the day, my lord,
	when you make them pay
	with that hand of yours that kills so many, and its lance.

Rhesus. That is the sort of thing I am ready to do for you, to make up for the long time I was away. I say it with Adrasteia's leave. Once we have set this city free of its enemies, and you have picked out the first fruits for the gods, I want to march with you against the country of the Argives and go through the whole of Greece and lay it waste with the spear, so they can learn in their turn what it is to be treated badly.

Hector. If I could be rid of the trouble in front of me and run this city the way it was, safe as it used to be, I would owe the gods a great deal of thanks. But Argos, and the pasture lands of Greece: those are not so easy to sack with the spear as you say.

Rhesus. Do they not say the best of the Greeks came here?

Hector. And we do not think little of them. We have as much as we can drive.

Rhesus. Then when we have killed these men, is the whole job not done?

Hector. Do not let go of what is close and stare at what is far away.

Rhesus. It seems to be enough for you to be hurt and never hurt back.

Hector. I rule a great kingdom, even standing here. Now: the left wing, or the right, or in the middle among the allies. You can plant your shield wherever you like and set your army up.

Rhesus. I want to fight the enemy alone, Hector. But if you think it is shameful, after all your long work before this, to have no hand in burning the ships' sterns, then post me facing Achilles and his troops.

Hector. You cannot set that raging spear of yours against that man.

Rhesus. But the word was that he sailed to Troy.

Hector. He sailed, and he is here. But he is in a rage with the commanders and does not lift a spear with them.

Rhesus. Then who has the next name after him in their army?

Hector. Ajax seems to me to fall short of him in nothing, and neither does the son of Tydeus. And there is Odysseus, the smoothest piece of work alive, bold enough in spirit, and the man who has done more outrage to this country than anyone. He came into Athena's precinct by night, stole her image and carried it off to the Argive ships. Another time he got inside our walls dressed as a beggar collecting for a god, cursing the Argives out loud, and he had been sent to Troy as a spy. Then he killed the guards and the men beside the gates and got out again. He is always turning up in an ambush around the altar of Apollo of Thymbra, close to the town. He is a cunning piece of trouble to wrestle with.

Rhesus. No brave man thinks it is right to kill an enemy in secret. He goes straight at him. This man you say sits in a thief's hiding place building schemes: I will take him alive, drive a spike up his backbone at the way out of the gates, and stand him there as a feast for the vultures on the wing. He is a pirate and a robber of the gods' shrines, and that is the death he ought to die.

Hector. Now make your camp, since it is night. I will show you myself where your army has to sleep, apart from the line we have drawn up. Our password is Apollo, if we should need one. Hear it and remember it, and pass it on to the Thracian army. And you sentries must go out ahead of the ranks and keep an alert watch and receive Dolon, our spy on the ships. If he is safe, he must be getting close to the Trojan camp by now.

Chorus.
	Whose watch is it? Who takes over from mine?
	The first stars are going down,
	and the seven Pleiades are climbing the sky.
	The Eagle is flying in the middle of heaven.
	Wake up. What are you waiting for?
	Up out of your blankets and on watch.
	Do you not see the moonlight?
	Dawn is close. Dawn is coming,
	and that star there is one of the ones
	that run out in front of it.
	Who was called for the first watch?
	Coroebus, they say. Mygdon's son.
	And who after him?
	The Paeonians woke the Cilicians,
	and the Mysians woke us.
	Then is it not time to go and wake the Lycians
	for the fifth watch, the way the lot fell?
Chorus.
	Listen. I hear it.
	Down by the Simois, sitting on her bloody nest,
	the nightingale who killed her own child
	sings her grief out with a voice of many strings.
	Already they are grazing the flocks on Ida.
	I can hear the pipe going in the dark.
	Sleep is charming my eyes shut.
	It comes sweetest on the lids toward morning.
	Why has the scout not come back,
	the one Hector sent out to spy on the ships?
	I am afraid. He has been gone a long time.
	Has he blundered into a hidden ambush
	and been killed?
	He may have. It frightens me.
	I say we go and wake the Lycians
	for the fifth watch, the way the lot fell.

(The sentries move off into the dark. Odysseus and Diomedes come in from the other side, with their swords drawn.)

Odysseus. Diomedes. Did you not hear something? Or is it an empty noise dripping through my ears? Some clash of armour?

Diomedes. No. It is the harness on the chariot rails, the iron rattling. Fear went through me too, until I made out that it was the horses' chains knocking.

Odysseus. Watch you do not walk into the sentries in the dark.

Diomedes. I will watch. I am setting my feet down carefully, even in the black.

Odysseus. And if you do wake them, do you know the army's password?

Diomedes. The word is Apollo. I know it; I heard Dolon give it.

Odysseus. Ah. These beds here are empty. I am looking at the enemy's beds and there is nobody in them.

Diomedes. And yet Dolon told us this was where Hector sleeps. He is the man this sword is drawn for.

Odysseus. What can it mean? Has his company gone off somewhere?

Diomedes. To set up some trick against us, perhaps.

Odysseus. Hector is bold now that he is winning. Bold.

Diomedes. Then what do we do, Odysseus? We have not found the man in his bed. We have missed what we came for.

Odysseus. We get back to the ships as fast as we can. Whichever of the gods it is that keeps him lucky, that god is keeping him alive. We must not force our luck.

Diomedes. Then should we not go for Aeneas, or for Paris, the most hateful of all the Phrygians, and take his head off with the sword?

Odysseus. And how, in the dark, in the middle of an enemy army, will you hunt those two down and kill them without any risk?

Diomedes. Still, it is a shameful thing to go back to the Argive ships without having done the enemy any fresh harm.

Odysseus. What do you mean, none? Did we not kill Dolon, who was spying on the moorings? Have we not got his gear here, safe? Or were you expecting to sack the whole camp?

Diomedes. You win. We go back. And may the luck hold.

(Athena appears in the dark above them.)

Athena. Where are you going, leaving the Trojan lines, with grief biting at your hearts because a god will not give you Hector or Paris to kill? Have you not heard that a man has come to help Troy, and in no small way? Rhesus. If he lives through this night into tomorrow, neither Achilles nor the spear of Ajax could stop him from destroying the whole Argive fleet — tearing down the palisade and driving a wide charge with his spear right through the gates. Kill him and you have everything. Leave Hector's bed alone, and the cutting of his throat. His death will come from another hand.

Odysseus. Lady Athena. I knew that voice; I know the sound of it well. You are always there in my troubles, at my side, fighting for me. Tell us where the man is asleep. Where in the barbarian army has he been posted?

Athena. He is lying close by here, and he is not drawn up with the rest of the army. Hector has bedded him down outside the ranks until night gives way to daylight. Near him his white horses are tethered to the Thracian chariot, easy to pick out in the dark. They shine like the wing of a river swan. Kill their master and take them home; they are the finest spoils there are. There is no place on earth that hides a team like that.

Odysseus. Diomedes. Either you kill the Thracians, or hand that to me and take the horses yourself.

Diomedes. I will do the killing and you will handle the horses. You are practised at the clever business and you have the quick mind for it. A man should be put where he will do the most good.

Athena. Look. I see Paris coming this way, toward us. He must have heard from one of the guards some vague story that enemies have got in.

Diomedes. Is he with others, or coming alone?

Athena. Alone. He seems to be making for Hector's quarters, to report that there are spies in the camp.

Diomedes. Then should he not be the first one dead?

Athena. You cannot get more than what is fated. It is not allowed that he should die by your hand. Go, and be quick about the killing you did come here to do. And I will pass myself off as Aphrodite, his ally, standing beside him to help him in his trouble, and I will answer my enemy with rotten words. That is what I mean to do. But the man it is going to happen to knows nothing of it and has heard nothing, though he is standing close enough to the words to touch them.

(Odysseus and Diomedes go off into the dark. Paris comes in from the other side.)

Paris. You there. I am talking to you, my general and my brother. Hector, are you asleep? Should you not be up? Somebody hostile is edging in on our army. Thieves, or spies of some kind.

Athena. Courage. It is Aphrodite here, keeping watch over you, and kindly. I take your war as my own business. I have not forgotten the honour you did me, and I am grateful to you for the good turn. And now, with the Trojan army winning, I have come bringing you a great friend: the Thracian son of the goddess who makes the songs, the Muse. His father is the river; they call him Strymon.

Paris. You have always been good to this city, and to me. When I judged that quarrel and gave you the prize, I laid up the greatest treasure of my life for this city, and I say so. I came because I heard something — not clearly, but a rumour has got in among the guards — that Achaean spies are here. One man tells it who never saw them; another who did see them come cannot say what they were. That is why I came to Hector's quarters.

Athena. Do not be afraid of anything. There is nothing new in the army. Hector has gone off to bed the Thracian troops down.

Paris. You convince me. I trust what you say, and I will go back to my post and stand guard with no fear in me.

Athena. Go. Take it that everything of yours is my concern; I like to see my allies come off well. And you will find out for yourself how much I want it. Now I am calling to you two over there, the pair of you with far too much fight in you. Son of Laertes, put your sharpened swords to sleep. The Thracian commander is down, the horses are taken, and the enemy have noticed and are coming after you. Run for the ships' moorings as fast as you can. Why are you waiting, with the storm breaking over you, to save your lives?

(Athena goes. The sentries come running in out of the dark, and Odysseus and Diomedes are among them.)

Chorus.
	Ah. Ah.
	Hit him, hit him, hit him, hit him.
	Strike. Strike.
	Who is that man? Look. That is the one I mean.
	Thieves. Those are the men stirring up this army in the dark.
	Here. Over here, all of you.
	I have them. I have them in my hands.
	What company is this? Where have you come from? Where are you from?

Odysseus. That is not for you to know. You die today for the harm you have done.

Chorus. Give the password, before the spear goes through your chest.

Odysseus. Halt. Steady.

Chorus. Get in close. Everyone, strike.

Odysseus. Was it you who killed Rhesus?

Chorus. No. It was you, who came to kill us—

Odysseus. Everyone, hold.

Chorus. We will not.

Odysseus. Ah. Do not strike a friend.

Chorus. Then what is the sign?

Odysseus. The word is Apollo.

Chorus. Right. Everyone, hold your spear. Do you know where the men went?

Odysseus. Somewhere over this way. We caught sight of them.

Chorus. After them, all of you, on their tracks. Or should we raise the alarm? No. It is an ugly thing to throw our own allies into a panic in the night.

Chorus.
	Which of the men was it who got through?
	Who is it, so very bold,
	who will boast he slipped out of my hands?
	Where am I to find him?
	Who shall I put him next to,
	a man who came through the dark on a foot that never flinched,
	through the ranks and past the guard posts?
	A Thessalian?
	Someone who lives in one of the seaside towns of Locris?
	Or does he pick up a living out among the scattered islands?
	Who was he? Where from? What country?
	Which god does he call the highest of them all?
	Is this Odysseus's work, or somebody else's?
	If we are to judge by what he has done before, what else?
	You think so?
	Why would I not?
	He is bold enough against us.
	What strength? Who is it you are praising?
	Odysseus.
	Do not praise a thief's smooth-talking spear.
Chorus.
	He came into the city once before,
	with a running, bleary eye,
	wrapped in a rag of a coat,
	a sword on him, hidden in the folds.
	He crawled about begging his food like some hired vagrant,
	his head dusty and filthy.
	And he said a great deal of foul stuff
	about the royal house of the sons of Atreus,
	pretending he hated the generals.
	I wish he had died, died as he deserved,
	before he ever set a footprint on Phrygian ground.
	Odysseus or not, I am afraid.
	Hector will blame us, the sentries.
	Saying what?
	Suspecting us.
	Of doing what? What are you afraid of?
	That they got past us—
	Which men?
	The ones who came into the Phrygian army tonight.

(A man comes in out of the dark, holding his side.)

Charioteer.
	Io, io. The luck a god deals is heavy. Pheu, pheu.

Chorus. Ah. Ah. Quiet, all of you, get down low. Somebody may be walking into the net.

Charioteer. Io, io. A heavy disaster for the Thracians.

Chorus. That is one of the allies, groaning.

Charioteer.
	Io, io.
	I am destroyed. And you, lord of the Thracians,
	you who ever laid eyes on Troy, the hatefullest sight of your life,
	what an ending has taken hold of you.

Chorus. Who are you? One of the allies? In the night my eyes are dull and I cannot make you out clearly.

Charioteer.
	Where can I find one of the Trojan lords?
	Where is Hector sleeping,
	bedded down under his shield?
	Which of the officers of this army do I tell
	what has been done to us,
	what somebody did to us and then went off unseen,
	after winding up a grief for the Thracians
	that anybody can see?

Chorus. Something bad seems to have come on the Thracian army, from what I can make out of this man.

Charioteer.
	The army is gone. The king is down,
	killed by a treacherous blow.
	Ah. Ah. Ah. Ah.
	What pain grinds at me, deep inside
	the bloody hole of the wound. How can I die?
	Was this what Rhesus and I had to die for,
	with no glory, after putting in at Troy to help?

Chorus. There are no riddles in the trouble he is telling. He says plainly that our allies are dead.

Charioteer. It has gone badly, and on top of badly it has gone shamefully, and that makes the evil twice the size. To die well, if a man has to die, is still bitter for the one dying — how could it not be? — but for the living it is weight and a good name for the house. We died stupidly and with no glory at all.

When Hector's own hand had bedded us down and given us the password, we slept, beaten flat by the march. No guard was set over the army, no watches through the night. Our weapons were not laid out in their places, and no goads were fitted on the horses' yokes, because our king had been told that you were on top and lying in wait by the sterns of their ships. So we simply dropped where we were and slept.

I woke out of sleep with my mind on my work, and I was measuring out the horses' feed with a generous hand, expecting to yoke them at dawn for the fighting. And through the thick dark I see two men going round and round our camp. When I stirred, they ducked down and drew off again. I shouted at them not to come near the army. I thought they were thieves out of our own allies. They said nothing. And I said nothing more either. I went back to my bed and slept again.

And a sort of vision came to me in my sleep. The horses I had reared and used to drive, standing beside Rhesus, I saw them — thinking I was dreaming — with wolves up on their backs, sitting there as if they belonged. The wolves were lashing the horses' hide with their tails and driving them on, and the mares were snorting through their nostrils, breathing rage, tossing their manes in terror. I sprang up to beat the beasts off my horses, because the fear of the night had me on my feet.

And as I lifted my head I heard the choking of dying men. A hot spring of new blood hit me, from my master, from his cut throat, out of his hard dying. I come up straight, with nothing in my hands, no spear. And while I am peering about, hunting for a weapon, a man in his prime steps up beside me and drives a sword into my lower ribs. I felt the blade go in and take a deep furrow of a wound out of me. I went down on my face. And they took the horses and the chariot and ran with them.

Ah. Ah.

The pain grinds at me. I cannot stand up straight any more.

I know what has happened, because I saw it. But how the dead men died I cannot tell you, or by whose hand. Though I can guess this much: what we suffered came from friends.

Chorus. Charioteer of the Thracian who has come off so badly, do not suspect us. The enemy did this. And here is Hector himself, coming. He has heard what happened to you, and he shares the pain of it, as he should.

Hector. You. You who have done us this enormous damage. How did the enemy's spies come in on you without your knowing, to your shame? How was the army butchered, and you never pushed them out, going in or coming out? Who is going to pay the penalty for this if not you? You, I say. You were the guard set over the army. And they are gone, without a scratch, laughing themselves sick at Phrygian cowardice and at me, their general. Now understand this, and I swear it by Zeus my father: either the whip is waiting for you, or the block and the axe, for doing a thing like this. Or else you can count Hector as nothing, and a coward.

Chorus.
	Io, io.
	It was to you, yes, to you,
	the strength that holds this city up,
	that I came running,
	when I brought you the news that there were fires
	burning by the ships.
	Through the whole night I never put my sleepless eye
	to bed, I never dozed.
	By the springs of the Simois I swear it.
	Do not set your anger on me, my lord.
	I am guilty of none of this.
	And if in time you find out that I said
	or did one thing out of place,
	send me under the ground alive.
	I will not ask you for anything.

Charioteer. Why are you threatening these men? Why are you working on my barbarian judgement with your woven words — you, a barbarian yourself? You did this. Nobody else would be accepted for it, not by the dead and not by us who are wounded. You will need a long, clever speech before you talk me out of believing you killed your friends. You fell in love with the horses, and for their sake you murder your own allies, after all the pressing you did to make them come. They came. They are dead. Paris shamed a host's table more decently than you have, killing your allies.

And do not tell me some Argive came and destroyed us. Who could have got over the Trojan lines and reached us, and not been seen? You were camped in front of us, you and the Phrygian army. Who was wounded, who was killed among your allies, when these enemies you talk of came through? We were the ones wounded, out on the edge, and the ones who got worse than that are not looking at the sunlight any more. To put it simply: we blame no Achaean. What enemy could have come through the dark and found where Rhesus lay on the bare ground, unless some god pointed the way for the killers? They did not even know he had arrived. No. You engineered this.

Hector. I have had allies for as long as the Achaean army has been in this land, and I have never heard a wrong word said about me by any of them. You would be the first. Never let a longing for horses take hold of me like that, so that I would kill my friends. And this is Odysseus. Who else of the Argives would ever have done such a thing, or planned it? I am afraid of the man, and something in my mind is troubled: that he may have run into Dolon as well and killed him. He has been gone a long time now and there is no sign of him.

Charioteer. I do not know these Odysseuses of yours. It was no enemy's hand that struck us.

Hector. Then believe that, if that is how it looks to you.

Charioteer. Land of my fathers, if only I could die in you.

Hector. Do not die. There is a big enough crowd of dead already.

Charioteer. Where am I to turn, with my master gone?

Hector. My house will take you in and heal you.

Charioteer. And how will the hands of the murderers nurse me?

Hector. This man will never stop telling the same story.

Charioteer. Curse the man who did it. My tongue is not pointing at you, whatever you boast. But Justice knows how it stands.

Hector. Take hold of him. Get him into my house, and see to it he has nothing to complain of. And you men, go to the people on the walls, to Priam and the elders, and tell them to bury the dead at the turnings off the highway.

Chorus.
	Why is some other god bringing Troy
	back out of her great good luck
	into grief again? What is he planting?
	Ah. Ah. Oh. Oh.
	What goddess is that above our heads, my king,
	carrying the newly killed body
	in her two arms?
	I am afraid, looking at this pain.

(The Muse appears above, holding her son's body.)

Muse. You may look, Trojans. I am the Muse, one of the sisters, the one who is honoured among clever men, and I am here because I have seen my son, my darling, killed pitifully by his enemies. And the man who killed him, Odysseus the trickster, will in time pay the penalty he owes.

Muse.
	With a dirge out of my own country,
	child, I am mourning you,
	you, your mother's pain.
	What a road you put in on, coming to Troy,
	an unlucky road, a miserable one.
	You went against me, and I told you not to go;
	you forced your way past your father, who begged you.
	Oh, my grief for you.
	Dear head, dear head, my child. Oh.

Chorus. As far as anyone can who has no share of your blood, I pity your son and I grieve for him.

Muse.
	Curse Diomedes, who came out of Oeneus's house,
	curse Odysseus, the son of Laertes.
	They have left me childless
	of the finest child a mother ever bore.
	And curse the woman who left a Greek house
	and sailed to a Phrygian bed under Ilion.
	She killed you, dearest, for Troy's sake,
	and she emptied a thousand cities
	of good men.

Muse. Thamyris, son of Philammon, there was much you did to my heart while you lived, and much when you had gone down to Hades. It was your outrage that tripped you, and your quarrel with the Muses, and it is what made me the mother of this unlucky child. For I was crossing the running water and I came too near to Strymon's fertile bed, that time we Muses came to the crag of Pangaeus with the gold in its soil, all our instruments with us, for the greatest contest of song there ever was, against that clever Thracian. And we blinded him. Thamyris, who had said so much contempt about our craft.

And when I gave birth to you, I was ashamed in front of my sisters, and ashamed of the virginity I had lost, and I put you out into the eddies of your father, the beautiful water. And Strymon did not hand you over to mortal hands to be raised, but to the girls of the springs. There you were brought up as beautifully as anyone could be, by the nymphs, and you ruled Thrace, the first of men, my child. While you were arming yourself for the bloody fighting round your own country I never feared you would die. But I told you never to put in at the city of Troy, because I knew what was fated for you. And Hector's embassies and those endless councils of elders talked you into coming and helping your friends.

And you, Athena, are the cause of every part of this death. Odysseus did nothing, and the son of Tydeus did nothing, for all that they did it. Do not imagine it has escaped me. And yet we the sister Muses honour your city above all others and haunt your land. It was Orpheus who showed men the torches of the mysteries that must not be spoken of, and Orpheus is this dead man's own cousin, the man you are killing. And Musaeus, your own holy citizen, who went further in learning than any one man ever went, was trained by Apollo and by us, his sisters. And here is my wages for it. I am holding my child in my arms and singing over him. I will not be bringing you another teacher.

Chorus. So the Thracian driver was wrong to abuse us, Hector, for planning this man's murder.

Hector. I knew that. It needed no prophets to tell me the man had died by Odysseus's arts. And when I saw the Greek army camped in my land, of course I was going to send heralds to my friends and ask them to come and help this country. I sent. He came, as he owed it to me, to share the work. But I take no pleasure at all in his being dead. And now I am ready to build him a tomb and burn a great luxury of robes on his fire. He came here as a friend, and he goes away out of bad luck.

Muse. He will not go down into the black floor of the earth. This much I will ask of the bride below, the daughter of Demeter who makes the crops grow: to let his soul go free. She owes me, and she should show that she honours the friends of Orpheus. For me, from now on, he will be as one dead, one who does not look at the light. He will never come to me again, and he will never see his mother's body. He will lie hidden in the caves of that silver-veined ground, a man who is also a god, and looking at daylight, the way the prophet of Dionysus came to live under the rock of Pangaeus, a holy god to the people who know about him.

The sea goddess's grief I will carry more easily now, because her son has to die as well. First we sisters will sing you in our dirges, and after you Achilles, on the day Thetis mourns. Pallas Athena, who killed you, will not save him. That is the kind of arrow Apollo keeps in his quiver for him.

Oh, the disasters that come of having children. The trouble human beings carry. Whoever adds it up honestly will go through life without children, and will not bury the children he had.

Chorus. This man is his mother's business now, hers to bury. But you, Hector, if you mean to do anything about what is in front of you, now is the time. This is daylight.

Hector. Move. Tell the allies to arm at once and to fill the yokes with the horses' necks. They are to hold their torches and wait for the Etruscan trumpet's call. I am confident that I will get over their army and over their wall and throw fire into the Achaean ships, and carry this coming ray of the sun to the Trojans as the day they are made free.

Chorus.
	Do as the king says.
	Let us go and put our armour on
	and pass the orders to the allies.
	Perhaps the god who is on our side
	will give us the victory.

(They go out. The sun is up.)
